One Nation faces questions over volunteer that tribunal once linked to neo-Nazi group
In short:
A man who volunteered for One Nation during a West Australian by-election was previously named in a federal tribunal ruling as someone who promoted neo-Nazi ideologies.
David Donis handed out how-to-vote cards and attended the party's victory event, sparking questions about One Nation's vetting processes.
What's next?
WA's One Nation leader Rod Caddies appears to have pre-empted the revelation, saying if an extremist had infiltrated the party, they would be expelled.
A man who volunteered for One Nation during the party's successful West Australian by-election was previously named by a federal tribunal for promoting neo-Nazi ideologies.
David Donis handed out how-to-vote cards for One Nation in the state seat of Secret Harbour last month, sparking fresh questions about vetting months after Pauline Hanson revealed the party had shut branches she said were "infiltrated by extremists".
Mr Donis was a founding member and president of the Society of Western Australian Nationalists (SWAN), a now-deregistered organisation the Administrative Appeals Tribunal (AAT) found was a racist extremist group.
The tribunal's comments about Mr Donis were made in a 2023 case concerning an army reservist's security clearance.
Mr Donis was identified by other political volunteers at the Singleton Primary School polling booth on August 27 and later pictured standing near the stage at One Nation's victory party that night.
Two people told the ABC there was an incident during the day where Mr Donis yelled at a voter leaving the polling station, prompting other volunteers to intervene and calm the situation.
A One Nation spokesperson said the individual the ABC identified as David Donis was "not a member of One Nation".
"Our party does not condone extremist views, and where such issues are identified they're acted upon swiftly by the party," the spokesperson said.
It is understood Mr Donis was a volunteer rather than a formal member and would not be permitted to continue associating with One Nation.
A Liberal source told the ABC that Mr Donis had previously been a member of the party as a teen but ultimately left when it became known his views were "not welcome".
Mr Donis has previously denied promoting neo-Nazi ideologies, but the AAT said it was satisfied he and other SWAN members had done so.
One Nation's vetting has come under scrutiny in the past, with Senator Hanson revealing in June that the party had shut down four branches.
"I'm being infiltrated by these extremists, so it's all the time happening with One Nation; they set us up all the time," she told Nine papers.
One senior West Australian Liberal told the ABC that One Nation has had "years of warnings" about problems with candidates and people associated with the party.
They said background checks should be "second nature".
"That includes basic vetting to ensure people publicly representing the party do not have verifiable links to neo-Nazis, white supremacists or organisations advocating political violence," the Liberal said.
Man adhered to "neo-Nazi ideologies"
Three years ago, the AAT accepted evidence Mr Donis was a member of SWAN, which it determined was a "nationalist and racist extremist group".
Mr Donis denied the allegation, but the tribunal said it was satisfied he and other SWAN members "adhere to, and promote, racist and neo-Nazi ideologies" and supported politically motivated and communal violence.
The findings about Mr Donis emerged in a case in which the AAT upheld ASIO's decision that an army reservist posed a security risk and should lose his NV1 clearance.
The AAT said the reservist had close ties to Mr Donis and SWAN, which the tribunal accepted was a nationalist and racist extremist group after hearing "closed evidence" — classified material that could not be disclosed publicly.
The case noted SWAN came into existence around 2018 or early 2019, with Mr Donis as a "founding member and president".
Incorporation documents show SWAN members voted to voluntarily deregister the organisation due to "inactivity" three months after the AAT findings.
One Nation WA pre-empts volunteer revelation
West Australian One Nation leader Rod Caddies appeared to pre-empt potential controversy over a party volunteer last week in a video shared on social media.
Mr Caddies criticised state Liberal MP Anthony Spagnolo for submitting a series of questions on notice to the Labor government "probing some tie" between One Nation's "Secret Harbour campaign and neo-Nazis".
He accused Mr Spagnolo of taking a page out of the "radical left playbook" by "trying to take One Nation down and tie us to Nazis".
"I don't know what sad little 'gotcha' the member thinks he has. I suspect it's something about some low-level volunteer or some link like that,"
Mr Caddies said if that were the case it meant the Liberal Party would have to own "everything their volunteers have said or done".
"The next time someone loosely affiliated with the Liberal Party has a shady background or says something crazy, I'll make sure every one of their members are set to the same standard you set," he said.
Mr Caddies then said even if the Liberals did "uncover something" it would not prove anything.
"If it turns out some idiot has managed to weasel his way into One Nation, we'll expel him; that's simple. If an extremist has infiltrated One Nation, it's by hiding their extremism," he said.
Volunteer witnessed shouting at voter
Mr Donis initially attracted the attention of volunteers from other political parties at a Secret Harbour by-election polling booth last month after he yelled at a voter.
One witness said it was before midday when they saw Mr Donis interact with a mother and daughter leaving the venue after voting.
They overheard Mr Donis wish the pair a "good day" before adding he hoped they had put One Nation "first" and Labor "last" on the ballot paper.
The witness said the woman replied she was more likely to put One Nation last, which prompted Mr Donis to accuse her of supporting abortion and setting a "bad example" for her daughter.
They said the woman gave a dismissive response, but Mr Donis kept yelling as she walked away across the car park.
The witness said the One Nation "booth captain" at the school intervened to try and quiet Mr Donis, as did a nearby Liberal member who urged him to "settle down".
They said there were no further incidents at the booth involving Mr Donis that day.
Later in the evening, Mr Donis was spotted at an event for supporters of One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen.
The ABC has been unable to contact David Donis.

How Democrats Are Mobilizing to Counter Potential Election Interference Amid Trump Concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:38:45 UTC
06:38:45 KST

With the midterm elections less than two months away, Democrats are training thousands of volunteers on how to respond to any potential incidents of voter intimidation at the polls in November.
The New Battlefield Project—an initiative that is being coordinated by the Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), which operates under the Democratic National Committee (DNC)—involves training at least 10,000 volunteers so that they’ll be equipped to counter interference or intimidation at polling locations across the country if such situations arise, says Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic party and president of the ASDC.
The on-the-ground team—dubbed the “Democracy Protectors”—will be wearing blue to distinguish themselves, and will be trained in de-escalating conflicts and documenting any potential “bad actors and bad behavior.” Information about such incidents would then be passed along to the state party and the DNC to take action where necessary. Kleeb says the volunteers will also be helpful resources to voters—for instance, they can help direct people to the right polling locations. The trainings, Kleeb adds, are based on constitutional observer trainings that the Minnesota Democratic Party coordinated amid Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids in the state.
In addition to the Democracy Protectors, the New Battlefield Project includes teams that are focused on encouraging citizens to register to vote and to vote early, as well as on dispelling any misinformation or disinformation spreading online ahead of Election Day.
The DNC musters an election protection program every year, and states sometimes train volunteers to perform similar tasks. But this year’s effort is larger in its scope and is being coordinated nationwide.
Kleeb says Democrats were spurred to launch the initiative because of speculation and concerns they were hearing from voters, candidates, and elected officials that President Donald Trump could send federal agents to polling places.
“About six months ago, state parties really started to put in place a program that we thought would address the threat of Donald Trump and what we think his allies are doing this cycle,” Kleeb says. “We heard Trump and Steve Bannon talking about how they could potentially be sending the National Guard, the military, or ICE agents outside of polling locations.”
“We take them very seriously,” she continues.
Trump Administration floats sending federal agents to the polls
The Justice Department announced last month that its Civil Rights Division would be “monitoring polling sites in Florida and Wyoming for the states’ primary elections to ensure transparency, ballot security, and compliance with federal law.”
On Tuesday, FBI Director Kash Patel also indicated that he was not opposed to the idea of dispatching federal agents to voting locations.
Separately, Trump has deployed the National Guard to cities across the country, including Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., with the stated goal of helping combat crime, though the data indicates that crime rates in many of those cities have been falling for years. When asked in May if he would send members of the National Guard or ICE officers to the polls, Trump replied, “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections.”
The troops’ presence, as well as comments from the President and his allies, has raised concerns from some Democrats that the military could be sent to voting locations. Members of the military are prohibited under federal law from being sent to “any place where a general or special election is held,” however. And in August, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff told Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin in a letter that the “Joint Force has no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections. Likewise, the Joint Force has no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said earlier this month that ICE—which has also ramped up enforcement in cities around the U.S. since Trump returned to office—“isn’t there to patrol the polling places.” But he added that “We’re there to enforce specific threats,” a comment that exacerbated fears among Democrats, advocates, and voters that ICE agents may show up at the polls in November.
When asked about the possibility of ICE agents being stationed at the polls during the midterms, then-White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said earlier this year that that was “not something [she has] ever heard the President consider.”
“I can’t guarantee that an ICE agent won’t be around a polling location in November,” Leavitt said in February. “I mean, that's frankly a very silly hypothetical question. But what I can tell you is I haven’t heard the President discuss any formal plans to put ICE outside of polling locations. It’s a disingenuous question.”
Kleeb says that Democrats wanted to be prepared just in case.
“Maybe nothing will happen,” Kleeb says. “Maybe they don’t send anybody anywhere. Maybe that’s going to be true. But as the Democratic party … we do not want to wake up the next day after Election Day, saying to ourselves, ‘Damn it! They said that they were going to do this, and we didn’t believe them,’ or ‘We thought that it was just them thumping their chest.’ We’re taking them seriously.”
When asked by TIME about the New Battlefield Project, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement that “the only ‘fears’ Americans have about our elections are being fueled by extreme liberal Democrats who refuse to support commonsense legislation that ensures Americans, and Americans only, decide our elections and other basic election security measures like Voter ID.”
Bis’ comment appeared to be referring to the SAVE America Act, the restrictive voter ID bill that the President has forcefully championed during his second term that has been met with vocal backlash from Democrats and voting rights advocates. The measure passed the House, but Senate Republicans have said they don’t have the votes required for it to pass the upper chamber.
‘An air of menace’: Experts express concerns over Trump Administration’s actions
Experts have expressed concerns about potential election interference in the November midterms, in light of recent actions taken by the Trump Administration.
“The Trump Administration has been progressively trying to regulate and interfere in elections in ways which are not constitutional,” alleged Pippa Norris, a lecturer in comparative politics at the Harvard Kennedy School and founding director of the Electoral Integrity Project. “Most of his actions haven’t actually succeeded, but they have sown confusion, and therefore there’s been problems because they can undermine public trust in the system.”
She cites, for instance, recent reports that the Trump Administration has directed federal agents to comb through voter rolls, which are overseen by the states, in a quest to find non-citizens. Research overwhelmingly shows that voter fraud is extremely rare.
Richard Briffault, a professor at the Columbia Law School, says that Trump “has been consistently complaining about fraud and misconduct at the polls, always without evidence.” Trump has repeatedly falsely claimed that the 2020 election was “stolen” from him.
Briffault adds that the Trump Administration has dispatched federal officials—such as those from the Justice Department, the National Guard, and ICE—to various places, which could be sparking concerns among local elections officials and voters about potential conflicts at the polls. He also points to the Trump Administration’s effort to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots—a move that was blocked by the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday, which the President railed against on social media this week.
“It is not surprising that many people are nervous that [Trump] might do something to try and disrupt the election if he feels it’s going against him,” Briffault says. “We don’t know what he’s going to do.”
“There’s kind of an air of menace that the Administration has generated,” he continues. “Whether they do anything, we won’t know until Election Day or the lead-up to it and after.”
Norris says that the practice of sending people to polling places to counter intimidation is often used in other countries during contentious elections. But she cast doubt that the New Battlefield Project was “the most effective thing which the DNC can do,” expressing concern that there isn’t enough time before the November midterms to effectively train volunteers in recognizing and responding to potential issues and that that could raise the possibility of “disputes” or conflicts at polling places, particularly if Republican organizations also dispatch volunteers to those locations.
Training for the volunteers started about three weeks ago, according to Kleeb. She adds that Democrats are taking the concern of potential conflict “very seriously;” a critical part of the training, she says, is teaching volunteers how to de-escalate tense situations while making it “very clear” that they should not engage if any violence erupts.
Briffault says it’s not clear yet if the initiative will be effective at countering potential intimidation, but that it could foster “a level of comfort” for voters at the polls. He notes, though, that there are so many polling places across the U.S. that it’s not possible for the New Battlefield Project to have a presence at all of them.
“I do think it’s important for people to know that there will be other people there looking out to make sure the election goes smoothly and without disruption,” he says.
Kleeb says that the volunteers won’t be at every polling place in the country, but each state party will decide the locations that have the most need for them. In Nebraska, for instance, Democrats think the second congressional district is “the most flippable congressional seat” in the state, so the party plans to station volunteers in high-traffic precincts in that area. In some states, the party may look to dispatch volunteers to polling places in areas with high immigrant populations or with many young people who may be voting for the first time, she adds.
“Our elections are safe and secure,” Kleeb says. “The Democracy Protectors Program is put in place to ensure that voters have a friendly face outside the polling location to make sure that their vote is counted.”

US Federal Reserve defies Trump with interest rate hike

“Naza” is an acronym used by Israeli military intelligence to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike, according to the filmmakers.

AI rivalry hangs over Trump-Xi talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:38:05 UTC
06:38:05 KST

AI rivalry hangs over Trump-Xi talks: What are the key talking points and disputes?
- The US-China AI rivalry will dominate Trump and Xi's talks, focusing on military risks, technology copying accusations, and chip export restrictions.
- US accuses China of copying AI tech using "distillation" and restricts advanced chip sales, while China denies these claims.
- The two countries differ on AI regulation, with the US opposing new rules and China enforcing strict AI content and data laws.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The race for AI supremacy is set to hang over next week's meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.
Washington and Beijing view advances in AI as critical to their economic and military competitiveness, but they remain at odds over access to advanced chips, allegations of technology copying and regulation of the AI industry.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he will meet Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng this weekend to discuss AI-related issues before the leaders' summit. Here are some of the key talking points and disputes.
Military talks
An AI system that interfered with a nuclear command network or launched a military cyber operation could leave either government with minutes to decide whether the other government had attacked.
US and Chinese security experts are urging both governments to prepare for such scenarios. They have proposed red lines around nuclear systems, human control over consequential cyberattacks, and a hotline for incidents involving autonomous AI.
Open questions include how to stop an accident from being mistaken for an attack, which military decisions machines should never make and how nuclear-armed rivals communicate when technology behaves unexpectedly.
Copying US technology
Copying US technology through a technique known as “distillation” has become a flashpoint in the battle over AI model development.
Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using output from larger, more expensive ones to lower the costs of training a new AI tool.
The US government accused six Chinese companies in September of maliciously copying American AI products using distillation, with law enforcement officials saying in a statement that the firms did so "likely with Chinese government awareness”.
The US made a similar accusation in April ahead of Trump's visit to Beijing. The Chinese embassy in Washington called the allegations “baseless”.
Chip exports to China
Chinese access to key US technologies underpinning the artificial intelligence boom is a point of friction between the two countries.
Since 2022, the US has imposed sweeping restrictions on shipments of advanced chips and chipmaking equipment to China.
There is evidence of advanced AI chips being smuggled into the country, though the scale is unknown.
The US has been considering restrictions on the ability of Chinese companies to remotely access data centres in other countries to prevent those firms from benefiting from Nvidia’s advanced chips.
There have been some exceptions to this effort. Late 2025, Trump decided to allow sales of Nvidia’s H200 AI chips. H200s are not the most sophisticated chips available, but their sale prompted concerns from China hawks in Washington who argued the chips could bolster China’s AI capabilities.
Regulation
The two leaders have fundamentally different perspectives on how involved they should be in the AI sector.
Trump has brushed aside calls for new federal AI rules, saying on Sept 14 that the US only needs a strong president, which the country has "in spades”. He said calls from AI executives for regulation of the technology are a "hoax”.
The Chinese government has rules governing AI algorithms and the data used to train them, including requiring content generated by AI to be clearly labeled.
US v China AI development race
The estimates US officials typically give put Chinese AI models just a few months behind their American counterparts, although industry leaders increasingly describe them as neck and neck.
In 2025, then-White House AI adviser David Sacks said China was likely three to six months behind the United States on AI development. Earlier in 2026, the US Commerce Department put DeepSeek V4 Pro about eight months behind frontier models.
Many in the industry say the gap is shrinking quickly. In August, Hugging Face Chief Executive Clement Delangue said China was winning the race as far as open-weight models were concerned - and likely was not far off in terms of frontier models either. Frontier models are the most advanced AI tools and open-weight models have publicly accessible core elements that can be downloaded, inspected and modified.
“I wouldn’t be surprised if they start dominating at the frontier either by the end of this year or next year at the rate of progress,” Delangue told broadcaster CNBC on Aug 3. REUTERS

Houthi's Bab el-Mandab gains expose Saudi failures in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:35:42 UTC
06:35:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Houthi's Bab el-Mandab gains expose Saudi failures in Yemen
The Houthi capture of ground overlooking the Bab el-Mandab Strait has dealt Saudi Arabia its gravest setback in Yemen in years, exposing intelligence failures, the collapse of Yemeni allies and the limits of US protection.
A Houthi advance this week along the Red Sea coast and the capture of islands at the mouth of the strait, a vital artery for global oil supplies, has also left the kingdom scrambling for backing as Iran and its allies expand their reach.
Senior Western, regional and Yemeni officials and sources said the Houthi breakthrough reflected various factors: deep divisions among anti-Houthi Yemeni factions, an untested Saudi-led command structure that replaced Emirati oversight, limited Saudi air support and an underestimation of Houthi preparations.
The diplomat said the Houthis had quietly assembled about 100,000 fighters, vastly outnumbering forces on the opposing side, adding: "Everyone, including the Saudis, missed this build-up and miscalculated the Houthis' intentions.”
Neil Quilliam, a fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, described the offensive as a glaring intelligence failure, saying: "They just weren't picking up the signal. They just weren't seeing the signs."
Yemeni political analyst Farea Al-Muslimi added: "The Saudis were caught off guard in Yemen."
The collapse of Saudi-backed forces handed the Houthis another prize beyond territory — a sizeable cache of advanced U.S.- and Saudi-supplied weaponry abandoned during the retreat.
The haul, according to regional sources, is likely to bolster the group's military capabilities, provide valuable intelligence on adversaries' equipment and further reinforce perceptions of a humiliating Saudi defeat.
"The Yemeni government forces were like a house of cards. They didn't resist. Completely. Completely," said Abdulkhaleq Abdallah, a political analyst in the United Arab Emirates.
The setback has also exposed how limited international support for a counteroffensive may be. Two Western officials said neither the United States nor European countries were prepared to offer direct military backing, and that Washington and its allies had not even joined a Saudi-led maritime defence coalition announced in July.
Saudi officials did not respond to a request to comment for this article.
Allies collapse, partners hesitate
With Iran-backed fighters now holding territory that can threaten Saudi oil exports and Red Sea shipping, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MbS) went to Cairo to discuss military cooperation between the two countries as Saudi Arabia seeks to contain the fallout after Washington declined to directly intervene militarily.
Two regional sources familiar with the meeting in Egypt said Riyadh wanted Egypt to help play a role in Red Sea operations. One regional source said MbS asked President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi for military support on Yemen given the close ties between the two countries. There was no immediate word on whether Cairo would agree.
A Saudi source said the meeting was scheduled long before the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began in February and "while it obviously covered the latest developments, it had the full agenda of bilateral issues to discuss."
Egypt's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment when asked whether MbS had discussed Egyptian military support.
The Houthis also appear to be using their gains to press for broader political concessions.
Former U.S. negotiator Dennis Ross said the group wants Riyadh to lift restrictions on Hodeidah port and Sanaa airport, provide compensation for the war and scale back support for Yemen's internationally recognised government.
"I don't think the Saudis can easily give in to the kinds of demands that they're making," Ross said.
A Gulf official said Saudi Arabia now faced a narrowing set of choices. Allowing the Houthis to consolidate their gains risked turning tactical victories into lasting strategic leverage, while a larger military response could prompt attacks deeper inside the kingdom.
"If you don't inflict enough pain on the Houthis, you become hostage to them," the official said.
Control of territory around Bab el-Mandeb — which lies between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast — could deepen the Houthis' regional reach, putting the Horn of Africa within easier reach of their logistical and smuggling networks.
Combined with Iran's leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, another vital route for global energy supplies, the foothold gives Tehran and its allies influence over two critical maritime choke points.
MbS's foreign policy strategy, built on trying to stabilise the region via a détente with Iran, has unravelled since the start of the war as his economic transformation agenda comes under mounting strain, increasing pressure on the kingdom's de facto ruler.
The absence of Western military assistance in Yemen, and the absence of these powers from a newly formed defence coalition, exposed the limits of its ability to rally support at a moment of acute vulnerability.
Riyadh appears increasingly to have been outmaneuvered by its adversaries and left wanting by its allies.
The Yemen Trap
The Houthi offensive revealed a blind spot in Saudi and U.S. strategy: while Washington and its allies focused on containing Iran directly, Tehran widened the battlefield by opening fronts from Iraq to the Red Sea, using energy assets, shipping routes and proxies as instruments of pressure.
The larger significance of the Houthi breakthrough lies not only in the blow to Saudi Arabia but in the momentum it restores to Iran's influence across the region, after major setbacks to its allies in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon.
For Iran it's a "win-win-win," said Farea Al-Muslimi.
Some political analysts say the more consequential blow is not the battlefield reversal but Washington's reluctance to come to its ally's aid. That signal, they say, has emboldened adversaries, weakened Riyadh's leverage and reinforced doubts over the reliability of U.S. security guarantees.
Al-Muslimi described Washington's refusal to help defend Saudi territory as "the biggest dismissing of the Saudi-American arrangement" in decades.
"The Americans are saying No," he said. "That kind of understanding in the relationship between Riyadh and Washington has never been tested more than now."
Yemen's long record of defeating foreign powers - from Egypt in the 1960s to the Soviets and, more recently, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia - helps explain why Riyadh's search for partners may yield only limited results.
Few regional powers appear eager to be drawn deeper into a conflict that has repeatedly frustrated attempts at outside intervention and acquired a reputation as a graveyard for foreign military ambitions.
"Yemen is the Vietnam and Afghanistan of every power dragged into it," Muslimi said, referring to conflicts in which foreign powers were humbled.
"The Saudis failed in Yemen, the Americans failed in Yemen," he said, adding in reference to Egypt's costly intervention in Yemen in the 1960s: "The Egyptians failed in Yemen."
(Reuters)

aston martin and brough superior turn their track superbike into a road machine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:33:09 UTC
06:33:09 KST

Aston Martin and Brough Superior introduce the AMB 002 Roadster, their first motorcycle designed and certified for use on public roads. The new model follows the track-only AMB 001, unveiled in 2019, and the AMB 001 Pro of 2022, extending the collaboration between the British marques beyond the circuit. Developed from scratch rather than adapted from either predecessor, the AMB 002 is limited to 300 individually built examples, with first deliveries scheduled for the third quarter of 2027.
The roadster combines compact proportions with sculpted carbon fiber bodywork shaped by the Aston Martin Design Studio. A smooth carbon fiber fuel tank rises toward the rider, while crescent-shaped openings carved into the side fairings channel cooling air around the engine. Automotive references appear throughout: Aston Martin’s side strake passes through the fairing and wraps around the headlamp, twin oval exhausts reference the Vanquish, DB12 S and DBX S, and blade-like rear lights recall the Vulcan, Valkyrie and Valhalla. Keyless operation, a backlit ignition button and leather saddle pads add details more commonly associated with the company’s road cars.
the AMB 002 is built for public roads | all images courtesy of Aston Martin
A FIVE-KILOGRAM TITANIUM FRAME HOLDS THE NEW V-TWIN
At the center of the AMB 002 is an all-new 1,083cc four-stroke water-cooled V-twin, producing 130 bhp and 110 Nm of torque. Developed for stronger low- and mid-range response on the road, the engine is machined and assembled in-house at Brough Superior’s headquarters in Toulouse, France, including CNC-machined billet engine cases developed to reduce weight. It sits within a titanium backbone frame milled from a solid billet that weighs just five kilograms and contributes to a 50:50 weight distribution.
Carbon fiber body panels and fuel tank help keep the motorcycle’s overall weight to 190 kilograms, while concentrating mass low within the chassis. Up front, Brough Superior’s double-wishbone Fior fork separates steering and braking forces rather than relying on a conventional telescopic fork. Evolved from the system developed for the AMB 001 Pro, the suspension is intended to maintain the bike’s geometry under braking and reduce dive, particularly when braking while leaned into a corner.
sculpted carbon fiber shapes the roadster’s body
FROM TRACK-ONLY EXPERIMENT TO ROAD-LEGAL ROADSTER
The AMB 002 marks a shift in a collaboration that began with motorcycles conceived primarily as collectible track machines. The first AMB 001 paired Aston Martin styling with Brough Superior engineering, while the subsequent AMB 001 Pro pushed the partnership further toward circuit performance. For the new Roadster, the brands instead focus on making the same combination of lightweight materials, mechanical detailing and limited production usable beyond the racetrack.
Each AMB 002 will be hand-built by Brough Superior in Toulouse, combining carbon fiber, titanium and machined components with hand-finished leather details. Production remains capped at 300 motorcycles, continuing the limited-edition approach of its predecessors while significantly increasing the number that will reach owners. Aston Martin and Brough Superior have not announced pricing for the Roadster, but orders are already being accepted ahead of deliveries beginning in Q3 2027.

Left on brink of victory in Swedish election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:32:18 UTC
06:32:18 KST

Sweden's Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson speaks in Stockholm on election night on Sept. 13, 2026. | Jonas Ekstromer/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty Images
Social Democrat Leader Magdalena Andersson is on course to become Sweden’s next prime minister as her left-wing bloc holds an unassailable lead over the right and far right with 99.9% of results declared.
By 10.30 p.m. on Wednesday night, Andersson’s four-party grouping was three seats ahead of Ulf Kristersson’s alliance of the right and far-right parties in the race to control the 349-seat parliament.
The Swedish Election Authority is set to confirm the “preliminary” result when all the votes have finished being counted, expected on Thursday.
Advertisement
The election is one of the closest in recent Swedish history, and offered voters a sharp choice between electing a new left-wing government or allowing far-right ministers into power for the first time.
Swedish public broadcaster SVT called the election for Andersson’s side on Wednesday night. Her Social Democrats are Sweden’s biggest party and have enjoyed the loose support of three other opposition parties who are seen as her likely coalition partners: The Greens, the Center Party, and the Left Party.
Kristersson’s conservative Moderates have been campaigning alongside the Christian Democrats, the Liberals and the far-right, anti-immigration Sweden Democrats. His allies do not expect him to concede defeat until Andersson wins a vote in parliament to prove she can command a majority. That vote won’t happen before Sept. 29 at the earliest.
Coalition negotiations will begin in earnest once the final outcome is confirmed. In theory any combination of parties can form into a government but in reality, the two-bloc system is likely to hold, meaning Andersson will seek to govern with some or all of her left-leaning partner parties.
Andersson’s Social Democrats stand on 99 seats, with her most natural allies in the Greens on 22. But that still leaves her 54 seats short of a majority and with a potentially difficult task persuading the other two parties in her bloc to cooperate with each other.
The Left Party, which has a historic association with communists, is emboldened by increasing its seat tally at this election to 30. And it has said the price of supporting a government will be gaining ministers inside the new top team.
Advertisement
But the Center Party’s leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist has said she cannot support this, because the “fringes” must not dominate the next government. Thand Ringqvist, whose party is set to take 25 seats — enough to get Andersson’s bloc a majority — ideally wants to form a new centrist administration without either the Left Party or the far-right Sweden Democrats. But the parliamentary numbers do not add up to a majority for such a grouping.
The Center Party has said it will start talks with Andersson’s Social Democrats. Thand Ringqvist was clear on Wednesday night that Kristersson’s rightwing bloc had “lost their government mandate.” But she told SVT that “at the same time, the election result, as it stands, does not give a mandate for a political left turn.”
Kristersson had promised to elevate representatives of the far-right Sweden Democrats into ministerial positions in his government if he won. In the end, while his Moderates party increased their vote share, the SD fell backwards, bucking the recent trend that had seen far right populists gain ground elsewhere in Europe.

Why women in China are still at risk of abduction and forced marriage
The latest incident has exposed many failings in local authorities’ work in a country where a mindset of favouring sons over daughters still exists
One stormy night last month, a driver surnamed He saw two tall men get out of a car in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen and pull a young woman off the street and into the vehicle. During the struggle, her umbrella fell to the ground.
She did not appear willing. Suspicious, He followed the vehicle and later reported the incident to local police, supplying them with footage he had recorded. Thanks to him and the police, the abducted 18-year-old was rescued from a forced marriage.
According to media reports, the teenager, originally from Lanzhou, Gansu province, had been promised to a man by her parents without her knowledge or consent. After receiving the agreed price from the prospective groom’s family, her parents forced her to drop out of school.
The teenager sought help via online posts and eventually a non-profit organisation found her a job in a Shenzhen coffee shop. But her parents, intent on marrying her off, tracked her down and sent a team to stake out her workplace and ambush her, driving her over 20 hours back towards home before they were stopped by the police.

Ukraine begins sowing winter grain crops
That is according to the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food, Ukrinform reports.
As of September 16, winter wheat and triticale had been sown on 145,300 hectares, or 3.2% of the projected area; winter barley on 13,000 hectares, or 2.2%; and winter rye on 13,300 hectares, or 17.3% of the projected area.

17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
An Argentine federal court on ordered the suspension of work Wednesday linked to the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falkland Islands, involving Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and British firm Rockhopper Exploration, according to Argentine media
Federal Judge Mariel Borruto, based in the Rio Grande in Tierra del Fuego province, granted a preliminary injunction ordering the companies to refrain from starting or continuing work needed to develop the offshore oil project,
The order covers drilling, subsea installations and the start of commercial oil production, according to details of the ruling reported.
The Sea Lion project is located 220 kilometers (137 miles) north of the Falkland Islands, an archipelago administered by the UK but claimed by Argentina. Navitas and Rockhopper made a final investment decision on the project in late 2025.
The ruling came after a lawsuit was filed by the Center of Ex-Combatants of the Falkland Islands in La Plata, and an environmental lawyers’ association seeking to stop the project on environmental and sovereignty grounds.
Borruto ordered the suspension until an environmental impact assessment is carried out before the relevant Argentine authorities.
The judge also ordered the companies to provide information on the status of the project, its schedule, wells, floating production facilities, contractors, financing sources, insurers and environmental studies.
The court said the measure is provisional and does not constitute a final ruling on the companies’ responsibility or on all issues raised in the main case.
Argentina has stepped up legal and diplomatic action against oil companies operating around the Falkland Islands.
President Javier Milei’s government has opposed the development, arguing that the islands and surrounding maritime areas are part of Argentine territory.
The UK has administered the islands since 1833 and rejects Argentina’s sovereignty claim. London also supports economic activity on the territory.

Here are five key takeaways from Wednesday's Fed rate hike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:23:51 UTC
06:23:51 KST

The Federal Reserve on Wednesday delivered a much-expected interest rate hike, and Chairman Kevin Warsh followed with a notably terse news conference at which he stressed policymakers' staunch commitment to tackling inflation.
Here are five key takeaways:
- A fairly unified message: The Fed's quarter-percentage-point rate increase was largely in keeping with market expectations. At least somewhat surprisingly, the vote was unanimous. Given the range of views expressed by policymakers in recent weeks, there was widespread speculation that at least one voter would dissent, with much of the speculation centered on Governor Christopher Waller. In the end, however, all 12 voters on the Federal Open Market Committee agreed with the decision.
- The market didn't like it: Stocks were in the green heading into the rate decision and bond yields were lower. That didn't last long. Whether it was Warsh's hawkish tone on inflation or just the general prospect of multiple hikes, stocks sold off sharply after the decision. The Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 631 points and the 2-year Treasury yield, the security most sensitive to Fed rate expectations, rocketed more than 7 basis points higher. The sell-off was reminiscent of the reaction to the July FOMC meeting and Warsh news conference.
- Short statement, short presser: In keeping with the prior two meetings under the Warsh regime, the post-meeting statement was terse, to say the least. Clocking in at a meager 130 words, the statement was even shorter than July's, which was 166 words, and was tied with the June missive. Warsh followed that with a news conference in which he took reporters' questions for a grand total of some 22 minutes during a session that lasted barely half an hour total.
- Connecting the dots: The FOMC dot plot of officials' individual expectations for interest rates showed a fairly cohesive group for 2026 but a wide dispersion afterward. Sixteen of the 18 participants expected at least one more rate hike this year. For out years, though, there was considerable disagreement. Eight expected another hike in 2027, nine of 17 saw rates steady or higher in 2028 and 10 figured on no cuts through 2029.
- Bucking the president: Warsh deflected a couple questions with political overtones. That was significant because President Donald Trump has been rattling his anti-Fed saber again, going so far as to threaten to cut off trade with some countries unless the Fed cuts. "I've got nothing for you on a discussion with the president," he said at one point, later adding, "Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane. Independence is a two-way street."
What they're saying
"This is unlikely to be the end of Fed rate hikes …. It's hard to look at roughly 4% unemployment and a core PCE forecast of 3.5% and say the Fed shouldn't be focused on inflation. But monetary policy looks like a really costly way to solve this problem right now." — Mike Madowitz, principal economist at the Roosevelt Institute, a liberal think tank
"Risk assets were not enamored with the outcome of today's FOMC. Hopes of limited hikes ahead faded in the face of the Fed's resolve to address inflation. Still, after the initial reset, we believe Chair Warsh's clear messaging could actually help support Treasury prices further out the curve." — Andrzej Skiba, head of the BlueBay U.S. Fixed Income team at RBC Global Asset Management
"Warsh's press conference was coherent, confident and consistently hawkish without coming across as crazily so. He balanced a stern but disciplined message on inflation with an upbeat take on growth which he said has been strengthening since the start of the summer." — Krishna Guha, head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI

Ukrainian Parliament Passes Key First-Reading Reforms for Parcel Tax and Small Business Bankruptcy

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:09:29 UTC
06:09:29 KST

The Verkhovna Rada on Sept. 16 passed two significant draft bills in their first readings, advancing key fiscal and business reforms required under Ukraine’s international funding commitments.
Lawmakers backed Draft No. 16051-1, with 273 votes, to introduce a 20% value-added tax (VAT) on cross-border e-commerce parcels valued at under €150 ($170).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Under the proposed rules, foreign online marketplaces and digital platforms would be responsible for calculating and remitting the tax directly.
Personal non-commercial shipments worth up to €45 ($52), unaccompanied luggage worth up to €150 ($173), and imported goods designated for military and energy needs will remain tax-free.
The passage follows almost a year of political pushback: parliament had previously failed to pass the parcel tax twice, despite appeals from Serhiy Marchenko, the finance minister, and Serhii Koretskyi, prime minister, before President Volodymyr Zelensky directly urged lawmakers to support it.
The legislation aims to generate around Hr.10 billion ($224 million) annually for a dedicated state budget fund to support Ukraine’s armed forces, while leveling the playing field between domestic and foreign retailers.
The reform is one of several structural benchmarks under Ukraine’s updated IMF program, required to release an upcoming $692 million tranche.
The parcel -tax measure was included among commitments signed in November 2025 and is also linked to progress toward €3.7 billion ($4.27 billion) in EU macro-financial assistance.
Ukraine Plans War-Risk Insurance Fund, Considers 1% VAT Increase to Cover Business Losses
During the same session, parliament approved No. 15024 with 270 votes to institute simplified, lower-cost insolvency procedures for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs).
The measure limits proceedings to a maximum of 180 days, without extensions; safeguards employee wages; and harmonizes national law with EU Directive 2019/1023.
The bill fulfills one of several indicators under the Ukraine Facility plan needed to secure €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion) in EU funding.
To take effect, both measures still require approval in a second reading, alongside key amendments to the Customs Code.
According to the August 2026 Monitoring Report published by the RRR4U consortium, Kyiv is navigating critical bottlenecks across three major donor pipelines, creating severe risks for the national budget despite recent policy breakthroughs.
Ukraine still faces 13 unfulfilled reform indicators from late 2025 through mid-2026, leaving around $4 billion in macro-financial assistance for 2026 frozen. Koretskyi told lawmakers that Ukraine is counting on $30 billion from partners this year, contingent on parliament delivering the reforms it promised.

How do staffing numbers stack up?
Every senator and MP have five full-time electorate officers to help run their local community offices, though members with unusually large seats can apply for extra.
Then there are personal staff, like advisers and media officers, who assist parliamentarians with policy, legislation and media.
The prime minister has the sole discretion to determine the number and level of personal staff allocated to everyone, including ministers, the opposition and independents.
Data from May this year shows Payman is the only independent in parliament who does not have any additional personal staff allocated.
Le has one, as does Nicolette Boele and senator Ralph Babet.
The remainder of the crossbench independents have two personal staff, except for Jacqui Lambie who has three.
The Greens — who have one MP and 10 senators — have 17 personal staff, while One Nation — with two MPs and four senators — are allocated five additional staff.
In total, the Albanese government has 495 staff working across ministerial offices, special envoys and in other support roles.
The Coalition has 92 additional staff. There is also a handful of extra staff allocated to whips offices and the presiding officers.
Crossbench teams up to attack 'unfair' staffing standards
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and independents Fatima Payman and Dai Le have teamed up to attack what they say is "unfair" staffing double standards for non-government politicians.
The three are calling on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to provide "fair staffing allocations" for independent and minor party parliamentarians before next month, or they will seek to move legislation to strip him of this personal power.
In a statement, they argue the current system where the PM can determine personal staff allocations for independents and minority party leaders is negatively impacting their constituents.
"When a crossbench office is under-resourced, it is the people of that electorate who miss out," the statement says.
Hanson, Payman and Le want staffing allocations decided independently, arguing when the original system of prime ministerial discretion was designed, there were warnings the power could be easily abused.
"Anthony Albanese is showing that these warnings were not misplaced," the say.

"Of course we need to keep Australia safe, but make that work," Taylor says.

Fed approves interest rate hike, signals one more to come this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:07:51 UTC
06:07:51 KST

The Federal Reserve on Wednesday approved its first interest rate hike in more than three years and indicated another is to come, as part of an effort aimed at combating inflation brought on by spiraling oil prices and other factors.
In a move that markets widely anticipated, the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee voted 12-0 to increase its key interest rate by a quarter percentage point, or 25 basis points. The move brought the overnight funds rate to a target range of 3.75%-4%.
"Inflation remains elevated," the committee said in its brief post-meeting statement. "Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."
During a news conference, Chairman Kevin Warsh said inflation has been "too high ... for too long."
"We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective clearly and at sufficient speed," he said. "Today, the FOMC decided that this standard has not been satisfied."
Warsh further explained that recent economic reports showed the economy, including the labor market, was strong. However, inflation remained above the central bank's target, and added that tension in the Middle East also contributed to the decision.
"All three of those things lend themselves to a firm unanimous decision today," he said.
Highly anticipated
Despite a raft of conflicting recent statements from policymakers, markets had priced in a better than 90% chance that the FOMC would approve the increase, though there was chatter about the possibility of multiple dissents.
Persistently high inflation readings coupled with statements from Warsh a few weeks ago had convinced Wall Street that the Fed would OK its first rate increase since July 2023.
Updated projections the committee released Wednesday showed that a strong majority of officials think another hike is possible later this year.
The dot-plot grid of individual officials' expectations indicated that 16 of the 18 participants – Warsh has chosen not to submit a dot since taking the position – expected another rate increase, with four of those seeing two more as possible. Two participants expected the committee to stop at one hike.
However, there are no increases penciled in for subsequent years, with one cut each indicated for 2028 and at least one for 2029.
Officials also nudged up their expectations for inflation this year.
They see the headline personal consumption expenditures price index at 3.7% and the core excluding food and energy at 3.4%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than the last update in June. The Fed doesn't expect to reach its inflation target until 2029, though it sees both measures dropping off sharply in 2027 – 2.3% for headline and 2.5% for core.
The committee had been on hold all year and was expected to stay there, until the tide began turning toward a hike in late August.
Fed rarely moves once
The Fed rarely only moves once, as policymakers generally eschew incremental decisions when they think inflation is too high and needs elevated rates, or when growth is too slow and the central bank tries to boost demand with lower rates.
While the Fed's action was expected, the rationale behind the hike was unusual.
The Fed generally looks through the kind of inflation the economy is experiencing now, with the higher fuel costs from the Iran war and the lingering impacts from tariffs. However, officials in recent days have weighed the cost of continuing to look through the price increases, particularly in light of a stabilizing labor market. The committee lowered its outlook for the unemployment rate to 4.1%, down 0.2 percentage point from June.
The worry now is that the duration of the energy prices could raise inflation expectations and start to spread through the economy. Economists also see expanded investment in artificial intelligence as a potential inflationary factor.
Also, the "transitory" episode from a few years ago is still fresh in policymakers' minds, as Fed officials thought the supply and demand shock from the Covid pandemic eventually would fade. Instead, inflation readings hit 40-year highs before the Fed decided to act.
In July, the debate generated considerable dissent on the policy view, with three FOMC members voting against the decision to hold, preferring instead a quarter-point hike.
At this week's meeting, 2027 was a fairly close call, with eight officials pointing to another hike, six seeing the funds rate holding steady and four envisioning cuts.
Markets already have been pricing in higher rates across the spectrum. The S&P 500 rose after Wednesday's announcement.
Treasury yields have been surging. The 10-year note has risen about a quarter percentage point since Warsh's remarks at the Fed's Jackson Hole, Wyoming, symposium on Aug. 28. The benchmark is up about a full percentage point since its February low. The 2-year note, which is most sensitive to rate expectations, has seen even sharper gains.
Borrowing costs also have been on the move. A 30-year fixed-rate mortgage had soared to 7.19%, up some 38 basis points since the Jackson Hole speech and more than a full percentage point from a year ago, according to Mortgage News Daily.
In the wake of the decision, Treasury yields were lower, a signal that investors were encouraged by the central bank's attempt to tamp down inflation. Yields and prices move in opposite directions.
"Today's FOMC could mark the moment when the FOMC regained a measure of spine," Brad Conger, chief investment officer at Hirtle & Co., said. "There were many arguments for standing still. But for once, the committee sided with main street."
"Inflation is a pervasive concern, and its uncertainty is impeding decision-making among all businesses. One swallow doesn't make a spring, but we might have just caught a glimpse of Volckerian decisiveness as opposed to the eternal sycophancy of the Powell era," Conger added.

Russian Oil Profits Surge as Middle East Conflict and Kremlin Cash Counteract Ukrainian Drone Strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:06:30 UTC
06:06:30 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Oil Profits Surge as Middle East Conflict and Kremlin Cash Counteract Ukrainian Drone Strikes
Despite a relentless campaign of Ukrainian drone strikes that has knocked out roughly a fifth of Russia’s oil refining capacity, Russian refineries are raking in unprecedented profits, The Moscow Times reported on September 16.
According to data from Rosstat , the refining sector earned a staggering 938 billion rubles ($11.13 billion) in the first half of the year, a 16.2% increase from the same period last year. Financial analysts expect third-quarter profit margins to surge even higher, marking an era of extraordinary profitability for the domestic segment.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This windfall of “super-profits” is being driven by a combination of record-high wholesale prices on the St. Petersburg exchange and massive state subsidies through Russia’s fuel “damper” mechanism, The Moscow Times noted. Wholesale prices for petroleum products began climbing in March following the outbreak of war in the Middle East.
By July, exchange prices hit record highs, with AI-95 gasoline reaching 82,600 rubles ($980) per ton and diesel at 77,600 rubles ($921). In September, the price of AI-92 gasoline set a new all-time high of 73,100 rubles ($868) per ton.
To prevent these wholesale spikes from fully passing to consumers, the Russian government pays oil companies directly from the state budget. These “damper” payouts ballooned to nearly 350 billion rubles ($4.15 billion) per month during the second quarter, and reached 500 billion rubles ($5.93 billion) across July and August, The Moscow Times wrote.
For giants like Gazprom Neft, these state payouts and price surges have more than compensated for the reduced refining volumes caused by drone attacks and unplanned repairs.
However, this corporate windfall is being directly funded by the Russian public. Since the beginning of the year, retail gasoline prices have surged by 21.2%, while diesel has jumped 18.4%.
The Moscow Times reported that, while major oil companies can artificially hold down prices at their branded stations using state subsidies, independent gas stations are forced to buy fuel at inflated wholesale rates and pass the costs onto everyday drivers.
While the Kremlin tightly guards the exact financial toll of the Ukrainian strikes, the damage remains immense. The Ukrainian General Staff previously estimated that drone attacks have inflicted $13.5 billion in damages to the Russian oil industry since August 2025.
According to the Russian insurance broker Mains, direct losses to the oil and gas sector from drone strikes exceeded 100 billion rubles ($1.19 billion) last year, with total indirect costs and lost profits surpassing one trillion rubles ($11.87 billion), The Moscow Times added.
In addition to striking onshore refineries, Ukraine is also targeting the maritime logistics network Moscow uses to export its petroleum. As part of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces' “MoLoChKa” campaign to cut off shadow-fleet revenues, a Ukrainian naval drone recently maneuvered past a pursuing Russian interceptor helicopter to strike the sanctioned oil tanker Armada Leader off the coast of Sochi.
Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert Brovdi reported that the operation has successfully targeted 285 Russian-linked vessels over 10 weeks, culminating in 16 ship strikes.
While Ukrainian strikes on refineries and shadow-fleet vessels have constrained Russian petroleum exports, the current global fuel crisis is primarily driven by a massive supply shock due to war in the Middle East. Severe transit restrictions through the Strait of Hormuz have slashed Persian Gulf fuel exports by roughly one million barrels per day.
Combined with Russia’s drone-induced outages and self-imposed export limits, this unprecedented squeeze has drained 1.6 million barrels per day of diesel and gasoil from the global market, sending international prices soaring past the equivalent of $200 per barrel.

What’s Really Behind the Global Diesel Shortage—and How Much Is Actually About Ukraine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:06:18 UTC
06:06:18 KST

- Category
- World
What’s Really Behind the Global Diesel Shortage—and How Much Is Actually About Ukraine?
Global diesel supplies are tightening as Persian Gulf exports collapse and Russian refinery output falls. So what is really driving the shortage—and how much of it is actually about Ukraine?
The global diesel shortage has increasingly been linked to Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, but market data shows that the larger supply shock began thousands of kilometers away—in the Strait of Hormuz, where severely restricted shipping has slashed fuel exports from the Persian Gulf.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the International Energy Agency’s September Oil Market Report, Gulf countries and Russia together exported 1.6 million barrels per day less diesel and gasoil in August than in February, when they accounted for almost 45% of global seaborne trade in the fuels.
The IEA said Gulf diesel and gasoil exports alone had fallen to just 390,000 barrels per day—slightly more than one-quarter of their pre-war level.
That means the Gulf lost roughly 1 million barrels per day of diesel and gasoil exports, making disruption in and around the Strait of Hormuz the larger component of the combined Gulf-Russia decline.
Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz following US-Israeli strikes at the end of February, Reuters reported, cutting Europe off from roughly one-quarter of its diesel and jet fuel supply and helping push fuel inventories at Northwest Europe’s main trading hub to their lowest level in 12 years.
Traffic through the chokepoint remains heavily restricted. According to Reuters on September 16, only four vessels were visibly recorded crossing Hormuz the previous day, compared with a 10-day average of 18. Some ships are believed to be making so-called “dark” crossings with their tracking systems switched off.
The IEA has described the Middle East disruption as the largest oil supply disruption in the history of the global market, noting that around 15 million barrels per day of crude and another 5 million barrels per day of oil products normally passed through Hormuz.
The agency said restoring transit through the strait is the single most important measure for easing pressure on global oil and fuel prices. Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries have added another significant supply loss.
The IEA said disruptions to Russia’s refining system and the near-halt in product exports following intensified Ukrainian strikes compounded the decline from the Gulf.
Reuters reported on September 15 that six of Russia’s leading diesel-producing refineries—which together account for roughly half of the country’s diesel production—had reduced or halted output following drone attacks.
Russia has also removed additional supply from the international market through its own policy decisions. Moscow has restricted diesel exports as it tries to protect its domestic market amid refinery outages and fuel shortages, and is preparing to keep restrictions in place through October.
According to Reuters, not all of the Russian diesel missing from the global market reflects refinery outages alone. Moscow has also restricted diesel exports in an effort to stabilize domestic fuel supplies following disruptions at Russian refineries.
Meanwhile, the scale of the Middle Eastern disruption remains larger. The IEA estimates that refined-product and LPG exports from Gulf producers remain almost 60%, or 3.7 million barrels per day, below February levels, while nearly 3 million barrels per day of Gulf refining capacity has been shut because of attacks and limited export routes.
The consequences are now visible worldwide. US diesel and gasoil prices exceeded the equivalent of $200 per barrel in early September, according to the IEA, while Asian diesel refining margins reached a record of more than $87 per barrel on September 16.
Industry executives also warn that there is little spare refining capacity available to replace the missing barrels. Vitol CEO Russell Hardy said in September that the global market was missing large volumes of refined products from both Russia and the Middle East, while US refineries were already operating close to maximum levels.
The figures therefore point to a broader picture than Ukrainian refinery strikes alone. Those attacks have reduced one major source of global diesel supply, but they hit a market that was already severely constrained by the collapse in Persian Gulf fuel exports following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz. And for now, the Gulf remains the larger part of that supply shock.

Details

The exact amount of unused SAFE funds will become known after EU countries provide the European Commission with information on the implementation of their projects by the end of October. According to RMF24, Brussels is seeking additional funds to support Ukraine’s defense needs.

An interfaith coalition unveiled Wednesday a 100-meter (328-foot) memorial shroud bearing the handwritten names of more than 20,000 Palestinian children killed by Israel in the Gaza Strip at the UN Church Center in New York.
"Not a number, but a name," organizers emphasized, explaining that the project aims to restore individual identity to every young person killed in the enclave, while demanding an end to Israeli military operations and establishing accountability for war crimes.
The Gaza Children's Shroud memorial was prepared by Doctors Against Genocide, Priests Against Genocide USA, Justice for All and partner groups.
The ceremony at the UN Church Center featured the recitation of the Holy Quran and an interfaith gathering coinciding with the opening of the UN General Assembly.
The initiative draws inspiration from an Italian memorial created in Rome by Pastors Against Genocide, which originated from the tragic practice in Gaza of parents writing children's names directly onto their bodies to ensure identification if their homes were bombed.
Following its initial launch at Philadelphia City Hall on Sept. 1, the exhibition is scheduled to travel to Washington in October before touring a new city each month as part of a year-long global campaign.
Israeli military attacks have killed more than 20,000 children and injured 44,000 in Gaza since October 2023, according to UN reports.

NASA has discovered the largest recent impact crater in the Solar System on the Moon
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
00:02:26 EEST
06:02:26 KST

NASA has discovered the largest recent impact crater in the Solar System on the Moon
Kyiv • UNN
The crater, 222 meters in diameter, formed about two years ago after a piece of space debris crashed into the Moon. NASA confirmed the discovery in early 2026.
A new crater approximately 222 meters in diameter and up to 43 meters deep has been discovered on the Moon. It was formed by the impact of a fragment of an asteroid or comet approximately two years ago. It has become the largest known modern impact crater in the Solar System, Associated Press reports, according to UNN.
Details
The crater was recorded by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter spacecraft on the Moon’s near side in May 2024, shortly after the impact. However, the relevant images were found only in August 2025 among the enormous volume of data collected.
In the autumn, the spacecraft took more detailed photographs of the area, and in early 2026, scientists confirmed the discovery. The new crater is approximately three times larger than the previous record holder, discovered by LRO about 10 years ago.
Such impacts occur approximately once every 132 years
According to researchers’ estimates, an impact of this scale is extraordinarily rare. Scientists called it "a truly unique, once-in-a-lifetime observation."
The impact altered the Moon’s surface across an area of more than 100 km around the impact site. Another study also found a cold region approximately 7 km wide near the crater, whose formation is associated with the mixing of the upper layer of lunar soil.
The crater was named after the late director of the Lunar and Planetary Institute in Houston, Thomas McGetchin. The research findings were published in the scientific journal Science Advances.

Netanyahu steps up threats against directors of Gaza documentary 'NAZA'
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed on Wednesday to pass a law to revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames Israel's soldiers, his latest threat against the Israeli directors of "NAZA", a documentary about soldiers' killing of Gaza civilians.
Directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, NAZA documents how mass civilian deaths were routinely built into Israeli targeting decisions in Gaza.
The film, which won a major prize at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday, takes its title from an Israeli military term for expected "collateral casualties" and is built around anonymous interviews with intelligence officers and soldiers.
It has drawn a backlash in Israel, with the military examining potential legal action against those involved in it. But it has also played into the charged political atmosphere ahead of Israel's October 27 election, which public opinion polls show Netanyahu's right-wing coalition could lose.
On Tuesday, Netanyahu accused some of his election rivals of failing to take a tough stand against the documentary, saying this made them unfit for office. And on Wednesday, he pledged to advance two bills that he said aimed at addressing the "immense damage" done to Israeli soldiers.
"The first, to revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames (Israeli) soldiers, and the second to hit them in their pockets and increase the statutory damages for defamation they can be sued for by 20 times," Netanyahu said in a social media video.
"We will hit them both in their pockets and in their citizenship, as their place is not with us."
Netanyahu cited three incidents in proposing the bills: "the recent film NAZA which portrayed (Israeli) officers and soldiers as war criminals"; 2025 remarks by left-wing ex-general turned politician Yair Golan that "a sane country does not kill children as a hobby"; and a military legal officer's 2024 leak of a video showing soldiers abusing a Gaza detainee.
Reuters could not immediately reach the NAZA filmmakers for comment.
In 2022, Israel's Supreme Court upheld a law that permits stripping citizenship from Israelis who carry out actions that constitute a breach of trust against the state. Any new legislation would likely face similar court challenges.
The NAZA filmmakers say they believe it is important that Israelis watch the documentary and grapple with the narrative it presents.
Gaza health authorities say more than 73,000 Palestinians, most of them civilians, have been killed in Israel's military campaign that has left much of Gaza in ruins.

Washington Won't Be Regulating AI Anytime Soon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

For weeks, Washington has been abuzz with talk of needing to push through some sort of AI regulation amid mounting concerns about the risks of highly capable frontier AI models going rogue.
But there is no reason to think any one measure can win the support of the White House, where officials have paused work on creating a FINRA-style regulatory body after President Donald Trump soured on the idea, or of Capitol Hill, where lawmakers have competing proposals that lack the votes to pass.
White House aides initially started sketching out a framework for an AI oversight agency connected to the administration soon after Google DeepMind’s cofounder Demis Hassabis floated the idea in a July 14 essay and in briefings to senior officials, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The Treasury Department and the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy envisioned a body where leading AI labs would self-regulate the development of frontier models, and they put together a preliminary draft to see what it could look like if executed.
But when a chorus of tech executives—including Trump’s former AI czar David Sacks and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg—learned of the effort, they one by one called Trump in August to express their opposition. The proposal has since been left in limbo.
Since then, there have been no new AI oversight proposals seriously under consideration at the White House, the sources say, not least as Trump has doubled down in recent days of rejecting any overt regulation and called AI safety concerns a “hoax” in a recent Truth Social post.
Trump’s ire has stemmed at least in part from a 3,822 word missive by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on the dangers of frontier AI. Trump’s aides, one of the sources said, viewed it as stirring anxieties that caused unnecessary headaches for the administration—even as it represents a fairly moderate position within AI circles.
In the absence of the White House taking the lead, several bills have sprung up in Congress—but with no voting days left on the House calendar until after the midterm elections and a lack of unity around even one bill, the odds of anything passing are extraordinarily slim.
Independent Auditors
The bipartisan Frontier Act, a bill introduced this summer by House Democratic senior whip Lori Trahan and Republican House Energy and Commerce Committee member Jay Obernolte, is widely seen as having the most support inside the House Democratic caucus as well as among AI executives.
As drafted, the bill would enable the Commerce Department to have auditors embedded at AI labs, who could report critical safety incidents and empower the administration to stop development if a model poses catastrophic risk.
But despite public backing from OpenAI, the White House has been undecided on whether to support the concept of using independent auditors amid skepticism from AI accelerationists about regulatory capture and from national security hawks over China.
The principal argument against the idea from Trumpworld is that even if auditors determine that a model is dangerous and needs to be taken offline, there is no guarantee that China will also pause development or stop trying to reverse engineer frontier AI weights.
There would then be immense pressure to lift any emergency pauses in development in order to stay ahead of China, defeating the entire premise of having auditors to push the Commerce Department to take models offline.
Still, the main issue for the Frontier Act remains partisan politics. House Democratic leadership aides tell Inner Loop even if the bill does end up with enough votes for passage, Republican Speaker Mike Johnson has no interest in bringing it to the floor.
To get around the procedural hurdles, House Democrats are looking at putting some of the bill’s AI audit provisions into must-pass legislation like a continuing resolution to fund the government, according to two House leadership aides.
But it is also not clear whether the bill has enough votes. Even among House Democrats, there is not unified support; some key lawmakers like New Jersey congressman Josh Gottheimer, who served on the House Democrats’ AI commission, have not signed on to the bill.
Kill Switches
There’s also so-called kill-switch legislation that would enable the government to force an AI model to be shut down. The legislation has both bipartisan and bicameral support, but the idea has received only modest interest from tech executives in Silicon Valley.
There are two competing kill-switch proposals: one from House Democratic caucus vice chair Ted Lieu and another floated this week by Louisiana Senate Republican John Kennedy.
Tech leaders, sources say, have been largely ambivalent about kill-switch bills, since the main concern of AI engineers is not about models behaving badly when observed but rather how they behave when they believe they are unobserved and incentivized to take extreme steps to complete a task.
The Hugging Face hack, for instance, was not discovered until after it was over. If the idea of a kill switch is to stop an AI model going rogue, some tech executives have suggested privately to WIRED that there would be little point in turning it off after the damage has already been done.
So for now, even as conversations about AI models killing us all have taken over the airwaves, it doesn’t really look like the US government is going to do anything about it. At least until events force everyone’s hand.
This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Unknown

At least 12 injured, including children, in Kyiv following Russian missile, drone attack
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Russia launched a drone and missile attack on Kyiv on the night of Sept. 16-17, damaging an education facility and injuring at least 12 people in Ukraine's capital, officials reported.
Explosions rocked Kyiv's city center at around 12:30 a.m. local time, the Kyiv Independent's Deputy Chief Editor Toma Istomina reported.
Russia's attack resumed when ballistic missiles targeted Ukraine's capital at around 2:13 a.m. local time with "two big explosions in quick succession, then another after about a minute," War Editor Chris York said. Another eight explosions, "one after another," rocked the city at around 2:21 a.m., he added.
An air raid alert was declared across much of Ukraine, including briefly in far-western Lviv Oblast, where sirens sounded from 2:12 a.m. until 2:26 a.m.
Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitscko said that at least 12 people were injured, including two childred, with at least nine of the injured victims requiring hospitalization.
Earlier, a small fire broke out at a Kyiv education facility as a result of a Russian strike, with the blaze extinguished by first responders, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) wrote.
"The facade and windows of a four-story building of a higher education institution in the Holosiivskyi district were damaged," DSNS reported.
Another fire broke out at a private property in Kyiv Oblast's Brovary district, located just east of Ukraine's capital. A utility building, agricultural equipment, semi-trailers, and a car were also damaged, the Kyiv Oblast Military Administration reported.
Homes and commercial infrastructure were also damaged in the oblast's Fastivskyi district, the Military Administration wrote.
The full extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
Russia regularly launches fatal attacks on Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure as it continues to wage its war.
Russian forces attacked Kyiv on the morning of Sept. 15, killing one person and injuring at least 12 others, local authorities said.
A gas station in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district was hit at around 6 a.m. local time, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko. One person was hospitalized in critical condition and later died in hospital, according to the mayor.
