Istanbul submits documents to ICC over Ukrainian attack on Turkish ship in Black Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:59:03 UTC
05:59:03 KST

ANKARA, September 16. /TASS/. Complainants have filed a submission with the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague over a drone attack on the Turkish cargo ship Reyhan Sari in the Black Sea that killed a Turkish sailor; evidence collected in the case has been submitted to the ICC prosecutor’s office, the maritime news portal HaberDenizde reported, citing Nuri Koray Kurun, a lawyer representing the complainants.
The filing will next undergo a preliminary review by the relevant ICC bodies, which will then decide whether to open a formal investigation into the case. Kurun estimated that the initial review could take about six months and the entire process up to two years.
The complainants include the shipowner, 12 crew members, who were on board during the attack, and the family of Savas Cakar, the 54-year-old sailor who was killed. According to Turkish media, Reyhan Sari came under attack on July 22 while carrying coal from Russia's Taman port to Trabzon.
The Turkish side attributes the strike to Ukraine. According to Kurun, one of the key pieces of evidence consists of video materials related to a Ukrainian operation aimed at striking vessels linked to Russia in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. He said materials concerning the operation, as well as footage of vessels being hit, appeared on official Ukrainian social media accounts.
"We have concrete information and images showing that the attack was carried out by the Ukrainian side," Kurun said. He added that the complainants included the evidence they had collected in their submission to the ICC.
The complainants are asking the ICC to consider the attack on their vessel under Articles 7 and 8 of the Rome Statute, which concern crimes against humanity and war crimes.

Rachida Dati in court: French ex-minister on trial over Renault-Nissan corruption case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:58:12 UTC
05:58:12 KST

Former minister and MEP Rachida Dati is on trial in Paris in the Renault-Nissan case, accused of corruption and influence peddling after taking €900,000 from a group subsidiary for counseling. Carlos Ghosn is being tried in the same case in absentia.
The trial of Rachida Dati opened on Wednesday afternoon before the Paris criminal court. The former justice and culture minister is facing charges of passive corruption, passive influence-peddling, and concealment of abuse of power and breach of trust.
At the heart of the case are the €900,000 she received between 2009 and 2013 from a Dutch subsidiary of Renault-Nissan, while she was serving as a Member of the European Parliament.
The opening day was marked in particular by the absence of Carlos Ghosn. The former head of Renault-Nissan, who has been in Lebanon since fleeing Japan in 2019, is also being prosecuted, notably for active corruption and influence-peddling.
Tried in absentia, he asked in a letter to the court for the hearing to be postponed, arguing that he had not been properly served. He said he was willing to take part in the proceedings via videoconference.
Over six half-days of hearings, up to 28 September, the court is to examine the relationship between Rachida Dati and Carlos Ghosn and, above all, the nature of the services said to correspond to the €900,000 paid by RNBV, the Dutch subsidiary of the Renault-Nissan alliance.
Fees at the heart of the proceedings
Rachida Dati maintains she worked as a lawyer for the group and denies any lobbying activity in the European Parliament. Her lawyers denounce what they call an "intellectual construct" by the prosecution and insist their client has "exclusively" carried out legal work.
The prosecution, by contrast, argues that the fee agreement signed in 2009 was used to conceal lobbying activities. Investigating magistrates noted the paucity of documents that could, in their view, establish the reality and scope of the legal services provided. They also consider that the remuneration was "totally disproportionate" to the work for which evidence has been found.
Investigators are looking in particular at several interventions by Rachida Dati in the European Parliament, including three questions submitted in 2012 and 2013 relating to the automotive sector. The prosecution believes her parliamentary activity may have been influenced by her professional ties with Renault.
Rachida Dati faces up to ten years in prison and a €450,000 fine, as well as a possible ban on holding public office. She remains presumed innocent until the court reaches its decision.
Carlos Ghosn, for his part, will therefore not be in the dock. The former executive, who disputes the allegations against him, remains in Lebanon. His absence adds a particular dimension to a trial that is expected to help the court determine whether the €900,000 paid to Rachida Dati did indeed correspond to legal services or whether it concealed lobbying activity, which was banned at the time for MEPs.

Canada applies to join British-led military coalition
OTTAWA - Canada, seeking to diversify its defence ties away from the United States, has formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military coalition, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office said on Sept 16.
The force, a grouping of 10 North Atlantic NATO member states, is a rapid response military partnership.
“Prime Minister Carney announced that Canada has formally applied to join the Joint Expeditionary Force and welcomed the UK’s support for Canada’s participation in this important initiative,” Carney’s office said in a statement.
Canada, already a member of NATO, is seeking closer military cooperation with European nations as it tries to reduce its reliance on the United States.
Carney had earlier met British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in northern England.
The two men discussed opportunities for defence industrial cooperation through the Global Combat Air Programme, an advanced fighter jet project that Canada joined as an observer in July 2026, Carney’s office said.
The JEF comprises Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom. REUTERS

House votes to hold Leon Black in contempt of Congress over Epstein subpoenas defiance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:54:15 UTC
05:54:15 KST

The House of Representatives voted Wednesday to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for his refusal to comply with subpoenas issued to him related to a committee's ongoing investigation of the notorious late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The vote by unanimous consent sets the stage for House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to certify the matter to refer Black's conduct to the Department of Justice for possible criminal prosecution.
It came a day after the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, in a 41-0 vote, passed a resolution recommending the full House hold the former Apollo Global Management CEO in contempt.
It is not clear whether the DOJ ultimately will prosecute Black.
Defendants convicted of contempt of Congress face a possible sentence of not less than one month and not more than 12 months in prison.
A DOJ spokesperson, in a statement to MS NOW, said, "The Department of Justice is expecting to receive the referral from [the] House Oversight Committee and takes allegations of contempt of Congress seriously."
"For the past 18 months, the Department has repeatedly said it will follow additional investigative leads in all matters relating to Jeffrey Epstein," the spokesperson said. "The US Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia will review the referral of Mr. Black carefully and will not hesitate to pursue additional cases where the evidence supports."
The contempt action stems from Black's failure to appear for a transcribed deposition by the committee on Sept. 3 after it issued him a subpoena for that appearance, and his failure to comply fully with a separate subpoena seeking copies of nondisclosure agreements he has been party to.
Black gave the committee one of the NDAs, which his lawyers said was the "only" one that Epstein knew about, but withheld others.
"No one is above the law," House Oversight Chairman Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., said in a statement.
"Leon Black defied two subpoenas, and the U.S. House of Representatives acted swiftly to find him in contempt of Congress," Comer said. "We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors in our investigation of the federal government's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell criminal cases."
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking Democrat on the House oversight panel, said, "This vote is an important step towards justice and accountability."
"We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes," Garcia said. "We are just getting started."
Black's attorneys blasted the House for its contempt holding, calling it "an outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr. Black."
"The House of Representatives has rushed through every stage of this inquiry. First, the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and Chairman Comer rushed to issue him subpoenas," the lawyers, Susan Estrich and Aaron Cutler, said in a statement.
"Then, the Committee rushed to hold him in contempt, even in the face of active litigation and an ethics complaint. Now, the full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee's actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman [James] Comer.
"Mr. Black is a private citizen who has helped create hundreds of thousands of jobs, has given away more than $700 million in philanthropic and charitable contributions, and has supported research that has been at the vanguard of cancer treatment," the attorneys said. "To think, he is being held in contempt over invalid subpoenas is ridiculous. It is so out of line that the behavior of this Committee is reminiscent of the 1950's where another Congressional Committee abused its investigative authority and destroyed people's lives."
Black sued the committee and Comer on Sept. 3, seeking to block those subpoenas. That lawsuit is pending in U.S. District Court in Washington.
"The subpoenas are invalid to the extent they exceed [the committee's] delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection to [its] legislative purpose," the suit says.
The civil complaint says the subpoenas issued by the panel "would also expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the Committee."
In their statement Wednesday, Black's lawyers said: "Our lawsuit shows the Committee and Chairman Comer abused their Congressional power and broke the law."
They also said that they believe a confidential ethics complaint they filed against Comer "will further show that Chairman Comer violated the rules of the House."
Black has not been charged with any wrongdoing in connection with his dealings with Epstein, who killed himself in 2019 after being charged with child sex trafficking.
But he stepped down as Apollo's CEO in March 2021, two months after the firm disclosed that Black had paid Epstein $158 million for tax and estate planning advice from 2012 through 2017.
Black, who has said Epstein's advice led to significant savings for him, knew at the time that Epstein had pleaded guilty in Florida state court in 2008 to two prostitution-related charges, among them soliciting prostitution from an underage girl.
"Mr. Black has repeatedly said that he feels terrible for Epstein's victims and that he regrets ever doing business with Epstein," Black's lawyers said Wednesday.
"He never abused a woman. He never was with an underage woman. He never engaged in sex trafficking. He never paid Epstein for access to women. He was never blackmailed by Epstein. Mr. Black had no knowledge of any of Epstein's heinous conduct. He never forced any woman to sign any NDA."

Mearsheimer: There’s no diplomatic way out of the Ukraine war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:46:28 UTC
05:46:28 KST

Mearsheimer: There’s no diplomatic way out of the Ukraine war
American political scientist John Mearsheimer has claimed that the Ukraine conflict can’t be resolved diplomatically because the two sides’ goals remain irreconcilable and it will ultimately be settled on the battlefield. 
 Mearsheimer made the remarks during a visit to Moscow in an interview with Fyodor Lukyanov, chairman of the Presidium of the Council on Foreign and Defense Policy and editor-in-chief of Russia in Global Affairs.
 Fyodor Lukyanov: John, if a time machine brought great diplomats like Metternich and Talleyrand into the present day, what would they do to stem the bloodshed and bring today’s conflicts to an end? Would they succeed?
John Mearsheimer: Well, they were definitely skilled diplomats. And if we talk about the Ukraine-Russia war, they would go to great lengths to try to solve that. But I think that they’d be unable to do it. I don’t think that war, the Ukraine war, can be settled diplomatically. I think it’s going to be settled on the battlefield.
Now you say to yourself, why do I think it can’t be settled diplomatically? It’s because Russia’s goals are unacceptable to Ukraine, and Ukraine’s goals are unacceptable to Russia. For example, Ukraine wants the territory that Russia has annexed returned to Ukraine.
It views the Donbass, Zaporozhye, and Kherson as sacred territory. And from Ukraine’s point of view, it’s completely unacceptable that Russia be allowed to annex that territory. Furthermore, Ukraine, given what’s happened, wants a security guarantee, either from NATO or from the United States, to protect it moving forward.
This is unacceptable to the Russians. Furthermore, it’s unacceptable to the Russians to give up the territory that they’ve now annexed. So how can you have a diplomatic agreement between the two sides when there are such stark differences? Ukraine is simply unwilling to give up those four oblasts and Crimea, which Russia has annexed.
And Russia is unwilling to allow Ukraine to have that territory back. Furthermore, Ukraine wants a security guarantee from the West. It wants to be part of NATO, which is understandable from Ukraine’s point of view. But Russia certainly doesn’t want Ukraine in NATO. That was the principal cause of this war to begin with. So you see that the Russians and the Ukrainians are directly at odds on key issues where they’re unwilling to compromise.
So the question is, how do you get a diplomatic solution? And the answer is, you don’t. And this one will be fought out on the battlefield. And the final solution will be determined by who wins the war.
Fyodor Lukyanov: All right, then what would victory actually look like? Would winning the war mean eliminating Ukraine as such?
John Mearsheimer: I don’t think that the Russians are going to eliminate Ukraine. I think that’s almost impossible. I think what the Russians are going to do is they’re going to take a substantial portion of Ukrainian territory. They already have taken probably about 20%, and I think they’ll ultimately try to take considerably more territory from Ukraine. But they will not conquer all of Ukraine.
Furthermore, Ukraine will be, when this war is over, a dysfunctional rump state. And the Russians will have a vested interest in making sure that Ukraine remains a dysfunctional rump state, so that it can’t join NATO, and so that it doesn’t present a threat to Russia. So I think what you’re going to get here at some point is a frozen conflict, not altogether unlike what you have in Korea.
The Ukrainians will never accept the idea that Russia has conquered all this territory. The Ukrainians and the [Western] Europeans, for that matter, will not accept the new status quo. They’ll want to go back to the borders, the pre-2014 borders.
And the Russians, of course, will want to make sure that doesn’t happen, because the Russians live in fear that Ukraine will become part of the West, and it will become a Western bulwark on Russia’s borders. So what you see is that once you get this frozen conflict, Russia will have a deep-seated interest in making sure that Ukraine remains a dysfunctional rump state.
This is one of the reasons I think the Russians are likely to try to take Odessa and to take the Black Sea coast away from Ukraine, because the Russians will see that as an important way of weakening Ukraine in the future. And again, Russia will have a vested interest in weakening Ukraine.
And from Ukraine’s point of view, it makes perfect sense to see Russia as an existential threat, to want to have help from the West to deal with Russia, and to want to get its sacred territory back. I fully understand how the Ukrainians think, but that’s unacceptable to the Russians. So if you have these two parties to a conflict, one, the Russians, and two, the Ukrainians assisted by the Europeans, who have irreconcilable differences, there’s no diplomatic way out.
Fyodor Lukyanov: Does it mean that all efforts made by the Trump administration, Kushner, Witkoff and others are just a waste of time?
John Mearsheimer: I think that’s basically correct. I mean, in the case of the Trump administration, I think that it’s important to emphasize that President Trump himself has the right instincts. He wants to settle the war, the Ukraine war, and he wants to establish good relations between the United States and Russia. There’s no question that his instincts are right on this issue.
But there are two problems. One is the structural problem that I just described to you, the fact that the warring parties have irreconcilable goals. That’s point number one. And point number two is that President Trump is an inept or poor negotiator. He views himself as somebody who is brilliant at cutting deals, and he can easily shut down the Ukraine-Russia conflict in his own mind.
But exactly the opposite is true. He’s a ham-fisted, inept diplomat, and he hasn’t even come close to shutting down this war as a result of his ineptitude.
Fyodor Lukyanov: We have just marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks. Looking back a quarter of a century later, how would you assess their significance from the perspective of great-power politics?
John Mearsheimer: Well, 9-11 has nothing to do with great power politics. It’s just very important to understand that. 9-11 took place during the unipolar moment, when the United States was the only great power on the planet, and there was no great power politics, because you didn’t have rival great powers that could compete with each other.
And what happened with regard to 9-11 is that a small group called Al-Qaeda, which hated US Middle East policies, found a way to attack the United States and cause serious damage, and then led the United States to launch the global war on terror, which led to a number of the forever wars that we became involved in, especially Afghanistan and Iraq. And both these wars were disasters. Our response to 9-11 was badly mistaken. There was no need to launch a global war on terror. We just got ourselves into even more trouble.
But it had nothing to do with great power politics.
Fyodor Lukyanov: Could that moment be seen as the beginning of the end of the unipolar world, as some argue?
John Mearsheimer: I think that you can make that argument. I think that the 1990s were the heyday of the unipolar moment. But Russia was in terrible shape during the 1990s. And remember, Putin comes into power in roughly 2000, right? The end of ‘99, Putin comes into power. And I believe Putin resurrects the Russians from the dead.
But during the 1990s, Russia was badly weakened. And China hadn’t grown significantly by 2001. In fact, it’s not until 2001 that China joins the WTO. And when China joins the WTO, its economic growth really takes off.
So I think you can see that throughout the 1990s, up to around 2001, 2002, the United States is an incredibly powerful country. And the unipolar moment, except for what happened on 9-11, looks like it’s going very well. But after 9-11, things tend to go downhill pretty quickly. And I think the most important event here is the 2008 financial crisis, which hurt the United States badly. And then by about 2017, the Russians had come back from the dead, and I think Putin had created a situation here in Russia where Russia was once again a great power, by about 2017. And at the same time, China was also a great power in roughly 2017. So it’s around 2017 that you transition away from unipolarity to multipolarity.
And that’s a fundamental change that has drastically altered international politics. The United States was much freer to intervene around the world during the unipolar moment because there were no great power competitors, and it was free to get itself into all sorts of trouble in places like Afghanistan and in Iraq.
But then came multipolarity, and now the United States has to worry above all else about rival great powers.
Fyodor Lukyanov: Why do you single out 2017? As far as I can see, nothing particularly significant happened that year. In 2014, there was Crimea; in 2015, Syria. So why 2017?
John Mearsheimer: Well, what I’m concerned about is the balance of power. And the question is, when you look at Russia in the 1990s and in the very early 2000s, it has hardly any meaningful military power. Its military has really been wrecked. And what you see around 2015, 2016, 2017, is that the Russian military is much more effective than it had been in the previous decade and a half.
And I think this is largely the doing of Putin. I think Putin went to great lengths to help restore the Russian economy. And as the Russian economy began to flourish, the Russians were able to translate a lot of that economic might into military might.
So, by about 2016-2017, most assessments from places like the RAND Corporation about the Russian military say that Russian military power is now quite formidable. Obviously, the Russians in 2017 were not as powerful as the Soviet Union was at any point during the Cold War.
But the Russian military by 2017, and this of course is true of the Chinese military as well, looks like a quite formidable instrument. See, my argument is if you’re going to talk about going from unipolarity to multipolarity, you’re basically asking yourself the question, when do countries like China and Russia become great powers?
And for me, a great power is a country that has sufficient military power to put up a good fight against the most powerful state in the system. And of course, this is the United States. And again, I think by 2017, most security analysts in the United States believe that the Russian military was a quite formidable instrument and was quite well positioned to put up a serious fight against the United States.
And given that military power, the restoration of military power in Russia, I think that was the basis that people used to make the case that Russia was once again a great power. And just to say one more thing on this, I think everybody understood that Russia was and still is today the weakest of the three great powers.
I think the United States remains the most powerful state on the planet. I think the Chinese are now a close second. And I think there is a danger moving forward that China could overtake the United States.
And I think the Americans or most American foreign policy elites or the American foreign policy elite is very worried about that possibility. So China, in a very important way, is the real peer competitor, not Russia.
But Russia is still a great power, I think that everyone recognizes that. And I think that’s why the United States cares so much about the Ukraine war. And I think the reason that President Trump is interested in stopping or ending the Ukraine war and having good relations between Russia and the United States is because Trump understands that Russia is a great power.
And from an American point of view, it would make much more sense for the United States to be allied with Russia against China, or at least have Russia neutral, rather than create a situation where we have, in effect, driven the Russians into the arms of the Chinese.
I mean, if you think about living in a multipolar world where there are three great powers, if you’re the United States and this is China, you want Russia on your side of the ledger. But instead, because of our foolish policies regarding Ukraine, we’ve driven the Russians into the arms of the Chinese.
And again, I think Trump’s basic instincts about the importance of settling the Ukraine war and getting Russia on good terms with the United States is driven in good part by his insight or his belief that China is the real threat for the United States.

Russia’s veterinary watchdog finds live pseudorabies virus in a dog vaccine batch linked to mass deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:38:44 UTC
05:38:44 KST

Russia’s veterinary watchdog finds live pseudorabies virus in a dog vaccine batch linked to mass deaths
Russia’s federal veterinary watchdog, Rosselkhoznadzor, detected live Aujeszky’s disease virus in samples from batch No. 20 of the Multikan-8 vaccine, according to TASS.
The samples were collected in Russia’s Yaroslavl region. “This confirms a causal link between the mass deaths of dogs and their vaccination with Multikan-8 from batch No. 20, which was contaminated with an extraneous virus fatal to dogs,” Rosselkhoznadzor said in a statement.
Aujeszky’s disease, also known as pseudorabies, is an acute viral disease that affects the central nervous system in domestic and wild animals and is fatal in most cases.
In mid-August, dog owners began reporting in large numbers that their pets had died after receiving the Multikan-8 vaccine. The first reports came from the Yaroslavl region. The vaccine’s manufacturer, Vetbiokhim, recalled four batches. Rosselkhoznadzor ordered that batch No. 20, comprising 60,000 doses, be removed from circulation and destroyed. Vetbiokhim prepared settlement agreements with the affected owners. The company did not acknowledge a link between the dogs’ deaths and the vaccine but offered compensation to the owners of dogs that died.

Netanyahu steps up threats against directors of Gaza documentary NAZA
- Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu vowed to pass laws to revoke citizenship and increase defamation damages against those who defame Israeli soldiers, targeting the directors of the Gaza documentary NAZA.
- The documentary NAZA alleges that Israeli military routinely accepted mass civilian deaths in Gaza, sparking backlash and potential legal action amid Israel’s charged political climate before the Oct 27 elections.
- Netanyahu cited NAZA and other incidents to justify the bills, highlighting a tough stance on criticism of soldiers, while Gaza health authorities report over 73,000 Palestinian civilian deaths since the 2023 conflict began.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed on Sept 16 to pass a law to revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames Israel’s soldiers, his latest threat against the Israeli directors of NAZA, a documentary about soldiers’ killing of Gaza civilians.
Directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, NAZA alleges that mass civilian deaths were routinely built into Israeli targeting decisions in Gaza, something Netanyahu and the military reject.
The film, which won a major prize at the Venice Film Festival on Sept 12, takes its title from an Israeli military term for expected “collateral casualties” and is built around anonymous interviews with intelligence officers and soldiers.
It has drawn a backlash in Israel, with the military examining potential legal action against those involved in it. But it has also played into the charged political atmosphere ahead of Israel’s Oct 27 election, which public opinion polls show Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition could lose.
On Sept 15, Netanyahu accused some of his election rivals of failing to take a tough stand against the documentary, saying this made them unfit for office. And on Sept 16, he pledged to advance two Bills that he said aimed at addressing the “immense damage” done to Israeli soldiers.
“The first, to revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames (Israeli) soldiers, and the second to hit them in their pockets and increase the statutory damages for defamation they can be sued for by 20 times,” Netanyahu said in a social media video.
“We will hit them both in their pockets and in their citizenship, as their place is not with us.”
Netanyahu cited three incidents in proposing the Bills: “the recent film NAZA which portrayed (Israeli) officers and soldiers as war criminals”; 2025 remarks by left-wing ex-general turned politician Yair Golan that “a sane country does not kill children as a hobby”; and a military legal officer’s 2024 leak of a video showing soldiers abusing a Gaza detainee.
Reuters could not immediately reach the NAZA filmmakers for comment.
In 2022, Israel’s Supreme Court upheld a law that permits stripping citizenship from Israelis who carry out actions that constitute a breach of trust against the state. Any new legislation would likely face similar court challenges.
The NAZA filmmakers say they believe it is important that Israelis watch the documentary and grapple with the narrative it presents.
Gaza health authorities say more than 73,000 Palestinians, most of them civilians, have been killed in Israel’s military campaign that has left much of Gaza in ruins.
The war was triggered by Hamas’ Oct 7, 2023, attack on Israel which killed 1,200 people, most of them civilians, according to Israeli tallies. REUTERS

US stocks end midweek lower as Fed raises rates for first time in over 3 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:36:10 UTC
05:36:10 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
US stocks closed mostly lower on Wednesday after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years and Chair Kevin Warsh warned that inflation remained persistently high.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 631.33 points, or 1.21%, to 51,461.78.
The S&P 500 declined 33.92 points, or 0.45%, to 7,551.81, while the Nasdaq Composite was nearly flat at 25,978.43.
The Fed unanimously increased its federal funds rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75%-4%, marking its first rate hike since July 2023. Policymakers also projected one additional quarter-point increase this year.
Equities initially responded positively to the widely anticipated decision but reversed course as Warsh emphasized persistent price pressures during his post-meeting news conference.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long,” Warsh said, adding that inflation readings during the summer did not indicate a meaningful improvement in underlying trends.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note climbed back above the psychologically important 5% threshold, trading around 5.02%.
Banking shares led the decline amid concerns that further rate hikes and elevated borrowing costs could weaken lending and economic activity.
Shares of Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and Citigroup fell around 3%, while JPMorgan Chase lost around 1%.
Intel shares rose on reports that the US chipmaker was holding talks with South Korean memory producer SK Hynix about manufacturing semiconductors in the US, helping limit losses on the technology-heavy Nasdaq.
The US dollar index gained around 0.6% to 100.21, its highest level since late July.
Gold futures fell 0.6% to $4,266 per ounce, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude dropped 3.7% to $101.87 per barrel.
European stocks close higher
European stock markets, meanwhile, ended on Wednesday higher, led by gains in technology shares ahead of the Fed’s policy announcement.
The STOXX Europe 600 index rose 0.46% to 637.09 points.
Britain’s FTSE 100 advanced 0.28% to 10,688.47, Germany’s DAX gained 0.53% to 25,537.75 and France’s CAC 40 increased 0.62% to 8,140.59.
Italy’s FTSE MIB recorded the strongest gain among the major European indices, rising 0.8% to 51,969.12, while Spain's IBEX 35 also gained 0.41% to end at 19,635.80.

film stills leave the screen and become elaborate makeup compositions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:35:59 UTC
05:35:59 KST

Emerald Vysions turns the face into a cinematic stage
For Toronto-based makeup artist Emerald Vysions, the face becomes a small-scale stage for images, emotions, and cinematic memories. Working on her own face, the artist reinterprets film stills through saturated pigments, graphic lines, metallic textures, rhinestones, feathers, and highly constructed lashes. Vysions extracts the visual language of movie scenes and compresses it into eye looks that can be read in a single glance.
A film normally exists at a distance, projected onto a screen, framed by a rectangle, and experienced through the collective act of watching. Emerald Vysions relocates fragments of that spectacle onto the body. The screen becomes the eyelid; production design becomes color and texture; costume can become an arrangement of rhinestones or an exaggerated lash.
Pierrot le Fou (1965) | all images by Emerald Vysions
from screen to skin
Cinema is one of the starting points for Emerald Vysions, but her makeup does not try to reproduce a film scene exactly. The artist picks apart what makes an image stick: a particular color combination, a costume detail, the shape of a gesture, or the mood of a scene. These elements reappear across the face as pigment, crystals, unusual lashes, painted shapes and other small details.
Seen alongside the film stills that inspire them, the difference in scale is striking. A whole scene, its actors, costumes, interiors and lighting, is reduced to the area around the eyes.
One example draws on the rich reds and feathers of Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953), translating the excess of the original scene into red pigment, jewels and pale feathered lashes. Other looks pick up on the strong blues, yellows, greens and pinks of their respective references. Vysions seems to pull individual details out of the scenes and give those details a new life.
Vysions’ work lives in the gap between the original image and what she does with it. The film still gives her a starting point, but the makeup does not always follow it literally. A color might become more intense, a detail might be enlarged, or something almost incidental in the original scene can become the focus of the makeup, resulting in something familiar without being immediately legible. You recognize the mood before you recognize the reference.

Trump's Kennedy Center closure is 'unlawful,' Rep. Beatty tells judge in emergency hearing request
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:32:54 UTC
05:32:54 KST

Rep. Joyce Beatty asked a judge Wednesday to hold an emergency hearing on what the Ohio Democrat called the "unlawful" closure of the Kennedy Center by President Donald Trump and the performing arts facility's board of trustees.
Beatty's motion says the closure is in "apparent violation" of a prior order from Judge Christopher Cooper in U.S. District Court in Washington.
Cooper later Wednesday ordered Trump and the board to respond to Beatty's request by Thursday morning.
"The Court will schedule a prompt hearing if necessary after reviewing the response," Cooper said in his order.
Beatty's request came a day after the board, of which she is an ex officio member, voted to close the Kennedy Center for renovations. Trump later Tuesday said it would close "immediately."
Trump also said planned renovations and reconstruction of the Washington center would not begin until a federal appeals court or the Supreme Court rules that his name can be included in the facility's official name.
A staff member for a law firm representing Beatty visited the center Wednesday morning and was barred from entering, according to the congresswoman's motion. The staffer "was informed by several security staff members that the building is currently closed to the public," the motion said.
"In addition, the staff member was informed that construction is beginning on the interior of the building and that the public is completely barred from accessing the facility for 'safety reasons,'" the filing said.
"Closing the Kennedy Center without Judge Cooper's approval appears to directly violate his order. This is an assault on the rule of law," Beatty's lawyers, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, said in a statement.
"The board cannot simply ignore Judge Cooper's rulings whenever it suits them. In this country, no one — including the president — is above the law," the attorneys said.
The lawyers pointed to a May ruling by Cooper in which he ordered that Trump's name be removed from the center and which enjoined the board from shuttering the center "until the Board approves any closure consistent with" Cooper's ruling "and the Court issues a further Order dissolving or modifying this preliminary injunction."
The Kennedy Center's board, which Trump named himself to head, voted in December to rename the center, which honors the late President John F. Kennedy. The facility then became known as the Trump Kennedy Center, though Congress never formally changed its name.
Beatty filed a lawsuit in December seeking to reverse the board's action. Cooper ordered in May that Trump's name be stripped off.
"Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it," Cooper wrote in his ruling.
The Department of Justice, which represents Trump and the board in the case, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The DOJ is appealing a decision by Cooper issued on Tuesday that barred the board from adding Trump's name back to the building and naming the grounds of the center after him.
The board in an Aug. 13 resolution said it intended "to recognize and honor President Trump's future existential and unprecedented contributions to the survival of the Center."
The board planned to inscribe the words "renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump" underneath the words that currently say, "The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts."
The board also said it would name the center's physical grounds "The President Donald J. Trump Plaza."
Cooper, in his order Tuesday, said, "Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing."
""The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted," the judge said.

Daly Cherry-Evans has arrived at the end of forever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:32:41 UTC
05:32:41 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
analysis
Ahead of his last NRL games, Daly Cherry-Evans has finally reached the end of forever
Years ago, when Daly Cherry-Evans was merely in his early 30s, he'd say that he was going to play forever and he was only ever half-joking.
Every time he'd be asked about his future, be it at the beginning of a season or at the end, he'd grin widely and assure whoever wanted to know that he, in fact, would never, ever stop.
Most of the time it felt like a gag, a way for one of the slickest operators in the NRL to disarm the inquiry and Cherry-Evans follow with all the usual patter we hear from the greybeards — that he'd play as long as his body held up or as long as he was still enjoying it.
Plenty say that but Cherry-Evans has lived it. He lived it long enough that he reached the end of the "lifetime" deal he once signed with Manly, long enough that younger men than him succumbed to the ravages of age and long enough that maybe the joke was on us the whole time for not believing him in the first place.
It is only now, a few months before he turns 38 years old, that Cherry-Evans has finally arrived at the end of forever.
Win or lose, the Sydney Roosters sudden-death semifinal against Cronulla on Saturday is the beginning of the last days, the ones that seemed like they would never arrive.
A defeat will mark Cherry-Evans's final NRL match before he links with Hull FC in Super League next year where's he's odds on to, at least once, play with or against someone a full two decades younger than him.
A win will push the Roosters into a preliminary final against the Dolphins and keep the dream of a farewell premiership alive.
If the Tricolours do manage to go all the way, Cherry-Evans will break Lote Tuqiri's record for the longest gap between grand final wins by one season.
That premiership back in 2011 is still definitional to Cherry-Evans and what he's been for all this time.
In becoming the first rookie halfback to win a grand final since 1978 and because he was one of Manly's best through the finals and on the big day in their win over the Warriors, Cherry-Evans was able to transcend many of the slings and arrows launched during the rise of franchise playmakers.
Instead of the typical hero journey most halfbacks endure, with its peaks and valleys and rises and falls, Cherry-Evans's success as a rookie gave him a kind of instant validation.
There was never any talk of what he might be one day once he matures, or what he would eventually become once he developed this part of his game or not.
There was no debate whether he would one day be enough to lead a team to glory because he had already done it. It was instant proof of concept.
So many of young halfbacks are defined by their future, the possibility of what they might be, but ever since that first season, Cherry-Evans has instead existed in a blissful and seemingly eternal present.
His game has changed in subtle ways since that first year with Manly but through a bird's-eye view the similarities of his 16-year career is remarkable.
This season was the 15th of those years where he managed at least 20 games and he has as many try assists this year at age 37 as he did the year he turned 25.
Old halves are supposed to run less but his return in that part of his game this year (51 run metres per game and five line breaks from 24 matches) is not miles away from his return as a rookie (57 per game and 11 line breaks from 27 matches).
They're meant to be worse at defending as well, but this year Cherry-Evans has had the third-best tackle efficiency of his career.
That's not to say there hasn't been some ups and downs for Cherry-Evans through his long career, but because of where he started and how long he's been there it was always easy to ride out the downs because, even as he reached his mid-30s, he had more time.
A bad option or a poor game or a sprayed kick, as rare as they were, or even a season where his team didn't make the finals were easier to accept because there was always more to come. He could always come back to what he had always been.
The end of that reality was put into stark relief in Sunday's qualifying final loss to Penrith even as, at the end of all things, Cherry-Evans can absolutely still cut it in a game of such quality and intensity.
It was only a month ago that he scored both tries in a 12-6 Tricolours win over the Panthers that remains their best performance of the season.
This time, with Sam Walker sidelined, Cherry-Evans slotted back into halfback and taken the lion's share of the kicking game and his field position chess match with Brian To'o as he hunted a 40/20 in the second half was a highlight.
In the end, two kicks Cherry-Evans got wrong cost the Roosters badly.
First it was a screwball torpedo of a thing with ten minutes left that he launched from his own 40 metre line that found the grass and seemed perfect until it took one bounce too many and trickled dead.
It was unfortunate and nothing more. Not even someone as experienced as Cherry-Evans, who will likely bring up his 450th first class game next year, can predict how a ball bounces.
Penrith rolled up the field on the seven-tackle set and took the lead through a Nathan Cleary one-pointer but it was not necessarily a death blow given Cherry-Evans is the modern day field goal king.
He's kicked 31 of them in his career, the most of anyone in the NRL era.
He's kicked them to cap off big wins and to break stalemates at the last second — seven of them came in golden point extra time and his most recent match-winner was just a few weeks back against Newcastle.
He's kicked them off both feet, in howling gales and monsoonal rain.
He's never met a way he couldn't do it and he's met all the ways it can be done.
But this time his only attempt, from inside 20 metres and right in front, was a shank the likes of which we've rarely seen during his career.
Even the best can get it wrong, but both moments brought into stark relief just how things have changed for Cherry-Evans.
Roosters coach Trent Robinson was circumspect about it after the match, pointing out that Cherry-Evans had iced games before for the Roosters and would do so again.
The former is a fact but the latter is closer to a prediction than a guarantee.
There might still be a next week for Cherry-Evans, but it only might be. There will not be a next year.
On Saturday night against Cronulla, with Walker still out, Cherry-Evans must become the system once again.
He will play sharp and smart, like he always does, like he always has, and maybe it will be enough to earn another day.
But after seeming ageless for so long, he is running out of tomorrows. He has reached the end of forever and after seeming immune to time for so long it is coming for him at last.
The story might not have its final chapter against the Sharks or the Dolphins, but the last page is nigh and the final days of Daly Cherry-Evans in the NRL are a reminder of how the present, after seeming fixed for so long, becomes history wholesale — not at all and then all at once.

Zelensky Signs Law Targeting Scam Call Centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:31:14 UTC
05:31:14 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky signed the law that introduces criminal liability for the organizers and participants of scam call centers, after Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, approved tougher penalties for electronic fraud earlier on Wednesday.
In his evening address, Zelensky said the Verkhovna Rada had passed the legislation alongside other bills linked to Ukraine’s commitments to international partners. The measures are needed to help close the state-budget deficit Ukraine is currently facing and, by doing so, sustain Ukraine’s resilience during the fifth winter of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I just signed this law. It is important that there is a vote for laws that are in Ukraine’s obligations to partners,” Zelensky said, expressing gratitude towards the parliament for today’s “effective vote.”
“It is important that they supported criminal liability for fraudulent call centers,” he continued.
The measure comes amid Ukraine’s wider effort to address corruption and improve criminal law as it works towards its EU accession.
New penalties – up to 12 years in prison
The decision No. 10190, newly adopted Wednesday morning, adds a separate provision to Ukraine’s Criminal Code covering organized groups that use electronic communications to obtain property or property rights through deception.
It applies to groups of at least three people who act according to a coordinated plan and divide tasks among members. The offenses may include acquiring, storing, processing or using personal data, banking information, authentication codes or other payment details to facilitate fraud.
Zelensky’s Former Comedy Studio Hit in Russian Strike – But It’s the Symbolism Moscow Is After
Under the legislation, creating or leading such groups can carry a prison term of seven to 12 years, along with confiscation of property if convicted.
Participants who knowingly take part in the group may face five to 10 years in prison, with or without asset confiscation.
Additionally, recruiting others into such networks may carry a sentence of three to five years, rising to five to 10 years for repeat offenses.
At least 313 lawmakers voted to support the decision, which came after an alleged protection scheme for the scam centers that involved Ruslan Kravchenko, Ukraine’s Prosecutor General.
According to Ukraine’s anti-graft agencies; National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), Kravchenko allegedly protected the scam centers and helped launder millions in wealth, acquiring high-end real estate, expensive vehicles, and other luxury assets.
In the wake of the incident, Kravchenko resigned from his post.
He later left the country in haste and published a video message announcing notices of suspicion against officials from anti-graft agencies, though they were never officially served.
On Tuesday, Sept. 15, Verkhovna Rada dismissed Kravchenko.
Seven bills awaiting their first reading
Separately on Tuesday, Zelensky said lawmakers were also considering seven bills tied to Ukraine’s obligations to international partners, most of which were still awaiting their first reading.
“Some of these measures may be difficult, unpleasant, and unpopular,” Zelensky said, noting that Ukraine must adopt them regardless, as Kyiv is facing a defense funding shortfall of about $27 billion (€23 billion).

Putin issues historic call ahead of Russian elections
President Vladimir Putin has called on Russians to make their voice heard by casting ballots in the upcoming parliamentary elections. The nation is to elect a new State Duma in what the president described as a pivotal vote that will “shape our future.”
The upcoming elections are the first parliamentary vote that Russia will hold during the continued military campaign against Kiev. In 2024, the nation held presidential elections amid the ongoing hostilities, with Putin securing a landslide victory by gaining 88% of the vote.
“We know what Russia is fighting for,” the president said in the address published by the Kremlin on Wednesday. “Your choice and your will shall once again show that millions of people stand behind our fighters; that we are a united people, bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for the Motherland; and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us,” Putin said.
“I urge you to exercise your constitutional right and make a considered, responsible decision, so that the election results demonstrate the maturity and resilience of Russian society. This will be our shared response to those who seek to weaken Russia, hold back its development, and deprive us of our sovereignty and our right to determine our own destiny.”
The 2026 parliamentary elections will take place September 18-20, with a total of ten parties contending for 450 seats in the lower house of the Russian parliament.
In July, Putin accused Kiev of seeking to destabilize Russian society through “terrorist attacks” targeting civilian and energy infrastructure. ZHA rethinks benghazi’s urban growth through a digital planning hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:20:33 UTC
05:20:33 KST

BENGHAZI 2050 BUILDS AN ADAPTABLE FRAMEWORK FOR THE CITY
Benghazi, the historic port city on Libya’s Mediterranean coast, is looking toward 2050 with a new planning framework developed by a consortium including A&O TEC, Prior+Partners, Zaha Hadid Architects (ZHA), Homa, Buro Happold, Systematica and Fichtner. Conceived amid a period of urban growth, infrastructure investment and renewal, Benghazi 2050: Next Generation City Plan sets out to coordinate future development while reconnecting the city with its waterfront, historic center and expanding neighborhoods. Rather than defining a single architectural intervention, the proposal combines a spatial vision with a digital platform intended to guide projects across the metropolitan area over the coming decades.
The Vision and Spatial Strategy begins with an analysis of Benghazi’s existing character and collective memory, proposing what the team describes as an adaptable framework based on connection rather than fragmentation and restoration rather than demolition. Public transport and pedestrian routes would link the historic core and shoreline with residential neighborhoods and metropolitan centers, while new employment and knowledge districts accommodate future growth. Zones of nature are also integrated into the strategy to support water management and ecological diversity, allowing urban expansion to develop alongside environmental systems rather than independently from them.
benghazi 2050 maps the city’s long-term growth | all images courtesy of ZHA
DIGITAL DATA FORMS THE FOUNDATION OF A CITYWIDE TWIN
At the center of the proposal is the Benghazi 2050 Digital Planning Hub, conceived as a shared evidence base for understanding the city and testing its future development. The platform brings together information on existing urban, socioeconomic, environmental and infrastructural conditions within a common spatial interface. Its datasets range from Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and three-dimensional urban models to population and land-use information, transport networks, infrastructure, environmental resilience studies, ongoing developments and future planning scenarios.
This accumulated information provides the foundation for a dynamic digital twin of Benghazi. As new data is added, the system is intended to evolve alongside the city, allowing proposals to be considered in relation to their broader urban context rather than as isolated developments. In this sense, the Digital Planning Hub extends the spatial strategy beyond the format of a conventional static plan, creating what the team describes as a living environment for collaboration between authorities, local communities, planners, designers and investors.
the proposal coordinates growth across the metropolitan area
ZHA SHAPES THE SPATIAL VISION AND DIGITAL PLATFORM
The multidisciplinary consortium divides the project across different layers of urban research and design. Prior+Partners leads regional and urban planning, economic strategy and governance; Homa focuses on land use, built form and socioeconomic strategy; Systematica develops transport and mobility; Buro Happold addresses the natural environment and utilities; and Fichtner contributes energy and infrastructure expertise. ZHA is responsible for the spatial vision and scenario design, while also leading the interface design and technology integration of the Digital Planning Hub. Web services, deployment and hosting are developed by Silicon Shore.
Together, these elements frame Benghazi 2050 not as a finished image of the city, but as a system through which its transformation can continue to be measured, evaluated and adjusted. The concept proposal brings baseline research, growth scenarios, spatial planning and computational tools into a single process intended to connect Benghazi’s identity with its long-term development. The Vision and Digital Planning Hub were presented as part of the Next Generation City Plan at the Global Competitive Urban Planning Initiative – Benghazi, held from September 6–8, 2026.

US House votes for a third time to end the Iran war as conflict drags on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:20:17 UTC
05:20:17 KST

For a third time, the US House has voted to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution that would halt President Donald Trump’s ability to continue military action without congressional approval.
The vote took place late Tuesday, and for a third time, the US House voted to end the war in Iran, attempting to cut President Donald Trump's ability to continue military action.
The roll call, 220-204, was similar to earlier efforts this summer, with a few more Republicans joining all Democrats voting to bring an end to the conflict. None of the resolutions have made it to the president’s desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto the measure.
"Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?" said Democrat Representative Seth Moulton, who served as a Marine during the Iraq War and pushed the resolution forward.
He said it’s time for Congress to "actually ask tough questions, as the Constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration."
Republican Representative Brian Mast of Florida, the chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat.
Mast said Trump is against "forever wars, and that is what he is ending" — the decades of hostilities from Iran.
"They are a continuous ongoing threat to the United States," Mast said. "Enough is enough."
Last war powers vote before midterms
The action is likely the last House vote on the Iran war ahead of the midterm elections, where the conflict overseas is playing a substantial role in the political campaigns. The war that Trump launched on 28 February has dragged on, with on-again, off-again deadly missile strikes being exchanged and causing havoc in the region for nearly seven months.
Lawmakers are heading home at the end of the week to campaign nearly full-time, with less than 50 days to go before the elections that will determine control of Congress as Democrats try to wrest power from Republicans.
Voters are confronting high prices, particularly for gas at the pumps, as the conflict disrupts the flow of oil resources through the vital Strait of Hormuz.
The Congressional Budget Office said Tuesday that the war has cost more than $38 billion (€33 billion), as of 1 August, and is projected to be costing between $2 billion (€1.74 billion) and $3 billion (€2.62 billion) monthly, depending on the intensity of the fighting. The budget office projected inflation will be 0.5 percentage points higher than expected heading into 2027 due to the war.
Trump himself had promised not to involve the US in foreign wars when he won a second term in the White House, and his actions against Iran are weighing on the Republican Party that controls the House and Senate. Most Americans say the war in Iran has not been worth fighting, according to an AP-NORC poll in July.
In the previous House actions, four Republicans voted to halt the war in Iran, but that number rose to seven in Tuesday’s war powers vote, including GOP lawmakers from battleground Iowa, Representative Zachary Nunn and Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, and retiring Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina.
They joined GOP Representatives Tom Barrett of Michigan, Warren Davidson of Ohio, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky voting in favor of the war powers resolution, with all Democrats.
War powers put to the test
Congress has tried repeatedly to alter the trajectory of the war against Iran, but efforts to limit the Trump administration’s military action remain a long shot so long as the president is able to fend off or veto the measures.
The House first approved a war powers resolution in June, and followed up with another one in July, all seeking to halt US action in Iran. The Senate on its 10th try also approved a war powers resolution to end the conflict, but GOP senators quickly reversed course the next day after Trump berated them during a closed-door lunch.
While the Constitution gives Congress the authority to declare war, it also gives the president authority as the commander in chief to engage in some military actions. The War Powers Act, created in the aftermath of the Vietnam conflict, sought to put a more specific time limit on the president’s power, requiring congressional approval for sustained military actions after 60 or 90 days.
House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledged at a press conference Tuesday the need to bring gas prices down.
But the Republican speaker said he believes the Iran conflict is entering a "new phase" as allies step up to help stabilize the region. When that happens, he said, "you’re going to see, as the president said, anytime gas prices will go down again, the cost of groceries will as well."
Johnson said Trump expects the shift after the election, and the speaker added, "I’d love it to happen today."

Russia Exploited Migrants and Refugees for Ukraine War Recruitment, Amnesty International Reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:13:08 UTC
05:13:08 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Exploited Migrants and Refugees for Ukraine War Recruitment, Amnesty International Reports
Russia has used deceptive, coercive, and exploitative practices to recruit foreign nationals into its armed forces and send them to fight in Ukraine, a pattern that in many cases amounts to human trafficking.
This was reported by Amnesty International in a briefing published on its official website on September 10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The level of exploitation and coercion involved led us to conclude that in many cases this amounts to human trafficking," Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International's Secretary General, stated, adding that the practice fits the definition set out in the UN's Palermo Protocol.
The Palermo Protocol is the UN's 2000 anti-trafficking treaty and the source of the first internationally agreed definition of human trafficking. It sets out a three-part test: an act of recruitment or transport carried out through coercion, fraud, or abuse of vulnerability for the purpose of exploitation.
Under its terms, a victim's consent is void once deception or coercion is used, which is why signed contracts do not shield the recruitment from the trafficking label.
Amnesty International's research documented how recruiters lured individuals into the Russian Armed Forces under false pretenses and exploited the precarious circumstances of migrants and refugees already inside Russia. Those targeted came primarily from low-income countries in the Global South .
The briefing drew on interviews conducted at two Ukrainian prisoner-of-war camps between 2024 and 2026, with individuals from Brazil, Colombia, Cuba, Egypt, Sierra Leone, Sri Lanka, Somalia, and South Africa.
Amnesty International also gathered testimony from foreign nationals currently serving with Russian forces, their families, lawyers, and journalists.
According to the organization, recruiters typically presented military service as a non-combat role, such as work in a military kitchen or as a driver far from the front.
Two Sri Lankan men believed they had been hired as cooks but were sent to the front lines and captured within weeks. "The scale of fighting is unimaginable. You do not see Ukrainian soldiers, only drones. Drones everywhere," one recounted.
Amnesty International reported that misleading online job advertisements and local agents deceived recruits in their home countries with false promises of civilian work and expedited Russian citizenship.
A South African man who applied online for a driving job in Poland was instructed to fly to Moscow, where his documents were seized. "He was told that he would not be going to Poland and that he was becoming a soldier," his wife told the organization.
The briefing detailed severe restrictions imposed once contracts were signed. Recruits from Brazil and Sri Lanka described having passports and mobile phones confiscated before deployment.
Pedro, a Brazilian IT professional recruited under the pretext of a well-paid tech job, recounted asking his commander to leave and being told, "If you try to escape, you will either go to jail or we will kill you."
Amnesty International noted that most enlistees were deployed to active combat zones after roughly two weeks of training, with little regard for combat readiness.
The organization emphasized that recruiters weaponized irregular immigration status and pending criminal charges, presenting enlistment as an alternative to detention and deportation.
Amnesty International called on Russia to end the abusive practices immediately and urged states whose nationals are at risk to issue public warnings and pursue accountability.
The organization also directed a series of recommendations to Ukrainian authorities regarding third-country nationals held as prisoners of war.
Previous reports indicated that by mid-August 2026, at least 2,982 recruits from 37 African countries had been documented, roughly 486 of whom had been killed, with Kenya, Egypt, Ghana, and Nigeria among the largest sources.
Foreign nationals from more than 40 countries have since been identified in Russian ranks, many funneled in through deception after traveling abroad in search of civilian work.

Syria abolishes al-Assad-era ‘terrorism’ court as Kurdish tensions flare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:08:50 UTC
05:08:50 KST

Syria abolishes al-Assad-era ‘terrorism’ court as Kurdish tensions flare
Discontent is testing President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s ability to unify a country emerging from 14 years of conflict.
Syria’s parliament has voted to abolish an al-Assad-era “terrorism” court and nullify the legal effects of its rulings, in one of the first significant legislative moves by the country’s new assembly.
The vote on Wednesday formalised the abolition of the court, which Syria’s new authorities had already treated as defunct, state-run Al-Ekhbariya TV reported.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Explosion at depot storing weapons left from Syria war kills 14
- list 2 of 3Kurdish YPJ women fighters face exclusion from Syria’s new army
- list 3 of 3At least seven killed in fire at prison in northern Syria
The Counter-Terrorism Court, established in 2012, was used to prosecute thousands of Syrians for offences deemed “terrorism-related” under ousted former President Bashar al-Assad.
Wednesday’s vote came during the opening weeks of the first parliament formed since al-Assad was toppled. The chamber convened for the first time in July.
In June 2025, President Ahmed al-Sharaa issued a decree dismissing 67 judges who had served in what he described at the time as the “abolished Counter-Terrorism Court”.
Syria’s March 2025 constitutional declaration had also called for abolishing the effects of what it described as unjust rulings issued by the court, including returning confiscated property.
The United Nations Human Rights Committee said in 2024 that the 2012 law establishing the court failed to adequately provide key judicial guarantees and raised concerns over arbitrary detention, torture or ill-treatment, and the court’s independence.
The vote is among the assembly’s first major legislative decisions after it spent its initial sessions establishing its internal rules and committees.
The 53-year-long rule of the al-Assad family ended on December 8, 2024, after a lightning 11-day offensive that took Syria and the world by surprise. With it ended a brutal police state, notorious for its use of torture and disappearances.
Kurdish discontent amid government integration deal
Hundreds of oil tanker trucks were stranded in northeastern Syria’s Kurdish region on Wednesday after demonstrators blocked a major highway near the town of Tal Tamr in protest over rising fuel prices.
Discontent has been building in the Kurdish region amid a push to integrate a once-powerful Kurd-led armed force – the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) – into Syria’s army and bring them under the control of the central government.
The integration agreement with the SDF, minted in August, has been widely regarded as a victory for al-Sharaa’s government, but discontent is testing the president’s ability to unify a country emerging from 14 years of conflict.
Kurds, who made up about 10 percent of Syria’s population of 23 million before the civil war began in 2011, were long marginalised under the country’s al-Assad dynasty. During the war, they carved out a de facto autonomous zone in the northeast.
When northeast Syria – including its oilfields – was under the SDF’s control, fuel was heavily subsidised. After the central government took control, it removed those subsidies, leading to a price hike.
Syrian Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir is scheduled to be questioned in parliament on Thursday over the increase in fuel prices.
On Sunday, the government further hiked petrol prices by about 30 percent and diesel by 40 percent, citing rising global fuel prices due to the US-Israel war on Iran as well as repair work at the Baniyas refinery on the country’s coast.
Demonstrators shut down the M4 highway near the town of Tal Tamr, blocking trucks bringing oil from the Qamishli and Rmeilan oilfields, and announced that they would only reopen the route if the price increases were reversed.
Additionally, students in the cities of Qamishli and Hasakah staged mass protests in recent weeks over a government decree that makes Kurdish an official language of instruction for the first time in Syrian history but only provides for three classes a week in the language. By contrast, Kurds had set up a school system teaching mostly in Kurdish.
With the new post-war government reasserting control over the northeast, Kurdish communities have been anxious about losing the rights they had under self-rule. Al-Sharaa has promised constitutional protection for Kurdish language and political rights.
In January, the integration deal reached between the central government in Damascus and the SDF halted weeks of fighting. While some Kurdish politicians hail the integration as a door for the Kurds to participate in building the new Syria and to demand their rights through the constitution, others consider the step a result of pressure from Turkiye and the United States and potentially harmful for Kurdish interests.

Saudi Arabia accuses Houthis of targeting Mecca, calls it a 'red line'
Saudi Arabia accused Yemen’s Houthis on Wednesday of launching an attack on the holy city of Mecca, which the Iran-backed rebels denied. Saudi Arabia, a US ally which has been the target of large-scale Houthi strikes since early September, declared Mecca a “red line” as it slid deeper into the new front of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia accused Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels of trying to attack Islam’s holiest city, as the region responded with condemnation Wednesday but no sign of military support. The kingdom, a key US ally, declared Mecca a “red line” as slid deeper into the new front of the Iran war.
With the world’s biggest oil exporter under fire from the rebels backed by the Saudis' regional adversary, the kingdom needs a safe outlet for its crude as well as military assistance. There's no clear path to either.
A crucial Saudi pipeline has been shut down, reportedly for weeks, after an attack by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. The Houthis have been targeting infrastructure in the kingdom and its shipping on the Red Sea, where they have seized several islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. And Iran is still targeting ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices remain above $100 a barrel.
The Houthis denied firing drones toward Mecca, about 1,100 kilometres (680 miles) from Yemen’s border. The Saudis said they intercepted and destroyed the drone before it entered the airspace over the birthplace of the Prophet Mohammed.
The attacks are the first test of a new defence pact among Saudi Arabia, NATO member Turkey and nuclear power Pakistan. But officials from Turkey and Pakistan told The Associated Press they have not received a Saudi request for support in response to the Houthis' escalation.

Criticism also came from the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, representing over 57 Muslim states, which said the attempt violates the “sanctity of holy sites”.

The La Liga president Javier Tebas criticised three Real Madrid players on Wednesday, including Kylian Mbappé, for not wearing a T-shirt properly in support of the people of Ceuta, a Spanish autonomous city in North Africa that has been hit by a migration crisis.
Mbappé, Vinícius Júnior and Ibrahima Konaté wore the commemorative T-shirt with the sleeves partially rolled up before Real Madrid's 3-2 victory over Elche in La Liga on Tuesday. The rest of the players wore it in the usual way.
In doing so, the three players partially hid the message "We are all Ceutans", referring to the inhabitants of this Spanish territory in North Africa. "We saw three players who decided not to put it on. Wearing it halfway is the same as not wearing it at all... it's bad, very bad," Tebas told reporters.
The initiative for the teams to wear these T-shirts came from a group of business leaders in the Valencian Community. Tebas explained that the proposal had been approved but not organised by La Liga, and stressed that "it is not a political act of any kind".

No 'political purpose'

Villarreal hosted Real Betis on Monday and both teams wore the T-shirts in support of Ceuta. Levante also wore them before their match on Sunday against Barcelona, although the Catalan side chose not to wear it.
The controversy comes against a backdrop of mounting tension in Ceuta following the mass arrival of migrants. Tens of thousands of people entered the city from Morocco on 30 and 31 July. Most returned to Morocco a couple of hours after they arrived, but several thousand remained in Ceuta.
Local residents have been staging protests on a regular basis while the migrants continue camping on the beaches and sleeping in the streets. Protesters accuse the Spanish government of abandoning a city overwhelmed by a humanitarian crisis.

The former Barcelona player described the gesture as an expression of social support for the city's residents, "regardless of their nationality".

Election results proclaimed in southern Philippines' majority-Muslim Bangsamoro region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:00:50 UTC
05:00:50 KST

Saadet Gokce
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Final results were declared Wednesday in the southern Philippines' majority-Muslim Bangsamoro Autonomous Region, following the region's first-ever parliamentary elections.
The Regional Board of Canvassers (RBOC) of the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) said 2,018,478 voters cast ballots, with an 84.34% turnout in Monday's elections, according to a statement from the Bangsamoro government.
The 80-member parliament consists of 40 regional parliamentary party representatives, 32 district representatives and eight sectoral representatives.
For the Regional Parliamentary Political Party (RPPP) seats, the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) secured 16 seats, followed by the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) with 15. The BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC) had eight and the Raayat Democratic Party secured one.
For district representative seats, the BFP won 15, UBJP nine, Serbisyong Inklusibo Alyansang Progresibo (SIAP) six, while the Progresibong Bangsamoro Party (PBP) and Al Ittihad-UKB won one each.
In the sectoral races, Yul Adelfo Olaya and Mary Ann Arnado won seats representing settler communities. Aida Silongan, Sulffy Abbas, Muhammad Nadzir Ebil and Marjanie Mimbantas-Macasalong represented the women, youth, ulama and traditional leaders sectors, respectively.
The Teduray and Lambangian communities selected Jo Glenna Jover and Leticio Datuwata, respectively, as their Non-Moro Indigenous People representatives under customary laws.
The BFP is led by Bangsamoro interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua, while the UBJP is headed by former interim Chief Minister Murad Ebrahim, who is also the leader of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.
Officials will assume office Oct. 30 and will elect the region’s chief minister.

"The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long," he told a press conference.
And Wednesday's rate hike may not be the last — the vast majority of Fed policymakers indicated that at least one more rate hike was likely necessary before the end of the year, according to their Summary of Economic Projections.
US households and businesses have been battered by years of higher-than-target inflation, and prices have surged in the wake of Trump's war on Iran, his signature tariff policies and the ongoing AI boom.
Trump has launched an unprecedented assault on the Fed's independence since taking office, attempting to fire a Fed Governor and launching a criminal probe against Warsh's predecessor in his quest for lower rates to spur economic activity.
The president's Republican Party faces a stern test in upcoming midterm elections, with rival Democrats seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress and economic issues front-and-centre for voters.
