How growing up in East Germany affected cognitive health in later life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:00:21 UTC
05:00:21 KST

Older adults who lived in socialist East Germany before the 1989 reunification show better cognitive health and slower mental decline today than their West German peers. This unexpected advantage seems linked to the former East German educational system, which featured longer compulsory schooling and widespread early childcare. The findings were recently published in the journal Research on Aging.
Following World War II, Germany was split into two distinct nations with opposing political and economic models. The German Democratic Republic in the East operated as a socialist state with a planned economy. The Federal Republic of Germany in the West developed as a capitalist, liberal democracy.
When the countries reunited in 1989, citizens merged into a single legal and economic system. This unique history provides researchers with a natural experiment to study how entirely different societal structures affect human development over a lifetime.
The contrast between East and West Germany represents a rare situation where culturally similar populations were separated by completely different modes of governance. The East German welfare state prioritized collective investments, aiming to build a highly productive workforce through extensive health and education services.
Previous research has consistently shown that East Germans suffered worse physical health and lower life expectancies compared to West Germans. These physical disparities are largely attributed to differences in health behaviors, economic development, and cardiovascular health.
Sociologist Ariane Bertogg at the University of Konstanz and gerontologist Jeffrey E. Stokes at the University of Massachusetts Boston wanted to see if these political systems left a similar footprint on the aging brain. They tested two competing ideas about cognitive aging.
One theory suggested West Germans would perform better on cognitive tests in later life because they enjoyed stronger economic growth, better nutrition, and more civil liberties. Another theory proposed that East Germans might have an advantage due to their state funded educational system.
East Germany mandated ten years of compulsory schooling, compared to eight or nine years in West Germany. The East also provided universal early childcare and a less socially divided school structure.
Educational exposure early in life is a primary driver of cognitive reserve. Cognitive reserve is the brain’s ability to build dense neural connections, which helps it compensate for age related damage and delay the onset of memory loss.
To find out which societal effect dominated, Bertogg and Stokes analyzed information from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe. They looked at a large sample of 5,231 older adults who lived in either East or West Germany in 1989.
Participants were at least 50 years old during the study and were interviewed multiple times over an average of four years. The survey included four standard tests used to evaluate brain health and predict dementia.
Working memory was tested by asking participants to recall a list of ten words. Executive function, which involves planning and focusing attention, was measured by having people name as many animals as they could in a set time.
Orientation was scored based on whether participants correctly knew the current date and day of the week. Finally, numeracy was tested by having participants repeatedly subtract the number seven from one hundred.
The researchers used statistical models to map each person’s cognitive trajectory over time. They adjusted the results for factors like childhood health, household income, and overall educational attainment.
To account for early life conditions, the researchers utilized a special retrospective module of the survey. Participants provided detailed histories regarding their childhood health, their perceived math and language skills relative to peers, and the number of books in their childhood homes.
The data revealed that individuals who lived in East Germany before reunification performed better across all four cognitive tests. They also showed a slower rate of cognitive decline as they aged.
West German residents experienced a steady decline in immediate memory and verbal fluency over the course of the study. In contrast, East German residents maintained stable scores or even slightly improved in these areas.
East Germans also demonstrated less steep declines in their orientation and numerical abilities. The researchers noted that these advantages were especially pronounced in men.
The results present an unusual paradox in aging research. Usually, populations with poorer physical health and lower life expectancies also suffer from worse cognitive aging.
Despite East Germans having higher rates of cardiovascular disease and earlier mortality on average, their aging brains remained more resilient. This suggests that the early benefits of an egalitarian, intensive education system can offset some of the physical wear and tear associated with a lower standard of living.
Next, Bertogg and Stokes examined whether a person’s age at the time of reunification influenced their cognitive outcomes. They wanted to know if experiencing the transition during a specific life stage altered the trajectory of mental aging.
They found that the gap in memory and verbal fluency was widest between East and West Germans who were in their forties when the Berlin Wall fell. West Germans in this age group showed relative disadvantages compared to their Eastern counterparts.
For numeracy and orientation, the East German advantage was highest among those who experienced reunification in their twenties. The cognitive differences between the two populations were largely absent among people who were already nearing retirement age in 1989.
The researchers interpret this as evidence of critical periods in adult development. Entering the workforce during reunification may have helped young East Germans maximize the benefits of their schooling within the new, larger economy.
Conversely, West Germans navigating reunification in their forties may have faced intense economic competition and family stress. Mid adulthood is often a period of high financial responsibility, making individuals more vulnerable to the mental health impacts of economic shifts.
The two nations differed in many ways beyond education and economics. West Germans faced higher exposure to environmental toxins like lead from gasoline, simply because car ownership was much higher there.
Social and psychological experiences also varied wildly depending on the side of the border. West Germany fostered a more open civil society, while East Germany relied on secret police and informants, which negatively impacted social trust.
The dataset did not allow the researchers to measure the direct impact of these specific social and environmental stressors on brain health. Future investigations will need to look at similar differences across other post socialist and capitalist European countries to see if the pattern holds.
Future studies will also need to track clinical diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias, rather than just test scores. High performing individuals sometimes hit the maximum possible score on cognitive tests, which can mask early signs of decline.
Cognitive test performance does not capture the full reality of living with a neurodegenerative disease. Tracking actual medical records over time will clarify how these early life educational advantages translate into real world dementia prevention.
The study, “Is There a Cognitive Footprint of Political Systems? The Case of Separation and Reunification of East and West Germany and Its Association With Later Life Cognitive Health,” was authored by Ariane Bertogg and Jeffrey E. Stokes.

Greenland and Antarctica lost 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:58:00 EEST
04:58:00 KST

Greenland and Antarctica lost 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice
Kyiv • UNN
Between 1979 and 2023, the ice sheets lost 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice. This raised global sea levels by 3.14 centimeters.
A new study based on satellite data collected since the 1970s recorded significant losses of polar ice in Greenland and Antarctica — the regions home to Earth’s two largest ice sheets — contributing to a rise in global sea levels, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Between 1979 and 2023, according to data from 27 satellite missions, Greenland and Antarctica lost a combined 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice, causing global sea levels to rise by 1.24 inches (3.14 cm).
This study, which used the longest satellite data record to date on changes in ice sheets to provide the most comprehensive picture of ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica, was conducted by the Ice Sheet Mass Balance Inter-comparison Exercise team.
According to scientists, the findings provide new evidence of the consequences of human-caused global climate change.
"To better visualize the scale of this enormous figure: 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice is enough to form a cube 23 kilometers (14.3 miles) high," said climatologist Inès Otosaka of Northumbria University (England), the lead author of the study published Wednesday in the journal Scientific Data.
Of the total ice loss recorded in the study, about 60% occurred in Greenland and 40% in Antarctica, despite the fact that Greenland’s area is only about one-eighth the area of Antarctica.
"When ice sheets melt, this contributes to rising global sea levels. And for every additional centimeter of sea-level rise, 2 to 3 million people are put at risk of annual coastal flooding. At present, ice sheets are one of the main contributors to sea-level rise, accounting for about 25% of the total increase in this indicator," Otosaka explained.
El Niño may become the strongest in decades - UN03.09.26, 14:31 • 5166 views
"We extended the time span of our satellite data to cover the period since the 1970s, and this confirms that ice loss began in the 1990s and has increased since then. Our estimate indicates that the rate of ice loss quadrupled between the 1980s and the 2010s," Otosaka added. The study recorded a slowdown in the rate of ice loss between 2020 and 2023, although scientists said this was likely a short-term fluctuation rather than a change in the long-term trend. They noted that exceptionally heavy snowfall in East Antarctica provided enough ice accumulation to offset some of the losses from glaciers in other parts of the continent, while a relatively mild summer in Greenland significantly reduced surface ice melting.
About 84% of the ice loss was caused by glaciers rapidly flowing into the ocean, rather than by surface ice melting; this indicates that the long-term trend is driven by the ice sheets’ response to ocean warming, Otosaka explained.
The researchers noted that although the overall sea-level rise resulting from ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica may appear insignificant, it puts between 6 and 9 million people worldwide at risk of coastal flooding and soil erosion.
"These findings have important implications for coastal development planning and demonstrate the urgent need to develop plans to protect coastal communities around the world from the consequences of melting ice sheets," Otosaka concluded.

Lithuania to Build CAESAR Maintenance and Repair Center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:56:12 UTC
04:56:12 KST

Lithuania will establish a center for the maintenance and repair of French CAESAR self-propelled howitzers.
To that end, Lithuania’s Ministry of Defense has signed an agreement with French defense company KNDS France, LRT reported.
Investment in the new infrastructure and the purchase of specialized equipment will amount to €12 million.
Lithuania will become the first country in the world to receive technological expertise from France to repair the electronic and hydraulic components of CAESAR self-propelled howitzers.
This will allow Lithuania’s defense industry to maintain the artillery systems independently instead of sending them to France for repairs.
Lithuania signed a contract to purchase the French artillery systems in December 2022. The agreement provided for the purchase of 18 CAESAR Mark II 6×6 wheeled self-propelled howitzers.
Under the contract, the first howitzers are scheduled to be delivered to the Lithuanian military in 2026, with the full order to be completed by 2027.
The Lithuanian Army has not yet received any CAESAR self-propelled howitzers, as the systems are still undergoing production and testing.
All 18 CAESAR Mark II howitzers ordered will eventually become part of the artillery battalion of the Žemaitija Infantry Brigade, replacing the outdated 105 mm M101 towed howitzers.
In August 2025, Estonia received six French 155 mm CAESAR self-propelled howitzers. The Baltic states are seeking to standardize their artillery systems to reduce maintenance and repair costs.
The Lithuanian Armed Forces have also deployed medium-range NASAMS air defense systems on the approaches to Vilnius.
Lithuania currently has two batteries of these air defense systems, with a third scheduled to arrive in the country in 2028.

US President Donald Trump has claimed that an FBI probe into his attempted assassination in July 2024 was deliberately mishandled as part of a “Democrat plot” to prevent him from winning a second term. He also referred to “new info” that supposedly appeared in the case, but provided no details.
In 2024, Trump, then the Republican presidential candidate, narrowly escaped death at a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, when a 20-year-old man fired shots from a rooftop, grazing Trump’s ear and killing one attendee and injuring two others.
Trump claimed at the time that President Joe Biden and his Democratic rival, Kamala Harris, were partly to blame as they allegedly made it more difficult for the Secret Service to protect him, while peddling rhetoric that could have encouraged the shooter.
The would-be assassin, Thomas M. Crooks, was killed by the US Secret Service. An internal review released later that year concluded that the Secret Service made multiple mistakes ahead of the shooting.
“Everybody knows the Crooked Joe Biden FBI didn’t do what they should have with respect to the Lunatic who shot me in Butler,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social on Tuesday.
He also claimed that “most of the information [on the case] was missing, altered, corrupted, or gone” by the time he took office in January 2025. “This was all a Democrat Plot, to get me out of the Election, that failed,” the president stated, adding that some new information on the case had emerged recently, but provided no details.
Trump also blamed former FBI Director Christopher Wray for mishandling the probe and maintained he “should pay a price for the way he handled this assassination attempt, and certainly for the things he said.”
Wray, who was nominated by Trump himself during his first term in office, stated that his agency did not find any accomplices of the shooter during testimony to the House Judiciary Committee. He also said it was unclear if Trump had been hit directly by a bullet or by shrapnel, provoking sharp criticism from Trump at the time. Wray resigned before Trump’s inauguration in January 2025.
The current FBI director, Kash Patel, told the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday that his agency looked into Crooks’ possible connection to any accomplices but found none. “We found no evidence that that individual was literally even speaking to any other human being other than his parents, who he resided with,” he said.
Attorney General Todd Blanche mentioned during the same hearing that new information related to the case had surfaced recently. “It is new information about the shooter and about his background, about his history and that’s stuff that we didn’t know before,” he said while refusing to elaborate.
Trump has been targeted in several assassination attempts. Two months after the July 2024 incident, a pro-Ukraine activist was arrested after being spotted with a rifle near Trump’s golf course in Florida. He was later found guilty of trying to assassinate Trump.
In April 2026, the president and First Lady Melania Trump were rushed from the Washington Hilton after gunfire broke out at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner. The suspect, Cole Tomas Allen, was later charged with attempting to assassinate the president as well.

Reminder

The Criminal Code of Ukraine is also supplemented with new articles:
-  Article 2554 ("Creation of, management of, or participation in an electronic communications fraud organization");  
-  Article 2555, "Recruitment for participation in an electronic communications fraud organization," establishing new liability for the actions of such fraudulent organizations and participation in them.

Lebanon returns 37 artefacts smuggled out of Egypt six years ago
The artefacts date back to the pharaonic civilisation, more commonly referred to as ancient Egypt.
Lebanon has returned 37 artefacts to Egypt that were smuggled out of the country six years ago.
A ceremony was held at the National Museum of Beirut in the Lebanese capital on Wednesday to celebrate the handover of the artefacts, which date back to the pharaonic civilisation, more commonly referred to as ancient Egypt.

“After investigating the identity and ownership of these items, it was determined that they belonged to Egypt,” said Lebanon’s Culture Minister Ghassan Salame as he gave the items to Egyptian Ambassador to Lebanon Alaa Moussa.
“We are setting an example in the strict implementation of the 1970 international convention concerning the prevention of the illicit trafficking of cultural property,” he was quoted as saying by Lebanon’s National News Agency.
The artefacts were seized from the Port of Beirut in 2020. Lebanon spent years working with INTERPOL, Egypt and the country’s top public prosecutor to verify the ownership and authenticity of the items.
The collection consists of masks, wooden dolls, pieces of Coptic textiles, amulets made from glass paste, medium-sized statues and two wooden coffins decorated with colourful designs.
Laura Salloum, an official with Lebanon’s Directorate General of Antiquities, said the artefacts had been purchased by a Lebanese national without official documentation confirming their source.
Such items are regularly stolen from Egypt. Last month, 48 artefacts were returned to Cairo by the FBI Art Crime Team in the United States.
Egypt’s official press office announced on Wednesday that its embassy in the Swiss capital, Bern, had recovered an ancient golden mummy mask with the help of local authorities.

Tips for consumers hit with a debt collection notice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:41:59 UTC
04:41:59 KST

How to make sure you are not impacted by misleading debt collection notices
This year has been a perfect storm for financial stress.
With three interest rate hikes, rising cost of living, and a Middle East war driving up fuel prices, more Australians are falling behind on their debt repayments.
And that has led to a 12 per cent spike in the number of people calling the National Debt Helpline.
In fact, an additional 20,000 people contacted the organisation for debt advice in the year to August, taking the total to 187,905.
About 15,000 of those were directly related to debt collection.
Adding to the stress is the fact that debt collectors are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to ramp up their efforts to claw back money from debt-ridden consumers.
One woman was sent repeated legal threats, trying to force her to pay a claim she was never liable for, which legal experts described as the "worst kind" of bullying.
It comes as the ACCC takes ARMA Group and Force Legal to federal court, alleging that between them they sent 320,000 debt enforcement notices to individuals that were allegedly misleading.
So how is a debt collector meant to engage with an individual, and what rights does one have in the process?
What rights does an individual have?
The coordinator of the National Debt Helpline, Vicki Staff, said the first thing to do was work out if the debt was valid.
"For example, you may have already paid the debt … I recommend writing to the debt collector and letting them know that you have paid it in full and provide any copies of records if you have something to prove that the debt is repaid," she said.
If the debt is more than three years old in the Northern Territory, and more than six years old elsewhere, that means it is statute-barred, meaning the legal time limit to start court proceedings has expired.
"If it's an unsecured debt and you've not made a payment, you've not acknowledged the debt in writing, and there's no court judgment that's been entered against you, you're in a good position to be able to challenge it," Ms Staff said.
But if the debt was valid, she said "crunch the numbers" to see what was realistic for repayment.
"Get your ducks in a row first [and] get an agreement from the debt collector as to an affordable payment arrangement," Ms Staff said.
Under the National Credit Code, an individual may be able to change the terms of their consumer credit contract to allow them to pause or reduce payments for a period of time.
If you're not happy with the process, Ms Staff said there were other avenues.
"Check to find if your debt collector is actually registered with an external ombudsman, [and] you can make a complaint," she said.
There's also the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).
"If the creditor is a financial services provider, you can take a complaint to [AFCA]," Nicola Howell, senior law lecturer at the Queensland University of Technology, said.
"Financial services providers should have an internal dispute resolution process as well that you can go to and seek to resolve the matter."
Expectations of a debt collector
Just like other industries, debt collector conduct is governed under Australian consumer law.
That means there are standards and expectations in place when looking to recover costs.
"Being proactive and being open to affordable hardship arrangements for people … communicating really clearly with customers around what was expected," Ms Staff said.
Dr Howell said if a debt collector did not act appropriately, there were consequences.
"The prohibitions against misleading and deceptive conduct or unconscionable conduct apply to businesses that are engaging in trade or commerce," she said.
"There's no carve-out for lawyers in terms of how they're conducting their business in that interface with consumers."

'Mobilisation of fear': The deeper strategy behind One Nation's immigration policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:41:41 UTC
04:41:41 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Jyoti has called her migration agent three times this month. Each time, she asks the same question: Has there been any update?
Her application for a Skilled Independent visa, a pathway to permanent residency, has been sitting in the queue for months. It has felt like a long wait for Jyoti, who has lived in Australia for the better part of a decade. In recent months, that uncertainty has taken on a new urgency.
The 43-year-old is a secondary school teacher who lives in an outer northern suburb of Melbourne with her husband and their two children. She arrived from Punjab, northern India, eight years ago as an international student and is now in Australia on a work visa.
She asks that only her first name be used because she fears speaking publicly could affect her family's visa prospects.
I feel like the axe is going to fall on people like us before anyone else.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"International students, temporary visa holders ... we would be the first to lose our livelihoods and our place here if Pauline Hanson comes to power, or if her party keeps gaining momentum," she tells SBS News.
Jyoti says she is watching the lead-up to Victoria's November election closely. To her, the election will be an early test of how far One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's momentum could travel and what that could mean for her family's future in the only country her children have really known. It's a fear, she says, that everyone she knows in her position is carrying right now.
One Nation wants to cut 750,000 temporary visa holders from Australia over three years. Not one of them will get a say in whether the party succeeds.
"Our fate is being decided by political parties whose fate we have no say in," Jyoti says.
Australia is home to roughly three million temporary visa holders, including students, graduates and skilled workers.
As One Nation pushes for sweeping cuts to temporary migration, it raises a harder question about political power: are people with the least ability to influence an election also the easiest to target?
Who One Nation's visa cuts would hit hardest
One Nation's plan would tighten the student and graduate visa systems, restrict family members from accompanying temporary skilled workers, and close off "visa hopping" — the practice of extending a stay by switching between visa categories rather than leaving the country and reapplying offshore.
According to the policy announced on Monday, international students and graduates would absorb the biggest cuts.
The student visa population, including accompanying family members, would fall from about 590,000 to 350,000, and the graduate visa population from about 270,000 to just 40,000 over three years.
Family visas linked to temporary skilled workers would be phased out entirely, a change expected to shrink that cohort from about 263,000 to 160,000 over the same period.
"Tinkering around the edges will not fix the damage," Hanson said in the media release.
"This is about giving Australians breathing space by drastically cutting the stock of temporary migrants, restoring control and making sure migration serves Australia."
Speaking with ABC's Radio National on Monday morning, Environment Minister Murray Watt said One Nation's policy would trigger economic disruption.
"One Nation's policy is a recipe to destroy the Australian economy and drive the Australian economy into recession," he said.
For people already living that reality, the question isn't abstract. Jyoti says the proposed changes have made getting permanent residency feel less like the obvious next step in her journey and more like a race against time.
They are looking at us as just numbers, but there are actual lives and people behind these numbers.
Not everyone would be affected equally, says Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the Department of Immigration. Much depends on a migrant's professional skills and experience.
"Temporary entrants with skills in strong demand tend to secure permanent residency much faster than others," he tells SBS News.
For instance, a nurse's pathway to permanent residency looks nothing like that of a graduate in a field with weaker demand. For the latter, the road can be far longer, and far less certain.
One Nation has confirmed it would maintain a net overseas migration (NOM) ceiling of 130,000 a year once its proposed three-year reset is complete.
Rizvi says that target leaves the policy with nowhere else to land.
"Taking into account the fact that One Nation has said it wants to quarantine WHMs [Working Holiday Makers] and PALM [Pacific Australia Labour Mobility] visas from any cuts; cannot lawfully reduce places for partners and dependent children; can't easily reduce numbers of NZ citizens contributing to NOM and wants to maintain a flow of tradies and health workers, it leaves no room for students and temporary graduates," he says.
Essentially, One Nation policy would mean abolishing the international education industry.
"That would have massive consequences for university budgets and staff. Possibly 50,000 jobs would be directly affected. More indirectly."
The political cost of having no vote
Temporary entrants have never had voting rights in Australia and "never will", Rizvi says.
But it's a dynamic that has shaped migration policy for longer than many realise, says Emily Foley, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Canberra who studies social democratic and centre-left political parties.
She says temporary migration has quietly created problems over many decades that successive governments have had little reason to confront.
"For years, policymakers and governments knew there were significant issues with the temporary migration program essentially creating an underclass of exploited and marginalised workers," she tells SBS News.
"And yet, precisely because this cohort are not voters, there was minimal political incentive to actively discuss the policy area, particularly when migration was such a salient and politicised election issue."
One Nation is not alone in pushing for tighter controls on temporary migration. Labor has already moved to amend parts of its policy, including restricting visa hopping, shortening Temporary Graduate visas, raising the income threshold for temporary skilled migration and introducing managed limits on new international student commencements.
The Coalition has also promised to reduce migration by linking NOM to the number of homes built. It has separately proposed making compliance with an Australian Values Statement a universal visa condition, with breaches potentially leading to visa refusal or cancellation.
But One Nation's proposal goes considerably further, targeting the temporary migrant population with sharp reductions in student and graduate numbers and restrictions on accompanying family members.
Foley says the party's focus is consistent with its longstanding position on immigration.
Attacking temporary migrants is therefore not surprising.
"This cohort, despite many being Australian taxpayers, are without the civil, political and economic rights and privileges of Australian citizens and permanent residents. It is easy for parties like One Nation to attack and marginalise temporary migrants precisely because they have so little recourse."
Benjamin Moffitt, a senior lecturer in politics and international relations at Monash University, is more blunt about the electoral calculus.
"It removes the one thing that usually keeps rhetoric in check: the people it hits getting a vote on it," he tells SBS News.
"Temporary visa holders and prospective migrants can't punish a party at the ballot box, so there's no electoral cost to going as hard as you like on them.
"That's true of migration policy generally, not a One Nation quirk, but it's a big part of why this is the one area where the inflammatory rhetoric can run so far ahead of the actual policy detail."
But he stops short of saying One Nation is deliberately targeting temporary migrants for this reason.
What can be established, Moffitt says, is that the groups One Nation has identified most precisely — including international students, working holidaymakers and skilled visa holders — are among those who cannot vote.
"Whether that's a deliberate strategy of picking targets who can't retaliate, or simply where the populist radical right's usual scapegoating logic lands by default, isn't something you can necessarily tell apart from the outside."
One Nation did not respond to SBS News' request for comment on whether the lack of voting rights among temporary visa holders is a consideration in its immigration policies.
What temporary migrants contribute
Temporary migrants make up a significant part of Australia's workforce and international education sector. Their contribution extends beyond the visa system, with international students alone generating almost $55 billion in education export income in 2025.
According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, international students and their families accounted for 82.4 per cent of non-residents eligible to work in Australia in June 2025.
Andrew McKellar, CEO of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told reporters on Monday that cutting temporary migration to the degree proposed by One Nation could have a significant economic impact.
"You know, if you're going to cut overall visa levels by 750,000 over a three-year period and drive net overseas migration into negative territory, that's a COVID-level shock to the Australian economy," he said.
One Nation has pointed to Canada's recent cuts to temporary migration as evidence that immigration can be reduced without crashing the economy.
McKellar said the focus should instead be on the potential impact of the proposed cuts on Australia's growth.
"What the debate cannot be about is it cannot be about arbitrary targets. We can't have solutions which are extreme, which would cause very significant damage to the Australian economy."
Why immigration works for One Nation
Tiziana Torresi is the program director of the School of Society and Culture at Adelaide University and studies normative political theory and the governance of migration. She says immigration sits within a broader populist strategy that divides society between an "authentic" Australian public and groups portrayed as threatening to its interests.
"Anti-immigration rhetoric has been central to One Nation's political discourse from its emergence," she tells SBS News.
Torresi says the party's appeal taps into economic and social anxieties.
"The mobilisation of fear is a key strategy of populist far-right parties, enabling them to present themselves as the only true voice and defenders of an authentic national community threatened by 'outsiders'," she says.
Moffitt says this extends to issues such as housing, jobs and infrastructure. He describes this approach as 'nativism', where social and economic problems are attributed to outsiders, particularly migrants.
"Nativism doesn't identify a housing crisis and then, separately, decide migrants are to blame; it needs a scapegoat for social and economic ills, and the migrant is the figure built to supply one," he says.
The result is a message that can speak to voters worried about the cost of living, housing and population growth, while also tapping into deeper concerns about Australia's changing social and cultural identity.
Torresi says this allows One Nation to present itself as the party willing to restore a sense of control to voters who believe established political parties have failed them.
One Nation can exploit these various anxieties by claiming that 'ordinary Australians' are being left behind or displaced.
That is where the politics of temporary migration becomes more complicated. The people most directly affected may have no vote, but the issue is being used to speak to millions of people who do.
Beyond the ballot box
Torresi says the absence of a vote does not mean migrants are politically disconnected.
"Migrants are embedded in families, workplaces, neighbourhoods, unions, community organisations, and broader social networks, creating relationships with citizens who do possess electoral rights," she says.
Those relationships can give migrants an indirect political voice through the citizens around them, who can respond at the ballot box.
"Consequently, political attacks on migrants may have effects that extend well beyond the migrant population itself."
But temporary migrants may have fewer connections to Australian citizens who can advocate for their interests, Torresi says.
"Temporary migrants may be doubly vulnerable to anti-immigration politics because they can lack both direct and indirect forms of political influence."
Back in Melbourne, Jyoti says the fear she feels is being mirrored back to her.
"It's not just me. Everyone I know in this situation feels the same fear," she says.
We've built our lives here, and none of that means we get a say in what happens to us next.
Her migration agent still doesn't have an update. She'll call again next week.

Japan just hit a new longevity milestone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:41:37 UTC
04:41:37 KST

Humans are living longer and longer. Now Japan has broken a new record for longevity: more than 100,000 people in the country are centenarians—some 107,677 of them are at least 100 years old.
Japan has one of the highest life expectancies in the world. Researchers believe this national longevity is likely linked to low rates of obesity, healthy diets, widespread health screenings and affordable health care, which lead to lower mortality rates from heart disease and cancer.
“I am very happy that so many people have been able to stay active for so long,” said Japan’s health minister Kenichiro Ueno at a news conference announcing the milestone in Tokyo on Tuesday.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Japan is “exactly where you would expect to see this first,” says Jay Olshansky, an epidemiologist at the University of Illinois Chicago. But he expects more countries to follow as large birth cohorts hit the 100-year mark and medical advances continue.
“Most people at older ages now are living on manufactured time—time that was created for us by our physicians and by the public health community,” he says.
But more people living long lives isn’t all good news. Japan also has one of the lower birth rates in the world. And its lower fertility rates and smaller working-age population are squeezing public resources and making caring for its older populations more difficult. Additionally, a long life can be “a potentially dangerous scenario unless it’s accompanied by good health,” Olshansky says.
Japan’s oldest known person, Fuyo Kumamato, is 114 years old. (The oldest living person in the world, Ethel Caterham in the U.K., is 117 years old.) Researchers around the world are studying supercentenarians, people older than age 110, in hopes of keeping more people healthy for longer.
“What’s really critical about this is quality of life,” Olshansky adds. “Just living longer should not be the primary goal of medicine and public health anymore. It should be health extension or health span.”

ICC used as ‘tool’ to target Global South – political commentator

AfD, the far right, and the lessons Germany's mainstream forgot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:41:29 UTC
04:41:29 KST

Breadcrumb
AfD, the far right, and the lessons Germany's mainstream forgot
On 6 September, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a landslide victory in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, securing nearly 44% of the vote and 39 of the state parliament’s 83 seats. The result marked the first time since the Second World War that a far-right party has won a state election in Germany.
The party fell just three seats short of an outright majority, meaning it cannot govern alone and will need support from another party or lawmakers to form a government. However, other MPs, specifically from the Büdnis Sahra Wagenknecht Party (BSW) will most likely give the AfD the seats it needs to run the state.
The election should not be viewed in isolation. It is the latest and perhaps most alarming indication of how Germany’s political mainstream has increasingly adopted positions once associated primarily with the far right, particularly on migration, asylum and national identity.
Their 258-page manifesto, titled Das Land Zuerst (The Country First), details a fundamental shift in the country’s immigration system. It promises large scale deportations of immigrations and asylum seekers, and advocates for a “remigration program,” that might even affect German resident holders or those who do not sound or look German.
AfD leader Alice Weidel has been explicit about the party’s intentions. She has said that if elected to government, their first 100 days would bring about the deportations and a closed German border, adding that “if it has to be called remigration, then let it be called remigration.”
Years in the making
The AfD’s policies range from encouraging Germans to have more children through financial incentives, such as a €2,000 birth bonus (although only applying to German citizen heterosexual families), to bringing back coal mining, and restoring friendly relations with Russia to provide cheaper access to energy.
They also want to change their school curriculum to focus less on the Holocaust and more on the country’s history pre-World War Two, and severely restrict abortion access.
While many attribute the AfD’s rise to worsening economic conditions, including rising energy prices, fewer job opportunities, and stagnating wages, these factors alone do not explain the party’s growing support. The political conditions that have allowed the AfD to flourish have been developing for years.
Last year, many of us warned that the mainstream parties’ shift towards increasingly anti-migrant and xenophobic rhetoric could ultimately backfire. Rather than isolating the far right, mainstream politicians have increasingly attempted to compete with it by adopting policies that restrict migrants’ rights and treating migration as the defining political crisis of the country.
Under the former Socialist Democrat Prime Minister Olaf Scholz in January 2025, the German Bundestag passed the Repatriation Improvement Act, one of the most significant recent efforts to accelerate deportations by extending maximum deportation detention from 10 to 28 days, as well as significantly reducing the benefits of refugees and asylum seekers.
Meanwhile Freidrich Merz, while claiming that he and the Christian Democratic Party must isolate the AfD so they do not “carry out an ethnic cleansing of the country,” Merz’s own government representatives admitted that they needed to be even tougher on migration.
“Perhaps it was also a mistake by the CDU that in recent years it had not addressed the issue [of migration] enough,” Minister President Sven Schulze said.
The politicisation of migration became emboldened especially following the December 2024 attack on a Christmas market in Magdeburg, the capital of Saxony-Anhalt, in which six people were ultimately killed and around 300 injured. The suspect was a Saudi national who had lived in Germany for years and had publicly expressed strongly anti-Islamic and far-right views, including support for the Alternative for Germany (AfD).
Despite the attacker being an anti-Islam, AfD supporter himself, the media, political parties and AfD themselves became emboldened with anti-Muslim, anti-migrant rhetoric.
Weidel declared that “Magdeburg would not have been possible without uncontrolled immigration” and called for “a restrictive migration policy and consistent deportations.” AfD supporters subsequently gathered in Magdeburg, with protesters reported chanting “Deport, deport, deport.”
Integration
Instead of attempting to rectify emboldened far-right ideologues, Merz presented his policy platforms to revoke German citizenship from dual nationals, especially pro-Palestinian demonstrators, people he considers “terror supporters,” and those who he believes commit severe crimes.
And in fact, some months later a naturalised Palestinian man, Abdullah A., had his citizenship revoked over alleged support of Palestinian fighters on his social media.
Now, directly after the AfD win, the CDU is reportedly moving to tighten citizenship rules even further. According to a recent report, senior CDU figures are drafting proposals that would effectively reverse key elements of the citizenship reform introduced by the previous government, including the normalisation of dual citizenship.
This follows a historic 2025 total of 332,500 naturalisations in Germany, after a 2024 citizenship reform under Olaf Scholz reduced the standard residency requirement to five years and allowed naturalised citizens to retain their previous nationality.
The reported plan includes renouncing previous citizenship, passing a language examination, covering living costs entirely from their own income, and disavowing “all forms of antisemitism."
Already, this country’s politicians are looking for ways to make it harder for individuals to integrate into German society by forcing people to give up their passports from their country of origin.
The danger does not stop with only the AfD winning elections, as we are already seeing dangerous signs that the far-right party is willing to use the machinery of the state to escalate violence where it deems necessary.
Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, gave the people a glimpse of his viciousness when he did not condemn building arms manufacturers in his state because he wants to reserve the arms for his own “remigration offensive.”
Inspired by Trump’s America
I am reminded of the United States, of the armed, masked ICE officers abducting immigrants from their homes, on their way to drop off their children, and at their places of work while killing them or the protestors who object to their abductions. The images of detention centres and imprisoning migrant children, and the act of disappearing and separating families, might be closer to Germany’s front doors than we think.
In fact, the AfD mirrors important elements of the MAGA movement: far-right politics wrapped in the language of economic populism, alleged restoration of a national homeland, and allegedly against investment in foreign wars. Like Trump and his movement, the AfD presents itself as a defender of ordinary citizens against elitist, lying bureaucrats and progressive institutions and establishments.
They promise tax reductions, economic benefits, and making Germany German again.
It is also important to note that the AfD, while entrenched in an antisemitic history, is vehemently pro-Israel and, in fact, tells Jewish constituents that it is their party that would treat them the best because of its commitment to stand firm against pro-Palestinians, leftists, and “those who hate Israel.”
Germany’s memory culture and mainstream political discourse have allowed a far-right party to simply claim that they are not antisemitic due to the fact that they are simply Zionist.
The AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt is a warning about what happens when xenophobia becomes mainstream political currency, when deportation is presented as the solution to social and economic problems, and when mainstream politicians compete with the far-right by adopting its rhetoric and policies.
Offering a softer, more palatable version of the same politics only risks legitimising the far right without necessarily winning its voters. If voters want tougher deportation policies, they may ultimately choose the politicians they believe will follow through, rather than those who express similar sentiments in a palatable, politically acceptable vocabulary.
Hebh Jamal is a Palestinian American journalist based in Germany.

An ancient disease is surging in Australia — and it isn't always easy to detect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:41:26 UTC
04:41:26 KST

IN BRIEF
- Gonorrhoea and syphilis notifications have surged by more than half in the past decade.
- Indigenous health experts have warned of a serious need for investment in community-led health projects.
Reported cases of infectious syphilis and gonorrhoea have surged by more than half over the past decade in Australia, as experts warn education and testing urgently needs to improve.
In 2025, there were 42,393 gonorrhoea notifications and 5,986 infectious syphilis notifications — a 10-year increase of 57 per cent for gonorrhoea and 56 per cent for syphilis, analysis from the University of New South Wales' Kirby Institute has shown.
Syphilis was declared a communicable disease of national significance in late 2025, in response to "ongoing and concerning" rises in Australian case numbers.
Chief medical officer Professor Michael Kidd declared that awareness was necessary among all Australians, including healthcare professionals, and urged everyone to get tested.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Syphilis and gonorrhoea are common bacterial infections with ancient origins, now easily treated with antibiotics.
But both infections can present with either mild or non-existent symptoms.
If left untreated, syphilis progresses through stages and can spread to the brain, heart, eyes, and other organs. It can cause neurological problems including paralysis, and dementia, and cause soft, tumour-like growths to appear on the skin, bones or internal organs. Tertiary syphilis can eventually lead to death.
Notification rates for infectious syphilis among women increased 170 per cent in the past decade from 2016 to 2025. In contrast, rates increased just 39 per cent among males.
Syphilis during pregnancy can lead to congenital syphilis, which can result in miscarriage or stillbirth, or severe lifelong health impacts in babies that are born, including prematurity, low birthweight and other physical developmental abnormalities.
Kirby Institute epidemiologist Dr Skye McGregor said congenital syphilis is a persistent issue in Australia, with more than half of deaths in the last decade among First Nations infants. There were 14 cases of congenital syphilis in 2025, and 113 from 2016 to 2025, with 40 resulting in the death of an infant.
"This is an entirely preventable outcome with early diagnosis, testing and treatment of pregnant people," McGregor said.
Better approaches for at-risk populations
First Nations peoples were disproportionately affected by STIs, diagnosed with gonorrhoea at more than four times the rate of non-Indigenous people and syphilis at more than six times.
Kim Gates, community relations lead in the Kirby Institute's First Nations Point-Of-Care Program, said the disparities in diagnoses between First Nations and non-Indigenous Australians were an indication of broader inequities in healthcare.
Australian services needed to be designed better to reflect the experiences of First Nations communities, Gates told SBS News, adding that many First Nations peoples have a complex relationship with the Australian health system and "have good reasons to be sceptical of top-down services and approaches".
"This is why Aboriginal-led services are so important," she said.
Gates said that while the 149 Aboriginal Controlled Community Health Services in Australia provide comprehensive and culturally safe healthcare, "there are areas these don't reach".
For Gates, sustained investment in community-led initiatives, like the First Nations Molecular Point-of-Care Testing Program, was the solution to bringing down STI rates among Indigenous populations.
Improving community awareness is key
Dr Arthur Wong, sexual health physician and conjoint lecturer at the Kirby Institute, said that timely testing, treatment and retesting were "crucial", and that post-diagnosis care was also "essential" to avoid repeat infections.
Wong told SBS News that awareness was already affecting syphilis rates, where evidence shows a decline in incidence among gay and bisexual men.
"We do know that testing has increased in certain populations," Wong said. "Gay and bisexual men who are taking HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PReP) are tested more frequently for STIs."
But the data leaves out an often-overlooked section of the population — for homosexual, bisexual and transgender women, rates of syphilis and gonorrhoea remain largely unknown.
LGBTIQ+ Women's Project Lead at ACON (formerly AIDS Council of NSW), Lee Wang, says queer and trans women aren't routinely reported in surveillance data, which has adverse health outcomes.
"When queer and trans women are overlooked, it can create the false impression that STI prevention and testing are not relevant to them," Wang told SBS News.
"This can contribute to lower testing and missed opportunities for prevention and early diagnosis, with recent surveys highlighting substantial gaps in STI testing when compared with gay and bisexual men."
There was a need for targeted sexual health education resources, Wang said, like ACON's Word on the Sheets, a digital sexual and reproductive health resource for LGBTQ+ women, trans and gender diverse people.
"We shouldn't confuse a lack of data with a lack of priority," Wang said. "We need healthcare providers who are equipped to discuss sexual practices without making assumptions about sexuality or gender identity."
Wong said preliminary data from the most recent Australian Study of Health and Relationships show that just 17 per cent of people aged 16 to 49 reported having an STI test in the last 12 months.
Rates of chlamydia and gonorrhoea were highest among young people aged 15 to 29 years.
Studies in recent years have pointed to a waning use of condoms among school-aged people in Australia, with findings from a Secondary Students and Sexual Health (SSASH) survey analysis by Victoria University in 2024 stating that condom use in Australia was low and has declined over a decade.
Overall, Wong said, Australia needed a "sustained and enhanced" response to sexual health, "to ensure any gains are experienced equally across all populations."

‘Made in Europe’ law threatens UK plans for reset with EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:39:28 UTC
04:39:28 KST

The UK government’s EU reset summit will be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry, government sources have said.
The “Made in Europe” legislation – formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act – is designed to curb China’s increasing presence in European industry, but was not on the reset plan agreed by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, in London in May 2025.
A follow-up summit was due to be held in July this year, but was cancelled after Starmer’s resignation. The government is now looking to change the roadmap, with one source saying that “Made in Europe should be on the agenda”.
It is understood that Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister with responsibility for the reset, told the EU’s trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, this was the UK’s new priority when the pair met last week.
The trade minister, Anas Sarwar, told a gathering of UK business leaders on Tuesday they needed to let their EU partners know the risks posed by Made in Europe, which will prioritise EU suppliers in key industries including car manufacturing and defence.
Ministers have privately expressed fears that the reset has lost significant momentum since Andy Burnham became prime minister, with his focus on the domestic agenda. Agreements have yet to be reached on several key issues, including what tuition fees will be paid by EU students coming to the UK on a mooted “youth experience” programme.
UK sources say that while a food and drink deal and a youth mobility scheme are still on the agenda, the government will not agree to a new summit date until the bigger issues of the Industrial Accelerator Act are included in discussions.
There was talk in London and Brussels that a meeting could be convened on 6 November, but it is understood this could now be pushed backuntil the end of November or beyond.
One government source said: “We are willing to negotiate on the things that matter to them, but they have to be able to negotiate the thing that matters to us. Made in Europe should be on the table, definitely.”
The UK fears the Made in Europe laws could jeopardise billions of pounds worth of trade if British goods are not categorised as European, locking it out of key contracts on the continent.
France, which conceived the Made in Europe laws, is pushing to have the legislation passed by the end of the year, deepening fears that British manufacturing could be left behind.
It is thought that France is sympathetic to the UK’s position, but believes increasing competition from China makes it more important to get the legislation on the books now, and make allowances for third countries later, a process that could take years.
One EU diplomat said that there was substantial backing among key member states for the UK to be included in Made in Europe, though not all agreed. “The problem is the benefits are seen as asymmetrical,” the diplomat said. “The UK gets more out of it than the EU.”
It is understood the Netherlands, Germany, Poland and Italy are all in favour of the UK’s inclusion, but France remains unconvinced.
The government’s newly assertive approach could give the UK some leverage in negotiations over concessions on youth mobility, something that is a political priority for many EU capitals.
Another UK source said a deal on Made in Europe would be “a good faith demonstration that we can find answers and almost everything else”.
A government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.
“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”
The UK’s desire for a deal on manufacturing rules comes at time when the EU is under pressure from industry across the bloc to loosen China’s growing presence in supply chains.
Last week, manufacturing bosses warned of a potential loss of 300,000 jobs this year unless incentives were put in place to make European products more attractive than cheaper parts from China.
The EU’s deficit with China is now running at €1bn a day, with fears that European companies are being cannibalised from within.
In her state of the union address to the European parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said the EU needed to grow non-Chinese supplies of rare earths and critical minerals vital to manufacturing.
Her surprise offer of an associate membership deal with Canada demonstrated how far Brussels can go to court third-country partners.
Speaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, the EU chief said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships.”
The EU and Canada are to hold a summit in late October to develop their future relationship. The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, though it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, enabling deep economic integration with these countries, which follow many EU rules including free movement – a red line for the UK.
Carney, who is to address the European parliament on Thursday, has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU, as his country seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.
Burnham met Carney at a football match in Liverpool on Wednesday night, where the two Everton fans watched their team in the EFL Cup. Burnham is also due to meet the US president, Donald Trump, for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York next week.
The potential new alliance between the EU and Canada will worry UK ministers that the bloc’s priorities are shifting. Should Burnham fail to complete a food and drink deal that was already on Starmer’s reset agenda, it could have implications for October’s budget, as the economic effects of easing trade with the EU is priced in as part of growth calculations.
The Conservatives criticised the UK-EU reset on Wednesday, saying a future Tory government would build a wholly independent regulatory system.
Alex Burghart, the party’s deputy leader, and Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, warned the plans would make Britain less competitive.
Speaking at the Policy Exchange thinktank, Burghart said: “Labour’s EU reset is the worst of both worlds and will leave Britain unable to take advantage of our country’s future growth potential.
“The next Conservative government would not be bound by this arrangement and will begin work now on a genuinely independent regulatory system.”

Fed raises US inflation outlook while lowering unemployment forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:38:07 UTC
04:38:07 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The US Federal Reserve raised its inflation forecasts for 2026 on Wednesday, while lowering unemployment projections, signaling persistent price pressures alongside a resilient labor market.
The median forecast for core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation was raised to 3.4% for 2026 from 3.3% in June, according to the Fed’s latest Summary of Economic Projections.
The core measure, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, is expected to ease to 2.5% in 2027, 2.2% in 2028 and 2% in 2029.
The headline PCE inflation forecast for 2026 was also lifted by 0.1 percentage point to 3.7%. Inflation is projected to fall to 2.3% in 2027, 2.1% in 2028 and reach the Fed’s 2% target in 2029.
The upward revisions came despite upcoming methodological changes by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis that economists expect to mechanically lower measured core PCE inflation.
The changes, set to take effect with annual revisions Sept. 30, concern the measurement of prices for services including portfolio management, legal services and computer software.
The Fed, meanwhile, presented a stronger outlook for the labor market.
Officials lowered their median unemployment-rate forecast for 2026 to 4.1% from 4.3%. The rate is projected to remain at 4.1% through 2029, compared with the June estimates of 4.3% for 2027 and 4.2% for 2028.
Changes to the growth outlook were limited. The Fed raised its real gross domestic product growth forecast for 2026 to 2.3% from 2.2%, and its 2027 estimate to 2.4% from 2.3%.
The projection for 2028 was unchanged at 2.2%, while the economy is forecast to grow 2.1% in 2029.
The revisions accompanied the Fed’s decision to raise its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to a target range of between 3.75% and 4%, its first increase since 2023.

Free but not quite yet.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:37:19 UTC
04:37:19 KST

Mikhail Ryumin, Sergey Kanurin, Andrey Merkuryev and Alexander Zaytsev
After a year and four months in pre-trial detention, four Russian truck drivers accused of participating in the 2025 devastating Ukrainian drone strike on airfields across Russia dubbed “Operation Spiderweb” have been released. But their ordeal is far from over.
On September 16, the Moscow City Court released the four Chelyabinsk men from pre-trial detention. According to Kommersant daily, the ruling came after the Prosecutor General’s Office refused to approve their indictment, conceding that the evidence of their involvement was insufficient.
The truckers—Mikhail Ryumin (56), Andrey Merkuryev (62), Alexander Zaytsev (57), and Sergey Kanurin (48)—were arrested after June 1, 2025. They had been hired to transport prefabricated houses across Russia, unaware that their trailers concealed Ukrainian drones. The remotely controlled drones launched from their parked trucks to strike strategic military airbases, including “Olenya” in Murmansk and the Ivanovo airfield.
Initially, there was a fifth defendant in the case. Vasily Pytikov, 62, was killed when his truck exploded on a highway in the Amur region during the drone launch. The Investigative Committee quietly closed the criminal case against the deceased driver in February 2026.
Now, the surviving drivers have been freed under a “ban on certain actions”. A defense attorney who requested anonymity told Mediazona that the men are forbidden from communicating with each other or witnesses, and are banned from using the internet and mobile networks, except for emergency calls. Most importantly, the drivers cannot return to their families in the Urals: because the Prosecutor General returned the criminal case to the Investigative Committee, they must remain in Moscow, ready to be summoned by investigators at any moment.
“Nobody will go to Chelyabinsk, I think, because they need to appear before the investigator; investigative actions will still be carried out,” the lawyer explained. “The criminal case has not yet been closed. We hope it will be, but for now, we have only won, you could say, the first battle.”
The lawyer added that months of imprisonment has “negatively affected the health and psychological state” of the drivers, who had been facing decades in prison on terrorism and explosives charges.
“My client was so moved today, he had stopped hoping for anything,” the defender shared. “All of them were overjoyed.”
In the spring of 2025 the truckers accepted what they believed were routine jobs transporting dismantled prefabricated frame houses to four different regions across Russia. Unbeknownst to them, the cargo concealed Ukrainian drones primed for an attack.
On June 1, 2025, those hidden drones emerged from the trucks to unleash coordinated strikes on major Russian military airbases deep within the country. The targets included the “Olenya” base in the Murmansk region, “Belaya” in Irkutsk, “Dyagilevo” near Ryazan, and an airfield in Ivanovo, which houses Russia’s rarest A-50 “flying radar” reconnaissance aircraft.

US makes major wartime bet on Ukraine’s largest private energy company with 85 million euro investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:37:19 UTC
04:37:19 KST

US makes major wartime bet on Ukraine’s largest private energy company with 85 million euro investment
Ukraine’s biggest private energy firm, DTEK, has secured an 85 million euro ($97 million) loan from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation for a critical battery storage project, marking the DFC’s largest wartime transaction, DTEK announced on Sept. 16. 
With Russia continuing to target Ukraine’s energy facilities, particularly power plants, ensuring a reliable energy supply has become a major concern in Ukraine. During the war, Ukraine has increasingly searched for investors to bolster its grid by decentralizing energy generation and supply. 
DTEK, owned by Ukraine’s richest man, Rinat Akhmetov, has positioned itself as an entry point for foreign investors in the energy sector, recently inking agreements with U.S. and European firms. But despite a few deals signed over the last 18 months, Ukraine has yet to see a wave of large-scale foreign investment in its energy sector.
The company's CEO Maxim Timchenko believes the deal with Washington could open the door to further foreign investment in Ukraine and inspire confidence in wartime investing. It could also be a game changer for DTEK, which has had difficulties accessing financing from international financial institutions like the European Bank for Reconstruction over its ownership.
"For me, the financial part is very important, but much more significant is this signal that DFC is ready to support Ukraine and DTEK. They have made an assessment of the risk, understand how to manage it, and are saying that private investors should follow. That's how important this is," Timchenko told reporters.
DTEK opened the battery storage facility last September with American energy firm Fluence Energy Inc., which provided 698 Gridstack batteries. Together, the batteries form a 200-megawatt system that can power 600,000 Ukrainian homes for two hours — reducing blackout risks and helping to stabilize the grid in Kyiv and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
While the DFC loan will primarily refinance loans initially provided by Ukrainian banks, it will also help DTEK build more battery storage with Fluence, Timchenko said. Most developers in Ukraine purchase batteries with Chinese components, but DTEK wanted American products, creating an opportunity to partner with the DFC, he added.
Under President Donald Trump, the U.S. is investing in projects that strictly exclude Chinese parts to compete with sectors dominated by Beijing. In March, the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund — jointly managed by the DFC and Kyiv — inked a deal with defense-tech firm Sine Engineering, which builds software for drones without any Chinese components.
The DFC has long expressed interest in Ukraine’s energy sector and has been in talks with DTEK for several months, likely because it is the largest private player in a sector dominated by state-owned companies.
The company is preparing for winter and needs to restore 4 gigawatts (GW) of power generation by the heating season, when Russia is expected to launch another mass bombing campaign targeting power plants.
Last winter, all of DTEK’s thermal plants were hit, and energy workers have been repairing the damage around the clock ever since. Timchenko told reporters on Sept. 10 that he is confident the company will be ready for another harsh winter.

France picks exiled Russian director Andrey Zvyagintsev’s ‘Minotaur’ as its international Oscar entry. The Russian-language film previously won Cannes’ Grand Prix.
France has submitted Andrey Zvyagintsev’s film “Minotavr” (“Minotaur”) for the Academy Award for Best International Feature Film, Variety reports.
The French Oscar committee chose the film after meeting with the producers, international sales agents, and U.S. distributors of the five shortlisted films.
“Minotaur” was co-produced by Charles Gillibert’s French companies, CG Cinéma and MK Productions. It follows the director of a company as he prepares for mass layoffs when he is ordered to send 14 people to war. Meanwhile, he learns that his wife is having an affair.
The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences will announce a 15-film shortlist for Best International Feature Film on December 15. The nominees will be announced on January 21, and the 99th Academy Awards ceremony will take place on March 14, 2027.
Last year, France submitted Iranian director Jafar Panahi’s “A Simple Accident,” which had won the Palme d’Or at Cannes and later received a nomination.
“Minotaur” is Zvyagintsev’s first film in nearly 10 years. His previous film, “Nelyubov” (“Loveless”), was released in 2017. Zvyagintsev became seriously ill with COVID-19 during the pandemic and underwent a lengthy rehabilitation abroad. He did not return to Russia after the country launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. In May 2026, “Minotaur” won the Grand Prix at the 79th Cannes Film Festival.

Israeli team to compete in Texan 'Meat Up' with kosher Wagyu shawarma - with all the fixings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:36:02 UTC
04:36:02 KST

A 14-member Israeli team will make its debut at the Texas Open Fire Meat Up in October, aiming to win over judges and barbecue fans with an unlikely centerpiece: a roughly 200-kilogram kosher Wagyu beef shawarma cooked entirely over open flames.
The competition, held at Quail Crossing Ranch in Hondo, Texas, brings together pitmasters, chefs and barbecue personalities from around the world. Organizers say more than 30 teams will cook over live fire, with hundreds of pitmasters and influencers expected to attend.
The Israeli team’s entry will include a giant shawarma spit weighing about 440 pounds, mounted on a specially built iron cooking structure and roasted over coals. An Israeli from Or Yehuda, now living in Miami, is building the equipment, which will be transported to Texas for the competition.
The beef will come from a kosher Jewish supplier in Texas, making the shawarma fully kosher. Team captain Ruben E. Maislos, an Israeli meat blogger with around 600,000 Instagram followers, said the choice was intended both to distinguish the Israeli entry and accommodate members of the team who keep kosher.
“This is a great opportunity to represent Israeli and Middle Eastern cuisine,” he told Ynet. “Our twist is kosher Wagyu, because they’re not familiar with that there. Half of the team keeps kosher, so we wanted to respect them and the occasion because we’re representing Israel.”
Wagyu beef has increasingly appeared in the kosher culinary world, including in Israel. For Maislos and his team, however, the challenge will involve far more than simply putting premium beef over a fire.
“In the United States, anything kosher is considered higher quality, and with meat, that’s critical. You don’t want to end up with low-quality meat. We have to plate it Michelin-style, because you can lose points on color and appearance too. It has to look like a photograph. Everything has to look like a million dollars. It’s not only about whether it tastes good.”
The Israeli team will also include chef Charlie Fadida and chef Yehuda Amar, a former contestant on Israel’s Master Chef who now lives in Miami, alongside grilling enthusiasts, meat lovers and content creators.
Competitors are expected to be evaluated on presentation, technique and flavor, with cooking centered entirely on live fire rather than gas or electric equipment.
The team's menu will lean heavily into flavors familiar from Israel's street-food culture. Tahini, amba, zhug, and spices will be brought from Israel and used to prepare the shawarma's seasonings and accompaniments.
Maislos said the current plan is to serve the shawarma with a shot of mint-flavored arak and, if possible, provide an Israeli soundtrack with singer Omer Adam playing in the background.
Asked about criticism that could arise from presenting shawarma as Israeli cuisine, Maislos argued that the dish had become firmly embedded in the country's culinary identity.
“First of all, we’re a Levantine country, and Israel is made up of people who came here from many different countries. We also have an Arab chef on the team,” he said.
“Shawarma became part of Israeli culinary identity a long time ago, even if the Turks or Greeks tell a different story. The Turks will say it’s theirs and the Greeks will say it’s souvlaki. Everyone says something. There are arguments about asado too, and in South America everyone thinks it belongs to them.”
Campaigning in Jewish communities through United States and showcasing Israeli symbols
Maislos plans to campaign among Jewish communities in the United States ahead of the event to draw supporters to the Israeli stand.
“I’ll start a campaign in America telling people to come buy kosher shawarma,” he said. “This isn’t just another version of what they already know. What we’re bringing is completely different from the other teams, which are making steaks, wings, lamb cuts and sweet sauces.”
“We’re no suckers. Israel is fourth in [beef] consumption in the world. No Israeli doesn’t think he’s the world barbecue champion. I don’t want to lose. We’re coming to put on a show.”
The team is also preparing to compete openly under Israeli symbols, with plans to display Israeli flags throughout its stand.
Maislos said he was not overly concerned about possible hostility, citing his experience as a visitor at the event last year.
“I didn’t compete last year, but I visited the festival and competition, and I saw how warmly everyone received me and how impressed they were that I had come from Israel,” he said. “So from my perspective, we need to amaze them with our food, and everything will be fine.”
“Maybe someone will come and say something, because we’re going to put our Israeli flag everywhere. But it’s Texas. They like us there, and I hope they like Mediterranean flavors too. I just hope there won’t be a protest, but whatever happens, we’ll deal with it.”

Ukraine put an Italian-Swiss Skyguard into combat duty. The missile inside is a Cold War design derived from the American Sparrow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:36:00 UTC
04:36:00 KST

Ukraine's air defense forces have put another Western-supplied system to work as the country prepares for a fifth winter of Russian aerial strikes on its energy grid, Militarnyi reported. The 38th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment released the first public footage of the Italian-Swiss Skyguard/Aspide on combat duty.
Ukraine enters the 2026-2027 heating season with an interceptor gap that keeps widening. Patriot deliveries fell from 675 in 2023 to 364 last year and 264 projected for 2026, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. F-16 pilots have resorted to gun-only sorties when missiles run out. Every additional short-range system that covers drones and cruise missiles frees scarce high-end interceptors for the ballistic threats Russia keeps sending.
Ukraine just showed the system in action
The Ukrainian unit posted a video of crews loading missiles onto the launcher and the system standing watch.
The system arrived through two European pipelines. Spain delivered the first batch in November 2022, then-Defense Minister Oleksii Reznikov confirmed. A month earlier, 19 Ukrainian troops had trained on the system at Spain's Zaragoza base. Madrid also asked Switzerland for re-export permission, Texty reported, since the Swiss firm Oerlikon Contraves — now Rheinmetall Air Defense — built the Skyguard fire control unit the missiles are paired with.
Italy pledged additional Skyguard units in February 2023. The Italian launchers differ from the Spanish ones. They carry a target-illumination radar and a TV tracking unit mounted directly on the launcher.
A Cold War-era missile in a drone war
Skyguard/Aspide, a related variant of Italy's Spada, is a short-range air defense system built to guard military sites and critical infrastructure from aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and drones. It pairs a Swiss fire control unit with Italian Aspide missiles derived from the American AIM-7 Sparrow, a radar-guided weapon the US Navy developed starting in the late 1940s to shoot down jet bombers during the Cold War. The system can engage targets at distances up to 12–25 km and altitudes from 15 m to 6,000 meters.
