FBI chief Kash Patel warns online radicalization fueling threats to synagogues, public officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:35:58 UTC
04:35:58 KST

The ability to turn online activity and organization into real-world violence, including attacks against synagogues and elected officials, is the most serious domestic threat currently facing the United States, FBI Director Kash Patel told the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday.
The hearing was the Judiciary Committee's annual FBI oversight hearing, with Patel appearing as the bureau's sole witness. Asked by Republican Sen. Darlin Graham of South Carolina about the leading domestic threat, Patel said the primary mechanism was the "cyber landscape," adding that "the single greatest threat" was the ability to carry out violence through online spaces, whether against children, houses of worship or elected officials.
Patel stressed that he was not necessarily referring to cyberattacks in the sense of hacking computer systems, but rather to the use of the internet, social media and encrypted applications for radicalization, planning and coordinating acts of violence.
One example he cited was a plot foiled in June against the UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House. The US Justice Department said at the time that five people had been arrested and charged with planning an attack against elected officials and participants at the event.
According to the indictments, those involved moved their communications to encrypted chats and planned to use explosive-laden drones to create chaos, followed by snipers who would fire on people fleeing the scene. In some of their communications, the suspects also discussed harming members of Congress whom they claimed were connected to the pro-Israel lobby.
Patel's emphasis on houses of worship is particularly relevant to the Jewish community in the United States following several significant incidents this year in which the internet played a role in either the threat itself or the radicalization process.
On March 12, 41-year-old Ayman Mohammed Ghazali of Dearborn Heights attacked Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Michigan. Following an investigation, the FBI determined that the incident was "an act of terrorism inspired by Hezbollah" aimed at the Jewish community and the large Michigan synagogue.
FBI: Ghazali searched online for synagogues, Jewish institutions prior to attack
According to the FBI's findings, Ghazali began consuming pro-Hezbollah and Iranian content online as early as January. In the days before the attack, he searched online for synagogues and Jewish institutions in the Detroit area, and later searched phrases including "largest gathering of Israelis in Michigan," "Orthodox synagogues," and "Israelis near me." He also looked up planned events at Temple Israel.
On the day of the attack, Ghazali arrived at the synagogue in a Ford F-150 pickup truck containing commercial fireworks and containers filled with flammable material. He rammed the entrance door, opened fire from inside the vehicle and exchanged gunfire with security personnel.
Children and staff were evacuated from the building, and no worshipers or employees were killed. The attacker died during the incident.
During the investigation, the FBI found that minutes before the attack, Ghazali sent videos to his sister in which he described the synagogue as "the largest gathering place for Israelis in the state of Michigan," said he had prepared his vehicle for the attack, and that he intended to "kill as many of them as possible."
The bureau said it found no evidence that he had accomplices and concluded that the attacker had been inspired by Hezbollah ideology.
Other incidents this year have also highlighted the connection between antisemitic threats and online activity. In March, a Chicago resident was indicted after, according to the Justice Department, posting on X/Twitter that he intended to "shoot inside a synagogue." The information was forwarded to the FBI's National Threat Operations Center.
In April, a US soldier stationed at Fort Polk was charged after authorities said he threatened in Discord conversations to enter a synagogue with an AK rifle and kill Jews. According to the Justice Department, the investigation was opened after the FBI received an online tip.
Lone extremists, small groups most difficult to identify, FBI warns
The FBI has previously warned that extremists acting alone or in small groups who become radicalized online and target "soft targets" such as houses of worship are among the most difficult threats to identify in advance.
In June 2025, the FBI and the Department of Homeland Security issued a joint warning about heightened threats to Jewish and Israeli communities in the United States, cautioning that foreign terrorist organizations could exploit events in the Middle East to encourage violence inside the US.
Patel stressed during the hearing that confronting the threat requires closer cooperation between the FBI and state and local police departments. Following the Michigan attack, the FBI also called on houses of worship and schools to work with law enforcement authorities and participate in training for responding to shooting incidents.

Saudi Arabia facing growing pressure on multiple fronts as Houthis escalate in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:35:54 UTC
04:35:54 KST

Saudi Arabia is facing growing pressure from multiple directions as the Houthis in Yemen expand their capabilities and Iran threatens vital infrastructure, and that is causing “great anxiety and pressure” in Riyadh, a source close to the Saudi government has told The Jerusalem Post.
“They’re surrounded from the south and the north and the east,” the source said, adding that the Houthis and the Iran-backed Hashd al-Shaabi in Iraq are major security concerns.
At the same time, Iran poses a different kind of threat, with Riyadh concerned that a direct confrontation could expose critical infrastructure, including desalination facilities, to Iranian missile and drone attacks, the source said, adding: “They definitely thought that they were vulnerable, and they were against the war between Israel-US and Iran.”
Nevertheless, the Saudi approach has been markedly different toward the Houthis, whom Riyadh appears to have initially underestimated.
“I think they miscalculated,” a diplomat in the region told the Post. “They really thought that they had Yemeni forces who could really stand up to the Houthis.”
Riyadh has adopted two fundamentally different approaches toward its adversaries.
With Iran, the preferred strategy is negotiation and mediation rather than direct military confrontation. That is largely because of concerns over the potential consequences of an Iranian attack on Saudi infrastructure.
Houthis progressing along Red Sea coast
The calculation is different regarding the Houthis.
“When it comes to the Houthis, they have a much more aggressive, forward-leaning, military solution,” the source close to the Saudi government said.
Saudi Arabia is supporting Yemeni forces opposed to the Houthis while also providing air support.
But Riyadh’s initial reluctance to employ air power more aggressively allowed the Houthis to make significant gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
The Tihamah coastal plain is largely flat rather than mountainous, making it particularly vulnerable to air power.
“It could have easily been stopped with air power,” the diplomat said, citing platforms such as Apache helicopters and C-130 gunships.
Instead, Riyadh initially relied on anti-Houthi Yemeni forces to halt the advance.
“They had confidence that the Yemeni anti-Houthis would stop them, and there was a kind of hesitancy or reticence to get involved,” the diplomat said.
That hesitation gave the Houthis crucial time to consolidate their position.
“That gave the Houthis the 24 hours they needed to take over the entire coast,” the diplomat said, adding that the decision was a “huge mistake.”
The Saudis, it seems, are deeply disappointed with the performance of forces led by Tariq Saleh, which failed to prevent the Houthi advance despite receiving training, funding, and weapons from Gulf states.
The forces were initially supported by the United Arab Emirates and later by Saudi Arabia, the source close to the Saudi government said.
“In hindsight, they think that the Tariq al-Saleh forces who didn’t fight, despite being paid and trained and armed,... must have disappointed them,” the source said.
Riyadh is now making greater use of air power. The Houthis have claimed more than 40 airstrikes over the past 24 hours.
The shift in approach has so far helped prevent the Houthis from expanding eastward toward Marib and capturing additional territory around Taiz and other parts of Yemen.
Trump refuses to strike Houthis
US President Donald Trump has refused to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. While CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper did visit Saudi Arabia over the weekend, US officials also met in Oman with Houthi representatives, who reportedly gave them a commitment not to target US ships.
So, why is the US not assisting with the Houthis?
“If it’s for technical, strategic, and military reasons, I can understand,” the source close to the Saudi government said. “If it’s a political chasing away of America, then that’s really problematic.”
Trump’s approach toward Riyadh could be influenced by a number of factors, including disagreements over Saudi support for US-led regional security initiatives.
Trump might believe the Saudis have not been sufficiently supportive, or he could view the US military presence in the region as overextended.
Trump’s strategic thinking is often difficult to predict, the source stressed.
“He’s very capricious,” the source said, adding that a decision to reduce US support could have consequences beyond the immediate political dispute.
Israel assisting Saudi Arabia against Houthis, diplomats say
Despite the growing pressure, Saudi Arabia remains pragmatic in its foreign and security policy, including publicly seeking greater assistance from Israel, the source said.
Israel is assisting Saudi Arabia, with CENTCOM mediating the sharing of intelligence on the Houthis, diplomats in the region told the Post.
“If it gets really bad for the Saudis and they need help, and they’re not going to get it from anyone else,” Riyadh could potentially reconsider its current positions, the source said, adding that its decision-making would ultimately depend on the nature and severity of the assistance required.
“It depends on the nature of the help they need and how desperate they get,” the source said. “The Saudis are ultimately very pragmatic. Regime survival comes before anything else.”

US Federal Reserve hikes rates, sees more tightening in search of 'timelier' drop in inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:35:32 UTC
04:35:32 KST

The US Federal Reserve (Fed) raised interest rates on Wednesday and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the coming months, with new US central bank chief Kevin Warsh joining a unanimous decision that effectively acknowledges the Trump administration's so-far inability to control inflation.
While US President Donald Trump had promised to lower prices on his watch, the combined impact of his global import tariffs, an energy shock following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, and capital spending from the artificial intelligence boom has kept price pressures intense enough that the Fed felt it needed to raise its benchmark overnight interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to the 3.75%-4.00% range.
New policy projections showed 16 of 18 policymakers anticipate at least one more quarter-percentage-point hike by the end of this year, with only two seeing rates remain stable from here. Warsh apparently again did not submit a rate projection.
US dollar rises against euro following Warsh's first policy shift
This is the first policy shift under the new Fed chief, who took office in late May after Trump selected him with the expectation that he would cut rates.
The US dollar rose against the euro after the Fed's announcement, while US Treasury bond yields held largely steady, having already weakened in anticipation of the hike. After hitting a 19-year high above 5% on Monday, the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was trading at 4.958%, compared to 4.946% just before the announcement.
The 30-year bond yield dipped to 5.312% after trading at 5.327% just before the announcement. Stocks were mostly higher, with the S&P 500 index up 0.3% and the Nasdaq Composite up 0.7%.
Market bets on a rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in late October ticked up to 56.5% from 54% before the hike, according to CME Group's FedWatch Tool.
"The Federal Reserve's decision today to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point reflects its continued focus on addressing persistent inflation. While inflation has moderated from peak levels, it has remained elevated enough to prompt additional action from the Federal Open Market Committee," said Michele Raneri, head of US research and consulting at TransUnion in Chicago.
The Fed's new policy statement and economic projections, by contrast, show the central bank opening the door to tighter monetary policy through next year, with the policy rate rising to the 4.00%-4.25% range by the end of this year and ending 2027 at the same level.
"Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2% goal," the central bank said in its policy statement after the end of a two-day meeting.
While the statement withheld forward guidance on upcoming policy decisions, as is Warsh's preference, the decision is likely to ease doubts that the Fed chief would hold off on tighter policy out of deference to Trump, a lingering question during his first months in office.
The statement dropped a previous reference attributing current elevated inflation to "supply shocks," particularly in the energy sector, a nod to concerns among policymakers, including Warsh, that price pressures were too broad to be comfortable with.
Warsh is scheduled to hold a press conference beginning at 2:30 p.m. local time to elaborate on the decision.
Rate increase to determine results of upcoming US midterm elections
The rate increase was announced less than two months ahead of midterm elections that will determine whether Trump's Republicans maintain control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency. The Republicans are facing an uphill battle with voters angry about gasoline prices that are about a third higher than a year ago and interest rates on home mortgages that have been rising steadily this year. The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is approaching 7%.
Policymakers' new quarterly economic projections raised inflation estimates, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, to 3.7% versus the 3.6% projected at the Fed's June meeting. Inflation is not projected to return to the 2% target until 2029, a year later than previously expected.
Economic growth was raised slightly from 2.2% to 2.3%, while the unemployment rate is expected to end the year at 4.1%, versus the 4.3% projected in June.
Warsh's characterization at his press conference of the logic behind the rate increase and the likelihood of further action will be important in shaping the reaction in financial markets that have been raising yields on long-term US Treasury bonds. The rate hike on Wednesday was widely expected, but investors will look to the Fed chief for more information on what might prompt further increases in borrowing costs.
Warsh has pledged to lower inflation back to 2% "clearly and at sufficient speed" by raising rates as needed.
Trump calls for interest rates of 1% or lower
US President Donald Trump called for sharply lower interest rates on Wednesday, saying rates in the United States should be 1% or lower.
"Interest rates in the United States should be 1%, or less," Trump said.
Trump also called for rates to be lowered quickly, saying, "Lower interest rates for the United States of America, and fast."

Air Force Eyes New-Build F-16s to Boost Fighter Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:34:37 UTC
04:34:37 KST

The Air Force will consider acquiring new F-16 Fighting Falcon jets to help fill capacity shortfalls in its aging fighter fleet, multiple people familiar with the matter told Air & Space Forces Magazine. These discussions are happening as the Air Force is building its proposed fiscal 2028 budget and the five-year spending plan that goes with it.
Buying new F-16s—which would be the U.S.’s first in more than 20 years—is viewed as one way to quickly build back lost fighter capacity, as Lockheed Martin continues to operate a hot production line for the aircraft. Buying F-16s from Lockheed, which also produces the F-35 Lightning II, would have parallels to the decision to acquire F-15EX Eagle IIs from Boeing, which likewise came after a yearslong gap in USAF purchases.
The new-build F-16s, potentially dubbed “F-16G” to reflect upgrades from existing F-16C and D models, could be on the agenda for discussion when Air Force four-stars gather this fall for a Corona gathering of top service officials.
Lockheed Martin deferred questions to the Air Force: “This topic is best addressed by the U.S. government, but we stand ready to support the U.S. Air Force and its mission needs,” Lockheed said in a statement. “Our proven products are the backbone of the USAF fleet and provide the most advanced and versatile capabilities to ensure air dominance now and decades to come.”
The Air Force, in a written response to Air & Space Forces Magazine, said it is examining its options as it looks to the future.
“The Department of the Air Force is in initial phases of analyzing options for the next Future Years Defense Program,” an Air Force spokesperson said. “At this stage, we have neither defined the precise mission requirements nor the spectrum of options that could fill it.”
Lockheed currently produces F-16E and F models, single- and dual-seat variants respectively, for the United Arab Emirates. The company moved its production line for Block 70 F-16s in 2019 from Fort Worth, Texas, to Greenville, S.C.
If the Air Force decided to buy more F-16s, Lockheed would likely keep its Greenville production line going. The potential upgraded F-16 from that line is being referred to as a G model by those familiar with the discussions.
The Air Force today has 826 F-16s in its inventory, with 484 of those operated by the Active-Duty force. The jets average 34 years old, however, and the newest in the inventory have been flying since 2005.
USAF F-16s carry out a variety of critical missions, including air-to-air and air-to-ground strikes. F-16s that carry out suppression of enemy air defense missions are referred to as “Wild Weasels” and have seen heavy action in operations against Iran.
New F-16 purchases would drive other movement in the industry. Both Pratt & Whitney and GE Aerospace make engines that go on the F-16. Pratt, which is owned by RTX, announced Sept. 15 it has licensed Hermeus to manufacture its F100-PW-229 used on the F-15 and F-16, saying the agreement will strengthen the U.S. defense industrial base by creating a new source for the widely used engine.
Northrop Grumman, which is developing two major upgrades for existing F-16s, would also likely benefit. The company is working on the Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, or IVEWS, and an upgraded large aperture targeting pod called LITENING LA.
IVEWS, also known as the AN/ALQ-257, is an advanced electronic warfare system providing radar warning, active jamming, and detecting, identifying and locating of potential threats.
A source familiar with the issue, who asked not to be named to speak more freely, said any new F-16 would likely have IVEWS and multiple other new capabilities placing it not only beyond the legacy C and D fighters, but also the Block 70 fighters Lockheed is currently building.
“If the Air Force were to buy a new F-16, this would not be your grandfather’s F-16,” the source said. “This would be more akin to buying an F-15EX.”
The source said buying more F-16s would make sense for the Air Force, since Lockheed and Boeing are facing capacity constraints limiting how many F-35As and F-15EXs, respectively, they can build. And the service’s existing fleet of F-16s has been flown hard in the wars of recent decades, the source said.
“There’s only so many times you can do a service life extension program before you begin to lose the strength and integrity of the airframe itself,” the source said.

Strong economy, sticky inflation, geopolitical risks drove Fed rate hike: Warsh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:33:48 UTC
04:33:48 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
- US central bank unanimously raises federal funds rate by 25 basis points after holding it steady in July
US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said Wednesday that a strengthening economy, persistent inflation and heightened geopolitical risks prompted the central bank to raise interest rates after keeping them unchanged at its previous meeting.
Asked what had changed during the seven weeks between meetings, Warsh said recent data, particularly labor market indicators, showed that the US economy had strengthened.
Inflation trends during the summer, meanwhile, failed to demonstrate sufficiently rapid progress toward the Fed’s 2% target, while the geopolitical outlook also changed, he said without referring to the US-Iran war.
“All three of those things lent themselves to a firm, unanimous decision today,” said Warsh.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) unanimously raised the federal funds rate Wednesday by 25 basis points to a range between 3.75% and 4%, following its decision to hold rates steady in July.
Inflation ‘too high’ for ‘too long’
Warsh said the unemployment rate remained low at 4.1%, with job openings and average weekly hours increasing, allowing the Fed to concentrate on the price stability side of its dual mandate.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long,” he said. “This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.”
Based on the latest consumer and producer price data, annual headline personal consumption expenditures inflation was likely around 3.6% in August, while core PCE inflation was running at approximately 3.2%, he said.
Too many categories continued to register price increases above 3% on six- and 12-month bases, Warsh added.
Financial conditions not restrictive
The rate increase removed “a dose of accommodation,” said Warsh, adding that he and other policymakers were “hard-pressed” to describe broad financial conditions before the meeting as restrictive.
He dismissed suggestions that the Fed had followed financial markets, which had largely priced in the increase.
“We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation,” he said, citing the employment trajectory and the economy’s underlying strength.
Warsh declined to signal whether the move would begin a series of increases, saying he was “not in the forward guidance business.”
He also said estimates of the neutral interest rate had no operational effect on the Fed’s decisions.
Fed forecasts growth, inflation above target
Median projections released after the meeting showed real gross domestic product expanding 2.3% this year and 2.4% next year.
Headline PCE inflation was projected at 3.7% this year before easing to 3.2% next year, while unemployment was expected to remain around 4.1%.
The median policymaker forecast placed the federal funds rate at 4.1% at the end of this year and next.
Warsh said he did not submit his projection and emphasized that the forecasts belonged to his 18 colleagues.
Higher Treasury yields reflect economic strength
Warsh attributed rising long-term Treasury yields partly to stronger economic activity, increased competition for capital amid heavy technology-sector investment and geopolitical tensions.
The Fed also established an artificial intelligence task force that is expected to report by year’s end on the technology’s implications for the economy and monetary policy, he added.

Black has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and said he had no knowledge of Epstein’s criminal activities.
His lawyers criticized the contempt resolution shortly after it passed Wednesday. “This an outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr Black. The House of Representatives has rushed through every stage of this inquiry,” they said.
“We intend to pursue our litigation challenging this action and will hold the committee and Chairman Comer accountable in the courts.”
The committee, chaired by Republican James Comer, then issued two subpoenas: one demanding that Black produce all NDAs “to which he is a party” and another requiring him to appear before the committee again for a deposition.
Black did not appear for his scheduled 3 September deposition and did not produce all of the NDAs sought by the committee.
He instead sued Comer and the committee, arguing that the subpoenas were “invalid” and exceeded the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection” to its legislative purpose. He also argued that the subpoenas would “expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein”.
On Tuesday, Black’s attorneys said that the committee under Comer and the representative Robert Garcia, its top Democrat, had “lost sight of its legislative purpose and is abusing its power”. They described the subpoenas as “illegitimate, illegal and a textbook abuse of power designed to bully and destroy legal protections of private citizens” and reiterated that Black “never abused a woman”, “was never blackmailed by Epstein” and “had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s heinous conduct”.
On Wednesday morning, more than a dozen survivors of Epstein’s abuse praised the House oversight committee for their vote.
“Survivors have fought for years to bring the truth about Epstein’s network into the open and have helped create this moment of accountability,” they said on Wednesday morning before the House vote. “Congress now has an opportunity to build on that work by following the investigative leads contained in the Epstein files wherever they go and demanding answers from the powerful people connected to them.”

Ukraine is seeking to establish a First Loss Fund to support war-risk insurance for businesses, with a one-percentage-point increase in VAT being considered as a way to raise Ukraine’s contribution to the mechanism, according to speakers at the European Business Association’s “Global Outlook: The Next Economy” conference.
The proposed mechanism comes in response to mounting losses businesses have suffered from missile and drone strikes, particularly as companies in logistics and other sectors struggle to insure their assets against war risks. The fund is intended to make such coverage more accessible and help attract additional financing from international partners.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine wants to raise about $1 billion domestically and attract at least another $1 billion from international partners, with the potential for $2-3 billion in additional financing.
A one-percentage-point VAT increase was discussed as one possible source of Ukraine’s contribution to the fund.
Business leaders debate VAT increase
Speakers at the conference – Oleksandr Kravchenko, minister of economy and environment of Ukraine; Tomas Fiala, CEO of Dragon Capital; Oleksandr Komarov, CEO of Kyivstar; Oleksandr Farkosh, general director of JTI Ukraine; and Roman Yanovych, general director of Nestlé Ukraine and Moldova – supported the need for a functioning war-risk insurance mechanism but expressed different views on how it should be financed.
Lithuania Says Downed Drone Was Russian Gerbera
The proposal comes as war-risk insurance remains expensive and unavailable for some businesses and assets. Tomas Fiala, CEO of Dragon Capital, said that only about 5% of the company’s assets are currently insured, while insurance in Ukraine costs more than 6% of asset value.
Fiala also pointed to significant losses at Lloyd’s, saying reinsurance losses over the past two years had reached around 200%.
Fiala said international partners expect Ukraine to make a contribution of its own. He also said he had recently met with the World Bank, which is consulting the Ukrainian government on war-risk insurance. Businesses expected the government to pair the proposed tax increase with efforts to reduce the shadow economy and corruption, he added.
Regarding the proposed one-percentage-point VAT increase, Fiala said he understood the rationale behind the measure because he could see what the government wanted to achieve, while noting that Dragon Capital would not be a major beneficiary of the proposed fund.
Komarov of Kyivstar said a one-percentage-point VAT increase would be understandable if it was tied to a mechanism addressing the insurance problem.
He also called for greater efforts to reduce the shadow economy and increase state revenues from the gray market.
According to Komarov, the existing insurance process involves numerous conditions, bureaucracy, and reinsurers, with disputes potentially requiring proceedings in English courts. He also said Kyivstar had sought compensation for losses sustained in 2022 and received about 50% of the amount in 2025, worth more than $10 million.
Kyivstar currently pays 7-8% of the value of its assets for war-risk insurance and cannot insure some assets in central Ukraine, Komarov said.
Yanovych of Nestlé Ukraine and Moldova said he was concerned that a VAT increase could push up prices and weaken consumer demand for products such as noodles, ketchup and mayonnaise. However, he added that he did not see an effective alternative to establishing a war-risk insurance system and argued that such a mechanism is necessary to maintain Ukraine’s investment attractiveness.
Yanovych said the availability of war-risk insurance is important for companies deciding whether to continue operating and investing in Ukraine rather than moving production abroad.
Shadow economy as a potential source of funding
Farkosh of JTI Ukraine, said the tobacco sector’s shadow market accounts for 19.8% and costs the state approximately Hr. 27 billion ($604.8 million) in lost revenue.
The discussion suggested that reducing illegal tobacco flows could provide an alternative source of additional state revenues that could be directed toward financing the proposed mechanism.
Previously, Kyiv Post wrote that raising VAT can fuel inflation. An official familiar with the tax discussions who asked to remain anonymous told Kyiv Post that VAT increases are understood to push inflation upwards for the first 12 months before the impact eases:
“VAT is an indirect tax that influences the price directly, so the military levy is less inflationary. VAT is indeed paid by those who consume rather than earn. We counted that a 1% increase in VAT adds about 0.7–0.8% to inflation.”
The VAT option, of course, has the advantage of being collected from everyone.
“The vulnerable will always pay military levy, but entrepreneurs and shadow economy actors won’t pay it – a VAT increase would force them to do so,” the source added.

Labor's long-awaited migration overhaul targets temporary visas

Labor to unveil delayed migration overhaul targeting temporary visas
In short:
The federal government will tighten temporary visa rules in a bid to reduce net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.
Labor is turning to regulatory changes to achieve the target after talks with the Coalition over stronger legislation broke down.
What's next?
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke will unveil details of the temporary visa changes in a National Press Club address today.
Labor will rely on tighter rules for temporary visas to reduce Australia's net overseas migration rather than seek support for new laws to achieve its target.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke will use an address at the National Press Club (NPC) today to unveil long-awaited measures that target temporary migrants seeking to bring family members to Australia, switch visas or extend their stay.
The overhaul will be pursued through regulation, including changes to visa conditions and application processes, as the federal government has no clear path to pass stronger legislation after compromise talks with the Coalition broke down.
In a speech titled The Work of Managing the Migration Program: Who Arrives, Who Stays, Who Leaves, Mr Burke will outline how the government plans to meet its target of reducing net overseas migration from about 300,000 now to 225,000 by 2028.
Mr Burke had intended to announce the policy six weeks ago but was forced to abruptly postpone his address amid disagreement between ministers weighing competing priorities.
Today, Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said reporting on the disagreements had been "overstated."
"We've been having sensible, detailed conversations because that is what a mature government does," she said.
"We want to have a sensible policy as a government that recognises that some immigration is still very important to this country.
"We also want to make sure the debate retains at its centre the reminder that Australia has been built on migration."
The ABC reported on Wednesday that the policy would include an effective ban on international students bringing family members to Australia.
While international student numbers are expected to be left untouched, the ABC has been told they will effectively lose the ability to bring their families to Australia under the crackdown.
Last financial year, 337,427 student visas were granted. Of those, 45,991 went to secondary applicants, classed as dependents or family.
Burke says legislation would have been 'better' option
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor met twice last week as Labor sought potential support for its immigration reforms.
The government hoped to pass legislation that would restrict the time people had to make onshore asylum claims and limit international students' right of appeal to remain in Australia.
But talks stalled after the Coalition presented a list of demands including tougher restrictions on so-called ISIS brides and linking migration to housing completions.
Having effectively dealt itself out of the reforms, Coalition figures have since argued the government already has sufficient powers to curb migration through regulation.
During Question Time on Wednesday, Mr Burke said the "best" outcome would have been to tackle migration through legislation.
"In the absence of that, there are still more levers the government will be able to use," he said.
Labor accused of 'starving' regions
Under pressure to reduce overseas arrivals, Mr Burke has already made sweeping changes to the migration system, pausing or slowing down the processing of working holiday maker visas in July, and re-prioritising the processing of skilled visas.
The changes, under Ministerial Direction 119, mean any worker applying for a skilled visa from overseas is now at the back of the queue, pushing visa wait times from days to over a year in some cases.
Asked by Indi MP Helen Haines about the "go slow" on working holiday visas hurting regional Australia, Mr Burke told parliament the government needed to get net overseas migration "down".
"We need to make sure that we deal with the numbers overall and do so in a sensible, targeted way that provides the easiest pathway through for the Australian economy," he said.
Ahead of Mr Burke's NPC speech, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson released a statement also accusing Labor of "starving" regional Australia of labour and tourists.
"The government would rather destroy industries in regional Australia than face the problem of unskilled arrivals and students head on," she said.
One Nation and Coalition poised to critique Labor
Senator Hanson pre-emptively criticised Labor's migration proposal because the government's net overseas migration forecasts, if reached, meant an extra one million people in Australia over the next four years.
One Nation this week announced it would cut the number of visas by 750,000 over three years, resulting in net negative migration.
The proposal targeting international students and the families of skilled migrants has been criticised by the Coalition and Labor, with Environment Minister Murray Watt arguing it would "probably drive the Australian economy into recession".
The opposition is finalising its own migration proposal, which Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam has said it will release in the coming weeks.
Nationals Leader Matt Canavan insisted he was on a unity ticket with Coalition leader Angus Taylor who agreed immigration numbers "must come down."
"We've got to get this right in terms of balancing the impacts to the economy," he said.
Asked if it was a problem that the Coalition was going to be the last to release its immigration policy, Senator Canavan said the election was still a long way away.
"I don't see that as an issue seen as the election is not for another 18 months," he said.

Election analysis: Israel's 3.25% threshold has got to go
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:32:16 UTC
04:32:16 KST

- i24NEWS
- Analysis & Opinion
- Election analysis: Israel's 3.25% threshold has got to go
Election analysis: Israel's 3.25% threshold has got to go
The problem in Israel is that even this goal isn't achieved. Enter the "technical bloc." Parties merge with a wink and a nod: Have a shotgun wedding to register a joint list to pass the 3.25% mark
Israel's election campaign is dominated by a number, not by issues. On October 27, Israel will chart the future of its security after October 7, the future of its politics after the 2023 judicial overhaul protests, and the future of its society in the drafting of Haredi yeshiva students.
And Israeli television panels are dominated by none of these. Instead, politics in Israel are dominated by the magic number of 3.25%.
That's Israel's electoral threshold. A party that gets 3.25% of the vote in the October 27 election nabs four seats in the Knesset. Get 3.2499999%? Your party is shut out completely.
That difference can be decisive. A small number of votes cast can also cast a verdict on the result of the entire election. Whether a party gets 3.25% (four seats) or 3.249999% (zero) can swing the entire parliamentary math, especially in a closely divided country.
For example: The Amcha Israel Party of former general Ofir Winter sits in polls either just below or just above the threshold. Pass the threshold by a hair, and add four seats to the pro-Benjamin Netanyahu bloc. Miss the threshold by a hair, have votes wiped out, and give seats by default to the opposition. The difference in real-world public support is slight; the impact on real-world politics is great.
So great that Israeli analysts almost universally see the threshold as the single most important factor in deciding the entire election. While a campaign should focus on issues at play, discussion is instead bogged down by what, in practice, really matters in determining an outcome: a number with a decimal point, not critical issues about Israel's security or identity.
In a democratic process, that's a serious flaw. Even beyond the campaign chatter, the fundamental goal of an election is to translate public will into public policy. Setting a threshold high enough to decide an election foils that goal and even undermines public legitimacy.
Of course, every parliamentary democracy without first-past-the-post districts must set some threshold. Countries across Europe do, from Germany (at 5%) through Italy and Spain (at 3%) and the Netherlands (famously, or infamously, at 0.67%). Israel itself set a threshold at 1% before upping it to 1.5% in 1992, to 2% in 2006, and then to 3.25% in 2015.
A higher threshold does have merits. In principle, a higher threshold weeds out smaller parties with little public support but substantial leverage in deciding parliamentary majorities. To many, that was the goal in Israel: To streamline the work of the government and Knesset by forcing smaller players to merge. At 3.25%, the parliament might still be left with goldfish, but at least it wouldn't have minnows.
The problem in Israel is that even this goal isn't achieved. Enter the "technical bloc." Parties merge with a wink and a nod: Have a shotgun wedding to register a joint list to pass the 3.25% mark. After elections? Wink, nod, and break up.
Suggested articles
The Knesset has lax rules about factions breaking into smaller units. So what ran as a unit of four seats on October 27 could become two separate units of two seats come November 27. As a result, the 3.25% threshold did not even achieve the core purpose for which it was set. In Israel's recent history, these scenarios have frequently played out, for example, with the one-seat far-right Noam faction of sometimes-deputy-minister/always-nuisance Avi Maoz.
The time for change has come. Israel must lower the electoral threshold back to 2% and, constitutionally, find ways to penalize parties that break up as a technical bloc.
True, any threshold by definition wastes votes. But the electoral and democratic stakes are lower. The psychological—and mathematical—impact of a wasted 1.99999% of the vote is substantially lower than that of 3.2499999%. In the aggregate, a given election could still lead to a similar number of lost votes and even to a threshold playing a decisive role. But the risk is more distributed when the threshold number is distributed.
So after October 27, let's tackle the security, political, and cultural issues facing Israel. And let's also take on a critical constitutional one: Lowering a single critical number that does so much damage.

130 lawyers say UK Israel settlement sanctions 'fall far short'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:28:33 UTC
04:28:33 KST

Breadcrumb
UK sanctions on Israeli settlements ‘fall far short’, lawyers warn
More than 130 legal experts, including lawyers and legal academics, have called on British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to introduce wider UK sanctions on Israeli settlements, arguing that recently announced measures “fall far short” of Britain’s obligations under a 2024 International Court of Justice (ICJ) advisory opinion that found Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory unlawful.
The six-page letter was sent to Burnham on Tuesday, following Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s announcement of a ban on imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The measures prompted a scathing response from Israel.
"We note the Foreign Secretary’s statement that the sanctions regime targets illegal settlements and settlement expansion, and not Israel. The obligations identified by the ICJ in the 2024 Advisory Opinion, and the subsequent General Assembly resolution endorsing it, however, attach to the occupation as a whole, and the Government has itself found that ethnic cleansing is taking place," the letter read.
"It is notable, by contrast to the improperly narrow approach to the sanctions regime adopted towards Israel, the UK’s Russia sanctions are not confined to economic activity in occupied Ukrainian territory," it added.
"They extend to Russian banks, energy companies, state-linked enterprises, shipping networks, exports, imports, investment activity, financial services and other sectors of the Russian economy because those structures are viewed as enabling, financing or benefiting from Russia's aggression against Ukraine."
The lawyers also referred to Article 6(3) of the Arms Trade Treaty, which prohibits arms transfers where a state knows the items would be used to commit genocide, crimes against humanity or grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions.
The letter also called on the government to ensure that money raised by UK-registered charities is not used to support settlement activities.
Labour MP Melanie Ward previously said Israeli settlements had received at least £28 million in donations from 32 charities in England and Wales, as the Charity Commission announced a fact-finding inquiry into charities operating in settlements in August.
Ralph Wilde, a UCL professor of international law who has acted as senior counsel and legal adviser to the Arab League in proceedings before the ICJ, told The New Arab that the illegality of the way the occupation is conducted, including the establishment of settlements, should be distinguished from what he described as the more fundamental illegality of the occupation itself.
"Yes, the settlements are illegal. Yes, genocide is illegal. But even if there weren't settlements, and even if there wasn't a genocide, Israel would still be acting illegally because it doesn't even have a legal right to be there in the first place," Wilde told The New Arab.
"And that's a more fundamental illegality, because it goes to the very presence itself."
Wilde said the UK had previously argued that it was neither possible nor advisable to determine whether the occupation itself was illegal, maintaining that it could continue lawfully until a peace agreement was reached.
But he described Britain's acknowledgement last week that the occupation is illegal as a significant, albeit limited, shift.
"The big shift from last week is that the UK is now saying that the occupation is illegal," he said.
However, Wilde said Britain had essentially "just acknowledged reality" without following the ICJ's reasoning to its conclusion.
"They haven't followed through and said what the court said, which was that because the occupation is illegal, it should end."
Wilde argued that further action should be taken in response to the ICJ's findings on Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory, including sanctions against Israel and individual Israelis whom he said support the occupation, including political leaders.
"There needs to be a complete end of any form of assistance given to Israel-military assistance, intelligence, or other assistance-because there's no way to be sure that that assistance is not, in one way or another, assisting the illegal occupation, and the UK is under a legal obligation not to provide assistance," he told TNA.
Meanwhile, another signatory to Tuesday's letter, SOAS professor of law Nimer Sultany, emphasised in a statement that "the elephant in the room is that the occupation is not a bug, it’s a feature."
“Israel’s political consensus opposes Palestinian statehood. Thus, ending Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territories, as determined by the International Court of Justice, requires immediate, effective and comprehensive actions by the UK government, not a piece-meal approach.”
The latest remarks follow international outcry over escalating attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the West Bank and an Israeli tender for 1,200 homes in the E1 settlement, east of Jerusalem.
The developments prompted Britain to announce a ban on imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank, alongside targeted measures against settlements and those facilitating or profiting from them.
11 other countries, including France and Canada, subsequently announced similar measures.
Meanwhile, Israeli rights group B'Tselem said on Monday that Israeli actions in the occupied West Bank form part of a wider project aimed at making it impossible for Palestinians to exist collectively as a people.
It identified five interconnected tactics and policies in the West Bank: "violence, ethnic cleansing, movement restrictions, economic strangulation, social and political destruction".

Australian wheelchairs donated to Gaza stuck in Jordan warehouse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:25:12 UTC
04:25:12 KST

Australian wheelchairs donated to Gaza stuck in Jordan warehouse
In short:
Hundreds of wheelchairs, donated by two Australian charities to help injured children in Gaza, are stuck in warehouses in Jordan due to Israeli restrictions.
The shipments are sitting in storage facilities managed by the Jordan Hashemite Charity Organization.
What's next?
Israel says it has approved the entry of thousands of wheelchairs into Gaza "without any quantitative restrictions".
More than 900 wheelchairs, donated by two Australian charities to help injured children in Gaza, are stuck in warehouses in Jordan due to Israeli restrictions on aid deliveries into the war-ravaged strip.
Two shipments from New South Wales-based charity Kids on Wheels Alliance arrived in Jordan in February 2025, while a third, from Wheelchairs for Kids based in Western Australia, arrived in October 2025.
But instead of being delivered to children with severe mobility issues inside Gaza, they remain sitting in storage facilities managed by the Jordan Hashemite Charity Organization (JHCO).
At one of those sites on the outskirts of the Jordanian capital Amman, Abdullah Al-Balawi, a doctor with the Palestinian Australian New Zealand Medical Association (PANZMA), told the ABC he was "feeling great pain" seeing the boxes piled up.
"These wheelchairs that are dedicated to Gaza's amputee children and those paralysed as a result of the war … they do not pose any threat," he said.
The JHCO said the Israeli agency responsible for aid coordination in Gaza, COGAT, had blocked the chairs from getting into Gaza, but an Israeli government source denied that an application for the Australian wheelchairs had been rejected.
COGAT did not answer the ABC's specific questions about the Australian donations, but in a general response said it had let thousands of wheelchairs into the strip during the war.
The ABC has been told Australian officials have raised the blocking of the wheelchair donations with Israel multiple times.
Charity says the sooner chairs can get to kids, 'the better'
Wheelchairs for Kids WA has been making specialised wheelchairs for children for more than two decades.
Its factory in Wangara, in Perth's northern suburbs, is staffed by volunteers and can produce and pack 120 wheelchairs each week — complete with knitted rugs and toys for children.
The wheelchairs are built to handle difficult terrain and are designed to grow with the children, helping negate the need for a replacement every few years.
"We'd like to help any little kid in the world who needs a wheelchair," said the organisation's co-founder Brother Olly Pickett AM, the 2025 Senior Australian of the Year.
"We'd like to help them as best we can, and so that's the reason we sent them over there."
Brother Olly said his team was not "terribly pleased" to hear the wheelchairs it had produced and dispatched to the region were stranded in Jordan, and did not really understand the cause of the hold-up.
"The sooner they come out of there and get to the kids, the better, and the little kids can get a much better life," he said.
"I think there's a lot of children waiting for them who have had amputations, and so they won't be able to walk around or get around.
"Once they get a wheelchair, they can get out and about, which would be wonderful."
UNICEF, the United Nations children's agency, said the war had left more than 11,000 children in Gaza with potentially life-changing injuries requiring long-term rehabilitation and potential permanent disabilities.
That includes children who have suffered amputations and traumatic brain and spinal cord injuries.
'We want to deliver a message to the world'
The JHCO submitted an application in late February 2025 for the first two consignments of wheelchairs, from the Kids on Wheels Alliance, to be included in a convoy heading to Gaza.
It said the application was rejected soon after, with Israeli authorities saying medical equipment and medicines were not approved for inclusion in that convoy.
The organisation said its application had remained "pending" ever since, with Israeli officials not providing any update since the initial rejection.
Because of that, the JHCO said it had been unable to make a subsequent application for the third consignment of wheelchairs from WA.
"The wheelchairs are sadly, it appears, blocked from entering Gaza to the children that need them most," Shaoquett Moselmane, chair of the Kids on Wheels Alliance, told the ABC.
An Israeli government source told the ABC that no aid was allowed to enter Gaza from mid-March to mid-May after a ceasefire in the strip collapsed. The ceasefire resumed for a few months, before Jordanian military-coordinated aid convoys were suspended in September 2025 after a shooting at the Allenby Bridge crossing between Jordan and the occupied West Bank.
The source insisted there would have been an opportunity for the wheelchairs to be delivered in that window, and said Jordanian authorities could pass the shipment to other NGOs or the United Nations to ship into Gaza instead.
But PANZMA said even if it tried to deliver the wheelchairs to Gaza through a United Nations shipment, passage into the strip would not be guaranteed and the move would incur significant extra costs.
"We want to deliver a message to the world," Dr Al-Balawi said.
"What is the impediment to the entrance of these wheelchairs into Gaza and reaching the children?
"The humanitarian aid must not stop. This is part of the stubbornness of the other side by not letting in this aid, the wheelchairs being only a part of it."
Loading...
One informed source, from outside of the region, said the wheelchairs had been blocked because of concerns among Israeli authorities that the wheelchairs could be "dual use" — effectively classifying the civilian items as potential weapons.
Human rights organisations, including Gisha, have regularly criticised Israel for using a very broad definition of "dual use", arguing it goes so far as to include items like torches and tent poles.
COGAT says it has let thousands of wheelchairs into Gaza
The ABC sent a series of questions, as well as reference numbers and dates of application, to COGAT, asking why the wheelchairs have been blocked from being included in Jordanian humanitarian convoys.
COGAT did not answer those specific questions, instead responding in general terms about the amount of medical equipment it had allowed into Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire.
"The State of Israel allows and facilitates the entry of medical equipment and equipment required for people with disabilities into the Gaza Strip, in cooperation with aid organisations and the international community," it said in a statement.
"Since the beginning of the ceasefire, approximately 22,000 tons of medical equipment and medicines have entered the Gaza Strip, in accordance with requests submitted by international organisations."
COGAT insisted it had approved the entry of thousands of wheelchairs into Gaza "without any quantitative restrictions".
"In addition, in cases where dual-use equipment is required to address the needs of people with disabilities, COGAT works together with international organisations operating on the ground to find solutions that will enable the entry of the required equipment," it said.
Australian Minister for International Development Anne Aly said Australia had been among countries pressuring Israel to "allow humanitarian aid to flow unhindered to Gaza".
"We continue to call on Israel to comply with its obligations under international law, including the binding orders of the International Court of Justice to enable the provision of medical supplies to Palestinians throughout Gaza," Dr Aly told the ABC in a statement.
"This should include allowing wheelchairs for injured children that have been generously donated by Australian organisations, including ones made by Wheelchairs for Kids in my electorate of Cowan."

US Military Fits HMMWVs and HEMTT Trucks With Ukraine-Style Anti-Drone Cages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:24:28 UTC
04:24:28 KST

- Category
- World
US Military Fits HMMWVs and HEMTT Trucks With Ukraine-Style Anti-Drone Cages
US military forces are testing vehicle modifications based on lessons from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, outfitting HMMWV utility vehicles and Heavy Expanded Mobility Tactical Trucks (HEMTT) with anti-drone mesh cages, according to Defense Express on September 16.
During the Exercise Thunderstruck 3.0 military maneuvers, troops rehearsed convoy defense and casualty evacuation while operating under simulated aerial threats from uncrewed aerial systems.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Footage released from the event highlights HMMWV platforms fitted with full metal mesh enclosures reaching down toward the wheel lines, while heavy HEMTT logistics trucks featured protective overhead armor installed over their armored cabs to shield crews from drone strikes.
While these protective screens do not offer full defense against larger middle-strike systems, military observers note that added overhead and side mesh significantly lowers the risk of catastrophic hits from small drones.
Similar protective netting and metal frames were previously deployed by Ukrainian forces, including units like the 12th Special Forces Brigade Azov, to protect light transport and supply vehicles operating near active combat zones.
As reported by Defense Express, the integration of these field adaptations into US drills underscores a growing effort among NATO allies to absorb real-time technological lessons from Ukraine to increase troop survivability on modern battlefields.
Previously, the US military integrated Ukrainian drone defense technology at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia.
Ukrainian personnel arrived at the facility to train American service members on the Sky Map software, a command-and-control platform used to identify threats like Iranian-designed Shahed models and coordinate interceptor drones.
The deployment aimed to address long-standing gaps in US air defense as the Pentagon increased spending to counter growing low-cost aerial threats.

Both Democrats and Republicans Are Increasingly Worried About AI's Environmental Impact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:20:24 UTC
04:20:24 KST

As data centers break ground in communities across the country, Americans are growing more concerned about the environmental impacts. That’s according to a new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago, which found that about half (53%) of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about AI’s environmental impacts. The number is up from 41% last year.
The concern is shared across all party affiliations. More Democrats, Republicans, and Independents said they are “extremely or very” worried about the environmental impacts compared to last year—with 65% of Democrats, 42% of Republicans, and 49% of Independents reporting their concern this year.
There are currently 1,287 data centers in operation in the U.S., with more than 2,000 planned projects, according to Clearview, a market intelligence company tracking U.S. power infrastructure and data center development. Virginia and Texas currently have the most data centers in operation, but many new developments are planned in rural areas in the South and Midwest. The growth is driven by the rise in hyperscale data centers, which are larger, more powerful, and often used to train and run large-scale AI models.
Despite the boom, Americans seem to be increasingly supportive of measures to regulate growth. About 6 in 10 Americans said they would support limiting the number of new data centers that can be built—including most Democrats and Republicans—the survey found.
Democrats seem to be the most concerned by the environmental impacts of data center growth. About two-thirds say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about how AI will affect the environment, the poll found, compared to about half in 2025. By contrast, about half of Independents and 4 in 10 Republicans are highly concerned about the environmental impact of AI.
Republicans, on the other hand, are more likely to see the benefits of data centers. Yet about 3 in 10 Republicans still believe the centers are “not very” or “not at all” beneficial for improved infrastructure and job creation.
What are the main environmental impacts from AI that people are concerned about?
A majority (60%) of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built, according to the new poll.
The concerns are not unfounded. A U.N. report published in June estimated that the water used by AI is expected to greatly expand in the coming years—equaling the needs of 1.3 billion people by 2030 and threatening natural resources for billions around the world. In the U.S. alone, data centers could account for 11.8% of electricity consumption by 2030, according to a 2024 report from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory Report.
The poll found that Americans are more worried about the environmental impact of AI than other industries with a substantial environmental footprint like the meat industry or air travel. About two-thirds of U.S. adults are in favor of requiring data centers to use clean energy sources, like wind or solar, to supply their electricity needs. Roughly 8 in 10 Democrats support this, along with 56% of Republicans.
But in the absence of clean energy alternatives, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than most countries by 2035, according to a new report from BloombergNEF.
The Trump Administration—which has been undoing climate rules that could help spur clean energy—has strongly supported data center expansion, urging communities to "let Data Reign” in a social media post on Monday. "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” he wrote. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign."
Americans seem to be less certain. Roughly a quarter of U.S. adults surveyed said data centers are “extremely” or “very” beneficial when it comes to technological advancement, and only about 2 in 10 say the same about job creation. Many U.S. adults say data centers are “somewhat” beneficial or aren’t sure, while about one quarter say they’re “not very” or “not at all” beneficial for technological advancement, and around a third don’t see any benefit for job creation. (Some research has shown that, while data center construction can yield a number of temporary jobs, facilities tend to employ fewer permanent employees.)
The survey results come as a growing number of cities and states have been placing moratoriums on data center growth until the impacts are better understood. As of September 2026, 313 moratoriums have been enacted, affecting 44 states and more than 200 cities, counties, and localities, according to the Urban Institute.
Many believe it's essential to pause data center growth now—before the number of data centers across the country explodes. “We’re undertaking a massive experiment in real time, and I don’t think there’ll be any putting the milk back in the bottle,” Michael Greenstone, who directs the University of Chicago institute that collaborated on the survey, told the AP. “Change is scary, and I think some of that is being reflected here.”

A six-fingered Leonardo DiCaprio and the creature from Ridley Scott’s ‘Alien’ stuff a ballot box in this Russian PSA about AI-generated election fraud videos

A six-fingered Leonardo DiCaprio and the creature from Ridley Scott’s ‘Alien’ stuff a ballot box in this Russian PSA about AI-generated election fraud videos
The Telegram channel Voyna s Feykami posted an AI-generated video about ballot stuffing. It shows a six-fingered Leonardo DiCaprio, soccer player Cristiano Ronaldo, and the alien from Ridley Scott’s film “Alien” dropping ballots into a ballot box. A voice-over warns that videos purporting to show election violations may have been generated using AI.
“Stay alert! In the coming days, as the election approaches, pressure on Russians will mount. Don’t believe everything you see online,” the channel says in the post accompanying the video. The channel urges readers to rely “only on official sources” for information about the election.
By the time this article was published, the video featuring DiCaprio had been viewed more than 100,000 times and shared by several other Telegram channels.
Russians lost real elections a long ago. But you’ve still got a choice. If you live outside Russia, please donate to Meduza — for yourself or for those who remain inside the country and want to read independent news.
Voyna s Feykami is run by Dialog, an autonomous nonprofit organization established by the Moscow authorities in 2019 as an online “citizen feedback” center. As Proekt reported, Dialog was actually tasked with promoting political advertising ahead of the vote on constitutional amendments. During the pandemic, Dialog was also responsible for providing information about the coronavirus. After Russia criminalized spreading false information about the virus, the organization began searching for such content.
The organization’s responsibilities expanded after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Dialog employees handled communications for the Defense Ministry and also fabricated stories about Ukraine. During this period, Dialog launched the Voyna s Feykami Telegram channel and a website of the same name.
In 2023, Meduza, iStories, and The Bell published a joint investigation into Dialog’s work. We found that Sergei Kiriyenko, the first deputy chief of staff of Russia’s Presidential Administration, oversees the organization on the Kremlin’s behalf. Sources described Vladimir Tabak, who has headed Dialog since 2021, as “Surkov’s man,” whom Kiriyenko had “inherited” along with his position. According to the sources, Kiriyenko personally visited the organization’s office to celebrate their victory in the vote on the constitutional amendments.
The journalists also examined Dialog’s internal guidelines for “debunking fake news.” When there is no basis whatsoever for refuting a story, the guidelines instruct employees to discredit the source, point out that the report contains no photos or videos, or suggest who might benefit from spreading it.
Voyna s Feykami has claimed, for example, that Ukrainian air defenses caused a gas explosion — not a Russian missile strike — that killed 46 people in an apartment building in Dnipro. It also described the strike that killed 12 people at a pizzeria in Kramatorsk as an attack on “a deployment site for foreign mercenaries.”

Foreign YouTuber using AI to promote One Nation to thousands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:15:02 UTC
04:15:02 KST

This YouTuber promotes One Nation to thousands in an Aussie accent. He's a foreigner we traced to the other side of the world
In short:
An ABC NEWS Verify investigation has uncovered a YouTube political commentator from overseas who is using AI to fake an Australian accent and promote One Nation to tens of thousands of people.
The account, Oceania Unfiltered, has accrued more than 3 million views and receives thousands of comments on its Australian and New Zealand political commentary.
The investigation also uncovered groups and pages sharing tips on generating social media content for profit, with one describing Australia as an untapped market.
"G'day. Good to see ya. Pull up a chair. Grab a cold one if you've got it, because we need to have a serious yarn about what's been going on down in Canberra this week."
This YouTuber seems very Australian.
He often presents from a room with coloured lights, using colloquial language and slang to speak almost exclusively about one topic: Australian politics.
"Aussies cannot just sit back, have a whinge at the pub over a beer, and hope she'll be right," he says in a different video.
He frequently promotes One Nation and its leader, Pauline Hanson, and is critical of Anthony Albanese. He rails against the "uni-party" and the "political establishment".
A spokesman for One Nation said the channel and its creator were not associated with the party.
The channel has received thousands of comments across his videos from seemingly real Australians engaging with his content.
But this YouTuber is not Australian.
He appears to be a man ABC NEWS Verify has traced to the other side of the world. And artificial intelligence has been used to give this channel its distinct Australian voice.
Signs of AI
The channel is called Oceania Unfiltered and claims to deliver, "sharp, independent analysis on the political, economic and cultural issues shaping Australia and New Zealand".
The earliest video about Australian politics was posted in February and the channel has accrued more than 3 million views across dozens of videos.
The presenter appears to be a Brazilian man, named Junior Lutero De Alcantara, sometimes shortened to Junior Lutero. His commentary is often spliced between real Australian news clips.
He appears on several YouTube channels — mostly speaking in Brazil's official language, Portuguese — discussing everything from world politics to aliens to conspiracy theories.
On a second YouTube channel appearing to feature Junior Lutero, older videos are presented in Portuguese before suddenly pivoting to a thick North American accent in newer videos.
Many of these are critical of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and praise US President Donald Trump.
It is unclear whether the real Junior Lutero is running all these accounts, including Oceania Unfiltered, or if someone else is using his likeness.
ABC NEWS Verify attempted to contact Junior Lutero numerous times but received no reply. We also engaged a Brazilian producer to try to contact him. They also received no reply.
A day after our first attempt to contact him in May, warnings started appearing on some videos which read: "Made with AI. Sounds or visuals were altered or fully generated."
These could be seen after expanding the video caption box.
After ABC NEWS Verify sent questions to YouTube, all videos on the channel had the AI warning placed in the caption box. Another small AI label was also placed below the video title where it could be viewed without clicking.
"All content uploaded to YouTube is subject to our policies, which we enforce consistently for all creators on our platform, regardless of whether their content is generated using artificial intelligence," a spokesperson for YouTube said in a statement.
"YouTube also requires creators to disclose when they upload photorealistic or meaningfully altered and synthetic content, and we display clear disclosure labels to provide viewers with context at a glance."
We also asked experts in AI detection to look at the Oceania Unfiltered content, with one video from September 1 singled out for deeper investigation.
"The video is a lip-sync deepfake," said the University at Buffalo's Media Forensic Lab.
"AI-generated speech lip-synced onto real footage of a person, with synthetic audio and visuals manipulated to match it," the analysis by Siwei Lyu, Jialing Cai, and Regina Chen stated.
The experts found unnatural changes around the eye of the presenter and found one of his moles disappeared.
In an older video they found "unstable boundaries and texture flicker".
Put simply, AI has been used to manipulate Junior Lutero's face and voice.
ABC NEWS Verify found a 2021 video where Junior Lutero speaks in English with a Latin American accent.
The clip sees the content creator asking Facebook to review a decision that restricted the monetisation on his page and does not show signs of AI manipulation.
The real Junior Lutero has filmed several of his videos in a town in Brazil's São Paulo state. ABC NEWS Verify has chosen not to name the town.
The town was identified using landmarks in the backgrounds in three videos on other channels, which do not appear to show signs of AI manipulation.
Transparency information on the Oceania Unfiltered Facebook page, which also features Junior Lutero's likeness, shows the page is managed from Brazil.
After ABC NEWS Verify published this story, the Oceania Unfiltered channel posted a statement — admitting the use of AI to manipulate videos.
"These videos are NOT 'AI-generated'. They are videos ORIGINALLY RECORDED BY ME. I turn on the camera, I speak, I record the video, and then I use AI to modify my accent," it read.
"I've made it clear in several videos that I'm Brazilian. I've never hidden that. But I absolutely love Australia, and I've been following Australian politics for years."
Oceania Unfiltered now has more than 45,000 subscribers on YouTube with its clickbait-style headlines.
Timothy Graham from QUT's Digital Media Research Centre said the channel "crosses the borderline" of misleading its audience.
While the primary motivation appeared to be personal financial gain, he said the impact could still be political.
"The effects and the impact of this stuff is more or less identical to what the intended, if not actual, outcomes of foreign influence operations would be," he said.
"What you end up with is divisive content that is injected into organic communities in Australia."
The comments on the videos indicate at least some viewers are unaware the presenter might not be authentic.
"You are spot on in your comments. Thank you for your continual posting of issues that affect Australians," one said.
"You are one of my favourite go-to political analysts. Keep up the good work and thank god Aussies are waking up and using their vote for change!" another said.
Oceania Unfiltered is part of the booming online "slop economy" — where individuals can generate revenue through engagement on social media, using cheap AI content.
"It's just a way of getting a quick buck," said David Hobson, a researcher from Canada's Center for Media, Technology and Democracy.
'More attention … more money'
Monetisation allows content creators on popular social media platforms to earn a share of the revenue their posts generate.
"Essentially the formula is more attention, more engagement, more money," Dr Graham said.
ABC NEWS Verify has identified groups and pages where a network of creators have shared tips and tricks on how to generate revenue on Facebook, critiqued other AI slop pages, and even discussing finding the right niche to generate engagement.
The Oceania Unfiltered Facebook page history showed how the creator behind it searched for and settled on a niche.
Disclosure data gathered from Facebook revealed the page had been monetised.
Between 2013 and 2026 it was renamed seven times — mostly different variations of Junior Lutero's name — until it became Oceania Unfiltered in March.
Older reels talked about a range of topics before the pivot to Australian politics this year.
After ABC NEWS Verify asked Facebook's parent company, Meta, questions, the company disabled the page for violating its inauthentic behaviour policy, which a spokesperson said "prohibits people from misrepresenting who they are or where they are located".
"We require creators to disclose when they post realistic content that has been created or altered with AI, and content that breaches our policies is not eligible to earn money on our platforms," the spokesperson said.
ABC NEWS Verify identified this post which contained a step-by-step guide on making an Australian YouTube channel — and claimed the country was an untapped market.
We contacted dozens of creators on Facebook, in an effort to ask about their posting and business model, but none replied.
Mr Hobson said online money-making models have existed for a long time, but now there's a difference.
"AI now makes it possible to generate this content at incredible scales," he said.
"It's up to the platforms whether this changes or not."
Slop from all over the world
In 2022, independent think tank the Institute for Strategic Dialogue published a paper examining a "growing global industry" of disinformation targeting US audiences.
The report's author, Elise Thomas — now a senior open-source investigator with the Centre of Information Resilience — told ABC NEWS Verify that creators with a commercial interest were the most innovative.
"Their stuff has to work, otherwise they don't get paid," she said.
"They are the quickest to adopt new technologies, they are most precise and effective in terms of targeting."
Earlier this year, Canada's Center for Media, Technology and Democracy published research focused on the "slop economy", specifically on Facebook.
The report described "a coordinated network of 340 Facebook pages — largely operated from Vietnam — targets users in Canada, Europe, and the US with AI-fabricated stories about politics, celebrities, and sports to drive traffic to fabricated news websites and generate ad revenue".
"As far as we can tell, they do whatever it takes to get clicks," Mr Hobson said.
ABC NEWS Verify examined hundreds of Facebook posts using Australian political buzzwords, and clickbait terms, to try to measure the scale of the local "slop economy".
We found accounts being run by people from locations like Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Vietnam and Bangladesh.
The content ranged from low-quality posts fishing for engagement, to higher-quality AI-generated imagery.
There are also AI political slop pages, which carry names like "Australia Unyielding" and "The Real Australia". In some cases, transparency information reveals that these accounts are operated by people overseas.
These pages also post in groups with names like "Australia Pulse" and "Australia Life".
These groups are a hotbed for foreign individuals looking for engagement by posting their own AI-generated imagery.
Both the groups and pages have genuine Australian members, alongside the foreign accounts.
Australians who interact with the content, generate revenue for creators if the account is monetised.
"Australian people are lucrative when it comes to delivering us content," Dr Graham said.
"We are cash cows because when we look at content and engage with it … the revenue that comes out of that is just so much higher compared to other countries."
Mr Hobson said the currency creators get paid in might suggest why they targeted countries like Australia.
"If you're based in Vietnam or Sri Lanka, any of these countries, if you're getting paid in American, Canadian, Aussie dollars — that translates a lot into your local currency," he said.
Additional research by Maryanne Taouk
