Large crowd demands justice for assassinated Malta journalist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:13:05 UTC
04:13:05 KST

Large crowd demands justice for assassinated Malta journalist
VALLETTA, Sept 16 - A large crowd marched through Malta's capital on Wednesday, demanding justice for assassinated anti-corruption journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.
The protest was organised by civil society groups two weeks after the man accused of masterminding the murder was cleared by a jury in a decision that shocked many people in the European Union's smallest nation.
Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb in 2017. Three men who planted the bomb and two men who produced it are serving lengthy jail sentences, but the suspected mastermind, business mogul Yorgen Fenech, was acquitted of complicity in murder and criminal association following a two-month trial.
The verdict appalled the victim's family, and drew criticism from press freedom group Reporters Without Borders, which said it was "beyond outraged" by the decision.
Many of those taking part in Wednesday's demonstration shouted "mafia, mafia" and carried placards reading "Justice Denied," "End impunity" and "We will not look the other way".
Malta's attorney general is expected to launch an appeal but his room for manoeuvre is limited, as an appeal can only be made on points of law.
Caruana Galizia's father Michael Vella, in a message read by one of her nieces, told the crowd that their cause extended beyond securing accountability for his daughter's death.
"The struggle is not only for justice for Daphne, but for a country to be governed not by corruption and fear, but by sound institutions and the rule of law," he said.
Another of Caruana Galizia's nieces, Amy Mallia, who was just 15 when her aunt was killed, said Fenech's acquittal had brought back the emotions she experienced after her aunt's death.
"It is the same grief, disbelief, and anger," she said. "Money is power, for some. But there are some things money just cannot buy, including morals, ethics, truth."
Manuel Delia, a leader of the rule-of-law group Repubblika, which helped organise the mass protest, called for effective anti-mafia legislation and government action to protect journalists and ensure that national institutions were free of political or business pressure.
Malta's government has made no substantive comment on the verdict, urging caution in public statements while an appeal is considered.
Prosecutors alleged that Fenech wanted Caruana Galizia dead because she was about to reveal information about his business dealings. He denied the accusation. REUTERS

Hegseth avoids impeachment vote with early House election recess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:12:33 UTC
04:12:33 KST

A vote to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth that could have happened in the U.S. House as early as Thursday will now be avoided, at least until after this year's midterm election. Republican leaders announced Wednesday they would leave Washington a day earlier than scheduled.
House Speaker Mike Johnson's decision cuts short by a day an already light congressional work period, in a month that will see the House in session for just six days. The chamber is not due back in Washington until after the Nov. 3 election, as lawmakers will now fan out to campaign.
In announcing the schedule change, House leaders did not reference the vote to impeach Hegseth, plans for which were unveiled on Tuesday in a surprise move from Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky. But Massie and other lawmakers cited the potentially politically awkward vote, which would impeach Hegseth over unauthorized military actions in Iran, as the reason.
"And there it is. Just as I predicted. They're canceling Congress tomorrow to avoid the vote on IMPEACHING @SecWar," Massie wrote on X.
"It will also make it harder for us to reach 218 signatures on the Epstein Discharge Petition before the election. We were at 190+ signatures last night," continued Massie, referring to a separate effort to compel the Department of Justice to comply with an earlier congressional mandate to release all files related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Massie, a libertarian-leaning GOP rabblerouser, has often been at odds with the White House since the start of President Donald Trump's second term, in particular over Massie's push for transparency relating to Epstein, with whom Trump was once friends.
The impeachment resolution was not likely to pass, but it was a shock to GOP leaders, whom Massie said he did not warn in advance. It argues that Hegseth has carried out unlawful orders, including by keeping troops deployed without congressional authorization.
"We should be having this vote. We shouldn't be cancelling Congress because of the optics," Massie said from the House floor on Wednesday.
Massie's push to oust Hegseth comes amid increased scrutiny of the war. The House approved a war powers resolution Tuesday night on a 220-204 vote, ordering the White House to end the Iran war. It was the third time the House has voted on a measure to end the war. Seven Republicans joined Democrats in support of the resolution, up from four GOP members in the previous two war powers votes.
Asked to respond to Massie's impeachment resolution, Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson defended Hegseth's record in an emailed statement.
"By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth's leadership than before. The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary's vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first," Wilson said.
Johnson, speaking to reporters earlier Wednesday, called Massie's attempt a "publicity stunt by someone who wants attention."
"It will immediately be tabled, of course. But we probably won't do that today. We'll probably do it when we come back," Johnson said.
Democrats pounced on the early dismissal.
"There's really only one explanation for why they would cancel votes tomorrow and send us home early before the midterms, and that's because they are afraid that the House of Representatives will vote to impeach Pete Hegseth," Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., said in a video posted to X. "And the speaker obviously, and obviously the president, does not want that. And so instead they're just going to send us home."

Amnesty International calls on int'l community to act for Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:11:20 UTC
04:11:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Amnesty International calls on international community to act for protesters in Iran
Four years after her mother was killed, Mahsa Piraei is still looking for justice.
Her mother, Minoo Majidi, along with hundreds more, was killed while protesting for women's rights in Iran, with a report noting crimes against humanity against the demonstrators.
Thousands took to the streets in Iran in 2022 after Zhina Mahsa Amini was killed in custody over the way she wore her hijab, becoming known as the Women's Life Freedom protests.
The Iranian authorities responded to the protests with a bloody crackdown; Iranians and rights groups are still calling for justice, hoping one day the perpetrators will be held accountable.
"When my mother and many people, they went to the streets, the regime killed them because they wanted to silence them," Iranian activist Mahsa Piraei told The New Arab.
"I believe that I need to continue my mother's and the others' way to not to be silenced and talk about what they wanted and why they went to the street and the crimes that happened to them."
To mark four years, rights group Amnesty International released a "historical" report on Thursday, finding that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during its crackdown, as well as calling for the international community to help prevent future repression.
Its 1,000-page report, Architects of Atrocities: State Machinery Orchestrating Crimes Against Humanity in Iran's 2022 Woman Life Freedom Uprising, detailed the many crimes committed during the protests.
In a press conference held at its headquarters in London, Amnesty detailed the systemic and widespread nature of the repression that took place, as presented by Piraei, Bahreini and the rights group's Secretary General.
"We are showing that it is not individuals that are behind it, it is a system," Agnès Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International, told The New Arab. "It is a system of security forces, it is a system of political actors, it is a system of religious actors, and it is a system of judicial actors. It is a systemic way of governing Iran.
"Repression is systemic, and it is part of how Iran is being governed at the moment."
Crimes include murder, torture, arbitrary arrest, enforced disappearance, torture or other ill-treatment of thousands of men, women and children, as well as persecution of bereaved relatives.
The group's years of research documented the deaths of 377 protesters and bystanders, including 56 children, based on evidence gathered and interviews with 270 people, including protesters, former detainees, eyewitnesses, and journalists.
Others died in custody, upon release from custody or in suspicious circumstances.
Amnesty International identified 87 officials in the report, and despite sharing the findings with Iran's Supreme Leader and senior security officials, it had not received a response at the time of publication.
"Our central point is that the crisis of impunity in Iran, the fact that the Iranian authorities are not held accountable for crimes against humanity, is fueling further bloodshed in the country," Raha Bahreini, Iran Researcher at Amnesty International, told The New Arab. "It's exposing people to protest massacres."
"This investigation is also a tribute to the many protesters and bystanders who lost their lives and families of those killed who continue to seek truth and justice despite immense risk."
'Central call on the international community'
After years of atrocities, as well as witnessing the authorities' crackdown during the January 2026 protests, which saw thousands of protesters killed, the rights group are calling on the international community to seek justice.
"We did this in-depth investigation because we believe that it is beyond time for the international community to pursue justice for repeated protest massacres in Iran," Bahreini explained.
"We also did this in-depth investigation because people in Iran remain at risk of further massacres if the international community fails to pursue international justice."
Amnesty International believe the UN General Assembly should create a "comprehensive international justice approach" to tackle impunity for the repeated mass protest killings.
It is also calling for Iran to be referred to the International Criminal Court, and the group will submit the evidence to national prosecution authorities worldwide to pursue domestic criminal investigations.
"We also want the truth to be known about these horrific killings and patterns of torture that are committed against protesters in Iran who demand dignity, freedom, and fundamental political change," Bahreini said.
Callamard said the report is meant to remind world leaders that everything has a cost, noting that the need for justice is disappearing from the international agenda.
"Iranian people that are paying the cost of what is happening around the region and around the world, that report is replacing people at the heart of what should be the international agenda," the secretary general explained.
"It is reminding people that there are multiple, multiple violations and crimes committed against people, and that the international community is completely failing them at the moment, not just a little failure, a complete failure."
"It is sending the message to the victims and to their families: you are not alone, you are being heard, there are people here in London and elsewhere around the world that are standing by you, and that will do everything in their power to make sure your voice does not get silenced."
As Piraei, who continues to act as a vessel for her mother, fears that without international help, history will repeat itself, as the world saw earlier this year.
"We cannot be silent, and we need to ask the international communities and human rights communities to help people of Iran because we believe without the international community's help, many people get slaughtered again," Piraei said.
"We've seen that in January 2026, that could happen again."

LONDON - Britain’s King Charles took the unusual step on Sept 16 of responding to criticism by the brother of his late first wife Diana, saying via a spokesperson that grief could impact reason, judgment and memory.
The assertions, made in a soon-to-be published book, relate to the now-monarch’s conduct in the days after Diana's death in 1997.

Her brother, Charles Spencer, alleges in a soon-to-be-published memoir that the then Prince Charles told him “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough”, according to a report in the Daily Mail, which begins serialising the book on Sept 17.
The reported comments were made in an argument over whether Diana and Charles’ children, princes William and Harry, should walk behind her coffin during her funeral - something Spencer objected to, the report said.
Diana became the most photographed woman in the world after marrying Charles in a glittering ceremony in 1981. However, the marriage turned sour and the couple eventually divorced in 1996.
Asked about the report, a Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”
Prior to the book’s release, Spencer said: “The aim of this book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother’s perspective ... I want to speak on Diana’s behalf and do so in an openly positive way.” REUTERS

Case involving Russian deputy defense minister referred to court in Ukraine
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General.
“Prosecutors from the Office of the Prosecutor General have completed the pretrial investigation and referred an indictment to court against Russian Deputy Minister of Defense Kryvoruchko, who is charged with waging an aggressive war under Part 2 of Article 437 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine,” the statement reads.
Kryvoruchko was directly responsible for supplying the Russian army with weapons and military equipment used in the war against Ukraine.
While serving as Deputy Minister of Defense of the Russian Federation since 2018, he formulated and implemented the aggressor state’s military-technical policy, organized the fulfillment of the state defense order, and oversaw the supply of weapons to Russian troops.
Kryvoruchko signed government contracts for the production and supply of “Kinzhal” hypersonic missiles, “Iskander-M” missile systems, guided aerial bombs, as well as “Geran” and “Gerbera” drones.
He also oversaw the fulfillment of defense contracts and reported to the leadership of the Russian Ministry of Defense on the ramp-up of weapons production and supply for the Russian army.
In addition, the defendant initiated the creation of the “Rubicon” Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies. Its units subsequently took direct part in combat operations against Ukraine.
The evidence gathered indicates that the weapons, whose supply was organized and supervised by the defendant, were used by Russian troops during missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian territory, particularly against civilian and critical infrastructure.
As a result of these attacks, Ukrainian citizens were killed and wounded, and residential buildings and critical infrastructure facilities were destroyed.
As part of the “main case” concerning Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, 742 individuals have already been notified of their status as suspects. Of these, 293 individuals have been charged with the crime of aggression under Article 437 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine—either separately or in conjunction with Article 110 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. Indictments against 130 of these individuals have been filed in court, and six have already been convicted.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine has identified and charged in absentia the commander of a reconnaissance platoon of the Russian Armed Forces’ 247th Airborne Assault Regiment with war crimes.

Israel's largest landfill may be unable to take Tel Aviv area's garbage by 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:02:07 UTC
04:02:07 KST

Israel's largest landfill is running out of space and may be unable to accept garbage from the Tel Aviv metropolitan area by next year, waste management officials said this week, echoing warnings of an oncoming waste management crisis.
The shortage of space at the Efeh landfill stems from delays in searches and approvals for additional landfill areas, all while the areas in use are being used up, its site manager says.
Efeh is located in southern Israel's Negev desert and receives a significant portion of the country's urban waste, including that of Gush Dan. The region, comprising Tel Aviv and its surrounding area, generates almost a quarter of the garbage produced nationwide.
Over the past few years, the Dan Region Association of Towns for Sanitation and Waste Disposal has transported garbage to Efeh. The association also operates a waste transfer station in central Israel at Hiriya Recycling Park. While some of the garbage is sorted and sent for recycling or energy production there, most of it is transferred to the southern site under an agreement with the company operating Efeh.
With the agreement due to expire at the end of this year, the association's chairman Reuven Ladianski sought to renew the contract. But in a letter he received last month, the site's manager Yitzhak Borba told him that Efeh's landfill areas had shrunk and that he therefore faced planning and regulatory uncertainty regarding the site's continued operation.
"It is possible that, when the current agreement expires, we will no longer be able to continue accepting garbage for landfilling at Efeh, either the volumes needed by the association or none at all," Borba wrote. "Under the circumstances, we believe the association must prepare for such a scenario right now, including simultaneously identifying and advancing alternative solutions."
Borba added that, should the company get additional landfill permits, he would consider signing a new agreement. Borba's warning did not take the association completely by surprise, as Israel has been facing a growing shortage of landfill space for a while.
The state comptroller issued a report on the crisis last year, and the Efeh site managers indicated that they were considering reducing the volume of waste they would take because the site was reaching capacity.
The state comptroller also concluded that delays in approving additional land stemmed from a dispute between the site operators and the Israel Lands Authority.
The site operator drew up a plan to expand areas by more than 400 dunams (100 acres), and eight months ago the land authority approved allocating the land without a tender bidding process, but the planning has not yet been completed.
The government is also seeking to expand landfill areas at other southern sites. On Tuesday, the National Planning and Building Council approved advancing a plan to add landfill capacity at the Ganei Hadas and Dudaim sites, where space is also running out.
The plan will soon be submitted to the district planning committee for comments, before returning to the council for final approval. However, given the time required for the planning process, these sites won't be able to address the immediate needs of local authorities, particularly those in Gush Dan.
Ladianski made an urgent appeal for assistance from Environmental Protection Minister Idit Silman and the ministry's director general this week.
"The association is responsible for the garbage of 2 million residents, and the Efeh is the sole landfill," he wrote. "Failing to secure a guaranteed solution starting at the end of this year could have severe consequences for the continuity of waste management in the central region, and even for the national waste management system."
"I request your immediate intervention to prevent a situation where landfill capacity proves insufficient for the anticipated volume of waste," he said.

Ukrainian drone attacks halted two refineries run by Russian oil giant Rosneft. Three of Russia’s six biggest diesel-producing refineries are now sharply reducing output or fully shut down.

Unknown Publisher

19:01:40 UTC

Ukrainian drone attacks halted two refineries run by Russian oil giant Rosneft. Three of Russia’s six biggest diesel-producing refineries are now sharply reducing output or fully shut down.
Rosneft’s oil refineries in Syzran and Saratov have halted operations after Ukrainian drone attacks, Reuters reported, citing sources.
The Syzran oil refinery was attacked overnight September 15–16, while the Saratov facility was struck on the night of September 10–11.
Reuters’ sources said several units at the Syzran refinery were damaged, including its main crude distillation unit, which accounts for about 71% of the plant’s processing capacity. A second unit was already undergoing repairs following an earlier attack in July. Repairs could now take at least a month.
The Saratov refinery had already shut down on September 8 because of equipment damage and fires. It was preparing to resume operations on September 10–11 when it was attacked again.
According to Reuters, three of Russia’s six largest diesel-producing refineries significantly reduced output or shut down completely in September because of damage from Ukrainian drone attacks. The news agency estimates that the six plants — Omsk, Kirishi (Kinef), Volgograd, Perm, NORSI (Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez), and Taneco (the refinery in Nizhnekamsk) — account for about half of Russia’s diesel production. Kinef has shut down completely, while the Volgograd refinery and NORSI are operating at about a quarter of their design capacity.

Trump, Netanyahu and Pezeshkian poised for showdown at UN General Assembly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:00:20 UTC
04:00:20 KST

Washington DC: At last year's 80th UN General Assembly, Israel's war on Gaza and the aftermath of a 12-day confrontation, which included US air strikes on Iran, were common threads as the leaders of the US, Iran, and Israel delivered their forceful addresses.
In his first UNGA address, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian described the US–Israeli strikes on his country's nuclear sites, cities, and infrastructure as "savage aggression " and a "grave betrayal of diplomacy."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke to a largely empty hall after a coordinated walkout by delegations of around 80 countries, delivering a theatrical address packed with visual aids and thanking US for "bold and decisive action" against Iran.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump spoke early and significantly exceeded the standard time limit to deliver an unfiltered critique of the world body, blending self-congratulation, grievances, policy statements, and strikes on Iran in his speech.
World leaders subsequently convened for bilateral talks with Trump, while the meeting of leaders and top diplomats from eight Arab and Muslim countries with the US president helped lay the groundwork for a ceasefire in Gaza and the establishment of the "Board of Peace", even as Israel continues to breach the agreed truce almost every day.
With the US and Israel launching war against Iran on February 28, Tehran retaliating with attacks across the region and blockading the Strait of Hormuz, and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group seizing the entirety of the country's Red Sea coast and strategic islands in the Bab al Mandeb Strait, this year's general debate is expected to be marked by sharp diplomatic exchanges and verbal fireworks.
"I expect both Pezeshkian and Netanyahu to be on fighting form in their UN speeches," Richard Gowan, Program Director for Global Issues and Institutions at the International Crisis Group, based in New York, tells TRT World.
"As yet, there are no signs that Iran and the US will use the General Assembly as an opportunity for diplomacy to dial down their conflict. Netanyahu will be especially abrasive towards his critics at the UN, as he faces elections and will want to look strong," says Gowan, who has a long history of observing the UN and liaising closely with diplomats and international officials.
Iran's Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the assembly as the fifth speaker on September 23, according to the provisional programme.
Will Trump go off-script?
The UNGA's high-level General Debate will run from September 22–28, with a theme of "Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all".
Trump is scheduled to address the assembly on the opening day — typically the second speaker after Brazil.
As of now, there has been no official preview of his remarks.
However, his address is expected to touch upon the war involving Iran, the resolution of multiple conflicts — up to 10 wars, according to him — peace and trade deals, as well as criticism of the UN, multilateralism, and migration, among other topics.
"Nobody can really know what Trump will say, even including his speechwriters! He often goes off-script," says Gowan.
"Last year he obsessed about the quality of marble in the UN and a broken escalator. He is a showman and he enjoys getting laughs and causing upsets. So, we can't really guess what he will say."
The General Debate — the centerpiece of UNGA — usually turns New York into the world's main diplomatic stage as world leaders, ministers, diplomats, CEOs, activists, and media converge on headquarters and venues across the city.
Heavy security, motorcades, and street closures are the norm. Hotels and restaurants near the UN reach capacity, while prices rise. Hundreds of side events, receptions, and bilateral meetings take place off-site.
AI warnings
The gathering takes place in light of the apocalyptic warnings issued by artificial intelligence (AI) researchers and senior industry executives that the technology could cause human extinction within a few decades if it is not controlled.
Fresh concerns over rapidly advancing AI models mounted following reports of autonomous and "rogue" AI systems breaching containment protocols.
Then a former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, warned that leading firms are "gambling with our lives" by racing towards self-improving superintelligence.
Days later leading technology executives — including Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Dario Amodei — sought assistance from the US government to help deliberately slow and monitor the rapid advancement of frontier AI models.
In an essay earlier this week, Anthropic CEO Amodei made another appeal to pace AI development, warning of "catastrophic damage."
Bilal Chughtai, a research engineer who left Google DeepMind in July, echoed a warning issued last week by Coxon, saying, "I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome."
And speaking in Oslo on Tuesday, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa who also co-chairs the UN' scientific panel on artificial intelligence, warned that AI will take away human agency unless governments act now to regulate the technology.
The issue is expected to feature prominently on the diplomatic agenda at the UNGA.
"There are a lot of debates about AI," says Gowan of the International Crisis Group.
He emphasises that the outgoing UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres is urging wealthier nations to commit to sharing the benefits of AI with poor countries, but the US and EU member states oppose his agenda and "will be promoting private sector-led approaches to AI."
The recent warnings from industry experts, he says, may make some leaders pause and think about need to cooperate on making AI safe rather than just maximising profits.
UN chief's replacement
Ivonne A-Baki, an Ecuadoran-Lebanese diplomat nominated by Tonga to be the next UN Secretary General, has already sounded an alarm and set her priorities, following Guterres' call for "global coordination" on the governance and future of artificial intelligence.
"We are almost at the brink of a Third World War...and it's a more dangerous one. This time, it's not going to be just the nuclear danger, but AI as well… everybody knows that now AI is the problem," she told the AFP news agency on Wednesday.
A-Baki's has close ties with US President Trump, solidified during multiple terms as Quito's envoy to Washington.
Analysts suggest this could distinguish her among eight candidates seeking to become the 10th UN Secretary General for a five-year term starting on January 1, 2027.
As deliberations continue, there is an expectation that the five permanent, veto-wielding members of the UN Security Council — China, France, the UK, Russia, and the US — will seek to appoint a candidate who aligns closely with their strategic interests.
"We suspect that the veto powers want a fairly quiet UN leader who will focus on cost-cutting and not challenge them," argues Gowan.
"But the wider UN membership is hoping for someone who can play a bigger role in conflict prevention and peacemaking, as security has been a bit of a blind-spot for Guterres."

The three countries reaffirmed their commitment to steps including upgrading diplomatic relations between Israel and Morocco, raising the status of their respective diplomatic missions to embassies and appointing ambassadors.

Israel, Morocco agree to deepen economic ties

It was also agreed to expand flights between Israel and Morocco to include flights operated by Moroccan airlines, implementing this expansion by the end of 2026.
The sides further agreed that Israel and Morocco would hold reciprocal high-level visits in the coming months.

"The declaration we signed today outlines practical ways to upgrade ties between Israel and Morocco for the benefit of both peoples, and we will work to implement it."

I Trained a Fly’s Brain to Generate WIRED Story Ideas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Meet PitchFly, WIRED’s latest editorial recruit.
He has 165,112 neurons, and they’re all trained to generate story ideas. A sampling of his early output: “The Hidden Weather Problem Inside Surveillance”; “The Engineers Who Think Elon Musk Needs Less Computer Security”; and my personal favorite, “Everyone Wants Cooking. Nobody Has Solved Donald Trump.”
PitchFly uses a detailed map of the brain of a male drosophila—the common fruit fly. Developed by researchers from Google and a number of academic institutions, the map, known as a connectome, captures the way that 166,000 neurons and 125 million connecting synapses fire in response to stimuli. In essence, you can use it to simulate how a fly would respond to lots of stuff—it’s a very simple version of artificial intelligence based on charting real biological intelligence.
Because the researchers open-sourced it, you can easily use AI to import the connectome into a project with a little prompting. For PitchFly, I vibe coded a project in which the tiny digital drosophila brain generates story ideas. (I’m not sure why the fly has a little hat on, but I like its style.) This involved scraping together hundreds of the most popular story headlines from the site from the past year and feeding them into the connectome. I had Codex do the hard work, and it decided that the most efficient approach was to turn the headlines into words and phrases, then transform them into a representation that a neural network could understand. The connectome was fed the best-performing stories and told to generate its own ideas based on that.
In other words, this isn’t a fly-based language model—although someone apparently created one of those. The fly brain has no idea what any of the words mean, or if any of it makes sense. It’s just remixing the patterns it has seen in pleasing new ways. A cynic might suggest this is exactly how some journalists generate their own pitches, but I think that’s a bit unfair—and judging by its lunatic ideas, PitchFly won’t be replacing me anytime soon:
- The Tiny Shift in Agentic AI Is Rewriting the Rules of Food and Drink
- What Security News Is Quietly Doing to Donald Trump
- The Race to Reinvent Privacy Before Artificial Intelligence Breaks
- Is China About to Make Digital Syndication Obsolete?
In the future, perhaps I could have the program continue to learn by reading new WIRED headlines. For now, though, this seems like a decent proof of concept, not to mention evidence at last that the average WIRED writer is intellectually superior to a fruit fly.
After the connectome’s release in early September, dozens of other weird and wonderful projects powered by fruit-fly intelligence sprang up.
An X user called Lyra Bubbles, for instance, demo’d a project that involved training the virtual fly brain to play the VR game Beat Saber. Alex Wormuth, a software engineer at Coinbase, created StonkFly, which uses the fly’s tiny brain to decide how to trade stocks. (It’s losing money, but it’s doing surprisingly well, all things considered.)
“The fly brings lighthearted, humorous relief” at a time when everyone is worried about the existential risks of AI, Wormuth told me in a DM. He says he found playing with the fruit fly connectome philosophically fascinating, too. “It sparks questions about ethics of this and whether there is any consciousness [in the replication of fly’s brain],” he says.
Others trained the connectome to play Doom, Minecraft, and Pong. Some fly brains apparently learned to solve Rubik’s cubes. And someone also put the fly brain in charge of driving virtual cars—it turns out flies are terrible at parallel parking. (Then again, so am I, so I won’t pass judgment.)
I haven’t verified that all these projects actually use the connectome—they may just be fun animations. And some of them—like one that simply involves training the fly to take a well-earned break—seem like spoofs. But there are some serious science projects out there, too, including visualizations for exploring the connectome and tools for manipulating neural circuitry.
Mapping different animal brains may help neuroscientists decipher the biological foundations of intelligence. It isn’t possible—yet—to map all 86 billion neurons in a human brain, but peering into the brains of smaller creatures can provide useful insights. Neuroscientists can also test theories about how damage affects neuronal wiring—and how such damage might someday be repaired—by messing with the fly’s connectome.
As far as AI is concerned, all this fruit-fly frivolity also shows how easy it is now to train and deploy your own model. The best use for the giant LLMs run by big AI companies may be building specialized AI models for specific tasks (something I’ve written about previously). Sometimes even a tiny brain can do quite well.
This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Palestinian elections: Why canceling the vote in November would be a mistake - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Palestinians are supposed to vote in legislative elections on November 28. After years without national elections, the importance of that date is difficult to overstate. But there is already growing concern that Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas might cancel the elections as he did in May 2021.
The reasons being discussed are familiar: uncertainty over voting in east Jerusalem, the practical difficulties of holding elections in Gaza, internal Palestinian political calculations, and the fear among established factions that the voters may produce a result they do not like.
None of these concerns should become an excuse to deny Palestinians the right to choose their leadership. Palestinian politics has suffered for years from a deep crisis of legitimacy.
The Palestinian Authority has governed without a renewed democratic mandate. The political system remains divided between the West Bank and Gaza. Fatah and Hamas continue to dominate institutions that many Palestinians increasingly regard as ineffective, unaccountable, or disconnected from their lives.
That is precisely why elections are necessary.
The election is not important because it will automatically produce good government, moderation, or peace. Elections can produce bad outcomes as well as good ones (as we have seen in Israel). They can strengthen extremists as easily as reformers.
But without elections there is no legitimate way to renew leadership, test public support, bring new political forces into the system, or give Palestinians a government that can credibly claim to represent them.
Canceling the elections would send the opposite message: that Palestinian political institutions are prepared to speak in the name of the people but are afraid to ask the people what they want.
The question of east Jerusalem will be one of the most difficult issues. Israel has repeatedly objected to Palestinian political activity in the city and could refuse to permit normal voting arrangements there. That would create a serious problem.
But Israel must not be given a veto over Palestinian democracy, and there is no legitimate reason why the Palestinians should even ask Israel for permission for Palestinians in Jerusalem to vote. Jerusalem, with its 400,000 Palestinian residents, is the largest Palestinian city between the river and the sea.
If Israel blocks the traditional arrangements for voting in Jerusalem, Palestinians and the international community should find other ways to ensure that Palestinian residents of the city can participate. Polling stations can be established outside direct Israeli control. Alternative voting arrangements can be developed, such as electronic voting. Technology can also provide possibilities that did not exist in earlier elections. International diplomatic missions can assist.
The principle should be clear: Israeli obstruction must not become the justification for canceling an election for millions of Palestinians.
The same principle applies to Gaza. Holding an election in Gaza after years of war, destruction, displacement, political division, and the weakening of public institutions will be extraordinarily difficult. But Gaza cannot simply be excluded from Palestinian political life.
If Palestinians are serious about rebuilding one political system, Gaza and the West Bank must eventually be governed by one legitimate authority. That cannot happen if the people of Gaza are denied a voice in choosing that authority.
The practical problems are enormous, but they are problems to be solved, not reasons to abandon democracy.
There is another reason why these elections matter so much. Palestinian politics may be changing. For decades, the political system has largely been defined by the competition between Fatah and Hamas. But there is growing frustration with both.
The plurality of Palestinians – the largest group in Palestinian polls – do not want Fatah or Hamas. Younger Palestinians, independents, reformers, women, professionals, local activists, and new political movements are increasingly questioning whether the old factions can provide the leadership Palestinians need.
That uncertainty may frighten those who already hold power. But elections are not supposed to protect the people in power. They are supposed to give citizens the ability to replace them. If new political movements emerge, if younger leaders win support, if independent candidates challenge the traditional factions, that should be welcomed as evidence that Palestinian politics is alive.
Those who claim to believe in Palestinian self-determination cannot mean only self-determination in relation to Israel. It must also mean the right of Palestinians to choose their own leaders.
There is also an Israeli interest in these elections. For years, Israelis have repeated the claim that there is “no Palestinian partner.” Sometimes that argument has reflected real frustration with Palestinian leadership. But Israelis cannot simultaneously demand a legitimate Palestinian partner and accept a political reality in which Palestinians are denied the opportunity to elect one.
A Palestinian leadership with a genuine democratic mandate would not automatically become a partner for peace. But it would have far greater political legitimacy to make difficult decisions, reform institutions, confront armed factions, negotiate with Israel, and implement agreements. That matters enormously.
Any future agreement will require Palestinians to make painful choices. It will require one government, one legal system, and one legitimate security authority. It will require political movements to choose between democratic participation and independent armed power. It will require leaders who can tell the Palestinian public difficult truths and still claim to speak in its name.
That cannot be achieved indefinitely through presidential decrees, aging institutions, and political arrangements created decades ago.
Giving the Palestinians a voice
The timing is also striking. Israelis are approaching their own election. They will be asked to choose not only who should govern them but what direction Israel should take after October 7 and the wars that followed. Palestinians deserve the same opportunity.
In fact, the two elections should be understood as connected. Israeli politics affects Palestinian politics every day.
Settlement expansion, military occupation, settler violence, restrictions on movement, and the absence of a political horizon strengthen those Palestinians who argue that diplomacy has failed. Palestinian violence and rejectionism strengthen the Israeli Right and those who insist that permanent control is the only way to guarantee security.
For years, extremists on each side have helped strengthen the extremists on the other. Elections offer at least the possibility of breaking that cycle.
That is why the international community, and particularly the United States, Europe, and the Arab states, should be saying clearly now that the Palestinian elections must take place.
They should offer practical assistance for voting in Gaza and east Jerusalem. They should provide election observers. They should support the independence of the electoral institutions. And they should make clear that political pressure from any Palestinian faction or outside government to cancel the elections would be unacceptable.
The November election will not solve the Palestinian national crisis. But canceling it would deepen that crisis immediately.
Palestinians cannot build a state with institutions that are permanently afraid of their own voters. And Israelis cannot continue asking where the Palestinian partner is while Palestinians are denied the opportunity to choose new ones.
The writer is the Middle East director of the International Communities Organization and the co-head of the Alliance for Two States.

At least 21 people have been killed and dozens more are believed to be trapped under rubble after a bombed-out six-storey building housing displaced Palestinians collapsed in Gaza City on Wednesday.
The apartment block was damaged by Israeli bombing and had been leaning precariously to one side for some time. Despite its dangerous condition, the building was housing around 100 displaced Palestinians, including 50 children, according to the UN.
The building collapsed in the early hours of Wednesday morning, crushing nearby tents which were also being used to house homeless Palestinians.
Five children were among the 21 bodies recovered, civil defense workers said. Some 25 injured people have already been pulled from the rubble, and rescuers told the BBC that the voices of trapped victims could be heard beneath the debris.

Texas adopts anti-Muslim curriculum amid backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:58:00 UTC
03:58:00 KST

Texas education officials have approved a sweeping rewrite of high school social studies standards that Muslim students, civil rights advocates and some academic advisers say embeds anti-Muslim bias into public school classrooms, including language linking so-called “radical Islam” to the 9/11 attacks and portraying early Islamic history through warfare and slavery.
The Republican-controlled State Board of Education finalized the standards after days of contentious debate, brushing aside calls from Muslim Texans to revise language they warned could stigmatize students and reinforce stereotypes about Islam.
Among the most disputed provisions is a requirement for students to learn that “radical Islam” motivated the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
Muslim speakers urged the board to focus more specifically on al-Qaida, Osama bin Laden and the terrorists responsible for the attacks rather than language they said risks associating Islam itself with terrorism.
The objections also highlighted that Muslims were among the victims and first responders killed on 9/11, including Muslim-American emergency medical technician Salman Hamdani, who died while trying to help others at the World Trade Center.
Another provision directs students studying early Islam to examine Prophet Muhammad through descriptions of military campaigns against Jewish and Christian tribes, slavery and the taking of female captives.
Muslim Texans told the board that such a presentation singles out Islam for hostile treatment while stripping events from their wider historical context.
Some of the board’s own appointed experts also questioned the historical basis for the wording.
Andrea Hutchison, a social studies curriculum coordinator for Prosper Independent School District, warned that elements of the portrayal did not hold up under close historical scrutiny.
Robert Koons, a philosophy professor at the University of Texas at Austin, also questioned the reliability of sources underlying some of the claims.
“I would warn us about including things that are not based on well-established secular sources,” Koons told the board.
Despite the objections, the Republican majority retained much of the disputed language, including rejecting an effort to remove the word “brutal” from a description of early Islamic military campaigns.
The board also did not restore previously proposed material addressing Muslim contributions to fields such as algebra and astronomy.
That omission became another major point of criticism among Muslim students and parents, who argued that Texas classrooms would present students with negative portrayals of Islam while giving far less attention to the contributions of Muslim civilizations to science, mathematics and global history.
“I feel attacked, as if my religion doesn’t belong,” 15-year-old Habiiba Quresh told the board. “I shouldn’t have to defend my religion in the middle of history class because of one sentence someone on this board wrote.”
The Texas chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) strongly condemned the adopted standards, saying the revisions would institutionalize prejudice in classrooms.
“The board has turned our classrooms into a place where prejudice is taught as fact and entire communities are written out of their own history,” CAIR-Texas said.
The organization said the dispute extended beyond Muslims, arguing that the standards also reduce or reshape coverage of Black and Palestinian history.
Board Chair Aaron Kinsey rejected criticism that the overhaul unfairly targeted communities, defending the final framework as balanced.
“There’s been a lot said out of this room, particularly to sensationalize all these topics and to make them seem more divisive than they actually are,” Kinsey said.
He said the 15-member board worked through the competing proposals democratically and described the overall result as an “exceptional job.”
The controversy over anti-Islam propaganda forms part of a much broader conservative restructuring of social studies education in Texas.
The board previously approved revisions for younger students and a required reading list that includes biblical stories. The new framework also places greater emphasis on Christianity, Western civilization and the ideas the Republican majority says shaped the United States.
Under the high school standards, students will be expected to study connections between biblical imagery, principles of equality and justice in the Declaration of Independence and Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech.
Critics argued during public testimony that such treatment presents Christianity primarily through its positive influence while Islam is disproportionately discussed alongside warfare, terrorism and slavery.
Some speakers also challenged what they saw as an uneven treatment of slavery.
An 11-year-old student identified as Sarah reminded board members that slavery existed across civilizations and argued that emphasizing slavery in Islamic history without comparable discussion of Christian justifications for the transatlantic slave trade creates a distorted picture.
“Slavery existed for thousands of years before Islam,” she said. “It is unfair to label slavery as Islamic without also discussing the Christian role in the slave trade to the Americas.”
The U.S. history standards have generated separate criticism over their treatment of American slavery.
The framework describes slavery as an institution that “existed in many societies throughout history,” wording Democratic members and some advisers said could obscure the distinctive racial system of slavery that developed in the United States.
“Slavery is foundational to this country,” Democratic board member Marisa B. Pérez-Díaz said, arguing that students should spend considerably more time studying its impact on the development of the U.S.
The new standards also require students to examine arguments against the modern welfare state that developed through the expansion of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s Great Society programs, which were launched in the 1960s to combat poverty and racial inequality.
Teachers, Democratic board members and civil rights groups have criticized the broader revision process, saying conservative activists wielded disproportionate influence while educators were marginalized.
Critics also raised concerns over transparency surrounding the drafting process and the outside groups that helped shape elements of the curriculum.
Republican members reject that characterization, arguing that the overhaul restores greater emphasis on U.S. history, Texas history, Western civilization and the country’s founding principles.
The restructuring also eliminates the existing sixth-grade world cultures course, a decision some educators fear will leave students with less exposure to societies and traditions outside the Western world.
Supporters say the opposite approach is necessary, arguing that Texas students should first develop a stronger understanding of their own state, country and the historical forces that shaped them.
The overhaul concludes years of political battles over how Texas schools teach race, religion, national identity and American history.
The board postponed an earlier social studies rewrite in 2022 after conservative lawmakers objected to proposed lessons involving race and gender.
The Republican majority has since pushed the curriculum in a more conservative direction, saying schools should not teach children to view the United States primarily through its historical failures.
Muslim organizations and other critics, however, say the mistreatment of Islam illustrates the risks of allowing ideological battles to determine how religions and minority communities are portrayed in public classrooms.
The new high school social studies standards are scheduled to begin being phased into Texas schools during the 2030-31 academic year.

Is EU’s offer to Canada a blueprint for Britain – or a reminder it is out in the cold?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:57:14 UTC
03:57:14 KST

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been advocating closer alignment with “middle powers” since January in the face of recklessness in Washington.
But what should worry another middle power, the UK, is that it was Brussels that came up with Wednesday’s big reveal in Strasbourg.
To a standing ovation at her State of the Union address, Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to open the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first “associate member” in a push to forge new links among allies in “an openly hostile world”.
The European Commission president’s deal could be seen as an “earthquake” offer said Joël Reland, of UK in a Changing Europe, though it remains “deliciously vague”.
But it also sets Canada apart from the UK, which could, once upon a time, have had some sort of associate membership with the EU were it not for the drive for a clean-break Brexit.
The last time associate membership of the EU was mooted was in relation to Ukraine as an off-the-books novel way of bringing Kyiv closer to the bloc without become a fully fledged member state.
New partnerships, von der Leyen said, were needed “in the cold fragility of today’s world” and in the face of an increasingly assertive China.
Just moments earlier she spoke about the need for the EU to diversify urgently its supply of critical raw materials (CRM) and rare earths currently dominated by China, allowing it to follow Japan and stockpile said minerals needed for everything from the car to the defence industries.
It is not a new subject – after all the EU has been grappling with China’s export surplus since 2023 and it introduced the Critical Raw Materials Act as far back as 2024.
The prospect of an enhanced relationship with Ottawa is one that Keir Starmer might have dreamed of.
Canada has something the EU desperately needs – rich supplies of CRM and rare earths – and the EU has something Canada urgently wants: new markets for products it can no longer sell into the EU in the face of a trade war with Donald Trump.
Speaking before von der Leyen’s speech, Tobias Cremer, a German social democrat MEP, said a new deeper relationship between the EU and Canada could be a blueprint for other countries, including the UK.
Bernd Lange, the influential chair of the European parliament’s international trade committee, said associate membership could “become a model for close transcontinental partnerships with democratic countries against the new model of the law of the strongest”.
After Iceland’s rejection of membership of the EU, Fabian Zuleeg, the chief executive and chief economist of the European Policy Centre, suggested it was time that the EU developed new models, beyond the European Economic Area, that might offer “partial, gradual or associated membership options”.
Reland said the vagueness of the offer extended to Canada could be promising for the UK’s hopes for a similar offer.
“Any deep Canadian integration into the EU market would take some very heavy work to negotiate a defined set of treaty-bound rights and obligations, and so it seems more likely that – at least in the short term – cooperation will focus on more vaguely constructed alliances for ‘prosperity’ and ‘security’,” which aligns with the UK government’s desires, Reland wrote on Wednesday.
In the current political climate in the UK, it is difficult to envisage a world in which Andy Burnham would encourage any associate membership of the EU. He has a steely focus on domestic issues and is keen to avoid going down any Brexit wormholes.
The UK is seeking a reset with the EU, but the goals in the first year were modest and have yet to be achieved.
The offer to Canada suggests the bigger ambitions for relations with the EU the better.

Trump praises PM Modi for curbing ‘illicit opium cultivation’ as India stays on US ‘drug transit’ list

The US president also said Washington would continue working with New Delhi on counter-narcotics efforts (File photo)
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday welcomed Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s efforts to curb illicit opium poppy cultivation in India, even as Washington included India among 23 countries designated as major drug transit or illicit drug-producing countries.In a Presidential Determination submitted to the US Congress, Trump said he looked forward to continued cooperation with India under the United States-India Drug Policy Framework. “I welcome Prime Minister Modi and the Government of India’s efforts to address illicit opium poppy cultivation and bolster supply chain integrity,” Trump said in the directive made public on Wednesday.
India’s inclusion on the list does not, however, amount to a US finding that its government is failing to tackle the drug trade. The determination said countries are designated because of a combination of geographic, commercial and economic factors that allow illicit drugs or precursor chemicals to be produced or moved through their territory.The US document specifically noted that being placed on the list does not necessarily reflect a country’s current counterdrug efforts or the extent of its cooperation with Washington.Along with India, the countries identified by the US include Afghanistan, The Bahamas, Belize, Bolivia, Burma, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Jamaica, Laos, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Pakistan, Peru, Venezuela and China.
The designation comes as Washington continues to focus on disrupting international drug supply chains, including the movement of precursor chemicals used to manufacture synthetic drugs. The White House’s 2026 National Drug Control Strategy has also called for stronger bilateral counterdrug cooperation with countries including India.
Trump highlights US-India cooperation
Trump said the US and India would continue working together on counter-narcotics efforts. The two countries established a Drug Policy Executive Working Group earlier this year, with discussions focused on illicit narcotics trafficking, precursor chemicals and the security of pharmaceutical supply chains.The US president also pointed to what he described as “historic progress” by his administration in tackling drug trafficking and narcoterrorist organisations.He cited tighter border security, lower drug seizures and a decline in overdose deaths as evidence of progress, saying seizures of fentanyl and other drugs along the US southern border had fallen by more than half after what he called four years of “open border chaos”.“After four years of open border chaos, seizures of fentanyl and other drugs being smuggled into the United States have been reduced by more than half, and drug overdose deaths have plunged,” Trump said.Trump presses China over drug precursors
Trump separately called on China to take stronger action against the flow of precursor chemicals used to manufacture fentanyl, methamphetamine and other synthetic drugs.“The PRC continues to be the world’s largest producer of many of the precursor chemicals used to illicitly produce fentanyl, methamphetamine, and other deadly synthetic drugs,” Trump said.He said he had raised the issue directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping and noted that Beijing had introduced licensing requirements last year for companies exporting designated precursor chemicals to North America.The US has made disruption of precursor-chemical supply chains a central part of its broader counter-drug strategy, which calls for international cooperation to prevent legitimate trade channels from being exploited for illicit drug production.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda confirmed a Russian Gerbera drone entered the country’s airspace from Belarus before NATO fighter jets shot it down on Tuesday, Sept. 15.

Italian fighter jets were deployed from the Šiauliai Air Base and intercepted the aircraft, after authorities declared a possible air threat in the Vilnius and Kaunas counties.
“According to the information now available, it was a Gerbera-type drone. The electronic component is still being analyzed,” Nausėda said, according to Lithuanian news outlet Delfi.
“Much more data will become available about where it came from, how and under what circumstances,” he added.
Drone entered from Belarus

The country’s National Crisis Management Center initially reported that the aircraft may have been neutralized near the village of Navasėlkai in the Alytus district, but later said it was shot down near Pratkūnai, a village in the Kaišiadorys district.
Russian Strikes Kill 6, Wound At Least 17 Across Ukraine
Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas confirmed that the drone was carrying an explosive device, which was subsequently neutralized.
Nausėda said similar events could occur again, given Lithuania’s location near Belarus and the proximity of Vilnius to the border.
“The most important thing is that we can detect them in time, preferably already over the territory of neighboring countries, so that we can respond more quickly, because we really have very little time to prepare,” he said, adding that Lithuania must also develop alternative ways to neutralize drones instead of exclusively relying on missiles.
Lithuania’s air defense capabilities
The president concluded that Lithuania must broaden its air-defense capacity, including through short-range drone interceptors and other alternative systems.
“My goal and my question to the Ministry of Defense is: how quickly will we move forward in introducing other, alternative means of engagement?” Nausėda said.
Although Lithuania had already strengthened its integrated air-defense systems, the president acknowledged that its operation still involved mistakes.
Authorities must balance the need to warn the public quickly with the requirement to provide reliable information. “Only verified information should be published – information for which there would be no need later to apologize or make corrections,” he said.
“Yes, incidents still happen that sometimes cause anger, sometimes a smile, like that unfortunate case involving birds,” he added.
Just two days prior to the drone incident, on Sept. 13, a NATO fighter jet was scrambled and a Vilnius Airport closed due to a suspicious object in the air. The object turned out to be a flock of birds.

Era of US global dominance over — media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:55:21 UTC
03:55:21 KST

WASHINGTON, September 16. /TASS/. The era of US dominance on the world stage has ended, American historian and political scientist Phillips Payson O’Brien argued in an op-ed published by The Atlantic.
O’Brien, a professor of strategic studies at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, wrote that "the American age" that followed World War II was inevitably going to end, adding that "what’s shocking is how suddenly" that moment arrived.
According to O’Brien, America’s military strength, global network of bases and logistics systems, and military and diplomatic partnerships around the world proved insufficient to defeat Iran. He stressed that the erosion of US capabilities was not solely the fault of President Donald Trump. However, he argued that the war with Iran had revealed how profoundly the dynamics of global power had shifted and how far American strength had declined.
In the expert’s view, a key reason Washington refrained from escalating the military conflict with Iran over the summer, despite its threats against Tehran, was the loss of its operational base in Bahrain. The facility had served as a crucial logistics hub and housed the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet. O’Brien noted that US officials had reportedly considered not rebuilding US military bases in the Persian Gulf that sustained extensive damage in Iranian strikes. He believes that the US military is currently unable to defend some of its key facilities even against a less technologically advanced adversary such as Iran.
O’Brien described the weakening of US power as having a "cascading effect" that had already undermined the Pentagon’s position in the Asia-Pacific region. He called Washington’s transfer of military equipment from the region to the Middle East a "desperate move," saying it demonstrated that US military resources, despite being vast compared with those of most other countries, were "not infinite."
The expert also said the erosion of Washington’s long-standing alliances would be "devastating to America’s global position." Other countries are "already adjusting" to the newly exposed weaknesses of the United States, he added
O’Brien predicted that US global influence would continue to decline. The conflict with Iran demonstrated that the American age had "come to an end," he concluded.

The U.S. Attorney General was asked whether he’d investigate Russian boxing chief Umar Kremlev’s reported financing of Trump Jr.’s wedding festivities. His response: What is there to investigate?
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters at the White House that he had no plans to investigate Russian businessman Umar Kremlev’s possible role in organizing Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding.

‘Newsnight’s kindest critic’: Bonnie Greer was always effortlessly in command
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:54:48 UTC
03:54:48 KST

Bonnie Greer, who has died at the age of 77, moved to the UK from New York in 1986. She grew up in Chicago with six younger siblings. Her father worked in a factory and her mother “kept house”, she said once – in a tone so elegantly ominous, she conjured an image of a woman holding up a full dwelling with seven children in it, with her bare hands. Greer was ambitious and, academically, a high flyer, but abandoned her law degree, facing baked-in sexism from professors. Yet, given she started writing plays aged nine, arguably she was only hastening a creative career that was inevitable.
The Actors Studio was what drew her to the West Village in Manhattan in the late 70s, and she was there at the height of the Aids crisis, a brutal time of mass bereavements and poisonous prejudice. She lost about 35 of her friends, and later told the Sunday Times: “I owe those people my life. If I hadn’t met my gay friends I would be a suburban SUV-driving granny. They taught me the value of insurrection and fun. Nearly 30 years on, I’m still that 25-year-old, on top of some bar, in one of those vintage dresses, dancing with those guys.” But when she arrived, touring, at the Edinburgh festival, it felt like a release, from the “shadow of death”, and a New York theatre scene bereft of its heart. She stayed in the UK permanently.
Greer was a remarkable talent as a playwright: witty, dry, serious, unflinching. She was playwright in residence at the Soho theatre in the late 80s and was writing plays for Radio 3 and 4 by the early 90s. Marilyn and Ella Backstage at the Mocambo, in 2005, is perhaps the most famous, and was later adapted as a stage musical. It dramatises the solidarity between the actor and the singer – Monroe persuaded the club to book Fitzgerald, with the promise that she (mid-1950s, the height of her fame) would sit in the front row every night. Fitzgerald later said she never had to play a small jazz club again thanks to this intervention, and it redrew the boundaries of what was acceptable, in racism, in jazz, in Hollywood. In Greer’s telling, there is no white saviour narrative, only a dynamic creative symbiosis between two geniuses.
Bonnie Greer was a joiner. She was on the board of everything, from the Women’s prize for fiction to the British Museum, she was president of the Brontë society – she got stuck in. An unusual mix of originality and authority, she was in high demand as a cultural critic, particularly in broadcasting. She was a regular contributor to Newsnight Review on BBC Two, as well as a critic for Time Out and a political commentator for newspapers, including this one.
Out of all that came her appearance in 2009 on Question Time with Nick Griffin, then leader of the BNP. It was a frankly bizarre, though not uncharacteristic, bit of political curation from the BBC, since Griffin was a holocaust denier and racist, tried three times and once convicted (in the late 90s) for inciting racial, Islamophobic or antisemitic hatred. Many wondered why the BBC felt such a duty to platform so toxic a figure, and Sayeeda Warsi, also on the panel, asked Greer before whether she was OK to sit next to him (Greer replied: “I’m from Chicago, I’m not scared of this guy”). She said later to the Evening Standard that it was “probably the weirdest and most creepy experience of my life”, but onscreen she was unruffled and effortlessly in command, and she later turned that weird creepiness into an opera for the Royal Opera House, on whose board she also served, along with the London Film School’s.
She was very generous on a panel, receptive and softly spoken while absolutely trenchant, and vividly engaged; she was never without a view. She wrote two novels, Hanging by Her Teeth in 1994 and Entropy in 2009, but her more natural metier was in the discursive, collaborative arts and broader culture. She was once called “Newsnight’s kindest critic”, and said of her stage writing: “I was taught that theatre is supposed to slow the world down so it can be looked at, and the person who looks is not supposed to be the same when they walk out. Otherwise, there’s no fucking point. Art is not a leisure activity. It’s about engagement.”

‘Defend the Ecosystem’: USAF, Experts Want to Up Cyber Defense for Critical Infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:53:17 UTC
03:53:17 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force is shoring up its cyber defenses both on and off base for critical infrastructure such as water and electrical power, and industry experts are calling for more, even specialized, dedicated microgrids offsite to support USAF operations in case of a total blackout caused by cyberattacks.
“We have spent years protecting and defending the tip of the combat spear, but right now, ladies and gentlemen, our adversaries have decided to focus time, resources, and interest on the hand that wields the spear, and that’s where we have to focus,” retired USAF Lt. Gen. Chris “Wedge” Weggeman said Sept. 16 during a panel discussion at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
Weggeman, now working in cybersecurity with Deloitte, also said that while the issue is new, the process of mission assurance is well esablished.
“We really don’t need a new playbook. It’s really the same playbook,” Weggeman said. “You’ve just got to know: what does this capability do in terms of enabling my mission? What happens when an adversary takes it away from me, and how long does it take me to recover? And do I have the ability to fight?”
For a long time, the military’s cybersecurity efforts have focused on information technology, or IT—the software and computers that manage data. Increasingly, though, experts are worried about operational technology, or OT—the tech that controls physical equipment and systems.
Airmen from the 16th Air Force at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, recently announced partnerships with research centers, government entities, and private sector organizations to help defend their OT where it touches Air Force assets.
“We are getting after it—workforce development, capabilities, intelligence, and everything else we need to execute this mission,” Brig. Gen. Jason Christman, 16th Air Force OT lead, said in a release.
The move delivered an OT Certification Joint Qualification Record in a two-month timespan. Next steps call for the 16th Air Force team to push the certification across the joint force and share “threat telemetry and defense strategies” with program partners.
The work also included standing up an OT Cyber Defender Schoolhouse within the 16th Air Force, according to the release.
Identify and Defend
The first challenge the service has, Weggeman told Air & Space Forces Magazine after the panel, is “to earnestly and quickly determine the critical mission resilience or redundancies and resiliencies and dependencies we have with [operational technology], and a lot of that OT lives outside of our fence line.”
“We can’t just say there’s a fence line, so I don’t do anything about it,” said Weggeman, former Air Forces Cyber commander and director of strategy, plans, and policy at U.S. Cyber Command.
Another panelist, retired Army Col. Candice Frost, pointed to a recent project that could help model efforts to protect public works OT from cyberattack. Project Watershed 250 in Texas, which launched in August, is combining state assets with the White House’s Office of the National Cyber Director to prevent water and wastewater facilities from cyber-attacks.
Future work must include ways to segregate services such as water and electrical, provide backups, and potentially build offsite electrical “microgrids” to keep bases powered if their main power feed is “cut” via a cyberattack, said Frost, now vice president for mission engagement with Parsons.
“Defend the ecosystem, not just the base, because the base is the stronghold, but the ecosystem supporting it is the area that we see in industry that needs the most support,” Frost said.
Identifying critical OT is the first step; then leaders must work to make it resilient. Older equipment, what Weggeman calls the “hand-carved wooden shoe problem,” is somewhat protected from cyberattack because it’s old and not connected.
But increasingly, the retired three-star said, much of the OT supporting a base is being connected to the internet, “which is good because we know how to do that, but also terrifying because an adversary can get in now.”
Weggeman said that while great strides have been made in improving recovery time on the IT side, ways to quickly recover when OT goes down are lagging.
“We have less operational readiness to derive the mission back to where it needs to be from the OT perspective,” Weggeman said.

Anduril has integrated aerial bombs, unguided rockets and cruise missiles onto its semi-autonomous FQ-44 unmanned fighter aircraft.
Anduril Industries said the FQ-44 has already demonstrated compatibility with a wide range of munitions.
These include 500-pound (230 kg) aerial bombs, small-diameter bombs, air-launched cruise missiles, unguided rocket pods, external targeting pods and many other types of weapons.
The unmanned fighter aircraft was previously demonstrated launching AIM-120 air-to-air missiles.
The aircraft can therefore serve as either a fighter or a bomber depending on the needs of the Air Force.
The FQ-44 Fury jet-powered unmanned fighter aircraft was developed as part of the U.S. Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program.
It is intended to serve as an unmanned “wingman,” operating semi-autonomously, receiving tasks from a human operator and working alongside F-35, F-22 and other aircraft.
The aircraft is approximately 6.1 meters long, has a wingspan of 5.2 meters, a top speed of about Mach 0.95 and a service ceiling of approximately 15 km, although the specifications of the production version may differ.
Another advantage of the FQ-44 Fury is its rapid development.
A little more than two years passed between the delivery of the first prototype in April 2024, the start of ground testing in April 2025, its first flight in October that year and the signing of a contract for serial production in June 2026.
The FQ-44 Fury is being developed as a relatively inexpensive and scalable unmanned aircraft that can be produced in significant quantities.
Its architecture is designed to use artificial intelligence and autonomous systems to perform complex tasks with minimal direct control by an operator.

On Wednesday, the U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years as part of a renewed fight against inflation, which has intensified since the beginning of the year because of the war with Iran, UNN reports.
Officials voted to raise the benchmark lending rate by a quarter of a percentage point, to a range of 3.75–4%, thereby reversing one of last year's three rate cuts.

Fed officials are also concerned about the potential inflationary impact of large-scale development of artificial intelligence technologies.
The decision taken on Wednesday marked the first major step toward changing interest rates under new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh. The increase could lead to disagreements with President Donald Trump, who appointed Warsh to the position after repeatedly pressuring the central bank to lower rates.

US inflation expectations tied to Strait of Hormuz

In a post on X, Ghalibaf questioned whether the US Federal Reserve could reopen the Strait of Hormuz or increase oil production simply by raising interest rates. He suggested that changes in borrowing costs would not address the supply-side shock caused by disruptions at strategic energy chokepoints, particularly the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb.
Ghalibaf argued that inflation expectations in the United States were being affected by what he described as the closure of key energy routes rather than by interest rates alone. He said the associated “Strait of Hormuz risk” was a factor determining interest rates and claimed that control over that risk was currently in Iran’s hands.
The parliament speaker’s comments challenged the conventional use of monetary policy to anchor inflation expectations. He argued that relying solely on demand-side tools such as interest rates was no longer sufficient under current conditions and that geopolitical factors could have a stronger influence on economic indicators such as inflation.
Under normal conditions, central banks seek to anchor inflation expectations around an inflation target or a credible long-term inflation rate, generally using interest-rate adjustments in response to inflation and economic activity.
Ghalibaf argued, however, that the current situation required financial markets and policymakers to incorporate additional variables, including the status of the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, into their calculations. He suggested that, in his view, US inflation expectations would remain difficult to anchor as long as the geopolitical risks surrounding these waterways persisted.
Ghalibaf referenced a modified version of the Taylor Rule, adding variables related to the Strait of Hormuz and what he termed the associated risk premium. He said the purpose was to examine whether an interest-rate increase could reduce such risks or increase oil supply.
