was as warm-blooded as humans, new study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:48:27 UTC
03:48:27 KST

For years, paleontologists have been piecing together clues that suggest Tyrannosaurus rex may have been quite unlike modern reptiles—including the possibility that it may have been warm-blooded.
But you can’t stick a T. rex on a treadmill or put a thermometer in its mouth, so scientists must resort to more indirect methods to gauge dinosaurs’ metabolisms and internal temperatures—such as the chemical composition of fossilized teeth. And now, for the first time, researchers say they have pinpointed an exact body temperature for T. rex.
“The enamel chemistry is truly recording the temperature at which it formed, and 66 million years later, we can read it using those measurements on a mass spectrometer,” says Aradhna Tripati, a geoscientist at University of California, Los Angeles, and a co-author of the paper. “It’s the next best thing to sticking a thermometer up a T. rex’s ‘butt,’ which we wouldn’t have wanted to do anyway.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Using tiny remains of T. rex tooth enamel found in modern-day Montana, scientists measured isotopes within the sample to estimate the dinosaur’s temperature . They found that T. rex likely ran at around 36 degrees Celsius—similar to the internal body temperature of modern-day humans.
Researchers have estimated dinosaur metabolism and growth rates before, but Tripati says the new study’s method is especially precise at estimating internal temperature because tooth enamel and thermodynamic estimates aren’t as sensitive to confounding factors such as environmental temperatures.
Robert Eagle, a co-author of the study and a geobiologist at University of California, Los Angeles, pioneered this approach to measuring prehistoric body temperatures. He says the findings are a culmination of some 15 years of work. Eagle hopes to use the same technique to suss out the body temperatures of avian dinosaurs and ancient mammalian ancestors next.
“I’m excited that it worked so well because we’ve tried a lot of things with this technique, but this really seemed to be a clear result,” Eagle says. “This gives me optimism that it’s going to be useful looking at other exciting questions.”
The findings add to the growing body of research into how dinosaurs functioned. For example, a 2022 study showed that dinosaurs likely had a range of metabolisms and estimated T. rexes that were on the lower end of endothermy. This new paper, which finds T. rexes’body temperatures to be more similar to those of large mammals than those of smaller, hotter animals such as birds, complements those findings, says Jasmina Wiemann, a paleobiologist at Johns Hopkins University and lead author of the 2022 study.
The new study, published on Wednesday in Science Advances, is “absolutely mind-blowing” and “impressively precise,” Wiemann says. The findings suggest that, based on their temperature, T. rexes likely could have lived anywhere on Earth—even the Arctic, she says.
“It has been really, really exciting to be a young scientist in the field and watching how the collective evidence that we have from different isotope data is converging toward the same picture, suggesting that most nonavian dinosaurs were probably warm-blooded,” Wiemann says.

Partisans claim sabotage at Russian plant producing missile components
An agent of the Ukrainian partisan group Atesh sabotaged the power supply to an electronics plant in the Russian city of Voronezh, the group said on Sept. 16.
The facility produces components used in Kh-101 and Iskander-K missiles, as well as Pantsir-S1 air defense systems, according to Atesh.
"Our agent, after a long study of the facility, detailed planning, and searching for weak points, managed to infiltrate an electrical substation near the VZPP-Sborka plant," Atesh said. "After bypassing security, he destroyed the main distribution cabinet supplying the enterprise and safely left the city."
The sabotage caused a voltage surge and cut power to the plant's workshops, the group said. Atesh also claimed that restoring full electricity supplies took several weeks, disrupting deliveries of key electronic components and delaying the production of Russian missiles and air defense systems.
Atesh did not disclose when the operation took place, saying it delayed publication to protect its agents.
Voronezh, a city in southwestern Russia, lies roughly 250 kilometers (155 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
VZPP-Sborka is a Russian manufacturer of semiconductors, integrated circuits, and power modules whose components are used in several Russian weapons systems, according to Ukraine's military intelligence.
40% of Ukrainians ready to relocate if conditions deteriorate 'significantly' this winter, poll reveals
Some 40% of Ukrainians are prepared to relocate this winter if conditions in the country deteriorate significantly, according to a new poll released by the Gradus agency on Sept. 16.
The survey, conducted by Gradus on Sept. 4–7, polled 1,000 Ukrainians aged 18–60 living in cities with more than 50,000 residents, excluding the occupied territories and areas with active hostilities.
In the lead-up to winter, Ukrainians are preparing for Russia to once again target the country's energy infrastructure in an attempt to make the country unlivable.
Russia has already escalated its attacks on Ukrainian businesses in recent weeks, targeting supermarket distribution centers, postal facilities, gas stations, warehouses, railway infrastructure, industrial plants, and Black Sea ports.
According to Gradus polling, safety is the main factor that would prompt Ukrainians to relocate. However, only one in five respondents said they would consider going abroad — the rest would look for temporary relocation within Ukraine.
"Most" respondents said the decision to relocate would not be prompted by a "single inconvenience" but by multiple factors, such as infrastructure disruptions, safety concerns, and lack of access to healthcare, education, and other essential public services.
"There is an important shift in how Ukrainians are approaching the coming winter: they are increasingly less likely to see resilience as the ability to endure any hardship indefinitely," sociologist Evheniia Blyzniuk, Gradus' CEO, said.
"People are not panicking about possible difficulties, but nor are they relying on the assumption that things will somehow work out. They are assessing risks and preparing backup options."

Russia plans new prison complex in occupied Kherson Oblast among wider prison expansion
Russian authorities plan to build a new prison complex in the occupied part of Kherson Oblast under a program to construct seven such facilities across Russia and occupied Ukraine by 2035, The Moscow Times reported on Sept. 16, citing a Russian government program.
The new facilities will combine pretrial detention centers with penal colonies of different security levels and will have a combined capacity of more than 20,000 people, according to The Moscow Times. The capacity includes 5,380 places for pretrial detainees and 15,120 for prisoners serving sentences.
Apart from the occupied part of Kherson Oblast, Russia plans to build the complexes in Kaluga, Astrakhan, and Tyumen oblasts, Buryatia, and Zabaykalsky Krai, while the first is expected to open in Tatarstan by 2030.
Each facility is expected to cost between 13 billion and 20 billion rubles (around $154 million and $237 million), The Moscow Times reported.
Russia's Justice Ministry estimated that concentrating detention centers and penal colonies in the same complexes could reduce the cost of holding prisoners and detainees by 25-30%, allowing the projects to pay for themselves within about a decade.
Ukraine approves more than 80 companies for private air defense
Eighty-one companies are now authorized to form private air defense units amid near-constant Russian attacks on Ukraine, particularly Kyiv and the surrounding area, the Defense Ministry said on Sept. 16. 
As Russia shifts its bombardment tactics to near-hourly drone attacks throughout the day, increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure, more businesses are joining the program, bringing the number of units up by 30 since July.
The ministry said the program is designed to protect workers and facilities while reducing pressure on military air defenses, which now face increased strain beyond concentrated overnight barrages.
Established by the Cabinet of Ministers in November 2025, the private air defense program allows businesses to voluntarily form and finance air defense groups staffed by trained and certified civilian employees. Eligible companies include providers of essential services such as electricity, water, transport, and communications, alongside security firms protecting other businesses.
Companies apply to the Defense Ministry for authorization, then agree with the Air Force command on their units' operations. Under rules introduced in March, participating businesses can also temporarily receive military air defense equipment and ammunition unused by combat units, with Air Force approval.
Private air defense is just one component of Ukraine's multi-level system of airspace protection.
The first successful interceptions under the program were announced in March, when a company's unit downed Russian drones in Kharkiv Oblast. In April, the ministry reported a private group's first interception of a jet-powered Shahed-type drone.
By mid-July, private air defense had downed more than 50 Shahed and Zala drones, according to the ministry.

Nato leader warns of ‘most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:46:30 UTC
03:46:30 KST

Nato needs “more UK and more Europe” to deal with the most dangerous security environment faced by the west in a generation, the secretary general of the 32-country military alliance said this afternoon on a visit to the UK.
Mark Rutte praised Britain for promising to increase defence spending in line with US demands after a meeting prime minister Andy Burnham – but argued that the military and financial effort must continue into the future.
“It is essential that your armed forces continue to provide the hard power Nato needs,” Rutte said in a speech to a specialist audience at Ditchley Park, a wartime retreat used by Winston Churchill in Oxfordshire.
It was a plea for the UK to make progress towards an alliance-wide target demanded by Donald Trump of spending 3.5% of GDP by 2035, about £30bn in real terms, money that has to be found from extra taxation, borrowing or reducing other spending.
Britain has so far only budgeted to increase defence spending to 2.7% of GDP by the end of the next decade. Short-term financial pressures have meant that the army has been told to stop non-essential training by the end of the year.
Chancellor John Healey resigned as defence secretary from Keir Starmer’s government in June because the former prime minister would not commit to 3% by 2030, arguing that it would require too great a step up in the next decade.
But Healey refused to recommit to the interim target when he was appointed to the Treasury by Burnham a month later, raising questions that the new government was backloading spending increases until after the next election.
Rutte said that he had discussed Britain’s “Nato commitments” when he had met Burnham at a science business park in Oxford earlier on Wednesday, without offering any details, in the first one-on-one meeting between the two.
Prior to that meeting, Burnham acknowledged that he had replaced Starmer, but insisted that there was “never any change in the UK’s unwavering commitment to Nato and our Nato obligations”.
The Nato chief, a former Dutch prime minister, said many in Europe had made the “casual assumption” that the US would “always provide most of the muscle and pick up the bill, no matter what” until Trump returned to the White House.
Instead, he noted that during a summit in The Hague in 2025, the UK and other alliance members had agreed to increase their own defence spending to match US levels, in response to Trump’s demand that Europe take the lead in defending the continent.
“We need more UK and more Europe in the alliance,” Rutte said, because Nato “faces the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with a return to wars in Europe and the Middle East, and wider geopolitical uncertainty.
Citing “Russia and its war against Ukraine, terrorism, Iran and the tectonic shifts of global geopolitical competition”, Rutte argued that the UK and Europe needed to invest more, because otherwise “our collective defence will not be credible”.
Britain, he said, had “a central role in building this stronger Europe in a stronger Nato” and noted that the UK was spending billions to upgrade the Trident nuclear deterrent, which is pledged to the defence of Nato members.
The UK is also gradually upgrading its conventional forces, though the UK’s overall defence spending, long the second largest in the alliance, is now behind Germany. By 2029, Berlin’s military budgets are on track to be twice that of the UK.
The UK was “leading the pushback” against a Russian campaign of provocation and sabotage across Europe, Rutte said, and that the UK had been “a good friend to Ukraine”. Britain spends £3bn a year supporting Ukraine with weapons.
Meanwhile, Canada, seeking to diversify its defence ties away from the US, has formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military coalition, prime minister Mark Carney’s office said on Wednesday.
The a grouping of 10 North Atlantic Nato member states is a rapid response military partnership.
Canada, already a Nato member, is seeking closer military cooperation with Europe.
The JEF comprises Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the UK.

The Kentucky Republican read eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on the House floor shortly after the chamber convened on Tuesday, citing the war secretary’s violation of multiple provisions of the 1973 War Powers Resolution in launching and waging the war against Iran.
Massie said that Hegseth unlawfully initiated the war, defied the Congress order to withdraw US forces from the war and incurred unnecessary civilian casualties.
“By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable,” Massie said in a statement.
Under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, a president generally must end unauthorized US military hostilities within 60 days unless Congress has authorized the action, with an additional 30-day period allowed for an orderly withdrawal.
He added that “Hegseth’s constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran.”

Congress, Massie said, “must not turn a blind eye to Secretary Hegseth’s unconstitutional and illegal actions.”
The impeachment push marks a high-profile challenge to a senior Cabinet official by a member of President Donald Trump’s own party. The resolution would need a two-thirds majority in the Republican-controlled Senate to convict Hegseth and remove him from office.
The House is required to act on Massie’s impeachment proposal by Thursday, giving lawmakers little time to consider the measure before leaving Washington for an extended recess that will last through the November midterm elections.
Massie’s push for impeachment vote came as the Pentagon’s inspector general released the first formal assessment of losses and operational disruptions stemming from the war on Iran, reporting that Iranian retaliatory strikes damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US military bases across West Asia and contributed to shortages of key munitions.
Citing communications with US Central Command (CENTCOM), the special report said Iranian strikes damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan between February 28 and June 30.
The assessment also acknowledged the depletion of key US munitions stockpiles during the war, while noting that earlier attacks had destroyed critical military assets, including missile-defense radar installations.

Ukrainian border unit’s HIMERA B1 relay took 10 strikes from Russia’s FPV drones and guided bombs. Last one leveled building and tower, and relay kept working
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:42:55 UTC
03:42:55 KST

A Ukrainian-made radio repeater survived 10 Russian drone and bomb strikes and a building collapse, and kept transmitting from under the rubble. The HIMERA B1, used by border guards on a telecom tower in Kharkiv Oblast, held its communications link through FPV drones and guided bombs, the manufacturer said.
On what Ukraine's soldiers call the most heavily jammed battlefield in the world, keeping a radio link alive is one of the hardest problems there is, and a cheap, rugged device that outlasts direct hits is a real advantage.
The B1 in Kharkiv Oblast worked in tandem with a second one 10.5 kilometers away, each covering roughly 5 kilometers, until it took 10 strikes. The account is the maker's, HIMERA, but it fits the company's story: a Kyiv firm whose encrypted, frequency-hopping radios were built to survive Russian electronic warfare.
The relay outlasts 10 strikes
The B1 is an autonomous repeater, a box that extends the range of a mesh radio network. This one sat on a telecom tower used by the 1st Border Guard Detachment. During one attack, its power system was destroyed, HIMERA said.
Later strikes partly collapsed the building, and the repeater fell and was buried under debris, yet it kept working.
"Even after that, the repeater remained operational and continued to stay connected," the company said.
Soldiers went in and pulled it from the rubble precisely because it was still transmitting.
The signal beats the jamming
The device is built for a battlefield where Russia listens for radio traffic and uses it to aim, so a poorly protected link can give away a unit's position. HIMERA's radios use AES-256 encryption and pseudo-random frequency-hopping to make a signal hard to intercept, locate, or jam.
A volunteer's frustration built the firm
HIMERA grew out of the front's own shortcomings. One of its co-founders volunteered with the territorial defense in Kyiv Oblast early in the full-scale war and ran into a critical shortage of reliable tactical communications, the company said.
The idea was to build something hard to detect, resistant to jamming, simple to use, and cheap enough to mass-produce, using encryption and frequency-hopping that make a signal difficult to find or suppress.
Within months, the company said, the idea became a team and the team a product, one now fielded widely enough that its repeaters are sometimes dropped into forward positions by drone.

Bloomberg: Germany is preparing hospitals for a possible Russian attack on NATO. Its military says as many as 1,000 wounded troops could need care each day.
Government agencies across Germany are inspecting the country’s infrastructure and health care system to assess how well they could function under martial law, according to Bloomberg.
In a report modeling possible scenarios for a Russian attack on NATO, the Bundeswehr estimated that Germany could receive as many as 1,000 wounded service members a day. The country’s five military hospitals would quickly become overwhelmed. Civilian hospitals are required to provide wartime care, putting the health care system under unprecedented strain, Bloomberg notes.
The government’s challenges reportedly include finding enough hospital beds, strengthening medical supply chains, and improving coordination between military and civilian hospitals.
Training enough medical personnel is another pressing challenge. Only a few hundred doctors in Germany have experience treating combat trauma and gunshot wounds. Civilian surgeons are now being offered specialized courses.
Private companies in the health care sector are concerned that their employees could be called up as reservists or volunteer for military service — affecting as many as 20% of their workers in some regions. The companies are also considering how to maintain uninterrupted production of critical medicines if demand surges and assessing whether adequate physical security measures are available.
Germany has seen a surge in hybrid attacks since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to Bloomberg. One of the latest incidents involved the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig Airport near a Ukrainian cargo plane. Germany blamed Russia for the sabotage and responded by closing the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. Russia responded by closing the Goethe-Institut.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has said Russia could start a war with NATO in 2029, though some analysts believe it could happen even sooner. In that event, Germany would be obligated to defend the alliance and, because of its geographic location, would likely become a key transit hub for military personnel, according to Bloomberg.

Leaked emails reveal plans to ‘double up’ prisoners in one-person prefab cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:41:00 UTC
03:41:00 KST

The Prison Service has drawn up plans to “double up” hundreds of prisoners in temporary prefabricated cells built for one person, at the request of the Ministry of Justice, leaked documents show.
Amid an ongoing overcrowding crisis in England and Wales, governors of 10 category C prisons have been asked to sign off the installation of second beds in “rapid deployment cells [RDCs]”.
The units, some of which measure 2.9 metres by 3.4 metres and include a bed, toilet and shower, were placed in the grounds of more than 15 prisons as a temporary solution to past overcrowding problems.
Estimated to have a 15-year lifespan, the steel-framed “pods” can be stacked to be two storeys and are usually occupied by low-risk prisoners, some of whom have been allowed to move into them as a reward for good behaviour.
According to leaked emails, the planned doubling-up suggested by Ministry of Justice officials would increase the overall capacity of the prison estate by 476.
Responding to the leaked documents, governors and prison officers said the numbers being proposed by Whitehall could breach health and safety laws and make jails unsafe for prisoners, staff and the public.
The plans were disclosed in an email sent on 27 August by a senior Prison Service executive to governors.
“As you are aware, maximising available prison capacity is of high ministerial interest, and HMPPS [His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service] have been asked to explore the viability of crowding Rapid Deployment Cell accommodation,” the executive wrote.
“The physical viability of installing a second bed in these units has been worked through at pace, and the assessment … is that ground floor units only are suitable to install a second bed.
“Given continued high population growth, and less supply coming online than anticipated, it is important that all potential capacity is identified quickly, and as such the panels need to take place over the next few days.”
The email was sent three days before Andy Burnham announced a substantial narrowing of prisoners’ eligibility for the government’s early release scheme, blocking hundreds of violent criminals from being freed.
According to a second leaked document, the doubling up plans would include beds being added to temporary cells in the following prisons: Wayland, in Norfolk (43 beds); Littlehey, in Cambridgeshire (60); Erlestoke, in Wiltshire (66); and Rochester, in Kent (60).
Other prisons asked to find extra capacity in temporary cells include The Verne, in Dorset; Wymott, in Lancashire; Channings Wood, in Devon; Whatton, in Nottingham, which is a prison for people convicted of sexual offences; The Mount, in Hertfordshire; and Huntercombe, in Oxfordshire.
The second document also shows that the doubling up proposals would breach “operational capacity”, putting the number of prisoners above safe occupancy levels.
Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the Prison Officers Association, said capacity breaches could prompt industrial action by his members. “By law our members cannot strike, but I know they would walk out on health and safety grounds if asked to oversee prisons which cannot cope with the numbers being proposed,” he said.
“Creating more space increases the pressure on an already overcrowded prison estate and risks the stability of prisons. If the government are convinced that early release schemes are sufficient, you have to ask why they are now insisting prisons source every available bit of spare capacity.”
Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors Association, said a full risk assessment would have to be carried out on each prison to ensure the public and staff remained safe if doubling up occurred.
“RDCs are amongst the least secure accommodation in the prison estate and prisoners located in them will have to be risk assessed. If you don’t do this, the prison won’t be sufficiently safe or secure,” he said.
“Increasing the operational capacity of a prison isn’t as simple as putting bunk beds in cells. There needs to be staff available to supervise the additional prisoners and there needs to be additional regime activities.”
Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League for Penal Reform, said the proposal was an act of desperation.
“Rapid deployment cells were themselves meant to be a short-term response but, ironically, they have come to be seen as being among the more positive parts of the prison estate, with fewer issues related to violence, debt and drug misuse. The risk now is that all this will be undermined as more and more people get crammed in,” she said.
There are 87,111 people in prison in England and Wales. Under the Ministry of Justice’s own definition of safety and decency, the prison estate should not hold more than 81,616 people.
Reacting to the leaked documents, a ministry spokesperson said the department was investing up to £4.7bn creating 14,000 new prison places.
“As the public would expect, we’re pulling every lever available to ensure there is always space to lock up dangerous offenders,” the spokesperson said.
“Cells are only doubled up where it is safe to do so, and no final decision has been taken on these units.”

South Korea “cannot afford” to slow the development of artificial intelligence as it seeks to catch up with global leaders and create new markets, the country’s science minister said Wednesday.
“It is an entirely different matter for a country already ahead to adjust its pace, than for a nation that is catching up while simultaneously having to create new markets to slow down,” Science Minister Bae Kyung-hoon said in a social media post, according to Yonhap News.
“We cannot afford to slow down the pace of AI development,” he added.
Bae warned that the divide between countries possessing frontier AI models approaching human intelligence and those without them could extend beyond technology to industrial competitiveness, national security, and long-term economic growth.
He, however, cautioned against unconditional acceleration, saying AI safety and public trust must advance alongside technological development.
His comments came amid a widening global debate over the pace of AI development.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and SpaceXAI's Elon Musk have called for slowing frontier AI development to allow safety measures to catch up, while proposing greater independent oversight.
US President Donald Trump has rejected such calls, describing fears of AI threatening humanity as a “hoax” and arguing that slowing US development could benefit China.
China has also pushed back, saying “fear-mongering, confrontation and vicious competition” would hamper global AI governance, and calling instead for open and inclusive development of the technology.

The Surprising Health Benefits of Reading a Book
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:35:02 UTC
03:35:02 KST

When was the last time you sat down with a good book? Over the last couple of decades, the number of Americans reading for pleasure has been steadily dropping, with one large study finding that only 16% of people read for pleasure. Trends elsewhere are similarly in decline; in the U.K., the percentage of people who read regularly dropped 8% over the last decade or so.
This might seem like an unimportant, if slightly depressing, side effect of people’s attention being fixed on screens. But a new review published in Psychological Medicine suggests that reading for pleasure—sitting down and focusing on a book you actually look forward to cracking open—can have significant impacts on your brain and wellbeing.
This is your body on books
Reading has an effect from a very young age, says Barbara Sahakian, an emeritus professor of clinical neuropsychology at the University of Cambridge in the U.K. and an author of the new paper. In one study of about 10,000 children in the U.S., she and her colleagues found that kids who started to read for pleasure early in life were better adjusted later, regardless of their socioeconomic background. “They had better cognition, they had reduced symptoms of mental-health problems, they had better attention,” she says. They also spent less time on screens, slept longer, and performed better in school.
But reading for pleasure shouldn’t stop in childhood. Studies of adult reading habits show benefits as well. In the review, the authors note that readers often mention in surveys that they feel less lonely after they read. “‘It made me feel more connected to others. It made me understand other people's point of view better, and gave me more empathy.’ That comes up a lot in surveys,” Sahakian says.
There are neuroimaging studies to back up that finding, she continues. “When you read fiction, particularly stories that are rich in social content, it activates areas in the brain that we know are involved in social cognition, areas that always come up when you're doing studies of theory of mind or understanding things from other people's point of view,” she says.
Surveys indicate a link to stress reduction as well. “With reducing stress, it seems to happen really quickly,” Sahakian says. “If you get engrossed in a book, then your mind and your attention are really focused on reading and the content, which means it takes your attention away from other things. You don't start ruminating about problems that you have…you forget all of that. So it's a little bit like mindfulness in that regard, because the attention is so focused.”
The benefits of reading in older age
Some of the research Sahakian finds most exciting focuses on older people’s reading habits. She refers to one study in Taiwan that followed people over age 64 for 14 years. “People who just read once a week had a significantly reduced risk of cognitive decline over that 14-year period, and importantly, it didn't relate to educational levels,” she says. “What is so good about reading is that you get these benefits regardless of socio-economic background or educational level. It will improve your brain. It will improve your cognition. It will improve your well-being,” she says.
If it’s been a while since you’ve read for pleasure, there’s no need to start with War and Peace. Reading works best when it relates to something you are actually interested in, says Sahakian. Try a magazine or book related to a hobby or special interest to start.
Do audiobooks count?
There’s not as much research about the body’s response to listening to audiobooks, so the trends are less clear. One study found that students who studied written material did better on a quiz later than students who listened to the material on a podcast, suggesting that taking facts in through the ears can make it harder to absorb them.
Perhaps more importantly, when it comes to reading for pleasure, people often listen to audiobooks while they are doing something else—like driving, gardening, or doing the dishes. That suggests, says Sahakian, that they aren’t producing the same feeling of absorption that reading text does.

Putin Declares Children’s Minds a “New Front” as Russia Overhauls Education
Russia has transformed its educational system into a sweeping mechanism for military indoctrination and anti-Western propaganda, effectively rolling back decades of post-Soviet academic autonomy, The Economist reported on September 10.
Labeling the fight for children’s minds as a “new front,” Russian leader Vladimir Putin has mandated a nationwide “federal programme of upbringing” aimed at cultivating militaristic patriotism. This systemic ideological overhaul spans all educational levels, culminating in the formal introduction of state-sponsored patriotic curricula inside Russian kindergartens on September 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The state’s curriculum relies heavily on revising history and embedding combat narratives into daily learning, The Economist reports. Middle and high school teachers are instructed to frame the full-scale invasion of Ukraine as an existential defense of a “multipolar world” while blaming “the collective West” for prolonging the war.
Weekly mandatory classes, titled “Conversations about Important Things,” dedicate significant time to military themes and the “reunification” of occupied territories. Furthermore, Russian educational authorities have aggressively cut social science hours to expand mandated basic military training, drone operation, and standardized history courses crafted by Kremlin propagandists.
To compensate for the absence of a coherent national ideology, the state is heavily promoting militarized youth organizations.
State-sponsored groups like the “Movement of the First” attempt to mimic Soviet-era Pioneers, while the “Yunarmiya” military youth group—which teaches children as young as eight to march in formation—now claims over two million members, The Economist noted.
Concurrently, private military centers founded by combat veterans train children with behavioral issues using strict tactical discipline, drilling them to operate as combat units rather than individuals.
Despite the Kremlin’s efforts, the militarization campaign often breeds apathy and quiet resistance rather than genuine fanaticism, according to The Economist.
Independent reports highlight that many students view the propaganda as a burden, while teachers frequently allow pupils to use ideological class time to complete standard homework.
Educational psychologists observe that this top-down indoctrination is fostering a culture of “doublethink,” where lying and superficial compliance are accepted as a societal norm, ultimately damaging the educational standards and psychological well-being of Russian youth, The Economist wrote.
To enforce this ideological shift and curb growing student apathy, Russian educational authorities have recently started requiring teachers to monitor and report students who resist state narratives. According to updated Ministry of Education guidelines, educators leading the mandatory “Conversations about Important Things” classes must formally track pupils who ask provocative questions or display a “disagreement with value orientations”.
Teachers are instructed to record these incidents in specialized post-lesson assessments, providing school administrators with data to evaluate ideological compliance and strictly enforce the state’s patriotic curriculum.

====================================================================================================

COVID vaccines no longer free for many Australians from next month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Everything you need to know about COVID-19 vaccine changes in Australia
For the past five-and-a-half years, vaccines against SARS‑CoV‑2, the virus that causes COVID-19, have been free for everyone living in Australia.
But that's about to change.
From October 1, only people at highest risk of severe COVID-19 disease will get the jab for free.
What does that mean for Australians more broadly and their access to the jab? And will this lead to more COVID-19 cases?
Who can still get a free COVID-19 vaccine?
From October 1, free COVID-19 vaccines will still be available for:
- Adults 75 and over (two doses per year, about six months apart)
- Adults 65–74 years (one dose per year)
- Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 50–74 years (one dose per year)
- Adults aged 18–64 years with severely immunocompromising conditions (one dose per year). This includes people with chronic kidney disease on dialysis and people with leukaemia. If in doubt, have a chat to your doctor.
How much will the COVID-19 vaccine cost?
We don't know yet.
And we may not know until the last week of September, according to Pharmaceutical Society of Australia vaccination ambassador and community pharmacist Julianna Neill.
That's because conversations are still ongoing with manufacturers about what the wholesale price for Australia will be.
"Normally we go from knowing what a private vaccination cost is going to be, and then it becomes free," Ms Neill says.
"We've never really been in this situation before."
Australians typically pay between $25 and $35 for their annual flu jab, but Ms Neill anticipates the COVID-19 vaccine will cost "significantly more".
Why is the COVID-19 vaccine rollout changing?
COVID-19 vaccines, previously funded under the National COVID-19 Vaccine Program, are moving to the National Immunisation Program (NIP) where they will sit alongside respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza vaccines.
"This reflects the shift from an emergency pandemic response to a long-term, routine program focused on protecting people at highest risk of severe illness," a spokesperson for the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing says.
During the pandemic, vaccines were made available at no cost to reach as many people as possible but are now being targeted at those most vulnerable.
Jodie McVernon, director of epidemiology at the Doherty Institute, believes this may make the vaccine more accessible for high-risk groups already rolling up their sleeves for other jabs.
"Including it with the whole package should actually increase coverage by raising awareness, and make it a normal, regular seasonal event," Professor McVernon says.
Will this mean a lower vaccine update?
Potentially.
COVID-19 vaccination rates have been dropping in recent years.
So far this year, 1.7 million people in Australia have received the COVID-19 vaccine, about 6 per cent of the population, compared to 8.9 million people who have had the flu jab.
Loading...
Ms Neill says there may be a slight decline in vaccination rates following the introduction of a fee, as cost can be a barrier.
But instead of looking at Australia's overall vaccination rate, Professor McVernon says it is important to focus on vaccination rates in high-risk groups.
"The main burden of disease for COVID is in the over-75s, we actually see more COVID deaths than flu deaths," she says.
"But not even 40 per cent of people in that age group get the [COVID-19] vaccine."
Will this mean more COVID-19 cases?
It's hard to say.
Over the past few years, the number of reported cases of COVID-19 in Australia has decreased.
But Immunisation Coalition chairman Rod Pearce says many cases are not reported, which means the true number of infections is likely to be much higher.
Dr Pearce says there may be more COVID-19 cases if fewer people are vaccinated and more SARS‑CoV‑2 is circulating.
Professor McVernon says the decline in the number of hospitalisations and deaths over time is a "good indication" the health burden from COVID-19 isn't as significant as it once was.
"We see successive waves year-on-year, and over time, as the population becomes more immune through repeated exposure and vaccination, the infections we see overall are less severe."
Any other health advice?
If you want a COVID-19 booster but you're not eligible for a free jab, now is the time to contact your local clinic as changes won't come in until October 1.
You can find and book a COVID-19 vaccine online, or reach out to your GP or pharmacist for more information.
Even if you aren't in a high-risk group, getting vaccinated can still help protect you against long COVID and limit transmission of the virus if you do get infected, Dr Pearce says.
"Most of it is about having a rapid immune response, because your body is ready to fight the infection as soon as you get it," he says.
Professor McVernon says it is also important to remember basic hygiene principles to help limit transmission, including staying home if you're sick, washing hands frequently and wearing a mask if unwell.

This is the first time the Fed has raised rates since July 2023 and potentially sets Kevin Warsh, the current Fed chair, on a collision course with Donald Trump.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said on Wednesday. “This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.”
After the announcement, Trump said in a Truth Social post that interest rates should be 1% or less and criticized the US trade deficit. Trump said the US would make “at least 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year” if it were to stop trading with countries with which it has a deficit.
“We are ‘carrying’ almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!,” Trump wrote.
Though Warsh acknowledged changing geopolitics, he avoided calling out the US-Israel war with Iran by name.
“There’s no hiding from hotspots around the world, and our judgment about what is the most likely or least likely of the geopolitical situation has changed,” he said.
Warsh also declined to answer questions about how Trump would react but reiterated that Fed independence was “a two-way street”.
“We will let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane. That is the way we can stand up here and call them the way we see them,” he said.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
New projections showed a majority of officials penciled in another rate hike before the year’s end, with four officials predicting the Fed’s benchmark interest rate would reach a range of 4.25% to 4.5% by the end of the year.
And though estimates on the country’s economic growth and unemployment rate were upbeat, Fed officials believed it would take roughly until 2029 for inflation to reach its 2% goal.
At its last meeting in late July, the open market committee voted 9-3 to maintain rates, the first time in 10 years that so many members shared dissent on a policy decision. Since then, the US and Iran have renewed attacks against each other, driving up the Brent crude benchmark to its highest levels in month.
The war has driven up inflation, especially energy prices. Gas prices have remained, on average, $1 a gallon more expensive compared with a year ago. Diesel fuel, which is used for buses, trains and trucks, recently reached an all-time high of $6.31.
Concerns about inflation have induced a sell-off in the US bond market, with the yield on the 10-year treasury note hitting a 19-year high earlier this week, despite efforts from the US treasury to calm the market. Typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, trouble in the US bond market can lead to higher interest rates for consumer and business loans.
The Fed uses interest rates as a tool to cool price increases by slowing activity. Higher interest rates impact mortgages, car payments, student debt and other types of loans. After inflation reached a generational high of 9.1% in June 2022, the Fed increased rates 11 times from 2022 and 2023. Rates were brought up to a target range of 5.25% to 5.5% before the Fed eventually started lowering rates in 2024 and 2025.
At the beginning of the year, when the annualized inflation rate was 1% lower than current levels, a Fed rate hike seemed highly unlikely. A majority of Fed officials were actually predicting a rate cut before the end of the year. But inflation in August remained stubbornly high while unemployment was steady, which furthered the chances of a rate hike.
Higher prices have painted a grim economic outlook as voters prepare to head to the polls in November. Recent data and surveys have shown heightened inflation has wiped out wage gains for Americans and dampened consumer outlook. In August, hourly earnings for employees decreased by 0.1% year-over-year after accounting for inflation and fell by 0.3% from the month prior. Consumer sentiment has also rapidly declined, according to a monthly survey from the University of Michigan, while expectations for more inflation have increased.
Candidates on both sides of the political aisle have sought to make cost-of-living concerns and the economy a forefront of their campaigns, but voters are split on which party has the greatest advantage on this issue, according to recent Pew data.
Meanwhile, Trump has implored Republican voters to pretend as if they are voting for him on their midterm ballot and promised every American a $5,000 “Trump dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress.
Critics have likened the move to bribery and warned of the financial implications, especially after the US government debt reached a record-high $40tn last month.

Fed raises rates for the first time since 2023 in unanimous vote defying Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:25:58 UTC
03:25:58 KST

The Federal Reserve has raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to a range of 3.75% to 4%, its first increase since July 2023, in a unanimous 12-0 vote that puts Chair Kevin Warsh directly at odds with the US president who appointed him.
Kevin Warsh has broken away from US President Donald Trump in his first Fed move, and he has done it with the entire committee behind him.
The Federal Open Market Committee lifted rates on Wednesday after holding them at 3.5% to 3.75% since December, ending a pause that had grown harder to justify as energy costs pushed prices higher.
Not a single member dissented in a unanimous 12-0 vote.
That matters because the pressure ran in both directions as three regional presidents had voted for a hike in July, while the White House spent months demanding cuts.
Nobody voted for either extreme.
At the time of writing, the market reaction to the decision has been fairly muted likely due to the fact that the hike was widely expected.
On the other hand, Trump has already reacted negatively on social media by stating that "interest rates in the United States should be 1%, or less [...]".
A statement stripped to the bone
The Fed's communication was as striking as its decision.
The statement ran to three short paragraphs, a fraction of the length markets are used to, with no forward guidance and no hedging.
"Inflation remains elevated," it read, adding that "today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
The word "timelier" carries an implicit admission that the return had been too slow.
Then a sentence the Fed almost never writes: "The Committee will deliver price stability." Not seeks to, not is committed to. Will.
The economic assessment was also confident throughout.
Activity is "expanding at a solid pace", domestic spending "has been resilient", productivity growth is "strong" and capital investment "robust", while job gains "have kept pace with the workforce".
Uncertainty remains elevated, the Fed said, owing partly to "geopolitical developments", its formulation for the Iran war.
By describing an economy in good health, the committee removed the argument that higher rates would damage growth, which is precisely the case US President Donald Trump has been making.
Boxed in by the data
The decision had been building for months.
Three regional Fed presidents dissented in July in favour of an increase, the most in one direction since 2016, and several others said afterwards they were ready to move unless inflation eased which it did not.
The Fed's preferred gauge, the personal consumption expenditures index, ran at 3.7% in both June and July, with core inflation at 3.3%. Before the Iran war sent fuel prices climbing, core stood at 3%.
Consumer prices held at 3.4% in August, but the monthly increase of 0.4% was the sharpest since May, evidence the energy shock is feeding through. Inflation has now been above the 2% target for more than five years.
Warsh had effectively committed himself at Jackson Hole in August, telling the symposium he "would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive" and warning that unless underlying inflation moved to target "clearly and at sufficient speed", the Fed had "work to do".
Markets took him at his word as the CME's FedWatch tool put the probability of a rate hike above 90% before today's decision.
Defying the president who chose him
US President Donald Trump had spent months demanding the opposite, insisting the country should have the lowest interest rates in the world and choosing Warsh partly on the expectation he would deliver them.
Warsh himself said while campaigning for the job that rates could come down.
The treatment of his predecessor sharpened the stakes as Jerome Powell was publicly attacked for moving too slowly, and the US Justice Department opened a criminal investigation into testimony he gave to Congress.
Today's decision could also have a restoring effect on the perceived independence of the Federal Reserve as an institution.
The technical details point to a Fed settling in at the new level.
The interest rate on reserve balances rises to 3.90% from Thursday, the primary credit rate to 4%, and standing repurchase operations will run at 4%. Seven regional reserve banks requested the discount rate increase.
The Fed’s new dot plot shows 12 of 18 officials expect another 0.25% hike by year-end, taking rates to 4.125%, while four see rates reaching 4.375%.
The hawkish signal extends well beyond 2026 as 14 officials see rates ending 2027 above today’s level, while the 2028 median stands at 3.9% versus 3.4% expected.
The longer-run rate also rose to 3.2%, suggesting officials increasingly believe neutral rates have moved higher while economists also expect more to follow.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia could revive Israel-Saudi normalization efforts - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:25:03 UTC
03:25:03 KST

Hamas’s October 7 massacre was not designed to scuttle normalization ties between Israel and Saudi Arabia. It was planned long before talk about diplomatic ties between the two countries gained momentum.
But the attack did disrupt those ties, and from Hamas’s perspective, that was a very welcome side effect.
Before October 7, normalization between Jerusalem and Riyadh appeared to be a question not of if but of when. After the fallout from the attack, Saudi Arabia hardened its position, insisting that there could be no agreement without meaningful movement toward the establishment of a Palestinian state.
The strategic logic driving the two countries together, however, never truly disappeared. Israel and Saudi Arabia still share many of the same enemies, face many of the same threats, and look to the US to help construct a regional framework capable of confronting them.
Ironically, it may be one of the regional wars spawned by October 7 – the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia in support of Iran in its war with the US – that resuscitates Jerusalem-Riyadh ties.
Organized by CENTCOM, Middle East military commanders, including Israel, meet in Germany
Axios reported Tuesday on a meeting organized by US Central Command among the military commanders of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan, and Egypt in Germany last week to discuss tensions in the region.
And that was before the Houthis’ push toward Bab el-Mandeb Strait and attacks not only on Saudi oil facilities but also toward Mecca. Saudi air defenses intercepted a drone south of Islam’s holiest city on Tuesday.
There is more than a little irony in Saudi Arabia looking toward Jerusalem for help protecting Mecca. Yet that is where the region’s shifting alliances may now be leading: The country that presents itself as the guardian of Islam’s holiest sites may increasingly need the intelligence, technology, and missile-defense capabilities of the Jewish state to help defend them.
Neither Saudi nor Israeli officials are talking publicly about the meeting in Germany or about any cooperation – intelligence or otherwise – between the two countries. But it beggars belief that no such cooperation is taking place.
Indeed, Saudi Arabia’s immediate security needs may be creating facts on the ground that diplomacy has not yet acknowledged.
Saudi Arabia needs more than defense promises
Even though the Saudis recently signed the Mecca Defense Alliance with Pakistan and Turkey, under the rubric that an attack on one is an attack on all, neither country has exactly rushed to Saudi Arabia’s defense against attacks from an Iranian proxy.
Defense pacts on paper are one thing. The ability to detect an incoming drone, track a missile, share intelligence in real time, and intercept a threat before it hits an oil installation – or approaches Mecca – is something else entirely.
In these areas, Israel has a great deal to offer. Just look to the UAE, where Israel reportedly moved advanced air-defense assets and personnel during the war with Iran.
Even before the meeting in Germany, a recently retired senior official in Israel’s intelligence community said at the MEAD conference in Washington last week that Israeli-Saudi cooperation is “very good.”
Israeli intelligence official says Israel, Saudi Arabia have much in common
The official said the two countries have much in common in the region and expressed hope they would find the common ground needed to reach a normalization accord quickly.
Fighting the Houthis might – if leveraged correctly – provide precisely that common ground. It could give Riyadh a compelling reason to show greater flexibility on its demand for movement toward a Palestinian state before normalizing ties with Israel.
That does not mean Saudi Arabia will suddenly abandon the Palestinian issue. Nor does it mean that secret security cooperation will automatically produce open diplomatic relations. But shared threats have a way of clarifying interests, and interests – more than sentiment – ultimately drive states into new alliances.
That the US convened the meeting in Germany is also consistent with what has been developing in the region for some time.
US intermediates Israeli-Saudi military cooperation
A recently retired senior US military official at the MEAD conference spoke not of direct bilateral Israeli-Saudi military cooperation, but of a US-led architecture that enables countries that may not trust one another – or maintain formal diplomatic relations – cooperate indirectly through Washington.
In this model, Washington collects radar and intelligence information from different countries, processes it through American systems, and redistributes it under separate bilateral agreements.
That arrangement lets countries benefit from one another’s capabilities without publicly acknowledging the cooperation. It provides Saudi Arabia with access to Israeli intelligence and technology while sparing Riyadh, at least for the time being, the political cost of admitting that it is working with Israel.
The US official said every Arab country hostile to Iran wants Israeli cooperation despite the domestic political cost.
In other words, while Ireland won’t use an Israeli-made component in its new government jet that would allow it to land in the fog, the Gulf states are eager for Israeli technology to help protect themselves from Iran and its tentacles.
Arab governments may not be able or willing to acknowledge cooperation with Israel publicly. But they do recognize and are eager to benefit from the country’s intelligence and technological capabilities.
For months, there has been talk about a new regional security architecture. Then came the Mecca agreement, and it appeared that the Saudis were looking elsewhere rather than toward an American-Israeli-based system.
Pakistan, Turkey are not providing Saudi Arabia with the material assistance it needs
But Pakistan and Turkey are not providing Saudi Arabia with the material assistance it needs as it faces off against Iran and its Houthi proxy, and Riyadh is discovering that declarations of solidarity from distant partners are a pale substitute for real-time intelligence and proven defensive capabilities from countries confronting the same enemy.
This new regional security architecture may indeed finally take off, with the Houthis providing the impetus.
It is worth remembering that Israel had deep security cooperation with the UAE long before the Abraham Accords. In fact, one could argue those ties built trust between the two countries and ultimately paved the way for formal diplomatic relations.
The same pattern could now emerge with Saudi Arabia. Quiet cooperation builds familiarity, familiarity builds trust, and trust can eventually make possible what once seemed politically unthinkable.
The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia will likely push Israeli-Saudi security cooperation up several notches. Might that, in turn, become the precursor to normalization?

Norwegian Jews decry proposed criminalization of settlement trade - interiew
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:24:56 UTC
03:24:56 KST

Norwegian Jews decried a proposed law that would make certain forms of trade with Israeli settlements a criminal offense with up to 3 years in prison, calling it “deeply troubling” and “dangerous.”
Norway’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Espen Barth Eide made the announcement in an interview with the country’s public broadcaster, the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation (NRK), earlier this week. The consultation deadline on the bill is to be on Saturday.
He also told NRK he believed Israel had become “far too accustomed to being able to intimidate Western countries by saying they were antisemitic if they criticized Israel for abuses and violations of international law.”
“Now the Teflon coating that Israel has had in many ways is gone.”
Speaking to The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday, Ester Nafstad, co-founder of Kos & Kaos (the Nordic Jewish network), said: “The proposed ban is presented as a political signal, but a law carrying potential prison sentences cannot be treated as merely symbolic.”
Penalties range from fines to three years in prison
Under the proposal, intentional violations could result in up to three years’ imprisonment, while even negligent violations could carry a sentence of up to six months.
Nafstad said that criminal liability requires clear boundaries and a serious assessment of the consequences – including for Palestinians whose livelihoods depend on economic interaction with Israelis – but that she does not believe the proposal has been sufficiently examined.
Nafstad told the Post that the proposal is creating “real anxiety” among Norwegian Jews.
“Many fear that their family, religious or communal ties to Israel could expose them to scrutiny or investigation, even when they have no economic connections to the West Bank or to Israeli settlements,” she said.
“Whether or not that is the government’s intention, such fears must be taken seriously when introducing criminal legislation directed exclusively at Israel and Israelis.”
Nafstad responded to the specific comment by Barth Eide about Israel believing it can “frighten” Western countries by saying they were antisemitic if they criticized Israel.
She said this sentence was “deeply troubling.”
“Eide could have argued for stronger criticism of Israeli policies without invoking antisemitism at all,” she said. “Instead, he lends authority to the idea that accusations of antisemitism are primarily a cynical political weapon used to frighten critics into silence. That does not primarily harm the Israeli government; it harms Jews and educators who are trying to make society recognize antisemitism when it actually occurs.”
Norwegian Jewish author, podcaster, and public speaker Henrik Beckheim also spoke to the Post about Barth Eide’s comment.
“[This is] delegitimizing when Jews call out antisemitism for what it is. Just accusing us of pulling ‘the antisemitism card’.”
Beckheim called Barth Eide the “most dangerous man in Norway’s government since Quisling.”
Concerns grow over potential impact on Jewish community
Israeli educator, activist and speaker On Elpeleg, who lives in Norway, said: “This action by the Norwegian government against Jews in Judea and Samaria is not only aimed at ethnically cleansing Jews from their historical homeland, but also risks criminalizing Jews in Norway and spreading hostility toward Jews in Norway.”
“This is a very worrying and dangerous development for Jews in Norway, especially when the government still does not designate Hamas as a terrorist organization,” he said.
Robert Hercz, president of Det Jødiske Fellesskapet i Norge (Jewish Community in Norway (DJFN)) told the Post that DJFN is prepared to support challenging the proposed law in courts.
"The aim is to bring a case before the European Court of Human Rights," he said.
Last week, 11 countries joined Norway in confirming their intention to impose national restrictions on trade in goods from Israeli settlements: Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom.
The 12 nations jointly said that the Israeli government’s actions in the West Bank “damage the possibility of realizing the two-state solution.”
The Jerusalem Post reached out to Foreign Minister Eide on Monday, but he did not respond by Wednesday's publication.

Democratic and Republican US senators asked US President Donald Trump's administration on Wednesday to declassify and release all information about a proposed agreement with Saudi Arabia on civil nuclear energy, including two classified "side letters" reached with Riyadh.
In a letter to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Energy Secretary Christopher Wright, which Reuters saw, the senators noted that the government has reached dozens of these so-called 123 nuclear agreements with other countries without withholding such information.
"Access to the full text is required for the Senate and the public to have a clear understanding of the commitments being made on the nation's behalf and those being made by Saudi Arabia to the United States," the letter said.
The State and Energy departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Democrats Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Ed Markey of Massachusetts led the letter, and 13 other Democratic senators, one independent who caucuses with Democrats, and two Republicans, Rand Paul of Kentucky and John Kennedy of Louisiana, signed it.
Trump sent the proposed agreement with Saudi Arabia to Congress in August, opening a 90-day window for lawmakers to review it and an opportunity to pass a resolution of disapproval.
Lawmakers have since pushed to declassify the side letters, reached alongside the proposed deal, and release the related documents.
Trump says Saudi nuclear deal only possible if Riyadh normalizes Israel relations
The nuclear agreement has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia would get the deal without normalizing relations with Israel. Trump has said it will only go into effect if Riyadh does, but congressional aides have said nothing in the pact addresses that issue.
The letter sent Wednesday did not mention the Israel issue.
The 30-year nuclear deal calls for the construction of AP1000 reactors, a project worth tens of billions of dollars that would benefit Westinghouse, jointly owned by Canada-based Cameco and Brookfield Asset Management.
Deal faces criticism for not preventing Saudi uranium enrichment
Some Democratic lawmakers and nonproliferation advocates have criticized the nuclear pact for not barring Saudi Arabia from enriching uranium or reprocessing nuclear waste, two potential pathways for making a nuclear weapon. The United Arab Emirates agreed to such measures, known as the gold standard, in its 2009 civil nuclear deal with Washington.
The Trump administration says the deal has nonproliferation measures required by law.

US Fed raises key rate for first time in 3 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:24:00 UTC
03:24:00 KST

US Fed raises key rate for first time in 3 years
September 16, 2026
The US Federal Reserve (Fed) on Wednesday raised interest rates by 25 basis points in an attempt to tackle stubbornly high inflation in the world's largest economy.
This move is sure to anger President Donald Trump, who has called for lower rates and who recently nominated Kevin Warsh to the post of Federal Reserve Chair.
"Our predominant focus is on the price stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long," Warsh told a press conference.
Warsh has served as Fed Chair since May and during his confirmation process, he had assured Congress that central bank policymakers would "have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation."
"Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the committee's 2% goal," Warsh added.
The increase boosts the Fed's target rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%.
Trump had promised to lower prices in his 2024 election campaign, but things turned out differently after his inauguration. The US now faces the combined impact of Trump's global import tariffs, an energy shock following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, and capital spending from the artificial intelligence boom.
After the announcement of the rate increase, Trump said US interest rates should be 1% or lower and that the rates should be cut fast.
"I ... talked to Kevin," Trump said. "And I said you might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They're very political. They're doing the wrong thing."
Fed plans to 'stay in our lane'
Since his appointment to the job, speculation circulated around which direction Warsh would take the Fed, as Trump has pressured the institution to follow his lead.
But on Wednesday, Warsh joined the unanimous decision to raise interest rates, saying it had been made independent of what the market may be doing.
"We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation," he said. "I'll observe market prices and see what they have to say. But today was our decision."
"Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane," Warsh said. "We let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too. That's how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them."
Borrowers will feel some impact
The raise in interest rates will affect those who borrow money to make large purchases, such as a home, car or large appliance.
The new rate will also raise monthly payments and costs for those who are already paying interest on credit card debt.
Currently, household debt payments are relatively low overall as a percentage of after-tax income. So many households will not feel the burden on borrowing in the short term.
But the move could be good for those who are saving, as interest rates on savings accounts and certificates of deposit will rise.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points Wednesday, delivering its first rate hike in more than three years as inflation remained elevated.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) increased the target range for the federal funds rate to 3.75%-4% in support of the central bank's dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability.
The decision was approved unanimously in a 12-0 vote.
"Inflation remains elevated," the Fed said, adding that the policy action would support a "timelier return" to its 2% inflation target.
"The Committee will deliver price stability," it added.
The latest official data showed US consumer inflation remained well above the central bank's target in August.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.4% month on month in August, accelerating from a 0.1% increase in July, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Annual inflation stood at 3.4%, unchanged from July.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, eased to 2.4% annually from 2.5%, despite accelerating to 0.3% on a monthly basis.
Energy prices jumped 16.3% from a year earlier, including a 27.4% surge in gasoline prices.
The Fed said economic activity continued to expand at a solid pace, while domestic spending remained resilient despite uncertainty that remained elevated partly because of geopolitical developments.
Productivity growth was strong and capital investment remained robust, according to the statement.
The central bank also said job gains had kept pace with growth in the workforce and that the unemployment rate had changed little.
The FOMC said it would continue its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Deadly Gaza building collapse raises fears over war-damaged structures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:20:05 UTC
03:20:05 KST

A six-storey building, already cracked and weakened by earlier Israeli strikes during Tel Aviv’s genocidal war on the tiny Palestinian enclave, crumbles onto nearby homes and tents in Gaza City's Tal al-Hawa area, killing 21 civilians and trapping dozens more beneath the rubble.
The disaster lays bare a broader crisis engulfing Gaza, where the vast majority of buildings have been damaged or destroyed by Israeli strikes, construction materials remain critically scarce, and displaced families are left with no choice but to shelter in cracked, unstable structures the civil defence agency has flagged among nearly 2,000 buildings across the territory it considers at risk of imminent collapse.
A building collapses overnight
Gaza's civil defence agency said a six-storey building, with four apartments per floor, collapsed early Wednesday in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City.
The structure fell onto nearby homes and tents, according to the agency, which operates as a rescue service under Hamas authority.
Death toll includes 12 children
Authorities in Gaza confirmed 21 people died in the collapse, among them 12 children and five women.
Rescue teams said they pulled the bodies from the rubble "after hours of arduous work," and transported 45 injured people to hospital.
The civil defence agency said the building had sustained damage from previous Israeli strikes and was sheltering more than 100 displaced people at the time it fell.
The agency’s spokesman Mahmoud Bassal said the structure was hit multiple times, in 2024 and again in March 2025, prompting warnings for residents not to return.
Families had ‘no other choice’ but to stay
Bassal added the displaced families are living in cracked, damaged buildings because they have no alternative.
"With neither tents nor homes available, they are living in cracked, damaged buildings despite the risk of collapse," he said.
Ahmed Al-Ajla, who lost his uncle and other relatives in the collapse, described such structures as "nothing but ticking time bombs."
Around 2,000 buildings are at risk of collapse
Gaza's civil defence agency has identified roughly 2,000 buildings across the Palestinian elclave that it considers at risk of collapse.
The UN said the vast majority of buildings in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed since the war began, leaving construction materials in critically short supply.
Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN's humanitarian coordinator for the occupied Palestinian territories, said he is "devastated" by the collapse.
"Today's tragedy underscored the grave risks faced by families living in these structures and the urgent need for safer alternatives. No one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter," he said.
Israel launched its brutal war on 7 October 2023. The health ministry in Gaza, whose figures the UN considers reliable, said the genocidal war has since killed more than 73,700 people.
Israel has allowed limited aid into Gaza since a US-brokered ceasefire took hold in October 2025, but continues to carry out strikes and restricts entry of equipment it claims could have military use.

Sen. Blumenthal urges AI oversight: 'We're on the verge of losing control'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:18:09 UTC
03:18:09 KST

New artificial intelligence products should be subject to some form of "objective review" before their release, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told CNBC on Wednesday.
The senator, who has introduced bipartisan legislation aimed at addressing AI safety risks, stressed that any new regulation should be targeted and sensitive to concerns about stifling global competitiveness.
"I think there is a balance here to be struck," Blumenthal said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "But the point is that right now we're on the verge of losing control completely," he said.
The remarks came as tech industry leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, have sounded alarms about the major risks of rapidly advancing AI models and called for a slowdown in the technology's development.
President Donald Trump, however, has vehemently pushed back on those fears, calling them a "hoax" and a "scam." His administration argues that beating China in the race to AI dominance is an all-important goal.
Blumenthal, who has emerged as a prominent voice on AI safety, said he also worries that regulation could dull the U.S.'s AI edge.
"We have to remain competitive," he told CNBC.
But "China is understanding that it needs to regulate AI because it could be a threat to their regime," he added.
"Nobody wants a regulatory state. What we want is, in effect, some scrutiny to prevent the autonomous rogue bots out of the sandbox, infiltrating sites without the control of the developers who were responsible for them," Blumenthal said.
The senator said the Food and Drug Administration's model of pharmaceutical regulation is analogous to the AI debate.
"I think we need to delegate some of this responsibility to the experts," he said. "We are hardly experts in Congress on AI, and I think we need to understand our own limitations in this area."
He also warned of the consequences of delayed action.
"We should learn, by the way, from our experience with social media, where the horse is out of the barn, algorithms are driving toxic content at kids, and we're still trying to catch up," he said.
