Aircraft carrier arrives at on the Clyde in Scotland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:36:57 BST
02:36:57 KST

HMS Queen Elizabeth has arrived in Scotland, sailing up the Firth of Clyde and into Loch Long to the jetty at Glenmallan, the Royal Navy has confirmed to the UK Defence Journal.
Commander Adrian Visram, a Royal Navy spokesperson, told us: “HMS Queen Elizabeth is currently in Glenmallan completing a short logistics and engagement stop before continuing on operations.”
The 65,000-tonne carrier sailed from Portsmouth earlier this month for three months of training and operations around the United Kingdom and northern Europe, in her role as NATO’s command ship for the Allied Response Force, a role she assumed in July and one neither Queen Elizabeth-class ship had performed before.
Glenmallan sits on the western shore of Loch Long in Argyll, and its jetty is the only facility on the west coast able to take a ship of the carriers’ size alongside, which is why both Queen Elizabeth-class vessels have called there repeatedly since it was rebuilt.
The jetty itself underwent a £67 million upgrade under a contract awarded to VolkerStevin in 2019, with Jacobs as managing agent and Arch Henderson as designer. It had last been upgraded in the 1970s and had reached the end of its economic life. Around £20 million of that work went to local suppliers and small and medium-sized enterprises in Scotland, and the project extended the jetty’s life by an estimated fifty years while making it accessible to the carriers.
The work involved installing four new navigational aids to allow safe passage through the confined waterway, two modular fender spacer units that move with the tide to keep the flight deck clear of the jetty, and dolphin mooring points to hold a ship of that size securely.
As we reported at the end of April, the last Queen Elizabeth-class carrier to make the trip was HMS Prince of Wales, which called at Glenmallan ahead of Operation Firecrest. That deployment, announced by the Prime Minister at the Munich Security Conference in February, took the carrier strike group across the North Atlantic and the High North, with Prince of Wales leading the force.
Firecrest was designed to deter Russian aggression, protect critical undersea infrastructure and demonstrate the ability to project force at scale within a NATO framework, against a background of a 30 per cent increase in Russian naval vessels threatening British waters over the preceding two years. It included activity under NATO’s Arctic Sentry mission and exercises alongside Standing NATO Maritime Group One, which Britain has led throughout 2026.
Queen Elizabeth’s own programme runs on a different track from her sister’s, and she will undertake advanced training under Flag Officer Sea Training, exercising across the spectrum of modern naval warfare, and will rehearse how an allied naval force would operate together in a crisis. The programme continues into next year with participation in major NATO exercises, preparing her to take over from Prince of Wales as fleet flagship and high readiness strike carrier in late 2027.
The Royal Navy has linked the deployment to the £240 million committed in the Defence Investment Plan towards developing drones for a Hybrid Carrier Air Wing, including jet-powered types intended to operate alongside the F-35B.
The first visit by a Queen Elizabeth-class ship to the upgraded jetty came in March 2021, when Queen Elizabeth called there during final preparations for her maiden operational deployment, the first time she had visited western Scotland after becoming a familiar sight on the Forth during her assembly at Rosyth.
On the way up the Clyde the ship paused over the wreck of HMS Dasher, the escort carrier lost on 27 March 1943 with 379 of her company, and laid a wreath. The ship posted afterwards that “the lessons from the tragedy improved the safety of carrier aviation. We still benefit from those lessons.”
Dasher was a converted merchant hull operating in the Firth of Clyde when an internal explosion sank her within minutes, and the inquiry that followed changed how aviation fuel was stored and handled aboard carriers.

The Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefield | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:36:16 UTC
02:36:16 KST

Even in a region beset by turmoil and learning to expect the unexpected, the lightning advance of Yemen’s Houthis along the Red Sea coast has shocked observers. More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee in a country where immiseration and displacement have become routine and half the population depend on humanitarian aid. But outsiders are paying close attention, because by claiming thousands of kilometres in a matter of days, and seizing strategically important islands, the Iran-backed rebels now control the Bab al-Mandab strait – the other major regional energy chokepoint after the Hormuz strait.
The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to rely on moving oil via its east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports. Now drone strikes – blamed on an Iran-backed militia in Iraq – have shut the pipeline: on one estimate, a month-long closure could cut global crude supply by 120m barrels. The halt to shipping through the Bab al-Mandab strait could be much more protracted. Taking the oil north is a far slower and more expensive route to Asian markets, and does not preclude attacks by the Houthis, who are also targeting oil facilities.
Saudi Arabia had painfully extracted itself from a war with the Houthis which it recklessly spearheaded – nominally in support of the internationally recognised government – at astounding cost to its own coffers and Yemeni civilians. It apparently hoped that it could calibrate its response to a flight from Iran to Houthi-controlled Sana’a in July, the first in over a decade, sufficiently to save the 2022 truce. But bombing Sana’a airport gave the Houthis the opportunity to escalate while blaming Riyadh.
The Houthis are not mere proxies for Tehran, but their interests are increasingly aligned, thanks to Donald Trump’s unlawful war on Iran. They need to maintain Iranian support and the strait of Hormuz crisis has created a new opportunity to exert economic pressure, and perhaps create a new income stream, via strategic gains along the coast. The forces ranged against them, including the government and southern secessionists, are more fractured than ever. The United Arab Emirates, which has clashed with its former close partner Saudi Arabia, withdrew its troops at the turn of the year.
Saudi strikes alone will not be enough to push the Houthis back. But Mr Trump has rebuffed requests for help. The Houthis have been canny enough to say that they are targeting only the Saudis, though that message reinforces the fact that their leverage could be used more broadly in future. They are also closer than ever to Djibouti, home to US, Chinese and other military bases.
The Saudis face a choice between negotiations with an emboldened enemy now making increasingly maximalist demands – or returning to the kind of full-scale war they previously regretted, with little support this time. Turkey and Pakistan are not rushing to act on the new Mecca defence pact the three countries signed in August.
Yemen’s recent history amply demonstrates the futility of seeking a military solution. Ultimately, its citizens deserve a government not dependent on either Riyadh or Tehran. Outside parties should concentrate on promoting a political process within the country. They should stress that both sides must protect civilians, and support humanitarian efforts. Their priority, however, should be a resolution to the Iran war, without which danger in the region, and broader instability, will only grow.

The Guardian view on Sweden’s election result: an opportunity that progressive parties must not squander | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:35:23 UTC
02:35:23 KST

European progressives searching for reasons to be cheerful have been finding them hard to come by this autumn. In Germany, the dramatic rise of the Alternative für Deutschland party is threatening the liberal values that underpin the identity of the federal republic. In France, polls continue to point to a likely Marine Le Pen victory in a presidential election, which is months away. Across mainland Europe, centre-left parties are failing to muster an adequate response to nativist movements that have colonised swathes of the working-class support that they once relied on.
In such an ominous political landscape, the outcome of a cliffhanger Swedish election provides a much‑needed source of optimism – albeit one that comes with heavy caveats. Prior to last Sunday’s poll, the outgoing prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, was explicit that if his rightwing alliance won the largest number of seats, he would invite members of the far-right Sweden Democrats party (SD) to become ministers in the next government.
That would have meant the formal end of the SD’s pariah status in Swedish politics, after four years in which its parliamentary votes have propped up Mr Kristersson’s minority administration. In a Europe where firewalls and cordons sanitaires against the far right have never seemed less secure, another significant threshold would have been crossed.
Voters appear to have instead handed the narrowest of victories to the Social Democratic leader, Magdalena Andersson, and the progressive bloc of parties. The SD’s share of the vote fell for the first time since it began its political journey as an openly neo-Nazi party in the late 1980s, and it slipped from second to third place behind the conservative Moderates.
So much for the good news. As in Germany and France, the Swedish far right has not needed to win power for its agenda to become normalised and partially implemented. Mr Kristersson’s reliance on the SD resulted in a government that behaved with performative cruelty towards migrants, and enacted much of its draconian programme on deportations and citizenship restrictions. Ms Andersson has responded by offering a milder version of the same approach to immigration and asylum. As it leaked support on the left accordingly, her party recorded its lowest vote share for over a century.
Unless traditional powerhouse parties of European social democracy are more courageous in seeking to shift the dial of political debate, the far right will continue to set its terms. The SD’s chosen slogan for its campaign was “Make Sweden Sweden again” – varying the usual Maga trope in order to stress the core ethnocentric message. From the sidelines its rhetoric will become still more extreme, and the defeat of the rightwing bloc is already being invidiously attributed to foreign-born voters.
Should Ms Andersson eventually succeed in forming a centre-left coalition government, she should counter the forces of division by channelling the best of her own party’s traditions. The Social Democratic party historically dominated Swedish politics through the idea of the Folkhemmet, or People’s Home, which encapsulated the inclusive ethos of a welfare society admired around the world. Locating the resources and ambition to develop a similarly attractive politics of the common good for the 21st century is the urgent task for progressives, in Sweden and beyond.

Von der Leyen blindsides EU with Canada ‘associate member’ pitch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:33:51 UTC
02:33:51 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney greets European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the official welcome ceremony during the G7 Leaders' Summit on June 16, 2025 in Kananaskis. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Ursula von der Leyen wanted to make a splash in her big speech. Instead, the European Commission president’s audacious offer of making Canada the EU’s first “associate member” has created a major diplomatic headache.
The idea was not run past European capitals in advance and has caused considerable confusion, four diplomats told POLITICO. Ottawa also appears to be distancing itself from the label — hours before Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to give his own speech to the European Parliament.
Von der Leyen dropped the bombshell proposal during her State of the Union address Wednesday, directly addressing Carney from the floor of the Parliament.
Advertisement
“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” she said, drawing thunderous applause from MEPs and an embrace from Carney.
There is another big problem: No one seems to know exactly what associate membership would entail.
And within hours, Canada was tamping down expectations.
“We’re not there,” Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s incoming ambassador to the EU, told reporters in Strasbourg when asked about associate membership. “What we’re focused on is actually driving results.”
That leaves von der Leyen having publicly offered up a new status that the EU hasn’t agreed to create or settled on a definition for — and which Canada itself doesn’t appear exactly eager to embrace.
A 'dangerous' strategy
The idea didn’t come out of nowhere. As U.S. tariffs and Donald Trump’s “51st state” threats strain ties, Canada is seeking to reduce its dependence on its neighbor, which receives roughly 70% of its exports, by deepening economic and security ties with Europe.
Advertisement
Ottawa has been exploring whether it can establish an unusually close relationship with the EU, the Wall Street Journal first reported last week. Carney publicly confirmed the broader ambition on Sunday, saying Canada was not seeking EU membership but rather a “unique alliance” with the bloc.
But von der Leyen’s decision to announce the proposal, at the biggest annual set piece of her political calendar, caught EU member countries off guard, according to four European diplomats who said their governments were not informed. They were granted anonymity, like others in this article, to speak candidly about their reactions to the proposal.
One diplomat slammed the secrecy as “dangerous” and “unwise,” pointing out that von der Leyen had not even raised the idea at a recent lunch with EU ambassadors. Another diplomat said the copy of the speech their government received in advance did not include the words associate membership.
Mark Carney said last week he wanted a “unique” partnership with Brussels but shied away from using the words associate membership. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images
And a different diplomat with knowledge of the discussions with Canada raised a different issue: “Nobody really knows what it [associate membership] means.”
While the Commission president is under no obligation to flag any of the speech's content to capitals in advance, they would need to approve any formal plan to grant Canada an exceptional status.
The idea has also raised questions about whether Britain could seek a similar deal. But EU officials have moved quickly to rule that out, stressing the model is intended for countries that cannot join the bloc. “Unlike Ukraine, Moldova, Georgia, Norway and the U.K., Canada is not in Europe,” one senior EU official said. “It cannot join the EU.”
Advertisement
Under the EU treaties and the bloc’s established institutional practice, there is a sharp distinction between membership and partnership. The EU has close relationships with many non-member countries, but only its 27 members have a seat in the bloc’s core political institutions and a formal role in making EU law.
A new model of membership “would actually require a treaty change,” German Socialists and Democrats MEP René Repasi told POLITICO.
The lack of wide consultation was visible inside the Commission, too, with an official involved in enlargement telling POLITICO their team had not been involved in any discussions about the proposal and that they knew nothing about it.
In the hallways of the Parliament, the proposal drew mixed reactions. “No one was aware of this special membership granted to Canada,” right-wing ECR co-chair Nicola Procaccini told POLITICO, adding it's "not entirely clear what this membership actually entails" but that the United Kingdom should be the first to benefit from such an arrangement.
Von der Leyen’s announcement should be read as a branding exercise to package a set of deeper ties across certain sectors that Canadians seek, as there is no legal basis in the treaties for such membership status, argued two centrist MEPs and one Parliament official.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola’s office put out a statement following a meeting with Carney that, tellingly, avoided mentioning the topic at all, saying the two leaders talked about “areas with big potential for even closer cooperation,” from critical raw minerals to defense.
Advertisement
The Commission's spokesperson's service did not immediately respond to request for comment.
Ottawa hits the brakes — ish
The response from Canada was hardly an unequivocal embrace.
Carney’s office welcomed Brussels’ broader push to deepen ties, saying after von der Leyen's speech that Canada wanted to strengthen its relationship with the EU and move beyond the existing free-trade relationship to a “far stronger, more ambitious alliance.”
But Ottawa has been careful, at least publicly, to distinguish that ambition from any form of EU membership. Carney himself said last week he wanted a “unique” partnership with Brussels but shied away from using the words associate membership.
Even if Canada eventually warms to the idea, there is a much bigger question: What would associate membership actually mean?
It’s not hard to imagine what quasi-membership could entail, based on privileges extended to other non-members.
Advertisement
Iceland, Norway, Switzerland and Liechtenstein all participate in the EU’s single market via the European Economic Area and are in the Schengen passport-free zone, despite not being part of the EU. Moldovans and Ukrainians can make calls and send texts in the EU without additional charges thanks to the bloc’s “roam like at home” program.
Without treaty change, “what one could rather imagine is looking in the direction of the EEA,” Repasi said, calling it “essentially an associate form of membership.”
But the EEA model comes with its own complications. EEA countries are deeply integrated into the EU's regulatory system while having no vote when EU legislation is passed.
Associate membership wouldn’t simply be about rebranding the EU's existing relationship with Canada or a euphemistic catch-all for a closer relationship, but creating a new category of partners for enhanced free trade and cooperation on areas including defense, AI and high-tech science, according to an EU official with knowledge of talks.
There would be no political rights or free movement, at least for now. Canada would be the first, but potentially not the only, country in the club: Australia, New Zealand, Singapore and Japan have all been mentioned as possible future members, the official added.
But a fifth diplomat was skeptical about what the result of such an arrangement would be and how it would materially differ from the close partnerships the EU already has with its allies.
Advertisement
A different diplomat pointed out that 10 EU countries have not yet even ratified the bloc's free trade agreement with Canada, CETA, which was signed almost a decade ago, while three have yet to approve the Strategic Partnership Agreement. A more daring pact would likely require the political enthusiasm of EU governments.
Germany also struck a cautious tone at a press conference on Wednesday.
“Canada is an especially close partner for Europe. That is why we are open to discussing new models of partnership,” government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said. But on the “associate member” label, he added: “I think we should give that some more thought.”
Camille Gijs contributed reporting from Brussels. Zoya Sheftalovich contributed reporting from Strasbourg. Oliver Noyan contributed reporting from Berlin.

One of Ukraine's key industries almost disappears from GDP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:30:00 EEST
02:30:00 KST

One of Ukraine's key industries almost disappears from GDP
Before Russia's full-scale invasion, the metals industry accounted for up to 7% of Ukraine's GDP. Metinvest, an international mining and steel group headquartered in Ukraine, now estimates its contribution may be close to zero.
Source: Metinvest Chief Operating Officer Oleksandr Myronenko in an interview with Forbes Ukraine
Quote from Myronenko: "The metals industry as a whole used to account for up to 7% of Ukraine's GDP. Now it may be close to zero. Those are the losses."
Details: He said that, of the group's mining assets in Ukraine, only the Central and Northern mining and processing plants are currently operating, though at about 50% of capacity. They produce iron ore pellets and concentrate for export to the EU.
The Southern mining and processing plant is idle because seaports are effectively closed. The Inhulets plant has been shut since 2024 because of high electricity prices.
At Zaporizhstal (Zaporizhzhia Steelworks), Russian strikes have effectively broken the production chain. Myronenko estimated that restoring the damaged equipment would cost tens of millions of hryvnias.
For reference: Ukraine's mining and metals sector has traditionally been one of the country's largest industries. GMK Center, a consulting company focused on the European iron and steel market, estimates that it accounted for 10.3% of Ukraine's GDP in 2021 and 5.5% in 2025. Last year, mining and metals products also accounted for 15.2% of Ukraine's total goods exports, worth US$6.2 billion.
Background:
- Following a Russian ballistic missile strike on 11 August, Zaporizhstal completely halted operations. In late August, Metinvest said it is not yet possible to determine when the plant could resume operations.
- Ukraine's steel production halved in August. In September, Zaporizhstal was hit by four ballistic missiles, with the damage described as critical.

Russia’s 2026 parliamentary election has no meaningful competition. Independent observers still plan to document how paper and online results diverge.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:28:43 UTC
02:28:43 KST

Russia’s 2026 parliamentary election has no meaningful competition. Independent observers still plan to document how paper and online results diverge.
In the summer of 2026, Yabloko — the only party representing Russia’s anti-establishment opposition and one that had campaigned against the war — was barred from the State Duma elections. Yabloko candidates running in single-member districts also faced obstacles, and the authorities managed to remove some from the race. There is no longer any meaningful political competition in the upcoming vote, especially because Moscow and dozens of other regions use remote electronic voting, which the authorities have used in previous years to rig the results. Even so, independent observers still plan to monitor the elections. The Kremlin has spent years making it harder for them to enter polling stations, but they can still do so. Meduza asked one observer why it is worth monitoring an election whose outcome has already been decided.
Why is our source anonymous?
Russian authorities may treat a comment or interview published by Meduza as participation in the activities of an “undesirable” organization. A first “offense” can result in a fine of 5,000 to 15,000 rubles. Another “offense” within a year may lead to criminal prosecution and up to four years in prison. We trust our source completely and have no doubts about his expertise.
— Why did you decide to become an election observer?
— I’ve been monitoring elections in Moscow for more than 10 years. I’ve seen every change in election law unfold firsthand.
In the early 2010s, there was a huge surge in election monitoring and grassroots civic activity in general. Some people I knew invited me to join. Even then, like many people, I didn’t like what was happening in the country. I wanted to change something.
The person who invited me stopped doing this a long time ago, but I’m still at it.
— It seems that many longtime observers have burned out and that election monitoring is no longer as popular as it once was. Is that true?
— Some people really do burn out because you’re very rarely able to get a result overturned — to challenge fraud, that is — even at your own polling station.
Then, once the online votes are counted, the winners aren’t the candidates who came out ahead in the precinct election commission’s final tally but completely different ones. When people see all this, many decide that monitoring is pointless and leave.
On top of that, a great many people left the country in 2022 out of concern for their safety. Others simply got tired.
— Why do you keep monitoring elections? There’s essentially no political competition in this election, and the authorities are using remote electronic voting…
— First, we never know what might suddenly make a difference or when. Suppose Yabloko had not been removed from the race for some reason. That would have been a huge incentive to try to protect Yabloko’s vote count. Not all polls can be trusted, but even those we saw suggested that Yabloko would have made a significant showing.
In any event, by being present at polling stations, we keep the machinery of fraud from expanding. The process is still cleaner with oversight than without it. If we aren’t there, absolute madness will unfold at polling stations. Our presence at least helps keep it in check.
In some local elections in regions without remote electronic voting, there is a very good chance that observers at polling stations will be able to protect votes cast for anti-war candidates.
Moscow, where I work as an observer, is a different matter. Remote electronic voting will be used in these State Duma elections and will most likely upend the results. But even in Moscow, some Yabloko candidates remain in the race [candidates in single-member districts]. And even if online voting reverses the results, we’ll be able to see a huge gap between the paper ballots counted at polling stations and the online vote. That will be revealing, too. It will show people that remote electronic voting clearly distorted the results and misrepresented how they voted.
— So you no longer see your role as forcing the authorities to overturn potentially fraudulent results, but rather as documenting the fraud?
— Sometimes we do manage to get the results overturned. There were cases like that in Moscow during the last parliamentary elections, in 2021. But ultimately, remote electronic voting decided everything there, too.
— How have you managed to avoid burning out over more than 10 years?
— That’s a very difficult question. Maybe it has something to do with my personality.
— The authorities do not welcome independent election monitoring. The clearest example is Grigory Melkonyants’s sentence. How do you assess the risks you face?
— To some extent, anyone in Russia faces risks right now. I don’t think mine are any greater than anyone else’s. I can recall only one case, in 2017, when a member of an election commission faced persecution for his work.
The system is still trying to preserve the appearance of legality, and I can’t recall any cases brought against observers specifically for their work.
Some neighborhood activists even deliberately seek appointments to election commissions in their districts. They do this not only to protect election results but also because the federal law “On Basic Guarantees of Electoral Rights and the Right of Citizens of the Russian Federation to Participate in a Referendum” still says that a court may impose administrative penalties on an election commission member only with the approval of the regional prosecutor. So to some extent, the position actually offers protection.
— How is independent monitoring at polling stations organized these days?
— Political parties and candidates appoint observers. We’re still able to reach agreements with parties represented in parliament, including A Just Russia and the Communist Party. I’ve heard that in some parts of Moscow, even the Liberal Democratic Party does this. It all depends on the local party organization.
We can also have candidates appoint observers [candidates running in single-member districts]. If a Yabloko candidate is running, the easiest thing is to have that candidate appoint the observers. If there is no Yabloko candidate, we have to negotiate with the parliamentary parties.
— Why are the parliamentary parties themselves interested in this?
— Some of them still retain a little independence at the grassroots level. Every State Duma deputy votes as instructed. But in some districts where parties have municipal deputies, they have to work with the public. Regional branches are still willing to make small compromises.
And some parties may still hope they can come to power someday. Parties also have an interest in preventing fraud because the more votes they receive, the more government funding they get. That’s where our interests overlap.
Sometimes observers are dropped when the list is handed over to the party, so only some of them ultimately make it into polling stations. But that’s still better than nothing.
Overall, the authorities have severely curtailed independent election monitoring. For some time now, only someone eligible to vote in the same election has been allowed to serve as an observer. In Moscow City Duma elections, for example, only a Moscow resident can serve, while in municipal elections, observers must even come from the same Moscow district. This has made it much harder to recruit observers for local elections.
— These days, polling stations may also have representatives from pro-government organizations that only purport to monitor elections — the autonomous nonprofit Dialog, for example. Have you encountered them?
— At polling stations, you’re most likely to encounter observers from the Civic Chamber. They try to cover almost every polling station, and they’re a total crapshoot.
Sometimes a relative of the precinct commission chair arrives as the Civic Chamber observer. Other times, someone shows up who immediately starts acting like an observer rather than a bystander and genuinely helps the independent observers.
I don’t really understand how the Civic Chamber selects them, but because there are so many, you do occasionally find honest people among its “observers.” Unfortunately, that’s rare. More often, they turn a blind eye to fraud. Obviously, a relative of the commission chair will side with the commission, not the law.
— What else should people know about voting this year?
— Ever since the COVID era, voting has taken place over three days. It’s best to vote on the last day, Sunday, because the ballots are placed in sealed storage bags between voting days. After the last election, there were reports that these bags had been opened at night and the ballots inside replaced — despite the observers’ best efforts.
So it’s best to come on the third day. Unfortunately, a number of regions use remote electronic voting, which is best avoided. It’s better to go to a polling station and vote on paper. Ideally, you should cast a paper ballot at the polling station where you’re registered on the third day. You’ll receive two ballots there: one for a candidate in your single-member district and one for a party.
But if that isn’t possible — if voters are abroad, for example — then remote electronic voting is acceptable. It is being used in 33 regions this time.
— Is there no way to reverse the effects of fraud in remote electronic voting?
— I have no idea how it could be done. During the last State Duma elections, candidates filed complaints in court — but we know how the courts work. So unfortunately, nothing can be done for now.
In theory, if an enormous number of people suddenly came to polling stations and voted on paper, the prearranged, manipulated online results might not outweigh the paper-ballot vote. I don’t rule out that possibility. But is that likely to happen in this particular election? Probably not.
Still, we know in advance how many voters there are at each polling station, and that number cannot change dramatically during the election. If, after the paper and online results are combined, we see an anomalous increase in the number of voters, that will be the clearest possible sign that a huge number of fraudulent votes were added to the online tally.
— Who is signing up as an independent observer these days?
— Mostly neighborhood activists and young people. I’m speaking only from what I see in my own district. I can’t say what it’s like elsewhere. After all, 2022 dealt an enormous blow to the civic movement. As I said, a great many people left the country.
The influx of young people doesn’t make up for the losses in the election-monitoring movement. Overall interest is declining. Few people stay involved year after year.
— But you still find it meaningful?
— I’ll quote a good song: “In my city, the hardest job is loving someone, but somebody has to do it.” In other words, if we aren’t there, no one will ever know what happens at the polling stations.
No one will ever know what the country’s citizens really think. This is a very subtle point. I very much want the government in this country to change, but I really don’t want anyone to die. I don’t want a bloody regime change. Elections are the only realistic way for power to change hands without bloodshed. And if a window of opportunity ever opens when we can actually make a difference, it will have been worth all the time we had to spend waiting.
In any case, even now, we make things difficult for the authorities at polling stations. I believe it is right to make things difficult for the system of government that has emerged in our country.
Finally, if we all live to see the government truly change someday, elections will still have to be held. You might say we’re keeping the knowledge of how to conduct fair elections from being lost.
Here’s an example that comes to mind: Scientists today are trying to understand how the Egyptian pyramids were built. We shouldn’t let things reach a point where people in the future have to figure out how to hold elections. There should be people who know and remember how to conduct them and what to do to ensure they are fair. The more people like that there are, the easier things will be in the future.
Russians lost real elections a long ago. But you’ve still got a choice. If you live outside Russia, please donate to Meduza — for yourself or for those who remain inside the country and want to read independent news.

US pays $725 million to UN, easing its debt dispute with the world body

Unknown Publisher

17:28:01 UTC
02:28:01 KST

US pays $926 million to UN, easing its debt dispute with the world body
- The US paid US$725 million to the UN, reducing its debt and securing its voting rights at the upcoming General Assembly.
- The Trump administration criticised the UN and cut funding, demanding reforms before releasing payments.
- The UN is undergoing reforms and cost-cutting amid financial challenges, with China also making significant contributions recently.
AI generated
NEW YORK - The Trump administration paid US$725 million (S$926 million) to the United Nations (UN), the organisation said on Sept 16, reducing Washington’s large debt and ensuring it keeps its vote at the UN General Assembly convening in New York next week.
US President Donald Trump has criticised the global body for not living up to its potential and slashed funding to many UN agencies. When asked about the planned payment in August, a US official said any payments will be contingent on continued reforms of the UN.
“We received US$725 million yesterday from the United States for the UN regular budget, and we also received US$102 million from the US for peacekeeping on Friday,” said UN spokesperson Farhan Haq.
“The US still owes US$1.312 billion to the regular budget,” he said, adding that, “with these payments, the US is no longer in jeopardy of falling under Article 19 for 2027”.
Under Article 19 of the UN Charter, a member state loses its voting rights in the General Assembly if its arrears exceed two years in annual fees, although grace periods are possible.
The Trump administration has carried out an unprecedented shrinking of its federal government, saying it was bloated and has significantly cut back on domestic and foreign grants in an effort that it says was to put money into causes that aligned with US taxpayer interests.
The US is the biggest contributor to the UN budget, but under the Trump administration it has slow-walked mandatory payments to regular and peacekeeping budgets, and has slashed voluntary funding to UN agencies with their own budgets.
The second-biggest contributor, China, also paid US$641.4 million on Sept 1 in its regular budget contributions, according to the UN website.
The UN has been undergoing a reform and cost-cutting exercise known as “UN80” amid its financial crisis. REUTERS

WASHINGTON, September 16. /TASS/. The window of opportunity for modernizing the US army is closing, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff of the US Armed Forces, General Dan Caine warned.
"We must move together because the window to build the force that we need is closing. We can buy almost anything in life, but we cannot buy time," he said.
He called on the US military-industrial complex to "move faster," "to deliver quality weapons" on time and at lower costs. The Pentagon and the government should work more effectively, Caine told a conference of the non-governmental Association of the US Air Force and Space Forces near Washington.
"Future conflicts will demand that we operate without the assumptions of uncontested access, secure rear areas, or uninterrupted or uncontested sustainment," he said. He also argued that the US adversaries are cooperating more closely. "They share technology, intelligence, weapons, and economic support. They're studying our battlefields of the past and our battlefields currently, and they're adapting quickly and seeking new ways to challenge our advantages," Caine said. Mendel says she was denied entry to European Parliament building, links decision to sanctions against her

Former press secretary to the President of Ukraine Yulia Mendel said she was denied entry to the European Parliament building and attributed this to sanctions imposed on her by Ukraine.
"On the day of my speech, I was barred from entering the European Parliament. I directly attribute this to Zelenskyy's sanctions [imposed on September 13]. But the speech will take place anyway, because I know that I represent a huge segment of society that longs for peace and to be heard," she said in a video she posted on her Facebook page on Wednesday.
After the sanctions were imposed, Mendel said they had been imposed just a few days before her speech at the European Parliament. "A few days before my speech at the European Parliament, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, my former boss, imposed sanctions against me… I knew that "treason" was being orchestrated because of my interview with Tucker Carlson, and I suspected sanctions might be coming," Mendel said on Facebook on Sunday evening.
Zelenskyy's former press secretary was scheduled to be the keynote speaker at the event "Ukraine: Dare to Choose Peace – Diplomacy, Not Escalation" in Strasbourg. The event was organized and moderated by AfD MEP Hans Neuhoff.
However, Mendel's planned speech was not an official event of the European Parliament. Members of the European Parliament and political groups may organize their own events on the premises of the European Parliament. The European Parliament itself does not approve the content of such events but handles organizational matters, including security, venue, translation, and technical support.
Mendel served as Zelenskyy's press secretary from 2019 to 2021. In May 2026, she gave an interview to American journalist Tucker Carlson, during which she made a series of accusations against Zelenskyy and his inner circle.

Kazakhstan Again Sentences Activists for Supposed Attempt to Seize Power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:20:00 UTC
02:20:00 KST

On September 8, five men were sentenced to between five and five-and-a-half years in prison after standing trial in an Almaty courtroom for supposedly attempting to seize control of power in Kazakhstan last year. The judges found all five suspects guilty not only of advocating for the violent seizure of power, but also of organizing mass unrest against authorities in the country and a seizure of the presidential residence, known as Akorda.
Several of the convicted have a past in activism, having taken part in multiple civil protests in the country over the years. While doors were closed for the hearings, the case sparked some attention from both activists and national human rights organizations. Along with criticizing the verdict, focus was also given to similar cases that had targeted activists previously. These types of court cases, activists argue, are part of a strategy employed by the Kazakh government to control opposition in the country.
While all of the defendants, aged between 56 and 62, were found guilty of advocating for mass riots and the seizure of power in Kazakhstan, two were found to have committed additional offenses. Kaisar Ozbek and Talgat Ashirov were convicted of illegally acquiring and storing explosives in relation to the unrest. These charges originally led the state prosecutor to request eight years in prison for each of the defendants.
When the trial began in February, the five men all entered not guilty pleas to all of the charges. Speaking with RFE/RL at the start of the trial, lawyers representing two of the defendants stated that their clients were simply ordinary people coerced into committing crimes.
Zhanara Balgabaeva, lawyer of one of the defendants, claimed that security forces made use of plants who pretended to share the activists’ views, then provoked them into committing crimes. “The civil activists, under the influence of these provocateurs, engaged in destructive conversations and activities of which my client was unaware,” she told RFE/RL.
She further criticized the decision to let the trial run behind closed doors, citing concerns for the rule of law: “They [the courts] don’t want transparency. They want to quickly shut everyone down without any fuss.”
This newest case taps into a trend of activists being accused of attempting to incite mass unrest or directly seize power in Kazakhstan. Such charges have now landed at least 17 people in prison since 2024. The Kazakhstan International Bureau of Human Rights and Rule of Law has questioned the neutrality of the country’s judicial system as a result. They suspect that the cases are a tactic employed by the Kazakh authorities to silence political adversaries.
The best known instance is often referred to as “the tractor case” due to the court claim that the seven charged activists planned to drive a tractor into Akorda in 2022. This supposedly would have been done in order to cause unrest in the country in an effort to seize power.
Another such case was presented in court just last year. In that case, five activists were sentenced to four years of restricted freedom for allegedly attempting to organize mass unrest in the country in relation to the referendum on the use of nuclear power in 2024. As suspects were interrogated in relation to this case, one defendant later stated that he was asked about their intention to seize control of Akorda in connection to the supposed plans of mass unrest.
Similar to the most recent case of an alleged plan to seize power, these previous incidents also included defendants of retirement age accused of planning mass unrest. Zhanara Balgabaeva, who has had a client in all three abovementioned cases, has also previously criticized the way evidence had been collected, pointing to some of it being acquired through provocations.
“In the ‘tractor case,’ when we were defending our clients, we said that any actions carried out through provocations are not admissible as evidence. Now we are seeing the same thing,” the lawyer stated in relation to the case surrounding the nuclear referendum.
With the recent verdict against five activists, Kazakhstan has now imprisoned activists for allegedly planning unrest for the third straight year, prompting both lawyers and human rights organizations to call foul play. Whether their criticism will have any effect on the Kazakh judicial system going forward remains to be seen.

Meloni rules out snap elections and plans to remain in office until the end of her term
Kyiv • UNN
Giorgia Meloni said she wants to remain prime minister until the end of Parliament’s term. She denied rumors of early elections.
Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Wednesday that she intends to remain in office until the end of the term of the current parliament, dismissing media speculation about possible early elections before her term ends next autumn, UNN reports.
"I would like to remain in office until the end of the parliament's term. I am proud of the stability of this government," Meloni said at a press conference following a cabinet meeting.
Meloni, whose government this month became Italy's longest-serving government since World War II, heads a conservative coalition comprising her Brothers of Italy party, as well as the League and Forza Italia.
Growing support for National Future, a new far-right movement led by former General Roberto Vannacci, has drawn some votes away from Meloni's camp and sparked rumors that she may try to call early elections to prevent a further decline in her approval rating.

Nevertheless, the coalition's path has often been difficult in recent months, suggesting that Meloni may be losing full control over the alliance as elections approach.
In July, Italy's lower house of parliament unexpectedly rejected a government amendment related to electoral reform that Meloni had strongly supported; this happened because some lawmakers from the ruling coalition did not support the initiative.

Why has the response to Nepal’s floods been so muted?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:17:49 UTC
02:17:49 KST

Why has the response to Nepal’s floods been so muted?
Because wealthy nations do not want to take responsibility for their role in the current climate crisis.
It has been three weeks since the collapse of a glacier and rock mass from the Langtang Lirung mountain triggered devastating floods in Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli valleys. Officials have confirmed the loss of more than 1,380 precious lives, while around 5,100 remain missing. The disaster shattered thousands of homes and wiped out vital infrastructure.
Nepal government’s rapid assessment estimates that full recovery and long-term reconstruction will need $4.7bn. That is roughly 10 percent of Nepal’s annual gross domestic product (GDP), and more than a third of its federal budget.
And yet, despite considerable media and public attention, the international political response has remained strikingly muted.
We have heard some condolence messages from foreign governments, along with emergency supplies and pledges of help. These matter. But the response mainly targeted immediate humanitarian aid. For instance, the United States pledged $3.6m, the United Kingdom $6m, and the European Union $2.3m. But these meagre funds cannot meet the needs of affected communities and provide them with the shelter, food and infrastructure to survive the winter.
Why has the response been so inadequate? Why have so few political leaders spoken up about this disaster with the urgency its scale demands?
Part of the answer may lie in an uncomfortable question Nepal has now put directly on the table: who should pay for climate loss and damage?
Nepal is increasingly framing the floods not simply as another weather-induced catastrophe, but as a consequence of a climate crisis to which the country contributed almost nothing.
This points to a deeper inequality of climate crisis.
For over a century, wealthy countries have consumed a vastly disproportionate share of the atmosphere’s capacity to absorb carbon dioxide. They grew their economies through industrialisation driven by fossil fuel consumption. Meanwhile, countries like Nepal got little chance to use anything approaching an equivalent share of that atmospheric space.
The result shows a stark divide between those who benefitted disproportionately from burning fossil fuels and those who face growing consequences.
Nepal has argued that international support to deal with climate catastrophe is not a charity. It must be climate justice. It has asked the United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage for urgent support, and the fund’s board is now considering how to respond.
That changes the political conversation. And it takes us back to the bargain struck in Paris a decade ago.
Developing countries fought hard for the international climate regime under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change to recognise “loss and damage” or the destruction that cannot simply be prevented through mitigation or adapted to. They secured its recognition in Article 8 of the Paris Agreement.
But wealthy countries drew a line around what that recognition could mean. The decision text adopted alongside the Paris Agreement states that Article 8 “does not involve or provide a basis for any liability or compensation”.
It was a strange political bargain: the world could acknowledge climate-related loss and damage, but that acknowledgement could not lead to demands for compensation.
Nepal is now testing the limits of that bargain.
The legal picture is more complicated than simply saying that the Paris Agreement prohibits climate compensation. In 2025, the International Court of Justice ruled that countries have a legal obligation to protect the climate system; if they fail their obligations, they are liable for reparations or compensation for the damage they have caused. The decision sparked renewed attention to the questions around state responsibility under international law.
In the case of Nepal and other developing countries disproportionately affected by the climate crisis, the state does not need to prove that one particular country caused a specific flood before the international community can recognise a responsibility to address the consequences of climate change.
But there is another issue: the traditional international system for supporting developing countries is itself shrinking. At precisely the time climate losses are mounting, official development assistance is falling. It plummeted by 23.1 percent in 2025, the largest annual contraction on record. Humanitarian assistance also fell sharply.
And the problem is not simply that there is too little aid.
For decades, the global economy has transferred enormous amounts of wealth and resources through unequal economic ties between the Global North and the Global South. Climate finance won’t fix that imbalance if it simply returns a fraction of that wealth as loans or private investment options.
A country should not have to borrow its way out of a climate disaster it did little to create.
Nor can compensation substitute for mitigation. Wealthy countries cannot keep consuming a disproportionate share of the world’s energy and material resources while ignoring the consequences elsewhere. They must rapidly reduce their own emissions and ecological overconsumption.
The muted response to the floods in Nepal therefore raises a larger question about international cooperation.
Perhaps the world is comfortable acknowledging the growing cost of the climate crisis. It is much less comfortable when countries affected ask whether the costs should be borne by those who contributed most to creating the crisis.
The avenues for changing this already exist: the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, the UN climate negotiations, and the evolving body of international law on climate responsibility.
What is missing is the political recognition that the costs of climate destruction cannot indefinitely be treated as somebody else’s problem.
If climate justice means anything, it must eventually include reparations for the damage caused by an unequal appropriation of the atmospheric commons.
That conversation can no longer be postponed.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

No matter how deranged and delusional your podcast is, Liz Truss can go further | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:15:37 UTC
02:15:37 KST

Some things you can set your watch by. Like every time small boats are in the news, the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, will manoeuvre himself in front of a camera to suggest that all male migrants are either murderers or rapists. Probably both.
But some things feel older than time itself. Like Liz Truss trying to persuade the world she was right all along. Most former prime ministers leave Downing Street relatively quietly. Lord Big Dave, the Maybot and even Boris nurse their grudges in private. Rishi lives in semi-retirement – almost a recluse – and only attends parliament when it suits him. Keir has been almost totally airbrushed out of history in a couple of months.
Liz, though, is the outlier. She refuses to give up. The last cockroach alive after a nuclear apocalypse. Even now, she probably has a platoon of nuns locked up in her basement in south-east London where they are being forced to embroider a 70-metre tapestry dedicated to a revisionist history of her 49 days in office. One in which an old monarch dies and a new king ascends the throne. As one Elizabethan era ends so another Elizabethan era begins and a grateful nation bows down to her genius.
You have to wonder if this obsession is healthy. Most normal people might be slightly embarrassed to be remembered as the UK’s shortest serving prime minister. And by far and away the dimmest in living memory. But Truss seems devoid of affect. No sense of shame. If anything she seems proud of her 49 days. That long! In Liz’s mind, she was simply too good for us. We weren’t ready for her. Give it a thousand years and her tapestry will be on show in the British Museum.
One thing you can guarantee: offer Liz a platform to speak and she will bite your hand off. No matter how deranged and delusional it may be, Liz is confident she can be yet more deranged and delusional. She is every rightwinger’s favourite guest. Not only is she guaranteed to say yes, she will also make everyone else seem almost normal. Win-win. She’s done all sorts of weird stuff in the US, and in the UK she has her own podcast where she pretends to be interested in someone other than herself on Mike Graham’s YouTube channel. Graham, you might remember, is the man who thinks you can grow concrete. And Liz is sure he’s right.
The new kid on the podcast block is the former Tory Brexiter Steve Baker. So who else would he get as his first guest than the Trusster. If anything, Steve has got even more weird in the two years since he lost his seat. These days he has the look of a far-right survivalist holed up in a hut somewhere in the Montana wilderness. And his podcast surroundings have the same feel. All very basic, just a table and chairs. The table probably has a cache of semi-automatic rifles underneath it. Every so often, Steve will interrupt the recording to do an ad for gold. He no longer trusts traditional currencies.
And up steps Liz. Doing what only someone as half-witted as she can: talking non-stop nonsense. Often with a weird half-smile on her face. At times you are tempted to believe that she is in on the joke that she is the joke. But then you realise she’s deadly serious. She hasn’t quite understood that people aren’t laughing with her, they are laughing at her. There’s something almost unbearably sad about this. So much so you almost feel guilty for indulging her insanity. Then you remember that only 2,000 people are going to watch this. And only we dedicated few are going to make it to the end.
Labour has ruined the country, she says. Tony Blair and Gordon Brown had a secret plot to dismantle British civilisation and nothing has been the same since 1997. At which point, even Steve has to remind Liz that the Tories were in power from 2010. The Trusster doesn’t miss a beat. She is rushing on her run, her onboard computer set to auto-pilot. The Tories weren’t really the Tories. They were socialists in disguise. All of them. They were all part of the woke establishment. That’s why they were anti-Brexit. And austerity never happened.
At this point it would have been a kindness to wrap the podcast up. To remind Liz that antipsychotic help was available. Because to the best of my knowledge, Liz had been a minister in successive Tory governments since 2012. She had also been a vocal supporter of Remain.
Only it turns out that was a different Liz. A doppelganger. She had been temporarily captured by the wokerati and made to do and say a lot of things against her will. It was only when she became prime minister that she could self-actualise into her truest state and then she was thwarted by the Bank of England getting tough on quantitative easing. All a deliberate plot to destabilise her mini-budget. Nothing to do with the mini-budget being riddled with unfunded tax cuts.
There were only two trustworthy people left in the world, she said: Donald Trump and Javier Milei. It was time to disband the judiciary, the prisons and the civil service. The whole world order needed to be rebalanced. Steve readily agreed. He reckoned the NHS should also be included on the grounds that it had almost killed him and a friend of his. Not even Liz was going that far. But together the revolution was possible.
Then the big question. What next for Liz? Would she stand for election again? Maybe, she said. But who for? She’s long since been too mad for the Tories and might even be too bonkers for Reform. All she knew was that she would never go away. Not while there were still things to talk about that no one was talking about except her. Poor Liz. The problem isn’t that no one is talking. It’s that no one is listening. Steve chucked her a nugget of gold and they both ran for the hills. You’ll never take them alive.

EU to ban social media for under 13s, curb access until 15
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:15:15 UTC
02:15:15 KST

EU to ban social media for under 13s, curb access until 15
STRASBOURG, France - The European Union will ban social media for children under 13 and allow only limited, supervised access until the age of 15 under plans unveiled on Sept 16 by EU chief Ursula von der Leyen.
A global backlash against social media has piled pressure on policymakers, with a rising body of evidence showing negative impacts on children’s physical and mental health.
“It is time for Europe to act,” von der Leyen said during her annual keynote address to the European Parliament. “It is we who decide our rules, not big tech,” she warned.
Australia in 2025 became the first country to ban social media for under-16s, triggering similar moves elsewhere, but the European Commission chief said the 27-country bloc would take a more “gradual” approach.
“No social media under the age of 13. No personal account under the age of 15,” she said. “That means from 13 to under 15, only mini accounts, set up and supervised by parents or guardians, with limited features and time restriction to one hour a day.”
“And between 15 and 18, safe design will be an obligation for the platforms.”
Before outlining the EU’s approach, von der Leyen paid tribute to a 14-year-old girl in Belgium, named Olea, who killed herself one month ago after being bullied, and whose mother she quoted as saying: “I am convinced that without these omnipresent networks, my daughter would still be here.”
Von der Leyen made no reference to online games or AI chatbots, which according to draft legislation seen by AFP would also be hit by the restrictions.
The commission president and tech chief Henna Virkkunen will formally present the proposed “KIDS Act”, including the tiered age limits in Strasbourg, France on Sept 17.
Children’s rights and parents groups welcomed moves to make online platforms safer.
“The devil is of course in the detail. Tomorrow’s proposal must be coherent, comprehensive, future-proof and robustly enforceable,” the 5Rights Foundation advocacy group’s Leanda Barrington-Leach said.
“Finally, Europe is sending a clear signal: it’s time to act against the harmful design of platforms to protect our children from toxic algorithms and features,” said Arnaud Ducoin, part of a group of French families who have filed a complaint against TikTok over teenagers’ self-harm and suicides.
‘Arbitrary age threshold’
The new EU law will also ban addictive design features such as so-called infinite scrolling where children are concerned, according to a draft document.
If platforms break the rules, they face fines of up to six per cent of annual turnover, draft details show.
“We do not have to accept addictive features,” von der Leyen warned, saying “platforms will have to prove that they are safe”.
The “risk” is not limited to children, she noted. “Addictive design, for example, is harming everyone,” she said, telling EU lawmakers that Europe needed more rules that will be proposed in the autumn.
Simeon de Brouwer of digital rights group EDRi said making platforms safer across the board was an urgent necessity, telling AFP “if the design is harmful at 13, it does not magically become safe on their 15th or 18th birthday”.
Pressure from EU states
Von der Leyen had faced pressure from members including France, Denmark and Greece for action across the 27-nation bloc to limit online harms for children.
France, which has proposed its own legislation, welcomed the announcement. Government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon said it was “a step in the right direction”.
The EU has sought for years to rein in Big Tech, empowering itself with a strengthened legal armoury, but it believes additional tools are needed to limit online harms.
The bloc has already told Meta platforms Facebook and Instagram as well as TikTok to change their “addictive” design through its content law known as the Digital Services Act, but changes have taken longer than Brussels wants.
Digital and consumer rights groups have meanwhile raised concerns over a related age-check app due to be rolled out later this year which Brussels says will keep children off social media.
“Age verification is not a silver bullet and would raise serious privacy and data protection concerns,” said European consumer organisation BEUC’s Agustin Reyna.
The proposal on Sept 17 will only become law after negotiations between EU capitals and the European Parliament, which could take months. AFP

Houthis claim shootdown of Saudi jet (VIDEO)
Yemen’s Houthi forces claimed on Wednesday to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet, releasing a video of the burning wreckage of the warplane. If verified, the video is the first ever evidence of a Saudi jet downed by Houthi air defenses.
In a video statement, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said that the jet was shot down over Yemen’s Marib Governorate using “a locally manufactured surface-to-air missile.” Saree then claimed that Houthi fighters successfully repelled two waves of Saudi F-15s and Eurofighter Typhoon jets that were scrambled to search for the wreckage.
Saree did not say when the incident took place, and the Saudi military has not yet confirmed the loss of the jet.

Footage from the crash site showed Houthi fighters lifting the tail of the aircraft, which bore the Saudi flag. The militants posed in front of the tail section chanting “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
Before Wednesday, the Houthis, also known as the Ansar Allah movement, claimed to have shot down three Saudi fighters, one in 2017 and two in 2018. The group also claimed to have damaged – but not downed – a Saudi jet in 2018. Riyadh denied ever losing a warplane to Houthi fire, and without clear video evidence, these previous claims were impossible to verify.
Saudi Arabia has been waging war against the Houthis since 2015, although the fighting was paused by a ceasefire in 2022. Violence between the Saudis and Houthis erupted again this July, when the Saudi-backed government in Aden struck an airport in Houthi-controlled Sana’a. The Houthis responded with strikes on Saudi targets, while Saudi jets resumed large-scale airstrikes on Yemen. Last week, Houthi forces swept across Yemen’s western coast, seizing the port city of Mocha and solidifying their control over the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
The Houthi offensive threatens Saudi Arabia’s vital oil exports. The Kingdom recently shifted its exports from the Persian Gulf in the east to the Red Sea in the West, as the Strait of Hormuz remains shut due to the US war on Iran. With the Houthis in control of the west, Saudi exports are now threatened from both sides.
According to Saree, Houthi forces also struck a Saudi airbase in Khamis Mushait and Aramco oil facilities in Yanbu with drones and ballistic missiles on Wednesday.

The Gomel region borders Ukraine, while the M-10 highway, where one of the checkpoints was installed, leads to Gomel from the south.

Satellite data shows major ice losses for Greenland and Antarctica
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:13:06 UTC
02:13:06 KST

Satellite data shows major ice losses for Greenland and Antarctica
LONDON - New research based on satellite data going back to the 1970s has documented major polar ice losses in Greenland and Antarctica — home to Earth’s two great ice sheets — that have contributed to rising global sea levels.
Between 1979 and 2023, according to data from 27 satellite missions, Greenland and Antarctica lost a combined 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice, adding 3.14cm to the worldwide sea-level rise.
The study, employing the longest satellite data record of changes in ice sheets ever gathered to give the most complete account to date of ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica, was conducted by the Ice Sheet Mass Balance Inter-comparison Exercise team, an international group of polar scientists.
The findings, they said, offer fresh evidence of the effects of human-caused global climate change.
“To put this very large number into context, 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice is enough ice to fill in a cube that would be 23 kilometres in height,” said climate scientist Ines Otosaka of Northumbria University in England, lead author of the study published on Sept 16 in the journal Scientific Data.
Of the ice loss documented in the study, about 60 per cent came from Greenland and 40 per cent from Antarctica, even though Greenland is about one-eighth the size of Antarctica.
“When ice sheets melt, they contribute to rising global sea levels. And with every additional centimetre of sea-level rise, about 2 to 3 million people are put at risk of annual coastal flooding. The ice sheets are now a major driver of sea-level rise, accounting for about 25 per cent of all sea-level rise,” Otosaka said.
“We have extended our satellite data record backwards in time to the 1970s, and this confirms that ice losses started in the 1990s and have increased since then. Our assessment shows that the pace of ice loss increased by a factor of four between the 1980s and 2010s,” Otosaka said.
The study documented a slowdown in ice loss between 2020 and 2023, though the researchers said this appears to represent a short-term variation and not a reversal of the long-term trend.
Unusually high snowfall across East Antarctica provided enough ice to offset some of the losses from glaciers elsewhere on Antarctica, while relatively mild summers in Greenland substantially lowered surface melting, they said.
Some 84 per cent of the ice lost came from glaciers flowing more quickly into the ocean rather than from ice melting at the surface, showing that the long-term trend is being driven by the response of the ice sheets to a warming ocean, Otosaka said.
The researchers said the total sea-level rise attributed to the ice losses at Greenland and Antarctica may not sound like a huge number, but it puts another 6 to 9 million people at risk of coastal flooding and erosion globally.
“These findings have implications for coastal planning, showing that we urgently need to develop plans for protecting coastal communities around the world from the impact of ice sheet melting,” Otosaka said. REUTERS

Emory University launches new academic center intended to counter rising antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:12:19 UTC
02:12:19 KST

Emory University launched a new academic center earlier this month focused on developing practical, government-level strategies to combat rising antisemitism.
The Emory Policy Institute on Countering Antisemitism, known as EPICA, was founded and is led by Ambassador Deborah Lipstadt, a University Distinguished Professor, Holocaust historian, and former US special envoy to monitor and combat antisemitism under the Biden administration.
Funded by private donations, the institute is designed to bridge rigorous academic scholarship with public policy, operating under the belief that anti-Jewish hatred poses a fundamental threat to democratic societies.
Reflecting on her transition back to academia after nearly three years in diplomacy, Lipstadt told The Jerusalem Post, “When I finished at the State Department, a number of people, both from within universities and from the world of diplomacy, said to me, ‘Deborah, you have a unique perspective on the issue of antisemitism, anti-Zionism, and Jew hatred, which is a term I prefer nowadays, in that you bring to it decades of scholarly experience, you also bring to it a face-to-face encounter in the lawsuit that you faced with David Irving, and you’ve now been in the diplomatic world for close to three years, so you understand how diplomacy works, what governments can do and what governments can’t do, what are the limits, what are the possibilities. Don’t just squander that or write a book and think that’s enough.’ So I turned to Emory University, Emory College, and they were enthusiastic about my building something that would address this issue, that would involve students as well, but also have a research element.”
EPICA to include undergraduate fellowship program
The institute’s core mission centers on conducting interdisciplinary research, facilitating public dialogue, and training the next generation of policy leaders. A key component of EPICA’s educational programming is an undergraduate fellowship starting in January 2027.
The fellowship will allow third- and fourth-year students in good standing to engage directly with policymakers, participate in study trips to Washington, DC, and complete summer internships on Capitol Hill and at policy think tanks.
Student fellows will produce research related to the Global Guidelines for Countering Antisemitism, an international framework introduced by Lipstadt in a 2024 speech in Buenos Aires, Argentina, and endorsed by dozens of countries and multilateral organizations.
The framework includes recommendations for governments and international bodies, including adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism as a framework.
Institute will support ongoing fight against antisemitism 'virus'
Lipstadt emphasized to the Post that the institute deliberately chose the word “countering” instead of “combating,” explaining that “combats would just suggest a winner, and I don’t think that there’s a winner in this.” Instead, she views the initiative as supporting an ongoing fight against a virus that extends far beyond immediate horizons.
“It’s a counter-effort, it’s an ongoing fight,” Lipstadt noted. “This is a virus that mutates and lives long beyond and beyond anywhere we can look at today.”
Lipstadt stated that through the institute’s efforts, “I would hope that the research that would come out, that the students’ experience, that the work that they will do, would compel increasing numbers of universities to take this issue seriously.”
Lipstadt added that addressing governments also means looking broadly at institutional policies.
“When I say governments, I’m not just talking about federal governments, but even universities, how can they address this? How can they counter this? How can they recognize that this is a dangerous and serious issue? And so that’s what we will be working on,” Lipstadt concluded.

Iranian drone and missile attacks on US bases in the region during Operation Epic Fury might have been aided by Russian spy satellites, CNN reported on Wednesday.
The report, which cited two US officials, said these satellites may have passed information to Tehran after flying over areas with a US military presence, such as Prince Sultan Air Base, which was struck by Iran on March 27.
According to the report, Russian satellites played a "vital role" in the Prince Sultan Air Base attack, which injured 12 US soldiers.
CNN analyzed the tracking data of the satellites in question, revealing that they passed over targeted areas just prior to Iranian operations against said targets.
The satellites included those used for detailed imagery, all-weather radio signal detection, infrared imaging, and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), which is used to locate high-value targets.
According to CNN, one of these high-value targets was a US Air Force Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) aircraft, which was destroyed during Iran's attack on Prince Sultan Air Base.
The report noted the accuracy of such strikes as evidence of Iran's use of Russian satellites, saying that the precision would be impossible without them.
Other targets in question by the report include a CIA facility within the US embassy complex in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

He noted that Russia's reasoning for helping Iran is due to the US similarly assisting Ukraine in its efforts to strike Russian targets.
"This is Russian payback with interest," said Obaid. "It's monumental in terms of the consequences of what this has done, not just to the US's standing in the region, but to the security architecture of the region going forward."

Israeli AI English-learning startup Loora raises $22m. in Series B
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:11:45 UTC
02:11:45 KST

Israeli AI language-learning company Loora has raised $22 million in a Series B funding round, bringing its total funding to more than $43 million, the company announced Tuesday.
The round was led by Union Tech Ventures, with participation from vgames and existing investors Emerge, Hearst Ventures and QP Ventures.
Loora, which uses artificial intelligence to provide personalized English-speaking practice, said it would use the funding to expand research and development and accelerate growth in the US, Europe, Asia, and Latin America.
The company also plans to roughly double its workforce over the next six months, primarily by hiring for AI research and development and learning-science positions.
Founded in 2020 by CEO Roy Mor and CTO Yonti Levin, Loora has more than 15 million users worldwide, according to the company.
Mor and Levin met during their military service and served together in Sayeret Matkal, the IDF’s elite special operations unit.
The company previously raised $9.25 million during its seed round and $12 million in Series A funding in 2024. The latest investment brings its total disclosed financing to approximately $43.25 million.
AI as an English tutor
Loora’s app lets users practice spoken English through conversations with an AI tutor and receive feedback on grammar, pronunciation, and fluency. The system adapts conversations to a user’s proficiency level and interests.
The app is aimed primarily at adults seeking to improve their spoken English, including for job interviews, professional presentations, and workplace conversations.
Loora said users have held more than 200 million conversations with its AI system. It said revenue has more than doubled during the past 12 months, with annual recurring revenue now in the tens of millions of dollars.
Those financial figures were provided by the privately held company and are not independently disclosed.
Loora also said it had built a business-to-business operation over the past year and now works with more than 100 companies, governments and universities.
According to Loora, 72% of its users say career advancement is a primary reason for learning English, while its typical user is between 25 and 55 years old.
Loora targets limits of traditional language apps
The company is betting that conversational AI can address one of the central limitations of conventional language-learning software: giving users frequent opportunities to speak rather than primarily completing vocabulary and grammar exercises.
Loora says its system uses information from previous conversations to adjust lessons and identify areas where an individual learner needs more practice.
The company says its database now includes more than 200 million learner interactions, which it uses to analyze engagement and refine the way the AI tutor responds.
Some users appear to be treating the AI less like a conventional language course and more like a conversation partner.
One German user spent roughly 40% of his conversations discussing politics, according to data released by Loora. An Indian user discussed 38 subjects over 49 conversations, ranging from water sports to philosophy.
Another user logged practice sessions on 1,377 consecutive days.
English proficiency as a path to economic opportunity
Mor said the company sees English proficiency primarily as an economic and professional issue.
“People who already know English tend to underestimate the scale of the opportunities it creates,” he said. “For most of the world, English is the most significant gateway to advancement, a better job, a place at university or an entirely different future.”
Loora says its service costs about $10 a month in some markets, compared with substantially higher rates for one-on-one instruction.
Roxanne Horesh, a partner at Union Tech Ventures, said the investment firm was attracted to Loora’s combination of AI personalization and repeat usage.
“What stood out to us was the combination of mission and execution,” Horesh said.
She said the challenge extended beyond creating an AI capable of holding a conversation to developing a system that could track individual learners, measure their progress, and adjust instruction over time.
