Proposal for monitoring babies with SGA unveiled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:03 UTC
01:38:03 KST

Health officials and doctors yesterday unveiled proposed measures for the long-term monitoring of infants who are “small for gestatational age” (SGA), ahead of Sunday’s Growth Awareness Day.
The Health Promotion Administration (HPA) and Taiwan Society of Neonatology members made the remarks at a seminar in Taipei, saying that small body size in infancy is linked to a failure to thrive, obesity and other disorders later in life.
HPA Director-General Shen Ching-fen (沈靜芬) said the government is considering including SGA in the “infant healthbook” to ensure primary care pediatrians are fully informed about the health risks faced by babies.
Photo: CNA
The mechanism allow hospitals and clinics caring for a child to be aware of childhood problems such as SGA, which is crucial for their future health, she said.
Many parents are not aware that infants with SGA must undergo regular check-ups past the age of two, Shen said.
Infants with SGA often make up for their small size in growth spurts, if given good nutrition and care, but the health book could help track those who remain smaller, lighter or shorter than their peers, she said.
Monitoring the growth of such children is essential to making sure that they receive the care they need, in addition to tracking their vaccination status, Shen said.
The measure is in response to calls from the medical community to include SGA in health records, she said.
The HPA is inclined to agree with these suggestions, as many of the metrics used to evaluate SGA infants are the same as those already being recorded in the agency’s primary care pediatrician system, Shen said.
Association chairman president Yang San-nan (楊生湳) said SGA infants often undergo growth spurts at age two or older, but develop low bone density, insulin insensitivity and other conditions in adulthood.
People born as SGA babies must be tracked for disorders linked to these conditions to faciliate preventive care or early treatment, he said.

Photo courtesy of the Chiayi County Agriculture Department via CNA
Taiwan’s largest concentration of “crocodile,” spectacled caiman, farms is in Yijhu Township (義竹), Chang said.
Chang described crocodile meat as mild in flavor with a firm texture “similar to chicken.”
Restaurants have devised several ways to prepare crocodile, including grilling, deep-frying, boiling, baking and stewing with traditional Chinese medicine ingredients, he said.
The department recommended skinless crocodile leg for grilling, as the dish would stand out in a Mid-Autumn Festival barbecue for its fresh taste and as “a topic of conversation.”
In contrast, skin-on crocodile leg is best used in soups or dishes like “three cup crocodile,” where its taste and texture are similar to giant grouper, it said.
Chang also touted the high quality of Chiayi’s seafood, saying that the oysters and clams are remarkably juicy and release their natural savory flavors with just a brief turn on the grill.
Chiayi’s charcoal-roasted white shrimp offer sweet and tender meat, requiring nothing more than a light sprinkle of salt or pepper to shine, he added.
Taiwanese tilapia features a delicate texture suited for various preparation methods, whether as fillets, chunks, or whole roasted fish, he said, adding that with a squeeze of lemon and a dash of pepper salt, it makes for a nutritious, tasty grilled dish.
People can browse and purchase more than 220 Chiayi aquaculture products by visiting the county’s “Chiayum” Web site (https://www.chiayumfresh.com.tw/), the department said.
Taiwan is to celebrate Mid-Autumn Festival on Friday next week.

UN chief Guterres calls for countries fueling Sudan's war to be held accountable
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 16 - United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called on Wednesday for countries providing weapons to the warring parties in Sudan that are used to attack civilians to be held accountable.
"What is happening in Sudan is absolutely horrible. The humanitarian situation in Sudan is devastating. The level of suffering of the Sudanese people is intolerable," Guterres told reporters ahead of the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations in New York next week.
Sudan's war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
"It is true that the conflict is fueled by a number of countries from the outside," Guterres said. "In my opinion, there should be accountability for the kind of interference in which some countries provide weapons to parties to a conflict when those weapons are used massively to attack civilians."
A U.N. fact-finding mission said earlier this month that foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks are helping sustain Sudan's conflict and expanding the warring parties' ability to strike distant civilian areas with drones. REUTERS

SK Hynix mulling making chips in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:37:58 UTC
01:37:58 KST

South Korea’s SK Hynix Inc is in talks with Intel Corp about a deal that would see it manufacture memory chips on US soil for the first time, three people familiar with the discussions said.
Under one potential scenario, SK Hynix would lease part of Intel’s long-planned chipmaking facility in Ohio, they said. Under another scenario, it could form a venture with Intel and major cloud firms that are keen to lock in memory supplies, two of the people said.
A deal would relieve pressure on Intel, which has been struggling, and mark a big win for US President Donald Trump’s administration, which has been ramping up pressure on chipmakers to build in the US as relentless investment in artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers fuels an acute shortage of memory chips.
Photo: AFP
However, potential opposition from Seoul could be a major hurdle, the sources said.
One of the sources described the talks as exploratory and stressed that no decisions have been made, adding that SK Hynix might consider other ways to structure the deal.
SK Hynix’s product lineup includes DRAM chips used in servers, PCs and smartphones and NAND flash memory chips that provide long-term storage memory. It is also the leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI processing units.
Any agreement to produce advanced memory such as HBM or even DRAM could run into opposition from the South Korean government as those technologies are considered sensitive, said the three sources who declined to be identified as the information is not public.
SK Hynix said in a statement that it is “reviewing various measures, including establishing additional production bases, to strengthen the competitiveness of its memory business,” but “no matters have been determined at this stage.”
Intel declined to comment on what it called speculation, but added that it was continuing with investments in Ohio to ready the site.
Asked about a potential SK Hynix plan to produce chips in the US, South Korean Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said any decision would be at the company’s discretion, but if it involved a “national core technology,” it would be subject to a review under the Industrial Technology Protection Act.
The US Department of Commerce did not respond to a request for comment.
Manufacturing semiconductors in the US costs much more than in South Korea, the sources said.
Building in the US entails significantly higher labor and construction costs, and much of the semiconductor industry’s supply chain is located within Asia, which also increases US costs, one of them said.
Even so, SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won said in July that the company faces enormous pressure and lobbying from customers and countries to supply more chips.
“I think we need to build a factory in the United States. If possible, I believe we should build it,” he told reporters.

====================================================================================================

Book review: Confessions of an ex-Trumper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:37:52 UTC
01:37:52 KST

The most interesting chapter in Anthony Scaramucci’s All the Wrong Moves is the one where the hedge funder turned podcaster goes to work for Donald Trump. It’s summer 2017, and he’s been given the job of comms director, which he doesn’t know how to do, but he and Trump think it’ll work out because they’re both from New York. Or maybe he took it because he had “Potomac fever,” which afflicts Wall Street financiers who find themselves on the riverfront in Washington DC thinking they know how to run a country just because they’re “full of power and judgmental insight … about to fix everything.”
This appointment lasts only 11 days, not even enough time to be truly tainted by Trump’s first term, though it is enough time for Scaramucci to miss the birth of his son. The account is a mea culpa soup, with the author full of regrets for his hubris, his impulsivity, his “pride, egotism and asinine stupidity,” the fact that, despite the clear-sightedness bestowed by his humble beginnings, he’d come to assume the collective biases of the rich people he hung out with.
But what he doesn’t address is the fact that it was quite plain by then who Donald Trump was. Scaramucci himself identifies the beginning of Trump’s explicit use of racism and the politics of hatred, not in his first taboo-breaking statement that Mexicans were bringing drugs and rapists into the US (2015), but with the Obama birther conspiracy, which had been going on for years. Irrespective of all his pondering as to whether Trump was symptom or cause of a broken US, Scaramucci knew when he joined the White House that he was reporting to a racist, a chancer, an egomaniac and a liar. Bluntly, a person with decent values would not have joined this administration.
That doesn’t invalidate his analysis, but it does flatten it. The US is all about money, he tells us; the founding fathers were actually the investing fathers; anything not obviously a decision motivated by money is the unintended consequence of one. The very United States was “unified — by money,” because that was all Alexander Hamilton was thinking when he created a central bank. The fact that half the English-speaking world could sing the thousand other things Hamilton was thinking in a close harmony hasn’t occurred to the author, who can’t have seen the musical. It makes his potted history of the US a little brutish, and his organizing principle — that the rot started to set in from Clinton onwards, when leaders lost their “moral purpose” — contradictory. If there was never any value higher than money, how can Clinton’s purpose have been any less moral than Franklin D Roosevelt’s?
All of that is just backdrop to the book’s fatal flaw. Scaramucci details the three “catastrophic” errors that have created the US’s current doldrums, and this is all wisdom he came about the hard way, through wrong moves of his own, in the board room, in the situation room, in Trump’s inner circle. These were: privileging China during the globalization era; waging war with no corresponding tax hikes, post 9/11; and bailing out the banks.
It’s hard to disagree with any of it. If the world’s manufacturing all moves to a place where wages are lower, you correspondingly destroy the employment prospects of your own workforce. But these are arguments that were diligently made at the time; by political insurgents from the right, during the 1992 election; by protest movements on the left, in the so-called Battle of Seattle of 1999, and in anti-globalization demonstrations around the world subsequently.
Scaramucci writes that he should have taken this more seriously, they were right, he was wrong, but never reflects on how it came to be. It turns out that without institutional muscle — peculiar for Scaramucci to tell the entire history of his nation’s economy with only the most fleeting mention of Ronald Reagan’s union-busting — mere logic and reason aren’t enough, until it’s too late. He similarly tells the story of the war in Iraq as a cashflow snafu without considering whether anti-imperialists and pacifists might have a point, sometimes, and the story of the 2008 bailouts with only the swiftest nod towards the Occupy movement which, again, was broadly correct in its analysis.
It’s consequently a book of constant catch-up, a man who thought he knew it all, slowly surrendering to more sophisticated analyses when it is too late now anyway: China no longer looks to the US for its place in global markets; American wars are no longer waged with long-term strategic aims if patchy funding streams, but impulsively; and Wall Street no longer calls the shots, techbros do. He nods towards that last reality with a suggestion at the end to break up Silicon Valley monopolies, but never thinks seriously about how far from Kansas the world has actually strayed.
It’s nevertheless quite engaging, and no more or less infuriating than it would be if, say, Alastair Campbell (Scaramucci’s UK opposite number — both coming out with hard-boiled political realism on their Rest Is Politics pods) penned an excoriating critique of the war in Iraq. But it’s hard to choke down an argument whose kernel is “sorry, guys, I just wasn’t listening” from someone still stuck on broadcast.
For a time, it became popular to describe the tactics of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) in encroaching on sovereignty and militarizing islands in the South China Sea as “salami slicing.” Those slices have been getting chunkier. The People’s Liberation Army has been increasing its navy and air force activities in the region. The Chinese Coast Guard has likewise been ramping up their activities, and the civilian paramilitary People’s Armed Forces Maritime Militia has been backing up the navy and coast guard with alarming swarming maneuvers. The PRC claims most of the South China Sea through its U-shaped 10-dash
For most train journeys, where you are going is the main consideration. On the Shanlan train (山嵐號) in eastern Taiwan, however, it’s not the “where” but the “how” that matters. On this pricey but meticulously crafted train journey running between Hualien and Taitung County’s Chihshang (池上), what you’re paying for isn’t to get from Point A to Point B, but rather a sensory, aesthetic and cultural experience. On the platform, the train stands out vividly next to the other Taiwan Railway carriages. Its exterior is painted in a yellow-green gradient intended to blend harmoniously with the ripening rice paddies of the East

Building around US unreliability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:37:49 UTC
01:37:49 KST

The flurry of new defense agreements signed by Japan suggests Tokyo is attempting to reshape its own security posture. This shift would come in response to China’s geopolitical advances, compounded by the growing unreliability of the US and the associated risks of strategic disengagement.
New security alignments among US allies and partners, which affect various strategic arenas, are increasingly viewed as a reaction to the purported decline of US global leadership during US President Donald Trump’s administration.
The “Mecca Joint Defense Agreement,” signed last month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, is seen in a similar light: as an effort by key US allies in the greater Middle East to establish self defense mechanisms against Iran (and Israel) outside the traditional US security umbrella.
However, it remains unlikely that Japan is truly hedging against a future post-US world order dominated by China, even if Tokyo is undoubtedly developing and expanding a complex, multilayered network with allied and like-minded countries.
Japan has deployed fighter aircraft to India for the first time to participate in joint exercises running until Monday next week.
The deployment follows a visit to New Delhi last month by Japanese Minister of Defense Shinjiro Koizumi, who agreed with Indian Minister of Defence Rajnath Singh to deepen cooperation through joint drills amid growing security concerns in the Indo-Pacific region.
Similarly, beginning on Tuesday, Japan’s Air Self-Defense Forces is hosting a joint exercise with French forces on Japanese territory. In April, the two countries signed a defense roadmap providing for more joint military training and maneuvers to support regional stability.
In the past few months, Tokyo reinforced bilateral security cooperation with Australia, the Philippines, New Zealand, South Korea and Canada.
All countries that have enhanced military ties with Japan have conducted maritime transits through the Taiwan Strait or the South China Sea — where the Philippines is locked in territorial disputes with China — transits that consistently draw indignant reactions from Beijing. These nations are reinforcing military cooperation among themselves, rather than just with Tokyo.
Riho Aizawa, a Japanese Ministry of Defense researcher, does not view Tokyo’s efforts to boost regional defense ties with partners as a hedge against dwindling US engagement. She does not see these initiatives as a response to the Trump administration’s demands for increased military spending.
Rather, in her personal capacity, she told me that “Japan’s growing defense cooperation with these like-minded countries is better understood as part of a longstanding effort to respond to an increasingly severe security environment by maintaining the alliance with America as the cornerstone of its security policy.”
Indeed, Japan’s forces, even in combination with those of its regional partners, might not have the weight to stand against major threats from China without US support.
For instance, Starlink’s use would be vital for Tokyo. Much like its role in supporting Ukraine against Russia’s invasion, the satellite Internet service could keep Japanese and allied forces connected even if ground infrastructure were destroyed by Chinese attacks.
No US Indo-Pacific ally has an operational, fully deployed domestic equivalent to Starlink, although Japan, South Korea and Taiwan are building sovereign low Earth orbit satellite networks for the future.
Europe finds itself in a remarkably similar position, despite its drive to increase defense autonomy from Washington. NATO’s European members would be unable to support Ukraine without US intelligence, satellite and geospatial support.
Japan should build a united front of Indo-Pacific middle powers rather than relying solely on bilateral or trilateral interactions. This should include Taiwan, even though all these actors usually refrain from open cooperation with it.
Even this appears daunting. Just as there are doubts regarding whether NATO’s Article Five on collective defense would trigger an immediate response from member countries — a scenario that many suspect Russian President Vladimir Putin is probing at — it is equally uncertain that solidarity would materialize between Japan and its partners in the event of a crisis with China.
It seems unlikely that India would rush to help Japan if it finds itself embroiled in a conflict with Beijing over Taiwan or the China seas.
At the same time, it is unlikely that Tokyo would swoop to the rescue of India during a possible border conflict between New Delhi and the Chinese.
In the same way, the Mecca deal is already showing its limitations: Despite voicing support, Turkey and Pakistan have so far abstained from direct military intervention against Yemen’s pro-Iran Houthi rebels following the group’s attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Meanwhile, Riyadh is set to receive a US$5.75 billion US arms package, including tank engines and Joint Direct Attack Munitions-Extended Range kits.
Any new security framework developed by Japan, or another US ally, can only complement, rather than replace, the alliance with Washington.
Emanuele Scimia is a journalist and analyst covering foreign affairs and defense issues.

Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) yesterday laid out proposed policies to encourage four forms of environmentally friendly commuting in Taipei: walking, taking buses, riding bicycles and using shared electric scooters.
The policies would prioritize commuter safety and convenience, and include proposals to add shared electric scooters to the TPass program and provide 30 minutes for free on the electric YouBike 2.0E during commuter hours, he said at a news conference at the DPP headquarters.
Shen said he would improve pedestrian safety by establishing school commuter zones around all of Taipei’s more than 150 elementary schools within eight years.
Photo: Gan Meng-lin, Taipei Times
Official data showed that the peak period for traffic deaths and injuries in Taipei in 2024 was between 7am and 9am, when students are traveling to school, he said.
The central government recommends defining an area within 150m of a school as a school commuting zone, but the guidelines are advisory and Taipei has only established four this year, he said.
Secondly, Shen said he would enact bus safety reforms, focused on subsidizing bus drivers’ salaries, redesigning driver seats, establishing driver rest stations at major turnaround points and reorganizing bus networks by district.
Thirdly, Shen said he would work to connect, maintain and supplement Taipei’s bicycle network to promote bicycle riding.
After YouBike resumed making the first 30 minutes of rides free, the number of rides increased by 55 percent, surpassing 400 million rides, he said.
Shen proposed providing more crossings over rivers and embankments, including a bicycle bridge across the Keelung River connecting Yingfeng Riverside Park (迎風河濱公園) and Gangqian (港墘) in Neihu District (?湖) to link the riverside cycle route to Neihu Technology Park.
Shen said he would also make the first 30 minutes of YouBike 2.0E electric-assist bicycle rides free during commuter hours and add more bikes at hotspots, while including electric scooters in the TPass program.

Taiwanese book longlisted for National Book Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:37:44 UTC
01:37:44 KST

The English-language translation of Taiwanese writer Ping Lu’s (平路) To the East of the East (東方之東) has been longlisted for the US’ National Book Award for Translated Literature, marking the second such recognition for a Taiwanese writer after Yang Shuang-zi (楊?子).
Translated by Jeremy Tiang (程異), the novel follows a Taiwanese writer’s trip to Beijing in search of her missing husband and her encounters there, the National Book Foundation said.
The nonprofit announced the longlist on Tuesday.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Culture
To the East of the East was one of 10 titles — originally published in Arabic, Chinese, French, Indonesian, Norwegian, Russian and Spanish — selected from 159 books, the foundation said.
Nine of the longlisted works are novels, while the other is nonfiction, the foundation added.
The foundation said it would announce the finalists on Oct. 6, while the winner would be revealed live at the 77th National Book Awards Ceremony on Nov. 18.
To the East of the East is the first book in the Ping Lu’s “Taiwan Trilogy.” Published in 2011, the novel was followed by Ilha Formosa (婆娑之島) and Passing (夢魂之地). The trilogy was republished in 2024.
In an interview with reporters, Ping Lu, whose real name is Lu Ping (路平), attributed the recognition to Tiang’s translation, saying that he writes well in English and that “my contribution may only be about 10 percent.”
When the book was published in 2011, she had recently returned to Taiwan after working in Hong Kong as director of the Kwang Hwa Information and Culture Center, Taiwan’s cultural office in Hong Kong, the author said.
The novel reflected her circumstances at the time, exploring how a person examines their inner emotions from an outside perspective.
“Sometimes if you go far enough, you can hear the call from within your heart,” she said.
The novel is also about the relationship between an island and the mainland, as well as the betrayal and separation that lead to the realization that one’s ideal life is often linked to the pursuit of freedom, Ping Lu said.
Ping Lu has won several Taiwanese national book awards, such as the National Award for the Arts. Her works have been translated into multiple languages, including English, French, Japanese, Korean and Czech, the foundation said.
Tiang, originally from Singapore, has also translated works by other Taiwanese writers including Su Wei-chen (蘇偉貞), Lo Yi-chin (駱以軍) and Chi Ta-wei (紀大偉).

Chinese Minister of National Defense Dong Jun (董軍) yesterday urged nations to avoid provocative acts and curb the resurgence of regressive historical trends in remarks likely to be taken as veiled criticism of Japan.
Warning that the world had arrived at a “fragile moment,” Dong called for a fresher, more equal approach to resolving international tension, but offered few specifics or direct criticism of rivals.
“We must bear in mind the lessons of history and remain highly vigilant against all latent manifestations of hegemony, militarism and historical revisionism,” he said in an opening speech at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum on security.
Photo: Reuters
“We must not turn a blind eye or condone such behavior. By rallying broad-based forces of justice, we must suppress the resurgence of historical dregs and prevent them from exploiting the situation to cause harm,” he said.
Ties between China and Japan soured last year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested that a hypothetical Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger a Japanese military response.
That spurred Beijing to repeatedly warn that Japan was seeking a return to its militarist past, which included the Japanese occupation of northeast China’s Manchuria in 1931 before a full war between the then-Republic of China and Japan.
About 2,000 military officers, diplomats and academics from 100 countries are attending the three-day event set to run until today, with delegates including some regional defense ministers, a senior Pentagon official, Russian academics and Taliban representatives.
As some analysts predicted, Dong steered clear of direct criticism of the US or its regional allies, such as Japan, and appeared to hew closely to long-held Chinese positions.
Dong urged efforts toward a peaceful, multipolar world marked by “partnership rather than alliance, win-win rather than zero-sum.”
“We must show no leniency toward provocative acts that seek to hijack the overall interests of countries in the region for the sake of personal gain or the interests of particular cliques,” he added.

Israeli state institutions are at risk of collapse due to surging settler terrorism, a leading Israeli think tank warned on Monday, as anti-Palestinian violence sweeps the occupied West Bank.
The Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) said the empowerment of ultranationalist Israeli forces is weakening the military, eroding law and order, and deepening the country's international isolation.
"Jewish terrorism has evolved from a local enforcement problem into a distinct strategic threat to the State of Israel and its democratic character," it wrote in a strategic alert.
"We warn of a threat to Israel’s very ability to govern and function. As history teaches us, democracies that fail to restrain radical forces within them do not survive."
This is only the second time the INSS has issued a strategic alert. The other time was in March 2023 when it issued a warning about the political crisis triggered by the far-right Netanyahu government's attack on the judiciary.
Since taking power at the end of 2022, Netanyahu's coalition has presided over a surge in anti-Palestinian violence, facilitated by extremist ministers from the Jewish Power and Religious Zionism parties.
The rate of violence has increased every year since 2023, reaching a record high this year, according to the UN.
Israel's security establishment recorded 660 incidents of settler violence in the first half of 2026, up 63% on the second half of 2025 and 50% higher than the same period a year earlier.
The intensifying pogroms have been accompanied by the destruction of dozens of Palestinian villages and the forced displacement of tens of thousands of civilians by settlers and the Israeli military.
Settlers are also becoming increasingly aggressive towards Israeli soldiers and law enforcement, with such incidents climbing more than a third in the first six months of 2026, INSS said.
The report said that the failure to prosecute violent settlers, political support for the perpetrators, and the weakening judicial system are "creating a reality marked by lawlessness, non-recognition of state institutions, and the loss of the state's monopoly on the use of force".
The lack of a response to the violence "constitutes evidence that it is a policy directed from above", it said.
Among the most influential ministers in the settler movement is the extremist national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who has incited violence against Palestinians, armed thousands of settlers, and lifted restraints on police officers and prison officials' use of violence.
The report also warned that settler violence is increasing Israel's international isolation and inviting intensifying sanctions.
The UK announced last week it would cut ties with Israeli settlements, with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accusing members of the government of facilitating ethnic cleansing and encouraging settler terrorism in the West Bank. It has been joined by other Western nations including France, Canada, the Netherlands, Ireland and Spain in banning settlement trade.
"Jewish terrorism, together with an unchecked settlement policy, has become one of the most effective instruments in the international campaign against Israel," INSS said.
"This campaign portrays Israel as an aggressive, oppressive and racist state that effectively advances ideas of ethnic cleansing of Palestinians."
INSS is one of Israel's most prominent think tanks and has close ties to the country's security establishment.
The alert echoes several letters signed by retired defence and security officials in recent months, which have urged the government to rein in settler terrorism in the West Bank.

It was Lee’s ninth home run of the season, as Detroit extended their winning streak to six games.
Lee, who was playing third base, hit the solo homer off a 128kph curve ball from Joe Mantiply in the ninth inning.
Photo: Dan Hamilton-Imagn Images
Lee broke Chang’s single-season record for hits by a Taiwanese player last month, and he now has 74 hits and 32 RBIs, with two stolen bases and a batting average of .258 in 287 at-bats this season.
Chang reached the nine-homer mark while playing for the then-Cleveland Indians in 2021. He now plays for the CPBL’s Fubon Guardians.
Spencer Torkelson on Tuesday hit a three-run homer and Drew Anderson pitched five shutout innings.
Photo: AP
The Blue Jays have lost six of nine. Toronto fell two games behind Cleveland in the race for the final American League wild card after the Guardians rallied in the ninth to beat the Chicago White Sox 7-6.
The Tigers are 4-1/2 games behind Cleveland, with three teams in between.

“There’s a lot of history here with me,” Alonso said after receiving a beer shower from his Baltimore teammates. “It doesn’t matter where and when, I just want to help the team win. I’m just really, really happy for us to come back the way we did.”
The Orioles were two outs from a defeat that would have dropped them four games behind Cleveland for the last American League playoff spot when Alonso hit a 126m solo drive off Kodai Senga to tie the score 3-all.
A fired-up Alonso, who hit a club-record 264 homers for the Mets before signing with the Orioles in December last year, spiked his bat toward the Baltimore dugout. He rounded the bases as the Queens crowd of 28,097 — down from 35,800 for the slugger’s return on Monday night — roared.
Fans chanted his name until Alonso emerged from the dugout for a curtain call. Then chants of “Fire Stearns” began, aimed at Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns.
“Everyone in the dugout was saying go out there,” Alonso said. “And they were right.”
The rare curtain call on the road continued an outpouring of support from Mets fans for Alonso over the past two nights — and apparently annoyed at least one of his former teammates.
“As the 2026 Mets, I know we have definitely underperformed, but we are — the guys in here work their [tails] off every single day and to have that kind of reaction to an opposing player — could be anybody — is crazy to me,” said New York pitcher Sean Manaea, who started Tuesday night. “Again, I’ve got nothing but respect for Pete, but yeah, just never seen anything like that before.”

Two nations, two gates, one golden key
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:37:05 UTC
01:37:05 KST

Two nations, two gates, one golden key
TEHRAN — For six months, Washington’s story stayed the same: Iran and its allies are isolated, the resistance is finished, and the oil routes are safe under American control. Trump and his officials claimed all this happened in days, not years.
Ignore the press conferences and look at the map instead. Yemen’s Ansarallah now control Mocha. They hold Dhubab, the last mainland town facing the island across the Bab el-Mandeb strait. They hold Perim, the rocky island that splits the strait into two narrow shipping lanes. The Hanish islands appear to have gone the same way. That would put the entire Yemeni Red Sea coast under one authority.
This is the same movement that was supposed to be wiped out after seven years of Saudi bombing, joint American and British strikes, and Israeli air raids and assassinations. Boats crossed the water. An island changed hands almost overnight.
Mocha is not just a trophy — it is a working port. Dhubab is the last real stretch of mainland facing the narrows. Perim sits in the middle of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait itself: eighteen miles of water squeezed into two tight lanes with a rock in the center. Hold all three and you do not just threaten the strait — you own the checkpoint.
Washington wanted a war short enough to fit a news cycle. Tehran took the first punch, kept its underground capabilities intact, and let the real cost fall later on the Persian Gulf capitals that bankroll the project. What is happening on the Yemeni coast is not a coincidence. It is the second half of the same plan.
A short war favors air power and press briefings. A long war favors whoever is still standing once the cameras leave. Iran and Yemen are still standing.
Since fighting with Iran began in February, Washington and Tel Aviv have tried to weaken Iran from the air and sea. Iran’s response stayed simple: no tanker leaves the Persian Gulf without its permission. The Strait of Hormuz stopped being an open shipping lane and became a checkpoint. That pushed Riyadh, Kuwait, and Abu Dhabi onto their backup route — overland to Yanbu, then south through Bab el-Mandeb. That backup route now runs straight past Yemeni-held ground.
Ansarallah closed the loop. Mocha, Dhubab, Perim — three positions, one chokepoint. The backup plan is gone too.
The Persian Gulf has only one real exit. For decades, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi assumed Washington would keep that exit open forever. When that failed, the Red Sea corridor became the fallback. That fallback is now compromised as well.
Tanker lanes were already only a few miles wide. Now they run under the watch of a force that has spent a decade learning this exact stretch of water. The roughly four million barrels a day the Saudis used to reroute around Hormuz now has to cross contested waters. Add the rest of regional shipping and the figure easily reaches six million barrels a day. This is no longer a footnote — it is the headline. Oil is already above $100 a barrel.
 
 Insurance markets will price this risk in long before Washington issues a statement. Shipping companies do not answer to the Pentagon. They reroute, pay higher premiums, or stop sailing. A warship on a map does not set insurance rates. Whoever holds the shoreline and the island does.
American naval doctrine was never really about “freedom of navigation.” It was about keeping navigation under American supervision. When that model breaks at two of the world’s three key chokepoints at once, it is not bad luck. It is the postwar maritime order coming apart.
Malacca is a separate issue for another day. What matters now is that the old belief — that global chokepoints ultimately answer to Washington or its allies in Tel Aviv — has taken a serious hit at both ends of the Persian Gulf’s main export route.
Saudi jets are still flying. Air power is what you use when you cannot hold ground with soldiers. Ansarallah has lived under that air power for more than a decade and kept taking territory anyway. The highlands and the Tihama coast do not empty just because a coalition loses momentum. Bombing a place is not the same as occupying it, and only occupation decides who controls land. Yemen has proven that point more than once.
Part of the reason this offensive did not stall is simple: Ansarallah fighters are defending their own homes, not collecting a foreign paycheck. That gives a person a reason to hold a position after the next round of strikes that a hired fighter never has. On the other side are many people manning checkpoints for a salary, in someone else’s war, supporting a project that will drop them the moment the money runs out.
Officials in Washington will keep talking about naval escorts and “open” sea lanes. The shipping data says otherwise. Hormuz traffic has already dropped sharply and now moves largely on Iran’s terms. Bab el-Mandeb is heading the same way. You can call a strait open all you like — underwriters will not treat it that way if the people who actually hold the coastline say differently.
Ansarallah’s position has been consistent: safe passage for everyone except vessels tied to Saudi Arabia; blockade for blockade; escalation matched with escalation — until the war on Yemen actually ends. That is a stated condition, not an idle threat.
The fallout does not stop at trading desks in London. Egypt depends on Suez Canal revenue. Jordan needs Aqaba running. Israel needs Eilat running. Arab states on the southern side of the Persian Gulf built their financial security on an American security umbrella. Now their only real sea route passes through territory they do not control. Kuwait has almost no alternative and is already boxed in. Cairo cannot create canal traffic out of nothing. Amman cannot move a port. Eilat will not turn into Haifa just because Tel Aviv needs it to.
This was never just a Yemen story. It is a Persian Gulf story that happens to be playing out on the Yemeni coast.
The harder question is what comes next. Persian Gulf capitals built their entire security posture on the idea that Washington’s presence made these waters permanently theirs to use. That idea now has two visible cracks — Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb — and cracks in shipping insurance do not heal because a general holds a press conference. Trump is reportedly saying the war will wrap up after the midterms; his own people are said to be telling him to plan for years, not months. Sooner or later the real conversation about keeping oil moving will stop being a conversation with Washington and start being one with Tehran and Sanaa, on terms nobody in Riyadh or Washington is used to negotiating.
Whether that ends in a settlement or a long standoff, no one knows yet. What is no longer in dispute is who holds the ground on both ends of the route right now. Six months of claims that Iran and its allies were “isolated,” “degraded,” or “finished” were what officials wanted people to believe. The coastline tells a different story. The oil still has to move, and for the first time in this war, the routes it depends on run through territories Washington does not control.
The message from Hormuz to Bab el-Mandeb is simple: the gates stay open only on the terms of whoever controls them. That is the shift. Everything else is commentary.
Iran holds Hormuz. Yemen holds Bab el-Mandeb. Two nations, two gates, one golden key. And for the first time in decades, Washington — and the project it shields in Tel Aviv — is standing outside the door.

Russian agents plotted assassinations in U.S. and Europe in first documented Russian intelligence attempt to kill on U.S. soil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:36:53 UTC
01:36:53 KST

The United States has charged two Russian nationals, two Cubans, and one Venezuelan with working for Russian intelligence to prepare assassination attempts in America and Europe, including the murder of Russian dissidents, the U.S. Department of Justice stated in a press release. As The Insider notes, this marks the first documented attempt by Russian intelligence to kill on U.S. soil. Besides the planned killings, for which operatives were offered up to $40,000, the agents recruited people to carry out sabotage in “all the countries that are helping Ukraine.”
The U.S. Department of Justice unsealed charges against five individuals whom investigators believe worked for Russian intelligence. They are Yuri Khrameev, 63, a former colonel in the Russian intelligence services; his son Kirill Khrameev, 27, an FSB officer; Cuban national Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35; Cuban Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, known as Viking; and Venezuelan national Angel Eduardo Castro, 22. Commenting on the case, Attorney General Todd Blanche said:
“It is our job to stop America’s adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil.”
According to Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg, the perpetrators attempted to “recruit U.S. citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin.” Over the summer, the network recruited a U.S. resident to surveil a well-known Russian dissident, identified in the published documents as “Victim-1.” Suarez promised the recruit between $1,000 and $1,500 to take photographs and video of locations associated with the potential victim. After the assignment was completed, the recruit was offered $40,000 to kill the dissident. When the U.S. resident declined to carry out the killing himself, he was asked to recommend “someone [who] can do the work.”
As The Insider found, Russian intelligence deliberately used Cubans and Venezuelans living in Russia to recruit a Venezuelan living in the United States. Angel Eduardo Castro, who had previously played baseball in Venezuela, served as the go-between.
In late July, Castro contacted a fellow countryman living in the U.S. and instructed him to surveil a Russian dissident in Washington. They communicated in code: the surveillance assignment referred to the need to “measure the plot of land and provide the measurements,” while the killing itself was called “construction.”
The same network, the U.S. Department of Justice notes, recruited a U.S. citizen in 2025 to surveil another Russian dissident — “Victim-2,” who lived in Lithuania. In that episode, the father and son Khrameev played the leading role. The younger Khrameev asked the recruit to take photographs at the potential victim’s address, and the elder Khrameev offered him $25,000 to carry out the murder. The Justice Department’s statement describes:
“Yuri Khrameev further told U.S. Citizen-1 that they wanted Victim-2 dead because he was ‘spreading dirt about my country’ and ‘distorting history.’ Yuri Khrameev then sent U.S. Citizen-1 a photograph of Victim-2 and described that he could be murdered by ‘throwing a bottle of gasoline’ or ‘sticking a knife’ in him. After U.S. Citizen-1 declined to carry out the murder, Yuri Khrameev offered to give him a ‘simpler job’ which could include ‘set[ting] fire to a warehouse of property or food’ or ‘throw[ing] a bottle of gasoline at an electrical substation.’ Yuri Khrameev made clear to U.S. Citizen-1 that the purpose was to target ‘all the countries that are helping Ukraine’ and that he was offering ‘serious money for serious work.’ Finally, Yuri Khrameev confirmed that he was a ‘colonel of Russian intelligence agencies.’”
The Justice Department notes that the network likely recruited other individuals to carry out acts of sabotage in Europe. According to the department, Cuban national Durruthy coordinated an attack in Czechia in June 2024 and another in Lithuania in September 2024.
All five individuals have been charged with participating in a conspiracy to finance terrorism. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro are also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire. The first charge carries a maximum penalty of up to 20 years in prison, the second up to 10 years. All of them remain at large.

Angry Dutch farmers blamed for railway sabotage: What happened?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:35:28 UTC
01:35:28 KST

Angry Dutch farmers blamed for railway sabotage: What happened?
Farmers in the Netherlands have taken action in the past, protesting against the government’s nitrogen policy.
Railways in the Netherlands suffered massive disruption on Tuesday when pipes, cables and other materials were placed on dozens of tracks, halting trains and upending the commutes of hundreds of thousands of passengers.
While no one has been blamed for the suspected sabotage, the incident coincides with mass protests by farmers angered by government environmental policies, and took place amid reports in local media that farmers had discussed taking direct action against the railways.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Four railway workers killed by express train at station in Japan
- list 2 of 3Train crashes into truck at railway crossing in Gdansk, Poland
- list 3 of 3Trains get hack warning
The Tuesday, September 15 incident is being investigated by police.
So what happened, why are farmers under suspicion, and why would anyone target a railway?
What happened on the Dutch railways?
Trains in the Netherlands came to a standstill on Tuesday morning, causing delays and cancellations for passengers across central and northern parts of the country.
It emerged that items on the tracks had caused trains to be halted.
“Materials were found in several places along tracks that were deliberately placed there. This is causing section failures. It seems to be sabotage,” ProRail, the country’s rail infrastructure operator, said in a statement.
ProRail’s interim CEO Mirjam van Velthuizen said the incident demonstrated how dependent the Netherlands is on its railways and called for greater investment in contingency planning.
“In a world where uncertainties are increasing, we must ensure that the railway can absorb disruptions, that the impact remains limited as much as possible, and that we can recover as quickly as possible,” she said.
ProRail said there were no injuries reported.
“Placing materials on the tracks is extremely dangerous and unacceptable, and fortunately, it did not lead to any accidents today,” it said.
Sabotage is suspected by the Dutch police, which is investigating.
What sort of sabotage is suspected?
Pipes and cables had been fixed to railway tracks, causing at least 35 signal failures across the country’s network of trains, ProRail said.
“It appeared that pipes and cables had been laid on the tracks, causing our system to believe that a train was standing on the tracks,” the operator said. That caused the automatic system to change signals to red, preventing trains from passing.
“Unauthorised” materials were found in at least 20 locations in the rail network, the operator said.
The sabotage had been going on since Monday, according to some reports. In one case early on Monday, a train “struck metal” on the track near Steenwijk, in the country’s east, according to media reports.
ProRail said there was no damage because the train was not travelling at full speed.
Why are farmers under suspicion?
While the perpetrators have not been found, Dutch media has reported speculation that angry farmers are behind the sabotage.
ProRail sources told broadcaster NOS that they had spotted farmer groups discussing taking direct action, including by fixing metal pipes to train lines, on social media groups.
Farmers in the Netherlands have taken similar action in the past, in protest against the government’s nitrogen policy.
The Farmers Defence Force (FDF), a protest and advocacy group, said it was not behind the railway sabotage, but did not rule out individual farmers being responsible.
The activist group did, however, say members set hay bales and car tyres alight along various roads across the Netherlands on Tuesday afternoon, on the government’s budget day of Prinsjesdag, in protest.
What are farmers protesting about in the Netherlands?
FDF opposes planned government policies requiring farmers to reduce nitrogen emissions, arguing that they are being unfairly blamed for nitrogen pollution.
According to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), agriculture accounts for 60-80 percent of human-driven nitrogen emissions. “While nitrogen is a natural and necessary nutrient for growing food, modern industrial farming practices introduce far more nitrogen into the ecosystem than the earth and crops can naturally absorb,” the EPA states.
But farmers in the Netherlands say reducing these emissions will substantially increase the cost of livestock farming and force some agricultural businesses to reduce production or close down.
“We feel like the country is on fire. Farmers feel as though their businesses are on fire because of the government’s plans”, FDF spokesperson Sieta van Keimpema told Reuters.
The government has promised financial compensation for farmers whose businesses are hit by the proposals.
Why would saboteurs target railways?
According to the Mineta Transportation Institute (MTI) in San Jose, California in the US, railways have been targeted by groups ranging from al-Qaeda to India’s Maoist guerrilla fighters to extreme environmental groups in Europe.
“Derailments are intended to cause casualties, while attacks on tracks and other right-of-way infrastructure are primarily intended to cause disruption and attract attention,” a 2018 report by the institute explains.
Because of the expansive nature of a railway network, it is impossible to completely defend it from sabotage, making it an easy target for those seeking to cause disruption.
MTI’s database shows that between 1970 and the end of 2017, there were a total 282 attempts to deliberately derail trains and 817 additional attacks on railway infrastructure, including tracks, bridges, tunnels, signalling and other right-of-way equipment.
Western Europe has suffered the second-highest number of derailment attempts globally, at 10.6 percent, after South Asia, where the majority of railway attacks take place.
“The European groups have sought to attract public attention to their issues that motivate them and cause disruption. Their actions resulted in inconvenience, but no casualties,” said MTI in its report.
Where else has railway sabotage happened in Western Europe in recent years?
French media reported a derailment in Normandy on Friday that is also suspected to be an act of sabotage. A section of rail found on the track may have caused the crash, according to prosecutors, the BBC reported.
In July, the “Angry Birds Commando” group, a radical environmentalist group, said it had placed incendiary devices on the railway line between Cologne and Dusseldorf, in protest against industrial technology causing the destruction of the environment, Deutsche Welle reported.

Mostly sunny weather is expected in the mountains as well, with light to moderate easterly winds. Temperatures will reach around 19°C at 1,200 metres and 12°C at 2,000 metres.
Friday will bring more sunshine, though cloud will increase for a time around and after midday. It will be slightly warmer too, with daytime temperatures rising by another 1-2°C.
Across the Balkans, sunshine will dominate, with some temporary cloud developing in the afternoon but no rain expected.

Russia's military recruitment drive in Africa — Time to reassess relationship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:35:10 UTC
01:35:10 KST

Russia's military recruitment drive in Africa — Time to reassess relationship
Families of Kenyans allegedly recruited illegally to fight for Russia in its war against Ukraine hold photos of their missing relatives during a protest demanding answers and their return, in Nairobi, Kenya, on March 5, 2026. (Gerald Anderson / Anadolu via Getty Images)
Ieva Miyares
Independent consultant on illicit finance, anti-corruption, and governance
In February 2026, a group of women stood outside Kenya's parliament in Nairobi holding photographs of their sons and brothers.
One, Winnie Rose Wambui, was looking for her brother, Samuel Maina, who had left for Russia believing he had a job as a mall security guard; the last she heard was a distress voice note recorded from a forest.
Winnie's story is part of a bigger effort of illegal military recruitment conducted by Russia.
At least 3,000 Africans from 37 countries have been recorded fighting, or having fought, for Russia against Ukraine, according to Ukraine's Foreign Ministry. Russia, long tied to many African nations, has drawn their citizens into a war. It is also using African resources and financial channels to work around Western sanctions.
However, Russia's ties to Africa show that they are no longer aligned across the continent but are shifting towards a series of transactional arrangements — ranging from deep state capture in fragile, junta-led states (CAR, Sudan, and Mali) or to more cautious, interest-based cooperation in countries with stronger institutions.
Either way, it leaves African states absorbing the costs: exposure to secondary sanctions, complicated ties with Western partners, and citizens recruited into Russia's war, often without informed consent. The patterns show that the benefit seems to run one way.
That shift raises the question: how will, and should, African countries respond to Russia's changing role in the continent? And just as importantly, what should European countries do with the gap this leaves behind?
The recruitment scandal
By now, there have been numerous reports documenting the scheme. A young man looking for work is offered a job in Russia, with the recruiter promising a $3,500 a month, plus bonuses of as much as $13,000. The job usually offers driving, security, or technical work, so he takes the offer and travels to Russia.
Upon arrival, the Russian side confiscates his passport and hands him a military contract written in Russian. There is no lawyer or translator to explain what he is signing. Before long, the new recruit is pressured into signing the contract and sent into the trenches.
And even among those who know exactly what they are signing up for — some of whom willingly go in for the money — many never receive the pay they were offered in the first place.
The human cost of this recruitment has been severe: a fatality rate of 22%, with training as short as 1 to 1.5 weeks.
Russia denies illegally recruiting anyone, insisting enlistment is voluntary and lawful.
Yet it has been proven that Moscow recruits Africans through state-linked companies, intermediaries, military structures, and embassy officials. News reports indicate that even the Russian Orthodox church, which has expanded into at least 34 African countries in the last three years, has also encouraged citizens to travel there.
Even the top political elites are involved, former South African President Jacob Zuma's daughter has allegedly recruited men into fighting without their consent.
Russia’s presence in Africa — sanctions, gold, and guns
Russia's presence in Africa is largely a Soviet legacy: it armed liberation movements from Angola to Zimbabwe and positioned itself as an "anti-colonial ally against Western powers."
Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Russia has leaned on the African continent to keep its sanctioned economy afloat. The U.S. has identified African gold as a key tool for sanctions evasion, and Russia's "ghost fleet" tankers supply African ports to avoid Western price caps.
More than 40 African countries maintain some military cooperation with Moscow, but only the CAR, Mali, and Libya host large deployments.
There, Russian-linked networks (first Wagner, now Africa Corps) control mining operations whose gold moves through the UAE before re-entering global markets.
Beyond the military cooperation, Russian influence is spreading economically and through trade: Egypt and Algeria buy military equipment from Russia, whilst others, like Benin and South Africa, depend on Russian fertilizers.
Kremlin-backed A7 crypto-network is expanding, moving beyond sanctions evasion into direct integration with Kremlin military and strategic operations in Africa.
What Africa gets — and gives up
For Russia, Africa has become both a source of deniable manpower and a workaround for sanctions while framing itself as an anti-colonial ally against a "hypocritical West" — a narrative that many African governments have found convenient to embrace.
But this entanglement carries its own cost: researchers find Russian-backed forces have not improved stability in Mali, the CAR, or Libya, and the economic upside is concentrated among a political elite.
Hundreds of African-flagged ships have been sanctioned for participating in oil shipments that benefit Russia. South Africa's central bank has also warned that secondary sanctions on local banks facilitating Russian evasion would be "severe" for the economy.
African countries' response
African countries' response has been varied — in some cases, very cautious. Facing public anger, the Kenyan government forced Russia to agree to stop recruiting Kenyans. Kenya has since shut over 600 recruitment agencies.
Similarly, South Africa announced that two of its nationals had died fighting for Moscow. The Foreign Minister visited the families of returned citizens.
Nigeria's Foreign Ministry likewise warned its citizens against fighting in foreign conflicts, however, not naming Russia directly. But said several Nigerians "were deployed to combat zones after being misled and coerced into signing military service contracts."
With Russia's global power and wealth weakening after four years of war, African countries should ask a question: What is Russia actually giving them in return for their manpower, sanctions circumvention, and complicity in the war in Ukraine?
As sanctions scrutiny increases, the cost of that complicity will only rise, hopefully pushing African governments toward greater alignment with sanctions rather than their evasion.
Use of momentum
Ukraine, for its part, is trying to close a diplomatic gap.
Since 2022, it has opened new missions, pushing its total toward 18–20 missions, though many remain understaffed.
Europe should follow Ukraine's lead and use this opening in three ways: press African governments harder to stop facilitating Russia's gold, oil, and arms deals; build the partnerships Europe has long neglected — more embassies, trade, and scholarships — as well as offer credible security cooperation.
Without an alternative, many African countries will keep turning back to Russia, or to whoever else fills the gap.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

Bulgaria ties three exemptions from Russia sanctions to national interest
Wednesday 16 September 2026 19:21

PHOTO BGNES
Font size
“Bulgaria has, for the first time, openly raised objections within the EU to the 21st package of sanctions against Russia and requested that three individuals, Patriarch Kirill, Vagit Alekperov, one of the co-owners of Lukoil, and Iskander Makhmudov, who is linked to a company supplying spare parts for Sofia’s metro trains, be removed from the sanctions list.” Bulgaria''s Prime Minister Rumen Radev said this in a statement to the media at the Council of Ministers, alongside Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš during his visit to Sofia, BTA reported. According to Radev, the requests were granted. “It has become clear that there is nothing alarming about a member state, whoever it may be, standing up for its national interest,” he commented.
Sofia objected to sanctions against Russian Patriarch Kirill because Bulgaria believes that religion should not become an additional element in the escalation of the war in Ukraine, Radev explained. Regarding Vagit Alekperov, the government cited the risk to Lukoil’s companies in Bulgaria, while in the case of Iskander Makhmudov, it pointed to supplies of spare parts for the Sofia metro, which the government considers a matter of transport security.
“We have always been part of common European decisions, but we regard these three individuals as a matter of national interest and, if our request had not been granted, we would not have supported these sanctions,” PM Radev said.

The party shared footage of Eisenkot's meeting with the Bedouin leaders

“Any other publication on the matter is a complete lie,” it added.
Forming coalition could be challenging without Arab parties, polls show
The report came as recent polls show that both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition bloc seeking to replace him lack the ability to secure a majority, suggesting that forming a coalition without the support of the Arab parties could prove challenging.
In 2021, Ra’am joined the coalition with the Naftali Bennett-Yair Lapid government, marking the first time an Arab party was a formal member of a governing coalition. The move to include Ra’am was highly criticized.

Eisenkot’s Yashar party has been leading in recent polling with around 23 seats, surpassing Netanyahu’s ruling Likud party.
While the Likud has repeatedly said that Eisenkot is attempting to form a government with the Arab parties, and cannot do so without their support, the Yashar head has denied the accusations.
On Sunday, the Likud announced that it would file requests to the Central Elections Committee to ban both the Arab-led parties – Ra’am and the Joint List – from running in the October 27 election.
The CEC can vote to approve the petitions next week, but similar disqualification decisions concerning the Arab parties have been overturned by the High Court in the past.

Britain Plans Uncrewed Hector ‘Teammate’ for Ajax Infantry Fighting Vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:34:00 UTC
01:34:00 KST

Britain is considering developing uncrewed ground vehicles for its Ajax infantry fighting vehicles that could be controlled from the armored vehicle or remotely.
ARX Robotics UK told Militarnyi that it would study the possibility of such a project jointly with General Dynamics Land Systems UK, which manufactures the infantry fighting vehicles.
The Hector ground drone is being considered as an uncrewed “teammate” for the Ajax.
The companies are analyzing the use of autonomous systems alongside combat vehicles to extend their range, improve situational awareness and reduce risks to personnel.
The Ajax is designed as one of the most digitized ground platforms in the British military.
The Ajax has data collection, information processing and command-and-control capabilities that can be used to coordinate autonomous systems at the tactical level.
By integrating the Hector UGV with the Ajax through the Generic Vehicle Architecture (GVA), crews will be able to assign tasks, control and deploy autonomous systems for reconnaissance, surveillance, protection and combat.
Hector, developed by ARX Robotics, is a wheeled UGV designed for a range of missions.
It is powered by an electric motor and can reach speeds of up to 70 km/h.
Hector can be controlled by a crew to the edge of a mission area, after which it can be operated remotely or under supervised autonomy.
The vehicle is equipped with thermal imaging cameras and modular mounting points.
It can carry a payload of up to 500 kg and tow up to 1,500 kg.
Hector uses Mithra OS, an AI-based operating system running on an onboard computing module.
Mithra OS is designed for adaptive navigation, remote control, and the performance of complex tasks in hazardous areas.
The operating system connects vehicles and robotic platforms into a single network, enabling coordinated operations and real-time data exchange as well as collaborative behavior between platforms.
Last year, Britain disclosed problems identified with Ajax infantry fighting vehicles that affected units operating them.

More than 40% of West Bank Palestinians believe Israel doesn’t have a right to exist, poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:33:38 UTC
01:33:38 KST

More Palestinians in the West Bank believe Israel does not have a right to exist (46%) than those who believe it does (41%), according to a new poll published by the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) on Tuesday.
The survey, which interviewed 400 Palestinians by phone between June 27 and July 2, with a margin of error of 4.9%, also found that 42% believed it was possible to bring about the end of Israel’s existence, while only 32% said it was impossible.
More than a quarter (27%) said they favored a two-state solution to resolve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, while 22% said they supported a single bi-national state with full equal rights, and 26% expressed a preference for a single Palestinian state without a Jewish presence. Only 17% said they would like to see a Palestinian state that permitted Jews as residents or citizens.
Despite a significant portion of Palestinians not recognizing Israel’s right to exist, over half (52%) said they would prefer negotiations as a way to end the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, while only 12% said they preferred armed resistance.
Additionally, 57% were of the opinion that violence had failed and that international diplomatic efforts were more fruitful.
Over half of respondents say diplomatic efforts more fruitful than violence
Given that more than half (57%) of the Palestinians polled said they believed violence had failed and that international diplomatic efforts were more fruitful, it follows that 40% of those polled said Hamas should disarm, and the majority preferred that Hamas not govern the Gaza Strip.
The most popular choice for the administration of the Strip is the current US-backed National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), which was selected by 32% of respondents. An additional 21% favored the Palestinian Authority (PA), while 21% favored a Fatah-Hamas unity government; only 5% chose Hamas as the preferred sole authority.
Marwan Barghouti preferred replacement of Mahmoud Abbas
When asked who they thought should replace PA President Mahmoud Abbas, imprisoned Fatah leader Marwan Barghouti was preferred by 34% of those polled, followed by Abbas’s deputy, Hussein al-Sheikh, who received support from just 8% of the respondents.
Unemployment was the greatest concern among 97% of those polled, while 96% also identified settler violence as a major issue. Fourteen percent reported being direct victims of settler attacks, 22% said they had heard first-hand testimony from someone they knew who had experienced harm, and 33% said they were exposed to cases of settler violence through the media and social networks.
The majority, 91%, also expressed concern regarding IDF operations in the West Bank, while 60% said they had a low or very low sense of personal security.

Houthi blitz leaves Saudi Arabia exposed, Iran emboldened
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:33:06 UTC
01:33:06 KST

Houthi blitz leaves Saudi Arabia exposed, Iran emboldened
ANKARA, Sept 16 - The Houthi capture of ground overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has dealt Saudi Arabia its gravest setback in Yemen in years, exposing intelligence failures, the collapse of Yemeni allies and the limits of U.S. protection.
A Houthi advance this week along the Red Sea coast and the capture of islands at the mouth of the strait, a vital artery for global oil supplies, has also left the kingdom scrambling for backing as Iran and its allies expand their reach.
Senior Western, regional and Yemeni officials and sources said the Houthi breakthrough reflected various factors: deep divisions among anti-Houthi Yemeni factions, an untested Saudi-led command structure that replaced Emirati oversight, limited Saudi air support and an underestimation of Houthi preparations.
The diplomat said the Houthis had quietly assembled about 100,000 fighters, vastly outnumbering forces on the opposing side, adding: "Everyone, including the Saudis, missed this build-up and miscalculated the Houthis' intentions.”
Neil Quilliam, a fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, described the offensive as a glaring intelligence failure, saying: "They just weren't picking up the signal. They just weren't seeing the signs."
Yemeni political analyst Farea Al-Muslimi added: "The Saudis were caught off guard in Yemen."
The collapse of Saudi-backed forces handed the Houthis another prize beyond territory — a sizeable cache of advanced U.S.- and Saudi-supplied weaponry abandoned during the retreat.
The haul, according to regional sources, is likely to bolster the group's military capabilities, provide valuable intelligence on adversaries' equipment and further reinforce perceptions of a humiliating Saudi defeat.
"The Yemeni government forces were like a house of cards. They didn't resist. Completely. Completely," said Abdulkhaleq Abdallah, a political analyst in the United Arab Emirates.
The setback has also exposed how limited international support for a counteroffensive may be. Two Western officials said neither the United States nor European countries were prepared to offer direct military backing, and that Washington and its allies had not even joined a Saudi-led maritime defence coalition announced in July.
Saudi officials did not respond to a request to comment for this article.
ALLIES COLLAPSE, PARTNERS HESITATE
With Iran-backed fighters now holding territory that can threaten Saudi oil exports and Red Sea shipping, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MbS) went to Cairo to discuss military cooperation between the two countries as Saudi Arabia seeks to contain the fallout after Washington declined to directly intervene militarily.
Two regional sources familiar with the meeting in Egypt said Riyadh wanted Egypt to help play a role in Red Sea operations. One regional source said MbS asked President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi for military support on Yemen given the close ties between the two countries. There was no immediate word on whether Cairo would agree.
A Saudi source said the meeting was scheduled long before the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran began in February and "while it obviously covered the latest developments, it had the full agenda of bilateral issues to discuss."
Egypt's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment when asked whether MbS had discussed Egyptian military support.
The Houthis also appear to be using their gains to press for broader political concessions.
Former U.S. negotiator Dennis Ross said the group wants Riyadh to lift restrictions on Hodeidah port and Sanaa airport, provide compensation for the war and scale back support for Yemen's internationally recognised government.
"I don't think the Saudis can easily give in to the kinds of demands that they're making," Ross said.
A Gulf official said Saudi Arabia now faced a narrowing set of choices. Allowing the Houthis to consolidate their gains risked turning tactical victories into lasting strategic leverage, while a larger military response could prompt attacks deeper inside the kingdom.
"If you don't inflict enough pain on the Houthis, you become hostage to them," the official said.
Control of territory around Bab el-Mandeb — which lies between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast — could deepen the Houthis' regional reach, putting the Horn of Africa within easier reach of their logistical and smuggling networks.
Combined with Iran's leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, another vital route for global energy supplies, the foothold gives Tehran and its allies influence over two critical maritime choke points.
MbS's foreign policy strategy, built on trying to stabilise the region via a détente with Iran, has unravelled since the start of the war as his economic transformation agenda comes under mounting strain, increasing pressure on the kingdom's de facto ruler.
The absence of Western military assistance in Yemen, and the absence of these powers from a newly formed defence coalition, exposed the limits of its ability to rally support at a moment of acute vulnerability.
Riyadh appears increasingly to have been outmaneuvered by its adversaries and left wanting by its allies.
THE YEMEN TRAP
The Houthi offensive revealed a blind spot in Saudi and U.S. strategy: while Washington and its allies focused on containing Iran directly, Tehran widened the battlefield by opening fronts from Iraq to the Red Sea, using energy assets, shipping routes and proxies as instruments of pressure.
The larger significance of the Houthi breakthrough lies not only in the blow to Saudi Arabia but in the momentum it restores to Iran's influence across the region, after major setbacks to its allies in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon.
For Iran it's a "win-win-win," said Farea Al-Muslimi.
Some political analysts say the more consequential blow is not the battlefield reversal but Washington's reluctance to come to its ally's aid. That signal, they say, has emboldened adversaries, weakened Riyadh's leverage and reinforced doubts over the reliability of U.S. security guarantees.
Al-Muslimi described Washington's refusal to help defend Saudi territory as "the biggest dismissing of the Saudi-American arrangement" in decades.
"The Americans are saying No," he said. "That kind of understanding in the relationship between Riyadh and Washington has never been tested more than now."
Yemen's long record of defeating foreign powers - from Egypt in the 1960s to the Soviets and, more recently, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia - helps explain why Riyadh's search for partners may yield only limited results.
Few regional powers appear eager to be drawn deeper into a conflict that has repeatedly frustrated attempts at outside intervention and acquired a reputation as a graveyard for foreign military ambitions.
"Yemen is the Vietnam and Afghanistan of every power dragged into it," Muslimi said, referring to conflicts in which foreign powers were humbled.
"The Saudis failed in Yemen, the Americans failed in Yemen," he said, adding in reference to Egypt's costly intervention in Yemen in the 1960s: "The Egyptians failed in Yemen." REUTERS

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague sentenced former Kosovo president Hashim Thaçi to 25 years in prison on 16 September for war crimes during the 1998-99 Kosovo conflict. The 58-year-old former Kosovo Liberation Army commander was convicted of murder, torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention. He was sentenced alongside three other former KLA commanders: Jakup Krasniqi, also to 25 years, Kadri Veseli to 18 years and Rexhep Selimi to 13 years. All four were acquitted of crimes against humanity after judges found prosecutors had failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that civilians had been subjected to a widespread or systematic attack. They can appeal.
In Pristina, thousands gathered in the city centre to watch the verdict on a large screen, with many supporters weeping, booing and chanting “Thaci, Thaci” and “KLA” while waving Kosovo Liberation Army flags. After the judgment, some marched towards the EU rule‑of‑law mission (EULEX) headquarters, chanting and, in places, clashing with riot police.
Thaci resigned as Kosovo’s president in 2020 to face the trial.

Saudi announces 110 mln tonnes of uranium-bearing ore discovery

Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia announces 110 million tonnes of uranium-bearing ore discovery
Saudi Arabia says it has discovered an estimated 110 million tonnes of uranium-bearing ore in the Medina region, as the kingdom seeks to develop nuclear power.
Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman announced the estimate on Monday at the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) 70th General Conference in Vienna, saying Saudi Arabia was continuing uranium exploration while also examining the recovery of the metal as a byproduct of fertiliser production.
Arab News cited Abdulaziz as saying geological studies had identified an estimated 110 million tonnes of ore containing high concentrations of rare-earth elements, particularly heavy rare-earth elements, alongside promising concentrations of uranium.
Uranium-bearing ore is rock or mineral material containing naturally occurring uranium. It is not the same as pure uranium, and the quantity of ore alone does not indicate how much uranium could ultimately be extracted.
Factors including uranium concentration, mineral composition, recovery rates and the cost of developing the deposit would need to be assessed to determine whether the resource could support commercial production.
The discovery comes as Saudi Arabia seeks to diversify its energy mix and develop nuclear power alongside its traditional reliance on oil and gas.
In July, the United States and Saudi Arabia reached a civil nuclear cooperation agreement that provides a framework for a decades-long partnership and opens the way for US companies to participate in the kingdom’s nuclear energy programme. The agreement was transmitted to Congress in August for review.
The 30-year nuclear agreement is expected to facilitate the construction of US-designed AP1000 reactors, a project worth tens of billions of dollars that could benefit Westinghouse, which is jointly owned by Canada-based Cameco and Brookfield Asset Management.
The agreement and accompanying documents establish safeguards for US-Saudi nuclear cooperation, but the deal has drawn scrutiny over the level of safeguards and whether Saudi Arabia will be subject to the IAEA’s Additional Protocol, which provides inspectors with expanded access to nuclear sites and information.
The discovery of uranium-bearing ore could add another dimension to Saudi Arabia’s efforts to develop domestic nuclear fuel capabilities, although the amount of recoverable uranium and its commercial viability remain unclear.
(Reuters, The New Arab)
