Gaza rug maker revives 300-year-old family craft in ruins left by Israeli war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:44:25 UTC
23:44:25 KST

In a cramped room beneath his home in eastern Gaza City, Palestinian craftsman Hussein Mahmoud al-Sawwaf turns a wooden wheel by hand as strands of wool and acrylic stretch across a simple loom, gradually taking the shape of a handmade rug.
There is no electricity, no modern machinery and no trace of the large factory where al-Sawwaf worked before Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip.
All he has are simple tools, yarn salvaged from the destruction and hands that know the craft well.
At his modest home in the Tuffah neighborhood, near the “Yellow Line” where Israeli forces are deployed, al-Sawwaf has converted a small space into a workshop for making handmade carpets and rugs after his factory was destroyed and its warehouses burned during the war.
With carpets, rugs and floor mats scarce in Gaza’s markets and the few available products increasingly expensive, al-Sawwaf has revived a craft his family has passed down for about 300 years.
For him, rug-making is no longer simply about preserving his ancestors’ profession. It has become a way to provide a cheaper product for Palestinians exhausted financially by the war while restoring a source of income for some of the workers who lost their jobs when his factory was destroyed.
Demand for such products has grown as widespread destruction of homes and businesses has stripped Palestinians of livelihoods and household belongings.
Large numbers of people have also been forced to live in tents, shelters and temporary accommodation after their homes were destroyed, damaged or rendered uninhabitable.
 
A craft born again out of necessity
Several men who worked with al-Sawwaf before the war now sit beside him in the small workshop. The craft has brought them back together after the war scattered them and deprived them of work.
They operate a manual wheel designed by al-Sawwaf himself to cope with the prolonged electricity shortages that have affected Gaza since the war began.
Al-Sawwaf, the son of the late carpet maker Mahmoud Husni al-Sawwaf, said he was forced to stop working during the first weeks of the war and flee from northern Gaza to the south amid Israeli attacks.
As the war continued and carpets, mats, fabrics and raw materials disappeared from local markets, he decided to resume the family trade with whatever resources remained.
“After fabric, carpets and mats were no longer available, I began renovating the shop and resumed work so we can meet some of our people’s needs, especially those displaced in tents, given the continuing blockade and restrictions on the entry of materials,” he told Anadolu.
 
 
Factory reduced to rubble
Returning to work was not easy. The factory that had supported al-Sawwaf, his family and dozens of workers no longer existed.
He said Israeli attacks completely destroyed the facility and burned its stocks of raw materials, finished products and machinery. Only one machine and a small number of tools could be salvaged.
Al-Sawwaf estimated that 80% to 85% of the yarn and other materials stored in his warehouses were burned.
Another portion of his stock remains in a warehouse in an area under Israeli military control, and he does not know what condition it is in.
Among the materials that survived were wool and acrylic yarn imported before the war, which have now become a rare form of capital that he is using to keep the craft alive.
“We work with whatever resources we have available,” he said.
 
Back to basic tools
The workshop reflects the scarcity surrounding it. There is no regular electricity, modern equipment or steady supply of raw materials.
To overcome those limitations, al-Sawwaf designed a hand-operated wheel inspired by a machine used during his grandfather’s time and adjusted his looms so they can function with basic tools.
With repeated movements, he winds the yarn and turns the wheel as workers arrange and secure the threads around him, gradually forming each rug strand by strand.
The devastation in Gaza has extended far beyond homes, damaging factories, workshops, stores and other economic facilities and leaving many Palestinians without jobs or income.
At the same time, Israeli restrictions on the entry of goods and raw materials have contributed to shortages and higher prices, while many families have little purchasing power left after years of war.
 
A cheaper alternative
Against that backdrop, handmade rugs have become a practical response to a growing need.
Al-Sawwaf said demand for his products has been noticeable, particularly because handmade rugs are cheaper and better suited to what families can currently afford.
“I have seen significant demand from people for handmade rugs because of their low price and because they are affordable,” he said.
The rugs he now produces differ from traditional carpets in price and design but offer families a practical way to cover the floors of homes and tents.
Their light weight and ease of cleaning and transport have also made them attractive to customers, al-Sawwaf said.
 
A 300-year legacy
For al-Sawwaf, however, every rug carries meaning beyond its practical use. Each thread represents the continuation of a family profession that he fears could disappear because of the war.
He said his late father used to tell him that the craft had been inherited from earlier generations. He later learned that his family’s history in carpet-making stretched back roughly 300 years.
“This is the profession of our fathers and grandfathers, passed down to their children,” he said. “I remember my father telling me that it had been his grandfather’s profession many decades ago.”
Al-Sawwaf has brought several former factory workers into the small workshop in hopes of restoring at least part of the income they lost when the factory was destroyed.
 
Working near ‘Yellow Line’
Al-Sawwaf’s workshop is located near the Sanafor junction in Gaza City’s Tuffah neighborhood, close to the so-called “Yellow Line” marking areas where Israeli forces remain deployed under the ceasefire arrangements.
“I insisted on living and working despite the Israeli army forces being nearby,” he said. “We have to continue the journey after my father.”
The “Yellow Line” was established as an Israeli military deployment line following the ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025. However, Israel subsequently expanded its control to encompass areas estimated at approximately 70% of the Strip's territory.
Al-Sawwaf hopes conditions will eventually allow raw materials and machinery to enter Gaza again so he can expand production and rebuild the factory he lost.
Israel’s genocide in Gaza began in October 2023. Gaza health authorities have reported more than 73,000 Palestinians killed and over 174,000 injured, mostly women and children.

117 journalists displaced from Yemen’s western coast amid escalation: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:43:37 UTC
23:43:37 KST

Mohammed Sameai and Ikram Kouachi
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
At least 117 journalists and media workers have been displaced from Yemen's western coastal city of Mokha and surrounding areas amid a military escalation since the beginning of September, the Yemeni Media Freedoms Observatory said Wednesday.
The nongovernmental organization said in a statement that the journalists and media workers fled Mokha, in southwestern Taiz province, and nearby areas amid recent military developments and the entry of Houthi forces.
It said the displacement was sudden, with several journalists leaving their homes in the hours before Houthi forces entered Mokha, amid fears of arrest or detention because of their journalistic work.
Some journalists were forced to leave without taking their personal belongings or professional equipment, it added.
The observatory quoted journalists who fled Mokha as saying that “Houthi forces raided the homes of journalists and looted their belongings.”
Others said they left in haste and were able to take only a limited portion of their belongings and equipment.
The group also reported the death of journalist Zakaria Dahman, a staffer at at Al-Jumhuriya TV, owned by Presidential Leadership Council member Tareq Saleh, in the southern port city of Aden after his health deteriorated during the fighting and displacement from Mokha to Aden, according to his colleagues.
Information blockade from conflict-hit area
The organization said the departure of journalists and correspondents from Mokha had “reduced access to independent, firsthand information from inside the city, making it more difficult to verify developments on the ground and provide information to the public.”
It called on international and local organizations, donors and press freedom partners to “urgently support displaced journalists, including through temporary financial assistance, housing, psychological support, professional assistance and the equipment needed to continue their work safely.”
The western coastal areas of Yemen have witnessed a major escalation in recent days, coinciding with advances by Houthi forces and their reported capture of positions and areas previously held by government forces. The developments have reshaped the control map along parts of Yemen’s Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Meanwhile, Yemeni government forces have announced advances in the northern Al-Jawf province bordering Saudi Arabia. They have also said they were approaching Al-Hazm, the provincial capital.
Government forces have also announced airstrikes on Houthi targets in and around Mocha and in parts of Taiz, Lahej and Al-Dhalea provinces, saying they destroyed military vehicles and weapons and repelled a major attack on Marib.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has intensified since early July 2026 after years of relative calm.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Sweden's centre-left opposition wins election, SVT says
STOCKHOLM, Sept 16 - Sweden's centre-left opposition has defeated the incumbent right-wing governing bloc by the slimmest of margins, public broadcaster SVT said on Wednesday, after 99% of the votes in Sunday's parliamentary election had been counted.
Only 26,169 votes separated the two blocs at 1647 GMT, but with fewer than 1% of districts left to count, parties led by opposition leader Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats looked set to win 175 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, signalling a change of government.
"The likelihood of a turnaround at this stage is so low that we can confidently state that the opposition will secure the most seats in this election," SVT said.
The right-wing governing bloc of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, which includes the far-right Sweden Democrats, was meanwhile on track to win 174 seats, data from Sweden's election authority showed.
The agency is now counting late incoming ballots from home and overseas, and has said this process may go on until Thursday before all votes are accounted for. REUTERS

At a meeting following the presentation ceremony, Ambassador Auväärt and Governor General Arbour discussed the close and practical alliance between Estonia and Canada, as well as cooperation on security, support for Ukraine and economic affairs.
“Canada’s role in ensuring the security of our region and supporting Ukraine cannot be overstated. We greatly value the presence of Canadian forces in our neighbouring country Latvia and Canada’s significant contribution to NATO’s collective defence,” Auväärt said.
The Ambassador noted that economic ties between Estonia and Canada have grown increasingly close in recent years. Cooperation between the two countries encompasses, among other areas, critical minerals and global supply chains, including rare earth production and the magnet factory opened in Narva last autumn by the Canadian company Neo Performance Materials.
The Ambassador also highlighted the Estonian community in Canada, which is one of the most vibrant Estonian communities outside Estonia. A testament to this is KESKUS, the international Estonian centre that opened in Toronto a month ago.
“Amid the tragic events of the 20th century, Canada gave thousands of Estonians the opportunity to build a new home and a future, for which we are deeply grateful. We also greatly value Canada’s decision to be among the first countries in the world to recognise the restoration of Estonia’s independence,” the Ambassador said.
Gert Auväärt was born on 22 August 1980. He holds a master’s degree in law from the University of Helsinki and has undertaken further studies in cybersecurity at the Marshall Center and the European Security and Defence College. Since 2004, he has held various positions at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, including as Legal and Economic Adviser at the Estonian Embassy in The Hague and Legal Adviser at Estonia’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations. From 2017 to 2018, he was Head of International Relations at the Estonian Information System Authority (RIA), and from 2018 to 2021 he served as Deputy Permanent Representative at Estonia’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations, where his responsibilities included successfully completing Estonia’s first campaign for a seat on the UN Security Council and coordinating Estonia’s substantive work and presidencies during its membership of the Council.
From 2021 to 2026, Auväärt served as Deputy Director General of RIA and Director of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-EE). For the past five years, he also represented Estonia on the Management Board of the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) and was a member of the European Cyber Crises Liaison Organisation Network (EU-CyCLONe).

Copenhagen police announced temporary restrictions on drone flights over a large part of the capital in connection with a meeting of the NATO Military Committee on September 18-19. Similar restrictions were imposed last year in connection with an EU summit held in Denmark.
The measure was also introduced to enhance security amid an earlier incident involving unidentified drones near the Danish-German border.

====================================================================================================

China’s Free-Trade Offer to Africa Won’t Solve the Trade Imbalance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:41:00 UTC
23:41:00 KST

In Abuja on August 14, 2026, nearly 500 government officials, diplomats, scholars, and business representatives gathered for a seminar on China’s new zero-tariff policy and what it means for African economic transformation. Nigeria’s minister of state for agriculture, Aliyu Sabi Abdullahi, used the occasion to strike a cautious note. “Zero tariffs alone do not guarantee success,” he told the room. “The question before us, therefore, is not, can Nigeria export more? The question should be, can Nigeria export better?”
Since May 1, China has extended zero-tariff treatment across 100 percent of tariff lines to the 53 African countries with which it holds diplomatic relations. That gives nearly all of Africa (with the lone exception of Eswatini) duty-free access to one of the world’s largest consumer markets. The early results look encouraging: Chinese imports from Africa reached $28.7 billion in May and June, up 23.5 percent from a year earlier. During the seminar in Abuja, China’s ambassador to Nigeria reported that Chinese imports from Nigeria specifically had already grown more than 40 percent year-on-year in both May and June.
African governments have good reason to welcome China’s new zero-tariff policy. The problem is that lower tariffs alone cannot resolve the deeper imbalance that has built up in Africa-China trade.
Africa-China merchandise trade hit a record $348 billion in 2025, but the flows were badly lopsided. China sold Africa $225 billion in goods, Africa sold China $123 billion. For every dollar of goods Africa sold China, it bought back roughly $1.83. The resulting deficit, $102 billion, was 64.5 percent above 2024’s figure. In the same period, Chinese exports to Africa grew 25.8 percent, while African exports to China grew just 5.4 percent.
Market access – like China’s new offer to African countries – can change the volume of trade, but not necessarily the structure of trade. What is actually being exported by each partner matters more than the size of the deficit itself. Research from the Boston University Global Development Policy Center and the African Economic Research Consortium found that from 2000 through 2022, 89 percent of African exports to China came from extractive industries: oil, copper, iron ore, alumina. Over the same period, 94 percent of African imports from China were manufactured goods.
A 2026 update from the same researchers showed that not much had changed. Extracted natural resources still dominate Africa’s exports to China, while agriculture and manufacturing each account for a small share of export value.
Most African countries have clearly stated ambitions to move up the value chain. Lower tariffs alone will do little to accomplish that goal. The rising volume of Africa-China trade is easy to measure and just as easy to celebrate, but the overall numbers are less important than the composition of trade.
The tariff opening still matters, of course. African exports of avocados, apples, and oranges to China have risen sharply since implementation. Market access of this kind can pull real investment toward certification, cold-chain logistics, and packaging, some of the obstacles holding producers back. But that won’t happen automatically.
Take copper as an example. Copper can be exported from Africa as raw ore, or it can be refined and worked into components before it ships. Currently, that work – and the added value – happens almost entirely outside the continent. China’s zero-tariff policy doesn’t care whether the copper is raw or refined; the tariff line is the same either way.
Two recent examples show what greater processing and value capture inside Africa can actually look like. At a processing plant in Kenya’s Athi River Export Processing Zone, locally grown avocados are ripened, sorted, and cold-pressed into extra virgin avocado oil bound for China. In Rwanda, a company that began exporting dried chilies to China in 2022 shipped its first batch of pickled chilies in June – a deliberate move toward a higher-value semi-processed product made only after the tariff change. In both cases, more processing is happening before the goods leave the continent, which means more of the value is captured in Kenya and Rwanda rather than downstream in China.
African countries do have the capability to move up the value chain, and intra-Africa trade proves it. UNCTAD reported that 61 percent of trade happening within the continent consists of processed and semi-processed goods, far above Africa’s share of processed exports to the rest of the world. The opportunity is to pair China’s external market with the regional value chains the African Continental Free Trade Area is meant to build. Cotton grown in Mali or Burkina Faso can be baled and shipped directly to China for processing, or it can move first through mills in Cote d’Ivoire or Ghana and leave as finished cloth.
It’s not tariffs that are holding back African manufacturing. China’s zero-tariff policy won’t solve problems like unreliable electricity, expensive financing, inefficient ports, thin transport links, certification bottlenecks, or customs delays. UNCTAD estimated that road transport alone accounts for about 29 percent of the price of goods traded within Africa, compared with 7 percent for goods traded beyond it. According to UNCTAD, non-tariff barriers constrain intra-African trade roughly three times more than tariffs.
African governments need to treat China’s opening as one input into a larger industrial policy, not as a substitute for having one. Africa-China trade will likely keep setting records, but that alone won’t help African economies climb global value chains. The real test will show up in the breakdown of those trade statistics: whether Africa is still mostly exporting raw materials like crude oil and copper ore or refined metals and finished goods.

Celebrated playwright and novelist Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:39:35 UTC
23:39:35 KST

Greer was known for incisive TV and radio appearances and for her novels, plays and essays which delved into politics, culture and identity.
American and British playwright-novelist Bonnie Greer has died aged 77.
Her husband David Hutchins announced the news, saying: "It is with profound sadness that I announce that my beloved wife, Bonnie Greer, has died aged 77 after a brief illness."
"Bonnie was an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life."
Hutchins added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her. Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together."
Born in Chicago in 1948, Greer moved to Britain in 1986. She became a familiar face on British television, including as a panelist on shows like Newsnight and Question Time.
Greer was awarded the Verity Bargate Award for Best Play for "Munda Negra" and she was also the author of the novels "Hanging By Her Teeth" (1994) and "Entropy" (2009).
Other works include the biography "Langston Hughes: The Value Of Contradiction" (2011) and the play "Marilyn And Ella" (2008) about actress Marilyn Monroe and singer Ella Fitzgerald.
Greer was appointed to the British Museum's board of trustees in 2005 and later served as deputy chairwoman. She also served on the boards of the London Film School and Royal Opera House, and was appointed a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature in 2022. She also served as Chancellor of Kingston University in Kingston upon Thames, London.
In 2010, Greer was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) for her services to the arts.
RIP Bonnie Greer 1948 - 2026

EU moves closer to social media ban for under 13s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:39:26 UTC
23:39:26 KST

The EU will move forward with plans for an under 13s social media ban, the head of the European Commission has confirmed.
Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday that social media apps were “depriving children of their childhood” and big tech platforms needed to prove the safety of their products.
She promised a draft law for a total ban on social media for under 13s, while children aged 13-15 would be allowed “mini accounts” under parental supervision with time limits on apps.
The commission will publish its social media plan on Thursday, which will have to be agreed by the European parliament and 27 EU member states if it is to become law.
Von der Leyen also promised that the commission’s Digital Fairness Act, due to be submitted to the European parliament this year, would tackle features such as addictive design, which she said was “harming everyone”.
The commission president made the comments in Strasbourg as part of her annual state of the union address. In a wide-ranging speech covering the EU’s place in a turbulent world and plans for continent-wide legislation, she also promised a European heatwave plan and committed to an emergency response mechanism to deal with sudden inflows of migrants in response to events in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in August.
Von der Leyen also made an unprecedented invitation to Canada to become an “associate member” of the EU, and pledged to set out ideas for a European security council involving Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the UK.
The former German defence minister said the EU needed its version of Nato’s article 4 – an “emergency security protocol” that means all member states would convene at the request of another in response to a hybrid attack.
“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said. “We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents – those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security.”
Nato’s article 4, which is separate from the collective defence clause, article 5, means members of the alliance can consult when one of them believes their territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened.
European nations have recently faced a series of hostile acts attributed to Russia, including sabotage, incursions by jets into European airspace and a drone attack on Leipzig airport.
Warning that Ukraine faced a tough winter, von der Leyen suggested the EU may have reached its limits on economic restrictions against Russia. “What is needed is not necessarily new sanctions, but above all the enforcement of existing sanctions,” she said.
After 21 rounds of measures, EU member states have found it increasingly difficult to agree sanctions on the Kremlin’s war machine, wary of the cost to their own economies.
Von der Leyen also touched on Europe’s divisions over whether or not to introduce restrictions on trade with Israel and its illegal settlements in the West Bank. The commission has declined to publish a proposal to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements, though several EU member states and allies including France, Canada and the UK have moved in this direction.
“When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events,” she said.

More than 104,000 people displaced inside Yemen as fighting continues: UN migration agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:38:56 UTC
23:38:56 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
More than 104,000 people have been displaced inside Yemen as fighting along the West Coast continues, the UN migration agency said on Wednesday.
A total of 104,796 people from 17,461 households have been displaced, according to the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) latest Displacement Tracking Matrix.
Taiz remains the epicenter, with more than 63,000 displaced in its districts, including 21,018 in Jabal Habashi, 12,642 in Al Ma'afer and 8,250 in Ash Shamayatayn.
Nearly 26,400 people have been displaced in Lahj, while Aden has recorded more than 3,500. Displacement is also rising in Al Abyan, Hadramawt and Ma'rib as fighting spreads, said IOM.
"Yemen is a country torn by war, displacement, poverty, and climate impacts," said IOM Director General Amy Pope. “Overlooking the suffering of civilians is not acceptable as needs continue to rise.”
The agency said families are moving under fire, often at night and with few belongings, while the pace of displacement is outstripping aid workers' ability to track movements in real time.
The IOM added that as many as 2,776 people have crossed from Yemen into Djibouti, where the agency is providing emergency assistance.
20M need health assistance
Nearly 20 million people in Yemen need health assistance as escalating violence places further strain on the country's already fragile health system, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said.
"The recent escalation of violence is compounding an already severe health and humanitarian crisis," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told reporters in Geneva.
Tedros said fighting has caused a sharp increase in casualties and displacement, while attacks on health facilities, shortages of supplies and fuel, and disruptions to referral services are pushing the health system “closer to collapse.”
He warned that risks from cholera, measles, polio and dengue, as well as malnutrition, are growing, particularly among displaced communities living in overcrowded conditions with limited access to safe water and sanitation.
Tedros said the WHO is providing emergency medical supplies and working with partners to strengthen frontline response capacity. However, humanitarian access remains "severely constrained," while funding shortfalls threaten efforts to sustain and scale up the response.
He called for the protection of health workers and facilities, unhindered humanitarian access and increased international support to address rapidly escalating needs.

Russia's Syzran and Saratov oil refineries halt operations after drone attacks — Reuters
Reuters reported this in an article, according to Ukrinform.
According to the agency's sources, the Syzran refinery halted operations on Tuesday, while the Saratov refinery stopped processing oil last Friday.
Several facilities at the Syzran refinery were damaged in the drone attack, including its main AVT-6 crude oil distillation unit, with a capacity of 17,100 metric tonnes per day. The unit accounts for about 71% of the refinery's total processing capacity, the sources said.
According to the sources, repairs at the refinery could take at least a month.
The refinery's second crude oil distillation unit, AVT-5, has a capacity of 7,100 tonnes per day, or 29% of the facility's total capacity. At the time of the September 15 attack, it was already undergoing repairs following an earlier drone attack in July.
The Saratov refinery halted oil processing on September 11 following another drone strike. According to Reuters sources, the refinery had also suspended operations on September 8 due to equipment damage and fires caused by a previous UAV attack. It had been preparing to resume oil processing on September 10–11.
The Saratov refinery had previously suspended operations for several weeks following a drone attack on August 2.
The Syzran oil refinery is located in Russia's Samara Region and has a nominal crude oil processing capacity of 8.5 million tonnes per year (150,000 barrels per day).
The Saratov oil refinery has a processing capacity of 7 million metric tonnes per year (140,000 barrels per day).
According to industry sources, in 2024 the Syzran refinery processed 4.3 million tonnes of crude oil and produced 0.8 million tonnes of gasoline, as well as 1.5 million tonnes of diesel fuel and 0.7 million tonnes of fuel oil.
According to industry sources, the Saratov refinery processed 5.8 million tonnes of crude oil in 2024, producing 1.2 million tonnes of gasoline, 1.9 million tonnes of diesel fuel and 1 million tonnes of fuel oil.
As Ukrinform reported, following a drone attack on September 6, the Rosneft-owned Ryazan oil refinery also halted operations.

Syria parliament votes to abolish Assad-era terrorism court, nullify rulings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:37:52 UTC
23:37:52 KST

Syria parliament votes to abolish Assad-era terrorism court, nullify rulings
DAMASCUS, Sept 16 - Syria's parliament voted on Wednesday to abolish an Assad-era terrorism court and nullify the legal effects of its rulings, state-run Al-Ikhbariya TV reported, in one of the first significant legislative moves by the country's new assembly.
The Counter-Terrorism Court was established in 2012 as then-President Bashar al-Assad sought to suppress an uprising against his rule, and it was used to prosecute thousands of Syrians for terrorism-related offences.
The move formalises the court's abolition after Syria's new authorities had already treated it as defunct. In June 2025, President Ahmed al-Sharaa issued a decree dismissing 67 judges who had served in what he described at the time as the "abolished Counter-Terrorism Court".
Syria's March 2025 constitutional declaration had also called for abolishing the effects of what it described as unjust rulings issued by the court, including returning confiscated property.
The United Nations Human Rights Committee said in 2024 that the 2012 law establishing the court failed to adequately provide key judicial guarantees and raised concerns over arbitrary detention, torture or ill-treatment, and the court's independence. It also noted that the court was permitted to depart from ordinary procedures during prosecution and trial.
The U.N.'s International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism said in a 2024 report that the Counter-Terrorism Court formed part of the judicial system through which detainees held by Assad-era security agencies could be prosecuted. The report documented widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment across the government's detention system.
Wednesday's vote came during the opening weeks of the first parliament formed since Assad was toppled in December 2024. The chamber convened for the first time in July.
The vote is among the assembly's first major legislative decisions after it spent its initial sessions establishing its internal rules and committees. It held a hearing this week with Education Minister Mohammad Abdul Rahman Tarkou over the state of the country's schools and is due to question the energy minister on Thursday over a sharp rise in fuel prices. Why this fast-growing German AI start-up is moving its parent company from the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:37:13 UTC
23:37:13 KST

In a highly unusual move, fast-growing German AI start-up Langdock has moved its legal headquarters from the US to Germany as it seeks to become a "European hyperscaler".
Berlin-based Langdock has reversed the usual path taken by European start-ups by moving its parent company from the US to Germany.
The decision comes amid growing debate over how Europe can build its own AI infrastructure, retain promising technology companies and reduce its dependence on US cloud and AI providers.
Many European start-ups establish US holding companies in an effort to make it easier to secure funding. Langdock has now defied this trend and dismantled its US holding structure and brought its parent company under European law.
“Langdock has reorganised its corporate structure into a Societas Europaea (SE), registered in Germany, replacing the previous US holding-company structure,” a company representative told Euronews Business. The company said the process began in early 2026 and cost several million euros. It is now complete.
Founded in Berlin in 2023, Langdock is an enterprise AI platform serving about 13,000 organisations. It gives employees access to several AI models and allows companies to connect them to workplace data and applications, create AI agents and automate tasks.
Langdock said creating a US-registered parent company was initially a “vital step” that helped it attract investors and benefit from the support and network of US start-up accelerator Y Combinator. However, its operations and customer data remained in Germany.
Langdock has now replaced its US parent company with a European SE. The previous structure meant customers’ lawyers had to check whether the US parent created any legal or data-protection risks, even though Langdock said the US company had no employees, infrastructure or access to its production systems.
US laws, including the Cloud Act, have created concerns across the market that American authorities could seek access to customer data.
Removing the US parent makes Langdock’s European structure clearer to customers, the company said, particularly “in geopolitically uncertain times”. It added that it was now large enough to meet the stricter governance requirements of an SE.
“We believe Europe is a strong place to build a global technology company, and we want to contribute to its sovereignty and competitiveness,” the company told Euronews Business.
About 80% of Langdock is owned by founders and employees who live in the EU. The company said the new structure would not change its plans to serve customers worldwide or raise money from international investors.
Langdock says its annual subscription revenue reached a rate of $50 million (€42 million) in August, up from $1 million (€870,000) in October 2024. The figure estimates how much subscription income the company would receive over a full year if its current sales continued.
Langdock said its long-term ambition was to build “a sovereign, full-stack AI platform that can compete with US hyperscalers over time”. It plans to launch three new services by the end of the year and use its own data centre in Germany to run open-source AI models and provide computing power. The company said it would start small and expand as customer demand grew.
Despite its rapid growth, Langdock has a long way to go before it can compete with US tech giants. Its $50 million annual revenue run rate compares with the $128.7 billion (€108 billion) in revenue generated by Amazon Web Services in 2025.
Langdock’s decision to relocate its parent company offers a test of whether European regulation and concerns about digital sovereignty can become a competitive advantage, rather than simply a burden, for the region’s AI companies.

Thailand, Cambodia conclude 1st maritime boundary conciliation meeting
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:34:11 CST
23:34:11 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Thailand and Cambodia on Wednesday concluded their first three-day international conciliation meeting here over their overlapping maritime claims.
The proceedings were conducted under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). Compulsory conciliation under UNCLOS is a non-adjudicatory procedure in which a neutral commission assists the parties in seeking an amicable settlement of their dispute.
In his opening statement on Tuesday, Cambodian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn said Cambodia wished to conclude, with the assistance of the commission and in accordance with international law, a treaty with Thailand delimiting a single, all-purpose maritime boundary between the two states.
Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said Thailand aims to seek a solution to the maritime delimitation issue.
He said the proceedings were limited to maritime boundary delimitation between Thailand and Cambodia in the Gulf of Thailand and did not concern sovereignty over land.
The compulsory conciliation proceedings were initiated by Cambodia in June, after Thailand unilaterally scrapped a 2001 memorandum of understanding on their overlapping maritime claims in May, saying the agreement had produced no concrete progress.
The Thai foreign ministry has said the conciliation process is expected to take around 12 months, after which the commission will issue a report containing its conclusions or recommendations, which are not binding upon the parties. ■

Xinhua Headlines: China opens major river-to-sea canal, creating trade shortcut to Southeast Asia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:34:10 CST
23:34:10 KST

* China opened the Pinglu Canal on Wednesday, giving its southwestern hinterland a shortcut to the coast.
* It shortens the inland waterway journey for goods from southwest China to the sea by more than 560 kilometers.
* The canal could provide a new corridor for goods to flow in both directions between the vast markets of China and ASEAN.
NANNING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China opened the Pinglu Canal on Wednesday, giving its landlocked southwest a shortcut to the coast and overseas markets, particularly those in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the country's largest trading partner.
Built at a cost of 72.7 billion yuan (about 10.75 billion U.S. dollars), the 134.2-kilometer canal runs from Hengzhou, a county-level city in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, to the Beibu Gulf, the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China.
The canal stretches along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic trade route connecting China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets. It is the first river-to-sea canal project planned and coordinated at the national level since the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal shortens the inland waterway journey for goods from southwest China to the sea by more than 560 kilometers compared with traditional routes through ports in Guangdong Province. It is expected to reduce overall logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent and save more than 5 billion yuan in transportation costs each year.
Lu Xinning, vice chairperson of the regional government of Guangxi, said the canal creates a new link between China's market of 1.4 billion people and ASEAN's nearly 700 million consumers. Its impact, Lu said, could extend beyond the movement of goods, spurring new cross-border investment and deepening regional supply-chain integration.
The canal took over four years to build. Most of it was created by widening, deepening and straightening existing waterways, while a small section had to be excavated through dry land and mountainous terrain.
"There was no established model or ready-made precedent to follow," said Cheng Yaofei, chairman of Guangxi Pinglu Canal Construction Co., Ltd.
One of the biggest engineering challenges was a 65-meter difference in water level, roughly the height of a 20-plus-story building. Three navigation hubs, all featuring twin-line ship locks, were built to raise and lower vessels along the canal.
Engineers developed water-recycling systems at the hubs, enabling the canal to save more than 1 billion cubic meters of water annually.
Environmental protection was another priority during construction. More than 98 percent of the roughly 315 million cubic meters of earth and rock excavated during construction was reused. The canal also includes a fish passage more than 480 meters long and a dedicated wildlife crossing for land animals including leopard cats and squirrels.
The canal opens in the first year of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), as the world's second-largest economy seeks to promote more coordinated regional development and further expand high-standard opening up -- priorities outlined in the plan.
The new artery carries particular significance for China's southwest, which has long lagged behind the more prosperous eastern coast and faced higher costs getting goods to seaports. Coal, ore, grain, new-energy materials and auto parts from the region can now take a more direct route to overseas markets.
In the near term, the canal is likely to reshape existing cargo flows, with some freight shifting from road and rail to waterways and from the Pearl River Estuary to the Beibu Gulf, said Meng Shuang, an associate professor at Central University of Finance and Economics.
Over time, Meng said, the lower cost of reaching the sea could generate new trade, draw investment inland and reshape industrial development along the canal.
With China and ASEAN seeking closer economic ties and greater regional connectivity, experts say the Pinglu Canal could provide a new corridor for goods to flow in both directions between the vast Chinese and ASEAN markets.
China's trade with ASEAN exceeded 1 trillion U.S. dollars for the first time last year. In the first seven months of 2026, total trade between the two sides reached 744.41 billion U.S. dollars, an increase of 24.7 percent year on year, accounting for 21.8 percent of China's total foreign trade during this period.
BeBe Zhao, president of Singapore-China Integrated Developments (Guangxi) Pte. Ltd., said the canal could bring new opportunities for businesses on both sides. ASEAN products could move more efficiently into western China, while goods manufactured there could reach global markets through regional hubs such as Singapore.
"The new route will not only make trade more efficient but also strengthen Singapore's role as a regional transshipment and trade hub," Zhao said.
For Boonsub Panichakarn from the Faculty of Logistics and Digital Supply Chain at Naresuan University in Thailand, the canal's significance goes beyond the distance it saves.
It lies in how much the canal can reduce logistics costs, time variability and uncertainty across the entire ASEAN-southwest China supply chain, he said. ■
(Reporting by Cheng Lu, Huang Yaoteng, Zhu Lili, Huang Kaiying, Tian Zijun and Yao Yuan; Video reporters: Hong Jing, Qin Guanghua, Yang Chi, Liang Shun, Huang Kaiying, Li Yuhui, Wan Houde, Wu Yimeng and Hu Hanbo; Video editors: Hong Jing, Zhu Cong, Hong Ling and Hong Yan.)

"The EU's vision should therefore be to seek a peaceful, rather than a military solution," he added. ■

Afrikaners are a white ethnic group in South Africa, mainly descended from Dutch, French and German settlers who arrived at the Cape from the 17th century onward.
The U.S. administration has accused the South African government of mistreating White South Africans, while the South African government rejected claims that it was confiscating land and "treating certain classes of people very badly."
In February 2025, shortly after beginning his second term, U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the U.S. government to facilitate the resettlement of Afrikaners from South Africa as refugees, citing alleged racial discrimination and persecution. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Durian offers new growth to Vietnam's coffee heartland
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:33:39 CST
23:33:39 KST

Workers clean durians at a durian processing factory in Dak Lak province, Vietnam, Sept. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Hu Jiali)
by Xinhua writer Phan Hong Nhung, Hu Jiali
DAK LAK, Vietnam, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- In Thai Binh village in Ea Tul commune, Le Tuan Tai walks under a canopy of durian trees, with sunlight falling through the leaves. He taps a green-yellow fruit with a small knife. A dull thud. "It's ripe," he says.
For nearly four decades, Tai's family has farmed this land in Vietnam's central province of Dak Lak. First rubber, then coffee, now durian. Nearly 2,000 trees cover 10 hectares. The shift is personal -- and increasingly common.
Dak Lak, long known as Vietnam's coffee capital, has more than 214,000 hectares of coffee and annual output topping 530,000 tons. And currently, a new crop is spreading fast: durian. The catalyst was China. In 2022, Vietnam signed a protocol allowing official exports of fresh durian to China, ending years of small-scale border trade and giving farmers steadier prices.
Dak Lak Province is one of Vietnam's major durian-producing areas. Its durian acreage has expanded from 15,000 hectares in 2022 to 45,000 hectares in 2026, with output in 2026 expected to reach about 500,000 tons.
Last year, the locality contributed about 1.1 billion U.S. dollars to the country's total durian export revenue of 3.86 billion dollars, according to the Department of Vietnam Customs and the Dak Lak Durian Association. Separately, Vietnam's Lao Dong newspaper reported that with 940,000 tons of durian exported to China, Vietnam, for the first time, surpassed Thailand and became China's largest durian supplier.
Durian is a demanding crop. It needs more labor and capital than coffee. "You cannot leave a durian orchard for a week but can leave a coffee one for a whole year without much attention," Tai told Xinhua, comparing durian to a newborn that needs daily care. Yet farmers keep switching because the returns are hard to ignore.
Do Viet Hung, owner of Hung Toan durian orchard in Ea Tul commune, began planting durian in 2017. Before his first harvest, he invested more than 10 billion Vietnamese dong (about 391,000 U.S. dollars) in an automatic irrigation system, fertilizer and intensive care.
Hung said his orchard began bearing fruit three years after planting, when durian sold for about 25,000 Vietnamese dong (about 0.98 U.S. dollars) per kilogram. Prices have since climbed to 60,000 Vietnamese dong (about 2.34 U.S. dollars), he said.
Tai's orchard is expected to produce 350 tons this year, worth about 18 billion Vietnamese dong (about 703,000 U.S. dollars). "Coffee gave our family a stable but modest living," he said. "Durian prices in recent years have kept household spending comfortable." About 70 percent of his fruit is destined for China.
Le Anh Trung, chairman of the Dak Lak Durian Association, said the durian industry's future lies not in replacing coffee but in building a more diversified and sustainable agricultural base. Coffee retains special importance for Dak Lak, while durian is becoming a high-value export industry.
"In the next stage, we should not only ask how many more hectares can be added, but how much value can be created on existing acreage," he said.
He envisions a value chain that runs from standardized raw-material zones to inspection and traceability, packaging, deep processing, cold storage, logistics and international markets. China's rising standards for quality, food safety and traceability, he said, have already pushed the province's durian industry to professionalize production and strengthen its supply chain.
That shift has brought processors and exporters into the supply chain. Vietnam 001 Fruit Company Limited, founded in 2022, has exported more than 2,000 containers of durian worth over 236 million dollars. Its fruit now reaches consumers across China, from Kunming and Guangzhou to Shanghai and Beijing, covering high-end supermarkets and wholesale markets in lower-tier cities.
"We source our fruits through local cooperatives, covering combined growing areas of about 1,500 hectares," said Nguyen Thi My Duy, director of the company. As Chinese demand has room to grow, she said, competition will hinge on quality and trust, not volume.
"Quality starts in the orchard, not the factory," Duy told Xinhua. The company has worked closely with farmers from the start and plans to invest in deep processing, such as durian cakes and dried fruit, to add value and prepare for the day when the fresh market matures. "We do not want to sell just a durian. We want to maximize the value of durian," she said. "That is also how companies can respond more proactively to market changes and help farmers secure more stable sales."
As the sun sets over Thai Binh, the orchards turn gold. Trucks loaded with fruit rolled out of the village. For farmers in Dak Lak, durian is no longer just an alternative crop; it is a new crown jewel of Vietnam's coffee kingdom. ■

No more than 100 Ukrainian military personnel will be able to train in the Czech Republic at the same time – media
Kyiv • UNN
The Czech parliamentary committee supported the army’s foreign missions plan for two years. The limit on Ukrainian military personnel participating in training exercises in the Czech Republic will be reduced to 100.
To defend NATO’s eastern flank, the Czech Republic will be able to deploy no more than 1,600 troops over the next two years, instead of the current 2,000. This is provided for by the government plan for the Czech Army’s foreign missions, which was supported today by a committee of the lower house of parliament, with votes from deputies of the governing coalition. Another change concerns reducing the number of Ukrainian troops who will be able to train in the Czech Republic simultaneously, UNN reports, citing Radio Prague.
Opposition lawmakers abstained during the vote.
Strengthening NATO’s eastern flank remains a priority in the mandate for the next two years, Defense Minister Jaromír Zuna said. As the number of troops available for possible deployment in other missions increases, the army’s overall capability is strengthened as well, he said. “This corresponds to actual needs and planned rotations,” the minister stated.
Chief of the Army General Staff Miroslav Hlaváč added that no more than 510 Czech troops had been deployed on NATO’s eastern flank at the same time.
Last year, 966 Czech troops and 29 active-reserve soldiers rotated through Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Slovakia, which was 478 fewer personnel overall. The new proposal provides for the possibility of deploying troops also in Estonia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, and now Finland.
The number of Czech troops taking part in the training of Ukrainian soldiers in countries outside the EU is planned to increase from 40 to a maximum of 60, while within the EU the limit remains at 100. No more than 100 Ukrainian soldiers will be able to train in the Czech Republic at the same time, whereas previously there could be as many as 800.
The government justified this by citing a reduced need. The number of troops assigned to protect the Czech diplomatic mission in Ukraine is to increase from a maximum of 20 to 30.

Lebanese Culture Minister Ghassan Salameh (1st L) hands over the ancient Egyptian artifacts to Egyptian Ambassador to Lebanon Alaa Moussa (2nd L) at a ceremony at the National Museum in Beirut, Lebanon, on Sept. 16, 2026. Lebanon on Wednesday returned to Egypt 37 ancient artifacts that had been illegally smuggled into Lebanon, according to a statement by Lebanon's Culture Ministry. (Xinhua/Bilal Jawich)
BEIRUT, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Lebanon on Wednesday returned to Egypt 37 ancient artifacts that had been illegally smuggled into Lebanon, according to a statement by Lebanon's Culture Ministry.
Lebanese Culture Minister Ghassan Salameh handed the artifacts over to Egyptian Ambassador to Lebanon Alaa Moussa at a ceremony at the National Museum in Beirut.
The artifacts had been seized at the Port of Beirut in 2020, and their return followed years of cooperation among Lebanese and Egyptian authorities, Interpol and Lebanon's Public Prosecution to verify their authenticity and ownership.
The collection includes two painted wooden coffins, masks, wooden dolls, pieces of Coptic textiles, amulets made of glass paste, and medium-sized statues.
"We are giving an example of the literal application of the 1970 international convention concerning the prevention of the illicit trafficking of cultural property," Salameh said.
He said Lebanon expected other countries to follow the same approach and return Lebanese cultural property that had come into their possession illicitly. ■

====================================================================================================

Clyde maritime alliance launches with defence growth focus
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:33:12 BST
23:33:12 KST

A new Clyde Maritime Alliance has been launched to bring together major shipbuilding, engineering, skills and public-sector organisations around investment, workforce development and future maritime projects on the river, according to Glasgow Chamber of Commerce.
Founding members include BAE Systems, Babcock International, Dales Marine Services, Ferguson Marine, JFD, Malin Group and Peel Ports Clydeport, alongside Glasgow City Region, Skills Development Scotland and Glasgow Chamber of Commerce.
Scottish Enterprise and the UK Government are providing seed funding for the alliance, which has been established through a Memorandum of Understanding intended to give the Clyde maritime sector a more coordinated voice on skills, infrastructure, investment and supply-chain growth.
The organisation follows work by businesses operating along the Clyde to assess whether the region has enough people, skills and industrial capacity to deliver existing programmes while competing for further work.
A study carried out with RAND Europe found that five of the Clyde’s largest maritime employers, Babcock Marine, BAE Systems, Dales Marine Services, Ferguson Marine and Malin Group, employ almost 8,000 people between them.
According to the alliance, that total is close to the number of skilled workers recorded when RAND last benchmarked the workforce across Scotland’s shipyards in 2003.
The workforce spans structural trades, systems engineering, naval architecture, outfitting and other specialist maritime disciplines, with the alliance seeking to retain and expand that skills base as existing shipbuilding and support programmes continue.
Stuart Patrick, Chair of the Clyde Maritime Alliance, said: “This is an important step forward in how we enable industry on the River Clyde to deliver economic benefit to the region. Forming the Clyde Maritime Alliance is a clear signal of intent: that we are ready to work together to deliver growth and opportunity for the Clyde and the businesses, people and communities who depend on it.”
He added: “The River Clyde has a proud maritime heritage, and the businesses within this Alliance are the custodians of that legacy today, building, maintaining and supporting vessels that matter to Scotland and the UK. But this is about more than protecting what we have. It’s about looking forward: securing the skills pipeline that will allow the Clyde to win and deliver the next generation of work, invest in innovation, and ensure maritime engineering continues to thrive here for decades to come.”
Skills and infrastructure
The alliance builds on the Clyde Maritime Skills Programme, developed by maritime employers with Skills Development Scotland, Glasgow City Region, local authorities and colleges.
That programme was supported by £2 million of Scottish Government Economic Intervention funding and used to test approaches to workforce planning, training and collaborative delivery across the sector.
The CMA’s initial priorities include skills and workforce development, inward investment, joint funding bids and work on larger strategic projects along the river.
Among those priorities are the Scottish Maritime Technology Park and Inchgreen, with the alliance aiming to bring industry and public-sector bodies together around investment and funding for both.
A small secretariat team is also planned to coordinate activity and assist members with funding bids and delivery.
Stephen Flynn, Cabinet Secretary for Economy, Tourism and Transport, said the Scottish Government had provided more than £1.3 million to help accelerate the alliance and support engineering and maritime skills programmes across the Glasgow City Region, alongside £30,000 from Scottish Enterprise to establish the organisation.
Flynn said: “Maritime and defence are growth sectors and as investment in UK and allied defence capabilities continues to grow, Scotland is well placed to seize the opportunities that come with it.”
He added: “Realising that potential requires skills, investment and collaboration that no single organisation can deliver alone. The Scottish Government is proud to support the Alliance and will work with its members and partners as that work progresses.”
UK Government Minister for Scotland Melanie Ward pointed to defence activity on the Clyde and elsewhere in Scotland, including shipbuilding, submarine support, cyber, space, radar and electronic warfare.
She said: “The UK Government is delivering a defence dividend to support Scotland’s maritime sector – including through our Defence Investment Plan – as it continues to deliver critical national infrastructure. From Clyde and Rosyth shipbuilding, to Faslane and submarine support, to cyber, space, radar and electronic warfare, Scotland remains central to UK defence capability.”
Ward added: “This Alliance will help unlock high-quality jobs, boost skills, and drive inward investment across the Glasgow City Region and beyond.”
Lucia Retter, Deputy Director of Defence, Security & Justice at RAND Europe, said the earlier study had brought together industry, education, skills bodies and government to establish a common picture of the Clyde’s workforce requirements and economic potential.
She said: “The creation of the CMA shows how a clear vision based on robust evidence can turn shared ambition into meaningful change.”
The alliance is now seeking additional members from the maritime supply chain, education sector, investment community and public bodies as it moves from its initial formation into longer-term work on skills, infrastructure and industrial growth.

ASTRAKHAN, September 16. /TASS/. The Caspian 2026 international exercise with the participation of Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, and Turkmenistan, took place in Astrakhan for the first time since 2016, the Russian Emergency Situations Ministry reported.
It reported that Russian Minister of Emergency Situations Alexander Kurenkov arrived in Astrakhan on Wednesday on a working visit to open the international exercise at the corporate training center of PJSC Lukoil, with the participation of five Caspian states.
"The Caspian 2026 exercise allowed rescue workers to establish direct contacts and practice the skills necessary for rescuing victims and responding to emergencies," Kurenkov said following the event.

The rescue teams practiced six scenarios: water accidents, natural and man-made fires, biological contamination threats, chemical accidents, oil spills, building collapses, and traffic accidents. The main objective was the evacuation of injured people rescued from land, water, and the air. "The practical part allowed us to test the protocols for interagency and international cooperation in the context of a large-scale emergency," the ministry noted.
In addition, the minister presented departmental awards to foreign delegates for their active participation in the development of international cooperation in the field of emergency prevention and response, as well as in the preparation and conduct of the Caspian 2026 exercise. In particular, five representatives of the rescue services of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Turkmenistan received the Medal ‘For cooperation between rescue services.’ "I would like to note that today’s awards symbolize our partnership, trust, and shared responsibility for safety, as well as recognition of your conscientious approach to your professional duties and loyalty to your duty," the minister added.
Previously, similar exercises were held in Astrakhan in 2016, followed by exercises in Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan. At that time, the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained the return to this format of exercises by citing the growing risks of natural and man-made emergencies and the need to develop practical cooperation among the Caspian states.

Kyiv • UNN
The Syzran and Saratov oil refineries halted processing after drone attacks. The shutdown could exacerbate fuel shortages and export restrictions in Russia.
The oil refineries of Russia’s "Rosneft", located in the cities of Syzran and Saratov on the Volga, halted oil processing after Ukrainian drone attacks this month, three industry sources said on Wednesday. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
The Syzran refinery ceased operations on Tuesday, September 15, while the Saratov refinery stopped processing as early as September 11.
According to the sources, the attack on the Syzran refinery damaged several facilities, including the main CDU-6 crude oil primary processing unit, with a capacity of 17.1 thousand tonnes per day. It accounts for about 71% of the facility’s processing capacity.
Repairing the damaged unit could take at least a month. Another unit at the Syzran refinery – CDU-5, with a capacity of 7.1 thousand tonnes per day – is undergoing repairs following a drone attack in July.
The Saratov refinery suspended oil processing on September 11 following another drone attack. According to the sources, the facility had also halted operations on September 8 due to equipment damage and fires, but was preparing to resume processing on September 10–11.
The refinery was also forced to shut down for several weeks following a drone attack on August 2.
The shutdown of the two facilities could exacerbate the fuel shortage on the domestic Russian market. Against the backdrop of supply disruptions, Russia has already restricted exports of gasoline, diesel fuel and jet fuel.

Unknown

A drone that was shot down by a NATO fighter jet in the skies above Lithuania for the first time was likely directed at Ukraine and veered off course, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Wednesday.
“Most likely, it was a Russian drone intended for Ukraine that was diverted from its course by Ukrainian electronic warfare measures and entered our territory, where it was shot down,” Nausėda told reporters after a state defense council meeting.
Nausėda identified the drone as a Gerbera, a low-cost plywood long-range aerial drone used by Russia. Gerberas are often employed as decoys to overwhelm air defenses, but they can also carry explosives.
An Italian fighter jet that is part of NATO’s Baltic air policing mission intercepted the unmanned aircraft over central Lithuania early Tuesday.
Russia has not commented on the incident.
Suspected Russian drones have previously been shot down over Poland, Romania, Latvia and Estonia, all of which are NATO and EU members.
Lithuania’s public broadcaster LRT, citing government officials, reported that the drone entered the country from Belarus and crossed 100 kilometers (62 miles) of territory before it was shot down.
Belarus is not formally involved in Russia’s war against Ukraine, but it has allowed Russian forces to use its territory as a staging ground for military operations.
Nausėda said the Lithuanian army is analyzing the drone’s electronics to determine its targeting. He said Lithuania needs to have the means to intercept drones, but questioned the efficiency of using fighter jets to do so.
The president also said that the security situation in Lithuania and across NATO countries more broadly remains unchanged, but warned that “incidents, provocation, sabotage acts, including false-flag operations” are still possible.
Reuters contributed reporting.

Israeli election is a contest over how to continue Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:30:29 UTC
23:30:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli election is a contest over how to continue the genocide in Gaza
The electoral slates for the upcoming Israeli Knesset elections are in. A total of 38 parties have submitted their candidate lists, and while a few new names have emerged, the lists themselves hold no major surprises. The real surprise has been who is emerging as Benjamin Netanyahu’s strongest challenger.
For months, that role belonged to Naftali Bennett, who had a short stint as Prime Minister between 2021-22. Bennett and Yair Lapid have formed B’Yachad, a centre-right anti-Netanyahu party. But a relative newcomer has completely overtaken both: Gadi Eisenkot.
Eisenkot spent four years as Israeli army chief of staff before establishing a new centre-right political party, Yashar, in 2025. Yashar has surged in the polls ever since, and Eisenkot is now the frontrunner to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu.
Eisenkot is being pitched as the polar opposite of Netanyahu: where many see the latter as a slick, elitist politician, Eisenkot is cast as a straight-talking, blue-collar man. Eisenkot’s team are also highlighting his personal sacrifice. His son died taking part in the genocide in Gaza, whilst Netanyahu’s son, Yair, has avoided being called up for reserve duty – and has spent much of his time since 2023 in Miami. All of this paints a contrasting image of Netanyahu, one that does not reek of corruption or elitism.
Scratch the surface, however, and the two differ very little on the fundamentals. Unsurprisingly, Eisenkot is an avid supporter of the expansion of the settlement enterprise and the genocidal policy in Gaza. What is less well-known is that, as head of the Israeli army northern command in 2006, he was the one who articulated the Dahyieh Doctrine in Lebanon. Named after a neighbourhood in Beirut that was flattened by the Israeli army, this doctrine is a military tactic that calls for the deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure. International law has condemned it as illegal.
That underlying convergence is easy to miss beneath the noise of the election campaigns, with both Eisenkot and Netanyahu fighting aggressive publicity campaigns. This will be the first election since the start of the genocide in Gaza and will prove to be a real test for Netanyahu, whose coalition is being undone at the seams.
Indeed, Israeli politics is all about coalition; no government has been formed without one, and everyone is competing to show the Israeli public who is more genocidal.
That competition has played out most starkly on social media over the last few months. In late August, Bezalel Smotrich, the Israeli finance minister and a key figure in Netanyahu’s coalition, posted an AI campaign video in which he mocked Palestinians and called for the Judaizing of the Negev and the Galilee – areas which have large populations of Palestinian citizens of Israel.
In another AI video posted by Itamar Ben Gvir, the Israeli internal security minister and another key figure in Netanyahu’s coalition, depicted Palestinian political prisoners on an industrial conveyor belt entering into an Israeli prison and coming out emaciated. This reality has already been well documented. The caption to the video read ‘we promised – we delivered '. It amassed four million views before Ben Gvir’s account took it down.
Both Smotrich and Ben Gvir are vital to Netanyahu’s coalition. However, recent spats have threatened that unity. Ben Gvir has refused to enter into an alliance with Smotrich’s party, which could leave it below the election threshold. At the same time, Ben Gvir has also accused Netanyahu of plotting with Eisenkot to form a coalition behind their backs. These cracks could prove to be the final undoing of Netanyahu’s political career.
Meanwhile, his opponents are also throwing everything they have at him. One of the key weapons in the anti-Netanyahu politicians' arsenal is the accusation that he knew 7 October was going to happen. Haaretz recently published convincing new details on this in an exposé. According to the Israeli newspaper, UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed called Netanyahu and warned him, in a 45-minute conversation, of a major operation being planned by Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar. Netanyahu reportedly responded that he believed that any threat would be confined to the West Bank and that the Israeli regime was prepared.
The authors of the exposé conclude that Netanyahu did not take the warning seriously; he did not brief Shin Bet, Mossad or the army heads. This has also since been corroborated. Since the publication of this report, Netanyahu’s office denounced the story and has filed a defamation claim against Haaretz. But there’s no doubt serious damage has been done.
Nevertheless, being reviled is not the same as being defeated. Netanyahu has a remarkable ability to survive, not least because his opponents have repeatedly failed to come together. What we can be sure of is that, whichever way this election plays out, the contest is only between politicians who have no interest in ending the genocide in Gaza; the only difference will be how they will continue to manage it.

Yesterday, the Italian Embassy in Berlin hosted the opening event of Rare Book Week Berlin, which brings together the international community of rare and collectible books through September 20, with the participation of over one hundred antiquarian booksellers and galleries from fifteen countries. Two works by Johann Wolfgang Goethe were presented in the Embassy’s Fireplace Lounge. 40% of Ukrainians ready to relocate if conditions deteriorate 'significantly' this winter, poll reveals

The survey, conducted by Gradus on Sept. 4–7, polled 1,000 Ukrainians aged 18–60 living in cities with more than 50,000 residents, excluding the occupied territories and areas with active hostilities.
In the lead-up to winter, Ukrainians are preparing for Russia to once again target the country's energy infrastructure in an attempt to make the country unlivable.
