Scientists find an immune “false alarm” that may drive rapid aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:05:35 UTC
23:05:35 KST

Scientists find an immune “false alarm” that may drive rapid aging
- Date:
- September 16, 2026
- Source:
- The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that some severe genetic disorders linked to rapid aging may be driven not just by damaged DNA, but by the body’s overreaction to that damage. When broken DNA fragments leak into the wrong part of a cell, an immune sensor called cGAS can mistake them for signs of a viral infection, triggering chronic inflammation and even interfering with DNA repair itself.
- Share:
New research suggests that an overactive immune sensor may play a major role in severe genetic disorders linked to rapid aging. By reducing the activity of this sensor, scientists were able to improve tissue health across several biological systems, challenging long-held ideas about how DNA damage drives degeneration.
The immune system is designed to recognize and eliminate threats such as viruses. But under certain conditions, that protective machinery can mistakenly react to the body's own damaged DNA. When fragments of DNA are treated as if they came from an invading virus, the resulting immune response can trigger chronic inflammation that harms healthy tissue.
An international research team led by Dr. Marva Bergman and Prof. Itamar Harel at Hebrew University, working with Prof. Yehuda Tzfati, Prof. Ido Ben-Ami (Hebrew University and Sha'are Zedek Medical Center), and Prof. Bérénice Benayoun (University of Southern California), found that this misplaced immune reaction is a major contributor to tissue degeneration in severe, rapid-aging disorders.
When the researchers reduced this immune false alarm, they saw improvements across multiple biological systems.
Rethinking DNA Damage and Rapid Aging
The study focused on rare DNA damage-repair (DDR) syndromes such as Ataxia-Telangiectasia (A-T) and Bloom syndrome. In these disorders, the cellular systems responsible for repairing routine DNA damage do not work properly.
As a result, damaged DNA can accumulate throughout the body, creating genomic instability and contributing to neurodegeneration, increased cancer risk, and premature aging.
For decades, researchers largely assumed that the unrepaired DNA itself was the main force driving cellular decline. The new findings suggest the picture is more complicated.
"Our results show that the damage isn't acting alone," said Prof. Harel. "It's the body's response to that damage, an exaggerated, chronic inflammatory reaction, that drives much of the degeneration."
When Damaged DNA Triggers an Immune False Alarm
When DNA repair breaks down, pieces of DNA can escape into the cell's cytosol. Once there, they can activate a molecular sensor called cGAS.
Under normal circumstances, cGAS helps defend the body by detecting viral DNA. The problem is that the sensor cannot always distinguish foreign genetic material from fragments of the body's own DNA.
That confusion can lead to persistent sterile inflammation, meaning inflammation that occurs without an infection. Instead of protecting the body, the prolonged immune response begins damaging tissues.
The researchers also identified another unexpected role for cGAS.
In addition to activating inflammation, cGAS can move into the cell nucleus and directly disrupt DNA repair. That means the same molecule can contribute to degeneration in two ways: by promoting inflammation and by interfering with the cellular machinery that fixes damaged DNA.
Under normal conditions, cGAS is an important part of the body's defenses. But when DNA damage becomes overwhelming, its activity may become harmful.
Turning Down cGAS Restored Tissue Function
To determine whether reducing this response could change the course of disease, the researchers used a fast-aging vertebrate model that makes it possible to study aging-related biological changes over a relatively short period.
When cGAS activity was lowered, several major disease features improved. These included neuroinflammation, tissue degeneration, and loss of reproductive capacity.
"We weren't just slowing decline," said Dr. Bergman. "We saw broad restoration of tissue function. It suggests that the body can cope with more DNA damage than we assumed, if the inflammatory response is kept in check."
The results raise the possibility that treating disorders caused by DNA damage may not require repairing every individual DNA lesion.
Instead, future therapies could potentially focus on controlling how the body responds to that damage.
A Potential New Treatment Strategy
That approach could offer a different way to treat severe DNA repair disorders. Rather than trying to correct every damaged piece of genetic material, researchers may be able to reduce the harmful inflammatory reaction that follows.
There is an important complication, however. cGAS is also essential for detecting viral infections, so simply shutting the pathway down could weaken antiviral immunity.
Any future treatment would therefore need to reduce the damaging effects of cGAS without eliminating its protective role.
The findings may also have implications beyond rare genetic conditions. Chronic inflammation and genomic instability are both common features of many age-related diseases, raising the possibility that similar mechanisms could contribute to broader forms of degeneration.
Aging, Reproduction, and Long-Term Health
Other studies from the same research group have explored how basic biological programs, including reproduction and developmental timing, interact with aging and lifespan.
Taken together, the work supports a broader idea: biological systems that help organisms survive, grow, and reproduce early in life may also influence how long tissues remain healthy later on.
The researchers emphasize that reversing severe disease-related degeneration is not the same as slowing the fundamental biological rate of aging.
Even so, the study points to a potentially important shift in how scientists think about DNA damage. The damage itself may be only part of the problem. The body's own response to that damage can also drive decline, and controlling that response could open new possibilities for treating some of the most difficult degenerative disorders.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Marva Bergman, Uri Goshtchevsky, Tehila Atlan, Gwendoline Astre, Ryan Halabi, Hosniyah El Ayoubi, Eitan Moses, Aaron J.J. Lemus, Bérénice A. Benayoun, Yehuda Tzfati, Ido Ben-Ami, Itamar Harel. A dual role for cGAS in shaping cellular and organismal responses to genomic instability. Genes, 2026; 40 (11-12): 852 DOI: 10.1101/gad.352760.125

Axios first reported the Pentagon’s account of the incident on Tuesday. US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the attempted seizure to the outlet and several others, saying the targeted unmanned surface vessel “remains under US operational control.”
The Associated Press said Hawkins identified the platform as an 8-meter Saildrone. California-based Saildrone produces several models of autonomous craft featuring a distinctive sail-like structure that carries solar panels and instruments, including a 7-meter model known as the Explorer.

Earlier this month, the IRGC reported destroying a Saildrone Explorer and released footage showing the drone on fire.
The paramilitary force also published footage of what it described as “one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines” operated by the US Navy that had been seized by Iran. CENTCOM said the submersible drone was an older model and did not carry sensitive equipment.
Tehran has previously reverse-engineered American military technology in an effort to bolster its own capabilities. Iran’s Shahed 171 Simorgh and Shahed Saeqeh drones resemble the US RQ-170, one of which Iran captured after it crossed into Iranian airspace on a surveillance mission in 2011.
Iranian kamikaze drones have played a significant role in the ongoing conflict with the US, which Washington launched alongside Israel in late February.
The continuing confrontation has significantly disrupted global energy markets, as both the US and Iran have sought to pressure the other through restrictions on oil exports from the Persian Gulf.

Central Bank puts rate-cutting cycle on hold

Unknown Publisher

23:03:34 KST

Central Bank puts rate-cutting cycle on hold
The Central Bank did not cut its key interest rate for the first time since 2025, pausing the cycle of monetary policy easing that had been underway since last June. It said the pause was needed due to a challenging situation with rising prices, driven to some extent by Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
- At a rate-setting meeting on Friday, held against the backdrop of accelerating inflation, the Central Bank said it did not even consider cutting the rate, which had been lowered continuously from June 2025 over ten consecutive meetings. Although it described the increase in fuel prices caused by shortages resulting from Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries as a one-off factor, it has affected prices of a broader range of goods and services. Core inflation, which excludes the most volatile components, rose to 5-6% on an annualized basis in July, it said, mainly as higher logistics costs were passed on through the supply chain — a trend the Central Bank had previously explained.
- Ukrainian attacks on the warehouses of Russian online marketplaces are currently having a “negligible” impact on inflation, said Nabiullina. She did not provide specific figures.
- Inflationary risks remain greater than disinflationary risks, it said, mainly due to strong demand and supply shortages due to the “withdrawal of production capacity” (a formulation the Central Bank uses to talk in code about the shutdown of oil refineries due to Ukrainian strikes), as well as wages growing faster than labor productivity. Although wage growth is slowing and gradually converging with productivity growth, the gap between the two remains significant.
- The economy is growing at a moderate pace in the third quarter. The Central Bank did not provide specific figures, but Russia’s year-on-year GDP growth was 0.6% in July, down from 1.6% in June.
- Tight monetary policy is also necessary because of the large share of subsidized lending, Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina explained. In the corporate lending sector, for example, one-quarter of loans have been issued at interest rates at least two percentage points below the key rate.
- Going forward, the Central Bank may have to pursue a tighter monetary policy if the government projects a higher structural primary budget deficit than the regulator has incorporated into its baseline forecast (we wrote more about those forecasts here). Correspondingly, if the deficit shrinks faster, it would be able to cut rates faster.
Why the world should care
The “one-off factors” of fuel shortages and price increases caused by Ukrainian attacks have brought a halt to a rate-cutting cycle that had lasted more than a year. Vladimir Putin had last week effectively justified this pause in advance by publicly backing Nabiullina and saying that pumping more money into the economy was dangerous at a time when the government and the Central Bank were deliberately suppressing inflation.

Annual pay differs by about €10,000 between Spanish regions, but a 90-square-metre home can cost up to €383,000 more. In the Balearic Islands and Madrid, buyers need more than €129,000 saved for the deposit and other upfront costs.
In Spain, earning a good salary does not necessarily make it easy to buy a home. An analysis by iAhorro reveals wide disparities between regions: while salaries vary by around €10,000 a year across Spain, the price of a 90-square-metre home can differ by almost €383,000.
The biggest hurdle is the money that has to be saved before applying for a mortgage. To buy a 90-square-metre home, the buyer has to put down around 30% of the price to cover the deposit and other costs. In the Balearic Islands, that comes to about €144,000, compared with €29,000 in Extremadura and €30,000 in Castile-La Mancha.
Prices account for much of this gap. A 90-square-metre property costs around €480,000 in the Balearic Islands and €431,000 in Madrid. By contrast, it costs about €97,000 in Extremadura and around €100,000 in Castile-La Mancha. So a higher salary does not always offset the cost of housing.
Savings also make the difference. If a family sets aside 35% of its income to save for the deposit, it could gather the money needed in less than five years in nine regions: Galicia, Navarra, Aragón, La Rioja, Murcia, Asturias, Castile and León, Extremadura and Castile-La Mancha.
At the other end of the scale are the Balearic Islands, Madrid and the Canary Islands. In these territories, five years of saving would not be enough to raise the money needed for a 90-square-metre home. For someone buying alone, the effort is even greater: they would need to save for 14.2 years in the Balearic Islands, 10.7 years in Madrid and 10.1 years in the Canary Islands.
According to iAhorro’s head of communications, Laura Martínez, quoted in a statement, the main problem is not so much paying the mortgage as pulling together the money to get started: “The hardest part is managing to save.”
According to the analysis, young people and buyers living alone find it hardest to overcome this first barrier.

Amazon to launch Ring ‘neighbourhood watch’ app in UK amid US privacy fears

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:00:21 UTC
23:00:21 KST

Amazon’s doorbell camera maker Ring is to launch its Neighbours community app in the UK in an attempt to supplant neighbourhood WhatsApp or Facebook groups.
The service is intended as a modern equivalent of a community message board, where neighbours can post about safety, community matters or lost pets.
It is being made available free of charge inside the existing Ring app for UK users from 21 October and can be used by anyone, regardless of whether they own one of the brand’s products.
“We used to have the village noticeboard, but as things have changed we no longer have that local connection,” said Dave Ward, the managing director of international for Ring. “Instead what you see in WhatsApp or other services is quite a broad-stroked flood of information, the bins being left out, that sort of thing. It’s a big group that ends up getting muted.
“We’re trying to tailor this down to just the things that really matter to your immediate community and then it becomes super useful.”
Those who join the service set their address and a radius of between 0.1 and five miles to join the local community.
Some of the more controversial features of the Neighbours service from the US will not be immediately available in the UK. That includes the Neighbours Verified service, which allows entities and services such as the local fire brigade to post advisory messages to local communities.
The Community Requests feature, which allows the police to issue calls for footage from Ring cameras in a local area in response to incidents, has drawn the most ire from privacy campaigners. It allows those with footage of incidents to share it with the police on an opt-in and per-event basis. The police are not informed of those that choose not to share footage.
Both features are being developed for release in the UK but not until later this year at the earliest.
Neighbours will launch with basic anonymised posting narrowed into categories, which must conform to a strict set of guidelines barring illegal content, discrimination, speculation or multiple other conditions.
The posts are moderated by AI and humans before and after being published. Content can be shared from Ring doorbells and other cameras.
“We are going to coach people to make sure they’re creating the right sort of post, asking them if that’s really something they want to write or whether it really need that descriptive term, to help stop the type of content no one wants to see and make it more community focused. That’s very different to other places [such as WhatsApp groups],” Ward said.
Amazon bought the video doorbell and home security camera maker in 2018 in a deal reportedly worth more than $1bn.
The new service will also have a feature called “Search Party for Dogs”, which allows users of lost pets to post an image and report of a lost dog.
Those in the neighbourhood who have Ring cameras and a suitable cloud subscription can opt in to join the search. They will then be notified if their cameras see a dog, prompted to check whether it is the correct dog, and then can optionally notify and share the video with the pet owner.
In an attempt to negate some privacy fears, Ring recently announced a new default encryption mechanism for camera footage called TAKE (throw away the key encryption). This feature provides Ring’s systems time-limited keys to the recordings, blocking the company and others access to the videos after 24 hours. Further processing or access, including by law enforcement, requires user consent to issue replacement 24-hour keys from the user’s Ring app.

Even light drinking is linked to worse hand dexterity and balance as we age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:00:10 UTC
23:00:10 KST

A recent study suggests that even low-level alcohol consumption over a person’s lifetime is associated with worse hand dexterity and poorer balance. The research, published in Alcohol and Alcoholism, indicates that the combination of advancing age and a higher number of lifetime drinks might negatively affect motor coordination and postural stability in otherwise healthy adults.
Manual dexterity involves the ability to make coordinated hand and finger movements to grasp and manipulate objects. Static postural stability refers to the ability to maintain balance and hold the body upright while standing still. Both of these physical skills are necessary for independent daily living as people age, helping with everything from buttoning a shirt to avoiding falls.
Historically, public health guidelines often framed light drinking as safe or even protective against certain cardiovascular issues. “For decades, ‘low-level’ alcohol consumption at or below current guidelines (≤1 standard drink equivalent/day for females, ≤2 standard drink equivalents/day for males) has been proposed to carry minimal systemic health risks or functional consequences,” Timothy C. Durazzo, a professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences at the Stanford University School of Medicine and a clinical neuropsychologist at the War Related Illness and Injury Study Center within the VA Palo Alto Health Care System, told PsyPost.
However, the scientific consensus has been shifting. “There is increasing evidence that any level of alcohol consumption is associated with increased risk for at least six different types of cancer,” Durazzo noted. He added that even low-level drinking at or below previous federal guidelines “is associated with abnormalities in structure, blood flow and metabolite markers of cell integrity across multiple regions of the human brain.”
Building on this evidence, Durazzo and his colleagues aimed to explore how low-level drinking relates to physical motor skills. Prior structural imaging studies suggested that low-level alcohol consumption is associated with decreased brain tissue integrity, but it was unknown if these subtle brain changes translated to physical functional differences. “However, there are no published studies on the association of low-level alcohol consumption with concurrent measures of manual dexterity and complex motor coordination, and static postural stability in exclusively healthy, non-smoking adults,” Durazzo explained. “These measures are relevant because functional impairments in these areas may have significant consequences for the activities of daily living (ADL), particularly with advancing age.”
To test this, the researchers recruited 83 healthy, non-smoking adults between 21 and 69 years old. The participants were screened to ensure they had no history of psychiatric, neurological, or major medical conditions. They were also required to have a history of low-level drinking, meaning they consumed a limited number of drinks per month and had no history of binge drinking in the year prior to the study.
The researchers used a standardized questionnaire called the Lifetime Drinking History to calculate each participant’s alcohol consumption. From this questionnaire, they determined the total number of drinks consumed over the past year, the past three years, and over the participant’s entire lifetime, as well as their lifetime average drinks per month.
To assess physical coordination, participants completed two standardized behavioral tests. The first was the Lafayette Grooved Pegboard Test, which measures manual dexterity, complex motor coordination, and motor speed. Participants were timed as they quickly inserted 25 small pegs into randomly oriented slots, completing the task once with their dominant hand and once with their non-dominant hand.
The second test was the Sharpened Romberg Test, which measures static postural stability. Participants were asked to stand heel-to-toe with their arms crossed over their chest for 60 seconds. They performed this balancing task first with their eyes open, relying heavily on visual input, and then with their eyes closed, which forces the brain to rely on internal sensory and vestibular systems to stay upright.
When analyzing the grooved pegboard results, the researchers found that recent drinking over the past one or three years did not predict physical performance. Instead, the mathematical combination of a person’s age multiplied by their total lifetime drinks was a reliable predictor of their manual dexterity. A higher combined total of age and lifetime drinks was associated with slower completion times for the dominant hand, as well as slower times when adding the scores of both hands together. “The associations observed were moderate in magnitude and the relationship between the product of age and total lifetime drinks was stronger for the participants’ dominant hand,” Durazzo said.
The balance test yielded a slightly different pattern. Every participant successfully maintained their balance for the full 60 seconds when their eyes were open. For the more difficult eyes-closed condition, a higher lifetime average of drinks per month was related to poorer performance. For each standard deviation increase in lifetime average drinks per month, participants had 2.3 times lower odds of perfectly maintaining their balance for the full 60 seconds.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year. That earlier study, which examined brain tissue thickness and blood flow on MRI rather than behavioral motor coordination and balance, similarly found that higher lifetime alcohol consumption combined with older age was associated with subtle neurological declines in healthy adults.
“Our recent research on this topic, combined with the existing research on the effects of low-level alcohol consumption on the human brain, suggest that lifetime alcohol consumption considered ‘low risk’ combined with increasing age, may have functional and brain biological consequences in healthy adults,” Durazzo noted.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study had a modest sample size, particularly regarding female participants. Because there were only 22 women compared to 61 men, the researchers noted that any sex-specific differences would require further exploration with a larger group of people.
The study design is observational, meaning it cannot firmly establish that alcohol caused the physical declines. Unrecorded lifestyle factors, such as diet, exercise habits, or genetics, might also play a role in motor performance and balance. Future research could look at general health markers, like blood chemistry and vitamins, to see how they interact with alcohol exposure to influence physical coordination over a lifetime.
“Next steps are to investigate the associations of low-level drinking with measures of attention/concentration, learning and memory and processing speed in a similar sample of healthy adults with low-level alcohol intake,” Durazzo added.
The study, “In healthy adults with low-level alcohol intake greater age and lifetime alcohol consumption are associated with poorer manual dexterity and higher lifetime consumption is related to worse postural stability,” was authored by Timothy C. Durazzo, Nicole D. Evangelista, M. Windy McNerney, Ansgar J. Furst, Maheen M. Adamson, Keith Humphreys, and Dieter J. Meyerhoff.

The U.S. has weapons in space. Here’s what that could mean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
Since the dawn of the Space Age, the weaponization of space has been an international concern. Now the United States has announced, with few details, that it has weapons in orbit.
“The United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending … against hostile adversary action,” U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said September 14 at the 2026 Air and Space Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Md.
With such limited information, it’s hard to know what to make of the announcement. But “the world should be listening with open ears about this information because of the wide range of consequences,” says astrodynamicist Thomas González Roberts of Georgia Tech in Atlanta.
Space weapons are difficult to define and encompass many different possible technologies. “There’s real ambiguity about the term ‘space weapon,’” Roberts says. These weapons can involve satellites directly attacking other satellites, with projectiles, explosives, lasers or other methods. A satellite could physically grab and manipulate another satellite. Cyberattacks can incapacitate satellites or wrest control away from their operators. Space weapons could also affect life on the ground, for example, by disrupting GPS services.
And space weapons have a long history. In 1962, the United States tested a nuclear weapon at high altitude, which incapacitated many of the satellites orbiting at that time. Soon thereafter, the 1967 Outer Space Treaty banned weapons of mass destruction in space. (Although, recently, the United States has alleged that Russia is testing technology needed to put a nuclear weapon in orbit.)
Multiple nations, including the United States, have also tested antisatellite weapons that can take spacecraft down by launching weapons from the ground or air. Worryingly, some types of space weapons could make orbits unusable, by strewing dangerous debris that can collide with satellites or anything else in its path.
Science News spoke with Roberts about what we know and don’t know about the weapons Meink referred to. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
SN: What do we know about these space weapons?
Roberts: When I saw this news, my first take was that it’s missing a lot of adjectives. The way we describe a space weapon is by its method of attack and the consequences of using that weapon.
So when I think about what a space weapon is, I think about questions like is an attack attributable — can others see who did it? Is it reversible, meaning the effects on the target can be undone? And will there be public awareness about whether it was successful or not? Could the attacker themselves determine if it was successful or not?
And could there be collateral damage, meaning other satellites or other space assets would be damaged or degraded? This is what I’m curious about for these U.S. weapons.
So, what kind of weapon do I think it is? I think it’s one where the benefits in those categories are greatest.
SN: Could it be connected to plans for the Golden Dome missile defense system, which would put missile interceptors in orbit?
Roberts: I had the same thought. Could this be that? Could this be something different?
The hint [Meink gave] of “space control” as an adjective is bothersome to me. I want more information. Are we talking about affecting your adversary’s ability to control their satellites? Are you saying the capability is for the United States to control another satellite? The use of the word “control” really sparks my thought processes. There are weapons where you can steal control away from someone else: cyberattacks, grappling, noncooperative rendezvous and proximity operations. I don’t know what the statement means in this context.
SN: Should we be concerned about space debris if these weapons are used?
Roberts: Some space weapons produce collateral damage. A fragmentation event produces nondiscriminate debris, meaning debris that will run into you no matter what your nationality is. But many, many satellite attacks, you can easily focus them on just your target. I would imagine the U.S. is talking about that. The U.S. is the biggest actor in space. They can’t afford to jeopardize the environment.
SN: How could someone attack another satellite without producing debris?
Roberts: Jamming it is the best idea here. If you’re jamming the signals with which a satellite receives or sends data, that means it’s not useful to its operator. But that doesn’t mean that it’s dead.
A lot of these attacks are targeting certain subsystems. Shining a laser at a satellite is particularly damaging to an optical or infrared sensor. If you think a satellite is taking pictures of Earth, like any spy satellite or reconnaissance satellite, you might be interested in disabling just that optical sensor.
SN: What might the repercussions of this announcement be?
Roberts: It really invites criticism from U.S. adversaries. The global community has been working for some time on preventing an arms race in outer space. It offers evidence to some who might claim that it’s too late.
Right now, states obfuscate. There’s evidence for Russia and China developing space weapons, testing them and demonstrating them. But largely they deny it. In most cases, they pretend they’re not doing anything at all. And the U.S. is taking a different approach. Instead of obfuscating it, they’re telling everyone.

Eesti 200: Government to curb infrastructure investments to rein in deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:58:00 UTC

Eesti 200: Government to curb infrastructure investments to rein in deficit
Some planned infrastructure and real estate investments will have to be postponed or canceled to cut next year's budget deficit and, if possible, fund modest pay raises for teachers and rescue workers, Education Minister Kristina Kallas told ERR.
According to Kallas, the government has reviewed all revenue and spending in the budget negotiations and looked for savings across all areas.
"We have also reviewed the investment portfolio and the state's real estate costs, so all the reviews in the budget negotiations are complete and the budgets for the coming years are now broadly in place. We know where we are spending, but we still need to tie up the final loose ends on what we can invest additional money in next year," she said.
Kallas said there is no more room to cut investments in people, such as benefits and wages, so the government has turned to infrastructure investments and real estate costs.
"We cannot start cutting benefits, such as higher education funding or hobby education funding — in other words, the investments we make in people. I don't see any room for cuts there; we have already cut them significantly," Kallas said.
"Then there are real estate and infrastructure investments where the state spends quite heavily — Estonia ranks first in Europe in terms of the share of its budget spent on infrastructure and real estate investments. There are certainly some things that can be dropped, meaning we don't carry out those construction projects or that can be postponed until later. That's also possible, in order to improve the budget position," she added.
Erkki Keldo (Reform), who was economy minister at the time, has also previously said that some investments will have to be cut.
Improving the budget position has been the Reform Party's position both before and during the budget talks. More specifically, the party wants to reduce next year's deficit by half a percentage point to 4 percent of GDP.
Kallas said that while there is agreement on cutting investments, Eesti 200 and Reform have not yet agreed on the 4 percent target.
"No, we have not agreed on that target because we said from the outset that we first wanted to see where it was actually possible to make savings and where those cuts could come from. We have now gone through all spending and can see that savings can be made on infrastructure and real estate investments," Kallas said.
Infrastructure investments mainly involve road construction and Rail Baltica. "There are also port and building construction projects, but relatively few. The state invests most heavily in infrastructure. A couple hundred million euros' worth can either be dropped or spread out over a longer period," she said.
Kallas added that the government believes Estonia's infrastructure construction sector is close to overheating because of the construction of Rail Baltica, another reason for the state to scale back its investments for now.
"Estonia's infrastructure construction market is worth about €1 billion and is currently almost at capacity. If the state were to add significantly more investment, the market would overheat and prices would rise, so that may not make sense at all," she said.
Rescuers and teachers still have hope for pay rises
Kallas has previously said that while raising teachers' salaries is a goal in the budget talks, she saw no way to do so because no new spending could be added to the state budget.
She now said work is still underway to find the money.
"Our position is that we have to find the money to provide at least some pay increase because salaries for rescue workers and teachers have lagged behind average wage growth. From Eesti 200's perspective, it is important that the state is still able to invest in areas other than defense because all other areas have had to make cuts over the past four years. The state cannot function on just one area. We have to be able to provide healthcare and school education for children," she said.
"We are currently fighting, if I can put it that way, to find further infrastructure cuts so that we can also direct money toward salaries. So, to put it plainly: I can't promise anything, I don't dare promise anything, but we are working on it," Kallas added.
However, the government cannot meet the Education Personnel Union's demand to raise the minimum teacher salary to Estonia's average wage of €2,312 next year.
"That would require finding €112 million in the state budget next year. That's 0.2 percent of GDP," Kallas said.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal will submit the state budget to the Riigikogu in the final week of September.
Public transport to receive millions in additional funding
Minister of Regional Affairs and Agriculture Hendrik Terras (Eesti 200) told ERR that his areas of responsibility will face a one-time cut of €900,000. It has not yet been decided where exactly the cut will be made.
"We haven't decided on the details yet; we simply agreed that we would make the cut. But broadly speaking, it won't affect public transport. Public transport is our main focus anyway and accounts for most of our ministry's budget, and costs in that area keep rising. Once again, operating public transport has become €10 million more expensive compared with last year," Terras said.
As a result, public transport funding will actually increase next year. With fuel prices currently difficult to predict due to global developments, some of the funding will remain in the government's reserve.
"We agreed on an additional €7.5 million for transport. We also agreed that around €8 million to €10 million would be allocated from the reserve. That's because the situation with fuel prices is so uncertain that we can't currently estimate how much additional money may be needed if fuel prices rise," Terras said.
"In the second and third quarters of next year, we can look at actual fuel prices and how much was spent and the government can then allocate money for fuel from the reserve accordingly," he added.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal will submit the state budget to the Riigikogu in the final week of September.

Will Southeast Asia Actually Benefit From Its AI Boom?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:58:00 UTC
22:58:00 KST

Headlines have for years been touting the emergence of Asia as a global powerhouse in data center development. The nature of headlines is that all too often they prove to be horrendously wrong in the long or even the short run – but when it comes to data centers in Southeast Asia, they are repeatedly getting validated.
The Asia-Pacific’s data center development pipeline reached a record 26.5 GW in the first half of 2026. Southeast Asia accounts for roughly half of the capacity under construction: Malaysia leads with 1,039 MW, followed by Thailand with 859 MW.
All this investment is producing a division of labor among national markets: Singapore concentrates on high-value, power-constrained activity while Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam are absorbing different forms of large scale growth.
The question is not whether Southeast Asia will add more data centers. It undoubtedly will. The more pressing question is whether the infrastructure being built across separate national markets could become the foundation of a regional AI economy.
Numbers of course, matter still. They always will. But not all numbers tell the exact same story. Under construction figures, for example, do not describe current operational capacity. At about 1.46 GW, Singapore retains the largest operational base in Southeast Asia, but its new capacity remains tightly controlled. Limits on power, land, and sustainability all but ensure that the country is unlikely to compete with its neighbors simply by adding volume.
Instead, these constraints strongly favor higher value uses including premium workloads and research compute while reinforcing Singapore’s status as the region’s high trust, highly connected high tech hub, supported by its strengths in talent development, governance, research, and connectivity.
It’s of little surprise, then, that Singapore’s second Data Center Call for Applications and plans for a low-carbon park on Jurong Island both point toward increasingly selective, high specification projects rather than an expansion bonanza. On August 21, the government provisionally awarded 200 MW to four data center operators out of more than 20 applications. This latest and all too predictable display of Singapore’s constraints is bound to gradually push more investment across the Causeway.
Indeed, on the other side of the Johor Strait, Malaysia has emerged as the region’s leading scale market. More available land and comparatively lower costs combined with supportive industrial policy are attracting facilities designed for hyperscale operations and AI training workloads.
Thailand, by contrast, had been expanding from a smaller base, with investment approvals and partnerships with domestic power producers supporting rapid growth particularly around Bangkok.
Indonesia and Vietnam illustrate another approach in which domestic market size and questions of digital sovereignty matter alongside foreign investment. Indonesia is pairing the region’s largest domestic market of about 288 million with large foreign AI projects while still requiring government and other designated strategic data to stay onshore. CoreWeave’s planned 360 MW deployment in Greater Jakarta illustrates how the country is moving from a primarily domestic-demand story toward a major destination for foreign AI infrastructure investment. Meanwhile Vietnam, home to 102 million people, has sought to attract investment through regulatory liberalization, including allowing wholly foreign owned data centers.
Capital, as it tends to, is moving across national markets, potentially enabling workloads to be distributed according to different national advantages, and constraints in one country increasingly affect investment decisions in its neighbors. As a consequence, instead of viewing them as isolated national opportunities, investors increasingly view ASEAN markets as complementary locations within a broader infrastructure strategy.
On August 1, SoftBank’s Singapore subsidiary signed a memorandum of understanding with SC ZEUS, a Singapore-based data center developer, and Robust HPC, a Malaysian high-performance computing specialist, to develop AI data-center capacity focused initially on Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam.
However logical it might be, this cross-border approach also exposes a problem. Instead of removing physical constraints, moving investment across borders redistributes them. Both Malaysia and Thailand are now facing limits in grid connections, transmission capacity, and the speed at which new power can be delivered.
In early September Thailand asked developers to halt work on about 49 projects under construction and froze approvals for about 117 until it finalizes national rules on power, water, siting and local benefit. In Johor, the Malaysian state bordering Singapore, water supply has also been under pressure.
Neither Bangkok or Kuala Lumpur are in a unique place. The United States, which accounts for approximately 45 percent of global data center capacity, is struggling to connect new load to the grid as demand continues to rise. Although energy generation potential is crucial for data center developers, it is far from being the only factor: whether firm power can reach the right location on the required timetable is equally, if not more, important.
The ASEAN Power Grid seeks to make cross-border electricity trade more practical. An early example of what such a broader regional system could look like is offered by the Laos-Thailand-Malaysia-Singapore Power Integration Project, Rest assured, greater regional power connectivity will not eliminate local shortages or transmission bottlenecks, but it could give governments and developers a larger geography over which electricity supply and demand can be balanced. For an industry where expansion is increasingly constrained by access to reliable power, this matters almost as much as the movement of data.
As data centers spring up across the region, a thornier question is also taking shape: what do countries actually capture from all this infrastructure? Data centers bring construction. They bring engineering jobs, energy investment, and tax revenue. They also bring ceremonial ribbons to cut at opening ceremonies. But much of the higher-value activity associated with AI lies elsewhere: software, model development, research, specialized services and the use of AI across domestic industries.
This is similar to a country hosting large electronics assembly operations without capturing the design, chip-making, or software layers that creates most value. Southeast Asia might end up hosting substantial computing capacity without developing a correspondingly deep AI economy.
Hence the terms attached to investment matter a lot. Governments can use access to land, power, and incentives to seek commitments on local skills, research partnerships, supplier development, and access to computing for domestic firms. Keeping foreign operators out should not be the objective. Instead, governments should put the wider AI value chain in their sights by turning data centers from isolated capital projects into anchors for broader technology ecosystems. Data centers should bring skills, suppliers, research capacity, and firms that can continue to create value after the next generation of facilities is installed.
The first challenge is domestic: ensuring that infrastructure investment produces capabilities rather than merely capacity. The second is regional: ensuring that those capabilities and services can operate across borders. Success will not come easily. The SIJORI (Singapore-Johor-Riau) Growth Triangle’s almost four-decade-long history shows that such cooperation may progress at a snail’s pace, and the path is marked by friction and incomplete results aplenty.
While infrastructure is already becoming more geographically distributed, the rules governing its use remain largely national. A company may therefore place servers in various ASEAN countries while having to navigate different requirements for data governance, cybersecurity, licensing, and the cross-border provision of digital services in each market.
There is also a very real risk that infrastructure fragments faster than regulation can connect it. If this happens, the region could end up with growing computing capacity without capturing the economic advantages of regional scale. Facilities would primarily serve national markets, companies would duplicate functions across jurisdictions, and firms seeking to operate regionally would face higher compliance and operating costs.
ASEAN’s Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) may help to address part of this problem. Its scope extends beyond digital trade to areas including cross-border data flows, electronic payments, data protection, talent mobility, AI, and cybersecurity. Those areas are directly relevant to whether computing capacity located in one ASEAN country can support firms, services and users in another.
Naturally, DEFA cannot integrate the physical infrastructure itself. It cannot build transmission lines or address water shortages. Nor can it determine where data centers should be licensed. What DEFA can do is reduce some of the regulatory friction that makes a regional digital economy expensive to operate. Southeast Asia will need both forms of integration: physical connections for power and networks, and common or interoperable rules for data, services, talent and digital commerce.
Two months after signing DEFA, Singapore will assume the 2027 ASEAN chairmanship. The opportunity is ripe for the country to push not only for the agreement’s formal adoption but, in order to reduce cost of operation across the region, for practical implementation as well.
National ambitions for greater control over AI and data will obviously not disappear in an instant, nor should they. But regional integration does not require governments to surrender control over sensitive infrastructure or information. Instead, it requires common rules and interoperability for countries to retain that control while still capturing the economies of regional scale.
The goal should be to turn infrastructure investment into skills, research capacity, local suppliers, and wider AI adoption. These capabilities should regionally be able to reinforce one another: a company operating in one country, computing capacity located in another, and electricity supplied through a wider regional grid need not function as entirely separate national systems.
Ultimately, gigawatts are a crucial yet imperfect measure of success. They make superb headlines, but the real measure is what they enable the region to do next. Bringing infrastructure to various regional countries is hard. But the more difficult challenge is to make national systems work together at a regional level, requiring governments, investors, and ASEAN institutions to ensure that, instead of operating in isolation, projects developed in various countries complement one another. The November 2026 signing of the Digital Economy Framework Agreement followed by Singapore’s 2027 ASEAN chairmanship will show whether policy can catch up with the infrastructure that is rapidly taking shape.

Reddit co-founder says tech industry has been 'tone deaf' in explaining AI: 'Misinformation flying around'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:57:47 UTC
22:57:47 KST

The tech industry has been "tone deaf" in explaining AI and properly informing the public about real risks, Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian told CNBC on Wednesday.
Ohanian said the debate around AI should focus on substantive risks rather than issues that can be used to score political points, arguing that an informed public is essential to navigating the technology. He acknowledged that the tech industry has contributed to the problem by doing a "pretty tone deaf job" of explaining AI, while suggesting that its risks are more mundane than the "Terminator and Skynet" scenarios some fear.
Skynet is a fictional self-aware AI system in the "Terminator" movies that saw humans as a threat and sought to wipe them out.
The comments come days after warnings from researchers at AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic of the rapid advancement of the technology known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI.
RSI refers to AI systems helping develop more advanced models, potentially creating a cycle in which increasingly capable systems contribute to building even more capable ones.
The concern is that if AI systems take over the process of training new models, their human developers could eventually lose control over how those systems evolve.
Ohanian argued that while AI risks are real, apocalyptic "Terminator"-style warnings can distract from real concerns such as agent swarms, when multiple AI agents work together to perform a complicated task.
"There are risks, I do think they're more benign, or they're more banal than people are thinking," he said.
He compared AI to nuclear energy because both technologies are powerful scientific advances that can cause serious harm but also deliver major benefits if managed responsibly.
"I'm hopeful this goes in a healthy direction, and it's just going to require fewer tweets and more, like, thoughtful conversation," Ohanian said.
"The doomer tweet was discouraging," he said without specifying, adding it was "frustrating" when "the slogans are actually not real things."
Earlier this month, an AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic and accused the company and OpenAI of acting irresponsibly when it comes to developing the powerful technology.
Jacob Coxon, who has worked as a researcher at both companies, said on social media that he resigned because he was concerned that Anthropic and OpenAI are "gambling with our lives." He said the people building AI "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."
For Ohanian, nuance is crucial. "We should have a discussion about the important, like real stuff, instead of these things that maybe score some quick political points… I have faith that we can have this discussion."
"It frustrates me because I see all this misinformation flying around, but I do think in the long run, we [will] get it right, and that's what I'm hoping happens. So I'm not terribly worried about that part of it."

The comments come as Israel seeks to expand the network of Arab states formally establishing relations with it, six years after the UAE and Bahrain became the first signatories to the Abraham Accords.
But Kuwait has remained a prominent holdout, with opposition to normalisation deeply rooted in the country’s political and public spheres.
Unlike most other Gulf monarchies, the country has a politically influential parliament, where Islamic and Arab nationalist forces have traditionally opposed normalisation with Israel.

Shelley’s comments came as US President Donald Trump has called for the Abraham Accords to be expanded further across the region.
Trump has previously urged additional countries to join the agreements, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Pakistan, Turkey, Egypt and Jordan, alongside existing signatories the UAE and Bahrain.
In comments cited by the Israeli media, Trump argued that the countries should sign the accords simultaneously after extensive US efforts to advance the initiative.
The renewed push comes against a backdrop of major regional tensions and the continuing fallout from Israel’s war across the region.
Shelley also described Israel-UAE relations as strengthening, saying there had been “dramatic growth” in bilateral ties and cooperation.
He claimed the UAE and Israel were now “true partners at the moment of truth”, while acknowledging that some aspects of their relationship remain sensitive and are not publicly reported.

Taliban seeks US ties, urges Washington to address legacy of Afghanistan war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:57:32 UTC
22:57:32 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The Taliban wants formal diplomatic relations with the US but said Washington must first address the legacy of its two-decade war in Afghanistan, Taliban spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi told CBS News in an interview.
Five years after the Taliban returned to power following the US withdrawal, Balkhi portrayed the end of the foreign military presence as the administration's main achievement, while acknowledging persistent unemployment, economic difficulties and public dissatisfaction.
“The greatest achievement obviously Afghanistan has had is the end of occupation,” said Balkhi, arguing that the country had since seen improvements in security, trade, investment and infrastructure.
He claimed Afghan exports rose from $750 million in 2020 to nearly $2 billion, while the number of factories increased from 1,500 to 6,000. He also said the government had been able to pay civil servants and attract billions of dollars in investment.
Balkhi acknowledged, however, that “there are areas where we haven't met the expectation of the general population,” citing widespread unemployment and other challenges.
The interview on Tuesday also highlighted Afghanistan's continued diplomatic isolation. Russia is the only country to have formally recognized the Taliban government.
Balkhi argued that Afghanistan was already engaging diplomatically with several countries and questioned the practical meaning of formal recognition.
On relations with Washington, he said Kabul wanted diplomatic ties with “every single country of the world, including the United States,” and would welcome the reopening of the US Embassy and American investment in sectors such as minerals and gas.
He also rejected calls by US President Donald Trump for Afghanistan to return billions of dollars worth of American-funded military equipment left behind after the 2021 withdrawal. CBS reported that roughly $7 billion in US military hardware remained in Afghanistan.
“That’s the assets of the state of Afghanistan,” said Balkhi, rejecting any deal linking the equipment to the release of Afghan funds frozen abroad.
Asked about the argument that American taxpayers paid for the equipment, Balkhi responded, “The Americans did a lot of things. Americans killed a lot of people, destroyed the majority of the country. Should they not be paying for that first?”
Balkhi demanded the release of Afghan central bank assets frozen by Washington, saying the funds belonged to the Afghan state rather than the Taliban government.
On the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, Balkhi said the Taliban condemned attacks on civilians and reiterated its commitment under the Doha agreement that Afghan territory would not be used to attack the US or any other country.
The interview also focused on restrictions on women and girls. Regarding the suspension of public schooling for girls from seventh grade onward, Balkhi said alternative forms of education remained available and rejected reports of girls attending clandestine classes despite the restrictions.
“There is no such thing as secret schools,” he said, describing the arrangements as homeschooling or madrasa, or Islamic, education.
Looking back at the war that followed the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001, Balkhi said Afghanistan had learned that conflicts should be resolved through diplomacy.
“War is not the solution, and occupying Afghanistan certainly isn't to your benefit,” he said, urging greater cooperation for Afghanistan's reconstruction and development.

Why are election officials in the US preparing for chaos before midterms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:56:11 UTC
22:56:11 KST

Why are election officials in the US preparing for chaos before midterms?
Trump lashes out at justices who rejected his federal mail-in ballot plan, raising questions on his next electoral moves.
US President Donald Trump has lashed out at the Supreme Court for rejecting his push to curb mail-in voting, raising fears that the US president might use federal powers to meddle in November’s midterm elections.
“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” the president lashed out after the court verdict on Monday. The justices “are merely a shell of their original selves, a court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Selling the war: Purges, polygraphs and propaganda
- list 2 of 3Trump tells Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian diesel supplies
- list 3 of 3Tehran and Muscat delay talks, citing regional consensus need
The ruling means states can continue administering mail-in voting under their existing procedures. Mail-in and absentee ballots have been used in the United States for decades and now account for roughly a third of votes cast nationwide.
Despite the ruling, political analysts and some officials fear that Trump may not let the electoral process proceed as planned, and might pull some other strings to tilt the election in his favour.
So what voting rules exactly has Trump tried to change – and what other powers could his administration seek to use in the run-up to the midterms?
Can Trump use federal powers to tilt the elections in his favour?
Election officials across the country are concerned about the prospects of interference, from the potential for ballot seizures to voter-fraud investigations.
A Reuters investigation based on interviews with dozens of state and local election officials showed that they are adopting new strategies to prepare for political interference, misinformation, cyberattacks and intimidation tactics.
According to the report, more than a dozen local and state election officials said they are hiring outside lawyers or seeking legal training for themselves and their staff to prepare for potential demands by the administration for access to sensitive voting records or election equipment.
Nearly twice that many said they are expanding public outreach and social media campaigns to counter misinformation, including the false claims made by Trump and Republican allies that voting machines are unreliable and mail-in voting is inherently corrupt.
What have the opposition and campaigners said on Trump’s electoral agenda?
Campaigners have fiercely resisted Trump’s executive actions attempting to dictate federal voting procedures. Groups including the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and the Brennan Center for Justice have sued the administration, arguing that the Constitution gives authority over federal elections primarily to states and Congress, rather than the president.
The pushback has also come from Capitol Hill. A bipartisan group of 261 current and former members of Congress filed a brief with the Supreme Court challenging Trump’s executive order and the subsequent Postal Service rule. They argued that the measures violated the separation of powers by taking authority over federal elections that the Constitution grants to states and Congress.
“The Constitution is clear that the states and Congress make the rules for federal elections, not the President,” Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin, one of the lawmakers leading the effort, said.
As per the US Constitution, elections are conducted by local authorities working under the states.
Raskin described Trump’s attempt to use the US Postal Service to regulate mailed ballots as “a naked power grab”, accusing the president of seeking “to inject confusion and chaos into our elections in a last-ditch effort to keep his party in power”.
Senator Alex Padilla, the top Democrat on the Senate Rules Committee, similarly argued that neither the president nor the Postal Service had the authority to determine how states administer elections. He said restricting voting by mail could particularly affect military personnel, people living in rural areas, and Americans living abroad.
The White House rejected accusations that it is seeking to interfere in the midterms, saying its measures are aimed at preventing illegal voting and ensuring confidence in the electoral system.
Why does Trump oppose mail-in voting?
This is not the first time Trump has cast doubt on the security of mail-in voting, citing debunked claims of widespread election fraud associated with it. Trump falsely blamed his presidential election loss on mail-in voting fraud in 2020. Back then, he called the voting system “the greatest scam in the history of politics”. He and his supporters opposed changes made during the COVID pandemic to expand mail-in voting.
Trump and his supporters also claim that the mail-ballot plan enables a large number of non-citizens to register and vote illegally, corrupting elections. For this, he has pushed for the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act (SAVE Act) that would require citizens to provide “documentary proof” that they are American citizens when they register to vote. The legislation is stalled in the Senate over concerns that millions of voters will be disenfranchised.
Studies show that voter fraud is extremely rare. The Heritage Foundation, the conservative-leaning think tank behind Project 2025 – which inspired many Trump administration policies – documented 100 cases of noncitizens voting from 1982 to 2025. That is about 0.000008 percent of more than 1.3 billion votes cast in presidential elections during that time.
What has he done to change election rules?
Trump has been explicit about his desire to assert more federal control over the election, saying in early February that “Republicans ought to nationalise the voting”. The White House has dismissed concerns that federal actions could disrupt the midterms, arguing that the administration is enforcing election laws and safeguarding confidence in voting.
In March 2026, Trump signed an executive order directing the US Postal Service to take control of mail-in voting by designing new envelopes with special barcodes that would allow the federal government to ensure ballots are only from eligible voters.
For the midterms, that move would force all states to adopt a uniform envelope style in a short time.
The order also required states to provide the Postal Service with a list of eligible voters before elections. Several government departments, including Homeland Security and US Citizenship and Immigration Services, would also have the voters’ lists.
The postal agency was additionally empowered to deny mailed ballots if they did not comply with new standards or were not associated with registered voters on the states’ lists.
The attorney general has demanded that 47 states and Washington, DC, a federal district, hand over their complete voter registration lists, according to a tally from the Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan policy group. Eleven states have complied or agreed to comply. The Trump administration has launched lawsuits against the 20 others that refused.

Australia's pre-colonial Indigenous population may have been far larger than estimated: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:56:06 UTC
22:56:06 KST

Beril Canakci
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Australia may have had a much larger Indigenous population before European colonization than previously estimated, with new research putting the median at 2.22 million people.
The study, published Tuesday in the journal Nature Human Behaviour, used archaeological and genetic evidence, historical observations and computer modeling of the continent's environmental capacity to reconstruct the population before British colonization.
Previous estimates have generally placed Australia's pre-colonial Indigenous population between 250,000 and 1 million people. Researchers said earlier figures were affected by the lack of systematic population records and by disease and violence that had already reduced Indigenous communities by the time early colonial estimates were made.
The research estimated that about 93% of the pre-colonial Indigenous population was lost in less than 80 years after the arrival of the First Fleet in 1788, with researchers attributing the demographic collapse to the effects of colonization, including disease and frontier violence.
The study estimated that about 2.06 million excess deaths between 1788 and 1861 would be needed to reconcile its population estimate with historical census records.

How the Houthis are also putting Egypt under pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:56:00 UTC
22:56:00 KST

How the Houthis are also putting Egypt under pressure
September 16, 2026
Any and all ships may pass, at least at first. That was how the spokesperson for Yemen's Houthis rebel militia put it. Transit through the Red Sea would be safe, with one exception: According to the Houthi spokesperson, ships from Saudi Arabia would not be allowed to pass this stretch of the sea.
The comments came during a time when the Houthi militia has been fighting to increase its presence at the southern entrance to the ocean passage. The Houthis now control the tiny volcanic island of Mayun, also known as Perim, at the entrance to the Red Sea, as well as other parts of the Yemeni coast and some small islands.
With these moves, pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia, the country that opposes the Houthis and previously fought a war (unsuccessfully) with them.
But pressure is now also increasing in Egypt. Every decrease in shipping traffic through the Red Sea also impacts one of that country's most important sources of national income, the Suez Canal.
As yet, maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has not been significantly reduced. According to news agency Reuters, last Saturday 24 ships passed through it and on Sunday, 27 did so. That is around the same as the 10-day average. The Houthis appear to want to signal that their plan is not stop traffic altogether. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is a chokepoint between Yemen and and the Horn of Africa. Ships have to pass it to enter the Red Sea.
In general though, maritime traffic has decreased here, according to maritime intelligence organization Kpler. On Monday, 21 ships went through the strait. But in the middle of July, the average number of ships passing through was 47.
How will things develop from here?
"The Houthis could actually interrupt, or at least significantly disturb, the connection between Asia and Europe," says Stephan Roll, a senior fellow with the Africa and Middle East division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, or SWP, in Berlin. "So first we have to wait and see how big the actual disruption to the Suez Canal will be."
Even complete control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait doesn't automatically mean control of the Suez Canal. But it does give the Houthis a further opportunity to indirectly threaten traffic.
For Egypt, this new disruption comes at a particularly unwelcome time. Houthi attacks at the end of 2023 had already disrupted business at the Suez Canal. According to the International Monetary Fund, earnings at the canal in 2024 fell by around $6 billion (€5.2 billion). Before the current security crisis, Egypt had been making between $9 billion and $10 billion from the Suez Canal annually.
More recently things had actually been improving again.
"The situation is certainly problematic compared to 2023," Roll told DW. "But it is not so clearly negative compared to the situation one, two or even three months ago."
Thanks to rising oil prices and the resulting higher cost of circumnavigating Africa, shipping companies had been using the Red Sea as they travelled between Asia and Europe.
The Suez Canal's finances had recently improved. The Suez Canal Authority, which manages the passage, reported that during the 2025-2026 fiscal year, revenues had risen by 23% to $4.67 billion (€4.5 billion). Despite the various conflicts in the region, this actually represented a recovery for the Suez Canal.
Houthi offensive could change all that
There is also a second critical factor. After recent drone attacks that the Saudis blamed on Iraqi groups, Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline to the coastal city of Yanbu will be out of service for at least several weeks. Between 4 million and 5 million barrels of oil were going through the 1,200 kilometer pipeline per day as the Saudis attempted to circumnavigate the Strait of Hormuz, blocked due to the US-Iran war. This latest damage could put as much as 4% of global supply at risk, according to Reuters.
An analysis by Qatar-based think tank, the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, warns of a scenario where the Persian Gulf and Red Sea are both likely to become more precarious. The East Asia Institute, a think tank based in Korea, has also written about the dangers of dual choke points.
Neither route can be seen as an independent alternative because flows of oil and trade depend on secure connections at several points.
Certainly for Egypt, this will increase economic pressure.
What can Egypt do about this?
In geopolitical terms, there is not a lot that Egypt can do. The Houthis in Yemen have only impacted the country indirectly.
"Egypt's military capabilities are very limited," Steffen Krüger, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation's Cairo office, explained.
Egyptian interventions in Yemen in the 1960s are still remembered in Cairo — back then, the country sent thousands of troops to support a new government in Yemen, in a war that would eventually last years — so Egypt would prefer to exercise restraint there.
"Although Egypt formally remains a member of the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis, its participation is largely symbolic," Krüger told DW.
And there is no doubt that Egyptian officials have noted the lack of success other countries like Saudi Arabia and the US have had in their attempts to rein in the Houthis.
"The Egyptians simply have no real alternative," argues the SWP's Roll, adding that Egypt is likely to try diplomacy first. "Basically they have to try to put a positive spin on a bad situation and somehow negotiate appropriate arrangements with the Houthis."
London-based media outlet The New Arab wrote that the Houthis offered to talk directy to Cairo about shipping security via the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) in London. But the ICS rejected that claim and said that "no such request was ever made to ICS" and that the chamber hasn't had direct communications with the Houthis.
On Tuesday, Saudi Arabian leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, travelled to Cairo to try to get Egypt's support against the Houthis.
"The Egyptians are likely to wait and see," says Roll of the SWP about the next steps for Cairo.
Egypt has a difficult balancing act to perform. The country is closely allied with Saudi Arabia but is also bound to suffer economically in any further escalation between the Saudis and the Houthi group.
A decisive factor will depend on if, and how, the Houthis restrict maritime shipping, and if they go beyond vessels with Saudi Arabian ties, or whether they are just using their currenty improved military position to exert pressure on their enemies.
This story was originally published in German.

Ukraine approves more than 80 companies for private air defense

Eighty-one companies are now authorized to form private air defense units — up from 51 in mid-July — the Defense Ministry said on Sept. 16, as the country, and particularly Kyiv and the surrounding area, come under near-constant Russian attack.
As Russia shifts its bombardment tactics to near-hourly drone attacks throughout the day, increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure, more businesses are joining the program. The ministry says the program is designed to protect workers and facilities while reducing pressure on military air defenses, which now face increased strain beyond concentrated overnight barrages.
Established by the Cabinet of Ministers in November 2025, the private air defense program allows businesses to voluntarily form and finance air defense groups staffed by trained and certified civilian employees. Eligible companies include providers of essential services such as electricity, water, transport, and communications, alongside security firms protecting other businesses.
Companies apply to the Defense Ministry for authorization, then agree with the Air Force command on their units' operations. Under rules introduced in March, participating businesses can also temporarily receive military air defense equipment and ammunition unused by combat units, with Air Force approval.
Private air defense is just one component of Ukraine's multi-level system of airspace protection.
The first successful interceptions under the program were announced in March, when a company's unit downed Russian drones in Kharkiv Oblast. In April, the ministry reported a private group's first interception of a jet-powered Shahed-type drone.
By mid-July, private air defense had downed more than 50 Shahed and Zala drones, according to the ministry.

Catherine Ringer dies: grief in music and political circles

Catherine Ringer died at 68 from cancer on 14 September. Since then, artists, politicians and cultural figures have paid tribute to the voice and freedom of the music icon.
Some voices you recognise in a split second. Catherine Ringer’s was one of them. A voice that could laugh, rasp, scream, sing of love, desire or madness. A voice that never wanted to be put in a box.
The announcement of her death has triggered a wave of emotional reactions. Among them, French President Emmanuel Macron, who paid tribute to a personality he called "unclassifiable, irreverent, profoundly French".
On X, the president accompanied his message with a clip from 2024 in which the artist sang 'La Marseillaise' during a ceremony marking the enshrining of the right to abortion in the Constitution.
The Élysée also paid solemn tribute on Wednesday in an official statement. The text traces the journey of this "all-round artist", born in 1957 in Suresnes and immersed from childhood in an artistic family environment. After her first steps on stage at the Café de la Gare and then at the Palace, as well as "darker, more painful experiences" from which she managed to break free, 1979 marked a major turning point when she met Fred Chichin.
Together, they created Les Rita Mitsouko, a duo with an art "free and impossible to categorise", which broke through to the general public in 1984 with the resounding success of the song 'Marcia Baïla'.
Following the death of her partner in 2007, Catherine Ringer carried on her career "with deeply moving dignity", alternating solo projects with returns to the stage to revive the band’s cult tracks. Described variously as "a diva, a popular singer and an avant-gardist", she leaves, according to the presidency, "a singular, flamboyant artistic legacy" that has left a lasting mark on musical life in France.
Across the political spectrum, voices have spoken up to stress that she was also a tireless activist, but without a party label – feminist through her actions long before the word became a slogan – standing up to sexists on TV shows as much as to right-thinking orthodoxies. Among them, Dominique de Villepin on X (source in French) and France Insoumise MEP Manon Aubry (source in French).
Her peers pay tribute and thank her
Rock musicians, pop artists, rappers or icons of French chanson: all are mourning the loss of a "big sister" of the stage.
On social media, the music world seemed to freeze in order to salute the woman who injected a punk streak of madness into mainstream French pop.
Singer-songwriter Benjamin Biolay posted a powerful tribute on Instagram (source in French), recalling the formative shock of the album 'The No Comprendo', and honouring the memory of an extraordinary voice and the poetry of the mythical duo she formed with Fred Chichin.
Singer Étienne Daho (source in French), meanwhile, posted a photo with Catherine Ringer and simply her first name.
And then there are the words from legendary band Sparks, with whom Les Rita Mitsouko worked. The American band spoke of an artist that was "one of a kind", a "true force of nature", and a friend whose path they know they were lucky to cross.
Tributes are also coming from far beyond the world of music. Actors and performers like Josiane Balasko, Nikos Aliagas, Michèle Laroque, Julie Gayet, Flavie Flament and Alain Chabat, among others, have shared their memories and their emotions on social media.
One particularly beautiful tribute from a user spotted on X shows that the artist touched many generations, including the youngest, and will continue to do so.
Finally, there is no better way to end this article than with music. The music of Catherine and Fred, the soundtrack that accompanied and lulled a large part of this writer’s life. This song in particular is forever tied to a vivid memory: a concert in October 2000, in a venue in Lyon. Seeing them play that night and hearing this track live is etched forever.
'C'est comme ça' – Les Rita Mitsouko – album 'The No Comprendo' – video directed by Jean-Baptiste Mondino in 1986.
