EU heads to COP31 with a blunt message: climate pledges are no longer enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:21:00 UTC
22:21:00 KST

EU ambassadors want COP31 to deliver faster clean-energy deployment, a transition away from fossil fuels, greater electrification, tripling renewable energy, doubling energy-efficiency improvements and cutting methane and other non-CO2 emissions by 2030, according to a document seen by Euronews.
The European Union is increasingly worried about whether nations will actually implement existing climate targets as it prepares for the United Nations' climate summit, COP31, according to a Council document seen by Euronews.
"(The Council highlights with concern) that current ambition and implementation remain insufficient to limit warming to 1.5°C," read the draft Council conclusions dated 14 September, referring to the Paris Agreement.
Similar concerns were recently shared by the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP), which warned the world is set to cross the 1.5°C global warming threshold, but can still limit, adapt to and return from higher temperatures.
Early in the summer, Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said that the latest COPs have fallen short of the urgent progress needed to tackle the climate crisis, calling their outcomes "underwhelming" compared to scientific demands.
In Antalya, where COP31 will take place in November, Brussels wants to defend the Paris Agreement and keep 1.5°C at the centre of international diplomacy, but it is also shifting the emphasis towards delivery, investment and implementation, according to the draft.
Rather than agreeing on new targets, the EU wants COP31 to deliver concrete outcomes: faster clean-energy deployment, a transition away from fossil fuels, greater electrification, tripling renewable energy, doubling energy-efficiency improvements and cutting methane and other non-CO2 emissions by 2030.
EU ambassadors want COP31 to produce “tangible progress” in closing the global ambition and implementation gaps and to set the direction for the next Paris Agreement cycle as the bloc of 27 nations concedes that pledges alone are no longer enough without active action.
The draft also calls on major polluters to raise their ambitions and minimise both the scale and duration of the overshoot, which UNEP and many other climate scientists have warned must be tackled with urgency.
"(The Council) urges all parties, particularly major emitters, to act with the highest possible ambition and make all efforts to return to a 1.5°C compatible trajectory and to minimise the magnitude and duration of the overshoot," reads the draft document.
Ironically, COP31 host Turkey keeps prioritising fossil fuels, despite its vast potential to replace them with clean power and recent success in increasing renewable energy capacity, according to a study of the country's power sector released on Wednesday by the Climate Action Tracker.
Energy transition and climate adaptation
Having becoming hostage to global price volatility due to disruption in the Middle East, the EU now frames the transition away from fossil fuels not as a purely environmental climate policy but as a matter of energy security and affordability.
It argues that renewables, low-carbon energy, energy efficiency and electrification can simultaneously strengthen energy security, reduce strategic dependencies and improve resilience.
On international climate, the Council is following the same energy policy touted by the European Commission, even if some divergences persist at home with consequential legislative files, such as the future of the bloc's carbon market or the ban on new cars and vans powered by diesel or petrol.
The EU also suggests that climate resilience is a paramount prerequisite for safe and prosperous economies and stresses that mitigation and adaptation must go together – a reality that Europeans are increasingly facing at home after a summer marked by intense heatwaves, wildfires and drought.
To address the issue, the EU wants all the nations at COP31 to incorporate their National Adaptation Plans into national investment plans and development strategies, reflecting a broader recognition that climate policy is no longer simply about preventing future warming but dealing with damage already occurring.
However, climate finance is likely to be one of the harder political negotiations.
Elephant in the room
In an echo of COP30 in Brazil, the EU will call for increased finance for developing countries covering mitigation, adaptation and loss and damage. It will also reaffirm its efforts to triple adaptation finance. However, it simultaneously stresses that public money alone cannot meet the scale of investment required.
The draft also highlights carbon pricing as an efficient way of cutting emissions and redirecting financial flows towards climate action.
After the absence of the biggest polluters at last year's COP30, the EU will reaffirm its commitment to multilateralism and call for reforms to make the system more effective and inclusive – a key point expected to become very contentious.
Given the current geopolitical scene, the EU's pursuit of multilateralism suggests COP31 will be about defending the international climate architecture as well as negotiating individual emissions measures.
Reacting to the draft document, Sven Harmeling, head of climate at the NGO Climate Action Network Europe, welcomed the EU's position in backing the 1.5°C, tripling renewables, just transition and climate adaptation, but criticised the persistent lack of ambition on climate financing.
"The draft still avoids the central question: what will the EU actually put on the table?" Harmeling said.
"Reaffirming the goal of tripling adaptation finance is welcome, but without clarity on Europe’s own contribution, the mandate risks asking more of others than it commits to itself."

Prolonging US-Iran Conflict Not Meeting Interests of Int'l Community - China's Wang Yi

What Do Taiwan’s People Think About Its Annual Military Exercises?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang military exercises were difficult for ordinary citizens to ignore this year. Mobile internet was deliberately slowed for 30 minutes to simulate wartime communications disruptions. Troops barricaded Guangfu Bridge, a key route connecting New Taipei City with the capital, setting up metal barriers and barbed wire as they rehearsed stopping enemy forces from advancing into Taipei. Hospitals also practiced moving medical operations underground as part of exercises designed to keep essential services running during a conflict. These scenes showed how Taiwan’s preparations for a possible war are moving beyond conventional military exercises and increasingly into the spaces of everyday civilian life.
The shift reflects a broader change in Taiwan’s approach to defense. This year’s Han Kuang exercises placed greater emphasis on realistic wartime scenarios while more closely integrating military training with urban resilience exercises. Preparing for a potential conflict is increasingly not only a task for the armed forces, but also a challenge involving civilian infrastructure, local governments, reservists, and ordinary citizens. But as Taiwan brings society more directly into its defense preparations, a basic question becomes more important: What do Taiwanese themselves make of the country’s most important annual military exercise?
To answer this question, the Institute for National Defense and Security Research (INDSR) commissioned a nationwide telephone survey shortly after this year’s exercises. Conducted by National Chengchi University’s Election Study Center from August 20 to 24, the survey interviewed 1,215 adults across Taiwan. Public satisfaction with the Han Kuang exercises reached its highest level in our survey series, yet most respondents said they knew relatively little about what the exercises actually involved. The findings suggest that as Taiwan expands whole-of-society defense, public approval and public understanding should not be treated as the same thing.
Public satisfaction with the Han Kuang exercises reached 60 percent this year, the highest level in our survey series. As shown in the chart below, satisfaction had generally hovered around 50 percent in previous surveys. It stood at 51.9 percent in 2021 and 53.6 percent in 2022, before falling to 45.5 percent in 2023. Satisfaction recovered to 51.3 percent in 2025 (there was no comparable survey in 2024) and rose further this year. The longer-term pattern has therefore fluctuated rather than followed a steady upward trend, but the 2026 result is noticeably higher than the levels recorded in previous surveys.
The figure also shows another shift. The share of respondents who did not offer a clear evaluation of the exercises – whether they chose now to answer or were unaware of the exercises at all – fell from 36.7 percent in 2021 to 25.3 percent in 2026, the lowest level in our survey series, although the decline was not consistent across years. Among those who reached the satisfaction question this year, about three-quarters expressed either a positive or negative view of the exercises.
These comparisons require some caution because the screening questions and skip patterns were not identical across survey waves. More importantly, being able to evaluate the exercises does not necessarily mean understanding them better. When we asked respondents directly how well they understood the Han Kuang exercises, the results told a different story.
Only 2.3 percent of respondents said they understood them very well and 22.6 percent somewhat well. By comparison, 46.1 percent said they did not understand the exercises very well, while another 26.4 percent said they did not understand them at all. In other words, nearly three-quarters of respondents described their understanding of the exercises as limited.
These findings do not necessarily contradict the relatively high level of satisfaction with this year’s exercises. People can form an overall impression of Han Kuang through news coverage, social media, or the activities they encounter in daily life without knowing in detail what individual drills are designed to test. Satisfaction captures how people evaluate the exercises, but it tells us less about how well they understand their purpose.
As Taiwan places greater emphasis on whole-of-society defense, the distance between approval and understanding becomes harder to ignore. Citizens are no longer simply an audience observing how well the military performs. They are increasingly expected to understand how society would function under crisis conditions and how civilian preparedness connects to national defense. That makes public understanding more consequential than it was when military exercises were viewed mainly as the work of the armed forces.
Satisfaction, understanding, and preparedness are therefore related but distinct. A citizen can support the Han Kuang exercises without knowing what they are intended to test or how they fit into Taiwan’s broader defense planning. Such support is still valuable. It gives the exercises public legitimacy and suggests that many people see value in continued preparation. But support alone does not tell us whether citizens are better prepared to interpret official instructions, understand disruptions during a crisis, or recognize their own responsibilities.
Of course, not every citizen needs detailed knowledge of military operations. What is needed is a more basic level of understanding. People should know what the exercises are trying to prepare for, why civilian participation is necessary, and how individual drills connect to the wider goal of national resilience. Public communication should therefore do more than make Han Kuang visible. It should help citizens make sense of what they are seeing.
For Taiwan, the next challenge is not simply getting citizens to watch Han Kuang, but helping them understand what they are watching and why it matters.

From Fugitive to Federal Custody: Inside the Takedown of South America’s ‘King of the South’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:19:00 UTC
22:19:00 KST

Reported by
When federal agents reached out to Sebastián Marset through his girlfriend in March 2025 to persuade him to surrender, the Uruguayan drug lord who styled himself the “King of the South” mocked them, boasting that he was "smarter than the entire D.E.A. put together."
“I’m not going to surrender,” Marset declared, according to court records. “I’ll be a criminal for the rest of my life.”
Almost a year later, heavily armed Bolivian special forces raided a residential neighborhood in Santa Cruz in the pre-dawn hours, capturing the fugitive who had evaded international law enforcement for years.
By that evening, one of the most powerful drug barons in South America’s Southern Cone - wanted by federal prosecutors for laundering millions of dollars in illicit proceeds through American banks - landed on U.S. soil in handcuffs.
Now held in a federal detention center in Virginia, Marset is mounting an aggressive legal defense. A new series of court filings has laid bare a detailed record of his global operations, missing evidence, and his own cynical view of regional law enforcement.
Federal prosecutors disclosed last week that agents seized three cellphones from Marset that provided access to $4 million in cryptocurrency. During questioning, Marset confessed to holding financial stakes in 10 tonnes of active cocaine shipments at the time of his arrest.
They charged him with conspiracy and incitement to violence for personal gain. He allegedly ordered the murder of an associate in Paraguay for betraying him.
Prosecutors also maintain that Marset laundered tens of millions of dollars through European banks and their U.S. subsidiaries with the help of financial operatives like Federico Santoro, a Uruguayan broker sentenced to 15 years in prison in 2025.
The filings further illustrate Marset's disdain for judicial systems. When asked by federal agents about pending charges in Paraguay, Marset reportedly dismissed the threat, stating he would resolve the matter "with money" because "there is no justice."
Defense attorneys, on the other hand, filed motions this week seeking to dismiss individual counts or throw out the indictment entirely. Among their central arguments is a challenge to a 1.6 tonne cocaine shipment that forms the basis of a key charge. The defense contends that the drugs were confiscated by Colombian authorities within national waters - placing them outside U.S. jurisdiction - and were subsequently destroyed by local police, rendering the evidence lost.
Attorneys also challenged efforts to connect Marset to Colombia’s Clan del Golfo and Brazil’s First Capital Command, noting those organizations received official U.S. terrorist designations after the alleged conduct occurred.
Marset’s trial is scheduled for January 2027.

EU chief von der Leyen proposes ‘associate member’ status for Canada
Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this week that Canada was seeking a ‘unique alliance’ with the European Union.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has raised the prospect of Canada becoming the 27-nation European Union’s first “associate member”, a striking overture as both seek to pivot away from a hostile United States under President Donald Trump.
Von der Leyen’s statement on Wednesday came after Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this week that Canada was seeking a “unique alliance” with the EU, but not membership.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Europe, Canada condemn Israeli plans for new West Bank settlement
- list 2 of 3Five key takeaways from the NATO summit in Ankara
- list 3 of 3‘A global rupture’: Carney calls for Canada-EU unity before G7 summit
Von der Leyen told the European Parliament in Strasbourg that, as democracies are facing a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together.
“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen told Carney, who was attending her annual keynote speech.
The first foreign head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” address, his visit comes in advance of an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next month. Carney will deliver his own address to the European Parliament on Thursday.
Von der Leyen said it was time to move from cooperation based on a trading relationship to a broader “alliance for the future” and “bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible”.
She said that the EU and Canada would work together on sectors ranging from manufacturing to AI, critical minerals and energy.
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she added.
EU treaties do not envision the possibility of becoming an “associate member”. But the idea was first proposed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz this year regarding Ukraine.
Under the plan, which met a cold reception in Kyiv as it pushes for full membership status, Ukraine would have been allowed to attend the bloc’s summits and have a representative in the European Commission.
It would have also benefitted from parts of the EU budget, but without full voting rights.
Buffeted by US tariffs and competition from China, Brussels and Ottawa already enjoy considerable cooperation.
A free-trade agreement (CETA) that abolished almost all tariffs has been credited with boosting trade in goods and services by more than 80 percent since 2016.
Furthermore, Canada became the first non-EU country to join a flagship defence loan programme this year.
“We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest – but to all of us. That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work,” von der Leyen said. “So, we are joining forces voluntarily.”

Responsible for supplying weapons to the occupiers: Russian Deputy Defense Minister Krivoruchko was charged in absentia
Kyiv • UNN
The Russian officer is accused of waging an aggressive war against Ukraine. He organized the supply of missiles, aerial bombs, and drones to the Russian army.
Prosecutors from the Office of the Prosecutor General have completed the pretrial investigation and referred to court an indictment against Russian Deputy Defense Minister Alexey Krivoruchko. He is suspected of waging an aggressive war or aggressive military actions, as provided for by Part 2 of Article 437 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Details
According to the investigation, Krivoruchko formulated and implemented the aggressor state's military-technical policy, organized the fulfillment of the state defense order, and controlled the supply of weapons.
It was established that Krivoruchko signed state contracts for the production and supply of Kinzhal hypersonic missiles, Iskander-M missile systems, guided aerial bombs, as well as Geran- and Gerbera-type drones. He also controlled the fulfillment of defense orders and reported to the leadership of the Russian Defense Ministry on the expansion of weapons production and supplies for the Russian army
In addition, according to the investigation, the defendant initiated the creation of the Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies. Its units subsequently took a direct part in combat operations against Ukraine.
The evidence collected indicates that the weapons whose supply was organized and controlled by the accused were used by Russian forces during missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian territory, in particular against civilian and critical infrastructure. As a result of such attacks, civilians were killed and injured, and residential buildings and critical infrastructure facilities were destroyed
The article provides for a sentence of 10 to 15 years in prison.
Reminder
The Security Service of Ukraine and the prosecutor's office notified Russian Colonel General Sergei Kuzovlyov in absentia of suspicion over the strike on Kramatorsk in June 2023.

Five reasons you might unexpectedly need a temporary Dutch home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:18:08 UTC
22:18:08 KST

Partner content
Five reasons you might unexpectedly need a temporary Dutch home
A new job, a burst pipe, a divorce, a renovation gone on too long: there are more moments than you’d imagine when you might suddenly need somewhere to live. Here’s how serviced and flexible housing can step in, whatever the reason.
1. The new job or the temporary assignment
 Relocating for work is the classic reason many people need a home in the Netherlands, but it’s far from the only version of it. Travelling nurses posted to a new hospital, researchers starting a fellowship, or consultants sent in for a few months on a project all arrive in the same position: they need somewhere to live, quickly, without signing up for a permanent rental contract.
Corporate Housing Factory (CHF) provides fully serviced apartments across the Netherlands – offering comfortable, home-style living for stays from one week up to a year, combining the convenience of a hotel with the privacy and space of a residence.
You request a quote, the team confirms availability, and in some cases you can get the keys as soon as the next day. Apartments come fully furnished, from kitchen appliances to Wi-Fi, with cleaning included. Companies are invoiced directly, and the booking system is connected to the Global Distribution System (GDS), so travel management companies can book on a client’s behalf just as easily as they could book a hotel.
CHF’s newest property, in Arnhem, is a case in point. The building dates back to 1878 and survived the bombing of the Second World War – one apartment still has a shrapnel hole, deliberately unfilled. It’s since been transformed into an industrial-chic block with high ceilings and top-quality furniture, right by Arnhem Centraal station and a local supermarket. The location was chosen for the wider Nijmegen-Arnhem-Wageningen region, where technology, healthcare, sustainability and logistics employers have long struggled to find decent corporate housing for their staff.
2. The housing emergency
 Then there’s the reason nobody plans for: a fire, a mould problem, a burst pipe or damage that suddenly makes your own home unliveable. It’s the kind of situation that can leave the victim feeling like an emergency bunker is the only option. And after an already stressful event, most people would rather not compromise on comfort.
This is where Thuis in de Stad comes in: “Until recently, we focused on corporate clients, so it was always relocations, work trips or internships,” says Claudia Vrancken from CHF. “With Thuis in de Stad, we’re opening the spectrum more broadly to the other unexpected reasons someone might suddenly need temporary housing.” You can anticipate fully furnished apartments, all utilities included; arrive with a suitcase and the rest is taken care of.
3. The renovation project, or getting caught between selling and buying
 The same goes for two other reasons someone might need to move out temporarily: a renovation that makes the house unliveable for a few weeks, or the gap between selling one home and getting the keys to the next. Neither is an emergency, but both mean needing a comfortable base at short notice, for an unpredictable length of time.
One detail that matters more than people expect in the Netherlands is the ability to register at an address – something most short-term rentals don’t allow, but which is essential for things like getting a BSN number or opening a bank account. (Just don’t forget to deregister when you leave!)
4. The divorce process
 Separation is another situation that can leave someone needing a home almost overnight – often with the condition of staying close to children and family during a period of transition. Flexible, furnished housing means not having to make a long-term commitment while things are still being worked out, while still having a proper place to call home in the meantime.
It’s also worth knowing, whatever the reason for the move, that pets are welcome – unlike with most hotels or holiday rentals. “Our apartments are all located in mixed-use buildings, so you really have the feeling you’re living somewhere with local families, kids and pets, instead of in a hotel,” says Claudia.
5. The sudden business trip elsewhere in Europe
 Not every unexpected need for a home happens in the Netherlands. A consultant might have to jump on a plane at short notice for a project in another European city, with everything needing to be arranged just as quickly as it would be here.
For that, there’s Your Serviced Apartment Agency (YOSAA): a boutique Europe-wide apartments platform. The general idea of YOSAA – connecting living, hospitality and real estate – is the same as CHF and Thuis in de Stad: the convenience of a hotel with the freedom and flexibility of your own apartment.
Whatever the reason – a new job, an emergency or a sudden change of plans – temporary housing isn’t just for expats. Sometimes life itself creates the need for a home between homes. If that sounds like you, contact the booking team via email at bookings@corporatehousingfactory.com to find the right temporary home for your situation.

Ukrainian drone commander says his forces killed decorated Russian general
KYIV, Sept 16 - Ukrainian drone forces killed a Russian general in eastern Ukraine on Saturday, a little over two weeks after he received a Hero of Russia award for his wartime service, Ukrainian drone commander Robert Brovdi said.
Major General Anton Grunis had won praise from President Vladimir Putin earlier this year after reporting how troops under his command helped Russia capture the Ukrainian stronghold of Kostiantynivka, a territorial claim disputed by Kyiv and independent military analysts.
Brovdi, who commands Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, said one of his units had killed Grunis in a nighttime strike on his position in a Russian-held part of Ukraine's Donetsk region.
"General Grunis was eliminated on September 12," Brovdi wrote in a Telegram post on Wednesday, adding that the general was the seventh Russian military commander killed by his drone forces. Reuters could not independently verify Brovdi's assertions.
Russia's Defence Ministry does not routinely confirm battlefield deaths of senior personnel, but Russian commander Apti Alaudinov, in a post on the Telegram messaging app, said Grunis had died, without giving further details.
A solemn-faced Grunis received the Gold Star Hero of Russia award at a ceremony in late August, standing first in a line of officers in dress uniform.
On July 3, he had addressed Putin via video link at a televised security meeting and described in detail how troops of his 4th Separate Guards Motor Rifle Brigade had participated in the claimed capture of Kostiantynivka.
Putin congratulated him and said: "Luck comes to those who do the work."
At the time, Ukraine denied that Russia had captured the city and said its forces retained control. The U.S.-based Institute for the Study of War said Russian forces had infiltrated but not fully seized the city and said Russia's claim was part of a wider information campaign to "portray the Ukrainian frontlines as collapsing."
Russia’s overall advances have slowed this year, but its forces have continued to press strategic cities such as Kostiantynivka. Moscow wants to control all of the broader Donbas region and has made that a central territorial demand in stalled negotiations with Kyiv. REUTERS

Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Plant Faces Falling Water Levels, Blackout Risk, Ukraine Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

Falling water levels and repeated losses of external electricity are creating an increasingly difficult safety situation at the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency said.
None of the plant’s six reactors is generating electricity, and all remain in cold shutdown, the Military Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR) said in a statement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
HUR said a work shift of about 1,150 employees, described as the minimum staffing level, was maintaining the facility’s safety systems.
The agency said the water level in the plant’s cooling pond had fallen from 12.86 meters in July to 12.63 meters in early August and 12.55 meters by the end of the month. It said the level was continuing to decline, while at least 15 meters was required for the facility’s normal operation.
The plant lost external electricity three times in August, on Aug. 1, 4 and 8, because of problems with the Ferrosplavna-1 power line, according to the intelligence agency.
HUR said the facility had experienced between 23 and 25 external power outages since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Backup diesel generators were activated during the August outages. However, their operation placed additional pressure on fuel supplies in the occupied region, the agency said.
“In the event of a prolonged total blackout, the plant would require about 150 metric tons of diesel fuel per day,” HUR said.
Ukrainian Businesses Expect Hryvnia Revenue Growth, Brace for War Through 2027
Nuclear plants depend on a continuous electricity supply to operate cooling and other essential safety systems even when their reactors are shut down.
Backup generators are intended to provide temporary power only if external supplies are lost.
Russian forces also disconnected internet access at the plant on Aug. 13 and 14, disrupting communications, the monitoring of key indicators and international oversight, HUR said.
The Zaporizhzhia plant, Europe’s largest nuclear power station, has been under Russian control since the early months of the full-scale invasion. The facility is located near the occupied city of Enerhodar in southeastern Ukraine.
HUR said residents of Enerhodar were experiencing repeated disruptions to electricity, water supplies and communications, as well as severe shortages of food and fuel.
The agency accused Russian forces of deliberately isolating the city’s information environment and mistreating civilians.
HUR also alleged that Moscow was seeking to incorporate the nuclear plant into Russia’s regulatory system by involving inspectors from Rostekhnadzor, the Russian agency responsible for technical and nuclear oversight.
It further accused Russia of using its representatives at the International Atomic Energy Agency to help legitimize the occupation. The intelligence agency cited a visit to the plant by IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi on Sept. 4, shortly before the agency’s General Conference in Vienna.
HUR claimed that Mikhail Chudakov, a Russian deputy director general at the IAEA, had secured changes to the agency’s Power Reactor Information System that displayed occupied Crimea as part of Russia and rendered the names of Ukrainian nuclear plants in Russian.
The intelligence agency also said Russian forces continued to use the Zaporizhzhia plant as a military base and shelter for occupation troops.
Russia has controlled the plant since March 2022, but Ukraine and the international community continue to recognize it as Ukrainian territory.

The movement said the agent escaped the city after the operation.
VZPP-S is a Russian producer of semiconductor devices, integrated circuits and power modules. Ukraine’s military intelligence lists the company as part of Russia’s defense-industrial supply chain and says it has produced electronic components for Kh-101 cruise missiles, Iskander-K missiles and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.
ATESH claimed the sabotage caused a major voltage surge and shut down production workshops. The movement said full power was not restored for several weeks, causing delays in deliveries of components for Russian weapons and, consequently, delays in missile and air defense production.
The movement’s claims have not been independently verified.
ATESH is a pro-Ukrainian partisan movement operating in Russian-occupied territories and inside Russia. It says it recruits local residents and Russian military personnel to conduct sabotage, gather intelligence and pass information to Ukraine. The movement regularly publishes claims of attacks and acts of sabotage against Russian military and defense-industrial targets, though individual operations are often difficult to independently verify.
The plant has already been targeted
The reported sabotage comes after the VZPP-S facility was struck in a Ukrainian attack in June.
Ukraine’s military intelligence says VZPP-S produces components for the Kh-101, including transistor assemblies and matrices used in the missile’s electronic systems. It also says the company supplies semiconductor components for the onboard computer of the 9M727 cruise missile used by the Iskander-K system, as well as components for the Pantsir-S1’s television channel.
The company itself describes VZPP-S as a major Russian producer of electronic components, with more than 900 products in serial production.
ATESH said it delayed publication of its claim to protect its agent.

Tropical Smoothie Cafe is getting a makeover as it prepares for its 'next 3,000' locations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:16:40 UTC
22:16:40 KST

Tropical Smoothie Cafe on Wednesday unveiled a new look as the restaurant chain prepares to continue its streak of rapid growth under Blackstone's ownership.
"We are a company and a brand that has evolved significantly over the last few years and really over the last 10 years," CEO Max Wetzel told CNBC. "We're thinking about what our next 3,000 cafes look like, and so it's a perfect time for us to roll this out."
The redesign comes as Tropical Smoothie prepares to introduce itself to more consumers, both in the U.S. and internationally. The chain, which also sells bowls and wraps, surpassed $1.6 billion in system sales over the 12 months ended in June. By the end of the year, it is projecting it will exceed 1,800 locations nationwide, up 50% since the end of 2022. Tropical Smoothie has plans to expand outside of the U.S., too.
But its bold plans come during a tricky time for the restaurant industry. Diners have been eating out less frequently, trying to save money while paying more for gas, groceries and other necessities. As a result, eateries have been battling for a smaller pool of customers and often leaning on discounts to win them over.
Tropical Smoothie last tinkered with its logo a decade ago. The new design, which will be found everywhere from packaging for its wraps to its mobile app interface, uses brighter colors and a uniform font, in part to try to set it apart from quick-service competitors.
"The color palette is entirely created by the ingredients that you can find in our cafe," Wetzel said. "All these ingredients are very different than a category that's really dominated by browns and beiges and fried food."
It also introduces the "Palm T," a frond-shaped icon that will represent the brand in "shorthand," particularly on digital platforms, according to Wetzel.
Tropical Smoothie has been working on the new branding for more than a year. But it is just one step toward what Wetzel called his ultimate goal: "building a best-in-class company."
In late 2024, Tropical Smoothie consolidated national and local media budgets into a single advertising fund. Franchisees pay 5% of their gross sales in marketing fees, meaning that the fund will grow as system sales — lifted by successful marketing initiatives — increase.
Tropical Smoothie's $80 million marketing budget is now deployed "much more effectively," according to Wetzel. As a result, its national brand awareness has increased from 34% of consumers a year ago to 42%, he said.
Tropical Smoothie has also been trying to improve its cafe operations. Earlier this year, it started to rearrange its food and bowl assembly lines for better speed and accuracy.
Outside of the cafes, Tropical Smoothie has also invested in what Wetzel called "the digital front door" of the brand. By the end of the year, the company will roll out an improved version of its mobile app and website, all with the new unified look. It is also testing self-ordering kiosks.
Those improvements tie into its efforts to win over repeat customers. Its loyalty program has grown to 13 million members, up 25% from the year-ago period. About 1 in 3 orders comes from a loyalty program member, according to Wetzel.
"Those are some of the bigger types of investments that we've built since Blackstone got here," Wetzel said.
Wellness winners
In 2024, Blackstone bought Tropical Smoothie Cafe for a reported $2 billion, including debt. The company was started in Florida in 1997, but its founders cashed out more than a decade ago. Blackstone is Tropical Smoothie's third private equity firm owner.
Wetzel joined the chain in late 2024, after the sale. Previously, he was CEO of CKE Restaurants, the parent company of Carl's Jr. and Hardee's, and chief operating officer at Papa John's.
In fiscal 2025, Tropical Smoothie reported net income of $115.4 million on revenue of $131.4 million, according to franchise disclosure documents. With just one company-operated location, Tropical Smoothie makes the majority of its revenue from franchising the brand.
As a chain that began on the East Coast, Tropical Smoothie sees the most growth opportunities out west, particularly in the Midwest and Southwest. And the chain is a big hit in cold climates like Michigan, too.
"What's exciting is as we hit critical brand awareness levels in these markets, we're seeing a nice increase in overall [average unit volumes]," Wetzel said, referring to the industry term for annual sales for the average restaurant in its footprint.
Wetzel said that Tropical Smoothie is not currently working on an initial public offering, but "over time" the company will evaluate its options. Sandwich chain Jersey Mike's, which was also owned by Blackstone, went public in late July, less than two years after the private equity firm bought it for a reported $8 billion.
Based on both system sales and number of restaurants, Tropical Smoothie is larger than its older rival Smoothie King, which has also grown rapidly recently. Last year, Smoothie King sold a minority stake to private equity firm Main Post Partners to accelerate the chain's growth.
But both smoothie chains are seeing similar trends boost their sales. Wetzel credited increased "health literacy" as one tail wind for the business; the growing adoption of GLP-1 drugs and the "Make America Healthy Again" movement have further boosted wellness trends that had already been percolating for years.
Plus, brightly colored drinks are buzzy now, too.
"We're a beverage-led concept, and beverage has gone from being the sidekick to the main event," Wetzel said, adding that about 85% of the chain's transactions include a smoothie, but the fruity drinks only account for about half of sales.

US-Houthi talks focus on Red Sea shipping and Bab el-Mandeb: Houthis pledge not to target US vessels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:16:23 UTC
22:16:23 KST

U.S. officials met earlier this week in Oman with representatives of Yemen’s Houthi rebels, just days after the Iran-backed militia seized a strategic strip along the Red Sea coast in an offensive that defeated forces loyal to Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, Reuters reported Wednesday. According to the report, the Houthis told the United States during the meeting that they intended to refrain from attacking American vessels in the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which they have effectively taken control of.
According to Reuters, the meeting was not made public but was confirmed by three sources. It took place Sunday at the U.S. Embassy in the Omani capital, Muscat, where the Houthis told American officials they remained committed to the ceasefire agreed with the United States in 2025 and therefore had no intention of attacking U.S. vessels. One source, a Yemeni official, also told Reuters that the militia’s representatives said they would not attack Israeli ships or any other commercial vessels, with the exception of those belonging to Saudi Arabia.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis a “foreign terrorist organization” in March 2025, making any support for the group a criminal offense. Washington nevertheless continued negotiating with them afterward, and in May last year, after two months of U.S. strikes aimed at halting Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping lanes, the sides reached a ceasefire. The Houthis continued attacking ships near their coast but appeared to avoid striking American vessels.
Over the weekend, following the Houthis’ territorial gains near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which effectively gave them control of the waterway, questions mounted over whether the United States and other countries would mobilize to help Saudi Arabia drive the Houthis from the area. The concern was that, alongside the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait could also be completely blocked, further disrupting global supplies of oil and goods.
But on Saturday, U.S. President Donald Trump said the Houthis had “called” his administration and asked the United States to stay out of the war in Yemen. On Monday, Vice President JD Vance said Washington was in direct contact with the group, without elaborating. At the same time, it emerged that Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, had called Trump last week to request U.S. military assistance in light of the Houthis’ dramatic advances, but Washington made clear to Riyadh that it would not intervene directly in the conflict.
Houthis say they did not fire at Mecca, claim to have downed F-15
The current situation has left Saudi Arabia in a strategic bind. Even as the Houthis and other Iranian proxy groups fire into its territory and strike its oil facilities, Washington is not stepping in actively to assist, and neither are Riyadh’s new partners in the so-called “Mecca Alliance,” Turkey and Pakistan. The two countries signed the defense pact with Saudi Arabia only last month but have so far limited themselves to condemning the attacks on the kingdom.
Officials in Turkey and Pakistan said efforts to “institutionalize” the alliance must be completed before it can become operational, and that Riyadh had not, in any case, asked either country for help.
According to Wednesday’s Reuters report, one source who confirmed the meeting in Oman said the U.S. side was represented by embassy personnel and that one member of the Houthi delegation was Mohammed Abdulsalam, a senior official based in Muscat who is under U.S. sanctions. Those sanctions, it emerged, did not prevent the talks from taking place.
The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014 and have been fighting for more than a decade against a coalition led by neighboring Saudi Arabia. More than 100,000 people have been killed in the war, while Saudi Arabia has faced heavy international criticism over its bombing campaign. In recent years, the fighting subsided following the declaration of a ceasefire, but it resumed in July after the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea in response to a Saudi blockade of Yemeni ports.
The current wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia has left the kingdom without a secure outlet for its crude oil, in part after pro-Iranian militias in Iraq struck one of its most important oil pipelines.
According to Saudi Arabia, the Houthis on Tuesday launched a drone toward Mecca for the first time in the current round of attacks. Mecca is Islam’s holiest city and home to the Kaaba, with millions of Muslims making the pilgrimage there each year. Riyadh said it intercepted the drone but declared Wednesday that firing toward Mecca, about 1,100 kilometers from the Yemeni border, amounted to “crossing a red line."
The Houthis, for their part, denied launching an unmanned aircraft toward Mecca. The last time they apparently attempted to attack the city was in 2017, when they fired a ballistic missile in its direction.
Meanwhile, the Houthis claimed Wednesday morning that they had shot down an F-15 fighter jet belonging to the Saudi-led coalition over Marib province in central Yemen. They provided no evidence and did not say when the alleged shootdown took place.

Gold mine collapse kills at least 70 people in Sudan’s West Kordofan
Dozens of artisanal miners have been killed, and many remain trapped after a series of adjoining mining shafts collapsed.
At least 70 people have been killed after a gold mine collapsed in Sudan’s West Kordofan state.
Dozens of artisanal miners were killed and a number of them were trapped after a series of adjoining mining shafts collapsed at al-Zaraa mine, near al-Nuhud town, on Tuesday, the Kordofan Observatory monitoring group said on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Sudan aid networks at risk of collapse, UN agencies warn
- list 2 of 3Dozens killed in rebel attacks on Sudan’s Kordofan, medical group says
- list 3 of 3At least five killed in Sudan’s South Kordofan in attack by rebel group
The group added that no specialised rescue teams had joined the rescue effort and residents with rudimentary tools were struggling to pull survivors out in loose and sandy soil.
A source in the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which controls the area, told the AFP news agency that at least 82 people were killed and another 50 wounded. “There is an unknown number of people still trapped under the rubble and rescue efforts are being conducted with rudimentary methods,” the source, who requested anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the media, said.
Khair al-Sayyed Jabara, who survived the incident, told AFP on Wednesday that he and fellow miners had dug throughout the night using their tools to reach survivors, adding that heavy equipment was needed.
“We don’t know how many more are still inside,” he said.
Survivors question absence of safety procedures
Another miner, Amin Suleiman, said the shafts were packed so closely that each one pulled down those beside it when it collapsed.
Local sources told the Reuters news agency that the high death toll was due to a lack of safety procedures and rescue equipment.
Sudan Doctors Network, a Khartoum-based medical group, said search efforts were ongoing and the casualty figure could rise, adding that the site was missing basic safeguards for workers.
The group condemned the “negligence” it said put miners’ lives at serious risk.
West Kordofan is held by the paramilitary RSF, which has been fighting Sudan’s army since April 2023. Smuggled gold has been a key source of revenue for the group.
“Mining activities in areas under RSF control, in the absence of safety standards and adequate protection and rescue equipment, turn mining into a direct threat to the lives of civilians,” it said in a statement.
It called for the search to continue and for medical and logistical help to be provided, and urged those in control of the area to end unregulated mining.
Sudan ranks among Africa’s leading gold producers, and most of its yellow metal comes from dangerous, informal mining at disused or unofficial sites.

Yemen's Houthis say they attacked Saudi airbase in Khamis Mushait, Aramco facilities in Yanbu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:13:48 UTC
22:13:48 KST

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Wednesday that the group had attacked an airbase in Khamis Mushait as well as Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
Saudi Arabia did not confirm either of the attacks.
The Houthi capture of ground overlooking the Bab el-Mandab Strait has dealt Saudi Arabia its gravest setback in Yemen in years, exposing intelligence failures, the collapse of Yemeni allies and the limits of US protection.
A Houthi advance this week along the Red Sea coast and the capture of islands at the mouth of the strait, a vital artery for global oil supplies, has also left the kingdom scrambling for backing as Iran and its allies expand their reach.
Senior Western, regional and Yemeni officials and sources said the Houthi breakthrough reflected various factors: deep divisions among anti-Houthi Yemeni factions, an untested Saudi-led command structure that replaced Emirati oversight, limited Saudi air support and an underestimation of Houthi preparations.
The diplomat said the Houthis had quietly assembled about 100,000 fighters, vastly outnumbering forces on the opposing side, adding: "Everyone, including the Saudis, missed this build-up and miscalculated the Houthis' intentions.”
Neil Quilliam, a fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, described the offensive as a glaring intelligence failure, saying: "They just weren't picking up the signal. They just weren't seeing the signs."
Yemeni political analyst Farea Al-Muslimi added: "The Saudis were caught off guard in Yemen."
The collapse of Saudi-backed forces handed the Houthis another prize beyond territory - a sizeable cache of advanced US- and Saudi-supplied weaponry abandoned during the retreat.
The haul, according to regional sources, is likely to bolster the group's military capabilities, provide valuable intelligence on adversaries' equipment and further reinforce perceptions of a humiliating Saudi defeat.
"The Yemeni government forces were like a house of cards. They didn't resist. Completely. Completely," said Abdulkhaleq Abdallah, a political analyst in the United Arab Emirates.
The setback has also exposed how limited international support for a counteroffensive may be. Two Western officials said neither the US nor European countries were prepared to offer direct military backing, and that Washington and its allies had not even joined a Saudi-led maritime defense coalition announced in July.
Saudi officials did not respond to a request to comment for this article.
Allies collapse, partners hesitate
With Iran-backed fighters now holding territory that can threaten Saudi oil exports and Red Sea shipping, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MbS) went to Cairo to discuss military cooperation between the two countries as Saudi Arabia seeks to contain the fallout after Washington declined to directly intervene militarily.
Two regional sources familiar with the meeting in Egypt said Riyadh wanted Egypt to help play a role in Red Sea operations. One regional source said MbS asked President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi for military support on Yemen given the close ties between the two countries. There was no immediate word on whether Cairo would agree.
A Saudi source said the meeting was scheduled long before the US-Israeli war against Iran began in February and "while it obviously covered the latest developments, it had the full agenda of bilateral issues to discuss."
Egypt's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment when asked whether MbS had discussed Egyptian military support.
The Houthis also appear to be using their gains to press for broader political concessions.
Former US negotiator Dennis Ross said the group wants Riyadh to lift restrictions on Hodeidah port and Sanaa airport, provide compensation for the war and scale back support for Yemen's internationally recognized government.
"I don't think the Saudis can easily give in to the kinds of demands that they're making," Ross said.
A Gulf official said Saudi Arabia now faced a narrowing set of choices. Allowing the Houthis to consolidate their gains risked turning tactical victories into lasting strategic leverage, while a larger military response could prompt attacks deeper inside the kingdom.
"If you don't inflict enough pain on the Houthis, you become hostage to them," the official said.
Control of territory around Bab el-Mandab - which lies between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast - could deepen the Houthis' regional reach, putting the Horn of Africa within easier reach of their logistical and smuggling networks.
Combined with Iran's leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, another vital route for global energy supplies, the foothold gives Tehran and its allies influence over two critical maritime choke points.
MbS's foreign policy strategy, built on trying to stabilize the region via a détente with Iran, has unraveled since the start of the war as his economic transformation agenda comes under mounting strain, increasing pressure on the kingdom's de facto ruler.
The absence of Western military assistance in Yemen, and the absence of these powers from a newly formed defense coalition, exposed the limits of its ability to rally support at a moment of acute vulnerability.
Riyadh appears increasingly to have been outmaneuvered by its adversaries and left wanting by its allies.
The Yemen Trap
The Houthi offensive revealed a blind spot in Saudi and US strategy: while Washington and its allies focused on containing Iran directly, Tehran widened the battlefield by opening fronts from Iraq to the Red Sea, using energy assets, shipping routes and proxies as instruments of pressure.
The larger significance of the Houthi breakthrough lies not only in the blow to Saudi Arabia but in the momentum it restores to Iran's influence across the region, after major setbacks to its allies in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon.
For Iran it's a "win-win-win," said Farea Al-Muslimi.
Some political analysts say the more consequential blow is not the battlefield reversal but Washington's reluctance to come to its ally's aid. That signal, they say, has emboldened adversaries, weakened Riyadh's leverage and reinforced doubts over the reliability of US security guarantees.
Al-Muslimi described Washington's refusal to help defend Saudi territory as "the biggest dismissing of the Saudi-American arrangement" in decades.
"The Americans are saying No," he said. "That kind of understanding in the relationship between Riyadh and Washington has never been tested more than now."
Yemen's long record of defeating foreign powers - from Egypt in the 1960s to the Soviets and, more recently, the US and Saudi Arabia - helps explain why Riyadh's search for partners may yield only limited results.
Few regional powers appear eager to be drawn deeper into a conflict that has repeatedly frustrated attempts at outside intervention and acquired a reputation as a graveyard for foreign military ambitions.
"Yemen is the Vietnam and Afghanistan of every power dragged into it," Muslimi said, referring to conflicts in which foreign powers were humbled.
"The Saudis failed in Yemen, the Americans failed in Yemen," he said, adding in reference to Egypt's costly intervention in Yemen in the 1960s: "The Egyptians failed in Yemen."

2026-09-16
13:13:43 UTC
22:13:43 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she would work with Canada to become the EU's first "associate member" in her annual speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Wednesday.
"We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible," von der Leyen said. "So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU."
She further stressed the need to maintain European independence in various sectors, including energy, raw materials and clean technologies.
To do that, EU countries will not only need to work together, but also have strong partners like Canada, whose Prime Minister, Mark Carney, is in Strasbourg and was warmly applauded by EU lawmakers as he arrived to listen to von der Leyen's speech.
Von der Leyen, now in her second five-year term at the helm of the EU executive arm, walked up to and embraced Carney after mentioning the "associate membership" issue for Canada, and Carney got a standing ovation from the chamber.
Through its partnership with Canada, she called for EU states to tackle climate change, competition from China and other major challenges.
The bloc was dealing with "an openly hostile world", von der Leyen said, setting out priorities for the 27-nation EU for the year ahead.
Von der Leyen: Solidarity among EU states necessary for facing challenges
She said solidarity among member states was the only possible solution. "Our path is clear. Building an independent Europe that has the power to act."
The 27-nation bloc faces war at its borders, with Russia's invasion of Ukraine. On trade and other issues, it also faces stiff rivalry from US President Donald Trump's United States and an increasingly assertive China.
The EU faces major headwinds at home as well, including the increasing popularity of a eurosceptic far-right, seen in regional elections in Germany that have weakened Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Opinion polls see Marine Le Pen as the strongest contender in next year's presidential vote in France.
"The state of our Union is the strongest it has ever been. The state of our Union can also feel as precarious as it has ever been," von der Leyen said.
EU to use any means necessary to reduce 'unsustainable' China trade deficit
Turning to trade, von der Leyen said the EU will use every possible means to reduce its "unsustainable" trade deficit with China. She said that the imbalance, with a goods trade deficit of €1 billion ($1.15 billion) a day last year, had reached a tipping point.
"Let me be clear: we will use all the tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship. Words are good. But deeds are better," she said.
Von der Leyen also said the bloc will need to stay its ambitious course on mitigating climate change but also step up efforts to adapt to it, drawing on experiences from the last three months when the continent was hit by unprecedented heat waves and wildfires.

Will militaries pivot on drone technologies after major Reaper losses in Iran? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:13:14 UTC
22:13:14 KST

The US lost around 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones in the conflict with Iran. This is according to a new Lead Inspector General Report to the United States Congress. Operation Epic Fury, which covers the fighting from April to June 2026. Since June, more Reaper drones have been lost in the conflict.
These types of drones, the Reaper and the Predator, are legacy US drone platforms. However, they have been lost in larger numbers as they have been pressed into service in places like Yemen and now Iran.
The losses may point to these types of larger drones becoming obsolete. The drones are vulnerable to air defenses. The reason they are so vulnerable is due to their history. They are a legacy of the US global hegemony after the Cold War. The drones are a symbol of American power. Now they could also be seen as a symbol of the changing world order.
The MQ-1 Predator and MQ-9 Reaper helped transform US unmanned aircraft from reconnaissance platforms into strike systems. What that means is that the Predator was first rolled out to do slow intelligence and reconnaissance missions, monitoring areas.
This was considered a dull and dangerous job. Losing reconnaissance planes and pilots has historically been a problem. For instance, Francis Gary Powers was an American pilot whose U-2 spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960.
Hellfire missiles: An early breakthrough in drone warfare
The Predator was an answer to this problem. No need to send pilots. Send drones. America’s General Atomics developed the Predator during the 1990s. The prototype first flew in 1994, and the RQ-1 entered operational use as an intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance aircraft, including deployments over the Balkans.
Then it became clear that the drone can and should be armed. A breakthrough came when the US began experimenting with arming it with the AGM-114 Hellfire missile. The first airborne Hellfire launch from a Predator occurred in 2001.
By October 7, 2001, armed Predators were flying combat missions over Afghanistan. This was too late to take out Bin Laden. However, the drone became a symbol of the war on terror.
The terrorist groups being hunted by US drones in Afghanistan, Iraq, Somalia, and Pakistan did not have air defenses. However, much has changed since then.
The MQ-9 Reaper first flew in February 2001. Reaper entered operational service in 2007. Compared with the Predator, it offered substantially greater speed, payload, and weapons capacity, including Hellfires and bombs. The Reaper was a natural evolution of the Predator.
The challenge in Iran, Yemen, and other places is that the Reapers are being lost at a higher rate than they will be replaced. It’s not clear if they will actually be replaced as the US transitions to other drones. The war in Ukraine and also in Iran has shown the need for large numbers of other drones.
The US knows it not only needs a Reaper replacement, but also needs tens of thousands of other smaller drones. Back in May, Aviation Week noted that the US Air Force had approved requirements for an MQ-9 Reaper replacement. It was supposed to be attritable, meaning it can be lost in larger numbers. Mass production and open architecture with a 1,500 km. range and 20-hour endurance.
Tyler Rogoway at TWZ noted that the requirement was for a drone “cheap enough to risk losing. “The Air Force’s MQ-9 Reaper successor will trade survivability for lower cost, broader missions, and mass production.”
New drones in development for replacement, supplementation
Armed Forces Press recently noted Swarm Aero had unveiled Gamera, a potential replacement. “After the US lost dozens of its MQ-9 Reaper drones to fighting in Iran, newcomer drone-maker Swarm Aero announced Monday that it had developed a drone in the same medium altitude, long-endurance (MALE) class, capable of executing swarm missions and cheap enough to afford losing, even in large numbers.”
It is said to have “a wingspan of about 72 feet, a payload capacity of 2,800 pounds, a ‘Pacific-spanning’ range of 9,000 miles and a combat radius of 2,300 miles with ‘hours’ of on-station time once at its patrol area.
Kitted-out Reapers, which reportedly cost $30-50 million apiece, have a payload capacity of up to 3,800 pounds.” In addition, another report at Aviation International News noted that General Atomics “has unveiled its Wildfire uncrewed air system” as a potential replacement.
The point is that the replacements are coming. In addition, many other drones are being used. The US is worried about munition shortfalls due to the Iran war. However, the lesson will be that the US needs new and cheaper munitions and drones. Rather than try to replace what was lost, the war will lead to major changes, much as World War II and other conflicts have.
The US military is already investing in lower-cost drones and missiles that can be produced and employed in large numbers, reflecting lessons from Ukraine and the 2026 conflict with Iran. One example is the Low-Cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System (LUCAS), a one-way attack drone similar to Iran’s Shahed 136.
Cheaper missiles are also a good move to get around the losses of the Reapers. Anduril’s Barracuda-500M is designed as an affordable, mass-producible cruise missile. Another entrant is Covenant’s Anthem, a long-range cruise missile carrying a payload exceeding 200 kg.
The future is clear. Cheaper and mass-produced drones and missiles. The era of the Reaper and Predator as a symbol of American warfare may be ending. Many other countries that use large drones, including Israel, will be learning from this.

Koos party still struggling to open a bank account in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:13:00 UTC
22:13:00 KST

Koos party still struggling to open a bank account in Estonia
The Koos party is still struggling to open a bank account after banks refused to provide one, leaving it unable to pay the election deposit for the upcoming Riigikogu elections.
ERR's news portal reported in April that the Koos party had been unable to open a bank account with credit institutions operating in Estonia, raising the question of how the party would be able to pay election deposits for its candidates.
The party has now sent a new letter to the National Electoral Committee confirming that it intends to participate in the Riigikogu elections on March 7 next year.
In the letter, sent on September 15, the party said the situation had not changed: It still does not have a valid bank account through which it can make payments.
"The party has repeatedly approached banks with the aim of opening a bank account but has received refusals," Koos board member Igor Hopp said, attaching confirmations of the banks' refusals.
This has left the party in a catch-22: It must pay an election deposit to participate in the elections, but doing so requires a bank account. Without an account, it cannot make the payment. And without confirmation of the payment, the party cannot submit a complete set of documents to register its candidates.
The party is asking the National Electoral Committee to establish a specific, lawful and practically feasible mechanism that would allow it to meet the legal requirement in a situation where it objectively has no bank account despite its efforts to open one.
"For us, it is fundamentally important to receive practical guidance: What exactly must the Koos party do to pay the election deposit, obtain proper confirmation that it has been paid and be allowed to register candidates for the 2027 Riigikogu elections?" Hopp wrote.
Arne Koitmäe, head of the State Electoral Office, has previously said that under the Riigikogu Election Act, before submitting candidates for registration, a party must transfer the required election deposit for each person submitted for registration to the Ministry of Finance's bank account. The documents submitted must include a copy of the payment order proving that the deposit has been paid.
"In practice, this requires the existence and use of a bank account controlled by the party. The law does not provide for alternative payment methods or special procedures," Koitmäe explained. He added that a third party is not permitted to pay the election deposit on behalf of a party.
The Koos party was registered on May 8, 2023. It initially sought to register under the name Estonian Patriots Party Koos, but the registration department did not approve the application. The party has 723 members, the best known of whom is Aivo Peterson, who has been convicted of treason by two court instances. According to the latest Norstat poll, the party's support stood at 1.0 percent.

Swiss passenger rail traffic reaches record high in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:13:00 UTC
22:13:00 KST

Swiss passenger rail traffic reaches record high in 2025
In 2025, rail transport volume totalled 23.7 billion passenger-kilometres, according to figures published on Wednesday by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO).
In a direct year-on-year comparison, rail demand rose by 3.2% compared to 2024 (22.9 billion passenger-kilometres), representing an increase of 737 million passenger-kilometres in one year. A passenger-kilometre corresponds to the transport of one person over a distance of one kilometre.
This growth is part of an ongoing trend: 2024 had already seen a 3.1% increase over 2023. Over a ten-year period, rail passenger numbers have shown a clear upward trend despite the impact of the pandemic.
Between 2015 and 2025, rail transport volume rose by 16.3%, from 20.4 billion to 23 billion passenger-kilometres. After plummeting to 13.3 billion in 2020 at the height of the health restrictions, rail travel recovered and surpassed its pre-crisis level as early as 2023.
Road transport dominates
Compared with other modes of transport, the rail network remains second behind road transport. According to 2024 data, private motorised transport (mainly passenger cars) accounted for 70.6% of the overall transport market, with 94.6 billion passenger-kilometres.
More
We travelled from Switzerland to Denmark by train – the journey took 24 hours
Railways account for 17.2% of the total volume of travel, ahead of non-motorised transport (5.9% with 7.8 billion) and public road transport such as buses and trams (3.5% with 47 billion). In total, public transport as a whole (rail, road, cable cars and waterways) accounts for 21.1% of passenger travel in the country.
Within this collective transport system, conventional rail accounts for more than 81% of passenger-kilometres travelled, confirming its position as the backbone of public transport in Switzerland.

St John of Rila brings Athens Bulgarians together for a four-day celebration

Wednesday, 16 September 2026, 15:10
PHOTO St John of Rila the Wonderworker Orthodox Church in Athens
Font size
Tens of thousands of Bulgarians live in Athens, and for nearly two decades the Bulgarian Orthodox church dedicated to St John of Rila has been the place that brings the community together. This October, the community is preparing a particularly large celebration of its patron saint, marking 1,080 years since his death.
The Days of St John of Rila will run from October 22 to 25, with an international academic forum, a children’s exhibition, a translation competition and festive church services involving clergy from both the Bulgarian and Greek Orthodox churches.
“The Bulgarian community in Athens is large – several tens of thousands of people. What brings us together is the Bulgarian Orthodox church in Athens, dedicated to St John of Rila. It has a history of nearly 20 years. Every year, on the feast day of the Wonderworker of Rila in October, we hold a major commemoration of the patron saint of the Bulgarian people,” Gencho Banev told BTA.
Banev teaches Bulgarian language, literature and culture at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and is an active member of the Bulgarian church community in the Greek capital. This year’s anniversary, he says, has given the celebrations a much larger scale.
Researchers and university lecturers will take part in the academic forum. The forum is open to anyone wishing to participate, with applications for competitions, papers and projects accepted until October 15.
And there is another, much older link between St John of Rila and Greece. Banev says the saint is well known there through a significant body of texts and church services. Even more intriguingly, research shows that his right hand is preserved on the island of Tinos. When it was separated from his body, and how it found its way to the Greek island, are questions that remain unanswered.
Radio Bulgaria will soon bring you a special interview with Gencho Banev about the celebrations in Athens and research into St John of Rila in Greece.

Experts: Energy truce between Ukraine and Russia will not lower price of oil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:11:00 UTC
22:11:00 KST

Experts: Energy truce between Ukraine and Russia will not lower price of oil
Estonian experts say restoring oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz would have a far greater impact on global markets than an energy infrastructure truce between Ukraine and Russia.
On Monday evening, U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on social media that Ukraine had agreed not to strike targets related to Russia's energy infrastructure and that Russia had agreed to do the same. The president said the rise in global diesel prices was mainly due to the war between Russia and Ukraine, rather than Iran.
Alan Vaht, a member of the management board of Estonian fuel retailer Terminal, disagrees with that claim.
"Russian diesel exports have fallen by 500,000 barrels per day, while the decline in the Persian Gulf region has been more than 1.1 million barrels per day. So we're actually talking about figures that aren't comparable at all," Vaht said.
Economic expert Raivo Vare believes Trump himself is the one who primarily needs an energy truce between Moscow and Kyiv.
"Now gallon prices have risen from $3.80 (€3.29) to $6.30 (€5.43) and continue to rise. The midterm elections are coming up and that's why Trump is worried. Why? Because he needs those prices to come down," Vare said.
Ukraine immediately agreed to the proposed energy truce. But why does Russia need it?
"Russia is having difficulty supplying itself with gasoline and diesel and that has been a strong argument for Ukraine. If that leverage is now taken away, Ukraine's position objectively becomes weaker and that has to be taken into account," Vare said.
However, Russia wants more than simply an end to Ukrainian attacks on its oil refineries.
"Second, of course, the sanctions, those illegal restrictions on supplying energy resources to the global market, must be lifted. Only then can the world, the global market, be supplied with petroleum products and prices begin to fall," Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.
For now, however, fuel prices at filling stations are rising not only in the United States but also here in Estonia.
"The only thing that would genuinely help the world and the global fuel market, including Estonia's fuel market, is an agreement between Iran and the United States and the resumption of flows of crude oil and refined petroleum products through the Strait of Hormuz. That is the only effective solution for bringing fuel prices down," Vaht said.

Kosovo’s former president jailed for 25 years over war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:09:41 UTC
22:09:41 KST

Hashim Thaçi, the former president of Kosovo, has been sentenced to 25 years in prison by a tribunal in The Hague for war crimes, including dozens of murders, committed during his time as a senior commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army during the country’s war for independence from Serbia in the late 1990s.
The European-backed Kosovo Specialist Chambers, convicted Thaci, 58, and three other former senior commanders of 96 murders, and counts of torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention directed at political opponents and civilians.
The convictions come at the end of a years-long process, strongly opposed by many in Kosovo, to bring accountability for crimes committed by KLA commanders during the 1998-99 war in which war crimes were committed by both sides.
Thaçi, who resigned from office nearly six years ago to face charges, stood in silence in The Hague as the presiding judge Charles Smith read out the sentence.
The former president, who served as the head of political directorate of the KLA’s general staff, faced multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity alongside the three other former leaders of the KLA who are widely regarded as national heroes in their homeland.
In addition to the murders, Thaçi was also convicted for the illegal detention of 385 people, torture of 303 people and cruel treatment of about 50.
Once a hardliner, Thaçi shifted towards a more moderate political identity after being courted by western diplomats who suggested he could be a central figure in Kosovo’s post-war settlement.
At the heart of the prosecution’s case was the degree to which the convicted men had senior operational command over the KLA as a centrally-led armed force and whether the crimes amounted to a pattern of abuse.
The court ruled that Thaçi had “actively participated in and encouraged crimes”. Smith said: “The scale and nature of the crimes committed were very serious”.
He added: “The so-called intelligence on which many of these victims were arrested, detained and killed was little more than unverified rumours. Based on that information, victims were called and described as spies and collaborators and violently treated.”
Smith said Thaçi “used his position, leadership, authority and standing” to encourage crimes but insisted the trial was “not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army” or its ultimate goal of securing independence for Kosovo, which at the time was a province in Serbia. Thaçi could appeal the verdict.
Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers court in The Hague had asked for a maximum 45-year prison sentence for Thaçi and the other defendants, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi who had all denied the charges against them.
Krasniqi received 25 years in prison, Selimi 13 years and Veseli 18 years. Thaçi also faces separate charges of intimidating witnesses with judgement in the case still to come. He has plead not guilty.
The three-judge panel dismissed six charges of crimes against humanity and said prosecutors had failed to show these happened as part of widespread or systematic attacks against the civilian population as a whole.
Known by the nom de guerre of Commander Snake during the war, Thaçi stood out among the KLA leadership as an intelligent and articulate figure who would later charm diplomats – most notably the US secretary of state Madeleine Albright – at the negotiations in Rambouillet that ended the conflict.
But behind the self-assured image he projected as a senior political figure, he was long dogged by allegations of a darker and more ruthless side from his time as a wartime commander.
Thaçi’s defence partly rested on the notion that while serious abuses did occur, the KLA was a not a strictly centralised organisation, claiming that Thaçi’s senior position in the rebel group did not indicate culpability for crimes committed by local units.
“Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the western ideals of democracy, equality and justice,” Thaçi told judges in February.
The trial was opposed by many in Kosovo. Outside the court, Kosovo foreign minister, Glauk Konjufca, told the media: “A terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war. It is a sad, unjust, undeserved decision,.”
Thaçi’s PDK party called the verdict “a great injustice, because it is based on claims and materials that we consider fabricated and nurtured over the years by the state apparatus and Serbian propaganda to criminalise the just war of the Kosovo Liberation Army”.
In Kosovo’s capital, Pristina, thousands of people watched the reading of the verdict live on a huge screen and were stunned at the sentence. Some started shouting “UCK,” the Albanian-language acronym for the KLA.
Thaçi, who was born in Kosovo’s rugged Drenica mountains – the KLA heartland – was a philosophy student who rose through the KLA’s ranks, returning from what he described as political exile in Switzerland to join Kosovo’s struggle for independence.
Thaçi served in a series of senior political roles after the war but resigned as president to defend himself before the The Hague. After the war, Thaçi became a central political figure and was instrumental in Kosovo’s 2008 declaration of independence.
Most of the 13,000 people who died in the war in Kosovo were ethnic Albanians. A 78-day campaign of Nato airstrikes against Serbian forces ended the fighting. About 1 million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes.
