Ukraine proposes record defence spending next year as war costs soar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:08:00 UTC
22:08:00 KST

Ukraine proposes record defence spending next year as war costs soar
KYIV, Sept 16 - Ukraine is proposing record defence spending for 2027 as the cost of the war with Russia, now in its fifth year, rises and the country needs more financial support from its partners, officials said on Wednesday.
Defence spending is expected to hit 4.89 trillion hryvnias ($110 billion) in 2027, 12% higher than this year. It accounted for about two-thirds of the total spending in a draft 2027 budget of 7.27 trillion hryvnias presented to parliament on Wednesday.
Budget revenues are forecast at 5.6 trillion hryvnias.
"This is the sixth budget of the full-scale war, and it's again bigger than the previous one. During these years, the war has become more expensive," said Roksolana Pidlasa, head of the parliamentary budget committee told lawmakers.
"At the same time, state revenues ... are not growing at the same pace as spending is increasing."
The daily cost of the war has risen to $190 million this year compared with $116 million in 2022 at the start of Russia's invasion, Pidlasa said.
Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said told parliament that Ukraine would require more than $52 billion in international financial aid next year.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's government has secured commitments from partners to cover around $20 billion and was in talks on how to cover the remaining amount, he said.
Marchenko said that Russian assets frozen by Ukraine's European allies could become a key source to cover the budget gap in 2027.
Lawmakers have until October 1 to review the draft budget and submit their proposals. The spending plan must be passed by parliament in three readings by December 1.
UKRAINE'S FINANCIAL SITUATION MORE COMPLICATED
Ukraine's financial situation was getting more complicated this year as Russia intensified its strikes on Ukrainian businesses and infrastructure, the finance minister said.
As the damages has grown, budget revenues have started falling, but at the same time the Ukrainian armed forces have required more funds, Marchenko said. Currently, Ukraine faces an unfunded additional gap for its defence spending of $27 billion this year as the country seeks to increase army wages and further increase its weapons production.
During the earlier years of the war, Ukraine covered its defence needs with its own revenues and relied on foreign financial aid to finance its social and humanitarian spending.
Since the start of the invasion, Ukraine has received about $198 billion in fiscal aid from its foreign partners with the EU providing the bulk.
But to ensure smooth financing from partners, Kyiv needs to push through tax and governance reforms, and meet a number of financial and budget requirements despite wartime challenges.
On Wednesday, parliament passed a bill to impose taxes on foreign parcels in the first reading, moving closer to satisfying one of the key conditions to unlock funds from the International Monetary Fund and the European Union.
"Parliament advanced two essential tax and customs reforms that bring Ukraine's e-commerce framework closer to EU standards, strengthen fiscal resilience and support fairer competition for Ukrainian businesses," Marchenko said.
"This progress also paves the way for around 4 billion euros in EU macro-financial support." REUTERS

Zelenskyy says he is ready to hold elections "tomorrow, but..."
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stressed that elections cannot be held while active hostilities continue due to a number of factors: legislation, the logistics of organising voting abroad and in temporarily occupied territories, and safety concerns.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with CBS
Quote: "I am ready to do it [hold elections – ed.] tomorrow. But if we have the war, you can't do it according not only to the constitution and the election law, [but] according to security first of all. Children can't go to school. How do you want to make elections? What elections? How to make elections with the 9 million people who are abroad?"
Details: Zelenskyy said that normally around 500,000 Ukrainians would vote abroad. He also mentioned the people who are living in temporarily occupied territories.
"Will they vote? How will they vote? Who will control their voting? There are Russian soldiers there," the president said.
Zelenskyy pointed out that Ukraine has repeatedly proposed a ceasefire that could be used to prepare for elections and as a step towards de-escalation and ending the war, but Russia has rejected these proposals.
When the interviewer noted that some people from the country's higher echelons of power, including former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, are calling for elections to be held, Zelenskyy said he considers this a mistake. He said he believes that these people "want to be in politics".
Quote: "I think it's a mistake. During the war, peace is [priority] number one. Politics is not even number two. Even for politicians, it's number 10. For people, it's number 100. The priorities are [different]. How to survive, how to live, how to go to school, as I said. What to do with all of this?"
Background:
- In an address on 18 August, Fedorov called for measures to ensure that Russia does not get to decide when Ukrainians can once again elect their government.
- A source from the President's Office told the BBC that Fedorov's idea of holding elections demonstrates a "lack of realism".
- Fedorov's team told Ukrainska Pravda that his call for elections did not mean he wanted them "tomorrow", but was intended to highlight the need to make thorough preparations and resolve all the issues related to the process in detail.

Iran warns against growing use of AI in wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:05:59 UTC
22:05:59 KST

Addressing UNESCO’s 2026 Global Forum on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (GFEAI 2026) in Riyadh on Wednesday, Hossein Simaee Sarraf stressed that technology is not neutral and warned that AI could be used as a means of oppression.
“Artificial intelligence does not act fairly by itself,” Simaee remarked, adding that algorithms can sometimes destroy more than they create and platforms can become sources of harm instead of development.
He also cautioned that even surveillance must have limits, noting that greater oversight of governments and those in power is desirable, but monitoring ordinary citizens’ behavior, relationships and intentions could create an “invisible dictatorship.”
“Today, data is being used in actions that violate human rights and even lead to the killing of children,” the minister noted, questioning whether AI platforms and technology developers should bear responsibility for how their systems are used.
Simaee pointed out that AI can also be used “to identify and precisely target human beings with missiles,” raising serious ethical questions over its military applications.
Referring to the attack on a school in southern Iran by the US using AI, which resulted in the martyrdom of 168 students and teachers, Simaee highlighted that the issue required deep consideration and urgent solutions.
The minister further cautioned that AI could widen existing inequalities, noting that an ethical framework should not only prevent harm but also guarantee equal access to the technology.
“Technology must serve humanity, and artificial intelligence must expand human freedom, rather than restrict it,” Simaee stressed, calling on developing countries to build AI systems suited to their own languages and cultures.
According to Press TV, his warnings come as AI-assisted warfare has increasingly featured in Tel Aviv and Washington’s military operations.
Investigations suggest that Israel has extensively used digital tools Lavender and the Gospel to identify and target Palestinians in Gaza, where the regime has killed more than 73,000 people and wounded 173,000 others.
Reports have also linked AI-assisted surveillance and targeting technologies to the regime’s military aggression in Lebanon, where its forces have killed 4,383 people and wounded 12,406 others.
Furthermore, during the US-Israeli aggression against Iran, several AI platforms developed by major technology companies, including Microsoft, Apple and Amazon, were combined with satellite imagery, radar, drone and communications data to create a battlefield picture and support targeting decisions.
He underscored that the region’s most important priority is now an end to unilateral coercive measures and the establishment of peace, describing sanctions as “unethical” and peace and security as an ethical necessity.
Simaee also noted that Iran enjoys capable universities, researchers, knowledge-based companies and specialized institutions, stressing that these capacities should be brought together through greater cooperation, data sharing and joint use of infrastructure.

Balyasny hedge fund boosts Swiss presence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Balyasny hedge fund boosts Swiss presence
Balyasny Asset Management is opening a presence in the Swiss tax haven of Zug, adding to the numbers of global hedge fund roles located in the country.
The Chicago-based firm with $38 billion assets under management is currently hiring for two commodities-related roles with Zug as a location option, as well as other analyst roles, according to the firm’s recruitment web page.
The firm co-founded by billionaire Dmitry Balyasny already has a presence in Geneva, among more than a dozen locations worldwide. It is currently awaiting a license to trade in Zug, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The canton is well established as a low corporate-tax centre, and commodity trading powerhouses including Glencore are also located there.
Balyasny declined to comment.
Ranked among the biggest global multi-strategy hedge funds, Balyasny, like its peers, employs multiple teams of traders across asset classes to earn steady returns.
As demand for multistrat services remains strong, firms are constantly on the lookout for more ways to recruit and retain top talent to run their growing assets. Aside from setting up in new locations to tap locally, some firms have been known to establish outposts for existing teams.
Switzerland has recently seen a flurry of hedge funds setting up a presence there including Capula Investment Management which established a Zug branch earlier this year. New York-headquartered Schonfeld Strategic Advisors plans to open in Zurich later in 2026, Bloomberg has reported.
Millennium Management has offices in both Geneva and Zug, while Brevan Howard Asset Management and Diego Megia’s Taula Capital Management each have offices in Geneva.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday announced plans to restrict children's access to social media, saying the EU will propose a new "Kids Act" aimed at protecting minors from online harms.
Addressing the European Parliament, von der Leyen said the commission would propose the legislation Thursday, introducing different levels of protection based on children's ages.
"No social media under the age of 13. No personal account under the age of 15," she said.
Under the proposed approach, children aged 13 to under 15 would only be allowed to use limited "mini accounts" established and supervised by parents or guardians, with restricted features and a time limit of one hour per day.
For those aged 15 to 18, social media platforms would be required to implement "safe design" measures, she said.
Addictive digital design
Von der Leyen said the initiative was prompted by concerns over the impact of social media and addictive digital design on children, including sleep loss, anxiety, bullying and self-harm.
She also said the EU would seek to shift responsibility toward technology platforms.
"We are reversing the burden of proof. Now, platforms will have to prove to us that they are safe," von der Leyen said, adding that the issue was not simply about minors accessing social media, but about the conditions under which social media platforms can reach children.
"Europe has the power to act. It is us who decide the rules, not the tech," she said.
Von der Leyen said the EU's approach would extend beyond minors, noting that addictive digital design can affect adults as well.
The European Commission plans to propose a broader "Digital Fairness Act" in the autumn, she added.

Sanctions relief for two Belarusian companies

Bellesbumprom is a state-owned industrial concern overseeing companies in Belarus’s forestry, woodworking, pulp, and paper industries. Washington imposed restrictions on the organization in 2023.

Oleshky Starving: The Human Cost of Territorial Concessions

A crisis on two fronts: Saudi Arabia's mounting security dilemma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:03:54 UTC
22:03:54 KST

Breadcrumb
A crisis on two fronts: Saudi Arabia's mounting security dilemma
A drone attack launched from Iraqi territory last week against Saudi Arabia’s main pipeline to the Red Sea has revived the prospect of a two-front confrontation for Riyadh.
As the situation in Yemen spirals further out of anyone’s control, Saudi Arabia’s options for managing both fronts are narrowing.
The Houthis have completed their takeover of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, seizing Mocha and the islands of Perim, Zuqar, and Hanish, which command the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
While the Yemeni government’s counteroffensive has since shifted toward Marib and Jawf, the front lines remain fluid.
A second front opens
On Thursday, several drones struck Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline south of Medina, causing injuries and damage and forcing Riyadh to shut the pipeline as a precaution.
The Saudi foreign ministry said the drones had been launched from Iraq and would not retaliate “at this stage,” at the request of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.
Baghdad dismissed the commander who led operations in Missan province after an investigation traced the drones to launch platforms near al-Shib, on the Iranian border, and closed three crossings, Shalamsheh, al-Shib and al-Mandali, to stop the attackers fleeing into Iran.
Al-Zaidi has accepted an Iranian request for a joint investigation. No group has claimed the strike, and an alliance of Iran-backed factions has denied hitting the pipeline.
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq called it “an honour that we do not claim”. Shalamsheh and al-Shib reopened to passenger traffic on Sunday, though not yet to trade, with a full reopening due by Thursday.
It is not the first time Riyadh has traced an attack on its oil infrastructure to Iraq. On 29 July, US and Saudi forces struck Iran-aligned Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) factions accused of hitting Saudi facilities in the Eastern Province. Twenty PMF fighters and five Iranian advisers were reportedly killed. Riyadh called it self-defence.
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq initially threatened retaliation over the July strikes before backing down under pressure from Iraqi figures, including Hadi al-Amiri. Diplomatic efforts through August did not stop last Thursday’s attack.
The Shia Coordination Framework in Baghdad remains divided over how to disarm Iran-backed factions ahead of a 30 September deadline. Part of the problem is that some factions are deeply embedded in Iraq’s security apparatus and maintain close ties to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
That disarmament push may not even solve the underlying problem. Tamer Badawi, an Iraq analyst and associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab that the Islamic Resistance in Iraq’s denial, if it “proves accurate,” could mean Iran’s Quds Force “may be conducting attacks via new groupings”.
Even if known factions like Kataib Hezbollah, Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba, and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada disarm, “other new and unknown groups can launch transborder attacks from Iraqi territories”.
Baghdad, Badawi added, lacks “consistent control over the Iran-aligned groups” and the “ground-to-air capabilities” needed to stop such strikes.
“It’s most certainly the case that there is coordination between Tehran, armed networks in Iraq, and Ansarallah,” he told The New Arab, though it is “taking much less of a public and celebrated appearance” than when Iraqi factions and Ansarullah synchronised attacks against Israel after 7 October.
The Institute for the Study of War described the strike as part of “a coordinated effort with other Axis of Resistance members to coerce Saudi Arabia to meet Houthi demands by attacking Saudi energy infrastructure”.
The same assessment linked the attack to the Houthi campaign around Bab al-Mandeb, saying the Houthis are “setting conditions to establish” the strait “as an Axis of Resistance-controlled body of water,” which it called “unacceptable for US national security and economic interests”.
Saudi strategy under pressure
The latest Houthi offensive began on 3 September across Taiz and Hodeidah, producing Yemen’s biggest territorial changes since a 2022 truce halted the civil war. It also undoes years of Saudi effort to reduce exposure.
Riyadh led a coalition against the Houthis from 2015, scaled back after a costly air campaign, and pursued a peace roadmap from 2023.
Direct hostilities resumed in July, after Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa airport and the Houthis blockaded Red Sea ports. Last Tuesday, Houthi missiles and drones hit four southern Saudi cities, injuring at least 73 people. Riyadh has relied on tens of thousands of Yemeni troops rather than deploy its own.
The Houthis claimed a fresh strike of their own on Sunday, saying they hit weapons depots and command centres at the Sharurah military base in southern Saudi Arabia. An Iranian commercial vessel was struck the same day in the Strait of Hormuz, a reminder that Riyadh’s other maritime exit remains unsettled too.
Those forces have struggled for familiar reasons. Coordination between units has been patchy, reinforcement mechanisms weak, and Saudi air support limited. Someone still has to fight on the ground, and the units expected to do that are the ones already exposed as weakest.
Ahmed Nagi, a senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG), said the Houthis’ hold on Bab al-Mandeb has already changed their leverage.
“It’s clear that the Houthis now have a greater influence over the Bab al-Mandab,” he told The New Arab. “It also gives them room to expand toward the other side of Yemen and further weaken the government forces that Saudi Arabia is supporting.”
Nagi said Riyadh has few good options left. “I don’t think the Saudis have many good options to contain the situation now,” he said.
“Things have basically gone from bad to worse. If they want to contain it, they’ll probably have to make some concessions, because the Houthis are now negotiating from a much stronger position.”
That bind predates last week’s advance. Reversing the Houthi gains risks pulling Saudi Arabia back into the ground war it spent a decade trying to leave. Leaving them unanswered risks losing the coastline and the pipeline’s approach to Yanbu for good.
Mohammed al-Basha, founder of the risk advisory firm Basha Report, said that “the situation on Yemen’s West Coast remains fluid”.
The coalition, he told The New Arab, “appears to have resumed limited airstrikes against Houthi positions,” while the Southern Giants Brigades and National Shield Forces “have stabilised a new defensive line south of the strait,” with units withdrawn from the coast regrouping elsewhere.
Houthi casualties from the offensive that ended 9 September are “heavy,” though unconfirmed.
Washington stops short
The Houthi advance has already pushed Riyadh to seek military help it said only two months ago it did not need. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called President Donald Trump twice on Thursday as Saudi-backed forces retreated, asking in the second call for the US to authorise strikes against the Houthis. Trump declined.
Adm. Brad Cooper, the CENTCOM chief, travelled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday, and around 200 US personnel are now in the kingdom, with more than 100 focused on intelligence and targeting, according to reports.
In practice, Riyadh is managing the war largely alone, with indirect support, limited airstrikes, stronger air defences, and a parallel push for Oman-mediated talks.
That mix of escalation and diplomacy is not necessarily a contradiction. It reflects a Saudi calculation that military pressure and a negotiated off-ramp serve the same goal, keeping the Houthis from consolidating gains without a return to the costly ground war Riyadh spent years trying to exit.
Saudi oil route comes under pressure
The pipeline gives Saudi Arabia only a partial way around Hormuz. It lets crude bypass the strait and reach Yanbu, but tankers carrying those exports south still have to cross the Red Sea toward Bab al-Mandeb. Bypass capacity, in practice, is not secure supply.
Markets are already registering some of that risk. Saudi Arabia’s benchmark stock index fell 1.3% on Sunday, and Aramco shares 1.6%, as investors weighed the pipeline’s precautionary shutdown. Reuters put the exposure at roughly 4% of global oil supply.
The Houthis say their blockade targets only Saudi vessels. Saudi crude supply fell 2.3 million barrels a day in August to 6 million bpd, its lowest level in three decades, according to the International Energy Agency, partly due to attacks on ships transiting Bab al-Mandeb.
Nagi sees a deliberate logic behind the timing. Iran, he argued, has a clear interest in pressuring Saudi Arabia while Hormuz is already disrupted, and in hitting Saudi energy exports via the Yanbu reroute now within Houthi reach.
It also challenges the regional order Washington has been building ahead of the midterms.
“That obviously benefits Iran at this moment,” he said, “because it gives Tehran another way to put pressure on its regional adversaries and the global economy.”
Regional test
The escalation is also testing the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement Saudi Arabia signed with Pakistan and Turkey in August, committing each to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. Whether it extends to an Iraq-origin attack is untested.
The East-West Pipeline was built to solve one problem, Saudi Arabia’s exposure at Hormuz. It is now exposed from both directions. Drones from Iraq can hit the infrastructure carrying crude to Yanbu, while Houthi forces at Bab al-Mandeb can threaten the ships carrying it onward.
That vulnerability-reduction strategy has instead multiplied where Riyadh can be tested.
But the coordination of strikes looks strategic more than operational. Tehran does not need to order a specific attack for it to serve the same purpose as the Houthi campaign at Bab al-Mandeb.
Confirmation of an operational link between the two fronts would turn this from two crises into one campaign against the infrastructure Saudi Arabia built to feel safe from either.
For now, Riyadh is reinforcing Yemeni forces, working with Baghdad to trace last week’s drone attackers, and leaning on Oman’s channel with the Houthis.
It is, for the moment, a strategy of management rather than resolution.
Francesco Salesio Schiavi is an Italian specialist in the Middle East. His focus lies in the security architecture of the Levant and the Gulf, with a particular emphasis on Iraq, Iran, and the Arab Peninsula, as well as military and diplomatic interventions by international actors

Belgian court rules country's treasury department lacks authority to decide on Russian bank's frozen assets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:03:22 UTC
22:03:22 KST

Belgian court rules country's treasury department lacks authority to decide on Russian bank's frozen assets
BRUSSELS, Sept 16 - Belgium's top administrative court ruled that the country's treasury department lacked the proper legal authority to refuse the release of frozen assets of Russian bank BCS held at Brussels-based clearing house Euroclear.
The Council of State did not order the release of the assets, however, and it was unclear whether the ruling offered the Russian bank a route towards getting the securities and funds back.
While the ruling only applies to BCS Bank, other treasury department decisions taken under the same mechanism could also be vulnerable to challenges unless Belgium revises the legal framework.
The ruling was made last Friday and first reported on Wednesday by Belgian newspaper De Tijd.
A spokesperson for the Belgian Finance Ministry said it was studying the ruling and its possible consequences. Euroclear and BCS Bank did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
BCS Bank held securities and funds at Euroclear through Russia's National Settlement Depository, which was placed under EU sanctions in June 2022 following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. This resulted in the freezing of the bank's assets held by Euroclear.
BCS Bank asked Belgium to have its assets released in July 2024, which the treasury department refused. BCS then appealed against the refusal to the Belgian Council of State in October 2024.
Friday's ruling said that under EU sanctions rules, Belgium must designate a "competent authority" to decide on requests to release frozen assets.
Belgium gave that power to the finance minister, who then delegated it to the administrator-general of the ministry's treasury department. The court ruled that this delegation was too broad and insufficiently defined.
Most of the roughly €200 billion ($230.7 billion) in frozen Russian assets held in Europe are kept at Euroclear.
The European Commission last year proposed using the assets to back a loan for Ukraine. But Belgium opposed that, saying it did not provide sufficient guarantees that it would not be left alone to deal with potential lawsuits and demands of damages from Russia. As a result, the plan was dropped.
However, several EU member states have recently asked for the EU to reopen the debate. REUTERS

Duterte in person at ICC for first time over ‘war on drugs’ killings
Former Philippine president accused of setting up death squads faces trial starting on November 30.
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte has appeared in person for the first time at the International Criminal Court (ICC), where he is charged with crimes against humanity for killings during his “war on drugs“.
Prosecutors accuse Duterte, who was arrested and transferred to The Hague-based court in March 2025, of creating, funding and arming death squads that targeted drug users and dealers. Duterte denies the charges, saying he only ordered police to act in self-defence as part of his anti-drug offensive.
Recommended Stories

The 81-year-old remained silent during Wednesday’s session, which covered his health, evidence disclosure and the timetable of the trial due to open on November 30. He had missed earlier hearings on medical grounds, with his lawyers saying cognitive decline has left him unfit to take part.
In a filing on Tuesday, the defence said serious memory loss leaves him unable to absorb new information or reliably recall the past.
Citing tests in an unpublished report by three medical experts, the lawyers said Duterte believes the year is 2007 or 2008, believes that he is 84 or 85, and could not name the sitting president of the United States.
In January, however, judges ruled that he was healthy enough to stand trial and requested that he be present for proceedings.
The charges cover Duterte’s alleged role in at least 76 murders between 2013 and 2018, when he was mayor of the southern city of Davao, and later as president from 2016 to 2022.
“Decades of murdering his own people, murdering the children of the Philippines, and he claims that he did it all for his country. He doesn’t deny it,” said Julian Nicholls, summing up for the prosecution after the hearings.
“His promise was to kill thousands, and he did.”
Philippine police say 6,200 suspects were killed in anti-drug operations, while rights groups and ICC prosecutors put the overall toll as high as 30,000.
Randy Delos Santos, a Filipino whose teenage nephew was killed by police under Duterte’s presidency, told the AFP news agency he was glad the former president was able to attend.
“Seeing that he is physically fit, we believe this could be the start of a process that will finally bring us, the victims, the justice we have been waiting for,” he said.
Lawyers for other victims of Duterte’s draconian anti-drug campaign have argued that a full trial could encourage more families to come forward.
Duterte is the first former head of state from Asia to face trial at the ICC.
In 2018, he had announced the Philippines’s withdrawal from the court after it opened a preliminary investigation into his conduct, but judges last year refused to dismiss the case on those grounds.

Strikes on UN warehouses push aid money from delivery to protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:01:12 UTC
22:01:12 KST

The UN is considering moving humanitarian supplies into underground facilities after strikes hit 10 of its warehouses in Ukraine this year and destroyed millions of dollars' worth of aid, UN Humanitarian Coordinator in Ukraine Matthias Schmale said on 15 September.
Repeated strikes on aid warehouses have forced the UN to rethink how it stores and buys supplies in Ukraine, including moving them underground. More of the humanitarian budget now goes to protecting aid rather than delivering it.
"These deliberate attacks on warehousing capacities … is a new trend of the last few months," Schmale told Reuters after briefing states in Geneva.
Strikes destroyed medical supplies, food, and generators worth millions across Ukraine
On 3 September, an air attack destroyed a major medical-supplies warehouse in the Kyiv region. The attack came after two other medical-supply warehouses were destroyed in the previous three months, including a double strike in Dnipro in late August that wiped out half the supplies earmarked for some 225,000 people in frontline and hard-to-reach areas.
In July, a strike on a warehouse near Kyiv destroyed nearly $3.9 million in UNICEF supplies, including power generators, water supplies, and hygiene kits. In May, an Iskander missile strike on a World Food Programme warehouse in Dnipro destroyed food meant for around 130,000 people.
Added security costs strain an already underfunded aid operation
Schmale said the UN is now weighing whether to store supplies underground rather than in conventional warehouses, and is delaying some purchases while it works out how to protect what it buys. The added security costs come on top of an already strained budget: the UN's 2026 humanitarian appeal for Ukraine seeks $2.3 billion to reach 4.1 million people.

BNN IN FOCUS | Political party review: New Unity – from election winner to fighting for survival in the Saeima

Author: Ilona Bērziņa
New Unity (JV) is very fond of playing the role of the “adult in the room”. But when that “adult” starts behaving like a petulant child, it should come as no surprise when someone else comes along and picks up the toys it has scattered around. For the winner of the 14th Saeima election, hovering on the edge of the 5% threshold is an extremely poor performance. It almost seems as though the political force has been thrown back to where it stood before the 13th Saeima election.
In the autumn of 2018, it seemed that little remained of JV’s former political strength. In the 13th Saeima election, it won just 6.7% of the vote and eight seats – the smallest parliamentary faction. Four years later, with the support of 173,425 voters and 26 seats, the party was back on top.
Another four years on, the situation has turned upside down once again. In an August 2026 SKDS poll, only 4.2% of all surveyed citizens said they were prepared to vote for JV, while a poll conducted at the end of August by Latvijas fakti in cooperation with Faktu logs put the party at 5.9%.
The party would still make it into the Saeima, but instead of contemplating another election victory, it now has to think about how to salvage what remains of its political influence. The fall has been dramatic, and it cannot be concealed behind the fig leaf of unpopular but supposedly necessary decisions.
The Progressives factor
As mentioned at the outset, once JV began behaving like a petulant child, a resourceful “classmate” from another group came along and took whatever it could. That classmate is the Progressives – a party JV initially feared leaving in opposition because the two parties’ electorates overlapped, and which it later brought into government itself.
Contrary to the view that JV’s turn towards the Progressives began only in the summer of 2023, when Kariņš set about dismantling his second government, the flirtation had begun considerably earlier.
Recall the metaphor of four-legged and three-legged stools, when Krišjānis Kariņš began forming a government after the 2022 election and JV considered a four-party coalition with the United List, the National Alliance and the Progressives.
Moreover, JV voters had no particular objection to the Progressives. In an SKDS poll conducted two weeks after the election, 60% of JV voters supported a four-party government that included the Progressives. Only 34% preferred a coalition of JV, the United List and the National Alliance without them. The inclusion of the Progressives was blocked mainly by opposition from the United List and the National Alliance.
After Kariņš resigned, JV eventually got its “three-legged stool” in the form of Evika Siliņa’s government. At the same time, however, JV’s rating fell from 10.3% in August 2023 to 7.7% in September – the largest decline among political parties that month.
JV and the Progressives – closer than they may seem
Following the collapse of Siliņa’s government in 2026, Siliņa herself acknowledged that the Progressives were ideologically the closest political force to JV in parliament.
Both parties are pro-European, pro-NATO and strongly supportive of Ukraine. Both emphasise the rule of law, a Western democratic orientation and investment in education and science.
On social values, JV is much closer to the Progressives than to conservative parties – something demonstrated by the debates over partnership legislation and the Istanbul Convention.
Where they differ is economic policy. JV defines itself as a centre-right party, emphasising fiscal discipline, entrepreneurship, investment, capital markets and competitiveness. The Progressives, meanwhile, define themselves as a social democratic and green political force. Their programme places much greater emphasis on progressive taxation, public investment, social security, affordable rental housing, climate policy and prioritising public transport.
If you are wondering why so much space in a pre-election review of New Unity is being devoted to the Progressives, the answer is simple: JV hoped to take a large share of the Progressives’ voters. Judging by the polls, the opposite happened.
Here is, in my view, a particularly telling example. In a 2025 SKDS poll, prospective Riga voters were asked who they considered the most suitable candidate for mayor. Among potential JV voters, 33% chose the Progressives’ Viesturs Kleinbergs, while only 16% considered New Unity’s own candidate, Vilnis Ķirsis, the best choice.
The fact that a JV voter can see a politician from the Progressives as a perfectly normal alternative to their own party’s candidate is already a warning sign that should not be underestimated. Otherwise, before the next Saeima election, the story of New Unity may begin like an old Latvian folk tale: “Once upon a time…”
Kariņš and the “adult in the room”
The expression “adult in the room” is a long-standing Washington political metaphor used to describe a pragmatic and predictable politician who keeps a cool head amid chaos. In Latvian politics, the label stuck almost perfectly to Krišjānis Kariņš and JV.
Here, another brief excursion into the past is necessary.
After the 2018 election, the largest parties were unable to form a government for several months. Only 109 days after the election, Krišjānis Kariņš – a politician from parliament’s smallest faction, with just eight MPs – succeeded in forming a five-party Cabinet comprising JV, Development/For!, the New Conservative Party, the National Alliance and KPV LV.
The political message was elegant: the election winners could not reach an agreement, so the calm, technocratic Kariņš arrived and put everything in order.
JV secured the prime minister’s office, constant public visibility and a reputation as the party that might not be the loudest, but was nevertheless the aforementioned “adult in the room”.
Climbing the mountain
By the 2019 European Parliament election, JV had won 26.24% of the vote and finished first. Of course, turnout in European Parliament elections was different, and the party had two very strong candidates – Valdis Dombrovskis and Sandra Kalniete – but the political signal was unmistakable: the party was back, and stronger than ever.
Meanwhile, some of the political newcomers of 2018 dissolved, split apart or lost voters’ confidence over the following four years. KPV LV effectively self-destructed, the Conservatives lost support, and Development/For! failed to clear the 5% threshold in 2022.
Against this backdrop, JV stood out as an island of stability in Latvia’s otherwise turbulent and rather murky political swamp.
Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, JV had become the leader in SKDS polling by March. In a crisis, public support for the incumbent government increased, while foreign policy and security moved to the forefront – areas in which JV had both Prime Minister Kariņš and the popular Foreign Minister Edgars Rinkēvičs.
That is how eight seats in the 13th Saeima became 26 seats in the 14th.
The price of arrogance and mistakes
The image of the “adult in the room” has one unpleasant characteristic: more is expected of the adult than of everyone else.
If a party has spent years presenting itself as the benchmark for competence, professionalism and integrity, its mistakes are judged by a different standard. And that became the proverbial banana peel on which JV stepped with remarkable enthusiasm time and again.
One of the biggest scandals concerned Kariņš’s special flights, and it struck precisely where the party’s image was most vulnerable.
In its 2022 programme, JV presented itself in terms of competence, foresight and integrity. Against that backdrop, the findings of the National Audit Office looked particularly damaging: approximately 1.2 million euros had been spent on special flights between 2021 and 2023, including at least 221,566 euros in state budget funds spent unlawfully and 323,688 euros in Council of the European Union funding used uneconomically.
Of course, a scapegoat was found – former State Chancellery Director Jānis Citskovskis – but that did little to reduce the political damage suffered by JV.
Once again, the polls tell the story. In November 2023, when the scandal over Kariņš’s special flights had just erupted, New Unity stood at 11.1% in SKDS polling. By December, it had fallen to 8.3%.
Kariņš “threw in the towel” on 14 August 2023, and just ten days later, on 24 August, the President nominated Evika Siliņa for the post of Prime Minister. She quickly reached an agreement on a coalition with the Progressives and ZZS.
What was done – and what was not
JV does have achievements it can put on its record.
Defence spending in 2026, based on the updated GDP forecast, amounts to approximately 4.73% of GDP; compulsory State Defence Service has been introduced and strengthened; in February 2025, the Baltic states synchronised their electricity grids with continental Europe, ending their dependence on the Russian and Belarusian power systems; and in education, the transition to Latvian as the language of instruction was completed and a centralised natural sciences examination introduced.
Admittedly, the decision to transition to Latvian as the language of instruction had already been taken by the previous Saeima. There are undoubtedly other positive achievements as well.
Now let us look at how several major promises made in 2022 have fared.
Ahead of the 14th Saeima election, JV promised in its programme to increase teachers’ salaries to a level 20% above the national average wage. Salaries have increased, but that target has not been reached.
The party also promised to make secondary education compulsory. No such requirement existed in legislation then, and none has been introduced since.
Another promise made during the previous pre-election debates – to introduce a property tax exemption threshold for a person’s primary residence – also remained unfulfilled.
The promised rapid transformation of the economy and narrowing of the gap with Lithuania and Estonia have likewise been slow to materialise.
Against this backdrop, the wording in the introductory section of JV’s 2026 programme about pursuing politics capable of correcting mistakes and delivering on promises to the very end seems particularly ironic.
Why should people believe that this new “contract with society” will work when previous election promises have been only partially fulfilled?
JV and a spectacular comeback
In theory, it is possible.
One example is Unity itself, which around 2017 had become associated in voters’ minds with political intrigue, arrogance and an inability to address social problems. According to SKDS, its rating hovered at around 2.7–2.9% in June and July 2018, while some Latvijas fakti polls put it as low as 1.5%.
Yet despite disastrous summer polling, the party managed to mobilise voters in the autumn by contesting the election under the New Unity name.
Could a similar leap happen again this autumn? Probably not.
JV is no longer the prime minister’s party, and instead of a clearly dominant leader, it now has a “team of heavyweights”. All of them carry the baggage of four years in government – and in the eyes of voters, it is hardly an appealing burden.
JV can still mobilise its disciplined core electorate and win over some undecided voters. However, the current data offer little indication that the party can repeat its 2022 triumph.

UN experts warn against glorifying convicted war criminals after Mladic funeral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
UN experts on Wednesday warned that glorifying perpetrators of international crimes can cause further harm to victims and survivors, after convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic was given what they described as a "hero's funeral" in Belgrade earlier this month.
The experts said official tributes to people convicted of atrocities can "deepen suffering and undermine memory, truth and accountability," expressing particular concern over the attendance of senior officials from Bosnia and Herzegovina's Republika Srpska entity at Mladic's Sept. 7 funeral.
Mladic, a former Bosnian Serb general known as the “butcher of Bosnia,” was convicted of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, including for the 1995 Srebrenica genocide. He died in August while serving a life sentence in The Hague.
According to reports cited by the experts, Mladic's coffin was transported to Serbia on a government plane and carried by uniformed soldiers, while military medals were displayed as thousands attended a Belgrade church.
"Lasting reconciliation is built on truth, accountability and respect for victims," the experts said, urging commemorative initiatives to uphold judicially established facts and reject denialism and historical revisionism.

Alzheimer’s damage may begin outside the brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Alzheimer’s damage may begin outside the brain
Immune cells in lymph nodes appear to kick-start inflammation
This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
Destructive immune cells tied to Alzheimer’s disease may get their marching orders from cells outside the brain rather than within it.
In mice, suppressing a small population of immune cells located in lymph nodes protects against neurodegeneration, researchers report September 3 in Nature Neuroscience. The findings raise the possibility of treating Alzheimer’s disease while bypassing the brain’s siege defenses.
For years, researchers have gone all in on efforts to remove toxic tangles of proteins like amyloid and tau from the brain as a way of halting Alzheimer’s, with limited success. But the immune system also plays an important role in neurodegeneration. What exactly that role is — protector or antagonist — has been unclear.
In 2023, neurologist David Holtzman and colleagues showed that immune system T cells accumulate around tau tangles — implying that they might cause damage. Halting these cells’ entry into the brain reduced inflammation, and also reduced neuronal damage, says Holtzman, of Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis.
Still, it wasn’t known how these T cells accessed the brain in the first place. “A big question has been whether the T cells passively enter the brain or are primed … to do so,” says Rudolph Tanzi, a neurogeneticist at Harvard Medical School who wasn’t involved in the study.
During priming, T cells are ordered to rally and multiply. The generals that bark out these orders are called dendritic cells, which capture signatures of cellular threats called antigens and present them to T cell infantry.
No one had looked closely at what dendritic cells in lymph nodes were doing during neurodegenerative disease, Holtzman says. So in the new study, he and his colleagues compared two groups of mice engineered to have tau-linked neurodegeneration, one of which lacked dendritic cells.
Blocking an attack
Alzheimer’s-like neurodegeneration can ravage a brain, as seen in the slice of a mouse’s brain at left. The attack may be planned in the lymph nodes, new research suggests. The brain slice depicted on the right came from a mouse in which that early stage of attack was blocked.
In old age, mice without dendritic cells still had brains packed with tau. But compared with the other mice, they were protected against neurodegeneration and performed better on cognitive tasks like nest building.
They also had far fewer T cells in their brains. This suggests that tau tangles aren’t working alone in driving neurodegeneration, Holtzman says. “A lot of the damage that tau is causing is due to the inflammatory response that it’s eliciting.” The results would need to be replicated in human brains, he adds.
Despite this seemingly important role, the researchers found few dendritic cells in the mice’s brains. Instead, they detected threat-mimicking brain proteins traveling to the lymph nodes, where dendritic cells used them to rally T cells. The team bred mutant mice with demoted dendritic cell generals that could no longer give commands to T cells. These mice also had fewer T cells in their brains and better-preserved brain structures.
It isn’t practical to disable dendritic cells from birth in people at risk of Alzheimer’s. But Holtzman says his colleagues are working on cellular targets that could suppress them in adulthood. The real promise of the study may be a dementia treatment that bypasses the nervous system’s locked vault — the blood-brain barrier, Holtzman says. “If this panned out, potentially you wouldn’t have to get [therapeutics] into the brain.”

The ministry said the crew detected a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter approaching the Russian warship that did not respond to calls over an international communications channel.
"The corvette's commander made the decision to fire two red signal flares to prevent a provocation by the Danish helicopter, after which the helicopter left the area," it said.
The incident prompted Denmark to summon Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin.
Danish authorities said the helicopter had been carrying out a routine operation near the Russian warship.
Denmark's military said one of the flares passed close to the helicopter and that no warning or radio contact had been made before they were fired.
Barbin, for his part, protested to the Danish side over what he described as dangerous maneuvers by Danish military helicopters near Russian warships.
He said Moscow was investigating the incident and called on Denmark to take measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.

UK allocates £800,000 to protect Ukrainian heritage under 100 Year Partnership Agreement
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:58:00 EEST
21:58:00 KST

UK allocates £800,000 to protect Ukrainian heritage under 100 Year Partnership Agreement
Ukraine and the UK have launched a joint programme to protect and preserve Ukrainian cultural heritage. The British government has allocated £800,000 (over US$1 million) to implement it.
Source: Ministry of Culture of Ukraine, following the inaugural meeting of the programme's Advisory Council in London
Details: The programme will run until 2029. It involves the exchange of expertise, training for Ukrainian specialists and joint projects in the field of cultural heritage preservation. It will be delivered by the British organisation Historic England, funded by the UK's Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS).
The programme's first project will be a collaboration with the Taras Shevchenko National Museum in Kyiv. British and Ukrainian specialists will work on preserving historical photographs from the museum's collection.
Plans include restoring photographs of Taras Shevchenko taken during his lifetime, which are held at the museum. Ukrainian conservators will also undergo training in the UK, so they can go on to work with such materials in Ukraine and pass on their knowledge to other specialists.
The Ministry of Culture reported that Ukraine currently has almost no specialists working in photograph restoration. Developing this specialisation will therefore be one of the project's goals.
An exhibition of Taras Shevchenko's work is also planned to be organised in the UK as part of the partnership.
The British side in the programme is represented by Historic England, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, and the British Council. Ukraine's representatives on the Advisory Council include officials from the Ministry of Culture, the Ukrainian Institute and the Ukrainian Cultural Heritage Foundation.
The council will meet twice a year until the advisory period concludes in March 2029. Its members will set priorities for joint work and consider new projects in the field of cultural heritage.

The vessels involved have not been officially identified. Sources cited by NDTV said the Pakistani ship was a Hunain-class corvette and that the incident occurred around 220 km east of Oman. The Indian vessel was described as a frontline warship.
A similar incident occurred in 2011 when the Pakistani warship PNS Babur brushed past the frigate INS Godavari, damaging its helicopter deck safety netting. Both ships were on anti-piracy patrols in the Gulf of Aden at the time.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:56:00 UTC
21:56:00 KST

The EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance held its first Board meeting in Brussels on Sept. 11, bringing together 18 founding companies from Ukraine and the European Union (EU) to establish priorities for cooperation in the unmanned systems sector.
The inaugural meeting focused on defining the Alliance’s key areas of work and outlining the next steps for its two-year mandate.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
For Ukrainian drone manufacturer Athlon Avia, which co-founded the Alliance, the long-term goal is to create a joint EU-Ukraine market for unmanned aerial systems.
According to Athlon Avia’s press service, such a market would give European countries broader access to Ukrainian drone technologies while allowing Ukrainian manufacturers to establish production capabilities in the EU.
The company said developing production outside Ukraine has become increasingly important amid the ongoing war and security threats.
“Ukraine should be not only a source of unique combat experience for Europe, but also a full-fledged participant in shaping Europe’s defence-industrial priorities and future capabilities,” said Artem Vyunnyk, co-founder of Athlon Avia.
“Together, we must focus on making the Alliance meaningful and influential. Our cooperation should result in solutions that carry real weight for both the Ukrainian and European defense industries,” he added.
The participating companies agreed on several priority areas, including strengthening supply-chain resilience, enabling secure cooperation between defense-industry companies, scaling up production, and creating opportunities for joint testing and innovation.
Hackers Breach Russia’s ‘Invulnerable’ Voting System Ahead of State Duma Elections
They also agreed to establish direct communication channels between member companies to facilitate cooperation.
Andrius Kubilius, European Commissioner for Defense and Space, described the inaugural Board meeting as a historic step toward deeper integration between Ukraine and the EU’s defense industries.
“Europe must learn to conduct drone warfare as one and learn from Ukraine. In a sense, this Alliance can become a kind of academy of Ukraine’s wartime experience,” Kubilius said.
“We’re trying to learn from them a lot, how the ecosystem functions, how the government and drone industries function together,” Simonas Šatūnas, head of Kubilius’s cabinet, said of the alliance in early September.
The EU–Ukraine Drone Alliance was established with a two-year mandate. At its next meeting, members are expected to agree on the Alliance’s governance structure and further define its operational priorities.
The group includes these 18 companies: ORQA, Indra Group, Fincantieri, WB Electronics/WB Group, Destinus, Delair, RSI Europe, TERMA A/S and Quantum Systems on the EU side; and Skyfall Industries, Greentech Harvest, Tencore, Deviro, Vyriy Industry, Scientifim, ATHLON AVIA Scientific Production Company, TAF Industries, UFORCE and F-Drones from Ukraine.
The Commission called for alliance members in early May, saying its main goals would be to “contribute to European efforts towards a comprehensive European drone and counter-drone capacity” and to “offer a multi-layered and multilevel framework, able to link sensors and effectors across Europe and to support decision-making processes.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen first proposed the drone alliance in her State of the Union address last year, as part of a broader set of measures aimed at responding to incursions into EU member states’ airspace.
Since then, the Commission has signed a new “defense industrial partnership” with Ukraine centered on an EU-Ukraine “drone deal.”
The agreement aims to “provide a single, coherent EU-Ukraine framework to facilitate, coordinate and support” the implementation of drone agreements Kyiv has signed with several EU and EFTA capitals.
The partnership could receive up to €10 billion ($11.6 billion) in unspent Security Action for Europe (SAFE) funds, von der Leyen said during a July 15 visit to Kyiv.
Eastern European countries have faced repeated drone incursions in recent months and are calling for the next EU budget to account for the impact of Russia’s war on frontline states.

Former Kosovo president sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:55:41 UTC
21:55:41 KST

Former Kosovo president sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci was found guilty of war crimes committed as part of the Kosovo Liberation Army including murder, torture and illegal arrests by a tribunal in The Hague on Wednesday. Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison alongside fellow former KLA figures who were also found guilty and sentenced.
Kosovo's former president Hashim Thaci was sentenced to 25 years by a tribunal in The Hague on Wednesday for war crimes, the court said in a long-awaited verdict likely to spark outrage in the Balkan country.
The judges said Thaci, who was tried along with three other former guerrilla leaders, was guilty of illegal arrests, torture, murder and cruel treatment committed by guerrilla fighters.
Read moreFormer Kosovo president Thaci pleads not guilty as war crimes trial begins
In Kosovo's capital, a large crowd gathered to watch live on large screens the sentencing of a man many revere as a hero.
As the decision was delivered, the crowd fell silent, with many appearing to be shocked by the decision – after weeks of preparation by his supporters for his possible acquittal.
Thaci's fellow former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) figures Jakup Krasniqi, Rexhep Selimi and Kadri Veseli were also found guilty and sentenced.
Krasniqi received 25 years in prison, Selimi got 13 years and Veseli 18 years.
All four were determined to be criminally responsible for the arbitrary detention and torture of hundreds of people and 96 murders, according to the court.
But they were acquitted of crimes against humanity charges.
The court also said Thaci, Veseli, Selimi and Krasniqi had "contributed significantly" during the Kosovo conflict to a common criminal purpose targeting perceived opponents of the KLA's political and military goals.
Thaci resigned as president and surrendered to the court after his 2020 indictment. He has remained in detention in The Hague ever since, with his time served counted toward his sentence.
'Sad, unjust'
For many inside Kosovo, Thaci and the KLA are symbols of its independence movement.
After the war, Thaci remained a central political figure and was instrumental in its 2008 declaration of independence.
Throughout the trial, images of the 58-year-old, who also served as prime minister, have regularly appeared on huge billboards around the country.
"A terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war. It is a sad, unjust, undeserved decision," Kosovo Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca told media outside the court.
Expectations of a possible release of Thaci and his co-accused drew huge crowds for a rally over the weekend and on Wednesday, hundreds gathered in the capital again ahead of the verdict as clocks ticked down to the decision.
But once it became clear the former president would remain in detention, the square was almost deserted within minutes.
Courting controversy
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC), although based in the Netherlands and staffed by international judges, was established under Kosovo law specifically to prosecute alleged crimes committed by KLA members during the war.
Before the court was established, earlier cases in Kosovo largely failed because of alleged witness intimidation and political interference.
Read moreWar crimes denial threatens peace in former Yugoslavia, Europe's top rights body says
Deeply unpopular from its foundation, the court's use of evidence supplied by Belgrade, which still refuses to recognise its former province's independence, has further inflamed accusations of political bias.
Prosecutors have tried throughout the trial to distinguish between the country's independence struggle and the men on trial.
They say all four men are responsible for crimes committed against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and neighbouring Albania, as well as the politically motivated murders of Serb, Albanian and Roma civilians.
The crimes were committed during and just after the Kosovo war, which claimed some 13,000 lives.
In response, the men's lawyers had argued that the KLA lacked a strict command structure and the senior figures could not control or be held responsible for fighters who committed crimes.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Around 170,000 older people homeless across Europe, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:55:39 UTC
21:55:39 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Around 170,000 older people are experiencing homelessness across Europe as the continent's overall homeless population climbs to an estimated 1.4 million, according to a report published Tuesday.
The 11th annual overview of housing exclusion by the European Federation of National Organisations Working with the Homeless (FEANTSA) and Fondation pour le Logement warned that homelessness among older people remains significantly undercounted.
The report estimates that 166,261 people aged 65 and over are living on the streets, in emergency accommodation or using homelessness services, a figure it rounds to about 170,000.
It said the true number is likely higher because data on older homeless people remain incomplete and vary widely between countries.
Across Europe, the report estimates that about 1.4 million people are homeless, including those sleeping rough, staying in emergency accommodation or using dedicated homelessness services.
Among 23 countries with recent data on homelessness, 17 recorded increases.
Ireland saw the steepest long-term rise among countries with comparable figures, with the homeless population increasing 367% from 3,738 in 2014 to 17,447 in 2026.
Portugal recorded a 228% increase, from 4,414 homeless people in 2017 to 14,476 in 2024, while France saw a 187% rise, from 110,894 in 2009 to 318,185 in 2024.
Finland was one of the few countries to record a long-term decline, with homelessness falling from 17,958 people in 1987 to 3,429 in 2023. However, the figure rose 34% between 2023 and 2025.
Growing old without secure housing
The report warned that housing insecurity among older people extends beyond homelessness to people living in inadequate homes, facing eviction or energy poverty or struggling to maintain housing they can no longer afford.
The share of older people among homeless populations also varies sharply between countries.
In Poland, 10,084 people aged 60 and over were recorded as homeless in 2024, accounting for nearly a third of the country's homeless population.
Portugal recorded 977 homeless people aged 65 and over in 2024, up 145% from 396 in 2018.
The report cautioned that national figures are not directly comparable because countries use different definitions, age thresholds and methods for measuring homelessness.
Its Europe-wide estimate of older homelessness was based on data from nine countries covering 105,446 people and extrapolated using the average rate among the population aged 65 and over.
Some countries exclude older people from official homelessness statistics.
In the Netherlands, for example, national figures exclude people over 64. A separate count across 57 municipalities in 2025 recorded 28,721 homeless people, including 6% aged 60 to 69 and slightly over 1% aged 70 and above.
The report linked housing insecurity in later life to falling income after retirement and the loss of a partner, and said women can be particularly vulnerable because their pensions are on average lower than men's in the EU.
The consequences of homelessness can also be severe for life expectancy.
In France, at least 735 homeless people died in 2023 at an average age of 49 – around 30 years younger than the general population.

Kyiv • UNN
A "Gerbera" drone was shot down in the Kaišiadorys District after veering off course. According to President Nausėda, "it was probably not an intentional action against Lithuania."
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said that a Russian "Gerbera" drone was shot down in the Kaišiadorys District on Tuesday evening. It had been intended to attack Ukraine but veered off course, UNN reports, citing LRT.
"At present, according to the information available, it was a 'Gerbera' drone," Nausėda told reporters after a meeting of the State Defence Council on Wednesday.
According to him, "it was probably not a deliberate action against Lithuania."

He warned that similar incidents could recur, and that countering them would require improving the identification of drones flying over foreign countries.
"Vilnius is located not far from the border, and, undoubtedly, after detection (...) we will have the capability and means to destroy drones or other aircraft," the President of Lithuania said.
According to him, Lithuania also needs alternative means of shooting down drones, since destroying them with fighter jets is ineffective.
In addition,
The BNS agency reported that on Tuesday evening, a drone that had arrived in Lithuania from Belarus was shot down in the Kaišiadorys District, near the Kruonis Pumped Storage Hydroelectric Plant, by Italian fighter jets stationed in Šiauliai.
When the drone was flying over Lithuanian territory, residents of Vilnius and Kaunas counties were sent warnings about a possible threat from the air.
Amid Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine, Lithuania has repeatedly warned in recent months about a possible threat from the air, but this was the first case in which a drone was shot down over the country's territory. Previously, this had occurred in Latvia and Estonia.
The last time residents of southeastern Lithuania were informed about a possible threat from the air was last Sunday, but it was later established that this occurred when radars detected a flock of birds.

A drone was found Wednesday in a forest in northern Lithuania, likely crashed months ago, prompting authorities to activate a bomb-response plan and send bomb disposal experts to the site, police said.

Drone discovered by foresters

Whilst doing this work, a forester walked over and spotted the drone in the grass. Whether it had become overgrown or had landed in the grass as it fell, I do not know, but in any case it was found in the forest in the grass. According to the forester, it is about three metres wide and shaped like an aeroplane,” Bronušas told LRT.lt.

EXPLAINER – Human misuse or rogue machines? How advanced AI could threaten society
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:53:56 UTC
21:53:56 KST

As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly powerful, warnings about the ways they could harm humans range from dangers already emerging today to fears of a future existential catastrophe.
Last week, Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon publicly resigned from the leading AI company, warning that developers were building systems that could ultimately destroy humanity.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon posted on US social media platform X. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
Soon after, leading AI executives backed calls to slow the development of increasingly powerful systems and strengthen safeguards, bringing concerns over the pace of AI development to the forefront of public debate.
"Recent warnings from AI researchers that advanced AI systems could pose a catastrophic risk to humanity should be taken seriously," Harin Sellahewa, dean of the Faculty of Computing, Law and Psychology at the University of Buckingham, told Anadolu.
While debate continues over whether highly advanced systems could themselves become a threat, Sellahewa said a more immediate concern is the possibility of people using increasingly powerful AI to cause large-scale harm.
"Advanced AI could amplify existing threats such as cyberattacks, misinformation, autonomous weapons, and other malicious activities," he said. “For this reason, the risks associated with both the technology itself and the ways humans may choose to use it warrant careful attention and appropriate safeguards."
Here are some of the ways AI could harm people:
AI is increasingly being incorporated into military systems, where it can analyze large amounts of battlefield information, identify objects, assist with targeting and help operate increasingly autonomous platforms.
Its use in warfare has raised concerns about what happens when machine-generated recommendations are wrong, insufficiently supervised or deliberately used to accelerate lethal decision-making.
Israel's use of AI-assisted systems in its war on Gaza has drawn particular scrutiny.
UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese, in her report From Economy of Occupation to Economy of Genocide, described how the Israeli military has used AI systems including Lavender and Gospel, as well as a system known as Where's Daddy?, to process information and generate or track potential targets.
The report also cited Project Nimbus, a $1.2 billion cloud-computing contract awarded by Israel to Google and Amazon in 2021, and said technology companies have played an expanding role in providing infrastructure and services used by Israel.
Albanese's report also said Palantir, whose work with Israel predates October 2023, expanded its cooperation with the Israeli government following the outbreak of the Gaza war.
Human Rights Watch warned in June that militaries were increasingly incorporating AI into life-and-death decisions, including targeting and weapons selection.
It cited reports that US forces used the AI-enabled Maven Smart System, integrated with Anthropic's Claude, during US-led strikes on Iran in 2026 to help identify priority targets and select munitions.
Anthropic said this month that it had also detected users in northern Yemen using Claude to support advanced weapons development.
The company did not identify the users as Houthis but said the activity originated in Houthi-controlled territory and included work on software for a guided rocket and a ballistic missile with a stated range of more than 2,000 kilometers (1,243 miles).
Cybersecurity is among the most immediate areas in which AI could contribute to physical as well as digital harm.
"In the near term, cybersecurity concerns, such as accelerated malware generation or automated vulnerability scanning, are the most plausible," Ruizhe Li, an assistant professor in the School of Computer Science at the University of Birmingham, told Anadolu.
Li said large language models are trained extensively on code repositories and software documentation, making them highly capable of understanding and generating computer code.
"Lowering the technical floor for sophisticated cyber exploits is therefore a tangible, near-term issue," he said.
AI can assist users in finding software vulnerabilities, writing malicious code, conducting reconnaissance and automating parts of cyber operations.
Anthropic said in its September threat report that it had disrupted attempts to misuse Claude in cyber operations, including activity involving phishing, malware and attempts to compromise computer systems.
An AI-assisted cyberattack targeting a hospital, electricity grid, water system, telecommunications provider or transport network could also disrupt services on which people's lives depend.
"What concerns me most are cyberattacks, attacks on critical infrastructure, and economic disruption," Sellahewa said.
"These are immediate and realistic risks because they can be amplified by human actors using advanced AI systems."
The same AI capabilities that can help scientists understand diseases, proteins and biological systems could potentially be misused to assist dangerous biological or chemical research.
Anthropic's September threat report described several cases in which users sought assistance for biological research that triggered the company's safeguards.
In one case, users sought assistance related to gain-of-function work involving the chikungunya virus, while others involved research into pathogens and toxins. Anthropic said it blocked the activity.
The concern is not that today's AI systems can independently create biological weapons, but that increasingly capable models could make specialized knowledge more accessible or accelerate work that previously required substantial expertise.
Li stressed the considerable gap between obtaining potentially dangerous information from an AI model and actually carrying out a biological or chemical attack.
"Catastrophic scenarios involving physical weapons, biological threats, or attacks on critical infrastructure require far more than generating text or code," he said.
"They demand complex coordination, specialized hardware, physical synthesis, and domain-specific infrastructure management. Current AI systems cannot autonomously navigate or execute these multifaceted physical pipelines."
AI can also cause harm by shaping what people see, hear and believe. It can already produce persuasive text, images, audio and video at scale and tailor messages to particular audiences.
Anthropic's September report documented AI-assisted influence operations involving fake accounts, websites and political content.
The risks can become particularly acute during wars, elections or public emergencies, when networks of AI-generated accounts could be used to spread false information, inflame tensions or encourage violence.
The riots that spread across parts of the UK following the killing of three girls in Southport in July 2024 offer an example of how AI-generated material can become part of a wider misinformation ecosystem.
False claims about the suspect's identity, religion and immigration status spread rapidly online after the attack and were amplified by far-right accounts before protests developed into riots in several cities.
Research by the London School of Economics found that one X account it examined posted dozens of AI-generated images promoting racist and Islamophobic narratives after the attack.
The researchers said 39 posts containing generative AI imagery attracted disproportionately high levels of engagement, with one receiving 11 million views.
Another category of concern involves direct interactions between AI chatbots and vulnerable users, with several lawsuits alleging that chatbot interactions contributed to fatalities including murders, overdoses and suicides.
In May 2026, the parents of 19-year-old Sam Nelson filed a wrongful-death lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that ChatGPT gave him dangerous advice involving kratom, Xanax and alcohol before his accidental overdose death in 2025.
OpenAI has disputed the allegations and says ChatGPT is not a substitute for professional medical care.
Another lawsuit concerns an alleged murder-suicide in Connecticut.
The estate of 83-year-old Connecticut woman Suzanne Adams sued OpenAI and Microsoft, alleging that ChatGPT reinforced her son's paranoid delusions before he killed his mother and then himself.
A review published in The Lancet Psychiatry this year warned that large language models might contribute to the onset or exacerbation of psychotic symptoms, including by reinforcing delusional beliefs in vulnerable users.
- AI fraud and impersonation
AI can also make fraud more convincing and easier to carry out at scale.
In 2024, Hong Kong police said an employee at a multinational company was deceived into transferring about $25 million after fraudsters used deepfake technology to impersonate the company's chief financial officer and other employees during a video conference.
The employee reportedly joined a call with several people who appeared to be senior company officials. Police said the fraudsters had created deepfake versions of the executives and used them to convince the employee to make the transfers.
US authorities have also warned about criminals using AI-generated voices and messages to impersonate public officials and other trusted figures.
The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report said investment scams involving artificial intelligence resulted in more than $632 million in reported losses that year.
For Li, many of the most credible near-term dangers do not depend on AI becoming conscious, developing its own intentions or deciding independently to harm humans.
They come from people using increasingly capable systems to do things that were previously more difficult, expensive or technically demanding.
"Because large AI models ingest massive amounts of human text and code, they reflect both constructive and destructive patterns present online," said Li.
Without appropriate safeguards, Li said, such systems can lower the technical barriers facing malicious actors, including by helping generate deceptive content, phishing campaigns or malicious code.
"AI models do not act on their own desires, and their behaviors and outputs are steered directly by user input and system prompts,” he said.
"The core risk is human misuse, not rogue machines."
