Africa is bigger than we’ve been led to believe – what next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:19 UTC
21:00:19 KST

This month, the UN passed a resolution, brought to the assembly by Togo, to phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe and replace it with another that shows the real scale of territories. That’s right – when it comes to size, the map of the world we have all grown up with is not accurate. The main loser of land on the Mercator map is Africa, and the new “Equal Earth” map reflects its true proportions. I spoke to our west Africa correspondent Eromo Egbejule about his extensive reporting on the map changes, and why people feel so strongly about it.
Seeing the new map transposed over the old might make you feel oddly disoriented. Logically, there is absolutely no immediate tangible impact on one’s life that comes out of knowing that the entire top part of the northern hemisphere is so much smaller than you were led to believe. And yet, there is still something agitating about it, like you’ve been the subject of a lifelong trick, or at least a breach of trust.
The vast geographical inaccuracies of the old map include the shortening of Africa, and the relative expansion of North America and Eurasia. The new projection shows Africa as taking up almost double the ratio of total land area shown on the map. It all feeds into a sense that there is something domineering about it, portraying some countries as not just political and economic powers, but geographical ones as well, and therefore natural hegemons. It is an emotional response more than anything, but a testament to how much our perceptions of the physical world are linked to our estimations of stature.
No, the world map has not gone ‘woke’
The Guardian’s west Africa correspondent Eromo Egbejule is struck by how, despite its disproportionality, there was still opposition to retiring the 16th-century map. The US was the only country that vetoed the UN resolution, and six other nations abstained. The US dismissed the effort as “superfluous”, but Eromo sees this as a euphemism for “ideological” or “woke”. “I don’t see why it feels so strongly,” he told me. “This is a scientific discussion. It’s not an imposition.”
There is nothing binding about the resolution, and yet, there is something revealing about the world’s superpower opposing it. It suggests that the US would like to preserve that connection between size and status, even when appearances are deceiving. US president Donald Trump’s interest in Greenland was reportedly influenced by its inflated size on the old map, an acquisition that would swell US territory in the political imagination. Greenland is “massive” said Trump – but in actuality, it’s a fraction of its size as shown in the Mercator projection. The old map depicts it as roughly the same size as Africa, despite it being 14 times smaller. Could huge geopolitical tensions, and confrontation with Europe, could have possibly been avoided by simply showing Trump an accurate map?
Do maps really matter?
“It does matter. Make no mistake,” said Eromo. In his view, the significance is in the momentum such a resolution triggers. “There’s two proverbs we have in pidgin,” Eromo said: “every dance begins with a clap” and “it’s grains of rice that fill up a pot”. In other words, this might feel like a small change, but the boost of one successful campaign could pave the way to what Eromo describes as a “multipolar world order”. He points out that this resolution comes on the heels of a separate landmark one – the UN vote to recognise the transatlantic slave trade as a crime and call for reparations, an effort also led by an African country.
There is a growing traction around a particular kind of advocacy: one that uses the procedures of high-profile international institutions to challenge dominant western understandings of history and reality. These interventions in how we make sense of the world may be symbolic – but they are meaningful, and they are gaining ground.
Moving towards a shared reality?
It is staggering that the Mercator map has pretty much remained the unchanged standard for over four centuries. In questioning what was once assumed to be fact, the resolution has not only addressed issues of accuracy. It has also, somehow, punctured the vast and abstract unrealities established throughout history by the west. The theft of resources and people is only one part of what was stolen from many regions of the world during colonisation. Countries were then stolen from, again, in terms of landmass on maps, and also the subordinating cultural and political associations that followed. There is something intangible and deeply political about the map’s significance – which is symbolic and threatening.
Eromo said that this sort of change makes people nervous because it ties in to all the ways in which legacies of literally carving out the continent and enslaving its populations still resonate. Hanging over the resolution are questions of precedent, of the floodgates being opened – the sort of building pressure that has resulted in calls to decolonise curriculums, for example. If the map that hangs in classrooms all around the world is changed, people may ask: “What else are my children going to be taught now?” Eromo said that there is something diminishing about learning that behemoths such as the US, China and Russia “can all fit into Africa with some space to spare.”
There are broader anxieties at stake – about what constitutes our shared reality, one that is increasingly fractured by social media and AI. These make tussles about maps a matter of holding on to the little that we can establish as concrete and true, in the face of vast political and digital forces that are warping our perceptions of the world. Eromo cites a statement that stood out for him, issued by Africa No Filter, an advocacy group that has been a part of the map justice campaign: “If we got something as basic as Africa’s size wrong for this long, what else about Africa have we simply accepted without questioning?”

Microplastics in soil pose global threat by acting like ‘Trojan horse’ to deliver toxins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:19 UTC
21:00:19 KST

Microplastics act like a “Trojan horse” delivering pollutants, pesticides and bacteria through the soil, a five-year multinational research project has found.
The EU-funded project, which has so far resulted in 22 peer-reviewed studies, found microplastics in the soil of all 227 agricultural fields it tested across 11 European countries. The researchers said this poses a global threat, with healthy soils essential for life on Earth.
In many cases, this contamination reflected current farming practices as well as historical land use, demonstrating that plastic pollution can persist for many years.
The researchers also found that microplastics could interact with other agricultural stressors such as pesticides and veterinary drugs.
One study in Switzerland found that fields with the highest levels of tyre-wear particles also had the highest levels of other toxic chemicals and metals.
Microplastics can create new microbial habitats on their surfaces. Known as the plastisphere, these surfaces form a hotspot for interactions between plastics, microbes and agrochemicals, the researchers found.
An increase of antibiotic-resistant genes was found within plastispheres when compared with controls. Pesticides appeared to amplify this effect further.
Edoardo Puglisi, a partner of the project and professor of microbiology at the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart in Piacenza, Italy, said the smaller the microplastics were, the more they tended to adsorb pollutants, microbes and DNA, leading to a “Trojan horse effect that can potentially increase the diffusion of pathogens and antibiotic-resistance genes”.
This Trojan horse effect can have an impact on earthworms and soil organisms by disrupting critical processes such as nutrient cycles, one study found.
Earthworms play a vital role in shaping the composition of the soil microbiome as well as the ecological functions of soils.
The EU-funded Minagris research project, in collaboration with the Countryside and Community Research Institute at the University of Gloucestershire, also found microplastics could affect plant growth and function. One study found that higher concentrations of microplastics reduced leaf area, chlorophyll content, photosynthetic efficiency and plant biomass in lettuce.
When drought conditions were added, these effects became even more pronounced, with plants performing less well than under either stress alone.
Environmental assessments often consider pollutants individually, but the findings show pollutants can behave differently when they occur together. The researchers say policy needs to recognise that plastic contamination is part of a wider picture of soil degradation and pollution.
In an effort to reduce plastic pollution, there has been an increase in the use of biodegradable plastics. However, the project found biodegradable plastics were not automatically safer and could still degrade into microplastics, potentially causing ecological damage.
“Once these plastics fragment into the ground, they’re practically impossible to remove, acting as vectors for agrochemicals and altering critical soil ecosystems,” said Dr Esperanza Huerta Lwanga, a research associate in soil physics at Wageningen University in the Netherlands.
“To protect long-term food production and soil health, policy must catch up. We urgently need standardised plastic monitoring, full manufacturer transparency, and risk assessments that evaluate through different species how microplastics interact with co-pollutants.”

How to turn excess olive brine into a lipsmacking salad dressing – recipe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:18 UTC
21:00:18 KST

Olive brine is a simple byproduct that has so much flavour, and it elevates a classic salade nicoise dressing while keeping things colourful, elegant and relatively simple.
Salade nicoise with olive-brine vinaigrette
Though this one-bowl wonder began life as a simple tomato and anchovy salad with olive oil, it has become more elaborate over time, and the addition of cooked green beans, eggs and even tuna all make sense to me. What’s worth preserving, though, is its Mediterranean simplicity, and the olive-brine dressing adds a lot of flavour without needing loads of extra ingredients.
In the spirit of simplicity, this vinaigrette keeps to just three wonderfully flavourful ingredients: olive brine for salt and depth of flavour, red-wine vinegar for acidity and olive oil for substance and piquancy. It won’t hold a stable emulsion in the way a mustard dressing does, so give it another good shake just before it goes on the salad. I buy whole olives with the pits in and pit them myself. They, and the brine, taste so much better that way.
Serves 4
For the vinaigrette 
2 tbsp brine from a jar of olives
  1 tbsp red-wine vinegar 
  6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
  Black pepper, to taste
For the salad
6 eggs
  200g green beans, topped
200g cocktail tomatoes, or cherry tomatoes
1 red pepper, stalk, seeds and pith removed, flesh sliced into rings
½ medium cucumber, skin on and seeds in, cut into large chunks
4 spring onions, cut into 1cm lengths (white and green parts)
1 small jar black olives
  Anchovy fillets, (optional) to taste; I used a whole standard 50g tin
1 small handful basil leaves, to finish
Put the olive brine, vinegar and extra-virgin olive oil in a jar, and add a grind of black pepper to taste. Screw on the lid and shake until the mixture emulsifies. It won’t stay emulsified for long, so shake again just before you’re ready to eat. The dressing will now keep in the fridge for up to a week.
Put the eggs in a pan of cold water and bring to a boil. Once boiling, add the green beans, bring back to a boil and cook for four minutes. Drain, then put the eggs and beans in a bowl of iced or cold water. Once cooled, drain again and put the beans to one side (they can be left whole or cut into pieces). Peel and halve the eggs.
Cut the tomatoes in half, then arrange all the vegetables on a platter. Scatter over the stoned olives and drained anchovy fillets to taste, then finish with the halved eggs, some torn basil leaves and the freshly shaken dressing. Eat straight away.

Army to replace Watchkeeper with Ukraine-proven drone
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:00:05 BST
21:00:05 KST

The Army is to bring the Tekever AR5 into service under a contract worth up to £400 million, replacing the Watchkeeper system in use since 2014, alongside a separate £16 million deal delivering more than a thousand small drones, the Ministry of Defence stated.
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, announced both at Defence Vehicle Dynamics, the biennial land warfare exhibition, on Wednesday.
The AR5 is a long-endurance surveillance aircraft able to carry up to 50kg of cameras and sensors. The deal begins with an initial order of six, rising to up to 24 by 2029, with the aircraft to be built at a new Tekever factory in Swindon. The type has already been used by Ukraine against Russia.
Mr Pollard said: “Our soldiers deserve the best technology, and that’s what we’re delivering. From small drones giving troops eyes on the enemy, to the AR5 offering commanders better intelligence over the battlefield, we’re transforming the Army’s ability to see, understand and act first.
“This is defence procurement that backs British industry, creates skilled jobs and keeps our Armed Forces ahead of our adversaries.”
According to the department, the Tekever contract will support more than 1,000 highly skilled jobs by 2030 across the company’s British sites, which include Bristol, Swindon, Lydd, London, Southampton, Edinburgh and West Wales Airport.
Karl Brew, Managing Director of Tekever UK, said: “We are proud to be delivering the AR5 to the British Army at this critical moment for national security. This investment allows us to grow our UK operations, create hundreds of skilled jobs and bring cutting-edge surveillance technology, proven on the battlefield in Ukraine, into service with British forces.”
The smaller aircraft come from three British small and medium-sized companies, with deliveries nearing completion. Evolve Dynamics of Hampshire is supplying 245 FOXE-NATO drones weighing less than 250g and fitted with infrared cameras for use at night. Marlborough Communications Limited of Surrey is providing 670 Skydio X10 INTL aircraft, which the department says can be ready to fly in under a minute and reach 45mph. A partnership between Brigantes Consulting of Exeter and Harmattan AI is delivering 110 SONORA drones, designed to help train soldiers before they use similar systems on operations.
That deal has created more than 30 new roles so far, with 18 already filled in Hampshire, Surrey and Exeter, including several veterans. The small drone contract was delivered by the National Armaments Director Group and forms part of Project Rapstone, the Army’s programme to bring new technology to soldiers faster, with the stated goal of doubling the Army’s fighting power by 2027 and moving new equipment from industry to the front line within 24 months.
Watchkeeper, the system the AR5 replaces, entered service in 2014 after a development programme that ran considerably over time and cost, and was withdrawn from service earlier this year. The Strategic Defence Review identified its replacement as part of a wider shift towards uncrewed systems, and the Defence Investment Plan commits new investment in the Army’s long-range surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities including the next generation of uncrewed aerial systems.

World News in Brief: Shipping alert from IMO, democracy vanishing in Nicaragua, alert over political ‘denialism’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

World News in Brief: Shipping alert from IMO, democracy vanishing in Nicaragua, alert over political ‘denialism’
Amid a rising number of attacks on shipping in key waterways in the Middle East linked to the US-Iran war, the head of UN maritime agency, Mr. Arsenio Dominguez, has insisted that the conflict is not a “pretext” to target “innocent seafarers”.
Since the current conflict in the Middle East began on 28 February, the International Maritime Organization, IMO, has verified 80 attacks on international shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz.
This has resulted in the deaths of at least 22 seafarers and injuries to many others.
In the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, dozens of fatalities have reportedly resulted from attacks on international shipping in recent months, although precise numbers are difficult to verify.
Attacks in the Red Sea have also resumed, with four fatalities confirmed in the latest attack by the Houthis on a merchant vessel on 11 August, the UN agency said.
Here’s Roel Hoenders, Chief of Staff at IMO:
“Apart from putting seafarers’ lives at risk, attacks on merchant shipping are having a severe impact on global supply chains and people everywhere around the world. - And let’s not forget that 22 crew have already been killed since the conflict in the Middle East began on 28 February.”
Mr. Dominguez stressed that in the Strait of Hormuz, the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, “it is not only one country attacking merchant vessels”.
UN rights chief warns democracy has almost disappeared in Nicaragua
Democracy in Nicaragua is being dismantled at an alarming pace, the UN human rights chief warned on Wednesday, as a new report detailed growing political repression, arbitrary arrests and the silencing of critics.
Presenting the findings, Volker Türk said power is becoming increasingly concentrated in the hands of the executive and the ruling party.
“The report traces the near-total capture of State institutions by the ruling party,” he said, describing a pattern of “systematic abuse of power” that has eroded checks and balances and left many people without protection when their rights are violated.
“The situation is utterly indefensible,” he added.
Basic rights dismantled
The report covers the period from June 2025 to June 2026 and paints a picture of a country where independent political activity has almost disappeared. It warns that proposed constitutional changes could block organized opposition groups from future elections and extend presidential terms to as long as seven years.
According to the report, the authorities also continue to use arbitrary detention as a tool against dissent. At least 46 people were reportedly still being held at the end of the reporting period, while UN investigators documented ongoing cases of enforced disappearance and deaths in custody.
Mr. Türk called on the Government to immediately free anyone detained without legal grounds.
The report also highlights a sustained crackdown on civil society and the media. More than 5,500 organizations have been dissolved over the past eight years, and at least 56 media outlets have been shut down.
“There is almost nothing left to shut down,” the High Commissioner said.
He urged Nicaragua’s authorities to reverse course and re-engage with regional and international human rights bodies.
AI’s role in ‘denialism’ trend must be stopped, says rights expert
The Human Rights Council has called on governments everywhere to counter the growing trend of so-called “denialism” politics, which often features the non-acceptance of genocide and other crimes against humanity.
Speaking at the council in Geneva, independent human rights expert, Bernard Duhaime, noted a recent wave of denialist statements by government officials, politicians and other actors worldwide.
Rapporteurs and other independent experts appointed by the council are not UN staff and receive no salary for their work.
Countries must actively counter any efforts to glorify those responsible for crimes against humanity, particularly considering the rise of social media and AI systems which amplify denialism, Mr. Duhaime insisted:
“We live at a dangerous time where ideologues and warmongers seek to fuel polarisation, hatred and chaos for their own political gains. It is high time to remind them of our collective commitment to human rights, accountability, and the rule of law.”
Mr. Duhaime, who works in an independent capacity, is tasked by the Human Rights Council to promote truth, justice, reparations and non-recurrence of crimes.
Delivering his report to the Council’s 47 Member States, he called on all countries to be vigilant about “politicians and corporate actors who seek to weaponize freedom of expression” and “manipulate history for political or other ideological ends”, while also inciting violence and silencing dissenting voices.
“Denialism” is increasingly used to undermine justice for vulnerable populations by spreading divisive narratives, Mr. Duhaime said, explaining that the trend risks eroding democratic institutions and accountability by replacing the truth with “emotionally-charged narratives”.
And although government oversight is key to combating supporters of denialism, the independent rights expert warned that “in too many cases” national legislation has become “tools of restriction and denial”.
“Combating denialism must never serve as a pretext for censorship or repression,” Mr. Duhaime told the Council.

Who should set the rules for AI? The UN is pushing for a safer digital future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Who should set the rules for AI? The UN is pushing for a safer digital future
Artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing rapidly, raising questions about how societies and governments can capture its benefits while managing risks that often extend beyond national borders.
Those concerns intensified after a former researcher at the AI company Anthropic warned on 8 September that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.
For the UN, the best way to address AI’s global risks is to bring countries together to adopt shared principles and commitments on AI governance.
Coordination is ‘indispensable’
“National action is essential, but global coordination is indispensable,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said on Wednesday.
The UN has worked for several years to provide a forum where countries can develop a shared understanding of AI technologies and discuss how they can cooperate – and provide a regulatory framework – on issues such as safety, human rights and disparities in access.
Rules-based development
The UN’s current work on AI governance stems from the Global Digital Compact, adopted by Member States in 2024 as part of the UN’s Pact for the Future, exactly two years ago.
The Compact called for international cooperation on AI and proposed two new mechanisms: an independent scientific panel to assess the AI’s risks and opportunities, and an annual global dialogue where governments and other stakeholders could coordinate approaches to AI governance.
In August 2025, the UN General Assembly – UNGA as we call it for short – formally established both.
The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI aims to provide governments with an independent assessment of what is known – and what isn’t known – about the rapidly developing technology.
The Global Dialogue on AI Governance, meanwhile, brings governments and other stakeholders together to discuss international cooperation, share experience and work towards greater compatibility between different approaches to AI governance.
The General Assembly designed the two institutions to complement each other: the Scientific Panel provides the evidence, and countries decide at the Global Dialogue what to do in response.
The Scientific Panel’s first preliminary report, released 1 July, concluded that AI capabilities are advancing rapidly – especially in areas such as reasoning, coding and science – creating significant opportunities.
It also identified risks such as misinformation, discrimination, privacy violations, cyberattacks and so-called “superintelligence” that could become difficult to control.
“We need a shared understanding of how to advance the safe, secure, and responsible development of AI – while identifying when increasingly powerful systems may require stronger safeguards, or additional measures to manage potential risks,” Mr. Guterres said in his pre-UNGA remarks to the world’s media in New York.
Working towards AI guardrails
The UN’s work comes as discussions move from whether AI should be regulated, to questions about which safeguards should be implemented.
On Wednesday, Mr. Guterres called for international cooperation to ensure that AI development remains safe, secure and responsible. He added that voluntary efforts to slow AI development will not be sufficient if they are isolated, unverifiable or unevenly applied.
Asked about how the UN could convene a summit as part of a process leading to effective regulation for humankind, he said it could not be done next week – but it should happen soon, with “everybody on board” from the public, private, scientific, and civil society sectors.
“If we believe AI development should slow when risks become too great, we need more than good intentions,” he said.
The Secretary-General has called for an AI Child Safety Pledge and a Global Fund for AI, which would support developing countries in building AI infrastructure and capacity.
He also stressed the need for guardrails that make AI “safe, transparent, accountable, with human dignity at the centre.”
While national and regional governments make their own decisions about AI regulation, the UN’s role will be to bring these governments together, provide a scientific basis for discussions and identify areas for international cooperation.
AI at UNGA
Some diplomatic sources quoted in news reports speculate that the Security Council will discuss artificial intelligence during the high-level week.
At UN Headquarters on the sidelines of the General Debate – where AI concerns will no doubt loom large at the podium – the UN’s SDG Media Zone will host an event on 21 September, and the AI and Human Development series will culminate with a discussion on 23 September. Both events will focus on the relationship between AI and human agency.
Mr. Guterres underscored during his press conference Wednesday that AI will be “a major topic” in his discussions with world leaders next week.
Comparing AI development to the Cold War-era arms race between the US and Soviet Union, the Secretary-General called for cooperation between countries at the forefront of AI – including the US and China – to slow down AI development while risks continue to be assessed.
“The countries that have the highest capacity in the frontiers of AI – I think they should establish mechanisms of contact, have an exchange of information and (create) some common guardrails in order to avoid a race to the bottom that could one day lead to a gigantic disaster at the global level,” Mr. Guterres said.
With the scientific and diplomatic mechanisms now in place, the UN will continue to work to turn that cooperation into concrete action as AI becomes increasingly powerful.

Belarus to release 25 more prisoners as US eases sanctions
September 16, 2026
Belarus will release 25 prisoners in exchange for a further easing of US sanctions, an envoy of US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday.
"We agreed on an interim agreement, and as a show of goodwill, Belarus will release 25 people. In exchange, the United States will lift sanctions on two companies," envoy John Coale told reporters in the Belarusian capital, Minsk.
Coale had reportedly requested the release of 250 prisoners during his visit last March. The US special envoy said both sides would work to resolve outstanding issues and secure the release of additional prisoners as well as the removal of further sanctions.
"We will continue to improve relations between the United States and Belarus and are working to secure the release of more people in the near future. We are not done!" he later posted on X.
Hundreds of people remain in prison in Belarus after President Alexander Lukashenko carried out a crackdown on protests against his reelection in 2020. Western countries then slapped sanctions on the country as a result of Lukashenko's repression of opposition.
Accusations against Lukashenko
Human rights organization Viasna, which is banned in Belarus, says the government still holds more than 900 political prisoners. The detainees have been accused of extremism, conspiracy to seize power, incitement of hatred, or insulting the president.
During Tuesday's talks with Coale, Lukashenko denied the existence of political prisoners and rejected Viasna's claims.
The two companies to be removed from the US sanctions list are Lakokraska, a manufacturer of industrial paints and coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned company that oversees the forestry, pulp, and paper sectors. These sanctions have been in place since 2008 and 2023, respectively.
Coale also announced the release of tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets currently held in US banks.

Apple iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max Review: For Camera Fiends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Stellar performance and cooling. Great battery life. Excellent and fun cameras with a customizable camera app. Bright, responsive screens with a smaller Dynamic Island.
TIRED
Pricier than ever. No base model (yet). Living in the iPhone Duo's shadow.
There is no iPhone 18 this year. If you were hoping to upgrade your smartphone right now, Apple is only offering the new iPhone 18 Pro models (and a very expensive folding iPhone coming next month). Don't let that be a reason to spend extra money on a phone you might not need.
Apple hasn't confirmed the next base-model yet, but the iPhone 18 is expected in spring 2027 alongside a mid-tier iPhone 18e. If you've historically been more than satisfied with the base iPhone model, you should absolutely wait to upgrade. Don't let the hype machine sway you.
That said, if you're a Pro connoisseur, the iPhone 18 Pro ($1,199) and its bigger sibling, the 18 Pro Max ($1,299), are very good phones, despite the $100 price hike over last year’s Pro models. No, you don't need to upgrade if you're coming from an iPhone 17 Pro, 16 Pro, or even a 15 Pro—hold onto your devices for longer!—but Apple's flagships deliver where it matters, even if they feel eclipsed by the spectacle of the foldable iPhone Duo.
Minor Refresh
Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro models have significant upgrades, but let's be a little more measured here.
Battery life has been stellar on the Pro models over the last few years, and that remains true here. The Pro Max is the more notable of the two because it packs a denser battery. With average use (around 5 hours of screen-on time), I hovered around 50 percent by the end of the day, and easily made it through day two on a single charge. I spent a little less time with the smaller Pro, but so far it has also comfortably gotten me through a day with around 40 percent left by bedtime. Safe to say, most people will very much enjoy the battery life, but the update doesn't feel drastic.
Next, there's the processor: the A20 Pro chip. I hardly run into problems with Apple's flagship silicon, and that hasn't changed. The phones run every app fluidly, and my benchmark tests show a surprisingly sizable leap over the A19 Pro in the 17 series.
It runs Control—a AAA game from 2019 ported to iOS earlier this year—decently well. However, aggressive upscaling makes the graphics look grainy, and character movements can feel a little sluggish. (I maxed out the graphics settings.) It's certainly not perfect, but I still can't believe I'm playing such a demanding title on an iPhone.
More impressive is Apple's thermal management on these phones. The company has expanded the vapor chamber's surface area by three times—the phone's cooling technology that helps spread heat around—meaning the entire phone felt toasty after close to an hour of gameplay in Control, with no uncomfortable localized hot spots. This larger vapor chamber also lets you game longer before phone’s thermal throttling kicks in and slows everything down.
The iPhone 18 Pro models come with iOS 27 out of the box, which features the all-new Siri AI. Yes, Siri AI is infinitely more capable than any version of Siri that Apple has offered before. It still doesn't quite have the spark or versatility of other AI assistants, but you might be fine with that. If you throw Siri AI a question, there's a good chance it can actually give you a satisfactory answer now. Remember that Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features aren't exclusive to the latest models, though you do need an iPhone 15 Pro or newer to access them.
The Dynamic Island, the pill-shaped bar housing the selfie camera and Face ID sensors, is noticeably smaller this year. To take full advantage of it, you can now view three live activities—like a DoorDash order status or your Uber ETA—simultaneously inside the Island, up from two. I was navigating in Apple Maps, chatting on a phone call, and had a DoorDash order en route to my home, and it spaced out all of these activities neatly.
Speaking of the iPhone 18 Pro design, I do like the new burgundy color, though I miss brighter, more playful options like last year's Cosmic Orange. But the real headline feature is almost invisible—embedded into the main camera on the back of the iPhone.
Aperture Priority
Apple is debuting a variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro models. This is by no means the first time we've seen a smartphone with a variable aperture—Samsung and Huawei both launched phones with the capability years ago. While Samsung abandoned the tech, Huawei and Xiaomi still ship it on their flagships.
What is a variable aperture? Simply put, the aperture is the physical opening that lets light reach the camera sensor. A wider aperture lets in more light and has a lower “f-stop” number, while a narrower aperture restricts light. Most smartphones rely on fixed apertures—the iPhone 17 Pro's main camera, for example, is locked at f/1.78. A variable aperture gives the lens mechanical blades that physically expand or contract in a circular shape, adjusting how much light hits the sensor. Apple gives you four f-stops to select from: f/1.48, f/1.78, f/2.8, and f/4.
Open the aperture to f/1.48 on the iPhone 18 Pro and more light floods in, delivering cleaner low-light shots and faster Night Mode captures. This also creates a real optical bokeh—the soft blurred background effect phone makers have spent years simulating with computational Portrait modes. Step it down to f/4, this blur recedes, keeping more of the scene and background in crisp focus. All of this can be very confusing for people unfamiliar with these camera terms, which is why Apple defaults the aperture to “Auto.”
I love it. I shoot manual on my mirrorless camera, so I immediately took to the new customization features in the Camera app to show Shutter Speed and Lens Aperture as easy-to-access settings. Shooting at f/1.48 delivers a nice bokeh effect—especially in low light—so I stopped using Apple's Portrait mode altogether. (Some parts of the image may look less sharp than on an iPhone 17 Pro because the plane of focus is narrower.) Apple will point out that Portrait mode is still useful, as you can always add more bokeh post-capture.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
iPhone 18 Pro Max, main camera with a one-second shutter speed.
Move to f/4 for group shots when you want everyone in the frame to be in focus. (Or if you want a very fun starburst effect with light sources!) As you change between the four aperture settings, you can see the blades moving on the main camera—it's very cool. In auto mode, the camera largely sticks to f/1.78, or f/1.48 in low light. It chooses the other two apertures for specific, usually brighter, scenes.
I have also enjoyed the ability to adjust the camera’s shutter speed. Yes, you can already do this with a third-party camera app, but now it's baked in! With a one-second shutter, you can capture some fun shutter drag to accentuate motion in a photo. However, you'll definitely need to buy a neutral density filter for super-bright scenes to balance exposure. It's fun to play around with.
I compared several of the 18 Pro’s photos with shots from Google's Pixel 11 Pro, and I do have to note that the iPhone tends to over-brighten scenes that should be very dark. So much so that it can misrepresent the dark mood you might be chasing. The Pixel tended to preserve more of those shadows, though it delivered more lifted blacks that made the image appear more matte. The iPhone can also struggle with backlit scenes, more so than the Pixel.
Apple has added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles, and this is a fun element to sink your teeth into and explore. Phone makers have realized that ultra-clean, sharp, “perfect” shots are perhaps not what most people want, and these stylings—like the new Camera Looks on Pixel phones—offer a new degree of “authenticity.”
The iPhone 18 Pro's camera system is fun without feeling overwhelming. You can pick and choose what degree of control you want, tweak Photographic Styles to your tastes, and add more depth after the fact, whether it's for videos or photos. Who knew people liked having more control? There aren't any sweeping improvements to the camera lenses or sensors, but this is a system that shutterbugs will love to experiment with, and that's what the Pro iPhone is all about.
Julian Chokkattu is Senior Editor, Gear at WIRED, overseeing personal technology, gadgets, and gizmos. He has been reviewing consumer products for a decade, specializing in mobile—from smartphones, tablets, and smartwatches to smart glasses and virtual reality. This is his sixth year at WIRED. Men estimate higher rates of sexual objectification than women report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Men and women have different perceptions of how often young women experience sexual objectification, with men sometimes estimating higher frequencies than women themselves report. The study, published in Sex Roles, highlights a disconnect in how different behaviors are perceived and measured. The findings challenge the assumption that men underestimate the everyday harassment women face.
Sexual objectification involves treating a person primarily as a body or a collection of body parts rather than a whole human being. This experience is common for many young women and is linked to negative psychological outcomes like depression, body shame, and a reduced sense of personal safety. In professional and public spaces, these experiences range from unwanted explicit sexual advances to everyday instances of inappropriate body evaluation. Researchers wanted to know if men and women had a shared understanding of how frequently these events happen in daily life.
Olivia A. Foster-Gimbel of Rutgers University and Renee Engeln of Northwestern University conducted the study. The researchers initially predicted that men would estimate lower rates of sexual objectification than women actually experienced. They reasoned that men might lack personal experience with being targeted or might be motivated to downplay the issue to maintain a positive view of their own gender group. Additionally, members of a dominant group often struggle to recognize the disadvantages faced by others.
On the other hand, the researchers recognized that the cultural impact of the #MeToo movement might have successfully educated men about the pervasive nature of these experiences. With so many public discussions about sexual harassment and assault in recent years, men might be highly aware of the issues women navigate on a regular basis. To test these competing ideas, the researchers designed a series of three investigations.
The researchers recruited 110 participants between the ages of 18 and 30 for their first study. Women were asked to report how often they personally experienced various objectifying behaviors on a scale ranging from “never” to “almost always.” Men were asked to estimate how often the average young woman had these same experiences using the identical scale. The behaviors were grouped into two categories: overt actions like catcalling or unwanted touching, and covert actions like staring or evaluating a woman’s physical appearance.
The results contradicted the researchers’ initial expectations. Men estimated that the average woman experienced both overt and covert sexual objectification more frequently than the women reported experiencing it themselves. There were no meaningful differences in how men and women perceived the emotional impact of these events. Both groups agreed on how bad these experiences made women feel, suggesting men understood the negative emotional toll of the behavior.
To explore whether men and women were simply interpreting the verbal rating scale differently, the researchers conducted a second study with 199 university students. Participants again provided ratings from “never” to “almost always,” but this time they also provided a specific numerical estimate, such as a set number of times per year. This allowed the researchers to see if words like “frequently” meant the same thing to both groups. Both men and women also read a short vignette about a fictional woman who was catcalled on her way home from work, and then estimated how often this type of event happened to women like the character in the story.
Once again, men estimated that the average woman experienced higher rates of objectification than the women reported for themselves. This pattern held true for both the verbal scale and the numerical count, showing it was not just a misunderstanding of the scale’s wording. When rating the fictional woman in the story, the pattern reversed. Women estimated that the character experienced this overt harassment more often than men did. This suggested that women might report lower rates of objectification for themselves than they do for other women, a phenomenon sometimes referred to as the denial of personal discrimination.
For the third study, the researchers recruited 165 university students and asked both men and women to estimate frequencies for the “average woman” aged 18 to 30. This approach allowed the researchers to compare expectations directly without the complication of women rating their own personal experiences. Participants evaluated both overt and covert behaviors using the verbal scale and the numerical count. They also provided written explanations for why men and women might differ in their estimates.
When imagining the average woman, the results depended heavily on the type of behavior in question. For overt behaviors like catcalling, women selected higher verbal frequency categories than men did, but their actual numerical estimates were roughly the same. Both groups estimated that overt objectification happened about 30 times a year. For covert behaviors like leering, the verbal scale ratings were similar between the genders, but men estimated a much higher numerical count, guessing that covert objectification happened 365 times a year compared to the estimate of 267 times provided by women.
The written responses revealed several potential reasons for these discrepancies. Nearly half of the participants suggested that men’s higher estimates might stem from their awareness of how often they or other men perpetrate these behaviors. Others noted that women might not always notice covert actions like being stared at from behind. Some respondents also proposed that men might deliberately guess higher numbers to avoid seeming ignorant or insensitive in a cultural climate that encourages believing women.
The researchers note a few limitations to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The study only included participants who identified as either men or women. This leaves out the experiences and perceptions of transgender and nonbinary individuals, who also face high rates of sexual objectification. A general reader might assume these findings apply to all age groups, but the research focused exclusively on perceptions of women between the ages of 18 and 30.
Future research could explore how estimates of sexual objectification change when considering older women or women of different racial backgrounds. Different communities experience and interpret objectification in varying ways, which could alter the numerical estimates and perceptions of frequency. Additionally, the data were collected in the years immediately following the peak of the #MeToo movement. Social attitudes continue to shift, and subsequent surveys will be needed to see if these patterns hold up over time. Ultimately, focusing workplace and social interventions on the negative mental health impacts of objectification might be more effective than debating exactly how often it occurs.
The study, “A Mile in Her Heels: Do Men and Women Agree on How Often Women Are Sexually Objectified?,” was authored by Olivia A. Foster-Gimbel and Renee Engeln.

Gaza: At least 20 killed in deadly building collapse, search for survivors continues
Search and rescue operations continued in Gaza City on Wednesday following the collapse of a bombed-out building that killed at least 20 people, according to reports.
The incident has highlighted the precarious situation of displaced Palestinians across the Gaza Strip who shelter wherever they can, including in structures damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas fighters.
“I am devastated by reports of people trapped under the rubble,” the UN Humanitarian Coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Ramiz Alakbarov, said in a statement.
Roughly 100 people, including 50 children, were living in the building at the time, he added.
Rush to support
The senior aid official commended the humanitarian community which quickly mobilized to support the emergency response.
So far, Egypt has provided heavy machinery while the United Arab Emirates and Qatar are set to deliver relief items.
The UN Development Programme (UNDP) also deployed available machinery and workers to support rescue efforts.
“Through the limited stocks available in Gaza, we will support survivors with health, shelter and other critical items and services,” Mr. Alakbarov said.
“Lives may still be saved, and every effort must be made to reach those trapped under the rubble.”
Unsafe shelter putting lives at risk
The senior aid official recalled that across the Gaza Strip, people are living in hundreds of damaged and unsafe shelters.
“Today’s tragedy underscores the grave risks faced by families living in these structures and the urgent need for safer alternatives,” he said. “No one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter.”
Ahead of the rainy season, aid teams are supporting people who choose to move from damaged buildings and flood-prone areas to safer sites.
“I call for urgent approvals for the entry of heavy machinery, specialized equipment, engine oil and fuel needed for search-and-rescue operations,” said Mr. Alakbarov, adding that tents, tarpaulins and other non-food items must also arrive in the next four weeks.
“Every possible effort must be made to save lives, protect people from further harm and provide families with safer places to live,” he said, stressing that “every minute counts.”

AI, climate and conflicts top Guterres’s agenda ahead of General Assembly

Unknown Publisher

AI, climate and conflicts top Guterres’s agenda ahead of General Assembly
Ahead of the UN General Assembly’s high-level week, Secretary-General António Guterres said the world had entered “an era of deep uncertainty” and urged governments to embrace international cooperation to address global threats.
Speaking to reporters six days before world leaders gather in New York, Mr. Guterres identified “three existential threats”: runaway artificial intelligence (AI), the climate crisis and deepening inequalities.
He also reiterated calls for a two-State solution in the Middle East and for a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.
While he acknowledged the need to reform global institutions, including the UN itself, the Secretary-General stressed that the UN’s promises to maintain peace and protect human rights remain the same.
“Updating our structures can never mean abandoning our principles – it must mean applying those principles with even greater determination,” Mr. Guterres said.
Need for peace
Now more than ever, Mr. Guterres called for Member States to uphold the UN Charter, defend international law, protect human rights, invest in sustainable development and push for peace everywhere.
He highlighted the decimation of Gaza and the Russia-Ukraine war as areas of particular concern, urging leaders to work towards “de-escalation, diplomacy and dialogue” to end these conflicts.
“At this crucial moment in the Middle East, de-escalation must be priority one, priority two and priority three,” the Secretary-General said.
All parties to the conflict in the Middle East must respect navigational rights in the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab Straits and must not harm civilians, Mr. Guterres said.
He also called attention to the suffering of the Palestinian people in Gaza and said Israel’s annexation of the West Bank “must stop.”
More than four years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Mr. Guterres said there is “no end in sight,” calling for an immediate ceasefire as the first step towards a “just, lasting and comprehensive peace.”
The General Assembly is expected to debate both conflicts next week.
Guardrails on AI development
The Secretary-General dedicated nearly half his remarks to what should be done about the rapid advancement of AI technology.
He recognised AI’s “enormous potential” on issues surrounding health, education and climate, but added that the world “cannot afford to ignore concerns” that AI development is progressing faster than human understanding of its risks.
Comparing AI to other issues of international concern Mr. Guterres said governments must protect their citizens from AI’s risks and that “global cooperation is indispensable.”
As fears mount of an AI arms race between the US and China, the Secretary-General acknowledged “geopolitical divides” and said voluntary pauses on AI development will not work if they are isolated – limited to only a few countries.
“The world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety,” he said.
Mr. Guterres pointed to the UN-founded Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, which he said will inform global discussions by providing the best available evidence on AI’s opportunities and risks.
As world leaders prepare to discuss solutions, the Secretary-General called for guardrails that build trust and “make AI safe, transparent and accountable, with human dignity at the centre.”
“International cooperation is more necessary than ever,” he said.

Repression continues in Venezuela in the face of ‘appalling’ human rights violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Repression continues in Venezuela in the face of ‘appalling’ human rights violations
In Venezuela’s El Rodeo maximum security prison, some of those detained for political reasons are subject to forced intubation – and prolonged confinement in a sealed underground cistern.
In the Fuerte Guaicaipuro military facility, prisoners have been confined in pit-like cells dug below ground level, exposed to cold, food deprivation and other degrading practices the UN qualifies as torture.
These observations from the independent Fact-Finding Mission on Venezuela published on Tuesday are part of a broader finding: following the US military rendition of then-President Nicolás Maduro in early January, State institutions responsible for repression, gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity remain fundamentally intact.
Despite some small improvements since the change of government at the top – most notably a significant decline in long-term detentions, enforced disappearances, and the release of hundreds of political prisoners – Venezuelans continue to endure severe human rights violations.
No institutional reforms
The independent Human Rights Council appointed investigators in Venezuela found that numerous laws used to criminalise opposition remain in force, and the country’s extensive intelligence services and security forces retain essentially the same structures, policies and practices.
No steps have been taken to disarm or dismantle the “colectivos” (pro-Government civilian armed groups) who have been the source of pervasive intimidation, violence and human rights abuses towards communities.
At least 19 officials previously identified by the Mission for their involvement in gross violations remain in, or have been reassigned to, key positions – while past human rights violations and crimes remain unpunished.
Journalists and other civil society actors also continue to be obstructed in their daily work.
“The reduction in some of the harshest forms of repression is notable, but it does not yet amount in any way to a transformation of the system that made them possible,” said Sofía Macher, Chair of the Mission.
Arbitrary arrests
Between 1 September 2025 and 29 July 2026, civil society organizations recorded at least 214 arbitrary detentions for political reasons, though 94 per cent of them occurred before the end of 2025.
After 3 January and the US capture of former President Maduro, the mission identified a recurrent pattern of short-term arbitrary arrests aimed at intimidating opposition activists, journalists, and other civil society actors.
Although the releases of dissidents following the US intervention have significantly reduced the number of political prisoners, non-governmental organizations estimate that between 379 and 500 people remain in detention – with the absence of official, transparent and verifiable information making it difficult to converge on a more precise number.
Torture continues
The mission documented torture and ill-treatment towards people detained for political reasons. It found 64 new cases of torture after 3 January alone, indicating that these practices remain widespread.
It also found that hundreds of people detained in State facilities are deprived of access to safe drinking water, adequate food, medicine and healthcare, leading to many in-detention deaths.
Víctor Quero Navas, a street vendor arrested for ambiguous reasons in January 2025, has become the face of the repression of Venezuelan detainees.
He died in custody while subjected to enforced disappearance, from acute respiratory failure secondary to pulmonary thromboembolism.
His mother, Carmen Teresa Navas, spent 16 months searching for him across detention centres, courthouses, public offices and even a morgue, and was told only in May 2026 that her son had died in custody nearly a year earlier.
Ten days after learning of his death, she too passed away.
“We call on the State authorities to take decisive steps towards accountability and to adopt a victim-centered transitional justice framework,” urged María Eloisa Quintero, one the mission’s experts.
“Venezuela should also reverse its withdrawal from the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court and cooperate fully with the Court and other international human rights mechanisms,” she added.
“Years of entrenched impunity must give way to accountability.”

Pope Leo says Middle East conflicts strain Jewish-Christian relations
VATICAN CITY, Sept 16 - Pope Leo said on Wednesday that recent conflicts in the Middle East had tested relations between Jews and Christians, adding that differing views of the ongoing violence had strained dialogue but not broken it.
In a new decree to mark the Catholic Church's last 60 years of efforts at inter-religious dialogue, the pope also reiterated the Church's condemnations of both antisemitism and Islamophobia.
"The conflicts that have erupted in the Middle East in recent years have ... left their mark on Jewish-Christian dialogue," said the decree, developed by three top Vatican offices and approved by Leo.
"Many channels of communication have been strained," it said. "Nevertheless, the pillars of dialogue among believers, built over 60 years of common effort, have remained firm. Upon these foundations, it is both possible and necessary to continue building."
The decree, issued to mark the anniversary of a 1965 Church document widely credited with improving centuries of acrimony between Jews and Christians, did not mention any specific Middle East conflicts.
Leo, the first U.S.-born pope, has previously criticised the Iran war, drawing the ire of President Donald Trump on social media.
Wednesday's decree described fighting antisemitism as a "shared struggle" for Jews and Christians. It also said attitudes of Islamophobia "fail to distinguish" between cases of extremist violence and the everyday lives of the world's Muslims. REUTERS

Auditor general: Defense scandals pose no security threat to Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:58:00 UTC
20:58:00 KST

Auditor general: Defense scandals pose no security threat to Estonia
Auditor General Janar Holm told ERR that the scandals that have emerged in the defense sector in recent months do not pose a security threat to Estonia. He said openly discussing problems instead makes the country stronger.
"I know many countries where it is not possible to talk about such things. This only makes us stronger," Holm said in response to a question about whether scandals in the defense sector pose a security threat to Estonia.
At the same time, Holm said the situation in the defense sector is concerning because several of the problems are systemic. He added that the more money that flows into the sector, the greater the confusion becomes.
The National Audit Office found problems with both the acceptance of goods and the awarding of contracts in 64 contracts handled by the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK). "Wherever we looked, there was some kind of problem," Holm said. In his view, a conventional inventory is not sufficient for accounting for Estonian Defense Forces stocks and a more digital system is needed.
EDF needs accounting rules
Holm said the Estonian Defense Forces, like all other government agencies in Estonia, must begin complying with accounting rules. He said this is important, on the one hand, for the Defense Forces itself, so that it has a quick and up-to-date overview of its assets and where they are located. On the other hand, the public must be able to see whether the money allocated to the defense sector has reached its intended destination.
However, because of problems with the accounting records, a situation arose this year in which the National Audit Office went to audit the annual report and the Defense Forces and Ministry of Defense said they had €1.2 billion worth of stocks. The National Audit Office cannot confirm whether the stocks are actually worth €1.2 billion because of the problems with the accounting records. "It seems to us that the figure should be somewhat higher," Holm said.
When there is confusion, it creates fertile ground for someone with bad intentions to take something for themselves at the state's expense. Efforts are now underway to determine what assets should be there in the first place in order to establish what is missing. Holm said there is also confusion surrounding the artillery shell deal, with the information lacking a clear audit trail.
Difficult to place blame without information
When information is lacking, it is also difficult to determine who is responsible. Holm said the parties are shifting the blame back and forth. "From the National Audit Office's perspective, what matters here is something that is often regarded as bureaucracy — namely, documentation," he said.
The National Audit Office has also told the Estonian Center for Defense Investments that the information does not provide a clear audit trail.
"We are now arguing over this and classified information is also creating a great deal of confusion, but presumably there will be clarity at some point," Holm said. He said primary responsibility always lies with the agency that enters into a transaction. In this case, the main responsibility lies with the head of the Estonian Center for Defense Investments, who signed the contract.

Not Mumbai, not Delhi: This North Indian city tops India in domestic expenditure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:57:31 UTC
20:57:31 KST

As per the study, an average household in Chandigarh spends nearly Rs 19 lakh annually.
Chandigarh has emerged as India's highest-spending city on a per-household basis, according to The Many Urban Indias, a report by People’s Research on India’s Consumer Economy (PRICE) and Tata Sons. An average household in the city spends nearly Rs 19 lakh a year, putting Chandigarh ahead of India's biggest metropolitan centres on this measure. The study examines how households across India’s 100 leading cities earn, spend, save and borrow.
Chandigarh has the highest average household spending in India
The report identifies Chandigarh as a Frontier city, a category comprising the smaller urban centres among India's top 100 cities by population.
Chandigarh is identified as the city with the highest average household consumption in the report. As per the study, an average household in Chandigarh spends nearly Rs 19 lakh annually. The distinction is about average spending per household, not the total amount spent across the entire city. This matters because larger cities have many more households and can generate a much bigger overall consumer market even when their average household spending is lower.The report identifies Chandigarh as a Frontier city, a category comprising the smaller urban centres among India's top 100 cities by population.
It places the city among the country's highest-spending urban centres, alongside Thiruvananthapuram in Kerala. The report also highlights Chandigarh's household financial position, noting that it has high levels of savings and low levels of debt.
Chandigarh and Bengaluru have the highest average household income
Chandigarh’s spending figures become more interesting when viewed alongside household income. According to the study, Bengaluru and Chandigarh have the highest average household income in India, at Rs 28 lakh per year. India's six largest metropolitan centres- Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata and Hyderabad are grouped together as the Big Six in the study. They have more than 10 million people each and account for a substantial share of the country's urban economic activity.
Delhi NCR is a major part of the report’s consumption story. The study says that Delhi NCR has a total consumption market worth $126 billion. This is nearly as much as Mumbai and Bengaluru combined. The report attributes this to two factors: Delhi NCR has around 7.5 million households, compared with 4.6 million in Mumbai. Its average annual household consumption is nearly Rs 15 lakh. This gives Delhi NCR a large overall consumption market, even though Chandigarh leads on average household spending.
Delhi NCR’s transportation spending alone is bigger than some cities
One of the report’s more striking findings concerns transportation. Delhi NCR households spend more than $33 billion annually on transportation, according to the study. That amount is larger than the total consumption market of Pune or Ahmedabad. The report also estimates that Delhi NCR’s annual dairy consumption is around $10 billion.
Mumbai: More high-income households, but not the highest average spending
Mumbai remains one of India’s major consumption centres, but the report places it behind Chandigarh on average household spending. The study says that Amritsar, Ahmedabad and Jabalpur have higher average household spending than Mumbai. At the same time, Mumbai leads the 100-city group in the share of high-income households.
The report defines high-income households as those earning more than Rs 36 lakh annually at 2025-26 prices. Their share across the 100 cities has increased to 12%, from 3% a decade earlier.
Bengaluru: Highest average income, but Chandigarh leads consumption
Bengaluru is another important comparison in the report. The city shares the highest average household income position with Chandigarh, at Rs 28 lakh per year. However, the report says that Chandigarh and Thiruvananthapuram have the highest average household consumption in India. It also identifies Surat as a city where average household consumption is higher than Bengaluru’s. This means Bengaluru’s high average income does not automatically translate into the highest average household spending.The report groups the cities into four categories:
Big Six: Cities with populations above 10 million.
Boomtowns: Cities with populations between 2.5 million and 10 million.
Breakout cities: Cities with populations between 1.5 million and 2.5 million.
Frontier cities: Cities with populations between 0.5 million and 1.5 million.
Chandigarh falls in the Frontier category, while Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru are part of the Big Six.

67 killed in gold mine collapse in Sudan’s West Kordofan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:57:18 UTC
20:57:18 KST

Ikrame Kouachi
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
At least 67 people were killed after the Al-Zara gold mine collapsed in Sudan’s West Kordofan state, with search operations continuing for survivors, the Sudan Doctors Network said Wednesday.
“More than 67 people were killed” when the mine collapsed near Al-Nuhud in West Kordofan, which is under the control of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the independent medical network said in a statement.
It said search operations were still underway for survivors or people trapped under the rubble, warning that the death toll could rise due to the mine’s lack of basic safety and protection measures for workers.
The network condemned “the negligence that had put miners’ lives at risk,” saying that mining in areas controlled by the RSF, without safety requirements or adequate protection and rescue equipment, “turns work into a direct risk to civilians’ lives.”
It called for search-and-rescue operations to continue and for the provision of the medical and logistical resources needed to deal with the disaster.
The Sudan Doctors Network also urged authorities controlling the area to “assume responsibility for protecting civilians and mining workers and to halt unregulated mining activities to prevent similar accidents.”
Artisanal mining employs more than 2 million people across Sudan under harsh conditions and accounts for about 80% of the country’s total gold production.
The Sudanese government does not prohibit artisanal mining but has sought to regulate the sector, which provides livelihoods for large numbers of Sudanese despite its risks.
Gold is a major source of foreign currency for Sudan after the country lost three-quarters of its oil revenues following South Sudan’s independence in July 2011, along with about 80% of its foreign-exchange resources.
Sudan has been gripped by war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, a conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced about 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Returning after unauthorized absence does not mean automatic reinstatement in service - Ministry of Defence
Kyiv • UNN
After a service member returns from unauthorized absence, they may continue their service only through the established procedure. Until the order is issued, duties, payments, and benefits are not restored.
Returning after unauthorized abandonment of a military unit does not mean automatic continuation of military service. This was reported by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
The ministry noted that, pursuant to Part Two of Article 24 of the Law of Ukraine "On Military Duty and Military Service," service members whose military service has been suspended:
-  are dismissed from their positions; 
-  are considered not to be performing (not carrying out)
the duties of military service; 
-  are not included in the personnel strength of the Armed Forces of Ukraine or
other military formations. 
After returning to the unit, service must be resumed in accordance with the procedure established by law. Only after the relevant order is issued may the service member be assigned duties, and their monetary support, benefits, and social guarantees be reinstated
To remind you
Earlier, the Ministry of Defense stated that Ukrainian service members who committed unauthorized abandonment of their unit while abroad may use a simplified procedure for returning to service.
Service members who committed unauthorized abandonment of their unit, including abroad, through June 12, 2026, inclusive, may use the simplified program for returning to the military.
UNN also reported that a new status has appeared in the "Army+" mobile application for service members returning after unauthorized abandonment of their unit.

Scotland imposes mandatory environmental assessments on new datacentres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:55:33 UTC
20:55:33 KST

Holyrood has voted to pause planning applications for all new AI datacentres for up to a year until the Scottish government has developed a national strategy.
On Wednesday, MSPs backed a Scottish Labour motion to halt new schemes for up to 12 months while rules on hyperscale datacentres are developed in what could be a blow to the British government’s AI strategy.
Scotland has seen a boom in planning applications for large datacentres as global investment in AI infrastructure has exploded, with British officials encouraging developers to include Scotland in the infrastructure buildout. Datacentres are critical for storing and processing data used by AI. One scheme in Auchtertool, Fife, has been billed as the second largest in the world, and is among more than 20 large datacentres proposed so far.
Campaigners have raised concerns about water usage and carbon emissions from large datacentres, and questioned whether Scotland has the capacity to cope with the resulting explosion in energy demand.
On Wednesday, MSPs voted to approve only projects that meet robust environmental impact assessments that consider the impact of neighbouring communities, and to make no decisions on planning for datacentre applications for up to a year until national planning guidance has been formalised by the Scottish government.
Kat Jones, the director of the NGO Action to Protect Rural Scotland, who has spearheaded demands for a datacentre moratorium in Scotland, said the vote was a “landmark day for all those communities across Scotland who have been extremely concerned about projects coming forward in their areas.”
“There’s much still to be done, but this is a huge step forward and we can all at least take a breath now,” she said. “That means the Scottish government must now urgently call in those applications which are approaching a decision date. The communities will expect nothing less.”
Ahead of the vote, the Scottish government announced that large-scale datacentres would face mandatory environmental impact assessments, as a result of growing concern about the ecological impact of the AI boom.
This month, hundreds from community groups protested outside Holyrood against the construction of large datacentres for AI until clear planning rules and the definition of a “green” datacentre had been formalised.
On Thursday, AI leaders will gather at Dumfries House in Ayrshire for a summit with King Charles on the future of the technology, amid warnings that the speed of its development threatens the survival of humanity.
After the vote, the Scottish Labour economy spokesperson, Daniel Johnson, said the economic potential of the AI boom needed to be considered alongside the impacts on the environment, communities and energy demand.
“So far the SNP has failed to do the work needed to get this right – that must change. It is right that the SNP government has accepted the need for national guidance before more decisions are made, and I want to see that guidance delivered with the urgency needed,” he said.
“The SNP must put in place the protections needed and ensure that any datacentres work for communities, create good jobs and deliver for Scotland.”
The Scottish government has been contacted for comment.

STRASBOURG, France, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed opening the door for Canada to become the first "associate member" of the European Union (EU), as she unveiled plans for closer security cooperation, tighter migration controls and stricter bans on children's social media use.
In her annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, von der Leyen said the EU and Canada would seek to upgrade their ties from the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) to an "Alliance for the Future," covering manufacturing, technology, defense, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals and artificial intelligence (AI).
"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," she told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who attended the address.
"We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics," she said, adding that she wants to bring the relationship with Canada to "the highest level possible."
Von der Leyen also proposed what she called "Europe's own Article 4," modelled on NATO's consultation mechanism, under which EU member states will convene when one country faces a serious security incident below the threshold of armed aggression.
She further proposed creating a European Security Council involving EU leaders and partners including Canada, Norway, Ukraine and Britain.
The State of the Union address sets out the Commission president's priorities for the EU for the coming year and is the centerpiece of the European Parliament's four-day plenary session, which opened Monday. ■

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16

PYONGYANG, September 16. /TASS/. North Korea has warned of the possibility of using nuclear weapons in accordance with the provisions of the law on policy regarding the state’s nuclear armed forces in response to the actions of the US and South Korea, the Korean Central News Agency reported, citing a Defense Ministry spokesperson.
The 2022 law provides for the use of nuclear weapons in the event of an attack on the country’s leadership and nuclear command and control system, as well as in the event of a threat to use nuclear or other weapons of mass destruction against North Korea.
"Such threats involving attacks and the use of weapons of mass destruction against our state by enemies can be considered the most serious challenge to our security, which requires the implementation of the relevant provisions of the law on the policy regarding the state’s nuclear armed forces," the statement said.
The defense official advised the US and South Korea to "analyze what the invocation of the relevant articles would entail and take this as a serious warning."
This statement came after a September 10 meeting of the US-South Korea Counter Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) Committee. According to Pyongyang, the parties agreed to improve information sharing, enhance joint response capabilities, and intensify relevant exercises.
However, the North Korean Defense Ministry viewed this as preparation for the potential use of nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons against the country. The statement also noted that similar scenarios were rehearsed during the US-South Korea Freedom Shield joint military drills.
