Merz's fate in the balance as second eastern German state goes to the polls
ROSTOCK, Germany, Sept 16 - Germany's struggling Chancellor Friedrich Merz will be relying on the popular centre-left state premier in the eastern region of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania to keep out the far right in an election on Sunday which may decide his political survival.
Fresh from its triumph in the Sept. 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party looks once again likely to come in first in the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election, which takes place on the same day as an election in the capital Berlin.
The AfD's first-ever victory in a state election sent shock waves through Germany's consensus-oriented political system, underlining the possibility of a far-right victory in Europe's largest economy at the next federal election due in 2029. National opinion polls currently put the AfD at between 27-29% against 18-20% for the CDU.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the other parties' hopes of keeping the AfD from power rest largely on the popularity of the Social Democrats' (SPD) 52-year-old state premier Manuela Schwesig, who leads a coalition with the Left Party and whose personal approval ratings are over 60%.
The latest poll for INSA polling institute put the AfD on 37%, ahead of the SPD on 35%, with the far-left Left Party on 10%, the environmental Greens on 5% and the far-left BSW under the threshold to enter parliament on 3%. Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) were at just 7%.
If confirmed on Sunday, that could be enough for a coalition between the SPD, Left Party and Greens, although the Greens are sitting exactly on the 5% threshold.
"It is, first and foremost, the Schwesig brand," said Wolfgang Muno, professor of political science at Rostock University. He said she was "by far the best-known politician in the state" and had succeeded in distancing herself from Merz's government in Berlin, where the SPD is junior coalition partner to the CDU.
"And that goes down very well here, because there has been an increasingly strong anti-party sentiment here in recent years," he said.
MERZ'S APPROVAL RATINGS HAVE PLUMMETED
In just over a year in office, Merz has seen his own approval ratings fall as low as 14% at national level and to single figures in the eastern states, as promised reforms have failed to show results, economic uncertainty has deepened and voter trust in the government has eroded.
The CDU is already on course for its worst-ever election result and it runs a serious risk of failing even to clear the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
For weeks, German media outlets have speculated over Merz's future, fed by leaks from within his own conservative camp, with expectations now widespread that another victory for the far-right could cost him his job, if not immediately, then over the coming months.
For the moment, senior CDU leaders have stood behind him, aware that replacing him would put the entire reform agenda at risk without solving the underlying economic problems that his government has struggled to address. But a poll at the weekend by the INSA institute found that 78% of people, including a majority of his own party supporters, no longer see Merz as the right person for the job of chancellor.
Schwesig, seen as a potential future SPD leader, has been a fierce critic of Merz, calling for more government action to curb soaring fuel prices and criticising his failure to connect with voters struggling with rising living costs.
"The Chancellor doesn't really give people the impression that he sees and understands their problems," Schwesig told a meeting with journalists in the Baltic port city of Rostock. "He simply ignores this problem."
MOMENTUM
Like other eastern regions, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a state with the one of lowest proportions of immigrants in Germany, suffers from a shortage of qualified workers and its health and aged care system depends heavily on foreign doctors, nurses and carers.
But the AfD's promises to restrict immigration and regain access to cheap Russian energy by restoring ties with Moscow have cut through with voters in the formerly communist states of eastern Germany, where many remain distanced from the western-dominated political establishments in the mainstream parties.
"There's a great deal of momentum building up again," Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD's lead candidate in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania told reporters last week. "The Chancellor is already completely out of his depth, and you feel at any moment that he might resign."
The state's resurgent shipbuilding sector, lifted by Germany's multibillion euro drive to rebuild its armed forces, and a flourishing tourism sector have helped revive an economy that was crushed in the years immediately following reunification.
But like the rest of the country, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania bears the traces of years of sluggish economic growth, exacerbated by surging petrol prices that hit especially hard in a largely rural state where many rely on their cars to get around.
Holm has struck a more moderate tone in the campaign than others in the party, including party co-leader Alice Weidel, insisting he welcomed foreigners with jobs and avoiding many of the culture wars issues that featured in the in Saxony-Anhalt campaign.
But although his party leads in the polls, the so-called "firewall" policies of the main parties means he is unlikely to be able to find a coalition partner.
Even so, he said the polls had underestimated the AfD's score in Saxony-Anhalt, where the party's success in an election which saw a turnout of almost 80%, had been fuelled by its ability to reach uncommitted voters who might otherwise have stayed at home. "And that's what I expect to happen here as well," he said. REUTERS

Meta admits mistake, to alert authorities on child sexual abuse material
NEW DELHI: Meta has admitted to a mistake and will immediately inform authorities about material related to child sexual abuse.Sources said that Meta will have to remove content related to the sexual abuse of children and material that could lead people to suicide.The government has told Meta that it can no longer be treated only as an intermediary but as a service provider, and will have to take responsibility for the content and services it provides. The development could have far-reaching consequences for Meta, sources added.The government believes Meta may no longer be entitled to legal immunity, although the issue will ultimately have to be decided by a court, they said.The development comes as Meta said it will report child-safety matters directly to India's National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, amid heightened government scrutiny over allegations that paid advertisements linked to child sexual abuse material (CSAM) appeared on Instagram.Until now, Meta primarily routed child-safety reports through the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) first issued a notice to Meta on July 3, 2026, seeking an explanation over advertisements allegedly linked to child sexual abuse material (CSEAM). Meta submitted its response a week later.The Commission subsequently decided to institute a formal inquiry to establish the facts of the matter and summoned Meta's India managing director and head to appear before it.The Meta head did not appear at the September 9 hearing, with the company instead represented by senior executives. Up to 34,000 hryvnias in fines for excessive noise from motorcycles and cars — Parliament supports the bill
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:32:16 EEST
20:32:16 KST

Up to 34,000 hryvnias in fines for excessive noise from motorcycles and cars — Parliament supports the bill
Kyiv • UNN
Parliament supported in principle a bill on fines for excessive noise from cars and motorcycles. Repeat violations may be punished by suspension of driving privileges.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted as a basis a bill providing for fines of up to UAH 34,000 for operating cars and motorcycles with noise levels exceeding the permissible limit. UNN reports this, citing a parliamentary session.
Details
Bill No. 15358 "On Amendments to the Code of Ukraine on Administrative Offenses and Other Legislative Acts Establishing Liability for Driving Vehicles with Noise Levels Exceeding the Permissible Limit" was supported as a basis by 261 members of parliament.
Under the bill, driving a vehicle with a noise level exceeding the permissible limit established by Ukrainian legislation for vehicles in operation entails a fine of UAH 8,500.
For the specified violation committed during martial law, the fine is UAH 17,000.
For a repeat violation within a year, a fine of UAH 17,000 with deprivation of the right to drive vehicles for a period of three to six months, or without such deprivation.
For a repeat violation within a year during martial law, a fine of UAH 34,000 with deprivation of the right to drive vehicles for a period of three to six months.
The first violation will be considered by the National Police authorities through an out-of-court procedure—to ensure prompt response and the inevitability of holding offenders liable directly at the scene. A repeat violation will be referred to court, since the application of a sanction in the form of deprivation of the right to drive, in accordance with the requirements of procedural legislation, may be carried out exclusively by a court decision.
After the law enters into force, the Ministry of Health, jointly with the Ministry for Communities, Territories and Infrastructure Development, is to develop and approve, within three months, maximum permissible standards for external noise levels from vehicles in operation, differentiated depending on the vehicle category, engine type and its displacement or power, as well as increased requirements for permissible noise levels at night (from 22:00 to 08:00).
We remind you
The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine rejected a bill on new fines for exceeding the speed limit. The members of parliament did not support the bill as a basis.

Special court for Kosovo sentences former president to 25 years in prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

11:32:07 UTC
20:32:07 KST

THE HAGUE, September 16. /TASS/. The Kosovo war crimes tribunal in the Hague found former president Hashim Thaci guilty of committing war crimes and sentenced him to 25 years in prison, taking into account the time he has already served, said presiding judge Charles Smith.
"The panel finds you, Hashim Thaci, guilty of the war crime of illegal or arbitrary arrest and detention, the crime of cruel treatment, torture as a war crime. The panel now sentences you to a single sentence of 25 years of imprisonment with credit for time served," Smith announced the verdict.
Taking into account the nearly six years he spent in custody, Thaci will have to serve about 19 years in prison. His associates -- former parliamentary speakers Jakup Krasniqi and Kadri Veseli, as well as former deputy from the Self·Determination party Rexhep Selimi -- were sentenced to 25, 18, and 13 years in prison, respectively. According to the indictment, all four were members of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) and, as such, are held responsible for the crimes committed during a non·international conflict in Kosovo. These crimes were part of widespread and systematic attacks on people who are believed not to have supported KLA’s actions.
The hearings in the Thaci case began on September 15, 2025. In total, about 140 victims of the crimes are participating in the proceedings. It took the Kosovo Special Court’s prosecutor’s office about two years to present all the evidence.

Deputy youth minister remembers Minab schoolchildren at IYF in Russia
YEKATERINBURG, Russia – Alireza Rahimi, Iran’s Deputy Minister of Sports and Youth Affairs and Chairman of the Supreme Council of Youth, began his address at a meeting of youth ministers from countries participating in the International Youth Festival (IYF) in Yekaterinburg by remembering Iranian schoolchildren killed in recent attacks.
The IYF is being held in Yekaterinburg from September 11 to 17, bringing together young people and officials from participating countries.
Rahimi particularly recalled the students of Shajareh Tayyebeh girls’ elementary school in Minab, southern Iran, who were killed when the school was targeted. He also referred to attacks in Lamerd and Kuhestak, where civilians, including children and teenagers, were among the victims.
Speaking on behalf of Iranian youth and the Iranian people, Rahimi condemned the US and Israeli military attacks against Iran, particularly attacks targeting civilians, children, schools and public gatherings.
“No political dispute, military calculation or strategic objective can justify the shedding of the blood of children and civilians,” Rahimi said, stressing that schools, homes, sports facilities and family gatherings should never become battlefields.
He said, however, that the message of Iranian youth was not one of hatred, but a call to defend independence and national dignity while pursuing just peace, lasting security and dialogue based on mutual respect.
Turning to broader youth challenges, Rahimi identified unemployment, the gap between education and future employment, unequal access to opportunities and the limited participation of young people in decision-making as major concerns.
He called for a shift from policies designed “for young people” to policies developed “with young people,” emphasizing meaningful youth participation, decentralization and cooperation between governments, universities, the private sector and civil society.
Rahimi also proposed the establishment of a Joint Youth Action Network among countries participating in the festival, with initial working groups focusing on future skills and artificial intelligence, entrepreneurship and social innovation, and voluntary participation and youth diplomacy.
He said Iran was ready to host the network’s first specialized meeting or one of its working groups.
Referring to recent discussions between Iran and Russia, Rahimi said the two countries had emphasized strengthening their joint youth platform and developing a joint action plan, adding that such cooperation could serve as a model for broader international youth cooperation.
“The future belongs to countries that trust young people sooner,” Rahimi said, calling on participating countries to turn youth dialogue into practical cooperation and joint action.

US officials met Iran-backed Houthis in Oman over the weekend, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:30:55 UTC
20:30:55 KST

US officials met representatives of Yemen's Houthis in Oman over the weekend, five sources familiar with the matter said, days after the Iran-backed terror group seized a strategic stretch of the Red Sea coast in a sweeping offensive that routed Saudi-backed forces.
The meeting, which has not been made public, was held at the US Embassy in Muscat, three of the sources said on the condition of anonymity. Two sources said that Oman's government, a longtime regional mediator, helped organize the meeting.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis a "foreign terrorist organization" in March 2025, criminalizing support for the group. But Washington has negotiated with them since, reaching a ceasefire in May last year after bombing the group for two months to halt a campaign of attacks on Red Sea shipping.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the Houthis had phoned his administration asking the United States to keep out of the Yemen war. US Vice President JD Vance said on Monday the United States was in direct contact with the group, without giving details.
Meeting was held at US Embassy in Muscat and helped by Oman, sources said
In the meeting, which one source said took place on Sunday, the Houthis told US officials that they had no intention of attacking American vessels and that they were committed to the 2025 ceasefire with the US, two sources said.
One of the sources, a Yemeni, said the terror group also said they would not attack Israeli ships or any commercial vessels, except those belonging to Saudi Arabia.
According to two of the sources, the US side was represented by embassy personnel.
One source said the Houthi delegation included a senior official based in Muscat who is under US sanctions, Mohammad Abdulsalam. Another source confirmed Abdulsalam's presence, along with another senior Houthi official, Abdelmalik al-Ajiri.
Asked whether the US had met with the Houthis in Oman, a State Department spokesperson did not confirm the meeting, but said safeguarding freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and preventing the export of terrorism from the Middle East were core US interests.
Oman's embassy in the US and senior Houthi official Abdulsalam did not respond to a request for comment.
The Houthis last week seized effective control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline, including the historic port of Mocha, and Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandab, or "Gate of Tears" strait, at the sea's mouth.
The Houthis, who seized Yemen's capital in 2014, have fought against a Saudi-led coalition for more than a decade. The war had quieted under a ceasefire in recent years, but fighting resumed in July when the Houthis declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea in response to a Saudi blockade of Yemeni ports.
Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, called Trump last week seeking US military support amid the dramatic Houthi advances. Reuters has reported that Washington told Riyadh it would not get directly involved.

Hague court sentences Kosovo ex-president Thaçi to 25 years in prison for war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:30:33 UTC
20:30:33 KST

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague on Wednesday found former President Hashim Thaçi criminally responsible for war crimes carried out during the 1998-1999 war with Serbia and sentenced him to 25 years in prison.
The court said Thaçi was responsible for the crimes of arbitrary detention against 385 individuals, cruel treatment against 49 individuals, torture against 303 individuals and murder against 96 individuals as part of a joint criminal enterprise.
The verdicts, which are expected to be appealed by the defendants, have sparked outrage from Kosovo and Albanian leaders, and sparked scuffles outside The Hague between assembled supporters and Dutch police.
Advertisement
Thaçi, a former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army, was tried alongside Jakup Krasniqi, Rexhep Selimi and Kadri Veseli. The four men were charged with six counts of crimes against humanity and four war crimes charges.
The charges of crimes against humanity were dropped, while Krasniqi was sentenced to 25 years, Selimi to 13 years and Veseli to 18 years for the other offenses.
According to the judgment, the court found that the prosecution had failed to prove the existence of widespread and systematic attacks against civilians, a key element for crimes against humanity.
Following the ruling, Kosovo’s Prime Minister Albin Kurti said that the KLA “was born as a response to the oppression of a genocidal regime and fought for the liberation of Kosovo.” He added that the country would continue to support the four individuals in the appeal procedure.
Thaçi’s brother, Gani, told the media that the family is convinced of his innocence and “we are waiting for the appeal.”
In a social media post, Krasniqi’s daughter Gresa called the ruling an “unjust, political, racist, and criminal” decision and claimed that many individuals responsible for war crimes against Kosovo Albanians remain free in Serbia today.
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama called the ruling a “shame.”
Thaçi was indicted in November 2020 and resigned as president in the same month to face the proceedings. He has remained in detention in The Hague since then. “I expect to be acquitted of every charge,” Thaci said in a recent interview in August. The other defendants have all denied the charges against them.
Advertisement
Kosovo Albanians gather at a rally in Pristina on Sept. 16, 2026, on the day of the war crimes verdict in the trial of former President Hashim Thaçi. | Elvis Barukcic/AFP via Getty Images
Thaçi also faces a separate trial later this month over alleged witness intimidation.
The 1998-1999 Kosovo war took place between the KLA and Serbian forces, who carried out a systematic campaign of ethnic cleansing, displacing over 1 million Kosovo Albanians, killing about 11,000, and injuring many thousands more.
The war came to an end in June 1999 after a 78-day NATO bombing campaign carried out against Yugoslav forces caused their withdrawal from Kosovo.
Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, but Belgrade has continued to refuse to recognize it. It is recognized as independent by more than 100 United Nations members. Relations remain tense despite years of European Union-mediated negotiations. “Our war was just, a war of liberation,” Prime Minister Albin Kurti said ahead of the verdict.
Former Kosovo President Vjosa Osmani said in an interview last week that she was worried about what a guilty verdict would mean for Kosovo’s security amid ongoing tensions with Serbia.
Thousands rallied in Pristina over the weekend and on Wednesday before the verdict in support of the four men, filling a central square with red-and-black Albanian flags.
Advertisement
Today’s announcement is a first-instance decision, and the parties have the right to appeal.
This article has been updated with comments from Prime Minister Albin Kurti.

US Army picks VIKING UGV for autonomous breaching trials
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:30:22 BST
20:30:22 KST

The US Army has selected IDV USA as one of four industry participants in a programme exploring autonomous vehicles capable of breaching complex obstacles and minefields while reducing the exposure of soldiers to direct fire, according to the company.
The Engineer Autonomous Breaching Capability initiative, known as EABC, is being led by the Army’s Capability Program Executive Office Mission Autonomy and is intended to examine how robotic systems could support engineering forces during some of the most dangerous phases of ground manoeuvre.
IDV USA, the American subsidiary of Leonardo-owned IDV, is offering a solution based around its VIKING Uncrewed Ground Vehicle.
The vehicle is being paired with ground autonomy software intended to support the integration of different mission systems and payloads, as well as autonomous navigation in environments where access to satellite navigation is degraded or denied.
According to IDV, the combination is intended to provide a common autonomy architecture that could eventually support missions beyond breaching, including other engineering and manoeuvre tasks.
The EABC requirement is focused on the particular problem of penetrating defended obstacle belts and minefields. Such operations can require engineering vehicles and personnel to work in areas deliberately covered by enemy observation and weapons, making the ability to push uncrewed systems forward potentially valuable.
IDV said the Army is seeking autonomous systems capable of carrying out those tasks “under direct observation and fire, minimising risk for human personnel.”
Corey Kashner, CEO of IDV USA, said: “We are honoured to be selected by the U.S. Army for the EABC initiative. The EABC program aligns directly with IDV’s vision for autonomous systems and robotic manoeuvre support.”
He added: “By combining the proven VIKING UGV platform with our autonomy framework, we are delivering a solution designed to enhance mission effectiveness while reducing risks to soldiers. We look forward to supporting the Army’s modernisation objectives.”
The selection does not represent a decision to field the VIKING system across the Army. IDV is one of four companies chosen to participate in the initiative, with the competing approaches expected to undergo further testing before the service decides how it wants to proceed. Following contract awards, the programme is expected to move through a series of demonstrations and operational assessments in environments intended to replicate realistic military conditions.
The process is planned to culminate in an assessment involving an Army unit, allowing soldiers to provide feedback on how the autonomous systems perform and how they could be employed in future breaching operations. That feedback will then inform subsequent decisions on next-generation autonomous engineer systems rather than immediately leading to a large-scale procurement.
The VIKING platform forms part of IDV’s wider work on autonomous military ground vehicles, with the company investing in mobility, autonomous navigation and the integration of mission-specific payloads. A key element of the proposed EABC configuration is the ability to continue operating in contested electromagnetic environments. IDV says the navigation architecture has been designed with GNSS-degraded operations in mind, reducing dependence on continuous access to satellite positioning during battlefield manoeuvre.
The Army’s interest in autonomous breaching reflects a wider effort to use uncrewed vehicles for missions where conventional engineering forces face particularly high exposure to enemy fire, mines and other obstacles.
For IDV, the next stage will be demonstrating whether VIKING and its autonomy software can translate that concept into a system usable by soldiers during realistic breaching operations, alongside the three other industry teams selected for the EABC initiative.

Second phase of CSTO Rubezh 2026 exercise begins in Kazakhstan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:29:54 UTC
20:29:54 KST

MOSCOW, September 16. /TASS/. The second phase of the Collective Security Treaty Organization’s (CSTO) Rubezh 2026 exercise, involving the Collective Rapid Deployment Forces of the Central Asian region, has begun at the Koktal training ground in Kazakhstan, Vladislav Shchegrikovich, press secretary of the CSTO Joint Staff, told TASS.
The total number of exercise participants is about 1,500, with more than 300 pieces of military and specialized equipment involved, including 115 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for various purposes. Military contingents from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan are participating, along with operational groups from the CSTO Joint Staff and Secretariat. The Russian contingent consists primarily of service members from the Central Military District, specifically from the 201st Guards Military Base, according to the CSTO Joint Staff.
"The second phase of the Rubezh 2026 joint exercise with the Collective Rapid Deployment Forces of the Central Asian region has begun at the Kotal training range in the Republic of Kazakhstan," Shchegrikovich stated.
He specified that during the Combat Operations phase, participants are practicing "two main training objectives: the occupation of the area of responsibility by the national contingents of the Central Asian Region’s Collective Rapid Deployment Forces and the elimination of illegal armed groups that have invaded the territory of a CSTO member state."
"Units are drilling practical maneuvers in both daytime and nighttime conditions for various tactical scenarios, including repelling attacks by a simulated enemy on checkpoints and populated areas, as well as detecting and destroying explosive devices and caches of weapons and ammunition belonging to illegal armed groups," said Shchegrikovich.
Using present experience to ensure safe future
The CSTO Joint Staff press service also emphasizes that experience gained in modern armed conflicts plays an important role during the exercise.
"The command and control bodies of the Collective Rapid Deployment Forces of the Central Asian region are carrying out training and combat tasks from hardened command posts. Various types of UAVs are actively being used for unit command and control, aerial reconnaissance, air and artillery fire adjustment, and delivering fire strikes," specified the CSTO Joint Staff press secretary. Significant attention is being paid to defense against UAVs of a simulated adversary, with an emphasis on mobile armed units, as well as to electronic warfare and air defense. Small assault groups are using motorcycles, quad bikes, and Ulan-1 and Ulan-2 tactical all-terrain vehicles.
In addition, according to the exercise commander, Commander of Kazakhstan’s Airborne Assault Forces Colonel Makhsut Guseinov, "a rapidly evolving situation with a steady escalation" has been created at the Rubezh 2026 exercise.
"The units drilled approximately 40 different scenarios within a tight timeframe. The results allow us to assess the personnel’s readiness for sudden changes in the situation, as well as their ability to respond to threats posed by the enemy’s use of unmanned aerial systems and improvised explosive devices," Guseinov stated.

OpenAI has begun preliminary conversations with investors about another funding round that could push its valuation beyond $1.2 trillion, following the launch of its newest advanced AI model, The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday.
The developer of ChatGPT was valued at $852 billion in March after securing $122 billion in financing from investors such as Amazon, Nvidia, and SoftBank.
If the new funding round moves forward, it would come ahead of the company’s initial public offering, which is now expected to take place next year, according to the report.

Since its previous fundraising round, OpenAI has reported that its number of active users has surpassed one billion, while more than 200 million businesses now use its AI models.
Its AI-powered coding tool, Codex, has also experienced significant growth. The company recently introduced Astra, a new model it characterized as the world’s most intelligent and aligned model.
OpenAI generated $6.7 billion in revenue during the three months ending in June, compared with $5.7 billion in the first quarter. However, its operating margin declined, pushing back expectations that the company could become profitable before an IPO.
Speaking with Fortune this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the company was unlikely to pursue a public listing this year, pointing to concerns surrounding AI safety.
“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman said.

Speaking ahead of European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen's speech before parliament, ex-Council President Charles Michel told Euronews that she has failed to rise to the occasion of the EU's challenges.
The European Commission President is "very slow" to make the necessary decisions on the current challenges facing the European Union (EU), Charles Michel, who headed the European Council during von der Leyen's first term as Commission chief from 2019 to 2024, said.
His comments came ahead of von der Leyen's highly anticipated annual State of the European Union address before the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday, in which she outlined her vision and priorities for the coming year.
Michel, however, was focused on her failure to fulfil the promises made in previous years.
"I'm observing that, today, the EU is facing complicated challenges because there are more and more conflicts; there is a war on European soil, and we are in a difficult position in terms of competition with China and the United States," Michel told Euronews' flagship morning programme Europe Today.
"We should focus on the core issues, and the core issue is not about communication; it's not about more initiatives. The Commission over the last years launched 400 initiatives. But where are the deliveries? Where is the improvement? When I meet entrepreneurs, they are disappointed because they don't feel a sense of urgency."
Over-regulation makes EU weaker
Michel argued that when it comes to strengthening the EU's competitiveness, identified by Michel as the top priority facing the bloc today, there is a deadlock.
"There is a question, a very simple question: 'Is the EU a better place to invest? Is the EU a better place to innovate?' We've seen a lot of regulations, over-regulation," he said.
Michel went on to say that there has been no significant progress when it comes to, for example, the capital markets union - essentially a single market for capital across the EU identified as a key pillar for strengthening competitiveness.
"It makes us weaker, too weak in the current context." While conceding this is not entirely von der Leyen's fault, he did emphasise that "she has a responsibility," adding that "there is no doubt that she is very slow in making her decisions. I have the impression there is a lack of focus on what matters."
The Commission chief addressed this matter in her speech on Wednesday, arguing that, with the EU single market and "world-class industry and services," the bloc has the foundations to compete and scale alongside major global powers such as China and the US, but that it is still too fragmented.
Von der Leyen argued the Commission is delivering on this front. "We now have the political agreement on the One Europe, One Market Roadmap. And together, by the end of next year, we can and must complete this historic overhaul of the Single Market."
'Blindly following US'
According to Michel, von der Leyen's approach to dealing with the US under Donald Trump's presidency has also put Europe's security at risk. She was criticised by MEPs, among others, for the so-called "Turnberry Agreement", the EU-US trade deal agreed to last summer, which some saw as lopsided.
"I have the impression that she decided to follow the United States blindly, even when it was against the fundamental interests of the European Union," Michel said.
"There was a kind of naivety, I think, and many of the European leaders - a few years ago I was one of them - made it very clear that it was important to build European sovereignty, this European independence that now she is starting to talk about, but a lot of time was lost."
However, Michel said he "remains optimistic" because "there is no Plan B."
"I think it is a question of time, and sooner or later there will be a clearer understanding that now it's time to act; it's time for a reset of this European project, and for this we need to focus on the core issues: businesses, economic development, making the lives of our entrepreneurs easier, smarter regulation, more investments. This is what is key, in my opinion."

Iran shakes with 94 earthquakes in a week
TEHRAN – A total of 94 earthquakes have been recorded across the country in a week from September 5 to 11, according to the seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran.
Statistically, 85 earthquakes with magnitudes smaller than 3, six earthquakes with a magnitude between 3 and 4, and three earthquakes with a magnitude between 4 and 5 have occurred in the country, irsc reported.
Of the total quakes, one had a magnitude of 4.4 on the Richter scale, which occurred on September 6th in Kordestan province.
Among the provinces of the country, Khorasan Razavi experienced the highest number of earthquakes with 13, followed by Yazd with 10, Semnan and Fars each with 9 earthquakes.
During the same period, two earthquakes hit Tehran. No earthquakes were recorded in Ardabil, Alborz, Chaharmahal-Bakhtiari, Zanjan, Gilan, and Hamedan provinces.
A total of 2,380 earthquakes with a magnitude of more than 2.5 on the Richter scale were recorded across the country over the past calendar year (March 2025–March 2026), according to the Seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran, Mehr news agency reported.
Out of recorded earthquakes, 910 had a magnitude greater than 3, 130 had a magnitude greater than 4, and 15 had a magnitude greater than 5 on the Richter scale.
The Iranian plateau is located in a very seismically active region of the world and is known not only for its major catastrophic earthquakes but also for the disasters relating to natural hazards, especially earthquakes.
About 2 percent of the earthquakes in the world occur in Iran, but more than 6 percent of the victims of the world’s earthquakes during the 20th century are reported from Iranian earthquakes.

Over half of eligible Iranians join Jan Fada campaign
TEHRAN – The “Jan Fada” (self-sacrificing volunteer) campaign officially launched on March 29 as a spontaneous public movement in response to persistent threats and aggression by the United States and Israel against Iran’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.
More than half of the country’s eligible citizens have registered for the initiative, according to Jan Fada spokesperson Sasan Zare, making it one of the largest public mobilization drives in the country in recent years.
Speaking at a press conference in Tehran on Wednesday, Zare said more than 31.3 million people had registered so far. He described the campaign as an initiative aimed at demonstrating public readiness to defend the country and contribute to various national sectors.

Another 20 percent selected social services, 17 percent volunteered for cultural, artistic, and media activities, and 13 percent offered to provide ongoing financial support. The remaining five percent were classified under miscellaneous services.
Organizers have described Jan Fada as a contemporary expression of Iran’s longstanding tradition of national resilience. The initiative, launched to demonstrate public readiness to defend the country amid heightened geopolitical tensions, quickly attracted millions of registrants nationwide.
The campaign has since expanded from a public registration drive into a broader framework for organized civic participation and national solidarity, bringing together volunteers from diverse communities.
The Jan Fada headquarters has also announced the launch of training and organizational preparations for 1,000 national resistance battalions.

Georgia’s top diplomat told Euronews that Tbilisi remains committed to EU accession and that Europe needs Georgia for its prosperity and security. But according to the FM, it all comes down to whether Europeans “are serious about enlargement”.

In a Euronews-moderated panel at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai, Botchorishvili outlined Tbilisi’s firm position that “Europe wants to enlarge, but Europe does not have experience of being represented in South Caucasus.”
"We both need to learn, we both need to exchange, and for that we need very intensive dialogue and working together.”
Botchorishvili, who also serves as Georgia’s vice premier, repeated her government’s long-standing position that Brussels must respect Tbilisi.
While Georgia remains ready to discuss EU accession, Botchorishvili said, “we expect that European partners will also realise it is important to have intensive dialogue and mutual respect with partners, which are very important for our common security and prosperity.”
Georgia’s EU accession process has all but stalled amid increasingly icy relations between Tbilisi and Brussels, with the EU accusing Georgia of a downturn in its democratic process and of a pro-Russian approach, while Tbilisi maintains it remains committed to its European belonging, but only by pursuing its own interests.
“European aspirations and identity are very deeply rooted in Georgia’s history and identity, and it is very natural for Georgians to have this aspiration towards Europe," the Georgian top diplomat told Euronews.
Once this principle was settled, there was a clear “but” from Georgia’s government representative, who explained that it is the “geopolitical context” together with “a very historic context” which makes this “a very delicate issue.”
“You will find the values that formed Georgia’s European aspiration, but also the same values that formed Georgian identity as well, so that is kind of a very delicate issue for Georgia,” Botchorishvili said.
Tbilisi is balancing its regional, or neighbourly, approach with its international ones, she explained.
'We have our history and our own resillience'
When asked about Georgia’s response to accusations of being pro-Russian and not pursuing real EU ambitions while having its territories still occupied by Russia, the foreign minister reverted to the geopolitical context by replying that “yes, Russian troops (presence) in Georgian regions definitely creates major security threats, but we are looking at this situation as well from the point of view of opportunities.”
Therefore, the foreign minister outlined Tbilisi’s current strategy towards Russia’s presence: “there are plenty of opportunities if you focus on preserving peace and stability, preserving economic development, and that's what we are doing today,” Botchorishvili said.
“Very often you will see different narratives flying around about Georgia, but the best message is to look at the numbers”, Botchorishvili continued.
She further implied that it is in Europe’s interests to engage, given that “Georgia has best economic growth in the region, in Europe, it's around 8%, which is impressive and is the best answer to all the false narratives that we hear about Georgia.”
"The South Caucasus is important for Europe’s security and prosperity (and) Georgia is the important place where not only energy passes through, but many other things which are important for European security from different perspectives," Botchorishvili said.
The foreign minister also insisted that as Georgia bridges Asia and Europe through its Black Sea access and given the current reshaping of global supply routes, it has "a very special place today in terms of connectivity."
"Talking about the Middle Corridor, which is not just a physical corridor, but it represents everything meeting together and from a European perspective, it is important for European security and prosperity.”
During the panel debate at the Arab Media Summit, the foreign minister blamed “a massive disinformation campaign against Georgia also because of its geopolitical meaning and importance” conducted by “some actors” who have “used this very sensitive and very delicate topic for different political purposes or reasons”.
“From our perspective, yes, it's quite complicated geopolitical context, but it is our history as well. We have experience and we have our own resilience as well. And we have our history which brought Georgia to this point,” Botchorishvili concluded.

ARKHANGELSK, September 16. /TASS/. The Orkan-2 unmanned boat for Arctic conditions was launched in Arkhangelsk, the region's Governor Alexander Tsybulsky wrote on Telegram. It will be tested in the White Sea on the route between Arkhangelsk and Pertominsk.
"The Orkan-2 unmanned boat has been launched today," the post reads. "The Orkan-2 has passed technical tests and its maiden voyage on the Arkhangelsk-Pertominsk route is due in a few days. This model has an increased load capacity of 400 kg, and a range of 600 km."
The boat will deliver diesel fuel to Pertominsk for a local diesel generator, some cargo for the Kenozersky National Park, as well as books for schools, and kindergarten coloring books on behalf of the Russian Post Company. The unmanned boat will be accompanied by a regular boat - for monitoring and safety reasons.
"These tests will check how unmanned vessels technologies can work in real northern conditions. Pertominsk is one of the settlements to where cargo delivery is complicated, and such voyages in future may become a reliable link with the regional center. If the experiment is successful, we will be able to talk about regular unmanned logistics for the Arkhangelsk Region's hard-to-reach territories," the governor added.
A research and environmental project
The new boat is the third unmanned vessel, developed by Sea Project and Unmanned Logistics companies, to operate in the Arctic. In 2025, the Breeze boat successfully completed an experimental route from Arkhangelsk to the Solovki. The second boat, the Orkan, since February has been at the Northern Arctic Federal University (NArFU).
"NArFU continues to develop the direction related to the operation of unmanned boats, both in educational and research aspects," NArFU's Chancellor Mikhail Danilov told TASS. "Our boat has been actively involved in the research program with a number of enterprises. In the near future, we plan to install hydrographic equipment on the boat."
The future of using transportation by unmanned boats in the region is quite promising, the Arkhangelsk Region's Deputy Governor and head of the local government Alexey Alsufyev said. "Therefore, it is necessary to plan how many boats of the kind are needed, what schedule they will have, what routes, and what they will be carrying. By the next navigation season, companies must have a confirmed cargo amount from every owner who will entrust to transport them," he explained.
The Kenozersky National Park has ordered the cargo transportation service. Right now, the park is working on the industrial and memorial complex dubbed Unsky Timber Factory: Access Allowed, and an unmanned boat will deliver construction materials there.
"Unmanned cargo deliveries are a very promising area for us, because the Onega Pomorie National Park is known for complicated logistics," Manager of the Kenozersky and Onega Pomorie National parks Alexandra Yakovleva said. "Most transportation options are connected with the sea, and we find this area interesting, both for cargo delivery and for monitoring and security."
The Orkan-2 marine robotic complex is designed to perform various operations at sea without a human on board. Generally speaking, the development of unmanned cargo transportation cuts delivery costs, increases the logistics availability for businesses, and creates new high-tech jobs.

====================================================================================================

The New Delhi BRICS Summit Sends Powerful Messages to America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:24:00 UTC
20:24:00 KST

India hosted the 18th BRICS Summit with considerable success and impact. This year’s summit generated consensus on several major issues that concern not only BRICS members but also much of the world beyond the U.S.-dominated West.
In the wake of this summit, one can legitimately argue that BRICS is emerging as a formidable grouping capable of challenging the global hegemony of the United States and the G7. More importantly, it is evolving into a global platform that can help its members move, as India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi put it, from being “rule takers” to becoming “rule makers.”
India achieved something that had seemed nearly impossible only a few months ago: securing the unanimous endorsement of a joint declaration by all BRICS nations. At the May meeting of BRICS foreign ministers, deep internal disagreements — particularly between India, which was reluctant to condemn Israel and the United States, and other members that sought such condemnation over the Israeli-U.S. attacks on Iran — prevented consensus. A separate dispute between the UAE and Iran over the wording of the document ultimately scuttled the proposed joint declaration, forcing the chair to issue only a summary of the discussions.
That failure highlighted the divisions within BRICS and raised serious questions about whether it could ever become a cohesive grouping. Its members include countries that are strategic rivals, such as India and China, as well as states directly at war with one another, such as the UAE and Iran. Yet India’s Ministry of External Affairs and its BRICS sherpas worked diligently to produce a draft acceptable to every member. All sides made significant compromises to reach consensus.
The resulting declaration sends a powerful signal: a united BRICS is prepared to engage with and reshape the global order — not by dismantling it, but by preserving its liberal foundations. This creates a striking reversal in global politics. The United States, which underwrote the liberal international order for more than seven decades, now appears determined to weaken it, tarnish its legitimacy, undermine core institutions such as the ICC and the ICJ, and render the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) increasingly irrelevant.
Contrary to the perception that BRICS seeks to challenge the U.S.-led global order, it is essentially pursuing a course correction. It seeks to ensure that the liberal order and its underlying principles are not diminished by double standards and unilateral actions, particularly those of the United States. BRICS is thus positioning itself as a defender of the fundamental principles upon which that order rests: state sovereignty, international law, international norms, and, above all, mutual respect among nations.
The New Delhi Declaration was remarkable and surprising in several respects. It remained consistent with the broad narrative advanced by India: that BRICS is not anti-American, anti-Western, or directed against any particular country. Rather, BRICS is an endeavor by states to come together to address common challenges and pursue mutually shared interests. What was particularly remarkable, however, was India’s ability to secure consensus on several highly contentious issues.
Four major features of the declaration deserve particular attention.
First, notwithstanding its carefully calibrated rhetoric, the declaration was strongly critical of U.S. trade and sanctions practices. It condemned unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures that distort trade and violate WTO rules. It also denounced unilateral economic and secondary sanctions imposed outside the authority of the UNSC, characterizing such measures as contrary to international law and harmful to the development, health, and food security of affected populations, particularly in the Global South (paragraphs 21–22).
Second, each of the three major BRICS powers — China, Russia, and India — managed to incorporate its particular priorities into the declaration. China secured a strong condemnation of unilateral sanctions, many of which are directed against it. Even sanctions targeting Iran indirectly affect China because it is the principal purchaser of Iranian oil. Russia, too, secured what it wanted: Ukraine was omitted. Far from criticizing Russia, the declaration remained entirely silent about the Ukraine war and its effects on global supply chains and the international order.
India, meanwhile, obtained the unified BRICS position it has consistently sought against cross-border terrorism, terrorist financing, and safe havens for terrorist groups (paragraph 40). The declaration condemns the April 22, 2025, terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir, in which 26 people were killed, and explicitly calls for combating the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing, and terrorist safe havens. Although the paragraph does not mention Pakistan, it clearly advances, legitimizes, and showcases India’s concerns about its problematic neighbor and its policies aimed at destabilizing Kashmir through cross-border terrorism.
Third, perhaps the most astonishing feature of the declaration was its treatment of the war against Iran (paragraphs 28–29). The document protects the United States and Israel to some extent by declining to name them, but its criticism of their attacks on Iran is nevertheless unmistakable. It expresses concern about escalating tensions in West Asia, stresses the protection of civilian infrastructure and the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, and condemns deliberate attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities operating under full IAEA safeguards as violations of international law. The declaration therefore affirms the protected status of Iran’s peaceful nuclear infrastructure and establishes that attacks against it are illegal, while offering no comparable criticism of Iran’s attacks on its Gulf neighbors.
Finally, the declaration’s extensive treatment of Palestine, followed by its discussion of Lebanon, constitutes a profound indictment of Israel even when Israel is not always explicitly named. It condemns forced displacement, starvation as a method of warfare, attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and the obstruction of humanitarian assistance. It reaffirms the Palestinians’ rights to self-determination and return, supports full Palestinian membership in the United Nations, and reiterates its commitment to a sovereign Palestinian state within the internationally recognized 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital (paragraphs 30–34). It then condemns violations of Lebanon’s sovereignty, calls explicitly on Israel to withdraw from occupied Lebanese territory, and denounces attacks against UNIFIL personnel and installations (paragraphs 35–36).
The declaration was not the only way in which BRICS spoke to the world; the summit’s optics were equally striking. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian received considerable prominence through several key bilateral meetings, his early arrival, and his participation in the BRICS Business Forum. The image of Modi, the host, walking hand in hand with Pezeshkian down the red carpet with visible warmth and affection was particularly telling. The red-carpet welcome suggested an Indian pivot away from Israel — a shift also reflected in the declaration’s direct condemnation of Israeli actions and its robust affirmation of Palestinian rights. Taken together, these developments indicate that India may now be moving away from the major mistake Modi made when he visited Israel in February, only days before Israel and the United States attacked Iran, and declared that India stood firmly with Israel.
Another highlight of the summit was the Iran-UAE meeting between the Iranian president and the UAE’s crown prince, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The meeting signaled that even states participating in the Abraham Accords and closely aligned with Israel and the United States now feel compelled to engage publicly with Iran. Moreover, the prominence accorded to the Iranian president, contrasted with the absence of the UAE’s ruler, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, suggested a noteworthy shift. Only four months earlier, the UAE had been able to block a BRICS declaration that would have condemned Israel and the United States. At the New Delhi summit, however, the UAE appeared — like India — to have recalibrated aspects of its foreign policy posture in a direction more accommodating toward Iran.
Although an important element of the BRICS narrative was that the grouping was not directed against the United States, the West, or any other country, the prominence accorded to Iran and Russia conveyed a more complicated message. Pezeshkian and Russian President Vladimir Putin participated prominently in numerous events both within and beyond the formal BRICS proceedings. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also held a significant meeting with a Kashmiri delegation comprising three leading religious figures — Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, Aga Syed Hassan Mosavi, and Molvi Imran Raza Ansari — a politically sensitive engagement rarely seen during a major summit hosted by India.
Taken together, these events appeared to send a clear message from India and BRICS to the West: however determined Western governments may be to turn Russia and Iran into pariah states, much of the Global South rejects their isolation and continues to embrace them as legitimate and consequential international actors.
Thus, while the New Delhi Declaration is softly critical of the United States, it is harshly critical of Israel, signaling a significant shift in the positions of countries such as India and the UAE. Without their support and concessions, such a forceful criticism of Israeli actions — and such an unequivocal affirmation of Palestinian rights — could not have secured unanimous approval. The summit also affirmed the growing convergence of interests among India, China, Russia, and Iran. All four states seek the emergence of a multipolar world and the resurgence of multilateralism in global governance. All in all, it was a highly successful summit for both India and BRICS.

President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen proposed granting Canada the status of the European Union’s first associate member. She made the statement during a speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, reports UNN.
Details
We want to move from CETA to an alliance for the future in order to create a common space of prosperity and economic security
She noted that the parties plan to develop cooperation in intelligent manufacturing, create a technology alliance and integrate their defense-industrial bases. Von der Leyen also named the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, battery technologies, artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, cybersecurity and economic security among the areas of future cooperation.

We want to bring relations with Canada to the highest possible level
She then said that she would like to work together with the Prime Minister of Canada to open up the possibility for the country to obtain a special status in its relations with the European Union.
I would like to work with you to open the door for Canada to become the European Union’s first associate member

Context

In addition, in 2026, Canada became the first non-European country to conclude an agreement with the EU on participation in the SAFE defense instrument.

Nina Yuzhanina, a member of Ukrainian Parliament from the European Solidarity faction and a member of the parliamentary Committee on Finance, Tax and Customs Policy, said that goods intended for security and defense purposes had been excluded, at the request of European Solidarity, from the list of goods that will be taxed in postal shipments if the bill on the taxation of parcels is adopted, which is required to receive financial assistance from the European Union.
"Once again about parcels. It was precisely the bills concerning the taxation of the value of goods in parcels that became among the most difficult and, in fact, divided the country into directly opposing views. They also became the reason for a large number of letters and appeals calling for support for the abolition of the exemption. The EBA, American Chamber of Commerce, Federation of Employers, Association of IT Enterprises, the Ukrainian Business Council, Ukrlegprom [the Association of Light Industry Enterprises], Retailers Association, Toy Manufacturers Association, Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and Ukrainian Council of Shopping Centers insist on abolishing the exemption and call for support for these bills," Yuzhanina wrote on Facebook.
According to her, a meeting of the tax committee was held Wednesday morning to reconsider decisions on the relevant bills, as four more alternative bills on the issue had recently been registered. The lawmaker noted that the European Solidarity faction had received individual appeals from European partners, so "we had to seek a compromise."
"So, as a result. Paragraph 100 of subsection 2 of Section XX of the Tax Code – the main provision that provides for an exemption from VAT for transactions involving the distance sale of goods specified in paragraphs 87¹ and 92 of the Tax Code – was supplemented, that is, the exemption was expanded: 'as well as transactions involving the distance sale of goods intended for security and defense purposes, the list of which shall be determined by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine,'" Yuzhanina said.
According to her, the list of such goods and the procedure will be approved by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine, and the tax paid upon receipt of a parcel will be refunded to the buyer. "Only in this way was it possible to preserve the exemption for goods intended for security and defense purposes. And this directly complies with the conditions of the Memorandum with the EU ratified by the Verkhovna Rada," the lawmaker wrote.
Yuzhanina also said that taxation of parcels, if the relevant bills are supported, would be introduced no earlier than July 1, 2027, and only 45 days after the day following the publication in the Holos Ukrainy newspaper of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine's decision ensuring the possibility of introducing the rules for the distance sale of goods.
"For me, it is important that at least one fundamental point was successfully defended: goods intended for security and defense purposes should not become more expensive because of the new taxation of parcels," she emphasized.
As reported, according to the draft state budget for 2027, the government expects UAH 11.8 billion in additional VAT revenues from the taxation of parcels with a declared value of up to EUR 150.

Formula 1 will return to the TOSFED Istanbul Park circuit from Oct. 1–3, 2027, organizers have officially confirmed, ending months of anticipation for the Türkiye Grand Prix.
The race weekend kicks off with practice sessions on Oct. 1, 2027, followed by crucial qualifying laps the following day. The main event will take place on Oct. 2, 2027, the Turkish Automobile Sports Federation (TOSFED) said.
Formula 1 management and local authorities finalized a five-year agreement ensuring Istanbul will host the top-tier races through the end of the 2031 season. Organizers opened pre-registration for ticket sales and official announcements on their website.
Tourism sector representatives expect the massive organization to trigger a significant surge in Istanbul’s tourism activity. Industry experts predict the influx of international visitors will provide long-term contributions to the local economy and improve the country’s global image rather than remaining limited to a single race weekend.
The 5.3-kilometer circuit last hosted a Formula 1 race in 2021, when wet conditions provided a thrilling spectacle for spectators. Designed by renowned architect Hermann Tilke, the anti-clockwise track is famous for its challenging Turn 8, featuring four distinct apexes that push drivers to their absolute limits.
This decision brings one of the most demanding circuits back to the global racing calendar. Local hospitality businesses prepare for an economic boom as tens of thousands of racing fans begin booking trips to the city, reserving regional hotels and premium restaurants months in advance.
The government projects significant tax income from hosting this prestigious, highly profitable international sporting event.

Majority of Americans see risk AI could destroy humanity: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:20:23 UTC
20:20:23 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
A majority of Americans believe advanced artificial intelligence poses at least a moderate risk of eventually destroying humanity, according to a Politico poll released Wednesday, highlighting growing public concern over the rapid development of AI technology.
About two-thirds of respondents said there is at least a moderate risk that advanced AI could destroy humanity, including 17% who said it is “almost certain” and 20% who described the risk as “significant.” Another 26% characterized the risk as moderate.
The survey found concern across political, gender and age groups. Among voters in the 2024 presidential election, 70% of those who voted for Democratic candidate Kamala Harris saw at least a moderate risk, compared with 60% of Donald Trump voters. President Trump has downplayed the fears about AI.
Americans also expressed greater support for slowing AI development than for continuing to build increasingly advanced systems.
According to the poll, 48% said AI is “good enough” and development should be paused to reduce risks, while 31% favored continued development because advanced AI could bring significant benefits. Among Harris voters, 58% backed a pause, compared with 44% of Trump voters.
The findings come as prominent AI industry figures have publicly warned about the technology's potential dangers. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, alongside billionaire Elon Musk, have called for slowing the development of advanced AI.
About half of Americans surveyed said AI leaders warning that the technology could ultimately kill humanity genuinely believe their warnings. By contrast, 26% said such statements are intended as marketing to make AI products appear more powerful or important.
Trump has continued to emphasize AI development as an economic and technological priority, while dismissing warnings about existential risks. Republicans and Democrats in Washington are nevertheless debating how to balance AI safeguards with the need for the US to remain competitive with China.
The poll was conducted online by London-based Public First on Sept. 13-15 among 2,064 US adults. It has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.2 percentage points, with higher margins for smaller subgroups.

US targets South Africa with visa curbs over ‘racial grievance’ claims

US targets South Africa with visa curbs over ‘racial grievance’ claims
The US has introduced a visa-restriction policy targeting South African officials and other individuals Washington accuses of enabling “uncompensated land seizures” and “race-based discrimination” against Afrikaners.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the measure on Tuesday, saying it would cover foreign nationals responsible for or complicit in policies permitting discrimination or inciting violence against racial and ethnic minorities.
Rubio accused the South African government of failing to “adequately address” Washington’s previously stated concerns. “The South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority,” he said in a statement. The policy creates a framework for denying or revoking visas but it did not name any individuals targeted by the restrictions.
Pretoria has yet to respond publicly. It has repeatedly denied persecuting white citizens or confiscating white-owned farms, while Ramaphosa has dismissed claims of a “white genocide” as false.
The dispute centers partly on the Expropriation Act signed in January 2025. It requires compensation for property acquired in the public interest but permits none in limited cases, including abandoned land. Pretoria says the law does not authorize arbitrary seizures and allows disputes to be settled in court.
The government describes land reform and black economic empowerment as necessary to address inequalities inherited from apartheid.
Relations between Washington and Pretoria have deteriorated sharply since Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025. The two governments have clashed over land reform, racial policies, Pretoria’s ties with Russia, China and Iran, and its genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
In early 2025, Trump froze US assistance and launched a fast-tracked refugee program for white Afrikaners, citing alleged racial persecution. Washington later expelled South African Ambassador Ebrahim Rasool over remarks accusing the Trump administration of mobilizing a supremacist movement. The US also boycotted the G20 summit hosted by South Africa and imposed tariffs on several major exports.
Pretoria has sought to reset ties. Ramaphosa met Trump in Washington in May 2025, rejecting claims that white farmers were being systematically killed and stressing that violent crime affects all races.
More than a year after Rasool’s expulsion, Pretoria appointed veteran apartheid-era negotiator Roelf Meyer as ambassador to Washington. It has also engaged US officials on trade and critical minerals and sought to retain access to the African Growth and Opportunity Act.
Ramaphosa has said he will respond to Trump’s demands, delivered by US envoy Leo Brent Bozell III. The South African leader has said Pretoria wants constructive ties but “will not be bullied.” His government has also rejected pressure to abandon its non-aligned foreign policy.
In June, after Bozell challenged Pretoria’s ties with China and Iran, the Department of International Relations and Cooperation said South Africa refused to be “drawn into geopolitical contestations” or pressured to take sides.

12 takeaways from von der Leyen’s State of the Union
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:19:12 UTC
20:19:12 KST

Ursula von der Leyen used her State of the Union speech to unveil a raft of proposals aimed at making Europe better prepared for a world of threats — from sweltering summers to hybrid warfare, migrant crises and social media.
What the Commission president chose to talk about in Strasbourg — and, just as importantly, what she left unsaid — will help define the rest of her term and the political legacy she leaves behind.
Here are the 12 biggest takeaways.
Advertisement
1. Canada could become the EU’s first “associate member”
Speaking directly to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was sitting in the Parliament hemicycle, von der Leyen proposed an ambitious, far-reaching new alliance spanning tech, defense, energy, critical minerals, AI, the Arctic and more.
In a message that could have been addressed directly to U.S. President Donald Trump, von der Leyen said: “This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength.”
While it remains to be seen whether EU member countries are on board with so-called associate membership — a model, it should be noted, that does not currently exist — the proposal is a striking signal of how badly Brussels wants to deepen ties with Ottawa.
2. Europe might finally get a security council
The idea of a European security executive body has been floated in various forms for years, but has taken on fresh urgency against the backdrop of Trump undermining the transatlantic security relationship and Russia’s war against Ukraine spilling over into the bloc.
Von der Leyen injected new life into the discussion by calling to create a European Security Council, saying it would bring together the EU and like-minded countries, including the United Kingdom, Canada, Ukraine and Norway (notably, there was no mention of the U.S.) to discuss and manage threats.
Advertisement
It would go hand-in-hand with a new “Emergency Security Protocol,” which EU countries could trigger in response to threats short of an actual attack or invasion. “In other words, a mechanism to flank NATO’s Article 4,” she said.
3. EU wants to work together on AI, but not with the U.S. or China
The Commission president is inviting the major AI labs to Brussels to discuss efforts to “pace the frontier” of AI development.
“AI comes with a balance of possibilities and risks,” she said. “Without addressing these risks, we will never be able to unlock AI’s possibilities.”
A woman uses her laptop at a metro station in Kyiv on Nov. 27, 2025. | Sergei Gapon/AFP via Getty Images
Von der Leyen called for cooperation with the United Kingdom, Canada “and others” on AI but did not mention the U.S. or China — the two countries leading the global AI race.
Von der Leyen said the remaining funds would be used for a new program involving joint projects with Ukrainian defense companies.
Advertisement
The announcement potentially turns an administrative problem — member countries such as Italy not taking up all the cheap loans available to them — into a way to integrate Ukraine's battlefield expertise and defense industry with Europe's.
5. Climate policy is becoming more about survival
Von der Leyen's climate message was notably focused on preparing for the worst rather than new emissions-cutting measures.
She defended the EU's existing climate targets but devoted much of her attention to dealing with the consequences of a hotter Europe, including a forthcoming European Heatwave Plan, a European Water Initiative and a Climate Insurance Alliance.
She said there can be “no repeat of this summer,” which was Europe’s hottest ever, causing its forests to burn and its rivers to dry up.
6. Von der Leyen wants to stop “gold-plating”
The Commission president wants EU countries to agree on a new “pact against gold-plating” — the practice of adding national requirements when implementing EU legislation.
“We are doing our best at the European level to cut red tape. But now I think it is time for the member states to step up,” she said.
Advertisement
While von der Leyen called for the overhaul of the single market to be completed by the end of 2027, she otherwise glossed over simplification and competitiveness in her speech.
7. Admitting defeat on Israel
Von der Leyen acknowledged the “deep suffering” in Gaza and condemned “unchecked settler violence” in the West Bank, while saying Europe must keep the two-state solution alive.
But she also openly acknowledged the EU's inability to agree on some of the measures she promised last year, with member countries unable to agree on action.
Destroyed buildings are seen in Gaza on June 10, 2026. | Ahmed Al Arini/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images
The failure to secure majorities for sanctions against Israeli settlers and ministers, she said, was “painful for many Europeans.”
“When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events,” she added.
8. Surprisingly little to say about finance
For a Commission that has spent much of the past year talking about making Europe a more attractive place to invest and scale up, financial policy was largely absent from the address.
Advertisement
Von der Leyen's main new financial announcement was a Banking Package focused on simplification and tackling fragmentation — a proposal the Commission had already announced in July.
There was little new on the broader ambition to turn Europe into a major investment hub.
“To be very clear, our budget is about our future. And any modern budget needs new own resources,” she said, referring to the term for EU taxes.
The Commission’s proposal to generate over €60 billion through new levies has been met with resistance in national capitals.
10. China got an ominous mention
One of the questions looming over the speech was how hard von der Leyen would go in on China.
Advertisement
On Wednesday, she slammed the EU's trade deficit with Beijing — “one billion a day. It has reached a tipping point,” she said — and highlighted “dangerous dependencies” on China for critical raw materials.
But on trade, she stopped short of calling for any dramatic measures — something she did in her 2023 speech — when she launched an anti-subsidy investigation into electric vehicles. “We will use all the tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship,” she said this year, in an apparent reference to the EU's still-under-construction diversification instrument, but did not go further.
11. Getting tough on migration
In the wake of the Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen called for a European Emergency Response Framework, which would give EU countries in similar scenarios “time-limited and strictly defined flexibility in standard procedures.” Translation: returning migrants faster without worrying about granting asylum.
She also wants the bloc to strengthen Frontex, its border agency, but did not mention raising staff numbers, as she has called for previously.
12. Banning kids from social media
Von der Leyen took aim at social media, which she said was stealing childhoods, and vowed tougher action to protect kids online, including keeping some minors off popular platforms like TikTok and Instagram.
“No social media under the age of 13. No personal account under the age of 15,” she said, adding platforms would also have to introduce “safe design” for under-18s.

Drone shot down in Lithuania was likely aimed at Ukraine, Lithuanian president says
VILNIUS, Sept 16 - The drone shot down in Lithuania by an Italian NATO fighter jet on Tuesday was of a type used by Russia and was most likely targeted at Ukraine, Lithuania's president said on Wednesday.
"It was a Gerbera drone," Gitanas Nauseda told reporters on Wednesday, referring to a cheap plywood long-range aerial drone used by Russia. Gerbera drones are often used as decoys but can also carry explosives.
"It was most likely not a conscious action against Lithuania. It [the drone] was probably targeted towards Ukraine but affected by Ukrainian electronic warfare and deviated off course," he added.
The Lithuanian army is analysing the drone's electronics to determine its targeting, Nauseda said.
The drone is the first suspected Russian drone shot down by the NATO Baltic Air Defence mission, which has patrolled the skies in the region since the Baltic states joined NATO in 2004.
Countries on NATO's eastern flank have seen repeated drone incursions, fuelling fears of the war between Russia and Ukraine spilling over the alliance's borders.
Russia has not commented on the incident.
"The security situation has not changed," Nauseda said. Although there is no large-scale operation against Lithuania or NATO, there could still be "certain incidents, provocation, sabotage acts, including false-flag operations," he added.
Attacks against Russian opposition activists or Ukrainian supporters are also possible, he said.
Polish prosecutors said on Wednesday that a drone spotted in the Baltic sea and later washed up on a Polish beach on Monday was a Russian Gerbera 2 drone according to preliminary findings.
Colonel Bartosz Okoniewski, the deputy district prosecutor for military affairs at the District Prosecutor's Office in Poznan, told state news agency PAP the drone was carrying a warhead which was neutralised on the beach overnight. REUTERS
