Rights abuses persist in Venezuela despite Maduro's removal, UN experts say
GENEVA, Sept 16 - A U.N.-mandated probe said on Wednesday that Venezuela's apparatus of repression remains largely intact despite a reduction in some abuses following President Nicolas Maduro's removal from power earlier this year.
The U.S. has locked Maduro up to face trial on drug-trafficking charges, but left his Socialist Party government largely intact, to the disappointment of Venezuela's opposition which says it was robbed of a 2024 vote and should be in power.
In a report to the U.N. Human Rights Council, the independent fact-finding mission said Maduro's capture in January led to a fall in long-term politically motivated detentions and related abuses, but did not amount to a fundamental break with years of repression.
"The measures of political liberalization adopted since that date remain partial, conditional and reversible at best," the mission said, adding a departure from the harshest forms of repression may not be a "genuine and sustainable departure".
Venezuela's mission to the U.N. in Geneva did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
The report, covering the period from September last year to July, described the U.S. intervention as a breach of international law.
Maduro's rule had been widely challenged by the opposition and numerous Western governments, including over the disputed 2024 presidential election.
SOME ADVANCES
The report noted that interim President Delcy Rodriguez – a Maduro ally – introduced measures including prisoner releases, an amnesty law and the closure of El Helicoide, a detention facility long associated with arbitrary detention and torture.
It also said that civil society groups and opposition figures had gained greater latitude to organize and criticize authorities.
However, the independent U.N. experts said senior officials linked to past repression remained in key positions and security agencies, intelligence services and laws used to restrict dissent had not undergone meaningful reform.
The mission said hundreds of people, including real or perceived opponents of the government, remained arbitrarily detained for political reasons and continued to face harsh prison conditions, torture and ill-treatment.
It documented allegations of beatings, electric shocks, prolonged isolation and other abuses at the El Rodeo I and Fuerte Guaicaipuro maximum-security prisons.
The report also found extensive links between the state and armed civilian groups known as "colectivos," saying they had played a key role in intimidating perceived opponents with political, financial and logistical backing from state institutions.
The mission said authorities had failed to advance accountability for past abuses and criticised Venezuela's decision to withdraw from the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court.
It urged the government to release all political detainees, investigate alleged crimes against humanity, reform security institutions and dismantle armed civilian groups involved in rights violations. REUTERS

Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi has disrupted Russia’s plan to encircle Ukraine’s heavily fortified “Fortress Belt” in Donetsk Oblast, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed, adding that Ukrainian forces have likely made additional gains beyond those publicly disclosed by Kyiv.
The assessment comes a day after Ukraine’s Third Army Corps publicly confirmed that it is conducting a counteroffensive against Russian forces north and northwest of Lyman. ISW said the Ukrainian gains have rendered Russia's plan to encircle the Fortress Belt from the north and south unfeasible.
Third Army Corps commander Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi said on 15 September that Ukrainian forces had cleared Russian infiltrators from several settlements and liberated Serednie. The corps said its forces had cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltrators and de-occupied another 10 square kilometers during the first phase of the operation.
Biletskyi said the operation, dubbed “Vivaldi,” was conducted under information silence and warned that the first phase was only one of four planned “seasons.”
Ukraine’s gains appear larger than initially disclosed
ISW assessed that Ukrainian forces have likely made additional gains beyond those announced by Biletskyi, with Russian sources beginning to acknowledge the deterioration of their position in the area.
In particular, Russian forces have been shelling Ukrainian positions in Kolodyazi, northeast of Lyman, according to geolocated footage. A prominent Russian milblogger also acknowledged that Russian forces were trying to push Ukrainian troops out of Kolodyazi – what ISW described as a “coy acknowledgement” that Ukrainian forces have likely liberated the settlement.
Russian sources have continued to report worsening conditions for Russian forces both north and south of Kolodyazi.
ISW also corroborated the Third Army Corps’ account of growing Russian logistical problems, noting that Ukrainian strikes have disrupted supplies for Russian forces in the Borova and Lyman directions. The corps said the pressure was severe enough that Russia moved some logistics and support elements across the state border into Russia’s Voronezh Oblast.
“Only the first season” – Ukraine unveils secret counteroffensive in a region Russia has been trying to seize for 12 years
Vivaldi disrupts Russia’s plan for the Fortress Belt
The operation’s broader significance lies in its effect on Russia’s campaign in Donetsk.
Russia has made capturing the remaining Ukrainian-held parts of Donetsk Oblast a central military objective, with its forces seeking to advance toward the heavily fortified cities of the Donetsk “Fortress Belt” from several directions.
The Russian military had also sought to create a northern route around the Fortress Belt through the Lyman area. ISW now assesses that Ukraine’s gains north of Lyman have made that plan unfeasible.
The institute said the Ukrainian counteroffensive will delay Russia’s planned offensive toward Sloviansk, the major objective Moscow had been expected to pursue after capturing Lyman.
Russian sources acknowledge setbacks
According to ISW, a prominent Kremlin-affiliated Russian milblogger similarly acknowledged that Ukraine’s gains will delay the Russian offensive toward Sloviansk and warned that the northern flank of Russian forces operating southeast of Lyman and east of Kramatorsk is now vulnerable to Ukrainian counterattacks and interdiction.
The Russian milblogger also claimed that Russian forces had lost positions south of Lyman and were struggling to recapture positions inside the city itself.
Russian sources have blamed the setbacks on the military’s culture of producing “beautiful reports” – exaggerated accounts of battlefield advances that can distort higher-level operational planning.
Another prominent milblogger reportedly claimed that some Russian commanders were attempting to conceal losses by rapidly assembling assault groups from inadequately trained personnel to retake lost positions.
Russia still presses its offensive elsewhere
Despite the setbacks around Lyman, ISW said Russian forces continue prioritizing frontal attacks against the Fortress Belt from the south and efforts to encircle it from the southwest, rather than advancing toward the cities from the east.
The institute said Russia may still be adjusting to the loss of the Lyman salient and the initiative in the area. It also assessed that Russian forces could seek to cut Ukrainian ground lines of communication to the Fortress Belt from the west.
For Ukraine, meanwhile, the counteroffensive is also undermining Russia’s ability to present advances in Donetsk as evidence of battlefield momentum.
And the full extent of Vivaldi remains unknown.
Biletskyi said the 85 square kilometers publicly disclosed by the corps represented only the first “season” of the operation, invoking Vivaldi’s Four Seasons.
“Vivaldi, as is known, has four seasons. And this is only the first one,” Biletskyi said on 15 September.

MOSCOW, September 16. /TASS/. Russia records about 20-30 bear attacks on people each year, while the situation in 2026 is not abnormal, with the country’s brown bear population rising from 182,000 to 308,000 over the past 15 years, the Russian Natural Resources Ministry's press service told TASS on Wednesday.
Brown bears have been attacking people in several parts of Russia in recent weeks. Five people have died in bear attacks in the Siberian Federal District over the past month alone. One of the most high-profile incidents occurred in the Altai Mountains, where a bear dragged a female tourist out of her tent and killed her. In recent years, Russia has recorded about 20-30 bear attacks annually, while the only unusual spike occurred in 2014, when there were 166 cases," the ministry's press service said.
The ministry stressed that the rapid spread of videos and information through social media and the internet contributes to the perception of such incidents occurring on a mass scale.
At the same time, Russia's brown bear population has grown considerably over the past 15 years, from 182,000 to 308,000, Tatyana Aramileva, director of the Natural Resources Ministry's department for state policy and regulation in wildlife protection, use and hunting, said at a TASS news conference on Wednesday.
"Over the past 15 years, the brown bear population in Russia has increased from 182,000 to 308,000," Aramileva said.

Duterte makes first appearance before ICC judges
September 16, 2026
Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines, made his first in-person appearance before judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) at a pretrial hearing on Wednesday.
The 81-year-old faces charges of crimes against humanity in connection with hundreds of murders committed during his "war on drugs" while in office.
Duterte, who served as president from 2016 to 2022, denies the allegations.
He has missed a series of hearings since he was arrested in March 2025 and has previously appeared in court via videolink.
Duterte's legal team have said he suffers from poor health, but the court's judges ruled in January that he was fit enough to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court.
The ex-president "suffers from a significant memory impairment that prevents him from retaining recent information and reliably accessing his memories," his lawyers said.
The prosecution, meanwhile, argued Duterte was "capable of meaningfully exercising his procedural and fair trial rights, and that he is fit for trial."
What is Duterte accused of?
Rodrigo Duterte is accused of crimes against humanity committed between 2011 and 2019, first when he was the mayor of the southern city of Davao and then as Philippine president.
Prosecutors say he is responsible for a systematic campaign that led to the deaths of at least 30,000 people, many of them during "anti-drug" raids.
Duterte's trial is scheduled for November this year.
During Wednesday's pretrial hearing, judges were to hear arguments about his health and decide whether he is mentally fit to stand trial.

Italy’s new Teseo missile completes 20-minute test flight
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:05:56 BST
20:05:56 KST

MBDA has completed a new validation firing of the TESEO MK2/E anti-ship missile for the Italian Navy, with the weapon undertaking an approximately 20-minute controlled cruise flight as the programme moves towards first deliveries in 2028, according to the company.
The firing was conducted as part of the multi-year development and qualification programme for the new missile, which is intended to replace and substantially expand the capabilities of earlier members of the TESEO family, known internationally as OTOMAT.
MBDA said the latest trial successfully validated the missile’s range and the overall design of the system, following an earlier firing in 2024 which focused on new missile components and aerodynamics.
The company said: “The test successfully validated the missile’s range, during an approximately 20-minute piloted cruise flight of the TESEO MK2/E.”
It added: “The trial validates the overall design of this new generation anti-ship system and paves the way for a swift conclusion of the development phase.”
The programme is now expected to move towards production within the timetable agreed with the Italian Navy, with MBDA targeting a first delivery in 2028.
Development of TESEO MK2/E began under a 2021 contract with Italy’s National Directorate of Naval Armaments covering development, integration and qualification. A separate production contract followed in 2025.
The missile is being developed for a broad range of Italian Navy surface combatants, including the PPA multi-purpose combat ships, future DDX destroyers, FREMM frigates and Horizon-class destroyers.
MBDA also said TESEO MK2/E will be integrated aboard the future FREMM EVO frigates and could be adapted for international customers.
The new missile is intended to do more than engage ships. Its guidance and mission systems are designed to support attacks against both maritime and land targets at greater ranges than previous TESEO variants. Among the major changes is a new Active Electronically Scanned Antenna radio-frequency seeker, intended to improve target detection and engagement performance in contested environments.
TESEO MK2/E also introduces shorter reaction times and more advanced mission planning, together with a satellite data link allowing the missile to be controlled and updated while in flight. That combination gives operators the ability to modify aspects of an engagement after launch rather than relying entirely on a pre-programmed flight profile. MBDA said the extended reach of the weapon should also allow launching ships to remain further away from defended targets, increasing stand-off distance for their crews.
Renzo Tosini, Executive Vice President Sales & Business Development and Managing Director of MBDA Italia, said: “I am extremely proud of this result, which will guarantee a unique sovereign capability to Italy and the Italian Navy and will pave the way for further international success for MBDA, thanks to the system’s cutting-edge anti-ship performances.”
He added: “The success of this firing once again demonstrates that working in total synergy with the customer is fundamental to achieving even more ambitious results.”

Europe strengthens its defense – Ursula von der Leyen explained what will change

Europe strengthens its defense – Ursula von der Leyen explained what will change
Kyiv • UNN
The EU is preparing its own "Article 4" for a rapid response to threats and is strengthening its defense. One of the key projects is the Freyja anti-ballistic system, developed jointly with Ukraine. Until it is fully operational, Europe plans to strengthen Ukraine’s air defense and support its energy sector.
The European Union is preparing its own emergency response mechanism for hybrid threats — a kind of European "Article 4." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said this during her annual address to the European Parliament, UNN writes.
Europe needs its own action plan in response to hybrid threats. We urgently need consensus on how to respond to certain incidents — those that are not yet armed aggression but already clearly threaten our national security. In other words, we need a mechanism that would complement Article 4 of NATO. And I believe the time has come for our own European "Article 4" — an emergency security response protocol. If it is activated by one member state, all member states must convene to coordinate a European response, deter further escalation and minimize its consequences
Ursula von der Leyen sees the creation of a European Security Council and a European Strategic Enablers Instrument as the next step. These would be cooperation formats that would allow European leaders to keep the continent's security under control and involve Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Canada and Norway, among others.
The war in Ukraine has shown us the importance of strategic enablers. These are critically important means of supporting and strengthening combat capabilities, without which no reliable defense is possible. From air and missile defense to strategic transport and aerial refueling, from space to cyberspace. These systems are vital, and we need more such capabilities. Only together does Europe have the necessary scale to create them. That is why I can announce a new European Strategic Enablers Instrument, which, of course, will be fully coordinated with NATO. After all, only a strong and credible European defense posture will guarantee our security. And there can be no doubt about this: Europe will defend every square meter of its territory
Freyja — an integral part of European security
The President of the European Commission said that Europe needs to build up its own air and missile defense capabilities and reduce its dependence on a single supplier. One practical solution will be the Freyja project jointly developed with Ukraine.
As of now, companies from 10 countries are working on it, while Fire Point, Kongsberg, Weibel, Saab, Diehl Defence, Hensoldt, Thales, Safran, Sener and Leonardo, among others, have joined its practical implementation.
Ukraine is responsible for a key part of the system — the interceptor missile and the launch vehicle. The partners are integrating radars, sensors, control systems and other components.
Ukraine is also setting the pace of implementation. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has already set a specific deadline: to obtain the first system by the end of December 2026, test its operation and then move on to scaling up production.
While Freyja is still at the development stage and Russia continues to attack Ukraine's civilian population every day, the EU plans to simultaneously strengthen its protection using the tools already available.

Scientists “truly astonished” by discovery that challenges Earth’s origin story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:03:10 UTC
20:03:10 KST

Scientists “truly astonished” by discovery that challenges Earth’s origin story
- Date:
- September 16, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- A new study suggests Earth formed almost entirely from material in the inner Solar System, challenging the idea that water-rich material from beyond Jupiter played a major role. If correct, Earth’s water may have been present much closer to the young Sun than scientists previously thought.
- Share:
Scientists have long debated where the raw material that formed Earth originally came from. Although our planet sits in the inner Solar System, many researchers have proposed that 6-40 percent of its building material arrived from the outer Solar System, beyond Jupiter.
That idea has been especially important for explaining how Earth acquired volatile substances such as water. If those materials came from farther out, then matter must have moved between the outer and inner regions of the Solar System while Earth was forming.
New research now challenges that picture.
"We were truly astonished"
Planetary scientists Paolo Sossi and Dan Bower of ETH Zurich compared existing measurements of isotope ratios from a wide range of meteorites, including samples associated with Mars and the asteroid Vesta, with the isotopic composition of Earth.
Isotopes are sibling atoms of the same element (same number of protons) that have a different mass (different number of neutrons).
Using a new approach to analyze those data, the researchers reached a striking conclusion. Their results indicate that the material that formed Earth came entirely from the inner Solar System.
Material from the outer Solar System appears to account for less than two percent of Earth's total mass, and possibly none at all. The study was published in Nature Astronomy.
"Our calculations make it clear: the building material of the Earth originates from a single material reservoir," says Sossi. His colleague Bower adds: "We were truly astonished to find that the Earth is composed entirely of material from the inner Solar System distinct from any combination of existing meteorites."
The ETH Zurich team based its analysis on existing measurements from ten different isotope systems found in meteorites. Earlier studies typically focused on only two isotope systems.
"Our studies are actually data science experiments," says Sossi. "We carried out statistical calculations that are rarely used in geochemistry, even though they are a powerful tool."
Meteorite Isotopes Reveal Earth's Origins
Scientists have used isotopes in meteorites for decades to trace where celestial objects formed, including which region of the Solar System they came from. For many years, however, oxygen isotopes were the main tool available for identifying that origin.
That changed in the early 2010s, when an American researcher showed that isotopes of other elements, including chromium and titanium, could also reveal where meteorites formed.
This discovery allowed scientists to divide meteorites into two broad groups. Non-carbonaceous meteorites formed exclusively in the inner Solar System. Carbonaceous meteorites contain more water and carbon and originated in the outer Solar System.
According to the new analysis, Earth is made entirely from non-carbonaceous material. The researchers found no evidence for the previously proposed exchange of material between the inner and outer Solar System reservoirs.
That suggests Earth grew in a relatively stable environment, gradually incorporating smaller nearby planetary bodies as it developed. It also means that most volatile substances, including water, must already have existed in the inner Solar System.
Jupiter May Have Divided the Solar System
Why did the young Solar System end up with two distinct reservoirs of material?
Scientists think Jupiter played a major role. As the gas giant grew rapidly, its enormous gravity carved a gap in the protoplanetary disc surrounding the young Sun. These discs are ring-shaped and consist of gas and dust; they are the birthplace of planets.
Jupiter appears to have acted as a barrier, limiting the movement of material from the outer Solar System into the inner region. Until now, however, scientists did not know how effective that barrier really was.
The new analysis suggests that very little material from beyond Jupiter ever reached the region where Earth formed.
"Our calculations are very robust and rely solely on the data itself, not on physical assumptions, as these are not yet fully understood," Bower emphasizes.
The results also show that Earth's material composition resembles that of Mars and Vesta.
Mercury and Venus May Share the Same Pattern
The researchers suspect that Mercury and Venus could fit the same pattern as Earth, Mars, and Vesta.
"Based on our analysis, we can theoretically predict the composition of these two planets," says Paolo Sossi.
For now, however, that prediction cannot be directly tested. Scientists do not currently have rock samples from Mercury or Venus, the two planets closest to the Sun, that could be analyzed in the same way.
A New Mystery About Earth's Water
"Our results shed new light on the formation history of our Earth and the other rocky planets," says Sossi.
The findings also raise a major new question. If Earth did not receive large amounts of water-rich material from the outer Solar System, scientists must explain how enough water could have existed in the hot inner Solar System to eventually produce Earth's oceans.
Sossi and his team plan to investigate that question next. They also want to determine whether similar processes could occur in planetary systems around other stars.
"Until then, however, Dan and I will have to engage in many heated debates about the material composition of Earth and its neighboring planets, because the scientific discourse over the building blocks of Earth is far from over, despite the new findings," says Sossi.
Story Source:
Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Paolo A. Sossi, Dan J. Bower. Homogeneous accretion of the Earth in the inner Solar System. Nature Astronomy, 2026; 10 (7): 972 DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02824-7

World Bank names Nobel laureate Michael Kremer as next chief economist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16

World Bank names Nobel laureate Michael Kremer as next chief economist
WASHINGTON, Sept 16 - The World Bank on Wednesday named Nobel laureate and University of Chicago professor Michael Kremer as its next chief economist, succeeding Indermit Gill, who retired last month.
Kremer, 61, won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences in 2019 jointly with Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty. He previously taught economics at Harvard University.
He starts his new role on October 1, shortly before the annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok, Thailand.
Kremer is known for using rigorous research to develop innovative solutions to real-world problems, often setting up programs that have helped small farmers and given millions of people access to vaccines and school health programs.
"Michael has spent his career not just identifying what works in development, but proving it at scale — and that is exactly the kind of thinking we need,” World Bank President Ajay Banga said in a statement.
"He joins us at a time when the world needs bold solutions to its most urgent development challenges, including creating jobs that meet the aspirations of more than 1.2 billion young people reaching working age in the coming decade."
Kremer joins the bank as developing countries grapple with rising interest rates and higher energy prices in the wake of the U.S. war against Iran. Those challenges come on top of a 23% drop in official development assistance in 2025, the sharpest on record, with the U.S. responsible for the lion's share.
He is the first economist to come to the bank with a Nobel in hand. Others, including Joseph Stiglitz and Paul Romer, received the honor after their tenure as chief economist.
Kremer currently serves the director of the Development Innovation Lab at the University of Chicago, where his research has been focused on innovation in education, health, water, finance, and agriculture in developing countries.
“The World Bank Group has tremendous research capacity to develop and test innovative solutions to development problems—and the operational reach to scale them up and improve people's lives,” Kremer said in a statement.
The world faced enormous challenges, but new technologies offered opportunities to boost growth, he said.
In 2024, Kremer gave a keynote speech at a World Bank event titled "The Great Incoherence: Growth and Human Development in an Era of Stagnation."
In that speech, he called for reforms to help countries meet ambitious development goals, including by funding innovative pilot projects and incentivizing research on new technologies, themes stressed by Banga since he took office in 2023.
Kremer is the husband of Rachel Glennerster, a British economist who served work for the UK government and the International Monetary Fund before becoming president of the Center for Global Development in Washington in September 2024.
Both joined Giving What We Can, a nonprofit group whose 10,000-plus members pledge to give 10% of their income to effective charities, when it was first launched in 2009.
In 2010, he co-founded Development Innovation Ventures, a fund administered by the U.S. Agency for International Development, which was shut down by U.S. President Donald Trump shortly after he returned to the White House last year.
He and Glennerster also pioneered the use of Advance Market Commitments, binding contracts made by donors to encourage pharmaceutical companies to research, develop and produce drugs for low-income countries, aiding development of a vaccine against the main cause of pneumonia globally.
Kremer's research on de-worming school children showed a sharp drop in absenteeism, prompting governments in Africa and South Asia to provide 2 billion treatments since 2014. He has also worked on AI-based agricultural weather forecasting, and co-founded Precision Development, which uses digital technology to improve productivity and incomes for smallholder farmers.
Winner of a MacArthur "genius grant" in 1997, Kremer is a member of the National Academy of Sciences and a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.
In the early 2000s, he also proposed a framework aimed at preventing dictators from looting their countries and saddling future citizens with illegitimate or "odious" debt. REUTERS

EU Proposes Creating European Security Council with Ukraine as a Member
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:02:40 UTC
20:02:40 KST

The European Commission has proposed creating a European Security Council — a new format for coordinating the actions of European states and partners in response to security threats.
Ursula von der Leyen, the President of the European Commission, stated this during her annual address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.
In addition to EU member states, the new format is expected to involve Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Norway, Canada, and other partners.
“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook. We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents,” von der Leyen stated.
At the same time, the European Commission proposes establishing an Emergency Security Protocol similar to Article 4 of the North Atlantic Treaty. If activated, an EU member state would promptly hold consultations and coordinate a joint response to the threat.
The framework would primarily address hybrid incidents, including acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, drone incursions, and other actions that do not necessarily rise to the level of direct armed aggression.
The initiative comes amid discussions in Europe about strengthening its own defense capabilities and creating security mechanisms that would complement existing NATO structures.
In March 2025, the European Union published its White Paper for European Defence, which identified Russia as a fundamental threat and set out a strategic development plan to strengthen the defense capabilities of the EU and Ukraine over the next five years.
Individual EU member states had previously supported the idea of creating a European Security Council. In January, Andrius Kubilius, European Commissioner for Defence and Space, called for the creation of a 100,000-strong European Union army for the bloc’s own defense and to replace U.S. troops in Europe if necessary.
European officials have also considered the Coalition of the Willing as a potential foundation for a new military alliance without U.S. participation, with Ukraine as a potential member.
On February 14, Ursula von der Leyen said that the EU should implement Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union on mutual defence.
In April, during an address to participants of the meeting of the heads of state and government of the European Union in Cyprus, Volodymyr Zelensky proposed that Europe create a comprehensive defense system capable of protecting its borders and infrastructure and countering drone threats.

Hackers Breach Russia’s ‘Invulnerable’ Voting System Ahead of State Duma Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:02:12 UTC
20:02:12 KST

At a meeting of Russia’s Central Election Commission (CEC), its head, Ella Pamfilova, provided an update on the GAS Vybory State Automated Election System (GAS Elections 2.0), which was unveiled earlier this year in preparation for the upcoming elections to Russia’s State Duma.
In August, Pamfilova claimed the system was “impossible to hack.” At the CEC meeting, however, she and Russia’s Deputy Minister of Digital Development, Oleg Kachanov, acknowledged that the platform had faced an unprecedented number of cyberattacks since its launch. They nevertheless insisted that it remained “maximally secure” and said its digital defenses would be reinforced by physical security measures protecting both the system’s infrastructure and polling stations.
Within hours of Pamfilova’s assurances, the anonymous hacker group CikLeak announced it had breached the CEC’s GAS Elections 2.0 infrastructure, as well as that of its contractor Tsifrotekh, a subsidiary of Rostelecom.
The hack included reams of internal company documents, source code, meeting recordings, passwords, and employee correspondence.
In its internet announcement, which was also released to media outlets including the independent Important Stories outlet, CikLeak was at pains to point out that its intention had not been to disrupt or interfere with the voting process itself, but to highlight how easily the system would allow the authorities to falsify the election results.
Oleshky Starving: The Human Cost of Territorial Concessions
The hackers said they wanted to send a message to Russian citizens encouraging them to vote in person. According to them, the new CEC remote electronic voting system is completely opaque and vulnerable to manipulation, allowing authorities to falsify election results.
The independent Russian outlet Important Stories said it had reviewed the trove of documents provided by CikLeak and verified their authenticity. The publication added that it would release its own assessment of the materials and their significance. They also contacted the director of Tsifrotekh, Alexey Gusev, for a comment, but he simply replied: “This is the first time I’ve heard of it.”
The GAS Elections 2.0 system, introduced at the beginning of 2026, replaced the older version that had been running since the late 1990s. Elections to the ninth convocation of the State Duma this month will be the first federal-level vote conducted using the new system.
Addressing the CEC meeting, Pamfilova described Russia’s new electoral system as a world leader in technological sophistication. According to her, the platform would allow the commission to uphold its “fundamental standards,” including remote electronic voting and video surveillance, throughout the upcoming State Duma elections.

Swiss parliament decides to abolish statute of limitations for murder
In Switzerland, murder will soon be one of the offences for which there is no statute of limitations. The House of Representatives and the Senate have reached agreement on this issue after years of debate. The bill still has to go to a final vote in the Federal Assembly.
On Wednesday, a minority within the Legal Affairs Committee prevailed in the Senate, proposing that, on this issue, the earlier decisions of the Senate and the House of Representatives should be upheld. Both chambers had already voted in favour of removing the statute of limitations for murder in March 2025 and March 2026 respectively.
The decision stems from a cantonal initiative submitted by the Canton of St Gallen as far back as 2019. The canton argued that advances in DNA analysis had provided investigators with technical capabilities that would allow evidence to be gathered even a long time after the offence had been committed.

Datacenter rush will create ‘tsunami’ of discarded electronics, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:00:19 UTC
20:00:19 KST

The ongoing campaign to build thousands of massive datacenters for AI will create a “tsunami” of discarded electronics, putting the world on a course to triple its annual generation of toxic e-waste in the next 25 years, a new report projects.
The electronic trash AI generates in the next 25 years could fill enough shipping containers to encircle the globe six times, it said. Yet, says the report by the non-profit environmental group Basel Action Network (BAN), there is no plan to deal with that waste – which typically contains toxins like lead, mercury, cadmium and forever chemicals, as well as valuable metals that are challenging to reclaim.
“Already electronic waste is the fastest-growing waste stream on the planet and only one-fifth is properly managed,” said Jim Puckett, co-founder of BAN, which works to see that toxic waste doesn’t end up getting dumped on the world’s poorer communities.
Experts concur. “We’re doing a terrible job of handling e-waste in the US,” said Vince Beiser, author of the book Power Metal, which details the global problems of trying to reclaim valuable metals inside electronic goods. “Some of it gets dumped overseas. Most of it just gets dumped in landfills, which is a problem because it can leach all kinds of nasty things into the water, into the soil.”
There are 4,871 new datacenters in the construction pipeline in the US, the report said, adding that, while not all are clearly designated for use by AI, many will be.
It calculated the volumes of e-waste related to computer servers used for AI, and to “the thousands of tonnes of copper, steel, concrete” for cooling, power distribution, networking and energy storage equipment needed to operate inside datacenters.
To estimate the total, the report approximated the amount of computing power analysts project will be built – totalling roughly 100 gigawatts of new capacity worldwide by 2030 alone and growing beyond that. It then analyzed how much equipment would be needed by weight – including racks of computer servers weighing 1,360kgs each, switches that weigh up to 30kgs, and hundreds of kilograms of copper cable connecting each rack.
Such equipment won’t be designed for repair and reuse, the report projects, and would need to be completely replaced every two to five years.
On top of this, it assumed that AI developments will force the rapid replacement of consumer computers, phones, and telecommunications equipment owing to the computing requirements of the new systems.
By taking this wide view of all the various types of e-waste that will be created, the BAN report projects that AI-driven equipment retirement will generate up to 13m metric tonnes per year by 2030 – a far higher estimate than a handful of previous studies.
AI datacenter construction has already created a groundswell of bipartisan opposition around the US for the huge amount of space and energy it requires, but the report comes when focus is turning to the long-term pollution AI could create.
A group of environmental and health experts last week called for the federal government to issue a pledge to protect citizens’ health from the repercussions of AI buildout. It cited estimates that the air pollution from the enormous amount of electricity generation needed for datacenters could result in hundreds of thousands of new asthma cases and as many as 1,300 premature deaths per year in the US alone.
The Trump administration has sought to weaken environmental safeguards that would normally govern such a massive technological buildout.
A 2025 report by McKinsey & Company estimates that, in order to achieve the tech industry’s planned rollout of artificial intelligence, nearly $7tn in capital outlays will be needed worldwide in the next five years to build datacenters running millions of computer servers 24 hours a day.
BAN’s white paper notes that this unprecedented spending “is roughly the cost of ending world hunger for the next 75 years – being spent in just five”.
“We all find ourselves unwitting participants in the AI horserace,” said the report, “as IT users everywhere find themselves using AI whether they would like to or not, and yet almost always, without being aware of the greater consequences of doing so.”

====================================================================================================

Allowing AI firms to collude to ‘pace the frontier’ is a dangerous proposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:00:18 UTC
20:00:18 KST

Anthropic’s Dario Amodei is not the first corporate CEO to suggest that excessive competition is driving the world to some socially undesirable outcome.
The safety breach disclosed by OpenAI after a swarm of its agents coordinated to breach their supposedly secure sandbox, get on the Internet and hack AI platform Hugging Face, warrants urgent action. It demonstrated the ease with which the technology can evade human control and gave concrete form to the existential fears about what it could do to humanity if not securely leashed.
The end of the world may well be nigh, as some in the AI industry have warned. These are truly scary times. But Amodei’s call for the leading artificial intelligence labs to coordinate to slow the breakneck pace of AI development, agree on safety standards and “pace the frontier”, (a call quickly endorsed by Open AI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google Deep Mind’s Demis Hassabis) is just a hi-tech version of an old proposition by corporate America – to get a pass from antitrust laws designed to protect the American economy from colluding businesses.
It is a dangerous proposition. Freeing the tech bros from antitrust constraints supposedly to allow them to get together and fix AI’s dangerous flaws, disenfranchises the everyday Americans who are most at risk from the thing, further empowering the very labs that, in their pursuit for wealth, greatness and who knows what other fantastical objectives, so casually blew past danger thresholds on many dimensions, bringing the existential threats into being.
Amodei et al’s argument, at heart, is that their businesses are trapped in a prisoner’s dilemma. If they unilaterally slow their fevered pursuit of artificial super-intelligence to make it safer, their rivals – less concerned about existential risks, of course – will get there first, with potentially devastating consequences for humankind, let alone the bottom line of the lab that took its foot off the pedal.
“Slowing down seems sensible,” said Jean Tirole, the Nobel prize-winning economist at the Toulouse School of Economics. “But that assumes coordinated slowing-down is feasible and sustainable. What happens when OpenAI, Anthropic or Grok conclude that US holdouts – or Chinese labs – are catching up? Will they resume immediately, perhaps covertly?”
As Bill Gates has written, “if someone had a credible plan for slowing down AI advances globally, I would likely support it. However, I don’t think that’s going to happen. The geopolitical and economic incentives are pushing too hard to go full speed ahead.” In this light, it might seem like a great idea for the government to encourage a friendly agreement for everybody to slow down. It is not.
The argument that excessive competition is driving a race to the bottom, is probably as old as capitalism, deployed to explain everything from environmental degradation to child labor. But it does not justify giving businesses a right to collude as they see fit. It is a call to craft government regulations to prevent businesses from competing using socially harmful tools.
Moreover, the case that excessive competition is encouraging reckless behavior is dubious. The AI labs are engaged in a winner-takes-all race, one that is extraordinarily expensive to keep going. That’s where the recklessness comes from
Amodei may be an unimpeachable guy. His call to slow the pace of AI development, bring external evaluators into the lab and increase the transparency of his operations suggests sincere concern over the risks. The drop in the price of leading tech stocks following the publication of his propositions suggests that he is willing to take a financial hit in the service of improved safety.
But the investors Amodei hopes will eagerly snap up shares in Anthropic’s IPO later this year may not be so altruistic. Tremors in capital markets suggest that raising the money to finance the trillion-dollar AI investment race is going to get tougher, discouraging strategies that might curb the leading labs’ edge over rivals. Given the incentives, granting the AI leaders a free hand to collude and self-regulate would be foolhardy.
Eric Posner, an antitrust expert at the University of Chicago Law School, said, we “shouldn’t trust companies in general about their motivations”. There is no reason to believe the AI labs, left to their own devices, would necessarily produce good, socially acceptable outcomes. Like any company, they will be calculating trade-offs, weighing risks against profits. And as Posner observed, “they don’t use the same weights as the public”.
So, how to regulate? Nothing is going to happen on this front while Trump is in office. Even after he is gone it will be tough to craft effective regulation to deal with the threats from AI without stunting innovation. There are questions about what rules to deploy, how they are enforced, and who they should apply to. And the peril of unilateral action is real. What if Beijing declines to participate? What are the risks of Chinese AI companies plowing ahead when American labs slow down? But if we could regulate nuclear power, we can probably regulate AI.
Moreover, there are viable ideas that might help even in the absence of government regulation and that don’t require stifling competition. There are proposals to tweak intellectual rights to encourage innovations that improve the safety of AI systems. Inventors of safety innovations would be rewarded by allowing them to release new AI models before their competitors. But the safety enhancements would be made immediately available to all firms.
On the stick side of the ledger, a legal liability regime could be designed to change the incentives of AI developers by punishing firms that gain from the design and deployment of an AI tool that caused harm, even if the harm was unintentional. For instance, the Hugging Face attack might have been prevented if OpenAI’s models had not been inadvertently rewarded for misbehaving during training. The fact that Amodei’s proposal does not mention legal liability suggests that AI leaders’ concern for safety does not override concern for the bottom line.
In any event, cementing in place the dominance of the frontier labs, protecting their rents and endorsing their heretofore gung-ho strategies, is not pro-safety. On the contrary, slowing down the leaders to let the laggards catch up is likely to make the AI ecosystem a safer place by inviting in desirable innovation and promoting competition along the safety dimension.
There is no fundamental conflict between safety and competition. Masters of AI who want to make this case should be viewed with skepticism.

The Politicization of ‘DEI’ Bike Lanes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

What do President Donald Trump and Pastor A.D. Cunningham of the United House of Prayer for All People (a predominantly Black church in Washington, DC) have in common? Neither seems to want to look out their window and see a bike lane.
The truth is that the ranks of anti-bike lane Americans are diverse, probably even more so than its advocates. When I first heard that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy pledged to rescind funding for “DEI bike lanes,” I immediately thought of the book Bike Lanes are White Lanes. The argument of the book is self-evident. Bike advocacy has long been largely the domain of white advocates pushing for bike infrastructure in largely white neighborhoods. To some, bike lanes are a symbol—and even a creator—of gentrification.
So, which is it? Are bike lanes white lanes or DEI lanes? And when did they become so controversial? Over the past century or so, bike lanes have come to represent more than just painted pavement.
Historically, the bicycle has been many things to many people: a toy for tots, a piece of exercise equipment, a tool for commuting, a way to explore a rugged mountain, a delivery vehicle, a device on which to do tricks and to trick out. Bicycling became truly popular in the 1890s, with many hoping it would become the great equalizer, a democratizing force that would open new spaces to women and afford everyone mobility. As the 1900 U.S. census declared: “It is safe to say that few articles ever used by man have created so great a revolution in social condition as the bicycle.”
Americans loved the bicycle—and loved to hate the bicycle. Many cyclists were white and so were most anti-cyclists. Perhaps the most common complaint was that bicycles were reckless. Cyclists, pejoratively called “scorchers,” spooked horses and endangered pedestrians, cried critics.
One solution was to divide traffic with separate bike lanes. Another idea was to create separate bicycle paths. The most vocal opponents were groups of cyclists. Serious cyclists wanted to be taken seriously. They thought (erroneously) the only way to do so was to have states recognize the bicycle as a vehicle and, accordingly, give it the same right to the road as every other vehicle. As they saw it, the problem was the notion that the bicycle was a plaything.
Earlier in his life, Trump actually endorsed the bicycle, or at least a bicycle race. The Tour de Trump was an American 10-day bicycle race, a mini-version of the Tour de France. It was 1989. Professional bike racing was then (and is still) largely the domain of white men.
Sadly, so is biking in general. Women account for only about 30% of all bicycle trips. Bikeshare programs, including DC’s Capital Bikeshare, skew white, male, and affluent, just like America’s first cyclists. When it comes to commuting, about .6% of white people commute to work by way of bicycle. That’s compared to .3% for the Black population.
Some of the disparities are cultural in the making—and don’t make a ton of sense. On the streets, men disproportionately ride, meaning cycling is masculine, right? Not really. Packs of cyclists are derisively referred to as “MAMILS,” as in Middle-Aged Men in Lycra. Meanwhile, step into a spin class, and you may likely see only women clipping in. Context, it turns out, is everything.
More broadly, exercise has become a luxury good. It was the Yuppies who made marathoning and high-end road bicycles so popular. Today, people are just as likely to commute by bicycle in households that have more than $200,000 in income as they are in households that bring in between $50,000 and $75,000. Many of the people commuting by bike are choosing to do so. They have alternatives.
Not everyone is so lucky. Transportation injustice is real. Too often, urban renewal projects destroy neighborhoods of color for the sake of white commuters’ convenience. We should be conscious of these historic injustices. But working to undo wrong and encouraging groups of people who don’t currently bike to do so don’t need to be mutually exclusive. And it shouldn’t be controversial.
The best way to get more cyclists is with more and smarter bike infrastructure. The primary reason people—of all types—say they don’t bike is because they feel unsafe. Bike lanes, especially protected bike lanes that are physically separated, really do work. Whether rich or poor, white or Black, hardly anyone currently bikes to work. Compared to similarly wealthy countries, it is an embarrassing reality.
President Trump and Pastor Cunningham bewail bike lanes in their backyard because they’ve identified the wrong culprit for very real issues. Getting around DC is a nightmare. The Greater Washington area is home to about 6.5 million people, and the federal city on the Potomac wasn’t built for all those people or cars. DC is swollen with Chevrolet Suburbans and Jeep Grand Wagoneers. Bicycles—comparatively slim, efficient, convenient, and much less likely to kill—are the solution, not the problem.
There’s nothing inherently left or right, feminine or masculine, about bicycles or bike lanes. A bike is just a bike. It is a simple two-wheeled machine with universal appeal.
The irony of recent criticisms, I would argue, is that bikes are as American as apple pie and ranch dressing. The bicycle gives many Americans their first taste of freedom in childhood. It doesn’t need to be fed gasoline. You can probably learn to take care of it yourself. You don’t need a license to operate it. All you need are your own muscles (or some batteries).
The government doesn’t even know if you own one.
What could be more American?

Palestinian youth may soon get to vote for the first time. Few believe it actually matters.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Palestinians in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip are scheduled to vote on November 28 for the first time in 20 years. For most of the electorate, it will be their first time at the ballot box. And for many of them, it may not matter.
Palestinian factions that have spent two decades in bitter — and at times violent — division are joining forces ahead of the upcoming legislative election, forming the broadest political coalition seen in the occupied territories in years. The Alliance of National Forces (ANF), formed following a series of talks in Cairo, includes Hamas, the two main dissident currents of Fatah led by Muhammad Dahlan and Nasser al-Qudwah, the Gaza-based paramilitary Popular Resistance Committees (PRC), which was never interested in politics, and the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ), a faction that has historically opposed elections in principle. The Palestinian left-wing factions, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) and the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP), are still considering whether to join.
Fatah, led by President Mahmoud Abbas, has said it will run independently and rejected the possibility of running on a joint list with Hamas.
In the background, Abbas has amended the elections law to require that any candidate subscribe to the official PLO political program, including all signed agreements with Israel — a condition that civil and legal groups have denounced as undermining political diversity and freedom. But the amended law also raises the number of legislative council seats from 132 to 200 and lowers the age of candidacy to 20 years. The Palestinian Authority (PA) says that these changes are designed to encourage broader participation.
According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, 64 percent of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza are under the age of 30. The majority of the electorate was either not born or too young to vote when the last elections took place in 2006. They are now being asked to choose between factions founded decades ago that are largely led by the same figures and run on programs that have not changed in years, divided along disputes that trace back to the Fatah-Hamas split of 2007 — decades before most of today’s first-time voters were old enough to understand what was at stake.
The energy of 2021
When Abbas announced legislative elections in January 2021, before calling them off a month before the vote, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were briefly swept by a surge of political energy. Thirty-six electoral lists were announced and began campaigning. Of those, only seven represented traditional factions. Five were explicitly youth lists, seen at the time as evidence of a generation hungry for participation and frustrated by the options available to them.
One, named “Karamati” — Arabic for “My Dignity” — included young professionals from both Gaza and the West Bank, and campaigned on democratic participation, opportunities for young people, and care for vulnerable sectors.
Another, the Generation of Democratic Reform, known by its Arabic acronym JAD, included intellectuals, professionals, and activists. JAD launched a virtual shadow parliament as an alternative to the official electoral process, campaigning — among other things — against the legal requirement of a $10,000 deposit as a condition for candidate registration.
The most outspoken and independent list was called Freedom and Dignity, headed by Palestinian activist Nizar Banat, a carpenter with a graduate degree in the Arabic Language and Law, and who had become an online political commentator known for his blunt, often scathing criticism of the PA. His list campaigned on fighting PA corruption, rejecting the Oslo-based order of negotiations with Israel, and opposing politically-conditioned European funding.
Then, in April of that year, Abbas canceled the elections. Nizar Banat criticized the decision and called on donor countries to cut off funding to the PA until it abided by the popular demand to hold legislative elections. A few months later, PA security personnel abducted and killed him, beating him to death while in custody.
Demonstrations broke out across the West Bank in protest over his killing, galvanizing a wave of popular outrage that was met with a swift PA crackdown. The assassination of Banat marked the denouement of political engagement in the Palestinian street, and with it the brief period of political enthusiasm around the legislative elections.
The scar of cancellation
The 2021 call for elections brought to light figures, ideas, and trends that were invisible in the Palestinian political mainstream, a far cry from the level of engagement demonstrated since the 2026 announcement of legislative elections. So far, only party lists have been announced, and the majority of Palestinians remain skeptical.
Much of the current detachment goes back to 2021 — not just to what the elections promised, but to what their cancellation cost.
Zein Abu Daqqa, Senior Fellow at The Institute for Social and Economic Progress, where he researches trends in Palestinian society, told Mondoweiss that “the cancellation of the 2021 elections had a deep and negative impact on how Palestinians think about elections.”
“Psychologically, the cancellation functions as an anchoring event which people remember vividly,” Abu Daqqa, who participated in the JAD initiative in 2021, said. “They also remember that some candidates sacrificed money, jobs, and other livelihoods to stand, only for the elections to be canceled shortly thereafter.” Abu Daqqa described the cancellation as “a real scar on the Palestinian psyche, which anyone considering forming a list now will have to reckon with.”
But Abu Daqqa also points to the compressed timeline. Elections were announced in late August with a vote scheduled on November 28, leaving barely three months for candidates to organize, register, and campaign. “Even in an open political environment, this would be a short window,” he explained, “and we have not had an open political environment or an active political life for many years.”
Haneen Abu Omar, a Palestinian in her early thirties who also participated in the JAD initiative, goes further, stating that many youth who showed enthusiasm in 2021, including herself, “have lost trust in the idea that Palestinian elections would fix things.”
“After a genocide in Gaza, and the ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, we saw a wholesale acceptance by Palestinian leaders from all factions of U.S. conditions, especially to the condition of creating a technocratic committee to run Gaza outside of the Palestinian political institutions, as if accepting the disintegration of Palestine,” she explained. “New elections seem designed to give legitimacy to this new order of things. I personally don’t trust this political system anymore, and I don’t trust that elections can fix it.”
She also points to the shock of the past three years. “Before October 2023, things weren’t rosy, and there were large Israeli raids in the West Bank, and people were arrested for no reason, but today things are on a whole different level,” she said. “Today, Palestinians feel that there is an existential attack on their presence in their country, and if I were a Bedouin who was expelled from his home and was still looking for a place to stay, or a mother from Gaza who is living under a tent and looking for food for her children, I don’t think that democratic participation in Palestinian institutions would be my first priority.”
As for Abu Daqqa, he sees this shift in attitudes reflected in his research. “Priorities have moved toward the economy and stability,” he said, drawing a historical parallel with the aftermath of the Second Intifada, during which stability and security also dominated Palestinian concerns. Yet, when elections were announced in 2005, Palestinians still participated in large numbers, with both presidential candidates, Mustafa Barghouthi and Mahmoud Abbas, campaigning on job opportunities, reconstruction, and fighting corruption, alongside national liberation goals.
“Attitudes toward the present elections are shaped by three perceptions,” Abu Daqqa noted. “Whether the elections will actually take place; whether they will be free and fair; and, following from these, whether they will have any bearing on people’s lives. If all three conditions are satisfied, the same hope and interest recorded in earlier questions on reform, democracy, and governance can be expected to return.”
‘Will it bring back our lost homes?’
In Gaza, the outlook for elections is grimmer still.
Razan Abdel Raheem, 26, is a children’s writer from al-Shati’ refugee camp in eastern Gaza. She has lived all the episodes of Israel’s genocidal war on the Strip, been displaced twice with her family, and lost her home to an Israeli airstrike. She now lives with multiple other families in a relative’s house.
In 2021, at 21, she also considered casting her first-ever vote for an independent youth list. Today, she told Mondweiss that she has no interest in the upcoming elections.
“I find it difficult to believe in anything at all after all that we have gone through,” Razan said. “What will a new legislative council do with the wholesale destruction here in Gaza? Will new elections fix all the injustices that we have been forced to live through since Hamas took over in 2007? Will it give us back the youthful years that we lost to Israel’s bombing campaigns? Will it bring us back our lost homes or our lost friends and family?”
Razan raises the questions that animate Gaza’s post-genocide politics with particular precision. “Will a newly elected council push back the Yellow Line that the occupation keeps moving toward us?” she said, describing Israel’s progressive expansion of the invisible line demarcating the Israeli-controlled part of the Strip. “Will it bring justice for Hind Rajab and the thousands of children like her who were killed? Will it make it possible for the people of Beit Hanoun, Rafah, and Khan Younis to go back to their land? Will it pursue cases to hold the occupying state accountable worldwide? Will it rebuild my parents’ house?”
“If the answer is ‘yes,’ then I will be the first to vote, and even demonstrate and campaign, too,” she said. “But I don’t think it is.”
Razan also points to a quieter demographic shift that she says is draining Gaza of the generation most likely to drive political change. “Most young people in Gaza who had a chance of leaving have left through scholarships or artistic residencies — I’m talking about the intellectual elite of Gaza’s youth who survived the genocide,” she explained. “Most of our friends from Gaza’s small Christian community also left, leaving a void in the city.”
Gaza, Raheem concludes, “is not what it used to be, and new elections are not enough to repair what has been broken.”
According to Abu Daqqa, the dark shadow that the Israeli genocide casts on elections is related to the precise moment Palestinians now experience. “Hope itself rises and falls with political events and with the political horizon,” Abu Daqqa explained. He believes it is “likely temporary, and will lift once people come to believe in a new process or new leadership.”
A generation disengaged
In mid-August, the Palestinian daily newspaper Al-Quds reported findings from the latest youth poll by the Palestinian Center for Polls and Survey Research, which surveyed 1,281 Palestinians aged 18 to 29 across Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem.
According to the findings, 72.4 percent of young Palestinians in Gaza aged 18 to 29, alongside 26.7 percent of the same cohort in the West Bank, did not follow the municipal elections held last April.
Up to 45 percent of those surveyed said they weren’t interested in internal Palestinian politics, 15.3 percent said they had lost trust in Palestinian elections, and 13 percent said they found no convincing candidate.
According to the report, 64.1 percent said they often or seriously think about leaving their country.
Yet Abu Daqqa’s research points to another aspect of the Palestinian youth’s outlook on their country’s politics. “When Palestinians are asked how they expect change to come about, they consistently point to elections,” Abu Daqqa said. “When asked about reform, most understand reform to mean elections. What people want is an electoral process through which they can choose their representatives. Elections, in short, remain both credible and a priority.”
The gap between the political energy of 2021 — with its youth lists, independent candidacies, and public debate — and the near-silence of 2026 reflects something beyond disillusionment with any particular party. It reflects a generation that watched elections canceled in 2021, a genocide unfold in 2023 and after, and a political class unable or unwilling to respond to either.
Abu Daqqa believes that the opportunity isn’t entirely lost for the current generation of Palestinian youth. “Each generation must develop the tools, tactics, and strategies through which it builds its own approach to liberation, and I am confident that the current generation will develop its own set of tools, principles, and strategies to do exactly that,” he said. “Innovation, creativity, and determination are everywhere in Palestine.”

Russia continues Ebola response in Uganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Russia continues Ebola response in Uganda
Russia is continuing its work in Uganda following the country’s Ebola outbreak, with specialists remaining on the ground, the head of Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor, Anna Popova, said on Tuesday.
Speaking at a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Popova said Russian experts were deployed to Uganda shortly after the outbreak began and helped local authorities bring it under control. “Efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak in Uganda are still underway right now,” she said.
The East African state was declared free of Ebola on August 27 after recording no new infections for 42 days. The outbreak, which began in May, caused 20 confirmed cases and two deaths in the country. Fifteen infections were imported from DR Congo, while five occurred among contacts and health workers linked to those cases, the authorities said.
“The test, which we brought there during the very first few days, proved to be highly effective,” Popova noted, adding that, after being further refined on the ground, the test has since passed the first stage of the World Health Organization’s qualification process.
Russia has provided Uganda with broader support in tackling Ebola and other infectious disease threats. Moscow sent epidemiologists to the country in May to assist with the outbreak investigation and supplied diagnostic tests, while a Russian mobile anti-epidemic laboratory was donated to Uganda in 2024. More than 80 Ugandan specialists have also received training at Rospotrebnadzor institutions in pathogen monitoring, laboratory diagnostics, biosafety, and other areas.
Earlier this month, ten specialists from the Ugandan Health Ministry and research institutions began a two-week course in Moscow covering disinfection, pest control, and field surveillance.
While Uganda has brought its outbreak to an end, Ebola infections continue to rise in neighboring DR Congo. The latest government figures show 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths, putting the case fatality rate at 48.4%. A total of 1,726 patients have recovered, while 905 remain in isolation or hospital care.
The outbreak has now spread to 62 health zones across seven provinces, with Ituri the worst affected. Cases have also been recorded in North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele, Tshopo, and Sud-Ubangi.

Prisma Peremarket files redundancy notice, 67 support jobs lost
Finnish-owned supermarket Prisma's Estonian arm, acquired by Coop this year, has filed a collective redundancy notice affecting 67 support unit employees.
This represents about 10 percent of its workforce, and the company said store staff will not be affected.
The Coop sale has meant existing support roles overlapping with the new owner's structure are redundant, the company said. Affected roles include product category coordinators and the communications manager.
Maren Penu, head of Prisma Peremarket's support units, said employees who received redundancy notices will be paid the compensation required under Estonian law.
"The final number of employees to be laid off will become clear during the process. The notice period depends on the employee's length of service and ranges from one to three months. Store employees will not be affected by the layoffs," Penu said.
Prisma Peremarket AS, formerly part of Finland's SOK Group, has been operating in Estonia since 2000. In September this year, Coop Eesti Keskühistu became the owner of Prisma Peremarket, following the sale announced in spring. The company had 13 stores in Tallinn, Harju County, Tartu, Narva and Rapla, and these are in the process of being reopened as Coop outlets, between now and year-end.

Belarus Frees 25 More Political Prisoners in Return for U.S. Sanctions Relief
Unknown

2026-09-16

19:58:42 KST

Belarus has agreed to free 25 prisoners in return for a further easing of U.S. sanctions, an envoy for U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday.
The deal was part of lengthy negotiations in which Washington is urging Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko to free hundreds of people, including human rights campaigners, political activists, journalists and lawyers in exchange for sanctions relief and an easing of his international isolation.
Trump's envoy, John Coale, told reporters in the Belarusian capital Minsk: "We agreed to an interim deal, and as a show of goodwill Belarus will release 25 people and in exchange the United States will lift sanctions on two companies."
The figure of 25 was much lower than the 250 that Coale persuaded Lukashenko to release when he last visited Minsk in March.
Coale said both sides would work to resolve outstanding issues to pave the way for another prisoner release and the removal of further sanctions.
"We will continue to improve U.S.-Belarus relations and are working to secure the release of more people in the very near future. We are not finished!" he posted later on X.
Belarusian human rights group Viasna said a new round of prisoner pardons had started, with relatives of some detainees being told they could pick up their loved ones from prison on Wednesday morning.
Viasna, which is banned in Belarus, says the former Soviet state still holds more than 900 political prisoners, even after Coale negotiated the release of hundreds since the middle of last year.
Among the most frequent charges against them are "extremist" activity, conspiring to seize power, incitement to hatred or insulting the president.
At Tuesday's talks with Coale, Lukashenko denied the people in question were political prisoners and rejected assertions by rights groups and the exiled opposition that he is steadily arresting more people to replace those he releases.
The two companies to be removed from U.S. sanctions are Lakokraska, a manufacturer of paints and industrial coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned industrial concern that oversees the forestry, pulp and paper sectors. Sanctions against them have been in place since 2008 and 2023, respectively.
Coale also promised Lukashenko on Tuesday to get U.S. banks to hand back tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets.
Coale's efforts since last year have led to the release, among many others, of Nobel Peace Prize winner Ales Bialiatski and leading opposition figures. His diplomacy has earned gratitude from many Belarusians, while also raising concerns.
"We should use every opportunity to save lives. But we should not confuse releases with political change. Repression continues, and Lukashenko continues supporting Russia's war," exiled opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said in comments to Reuters on Tuesday.
"The purpose should be to empty the prisons, not to rehabilitate the dictatorship."

IAI debuts new tactical vehicle for German special forces

Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) has introduced a new tactical vehicle for Germany’s special forces, marking the first public appearance of the TAHR, a platform built on IAI’s ELTA ZD chassis and produced by Flensburg Technology Systems (FTS).
The first pre-series vehicle was unveiled ahead of schedule at the annual conference of the German Special Forces Command, the Kommando Spezialkräfte (KSK), in Altensteig‑Wart on Tuesday.
The TAHR is based on the Israeli ZD platform developed by IAI ELTA, which has been battle-proven by Israeli special forces. FFTS, a joint venture between IAI’s ELTA division and German defense contractor FFG, developed and manufactures the vehicle in Germany.
Designed as a light, air‑transportable platform, the TAHR incorporates operational modifications requested by the KSK, including an open architecture for integrating weapons and sensors and a layout intended to improve situational awareness. Its compact dimensions also enable two TAHRs to be transported inside CH‑47 Chinook helicopters, with crews able to achieve combat readiness shortly after landing, a core requirement for airborne special operations.
The TAHR will be delivered to the KSK in two variants, a combat configuration and a support model. Both are based on an existing all‑terrain platform already in service. FTS adapted the design to meet the KSK's mission-specific requirements, which rely heavily on rapid deployment and mobility in demanding environments.
“The KSK’s mission is to conduct special forces operations worldwide and under all conditions successfully. To do this, the KSK requires not only high mobility but also a variety of suitable modes of transport depending on the situation, mission, and terrain,” said KSK commander, Brig.-Gen. Andreas Kühne.
“With the TAHR, we are getting an operational and combat vehicle that is air-droppable and ready for deployment in any terrain. Together, we have succeeded in advancing this important armament project for the KSK in such a way that the first pre-series vehicle can be presented within just one year,” he added.
FTS signed a framework agreement in October 2025 with the Federal Office of Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support, the German Army’s procurement authority, to supply up to 200 vehicles.
IAI’s leadership described the rollout as a milestone in the company’s cooperation with Germany.
“IAI views Germany as a strategic partner in developing joint defense capabilities over the long term. Our cooperation spans multiple domains, from air and maritime to land, and is grounded in the combination of technology, expertise, and industrial capabilities on both sides. We are committed to further deepening this cooperation and jointly developing solutions to address the evolving security challenges of the years ahead,” IAI CEO Guy Barlev said.
ELTA CEO Dror Bar noted that delivering the first vehicle ahead of schedule showed the effectiveness of the industrial collaboration and the ability to tailor proven Israeli platforms to German operational needs.
“We are proud to present the first TAHR vehicle ahead of schedule. This achievement reflects the strength of our industrial cooperation with our German partners and our ability to deliver advanced, proven platforms tailored precisely to the customer’s operational needs,” he said.
Europe has increasingly turned to Israeli defense technology over the past decade, especially after Russia invaded Ukraine and the growing demand for rapid, combat‑proven systems.
