'La bola negra' by Los Javis shortlisted to represent Spain at the 2027 Oscars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:05:10 UTC
19:05:10 KST

With further possible nominations for the civil‑war drama yet to be announced, the film, hailed at Cannes and TIFF for its three intertwined 'queer' stories, pulls ahead of the other Spanish contenders: "El ser querido" by Sorogoyen and "Los domingos" by Ruíz de Azúa.
Spain's film academy has chosen "La bola negra" to carry the country's hopes of securing a new Oscar for best international feature, a feat achieved only four times in the history of the US awards, most recently thanks to Alejandro Amenábar's "Mar adentro" ("The Sea Inside") in 2005.
This ensemble drama about queer desire and repression, set against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War and closely linked to the figure of Federico García Lorca, has already won the award for Best Director at the Cannes Film Festival after also competing for other prizes such as the Palme d'Or itself.
The final Oscar nominations will be revealed on 15 December. That is when it will become clear whether the creative duo made up of Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, Los Javis, will conclude at Hollywood's Dolby Theatre the promotional tour they have been immersed in for several months. This year's film awards ceremony will be held on 14 March 2027.
Film analysts are confident about its chances of picking up several extra nods from the Hollywood Academy in different categories such as best supporting actress, a nomination that could go to cabaret performer Nené Romero played by Penélope Cruz. The reactions coming in this week from the Toronto International Film Festival, an annual bellwether for US critics, appear positive among both specialists and general audiences.
This is Los Javis' second feature after their debut "La llamada", which was followed by several television projects such as "Paquita Salas", "Veneno" and "La Mesías". The cast of "La bola negra" is completed by singer-songwriter Álvaro Lafuente, Guitarricadelafuente, as well as Miguel Bernardeau, Carlos González, Milo Quifes, Lola Dueñas and a brief appearance by Glenn Close as a historian who travels to present-day Madrid.
The war film beat "Los Domingos" by Alauda Ruíz de Azúa, one of the most highly awarded films in Spain last season but unable to enter the 2025 preselection, and "El ser querido" by Rodrigo Sorogoyen, which tells the story of the relationship between an absent director (Javier Bardem) and his daughter, played by Victoria Luengo.
Pending the announcement of the final nominations, one of Los Javis' main rivals could be the Romanian film "Fjord", winner of the Cannes Palme d'Or for its portrait of an ultra-religious marriage (played by Renate Reinsve, who has experience in Hollywood, and Sebastian Stan) that explores the contradictions of progressive Norwegian society.

Belarus releases 25 prisoners in exchange for US lifting sanctions on two companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:05:01 UTC
19:05:01 KST

Belarus has agreed to free 25 prisoners in return for a further easing of US sanctions, an envoy for US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday.
The deal was part of lengthy negotiations in which Washington is urging Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko to free hundreds of people, including human rights campaigners, political activists, journalists and lawyers, in exchange for sanctions relief and an easing of his international isolation.
Trump's envoy, John Coale, told reporters in the Belarusian capital Minsk: "We agreed to an interim deal, and as a show of goodwill Belarus will release 25 people and in exchange the United States will lift sanctions on two companies."
The figure of 25 was much lower than the 250 that Coale persuaded Lukashenko to release when he last visited Minsk in March.
The American said both sides would work to resolve outstanding issues to pave the way for another prisoner release and the removal of further sanctions.
"We will continue to improve US-Belarus relations and are working to secure the release of more people in the very near future. We are not finished!" he posted later on X/Twitter.
Belarusian human rights group Viasna said a new round of prisoner pardons had started, and relatives of some detainees had been told they could collect their loved ones from penal colonies on Wednesday morning.
Belarus's Lukashenko denies replacing some prisoners with others
Viasna, which is banned in Belarus, says the former Soviet state still holds more than 900 political prisoners, even after Coale negotiated the release of hundreds since the middle of last year.
Among the most frequent charges against them are "extremist" activity, conspiring to seize power, incitement to hatred, or insulting the president.
At Tuesday's talks with Coale, Lukashenko denied the people in question were political prisoners and rejected assertions by rights groups and the exiled opposition that he is steadily arresting more people to replace those he releases.
The two companies to be removed from US sanctions are Lakokraska, a manufacturer of paints and industrial coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned industrial concern that oversees the forestry, pulp and paper sectors. Sanctions against them have been in place since 2008 and 2023, respectively.
Coale also promised Lukashenko on Tuesday to get US banks to hand back tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets.
Coale's efforts since last year have led to the release, among many others, of Nobel Peace Prize winner Ales Bialiatski and leading opposition figures. His diplomacy has earned gratitude from many Belarusians, while also raising concerns.
"We should use every opportunity to save lives. But we should not confuse releases with political change. Repression continues, and Lukashenko continues supporting Russia's war (in Ukraine)," exiled opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said in comments to Reuters on Tuesday.
"The purpose should be to empty the prisons, not to rehabilitate the dictatorship."
US envoy hopes Belarus will release hundreds more prisoners next month
Coale further told Reuters on Wednesday he expects to visit the country again around one month from now, hoping to secure the release of hundreds more prisoners.
"I hope hundreds (are released). I don't know. That's my hope," Coale said of his next planned trip to Minsk. "I'm confident that we'll get a lot more out."

Women, Life, Freedom uprising survivors honor Mahsa Amini on anniversary of her death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:05:01 UTC
19:05:01 KST

Four years after Mahsa Amini was murdered by the Islamic Republic, sparking Iran’s ‘Woman, Life, Freedom’ protests, survivors of that 2022 uprising spoke to The Jerusalem Post about the young Kurdish woman’s enduring memory, what they witnessed during the crackdown, and how those events changed their lives.
Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish-Iranian woman from Sanandaj in western Iran, was arrested by Tehran’s morality police on September 13, 2022, for allegedly wearing her hijab improperly. She collapsed at the Vozara Detention Center shortly afterward and fell into a coma. She died three days later, on September 16.
Iran’s Police Information Center claimed that Amini suffered a cardiac seizure while in custody. However, a UN human rights expert later said evidence indicated that Amini died “as a result of beatings,” and the UN Fact-Finding Mission on Iran said it had “established the existence of evidence of trauma to Ms. Amini’s body, inflicted while in the custody of the morality police,” which it said had demonstrated clear “patterns of violence.”
Outraged by Amini’s death, protesters took to the streets in at least 134 cities and towns and 132 universities across 26 of Iran’s 31 provinces. The Islamic Republic brutally suppressed the “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests, firing live ammunition into crowds and forcibly disappearing thousands of people. At least 49 women and 68 children were killed in the streets, according to United Nations estimates.
Iranian regime's security forces confirmed to have killed 551 people during protests after Amini's death
Yasser Fattahi’s father, Jowhar Fattahi, was among the 551 Iranians confirmed to have been killed by the regime’s security forces.
The son told the Post that on November 21, 2022, his 60-year-old father decided to join a march in their hometown of Javanrud, in Kermanshah Province, after Bahaeddin Vaisi and Erfan Kakayi, two members of their extended family from the town, were killed by security forces.
Jowhar was among several people from the town who stayed up through the night, guarding the bodies so that the regime could not “hold them hostage.”
He joined an estimated 30,000 people from the community in laying the men to rest before marching in their memory.
Though Jowhar lacked formal higher education, his son defined him as a principled, compassionate man.
“He always used to say at home, ‘Neither oppress anyone nor allow anyone to oppress you.’ He emphasized the first part more, not being an oppressor ourselves,” Fattahi recalled.
“He was not a violent or extremist person at all. He also always spoke about the injustices that the Iranian government had inflicted on everyone, and especially on the Kurdish people. He wished for a change of government, so that ordinary people would no longer have to bear the cost of living under a cruel and authoritarian regime.”
Fattahi, a nurse, was tending to wounded protesters in Sanandaj when the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) opened fire on the crowds in his hometown.
A family friend who marched alongside Fattahi’s father would later tell him how Jowhar stopped to help a young woman who had been shot and wasn’t moving. He refused to move away from her when directed to do so by IRGC members, so they shot him in the femoral region of his left leg.
“In those days, people preferred to die rather than go to the hospital because they knew that, either way, they would be taken from the hospital by the IRGC and held hostage, and ultimately they would be killed,” Fattahi said, explaining how he was stuck treating protesters in secret as his father lay at home begging those around him not to transport him to hospital.
Jowhar Fattari died of his wounds after losing consciousness due to IRGC violence
After he lost consciousness, Jowhar was taken to hospital, where he died of his wounds. Having witnessed the security forces abducting the bodies of those killed, the friends who took Jowhar for medical attention snuck his body out of the institute and buried him far from the city’s main cemetery.
Tens of thousands have been killed in the years that followed Jowhar’s death as the Islamic Republic continues to suppress dissent. Still, Amini’s name has come to represent a call for freedom and the sacrifices made in hopes of achieving it, Fattahi noted.
“‘Woman, Life, Freedom’ is not merely a slogan. It is far more complex, and at the same time, it is the simplest demand one could possibly make.” Speaking of the oppression faced by women in Iran, he said it is “beyond words.”
Describing the situation of women as “tragic,” Fattahi said, “Women are the ones who nurture and raise us, and without their freedom, we cannot expect free human beings to exist. So why should they be subjected to violence or killed because of these policies?”
The Woman, Life, Freedom movement gave women “living under repression and suffocation” an “opportunity to say ‘No’ to a fascist system that treated” them as “slaves” and “inferior to men,” he continued.
“One reason the name of Jina [her real, Kurdish name; Mahsa was her Iranian name] Amini and the Woman, Life, Freedom revolution has endured is that this revolution should not be reduced to the issue of the hijab. Women’s problems are not limited to the hijab.”
“Freedom does not simply mean having the freedom to choose whether or not to wear a hijab,” he concluded. “This is the most basic of women’s rights.”

Global Gender Gap Report: Women's hard-won gains 'fragile'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:05:00 UTC
19:05:00 KST

WEF report: Progress on gender equality remains 'fragile'
September 16, 2026
The Global Gender Gap Report 2026, published by the World Economic Forum (WEF) on Wednesday, reveals that gender parity worldwide is closer than ever — standing at 69.2%.
However, the Geneva-based nonprofit warned that full parity may still be 120 years away and that the progress made so far remains "fragile."
The report, which looked at gender parity across workforce participation, education, health and politics in 145 economies, found that women now occupy senior leadership positions in government and business at levels that were rare globally when the index began in 2006.
Yet, while women's presence at the top of politics has grown since the first report, the past decade has seen that trend reverse. The percentage of countries led by women peaked in 2022 and has now fallen back to 2016 levels.
WEF Managing Director Saadia Zahidi warned that while parity is a foundation for growth and competitiveness, it is "not inevitable."
"To accelerate, governments and employers need to learn from the policies that work and apply them faster. A new economy demands a new approach to talent," Zahidi said in a press release to accompany the report.
Women still missing in top power roles
The WEF found that women remain underrepresented in roles with the largest economic and political influence. They still hold fewer than a fifth of chief executive officer (CEO) positions, while only one in 10 ministerial roles held by women is considered high influence.
While the number of ministerial roles led by women has risen 26% since 2008, only one in 10 was considered weighty then — a share the WEF report said was "virtually unchanged today."
Despite nearly $1 trillion (€866 billion) being invested globally to develop artificial intelligence (AI), the report also revealed that fewer than one in five AI engineers are women, and they are underrepresented at every level of AI firms.
For the 17th consecutive year, Iceland leads the ranking with 93% of the gender gap closed, followed by its Nordic neighbors Finland and Norway. The three nations have made the Top 10, along with Sweden, every year since 2006.
Namibia ranked fourth globally, higher than Germany (9th), the United Kingdom (5th) and Australia (8th).
US falls in gender gap ranking
The United States dropped five places in the rankings to 47th, with 74.9% of its gender gap closed.
The country achieved full parity in education for a second year, ranking first in the world in that area.
In the US, women have long matched men in professional and technical jobs, but parity in senior management has fallen by almost 11 points since 2006, the WEF calculated.
The political score fell 4.1 points from last year after the share of women ministers dropped from two-thirds parity to one-half. The decline coincided with a lower share of women serving as Cabinet secretaries in President Donald Trump's second administration.
The WEF kept the head-of-state indicator for the US at zero as the world's largest economy has never had a female president.
India stuck while China moves up
India, the world's most populous country, remains at 131st in the rankings, with 64.5% gender parity closed.
The report noted India's overall gains amount to a 4.3 percentage-point rise since 2006, which the authors said was mostly due to educational achievement. Women's labor-market participation has barely moved over 20 years, the WEF noted.
India's economic parity score has varied significantly since the first report. Parity among professional and technical workers has almost doubled since 2006, to 49.9%. Among legislators, senior officials and managers, however, it is still only 13.1%.
In parliament, India has closed 16.1% of the gender gap, up seven points since 2006, while the share of women in long-serving Prime Minister Narendra Modi's cabinet has fallen recently, with parity slipping to 5.9% from a 30% peak in 2019.
China, meanwhile, rose seven places to 96th, closing 69.9% of its gender gap. Economic parity is its strongest pillar, at 72.3%, but politics has barely moved in 20 years, with women still accounting for only a fraction of ministers.
Large jumps for Namibia, Kenya and Ghana
Reaching 84.5% parity in the latest report, Namibia leads the way in Sub-Saharan Africa, climbing four places to No. 4 in the ranking.
Namibia has long been well represented by women on the political stage. Last year, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah became its first female president. The country also has a female vice-president and the parliament speaker is a woman, too.
Other African countries were among the biggest climbers in the 2026 rankings, with Kenya rising 33 places in a year to 65th, Ghana up 32 places to 56th and Angola climbing 30 places to 87th.
However, Africa shows the widest range of outcomes for women, the report found, with Chad recording the lowest score of 57.8% parity closed.
Other large climbers in the 2026 report were Guatemala, which rose 31 points to 50th place, and the Czech Republic, which climbed 25 points to 77th.
The WEF also ranked the countries that have progressed the most since 2006 in closing gender gaps, namely Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador, France, Guatemala, Iceland, Mexico, Namibia and Nepal.

Is Gadi Eisenkot's biggest selling point that he's 'not Netanyahu?'

Front-runner Gadi Eisenkot is drawing support precisely because he is "everything Netanyahu isn't," Jerusalem Post editor-in-chief Zvika Klein said in an election discussion with host Jacob Laznik.
Klein described Eisenkot's disciplined, low-noise operation as a "Swiss watch" that rolls out respected recruits at a steady pace and grants few interviews, contrasting it with what he called the "reaction politics" of Naftali Bennett.
The pair opened on the foreign sanctions targeting Israeli figures, which Laznik dismissed as "stupid" and poorly thought through, even as he noted the governments behind them track Israeli coalition politics closely.
From there, they turned to a right-wing camp Laznik called "in shambles," citing the failure of Ben-Gvir and Smotrich to run together despite Netanyahu's push and the mergers that never came together. Klein said Likud's candidate list was assembled "last second" and became "a mess," with the fight over reserved slots landing in the party's internal court and nearly splitting its base. Both flagged puzzling placements: a former hostage and a Channel 14 television host in high, coveted slots while a serious defense figure was buried at number 35.
Where they diverged most was on what the election is actually about. Laznik rejected the idea of an "exciting list," insisting the vote should turn on a bare-minimum agenda the country needs "yesterday," a state commission of inquiry into October 7, a haredi draft law, and honest budgets: items he called "non-negotiable." Klein pushed instead for a cross-partisan government, and the two weighed whether any coalition could rely on the Arab parties, the case for term limits, and how any incoming leader would inherit simultaneous pressure from Iran, Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, and Turkey.
Klein closed with three priorities regardless of who wins: resolving the draft through financial pressure rather than force, governing as "everyone's prime minister," and overhauling Israel's diplomacy at "Ariel Sharon magnitude."

Ukraine Parliament clears first reading of bill ending VAT exemption on packages under EUR 150
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:04:55 EEST
19:04:55 KST

The Verkhovna Rada supported at first reading bill No. 16051-1 on amendments to the Tax Code concerning the abolition of the value-added tax (VAT) exemption for international postal shipments worth up to EUR 150.
As reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, during Wednesday's plenary session, 273 members of parliament voted in favor of adopting bill No. 16051-1, against the required minimum of 226 votes, while one voted against.
"I am speaking from the Rada rostrum for the third time asking you to support an important bill that is part of our international commitments and provides for fair taxation conditions... We can no longer delay this. We have already taken certain steps to defer expenditures until December. A decision is now being prepared that will allow us to operate under conditions of a liquidity crisis. But this has a significant impact on the ability of central executive authorities and local budgets to exercise their powers under conditions of full-scale aggression," Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko said from the parliamentary rostrum.
He added that due to the postponement of the abolition of the VAT exemption for international postal shipments worth up to EUR 150, EUR 4 billion will already fail to be received in September. According to Marchenko, the government urgently resubmitted two bills on abolishing the exemption (No. 16051 on amendments to the Tax Code and No. 15460 on amendments to the Customs Code), as there is a chance to receive these funds in October if the vote is successful.
As noted in the explanatory note to the bill, the amendments were developed to harmonize national tax legislation with European Union law, in particular to implement the provisions of Council Directive (EU) 2017/2455 and Directive 2006/112/EC on abolishing the VAT exemption for imports of low-value goods. This will eliminate distortions of competition between suppliers inside and outside the EU.
The document provides for the introduction of special VAT rules for transactions involving the distance sale of goods (excluding excise goods) imported in international postal and express shipments addressed to individuals and valued at up to EUR 150, with enterprises providing electronic interfaces or their intermediaries designated as responsible for assessing and paying the tax. At the same time, the VAT exemption is retained for small noncommercial consignments worth up to EUR 45 sent from individuals to individuals free of charge, as well as for goods in unaccompanied baggage worth up to EUR 150 and goods for security and defense purposes (energy equipment and goods for the defense forces).
Implementation of the law's provisions is expected to bring an additional approximately UAH 10 billion per year into the state budget.
As reported, the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Finance, Tax and Customs Policy recommended that parliament adopt bills No. 15460 and No. 16051-1 on amendments to the Tax and Customs Codes concerning value-added tax (VAT) treatment of e-commerce transactions.
Earlier, on September 1, the Rada rejected the revised bill (No. 15112-d) and six alternative bills on abolishing the VAT exemption for parcels worth up to EUR 150.
The parliament also sent back for revision bill No. 15460 on amendments to the Customs Code aimed at abolishing the VAT exemption for international parcels worth up to EUR 150. In May, the Rada rejected a bill containing similar amendments to the Customs Code (No. 12360).
Consideration of bill No. 15460 for the second time is expected on Wednesday, September 16.
The Verkhovna Rada's adoption of bills abolishing the tax exemption for international parcels worth EUR 150 is a condition for Ukraine to receive the third tranche under its program with the International Monetary Fund, worth approximately $0.7 billion, and the second tranche of macro-financial assistance from the European Union, worth EUR 13.7 billion, under the EUR 90 billion Ukraine Support Loan.
In the updated Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies under the EFF program with the IMF, Ukraine undertook, as a new structural benchmark, to adopt this law by the end of July, whereas under the original version it was to be approved by the end of March along with other tax provisions. However, this structural benchmark was not met.

Building a drone bridge from Israel's Negev to NATO’s eastern flank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:04:51 UTC
19:04:51 KST

Rezekne, Latvia, early September 2026, is quiet in a watchful way. Looking at it first through my innovation diplomacy lens, then through my photojournalist's lens, the geography tells its own story: dense birch forests giving way to open, swampy lowland close to the Russian and Belarusian border, a pivotal node on NATO's eastern flank.
The Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum 2026 opened against that backdrop, and within minutes a warning came over the public address system with a chill I knew from home: "Given the geographical location of the region, you may receive a cell broadcast alert if a potential threat in the airspace is detected. If you receive such an alert, please remain calm. If necessary, the event will be paused." The room, packed with NATO commanders, Baltic defense innovators, venture capitalists, and government ministers, stiffened.
Addressing the assembly, Krists Avots, parliamentary secretary to the prime minister of Latvia, reflected candidly on the wake-up call that reshaped his country's defense establishment. "On May 7, in this very city, two drones came by," he told the audience. "The government fell. We were caught somewhat unprepared. I think it was something to remember: that we need to be always ready, and being always ready means having the right capabilities that match what's the latest and greatest."
That May incursion followed a pattern of low-altitude airspace penetrations, met at the time with hesitation and a lack of counter-UAS response. Baltic citizens now watch for emergency airspace alerts on their phones as a matter of routine.
I know that sound. Two decades ago, I spent time documenting the “Tzeva Adom” sirens over the Western Negev, the one that gives residents 15 seconds to find concrete cover from incoming rockets fired from Hamas-controlled Gaza. Standing in that Rezekne auditorium, tens of kilometers from the Russian and Belarusian frontiers, I heard the same acoustics of a border under siege. Later, at a drone integration workshop outside Riga, the security protocol mirrored an active combat deployment.
"Because of growing tensions on the Russian side, our location has been scrubbed from public maps," the site director told me as our names were checked against a vetted manifest. "Nobody takes photographs. Everything you see here was built in the last six months to keep pace with operational demands."
For a decade, my photojournalism has followed landscapes under pressure, from the salt chimneys rising along the receding Dead Sea to the kinetic friction of the Western Negev's border envelope. Along this cold, marshy front line, the collision of East and West creates a different kind of pressure, and it leads the same place mine does: back to the battle-tested innovation hubs of the Negev, where survival has long depended on technology built not to break.
Seven out of 120: The Tel Aviv prelude
Days before I landed in Latvia, I stood inside Start-Up Nation Central's Tel Aviv headquarters for the demo day of the SouthUp DefenceTech Accelerator's third cohort. SouthUp's home base and live sandboxes sit in the Western Negev along the Gaza border, but this event was brought to Tel Aviv deliberately, putting frontline southern founders in the same room as more than 20 defense venture funds, institutional investors, and senior officials from MAFAT, Rafael, and Elbit.
Jointly run by SouthUp and Hamitbah alongside the HLS Innovation Community, the accelerator’s selection process was uncompromising: out of more than 120 defense-tech startups evaluated across Israel, exactly seven companies made the cut. Tech7 Chairman Yoram Sadan and Program Director Ron Reis emphasized to the room that selection went far beyond raw technology. The non-negotiable bar was whether a venture could absorb rapid business growth, scale globally, and deploy solutions forged in Gaza border operations, such as directly into NATO’s eastern theatre.
Three of those technologies stood out as tools built for survival. SelfS has built a microchip lighter than a single battery that gives drones an offline digital brain, letting them map underground tunnels with no GPS signal, a direct answer to subterranean infiltration whether along the Gaza border or the forested Belarusian frontier.
Cipax has built a self-healing communications link that keeps drone pilots connected through complete electronic warfare blackouts. Baxera has built a passive acoustic array that detects incoming low-altitude drones by sound alone, without broadcasting a signal an adversary could trace.
These systems were forged in the world's most contested airspace, and taking them to Latvia tests them against dense pine forest, marshy bog, and freezing winter - conditions the Negev desert never offers. A system that can navigate both a dusty tunnel and a snowbound forest earns its place anywhere on NATO's flank.
That same battle-tested logic carries through the mature end of the SouthUp and Hamitbah portfolio, companies already at Technology Readiness Level 9. Robotican builds autonomous interceptor drones that capture hostile aircraft mid-air and scout inside confined buildings. CopterPIX, fresh off a major defense tender win for attack swarms, runs a 3,000-square-meter manufacturing facility, the mass production capacity a bilateral European partnership needs.
An Optical Target Seeker venture is already evaluating a Latvian assembly plant for its smart optronics, to keep production and intellectual property inside Europe. And an Agricultural Robotics Platform has pivoted from precision farming to rugged perimeter security, patrolling border stretches where human sentries face brutal weather and terrain.
Voices from the summit
Latvia's Economics Minister Viktors Valainis opened the forum without hedging. "The link between security and the economy has become very direct," he said. "For Latvia, positioned on the eastern border of the European Union and NATO, the dual-use sector is both an existential defense necessity and a strategic economic engine. Latvia has surged defense spending from 3% to over 5% of GDP. Our national goal is to double the size of our economy by 2035, and dual-use industries are the primary spearhead."
Avots reinforced the same mandate from a different angle: "We are allocating over 5% of our budget toward defense, which presents a rare opportunity for economic growth. But for our local defense companies to succeed, they must look outwards and build interoperable capabilities that integrate directly into allied markets. Our allied forces operate on a simple motto: fight tonight and fight tomorrow, and we must build tools that match those operational realities in real time."
That is the opening Hamitbah and SouthUp exist to fill. In a working session, Jevgenijs Rjascenko-Saraks, head of Innovation and Research Policy at the Latvian Defense Ministry, walked me through the integration pathway for Israeli innovators, routing our portfolio through Latvia's Autonomous Systems Competence Center for live trials under heavy jamming at the Selija military range, alongside a local corporate footprint to access joint European Defense Fund bids.
Laura Strovalde, deputy director of the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), described a two-billion-euro dual-use deal pipeline and stressed that international joint ventures need local incorporation to anchor long-term production. Behind both conversations stood Irina Rubincika, LIAA's representative in Israel, whose coordination set this pipeline in motion following the Latvian ambassador's recent visit to the Western Negev. UniLab Defence, the technology transfer consortium linking Latvia's four leading research universities, offered the academic foundation I am now working to connect directly to Sapir Academic College's Faculty of Technology in the Western Negev.
The resilience bridge
Israel's Ambassador to Latvia Sandra Simovich framed a wider vision for bilateral relations. While hardware and drones dominate the headlines, she pointed to another expertise forged in the Western Negev: societal resilience, first-responder methodology, and emergency community management. Two decades under security pressure have shaped a resilience triangle in Negev municipalities, linking rapid emergency response, mental health support, and community trauma infrastructure, a model she sees as directly relevant to Baltic societies now bracing for hybrid border threats.
That bridge had already been tested in practice. In mid-June, the Latvian ambassador to Israel joined a delegation to the Western Negev, visiting kibbutzim, Sha'ar Hanegev, and the Sderot International Resilience Center, where a multi-million-shekel emergency simulator is under construction to train diplomats, medical leaders, and first responders under fire.
This diplomatic vision aligns with the grassroots civil work of Lina Ferbere and her organization, Jewnited.lv, formed in the immediate aftermath of October 7 to lead public diplomacy delegations of Baltic parliamentarians, journalists, academics, and medical leaders to Israel.
During our exchanges in Riga, Lina described how border incursions are transforming Baltic public consciousness. "What people are not prepared for here is resilience tech, learning first responders and how to deal with emergencies," she told me, noting that phone-based airspace alerts have suddenly brought border threats into daily life. Her goal with Jewnited.lv is to deepen Latvia-Israel relations through long-term civil, academic, and societal bridges.
Preparing her next delegation for late November, which includes senior medical academy professors and military health directors, she described a shift already underway: "I would love to adjust the program to be less tragic, more looking to the future, looking to what Israel can give to the story through innovation and development in times of constant pressure."
A senior Baltic strategy consultant put the principle behind all of it plainly in a closed-door session at the summit: "Trust is an active piece of defense infrastructure. If companies do not share operational problems openly, development lags. Small countries cannot afford stovepiped innovation."
The horizon beyond it
Latvia sits at the front line with Russia and functions, for Israel, as a strategic gateway into NATO's eastern flank, the Baltic states, and the wider European Union. What happens on this border reverberates across the transatlantic alliance.
Standing on the historic battlefields that for centuries served as the brutal collision ground between Russian and German empires, I looked out across the pine woods, mist-covered lakes, and concrete boundary markers along the border corridor, a landscape that gave away nothing of the severe tension sitting just beyond it.
The electronic warfare disrupting GPS signals over the Baltic Sea runs on the same doctrine used against tactical networks in the Middle East. The loitering munitions crossing into Baltic airspace share a direct lineage with the ones I have watched fall near my own home.
Rezekne and Sderot share little more than a place on a border line. Sderot and the Western Negev have spent two decades building battle-tested defense and resilience technology under fire, an experience Rezekne is only now starting to recognize it needs. Latvia is already ranked the seventh-largest drone exporter in Europe, and that capacity - paired with the Negev's field-tested edge - is what innovation diplomacy is built to connect.
The author is the director of innovation diplomacy and strategic partnerships at Hamitbah- Western Negev Innovation Authority

Lapid calls on Netanyahu to convene defense budget committee, release NIS 11b. to IDF
Unknown

10:04:38 UTC
19:04:38 KST

Opposition leader Yair Lapid called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday to convene the Knesset committee overseeing the defense budget and immediately approve NIS 11 billion for urgent IDF procurement, arguing that the move could be carried out without breaching the state budget or raising taxes.
Lapid’s proposal would allow funds to be transferred to the IDF without reopening the state budget. The opposition leader had previously conditioned his support for the transfer on canceling coalition funds allocated to haredi (ultra-Orthodox) draft evasion. He also argued that Netanyahu’s earlier proposal would increase taxes.
“I am once again calling on Prime Minister Netanyahu: We have a legal way to resolve the issue of the IDF’s immediate stockpiles without breaking the budget framework and raising taxes,” Lapid said.
“Let’s convene the joint committee on the defense budget and immediately transfer NIS 11 billion that has been waiting for many months for urgent defense procurement,” he continued.
Lapid’s statements came after he held a security briefing with Netanyahu on Monday, during which Lapid said the prime minister requested that the state budget be reopened to allocate additional funds to the defense establishment.
The opposition leader said he would not support the proposal if it meant raising taxes. Instead, he conditioned his support for the prime minister’s proposal on canceling coalition funds being transferred “to finance haredi draft evasion.”
Lapid had noted that, in general, he supported transferring the funds to increase the defense establishment’s budget “because the IDF needs to be strengthened.”
Adjustments can be made to the state budget if they receive the required Knesset approval.
The Knesset is currently on summer recess ahead of the October elections, but the plenum can still convene under certain circumstances. As a result, opposition support would be significant for advancing Netanyahu’s proposal.
Netanyahu’s ruling Likud party said after Monday's meeting that Lapid was “misleading the public about the defense budget.”
Increasing defense budget without raising taxes
The party argued that it could increase the defense budget without raising taxes.
Defense Minister Israel Katz later said Lapid should support additional funding for the IDF, arguing that the “economic situation is good” and that the necessary funds were available but required formal legislation in the Knesset. He claimed the request was not connected to any tax increases or other budgetary items.
The 2026 state budget that was approved in March included an expenditure cap of about NIS 699 billion.
The Defense Ministry’s budget was set at nearly NIS 142b. The sum reportedly increased by about NIS 32b as a result of the post-Oct 7 war.
The 2026 state budget also included nearly NIS 6b in coalition funds, with hundreds of millions of shekels directed to haredi institutions as part of the proposal.

Former Philippines President Rodrigo Duterte appeared in public on Wednesday for the first time since being transferred to the International Criminal Court 18 months ago to face murder charges regarding his war on drugs.
Duterte, 81, served as president from 2016 to 2022, before being charged with crimes against humanity for setting up, funding and arming death squads that targeted narcotics peddlers and users. He was arrested and taken to The Hague in March 2025.
On Wednesday, he appeared in the ICC courtroom where judges heard arguments about his health and ability to stand trial, set to begin in November.
His lawyers have said he suffers from cognitive decline that affects his memory and daily functioning, and is not well enough.
Dressed in a black suit and white shirt, Duterte did not speak in court.
In January, ICC judges said Duterte's health was good enough for him to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court, rather than by video link from the detention unit.
Duterte is allegedly responsible for as many as 30,000 deaths
The warrant for Duterte says he was responsible for a widespread and systematic campaign that led to thousands of killings between 2011 and 2019, including his time as the mayor of the southern city of Davao.
ICC prosecutors have said as many as 30,000 people may have been killed in the crackdown, the details of which were reported in a Reuters investigation.
Police said 6,200 suspects were killed during anti-drug operations. Duterte said he instructed police to act in self-defense and told supporters he was ready to "rot in jail" if it meant ridding the Philippines of illicit drugs.

A Russian-made Gerbera drone shot down over central Lithuania early Tuesday was apparently headed for Ukraine but veered off course after being affected by Ukrainian electronic warfare, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Wednesday.
“Based on the information currently available, it was a Gerbera-type drone,” Nausėda told reporters after a meeting of Lithuania’s State Defence Council.
The president said the incident was most likely not a deliberate attack against Lithuania.
“Most likely, it was a Russian drone intended for Ukraine that was diverted from its course by Ukrainian electronic warfare measures and entered our territory, where it was shot down,” Nausėda said.
The drone entered Lithuania from Belarus and was shot down in the Kaišiadorys district, near the Kruonis pumped-storage hydropower plant, by Italian fighter jets stationed at NATO’s air base in Šiauliai, according to Lithuanian officials.
Residents in the Vilnius and Kaunas regions received alerts warning of a possible air threat as the drone crossed Lithuanian territory.
Nausėda warned that similar incidents could happen again and said Lithuania needed to improve its ability to identify drones and other airborne objects approaching from abroad.
“Vilnius is close to the border, and, undoubtedly, once we identify and detect them, we could and should have the means to destroy drones or other flying objects,” he said.
But the president said Lithuania also needed alternative ways of bringing down drones because using fighter jets was not an efficient solution.
The incident was the first time a drone had been shot down over Lithuanian territory as Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues. Similar incidents have previously occurred in Latvia and Estonia.
Lithuania has issued several air-threat alerts in recent months. On Sunday, residents in parts of southeastern Lithuania received an alert about a possible air threat, but authorities later determined that radar systems had detected a flock of birds.
Earlier Sunday, authorities near Varėna, in southern Lithuania, also detected an unidentified object crossing Lithuanian airspace and possibly entering Russia’s Kaliningrad region. The object was believed to have come from Belarus. No air-threat alert was issued because authorities said they lacked sufficient information about the object.

Venezuela opposition leader Machado weighs return home amid US reticence

Venezuela opposition leader Machado weighs return home amid US reticence
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado faces a growing dilemma over when to return home from abroad to rally support, amid reticence from the Trump administration about her homecoming, four opposition sources and two political analysts said.
Machado left the country late in 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after largely living in hiding since a contested 2024 election. She has repeatedly promised to return, including after the US ouster of President Nicolas Maduro in January and twin earthquakes in June. But US officials have privately asked her to delay her return after the quakes.
The question of Machado’s return could reshape the political landscape in Venezuela, where US-backed talks aimed at remaking the political system ahead of elections do not include her movement. Though she commands the highest approval rating among political figures connected to Venezuela, her support slipped in August.
Four opposition sources said Machado will return, but no date has been set. One added that the leader, currently in Panama, plans to travel to the US beforehand, although no itinerary has been established.
“She is going to return. She'll go to the United States, but not to ask for permission,” said one source close to Machado, adding that Machado’s focus upon her return would be to push for fair elections.
Machado sought to cultivate US President Donald Trump as an ally well before Maduro’s removal. But since the ouster, Trump has repeatedly expressed support for interim President Delcy Rodriguez, Maduro’s former deputy, and hailed oil deals by the US government and major energy companies.
Too soon for elections: Trump
Trump said in September that it is too soon to consider democratic elections.
Machado’s long-time associate, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, said in a September interview that while she had every right to return, she was playing an important role organising the Venezuelan diaspora.
The US worries Machado could disrupt its transition plans if she were to return and rally supporters to push for Maduro-era officials to leave power, said one political analyst, who asked not to be named. Asked about the timing of Machado’s return, a State Department spokesperson declined to discuss private conversations.
US-backed talks between a faction of the opposition and the interim government, aimed at remaking the country’s political system ahead of eventual elections, are set to resume this week.
Though another source close to Machado said she had proposed leading negotiations herself, the US instead backed the leader of the 2015 legislature, which it recognises as democratically elected, and the talks so far do not include Machado’s political movement.
Machado did not respond to a request for comment about her possible return, her relationship with the US or the negotiations.
Venezuela’s Information Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
Machado’s popularity slips
Machado commanded huge crowds while campaigning in 2024, as she travelled around the country calling for a return to democracy.
The opposition coalition she led, which posted most ballot-box-level vote tallies online, says it won 67 per cent of the presidential vote. Though international observers questioned the official results, which showed a win for Maduro, the government never published detailed tallies and the country’s top court backed Maduro.
Machado has the highest approval rating among 15 political figures connected to Venezuela – including Trump and Rodriguez – in the monthly Latam Pulse survey by AtlasIntel and Bloomberg, but her support dipped in August to 53 per cent approval from a high of 72 per cent in July.
“The positive boost Maria Corina received after the earthquake has faded amid growing uncertainty. The changes she promised, at least in the public imagination, seem increasingly out of reach,” AtlasIntel chief executive Andrei Roman said on social media platform X.
“Even if it is not her fault, the current situation is affecting her credibility and her ability to build the future most Venezuelans envisioned after Maduro's removal.”
Machado will pay a political price for saying she would return to Venezuela after the earthquakes, then not doing so, said one opposition figure who is not part of Machado’s faction, adding that her relationship with Washington is uncomfortable.
“It’s not an easy situation.”
The quakes killed at least 6,500 people and thousands more are missing.
Despite Maduro’s ouster and Trump’s oil deals, Venezuelans still suffer patchy public services and poor healthcare, said Maracaibo metal worker and local opposition organiser Gabriel Hernandez, 54, as he waited for a bus.
People would be ready to take to the streets to back Machado, he said.
“We’re all waiting for Maria Corina to return. We need the person we have placed our trust in to take the reins in this highly uncertain situation, and that can only happen with her presence here and then elections,” Hernandez said.
“Without a doubt, we would take to the streets with her and ensure that she becomes the candidate, the winner and the president of this country.” REUTERS

The Rada supported abolishing the duty-free allowance for parcels worth up to €150
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:02:39 EEST
19:02:39 KST

The Rada supported abolishing the duty-free allowance for parcels worth up to €150
Kyiv • UNN
Parliament approved in principle two bills introducing 20% VAT on parcels worth €0 and above. The new rules may take effect in July 2027.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted as a basis two draft laws that abolish the tax exemption for parcels worth up to 150 euros, reports UNN.
Details
Draft Law No. 15460 "On Amendments to the Customs Code of Ukraine Regarding the Specifics of Customs Formalities for Goods Moved (Sent) Across the Customs Border of Ukraine in International Postal and Express Shipments" was supported as a basis by 267 MPs.
The document amends the Customs Code of Ukraine (which regulates customs procedures, border clearance rules, and the 150-euro threshold for import duty).
According to the draft law, VAT would be introduced on imported goods purchased through marketplaces, starting from 0 euros.
Currently, international shipments worth up to 150 euros are not subject to import VAT or import duty. Under the proposed rules, the limit itself would remain, but its application would change: goods worth up to 150 euros would be exempt only from duty. Thus, VAT at the standard rate of 20% would be charged starting from the first euro of the value of the goods.
For shipments worth more than 150 euros, the basis for calculating the duty would change. It would be charged at a rate of 10% of the entire invoice value of the parcel, rather than only on the amount exceeding 150 euros.
At the same time, private gifts sent free of charge worth up to 45 euros are expected to remain exempt from taxation. The new rules would not apply to the distance sale of alcohol and tobacco.
Requirements are being introduced for the accounting of marketplaces, their representatives in Ukraine (for non-resident marketplaces), and a special guarantee for applying the distance-selling scheme.
A transitional period is предусмотрено for postal operators, express carriers, and marketplaces to adapt. During the first year, administrative liability would not apply for unintentional errors related to the incomplete or late payment of VAT for parcels worth up to 150 euros, provided that the tax itself is paid in full.
Draft Law No. 16051-1 "On Amendments to the Tax Code of Ukraine Regarding the Specifics of Value Added Taxation of Transactions Involving the Distance Sale of Goods Moved (Sent) Across the Customs Border of Ukraine in International Postal and Express Shipments" was supported as a basis by 273 MPs.
The document amends the Tax Code of Ukraine (which specifically establishes the rules for calculating and paying VAT on e-commerce and parcels).
It also provides that taxes on parcels will be credited to the special fund of the State Budget of Ukraine and directed toward meeting the needs of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
If the draft laws are adopted in their entirety, the provisions of the Tax Code and the Customs Code are to take effect no earlier than July 2027.

Gaza Cinema Academy: A new generation of Palestinian filmmakers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:02:14 UTC
19:02:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Their stories, their voices, their images: Inside Gaza Cinema Academy and a new generation behind the camera
"We are here" is the message behind the Gaza Cinema Academy, launched internationally at the 83rd Venice Film Festival. Its aim is to equip a new generation of Palestinian filmmakers with the tools to tell their own stories.
The academy was co-founded by Palestinian filmmakers Mai Masri and Ezzaldeen Shalh, with support from a group of Palestinian, Arab and international filmmakers and film-industry professionals including Tunisian director Kaouther Ben Hania, Palestinian director Annemarie Jacir, Palestinian actors Hiam Abbass and Saleh Bakri, Egyptian-American actor and filmmaker Ramy Youssef, Italian producer Graziella Bildesheim, and Egyptian film-industry professional Alaa Karkouti.
In Gaza, where electricity is scarce, equipment is difficult to access, and movement is severely restricted amid Israel's genocide and siege, the basic conditions for making films remain profoundly uncertain. At the same time, as Gaza is documented through an unprecedented volume of images, a more fundamental question has emerged: who gets to hold the camera, and who gets to tell the story?
It is from this tension that the Gaza Cinema Academy has emerged.
Internationally launched alongside an event at the Venice Film Festival celebrating the second edition of the Gaza International Festival for Women’s Cinema, the academy is an attempt to establish something more lasting than a series of workshops: a sustainable space for film education, production and exchange rooted in Gaza.
'A much greater need'
Its origins go back around two years, when filmmaker and educator Mai Masri and Ezzaldeen Shalh, who also runs the Gaza International Festival for Women’s Cinema, began discussing how to create a genuine pathway into filmmaking for young people in the besieged territory.
"We agreed that young people in Gaza needed more than occasional workshops; they needed a genuine training path that could provide them with knowledge, tools, and continuity," Mai tells The New Arab.
The first step was a Filmmaking Diploma, designed partly as a practical test of whether such an ambitious project could work under Gaza’s conditions. It quickly became clear to its organisers that the demand was considerably greater than a short course could accommodate.
"During the diploma, we saw the enormous passion among the trainees, both young men and women," Ezzaldeen recalls.
"We also realised that the need was much greater than a training course that would end after several months."
That experience eventually became the Gaza Cinema Academy.
For Ezzaldeen, establishing a film school during a devastating war is not a contradiction but the reason for doing it now.
"It may seem unusual to establish a film academy in Gaza at one of the harshest moments our people are experiencing, but for me, this is precisely what makes its existence necessary," he says.
"War does not only destroy buildings; it also threatens memory, images, and stories."
The academy’s central ambition, then, is not simply to teach technical skills. It is to shift young Palestinians from being subjects in images to becoming their authors.
"There is a generation living through an exceptional and extremely painful experience," Ezzaldeen continues, "and it is important that they possess the knowledge and tools that enable them to tell their own stories, rather than Gaza always remaining a story told by others."
Mai, whose long career in Palestinian cinema has centred on questions of memory, identity and human experience, sees the image in similarly expansive terms.
"I have come to believe that the image can be a means of preserving memory and resisting its erasure," she shares.
"Young people in Gaza are living through an extremely harsh experience today, but at the same time they have stories, perspectives, and creative energies that deserve to find their way into cinema and out into the world."
That distinction – between recording events and creating cinema – is important to both founders. The academy is not intended to produce an endless stream of images of destruction. It is meant to cultivate filmmakers capable of looking beyond the immediately spectacular to find stories in ordinary life, memory, relationships, and detail.
"We do not want cinema in Gaza to be limited to documenting tragedy, despite the importance of doing so," Ezzaldeen clarifies further.
"We want there to be a genuine cinematic life: education, production, films, festivals, and new generations capable of creating Palestinian cinema that carries their experience to the world."
Learning to look
For the trainees who came through the first diploma, the academy represents something more immediate: an opportunity to acquire a language they had often been approaching from the margins of journalism and media.
Raghda Al-Buhaisi arrived with a degree in Journalism and Media from the Islamic University of Gaza and years of experience in print journalism, radio, visual journalism and media coordination. Her turn towards filmmaking began with a photograph.
"I decided to join the diploma programme after creating a human-interest photo story – my first foray into the field of photography," she says.
"I wanted to learn more about the industry and hone my skills, particularly in film directing."
For Raghda, the attraction of cinema lies partly in its ability to communicate beyond the conventional structures of news.
"I realised this was the ideal way to convey our message as Palestinians – living under siege, genocide, and destruction to this very moment – through a seamless approach that reaches the minds and hearts of viewers worldwide, letting them know: ‘We are here.’"
The programme gave her a grounding in the mechanics of filmmaking – cinematography, shot selection, screenwriting, production, and directing – and made the transition from an idea to an actual film less abstract.
"I acquired numerous skills during my studies and through fieldwork – such as the art of cinematography, including angles, shot selection, and understanding what works best on camera," she explains.
"I also learned how to conceive, develop, and refine an idea, write a screenplay, and manage the production, execution, and directing processes."
Manar Abu Sha’ira, another trainee with a media degree and experience in television, radio and reporting, came to the programme with a related but distinct interest: visual storytelling as a way of getting closer to lives that might otherwise remain unseen.
"I am passionate about film, but for me, filmmaking is not only about art," she says. "I am also interested in documenting the reality around me and telling stories that might otherwise remain unseen."
Yet Manar is wary of reducing that reality to images of suffering.
"I want to learn how to tell these stories in a way that is honest and human, without simply showing suffering," she says.
"I want to show the people, their experiences, their resilience, and the small details of everyday life."
That emphasis on looking and listening before filming is fundamental to the academy’s approach.
"One of the most important things for me is that students first learn how to see and how to listen before they learn how to film," she says.
"Cinema is not simply technical knowledge of a camera or editing software; it is a relationship with people, place, memory, and detail."
Ezzaldeen makes a similar distinction. The academy, he says, will teach filmmaking "as an integrated process, not simply how to operate a camera."
Students will learn how to search for an idea, develop it into a treatment and screenplay, and move through all stages of filmmaking. But the deeper objective is to cultivate an individual point of view.
"Owning a camera does not necessarily make someone a filmmaker," he says. "What matters to us is that trainees learn how to observe, how to research, how to develop their own point of view, and how to use cinematic language to express it."
The insistence on practice is equally important. During the diploma, students were not confined to lectures but were expected to make films.
"We therefore want students to work on real films and projects, and to learn through experience, through their mistakes, and through collaborative work, rather than only through lectures," Mai explains.
For Manar, that practical component answers a personal difficulty familiar to many beginning filmmakers: knowing what one wants to say but not yet knowing how to make an audience see it.
"Sometimes I may have an idea in my head but find it difficult to translate it visually. I hope the academy will help me overcome this through practice and feedback," she says.
Women behind the camera
The academy’s early focus on young women and new voices is rooted partly in Mai and Ezzaldeen’s experience with the Gaza International Festival for Women’s Cinema, but also reflects a broader conviction that representation cannot stop with putting women on screen.
"For young women in Gaza, I believe there is an even greater need to open up opportunities for them, not only to appear in front of the camera, but to stand behind it, to write, direct, shoot, and make their own films," Mai affirms.
Ezzaldeen describes the same ambition in terms of who gets to shape the cinematic gaze.
Through their work with the women’s film festival, he explains, they became increasingly aware of "the importance of opening up more space for women, not only to be subjects in films, but to become the ones behind the camera, making decisions and shaping the vision, and to tell their experiences from their own perspectives."
The academy is nevertheless not exclusively a women’s institution. Its stated mission is to create opportunities for young women and men, with particular attention to people who have not previously had access to professional film education.
Mai describes this as part of a larger effort to allow new and diverse perspectives to emerge from Gaza.
"We want to give a new generation of young women and men access to cinematic knowledge and help new voices emerge that are capable of presenting Gaza and Palestine from diverse, personal, and human perspectives."
The trainees’ own cinematic preferences suggest the kind of filmmaking that may emerge from that approach.
Raghda is particularly drawn to documentary cinema because of its direct relationship with reality. “I feel it is perhaps the most capable medium for conveying a message,” she claims.
Her aesthetic instincts, however, are not purely journalistic, as she is attentive to colour, natural effects, close-ups and the expressive power of unforced human presence.
“A person appearing natural and unfeigned is more powerful than any special effect when it comes to conveying a message or idea,” she elaborates. “I am drawn to close-ups and love the details that conceal significant, moving elements.”
Manar, meanwhile, gravitates towards “realistic and human-centred cinema”, particularly films that appear simple but contain deeper meanings.
“I like documentaries and films that make me feel close to the characters and their real experiences,” she says. “In general, I am influenced by filmmakers who focus on honest storytelling, real emotions, and small details rather than relying only on dramatic scenes.”
There is a striking convergence here. The academy is being established amid an overwhelming historical reality, but the filmmakers being trained within it are interested not only in history at its most monumental, but rather in faces, details, ordinary experiences and the spaces between major events.
Making cinema when the basics are missing
Of course, the academy’s ambitions confront a brutal practical reality.
In most film schools, access to a functioning classroom, electricity, internet, editing computers and cameras would barely merit discussion. In Gaza, each can become a significant obstacle.
"Every detail that might be ordinary in any film school elsewhere in the world becomes a daily challenge here: the venue, electricity, internet access, transportation, equipment, and even the ability of students and trainers to reach the training location," Ezzaldeen says.
The problem is not simply that equipment is expensive, but also that getting it into Gaza can itself be extremely difficult. The academy needs cameras, lenses, sound technology, lighting, editing systems and storage devices, while existing resources have been depleted by destruction and displacement.
Raghda describes the situation from the trainee’s perspective: "We lack the logistics and tools needed to carry out our work as filmmakers; our computers are worn out, and we have no cameras – most of our equipment was lost under the rubble, broken, or left behind during displacement."
There is another obstacle that cannot be solved by acquiring technology: "People here are unwilling to talk or engage; they have lost their zest for life," Raghda says.
"They are preoccupied with securing basic necessities and have no desire to speak. They feel the world has let them down."
For a filmmaker attempting to document human experience, this creates ethical and emotional difficulties. The camera may be ready, but the person in front of it may not be.
"This is a major challenge," she says, "dealing with someone who has lost everything, while the world offers no sympathy."
Manar points to the more general constraints: "There are limitations in movement, electricity, equipment, and sometimes even finding suitable places or people to film."
The academy’s response is necessarily pragmatic. It has learned not to wait for normality. "Our experience over the past period has taught us not to wait for ideal conditions," Ezzaldeen says, "because if we wait for them in Gaza, we may never begin."
Instead, the organisers are trying to build the academy incrementally, using whatever resources are available while developing connections with filmmakers and institutions outside Gaza.
Mai stresses that the international network is not meant to substitute for the academy’s presence in Gaza.
"It is very important to me that the Academy remains rooted in Gaza and that the young people there remain at the heart of the project," she says.
"At the same time, we need to open windows to the world for them through trainers, filmmakers, institutions, and festivals that can collaborate with us."
That model is likely to be central to the academy’s survival. It is neither fully local nor an external programme delivered into Gaza. Instead, the organisers envision a structure in which training and resources can flow in both directions.
"Sustainability will not be achieved through financial support alone, although that is essential," Mai says.
"It also requires building a long-term network of relationships, cooperation, and exchange, so that filmmakers in Gaza feel that they are part of a wider cinematic community and that distance and blockade do not have to mean cultural isolation."
From Gaza to Venice – and back again
The decision to unveil the academy internationally at the Venice Film Festival was therefore deliberate. For Ezzaldeen, the symbolism matters.
"We chose Venice for the international announcement of the Gaza Cinema Academy because we wanted this initiative to move from Gaza into an international cinematic space," he says, "and to say that Gaza, despite everything happening there, is still capable of producing cultural and cinematic initiatives and of thinking about the future."
The launch was paired with an event dedicated to the second edition of the Gaza International Festival for Women’s Cinema. The two initiatives share an ecosystem but remain distinct: one focuses on education, training and production; the other on creating a platform for films and filmmakers.
Their connection, however, is straightforward. A film school can teach people to make films, while a festival can provide a platform for those films to be seen.
"For me, this is the deeper connection between the Academy and the festival: to help films be made, and then to help those films find their way to audiences and to the world," Mai says.
The festival’s second edition is being developed as a broader continuation of its inaugural experience, with fiction, documentaries and screenplays, alongside a stronger presence for women filmmakers and participants from different parts of the world.
For Ezzaldeen, bringing both initiatives into the international cinematic sphere is ultimately an argument against seeing Gaza only through the vocabulary of destruction.
"We do not want cinema in Gaza to be limited to documenting tragedy," he repeats. "We want there to be a genuine cinematic life."
That aspiration may sound modest in another context. In Gaza, it is anything but.
For Raghda, the desire to make films is inseparable from the need to insist on Palestinian presence. Her first photographic experience led her towards filmmaking precisely because she saw in it a way of reaching people beyond the immediate geography of Gaza.
Her ambition is now to continue developing the skills she acquired and eventually "establish a name for myself in this industry at both local and international levels."
Manar's ambitions are quieter but equally rooted in the future. She is looking to gain greater confidence, practical experience, and the chance to learn from other filmmakers and her colleagues. Her cinematic interest lies in the intimate rather than the spectacular: "simple stories" with "deeper meanings," honest emotions and small details.
The academy’s founders are betting that these individual perspectives are precisely what Palestinian cinema needs.
"Gaza has artists, filmmakers, and young people with dreams, imagination, and a desire to make films," Mai says.
"It is important that they themselves are able to hold the camera and tell their lives through their own eyes."
For Ezzaldeen, that is ultimately why the academy has to exist now, rather than waiting for a less impossible moment.
"Continuing to teach cinema inside Gaza is not a cultural luxury," he confirms. "It is part of protecting memory and giving a new generation the ability to express itself."
The Gaza Cinema Academy therefore begins not from a position of stability but from uncertainty. Its classrooms, equipment and future remain subject to circumstances far beyond the control of its organisers.
Yet its underlying proposition is remarkably concrete: that even amid devastation, cinematic education can create something that destruction cannot easily erase – the ability to look, to listen, to imagine, and eventually to say, in one’s own images, we are here.
Mariana Hristova is a freelance film critic, cultural journalist, and programmer. She contributes to national and international outlets and has curated programs for Filmoteca de Catalunya, Arxiu Xènctric, and goEast Wiesbaden, among others. Her professional interests include cinema from the European peripheries and archival and amateur films

The meaning of fake marble
Unknown

Humans have prized marble for its colours, patterns, texture and heft for thousands of years. In this video, Mary McGillivray, a digital creator and PhD student at the University of Melbourne, explores how, for as long as we’ve prized it, we’ve been inventing ways to fake it. McGillivray traverses Europe to investigate how, from ancient Rome to modern home-improvement stores, we’ve developed techniques to cast, plaster and paint imitations of the metamorphic rock. And, as McGillivray argues, this process has been about more than finding a cheap alternative to a luxury material. Rather, the millennia-long history of our fascination with marble, and of our attempts to recreate it, has much to say about how humanity is inspired by, and competes with, the natural world.
