EU opens door for Canada to become bloc's first 'associate member': European Commisison chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:31:36 UTC
18:31:36 KST

The European Commission president on Wednesday opened the door for Canada to become the European Union's first "associate member," calling for a fundamental rethinking of the bloc's partnerships amid growing geopolitical and economic challenges.
Addressing the European Parliament in her 2026 State of the Union speech, Ursula von der Leyen said Europe must "urgently reimagine our partnerships" and proposed working with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to bring relations between the EU and Canada "to the highest level possible."
"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union," she said.
Von der Leyen presented the proposal as part of a broader effort to deepen cooperation with like-minded partners on strategic areas, including energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, cybersecurity, and economic security.
The proposal would represent a new form of relationship between the EU and a non-EU country, although von der Leyen did not give details on what an "associate member" status would entail or what institutional arrangements would be required.
Von der Leyen said the EU had to secure access to critical raw materials, strengthen its energy independence, and develop its own capabilities in emerging technologies while cooperating with trusted partners.
She argued that Europe has chosen to pursue a more independent path, saying a stronger Europe is emerging that is better equipped to defend itself, secure its energy supplies, and protect its economic interests.
 
Economy and energy
Von der Leyen identified restarting Europe's economy as the EU's "number one priority," pointing to the bloc's large single market, industrial base, savings, and currency while acknowledging continued fragmentation in capital markets, networks and purchasing power.
She said the EU had reached a political agreement on a "one Europe, one market" roadmap and called for the overhaul of the single market to be completed by the end of next year.
Von der Leyen also announced a new international connectivity initiative linking the South Caucasus and Central Asia with the European market through the so-called Middle Corridor.
Von der Leyen said Europe cannot remain an industrial powerhouse if its energy prices stay structurally high.
She highlighted the EU’s efforts to reduce dependence on Russian gas through diversified supplies and investments in renewable energy and nuclear power.
Von der Leyen also called for greater electrification, saying the EU’s goal should be to double the share of electricity by 2040.
"In short, let's make Europe's future electric. This is a must," she said.
 
China and critical raw materials
Von der Leyen also warned that Europe's trade relationship with China had reached a "tipping point," citing an EU trade deficit with China of around €1 billion ($1.1 billion) a day.
She said the bloc is seeking dialogue with Beijing to rebalance trade, but insisted that the dialogue must produce results.
At the same time, she highlighted Europe's dependence on China for critical raw materials, saying the EU is more than 80% dependent on China for many such materials and 90% dependent for some rare earths.
She announced plans for a new “European Corporation on Critical Raw Materials” to help secure and stockpile supplies needed for electric vehicles, chips, batteries, clean technologies, and defense.
 
Artificial intelligence
Von der Leyen described the issue of artificial intelligence as the second major "tipping point" alongside climate change.
She cited concerns over cyberattacks, self-improving models, and AI systems acting beyond their intended environments, while defending the EU's AI Act as an important framework for establishing safeguards.
Europe, she said, should cooperate with partners including Canada and the UK on AI model evaluation, verification, early warning, and AI security.
At the same time, she stressed that Europe needs its own technological capabilities, particularly in areas linked to national security.

Amnesty says Iran committed 'crimes against humanity' in 2022 protests crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:30:07 UTC
18:30:07 KST

Amnesty says Iran committed 'crimes against humanity' in 2022 protests crackdown
In a report released Wednesday, Amnesty International said Iranian authorities committed “crimes against humanity” during the violent crackdown on the 2022 protests known as the movement “Woman, Life, Freedom” that was sparked by the death of Mahsa Amini.
Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in the crackdown on 2022 protests that left hundreds dead, Amnesty International said Wednesday, adding Tehran's suppression of new demonstrations this year bore the "same hallmarks" but on an even wider scale.
The crackdown in 2022 amounted to "crimes against humanity" including murder, torture, rape and enforced disappearance, Amnesty said in a report marking four years since those protests, warning that the authorities' actions earlier this year were "on an even deadlier and more staggering scale".
The London-based rights group named 87 national and regional officials, six of whom were subsequently killed in US-Israeli air strikes, who it believed were responsible in the chain of command and should face international justice.
Read moreIran sentences Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi to six years in prison
Several months of protests against the Islamic republic's theocratic authorities known as the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement erupted in September 2022 following the custody death of Iranian Kurdish woman Mahsa Amini who had been arrested for allegedly violating the strict dress rules for women.
These were the biggest protests in Iran in recent years until demonstrations earlier this year sparked by anger over the cost of living that peaked on the nights of January 8 and 9.
On both occasions authorities responded with a deadly crackdown that caused international outrage. Amnesty's 1,000 page report focused on the 2022 protests while making clear that the crackdown in 2026 followed the same pattern while being even more severe.
"The extensive evidence gathered and analysed in our report leaves no doubt: Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity to crush the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising," said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International's secretary general.
Amnesty urged the UN General Assembly to "create an international criminal justice mechanism aimed at prosecuting those most implicated".
'Unlawfully killed'
The 87 officials it named included former supreme leader Ali Khamenei and top figures in the Revolutionary Guards who were killed in the US-Israeli war this year.
But some others, including Ahmad Vahidi, who was then the interior minister and now chief of the Revolutionary Guards, are still alive.
Read moreIran’s youth on the front lines of protests face worsening crackdown
"The security forces deployed by the authorities unlawfully killed hundreds of protesters and bystanders, including dozens of children" in the crackdown from September to December 2022, Amnesty said.
"They subjected thousands more to arbitrary arrests, incommunicado detention, enforced disappearance and torture or other ill-treatment. They raped and committed other sexual violence against some of those arrested in connection with the protests," it added.
Amnesty said it had identified 377 protesters and bystanders, including 56 children, who lost their lives during the 2022 protests, of whom at least 326 were killed by security forces, including with metal pellets fired at close range.
'Unprecedented massacres'
One of those killed identified by Amnesty in the report was 62-year-old Minoo Majidi who was hit by metal pellets while protesting in the western city of Kermanshah in September 2022.
"She was killed on the street. She had gone to the street for change, to shout 'freedom'," her daughter Mahsa Piraei, who lives outside Iran, told AFP.
"The world thinks the protests were about freedom for women. They were, but they were also about freedom for people and the right to life," she added.
Read moreIran’s military-grade crackdown expands from Kurdish areas – and Kurds fear the worst
Amnesty described the crackdown this year as the "unprecedented massacres of thousands of protesters and bystanders" which "bear the same hallmarks as the crimes against humanity documented in this report, yet on an even deadlier and more staggering scale".
"Seeking justice is partly for my mum but to help the still many lives who are in danger," Piraei added, referring to the dozens of people arrested during the January protests who rights groups say are at risk of execution.
They include Ali Zarei, who was blinded in one eye during 2022 protests and then took refuge in Germany, but returned to Iran this year and was arrested and sentenced to death.
"We need to shout out their names," Piraei added.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

The speedy speech from the throne: What the papers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:30:03 UTC
18:30:03 KST

The speedy speech from the throne: What the papers say
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch papers found little to unite around in Tuesday’s king’s speech, with editorials picking at what was missing in substance and delivery.
The Volkskrant in its editorial remarked on the “lack of urgency” in the speech from the throne over measures to combat and alleviate climate change. Former climate minister turned prime minister Jetten’s green profile is “fading”, the paper wrote, as recent forecasts warn the Netherlands will come nowhere near realising its climate goals.
The less-than-emphatic reference to this year’s extreme temperatures in the king’s speech illustrates the prime minister’s wish to remain pals with everyone, by avoiding polarising issues, such as climate and a speedier energy transition, the paper said.
“Politicians too often believe that strict measures to protect the environment will weaken the country’s competitive strength but the reverse is the case in the long term,” it warned.
Trouw expressed surprise at the VVD’s stubborn and out-of-touch insistence on shielding the rich while raising taxes for everyone else when, according to a poll commissioned by the paper, voters across the board, including 50% of VVD voters, would support a rise in wealth tax.
“It is as if the VVD is fighting a rearguard battle over something a majority of voters want to get rid of, as economists and all manner of advisory commissions insist that it is wealth that should be taxed, not labour,” the paper wrote. “It will be up to the CDA and D66 to win that battle in the next few months.”
The Telegraaf commented on the fact that although the king’s speech contained few new measures, it was the longest in history, with 2,889 words, spoken in places at breakneck speed.
Fewer figures and less jargon went some way to make the speech more accessible and “the good news” was the king speedy delivery: an average of 2.5 words per second against his mother, former queen Beatrix’s, 1.6.
When the king mentioned the farmers and the “need for clarity regarding their long-term prospects,” they were actually setting fire to roads, “a standout moment”, the paper said.
The NRC, in its own analysis of the speech, has been totting up the number of times the word “cooperation” appeared. It’s 14, and that, the paper said, is a measure of how desperate this minority cabinet is to secure the support of the opposition both on the right and on the left.
The wars in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran are “only referred to halfway into the speech”, the paper noted, and while there is “violence” in Ukraine, the violence in Gaza and Iran is qualified as “a situation”.
In a scathing comment, the AD criticised the actions allegedly perpetrated by farmers during the king’s speech. “Those who want to save democracy don’t sabotage it”, the paper wrote.
“The most relevant passage in the speech was the one about polarisation. The one about the softer voice of people who are genuinely worried, which is increasingly being drowned out in the Netherlands.” The paper pointed out that sabotaging the railway system (which is still being investigated and has not been attributed to the farmers) comes with a penalty of 15-year prison sentence.

China Isn’t Buying Silicon Valley’s Call for an AI Slowdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

For years, many of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley have argued that the US is locked in an AI arms race with China and that the consequences of losing would be disastrous. But over the past week, those same executives have started emphasizing a different message. AI has the potential to become so dangerous, tech leaders say, that the two countries urgently need to work together to slow the race down.
“Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post published Saturday titled “We Must Pace the Frontier.”
China’s government and AI companies have made it clear that they’re deeply skeptical of Amodei’s proposal, but not because they want to keep blindly racing ahead or don’t believe the technology poses serious risks. The problem the Chinese government and Chinese AI companies see is far simpler. They think they’re being offered a bad deal.
“The AI safety community in China is growing and shares many of the same concerns that American labs do,” says Kevin Xu, founder of the technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital and a former White House staffer under President Barack Obama. “The gulf lies between an Anthropic-led vision that would only subjugate and restrict China first to maximize leverage before talking. Meanwhile, China would only talk if it’s being treated from a position of equals.”
Amodei wrote that a “key part” of the slowdown strategy should be ensuring that the US and other democracies maintain “as large as possible” a lead in AI development over autocracies like China. To do that, he urged the US to take steps including cracking down on chip smuggling and preventing unauthorized model distillation by Chinese companies.
“His essay specifically says the pacing of AI is conditional to increasing the lead over China," says Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis and a digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, “which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers.”
Amodei went on to make what might seem like a heroic leap in logic: He argued that weakening China’s AI industry would somehow give the US more leverage and make “an agreement more likely in the future.” How, exactly, that is supposed to entice Beijing to come to the negotiating table is left unexplained. (To Amodei’s credit, he later admitted in a television interview that he has “no idea how to negotiate with China.”)
The government officials, AI researchers, and other prominent commentators in China who responded to Amodei haven’t argued that AI poses no risks. But many of them clearly resent the idea that their country should simultaneously be treated as an essential governance partner and a competitor that needs to be constrained.
When asked about Amodei’s blog post on Monday at a press conference, Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, didn’t mince words: He described the proposal as “fearmongering, confrontation, and vicious competition” that would only hamper global AI cooperation efforts. The next day, the ministry also stressed that “China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI.”
The mixed comments are reflective of another reason that Beijing may be less receptive to the Anthropic CEO’s warnings than other audiences. Unlike many of the loudest voices in Silicon Valley, China’s leaders are not primarily concerned about so-called existential risks from AI, such as the possibility that a rogue agent could kill everyone on Earth. Like in many other policy areas, Beijing’s prevailing anxiety is that AI could disrupt domestic social stability or threaten the Chinese Communist Party’s grip on power.
“Beijing finds it difficult to take these calls at face value partly because it’s skeptical of the possibility of achieving AGI and doubtful of the narrative that AI poses extreme risks to humanity,” says Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow at the Center for a New American Security focused on national security and artificial intelligence. “Although Beijing is starting to recognize loss-of-control risks, the risk that Beijing seems most worried about is the threat AI could pose to CCP rule.”
In a recent essay, China’s minister of state security Chen Yixin warned that AI could fuel political disinformation, cyberattacks, espionage, social unrest, and new military threats. He spent far less time on the kinds of doomsday scenarios that frequently preoccupy people at US frontier AI labs.
“Chinese policymakers tend to read US companies’ calls for AI safety as instrumental,” says Nie. “They believe that US companies are seeking to inflate their own value ahead of potential IPOs or to slow down their competitors, which are primarily Chinese companies at this point.”
That skepticism is also shared by many people who work in China’s AI industry, which has broadly focused on releasing lower-cost, open-weight models. In a widely shared essay published on Sunday, a researcher at DeepSeek said he believes AI could move human society to one of two extremes. In the first, powerful AI is broadly available and raises living standards. In the second, a handful of tech companies control the most advanced systems and the resources that come with them, making it even harder for everyone else to catch up.
“That is why I still believe the most advanced intelligence should be made available to everyone in an open and inexpensive way,” the DeepSeek engineer wrote. “I do not trust Anthropic or OpenAI to do that. And I especially do not want Anthropic to control the most advanced artificial intelligence or AGI.”
None of this means that US-China cooperation on AI safety is doomed. Preliminary negotiations between the two countries are reportedly already underway ahead of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s planned visit to Washington later this month to meet with US President Donald Trump.
There are plenty of reasons to be hopeful that these discussions will result in some progress, even though it may be incremental. Both governments have expressed worries about some of the same things, including cybersecurity threats, the misuse of powerful models, and the possibility that increasingly capable AI systems could behave in unexpected ways.
“There are people who genuinely care about AI safety on both sides, and there’s a possibility they could engage in good-faith discussion in narrowly scoped issues,” says Nie. What might move the needle most, she says, is designing a credible way for each country to verify that the other is abiding by its commitments.
Still, others worry that rhetoric from Amodei and other US tech leaders about weakening China could erode the fragile trust that diplomatic talks depend on. Kristy Loke, a research fellow at the AI safety nonprofit MATS Research, says that Amodei’s missive may ultimately backfire. “Dario is undermining one of the few available levers for reducing the very risks he professes to take seriously,” she says.

Hague Court Finds Former Kosovo President Thaci Guilty Of War Crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:28:12 UTC
18:28:12 KST

An international tribunal in The Hague has found former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) commander and later Kosovo President Hashim Thaci guilty of war crimes and sentenced him to 25 years in prison.
The 58-year-old Thaci, and three other former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army who fought Serb forces in the 1998-99 war, was convicted on four counts of war crimes: illegal and arbitrary arrest and detention, cruel treatment, torture, and murder.
Judge Charles Smith said the men, widely regarded as national heroes in Kosovo, had been engaged in a "common criminal purpose" that involved arbitrary detention of at least 385 people at locations in Kosovo and northern Albania under KLA control.
Some 348 detainees were subjected to cruel treatment and 303 to torture, the court ruled. This included pulling out people's nails, breaking their limbs, and subjecting them to mock executions.
The court found the defendants guilty of 96 cases of unlawful killing. The victims had taken "no active part in hostilities."
The verdict was roundly condemned in Kosovo, where Prime Minister Albin Kurti called it an “unacceptable injustice." In Washington, a State Department spokesman told RFE/RL "we urge all parties to respect the court’s decision."
Detailed Atrocities
The judgement provided gruesome details of the crimes committed.
"One detainee held in Lapushnik recounted that when KLA members beat one of his co-detainees, the co-detainee pleaded with the soldiers, saying, 'Give me a bullet, don't have me suffer like this,' to which one of the soldiers responded, 'There is no bullet for you, we will take your life little by little,'" Smith told the courtroom.
The judgement described how the KLA identified and detained its opponents often on the basis of "unverified rumors" to consolidate their control over Kosovo during the period of April 1998 to August 1999. The detainees were accused of being collaborators, spies, and traitors.
They were tortured and mistreated in school buildings, cowsheds, and basements, Smith said, adding that some survivors endured long-term depression or were no longer able to walk due to their mistreatment.
For those who did not survive, death was not the end of their mistreatment, the court heard.
"Many of the murder victims' bodies were found in a condition that involved further outrage upon their dignity," Smith said. He described one case where a family learnt of a victim's death from a media report before finding the mutilated body by a roadside.
"The bodies of some murder victims were never found, thus further contributing to the pain of surviving relatives," Smith said.
The convicted men's ultimate aim was to secure power in Kosovo after independence by eliminating political opponents, the court ruled.
Thaci, who stood in silence as the judge read out the sentence, had denied all charges, as had the other convicted men. Selimi received 13 years in prison, Veseli 18 years, and Krasniqi 25 years.
All four men had "significantly contributed to the common criminal purpose," Smith said. This included, he said, both encouraging the crimes and participating in them.
A Brutal War
The KLA emerged in the mid-1990s, after years of peaceful resistance by Kosovo Albanians to the regime of Slobodan Milosevic.
From small guerrilla groups, it grew into a force fighting against ethnic Serb and Yugoslav troops. Hundreds of thousands of ethnic Albanians were driven from their homes in the conflict, raising the specter of a repeat of the ethnic cleansing practiced in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some 13,000 people were killed or went missing.
In March 1999, NATO launched air strikes against Yugoslav targets, leading to the withdrawal of Yugoslav and ethnic Serb forces. Kosovo declared independence in 2008.
"This case is not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army and its goal of independence for Kosovo. This case is not concerned with weighing the responsibilities of one side against those of the other," Smith said.
But in Prishtina, the verdict was met with protesters marching through the streets chanting "KLA, KLA" in support of the four convicted men.
"This is a catastrophic judgment, against the Albanian nation," a man in military uniform who said he had been a soldier told RFE/RL's Kosovo Service.
Crowds had watched Smith delivering the verdict on big screens erected across the country.
Later, a group of people ignored calls for calm from politicians and pelted the building of the European Union's civilian peacekeeping mission in Prishtina with stones before marching toward the main government building.
Police in the Hague had to use a water cannon to clear the area around the court after Thaci supporters began protesting. The unrest was quickly quelled.
Kosovo's Prime Minister, Albin Kurti, called the verdict an “unacceptable injustice and a severe and harmful punishment." He said the convictions must be overturned in an appeal process "as soon as possible."
Ramush Haradinaj, a former KLA leader and later Kosovo Prime Minister, said the verdict was "unacceptable, unjust," adding "the KLA fought a just liberation war."
In 2019 Haradinaj also appeared at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the international court set up to hear cases relating to the 1990s conflict, but was not formally indicted.
Thaci's lawyer, Richard-Pierre Prosper, called the verdict a “travesty of justice” and said the outcome was predetermined. Prosper said the defense would appeal but that it could take years for the process to reach conclusion. He called on Kosovo's parliament to stop cooperating with the Specialist Chambers.
The US State Department told RFE/RL it respected the judgement and urged all parties to do so, too. A spokesman said they should "avoid inflammatory rhetoric and continue working toward a peaceful, democratic future."
Serbia’s outgoing Interior Minister Ivica Dacic claimed the convictions were "confirmation" that the KLA was "a criminal and terrorist organization.”
The court, however, made no such ruling.
"This case concerns the acts and conduct of the accused," Smith said.

Von der Leyen announces near-term aid measures for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:27:41 EEST
18:27:41 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has announced measures to assist Ukraine this winter, including providing unprecedented support, strengthening air defenses, and tightening sanctions against Russia.
“We know that the coming winter will be tough for Ukraine. But we also know that North Korean missiles and Russian drones cannot break the Ukrainian spirit of resistance. Because the people of Ukraine are fighting for something. They are fighting for the survival of their country, for their identity and for their freedom. And they are also fighting for our freedom and our self-determination. Our task remains to support Ukraine as best we can,” she stated in Strasbourg on Wednesday during the European Parliament's plenary session, as part of the annual 2026 State of the Union address.
She named providing assistance to Ukraine as “our strongest-ever support to Ukraine over the toughest winter of the war.” “Together with our partners, we will provide humanitarian aid and reinforce Ukraine's supplies of power and heating,” the President of the European Commission explained.
As a second point, von der Leyen highlighted the strengthening of Ukraine's air defense. “Last week, for the first time, we approved the purchase of American Patriot interceptor missiles. These now need to be delivered urgently. But we must also jointly reduce our dependence on a single supplier. That is why we would like to develop with Ukraine an affordable, modular missile-defence system. At the heart of this collaboration is the Freya project. Here we are combining the Ukrainians' combat experience and innovativeness with Europe's technological leadership. And, of course, our substantial production capacity. But Freya is only the beginning. More is needed,” she explained.
In this regard, von der Leyen announced the launch of a new program of joint projects with Ukrainian companies, utilizing remaining funds from the SAFE fund.
The European Commission President identified the tightening of sanctions against Russia as the third element of aid to Ukraine. “What is needed is not necessarily new sanctions, but above all the enforcement of existing sanctions,” she explained.

India to question Google over 500k Gmail accounts linked to BRICS bomb hoaxes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:24:35 UTC
18:24:35 KST

India to question Google over 500k Gmail accounts linked to BRICS bomb hoaxes
India will question Google over a network of 513,847 Gmail accounts that were unearthed in a probe into recent bomb threats targeting government offices and countries that participated in the BRICS Summit in New Delhi.
Police in the western Indian state of Gujarat uncovered the database of email credentials from two people arrested over bomb threats to the state’s top lawmaking body, the Legislative Assembly, as well as the offices of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, and countries participating in the summit. Similar emails were also sent to ten schools and three courts in Gujarat. 
Gujarat is the home state of both Modi and Shah. The threats were later found to be hoaxes. 
Roshan Kumar Bhumihar, arrested from Bhagalpur in the eastern Bihar state, led the police to Gulshan Kumar Singh from Deoghar in neighboring Jharkhand state, who allegedly supplied the Gmail accounts used to send the threats out. Singh was also arrested, and the devices used to transmit the threats were seized.
Police say Singh had been generating email IDs in bulk since 2022 and supplying them as ready-to-use accounts. Investigators are surprised at how the large number of accounts were created and operated without getting caught in Google’s security systems. 
“We will write to Google, ask them to make some policy changes so [safeguards] cannot be bypassed,” senior Gujarat Police cybercrime official Vivek Bheda said, according to local reports.
Police also plan to formally make Google a subject of the investigation, although it is unclear whether the US-based tech major will face any charges.
The Gmail accounts were allegedly created specifically for sending email threats as well as for carrying out other cybercrimes. The investigators allege the suspects shared the email accounts to associates in Bangladesh and received financial support from them.
One of the people arrested was also in contact with a buyer in Bangladesh who purchased batches of accounts and paid partly in cryptocurrency, Reuters reported.

EU proposes new security strategy to complement NATO's Article 4 amid Russian attacks
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:24:00 EEST
18:24:00 KST

EU proposes new security strategy to complement NATO's Article 4 amid Russian attacks
In response to Russia's intensifying hybrid attacks on Europe, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has announced plans for a new security strategy for European countries to complement NATO's Article 4.
Source: von der Leyen during her annual address to the European Parliament on 16 September, as reported by European Pravda
Quote: "As the threat level climbs, so must Europe's preparedness. This is why I will propose, together with the HRVP [Kaja Kallas – ed.], a new European security strategy.
I believe it is time for Europe's own Article 4 – or an Emergency Security Protocol. When triggered by one member state, all member states would convene. To coordinate a European response. To deter further escalation. And to mitigate the impact."
Details: Von der Leyen noted that cyberattacks, sabotage, arson and drone incursions into the EU are intensifying every day.
She stressed that Europe needs its own response plan for hybrid threats.
"We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents. Those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security. In other words, a mechanism to flank NATO's Article 4," the Commission president said.
For reference: NATO's Article 4 enables any member state to request consultations with its allies if it considers that its territorial integrity is under threat. It is considered a preliminary step towards invoking NATO's Article 5.
Background:
- In August, members of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party called for NATO Treaty Article 4 consultations after a drone was spotted near a Ukrainian aircraft in Leipzig.
- In May, Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu also said that a Russian drone crashing into a residential building in Galați could justify invoking Article 4 for consultations with NATO allies.

Ukraine protests Finland's football match against Belarus
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:23:35 EEST
18:23:35 KST

Ukraine's embassy in Finland has sent a diplomatic note to the Finnish Foreign Ministry over the staging of a football match between Finland and Belarus in Helsinki, according to Helsingin Sanomat.
Finland will face Belarus in a Nations League tie at Helsinki's Olympic Stadium on 29 September.
Ukraine's ambassador to Finland, Mykhailo Vydoinyk, told HS that the embassy is disappointed the match will be held in Helsinki.
He said he hoped the game would be moved outside Finland.
In recent years, Russia and Belarus have used hybrid tactics against the European Union, including the weaponisation of migration. Last week, six people were found hiding inside a vehicle at the Port of Helsinki in a case linked to a wider phenomenon in which people who have entered the Schengen area from Belarus are transported through different countries to other parts of Europe.
Finland and Belarus were drawn in the same Nations League group in March. The Football Association of Finland initially said the home match against Belarus would be played at a neutral venue.
In May, however, Helsinki's Olympic Stadium was announced as the venue for the match. The Finnish FA cited the International Olympic Committee's policy allowing Belarusian athletes to compete in international events under certain conditions.
That decision also cited sporting fairness, the importance of home advantage for the Finnish team, and the players' readiness and desire to play the match on home soil. It also took into account the views of Finnish supporters.
Vydoinyk said he was surprised by the Finnish FA's decision, saying it ran counter to Finland's otherwise strong support for Ukraine.
Finland last hosted a Belarusian team in autumn 2024, when HJK faced Dinamo Minsk. In the spring of 2025, both Finland's women's and men's futsal teams played Belarus on neutral ground.
The Finnish Football Association meanwhile says it will use the match to raise support for Ukrainians, with the net proceeds from ticket sales donated to humanitarian efforts in Ukraine.
Finland will face Belarus twice in September. Although Belarus is the designated home team for one of the fixtures, the match will be played in Budapest.

Coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said the drone was intercepted at around 6.50 pm local time (1550GMT) Tuesday before entering restricted airspace, with its wreckage falling south of the city.

Incoming minister: Russia talk has made foreign investors more cautious
Talking about the Russian threat has made foreign investors looking at Estonia more wary incoming Economy Minister Liina Vahtras (Reform) said.
However, these discussions are necessary, and the resulting transparency has also earned more international trust in Estonia, added Vahtras, who also championed a move towards more automation and artificial intelligence (AI) for traditional industries.
Vahtras, a former head of the national e-residency program, was appointed minister of economic affairs and communications by the Reform Party on Tuesday.
Your new colleague [Defense Minister] Martin Herem has been talked about recently due to claims he is stoking fears of war in warning of a new Russian attack. A fear of war affects not only consumer decisions inside Estonia but also those by foreign investors. Should we be talking about how dangerous it is to be next door to Russia?
I think talking about the danger has actually earned Estonia a great deal of trust, and to a certain extent we definitely needed to do that. As far as foreign investment is concerned, that naturally also affects investors' decisions.
What should our message be?
Our message should be that we are prepared, we know what we are doing and we have the necessary capabilities. That falls somewhat within the remit of my new colleague, Martin Herem, but what we have actually seen at the Estonian Business and Innovation Agency is that the decision-making period for foreign investors has gotten longer. This is where we as the state can step in and explain what we have done, why we can still be trusted and that Estonia is protected.
Industrial companies are struggling. Wage-price inflation also affected by tax hikes have made production costly. What is the future of so-called traditional industry in Estonia?
What we have been seeing is that they certainly need to take even bigger and longer strides toward automation, digitization and the use of artificial intelligence. We are seeing that businesses are very interested in this. For example, the Estonian Business and Innovation Agency has developed an innovation loan which attracted a very large number of applications and expressions of interest, and the same was true of the AI grant. We had to close it off completely in less than an hour as more than 200 applications had been submitted. So the interest is strong, which means the need is clearly there. Businesses recognize that need, and this is where we can help.
The state is living on borrowed money. What are you prepared to cut from your area of responsibility in the new budget?
I can't answer that yet as I have not familiarized myself with the budget. However, I do know that a great deal has already been cut from the area of responsibility of the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications in previous years, so there are certainly things which can be done and reviewed, but unfortunately I cannot give you a more precise answer today.
Unfortunately, the public does not know very much about you, and your ministerial post is not exactly the most popular one — you are not going to be a star inside six months. What do you think will happen to you after the [March 2027] elections? The Reform Party is unlikely to have a very deep roster after the elections. How far ahead are you looking?
I will certainly do my very best and give it my all in standing in the elections and seek a mandate from the voters. If I do not attain that, I will have to seek out new challenges for myself, and I hope I will succeed in doing so.

Yemen's Houthis claim they shot down Saudi fighter jet, deny targeting Mecca
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:20:47 UTC
18:20:47 KST

Saudi Arabia vowed it would not hesitate to take "deterrent measures" against the Houthis after alerts were issued over possible drone attacks near Islam's holiest site, the first such alerts since the Iran war began in February.
Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday said they shot down a Saudi fighter jet, claiming they used munitions made by the group to target the warplane.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah's aid and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on social media, while accusing Saudi Arabia of launching 450 strikes.
He said the aircraft had been targeted "using a locally made air-to-air missile".
The spokesman also dismissed Saudi claims that the Houthis had targeted Islam's holy city of Mecca.
"Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites," he said, adding that "fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal al-Saud regime cannot deceive anyone."
The Saudi coalition vowed retaliation, warning that the security of holy sites was a "red line".
"The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line, and the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia," the coalition said in a statement shared by spokesman Turki al-Maliki on X.
Saudi Arabia had issued brief alerts on Tuesday over possible attacks in Mecca and across swathes of the kingdom's south, which borders Yemen.
The alerts, including the first one issued in Mecca since the Iran war erupted in February, came a day after a wave of ballistic missile and drone attacks launched from Yemen wounded 13 people in the kingdom's south.
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned on Wednesday "in the strongest possible terms the dastardly and heinous" attack on Mecca.
"The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act," he said on X.
The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, a 57-member bloc of Muslim-majority countries, also condemned the "heinous" attack.
The Houthis are Zaydi Shia Muslims, a specific branch of Islam historically rooted in northern Yemen that is theologically distinct from both the Twelver Shia Islam dominant in Iran and Saudi Arabia's Wahhabi-influenced Sunni tradition.
Mecca is Islam's holiest site, home to the Kaaba — which Muslims worldwide turn toward for prayer — and the destination of the Hajj pilgrimage, one of the faith's Five Pillars or main tenets.
Any confirmed attack on the city would put the perpetrators beyond the pale in the eyes of virtually the entire Muslim world, Shia and Sunni alike.
Warnings over Bab el-Mandeb spike
Formally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with the internationally recognised government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July.
The fighting in the Arabian Peninsula's poorest country has forced 82,000 people to flee their homes since the start of September, according to the UN.
Yemen's permanent representative at the UN Abdullah al-Saadi said his compatriots were fighting to restore "national institutions across every inch of their land", and called on the international community to take action against the Houthis.
The group has also declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and has been targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of the entirety of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
One of the world's crucial waterways connecting the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and the main chokehold on the cargo route to the Mediterranean and Europe has become vital to Saudi crude exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthis have insisted that there is no threat to navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb except for Saudi vessels.
Any attacks in the waterway are likely to make it less attractive to shippers.
Disruption in the strait could also endanger Egypt, as the Red Sea serves as the gateway to the Suez Canal, on which Cairo relies for crucial foreign revenue.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called on Tuesday for "ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation" through the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, the Egyptian presidency said.
On Tuesday, Qatar warned of dire consequences if Bab el-Mandeb was closed, saying it would be "catastrophic for the entire world".
US media reported last week that the Saudi crown prince made a personal request to President Donald Trump for US intervention, but it was turned down. Neither Riyadh nor Washington have issued any statements regarding these reports.
However, a US military task force is working to enhance intelligence-sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces as they face attacks, a US official told AFP on Tuesday.
Canal revenues are currently around half of what they were before the Houthis first started attacking Red Sea shipping in 2023, a campaign they said was in solidarity with Palestinians during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza.
The Houthis have also targeted oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the world's leading crude exporter, pushing global prices above the $100-a-barrel threshold.
The Saudi-led coalition said it would deal with the attacks "firmly to protect the sovereignty of the Kingdom", and would take "all necessary operational measures to deter this ... hostile and extremist approach".
The Houthis are tied to Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

Music helps brain recover from stress by reshaping regulation networks, study finds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:19:44 CST
18:19:44 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- A new study suggests that music may help people bounce back from stress not just by distracting them, but by reshaping how the brain handles stress over time.
The research, led by researchers from the Institute of Psychology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, was recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).
Scientists have long recognized that music can be relaxing, but it remains unclear whether it offers benefits beyond other soothing sounds, when those benefits are most significant, or what changes occur in the brain to produce these effects. To explore this, the researchers conducted two experiments involving 120 healthy young adults.
In the first experiment, participants listened to either relaxing music or calming natural water sounds before or after a stressful mental arithmetic task. Listening to music before the task did not clearly reduce the initial stress response. However, music appeared to be especially helpful during recovery after the stressful event. At that stage, participants who listened to music reported greater improvements in positive mood and faster recovery on several physical measures.
In the second experiment, another group of participants had brain scans while recovering from the same type of stress. The results showed that music changed communication between the auditory cortex, which processes sound, and the insula and thalamus, which are involved in monitoring the body, detecting important signals, and regulating arousal.
These brain changes followed a clear pattern during recovery. Early on, signals from the auditory cortex to the insula became stronger. Later, communication between the insula and thalamus increased, and this was linked to better mood. The researchers also found that as musical tension rose and fell over time, connectivity among these brain regions changed as well. Those patterns were tied to improvements in mood, heart rate, and autonomic balance.
According to Du Yi, a professor at the Institute of Psychology, music is a highly structured signal that unfolds through cycles of anticipation, tension, and resolution. The findings suggest the brain may use this evolving structure as a scaffold to reorganize its stress-regulation networks, helping both mind and body return to a more balanced state.
"The study points to musical tension as an important factor in how music supports stress recovery. It also offers a possible neural framework for designing music-based interventions to support stress resilience in daily life and clinical care," Du said. ■

New study links muscle loss to higher dementia risk
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:19:38 CST
18:19:38 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Losing muscle mass as people age could be an important warning sign for dementia risk, new Australian-led research has found.
Researchers analyzed more than 80 studies examining links between body weight, body fat, muscle health and dementia, finding that people with sarcopenia had a 42 percent higher risk of dementia, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's Curtin University.
Sarcopenia is a condition where people lose a greater amount of muscle mass, strength and physical function, often as they get older, according to the study published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition.
The study also found that the relationship between obesity and dementia depends on age: People with obesity in middle age, or before 65, had a 9 percent higher risk of dementia, while obesity among people aged 65 and over was linked to a 17 percent lower dementia risk, but researchers cautioned against interpreting the finding as a benefit of gaining weight.
The findings showed a complex relationship between body weight, ageing and dementia, with more long-term research needed to understand whether low muscle mass and excess body fat together increase dementia risk, said corresponding author Professor Mario Siervo from Curtin's School of Population Health.
Lead researcher Uraiporn Booranasuksakul from Thailand's Burapha University said body weight alone did not fully reflect dementia risk, with muscle strength and function also important as people age.
The researchers from Australia, Britain, Canada, Thailand and Italy said the findings reinforced the importance of taking a life-long approach to maintaining healthy body composition, including maintaining muscle strength and function as people get older. ■

Changchun 2027 to build bridge connecting young people worldwide, says FISU secretary general
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:19:28 CST
18:19:28 KST

by sportswriters Huang Yuhan, Li Dian and Tang Mingze
CHANGCHUN, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade will serve as a bridge connecting the world and create lasting memories for young people globally, Matthias Remund, secretary-general and CEO of the International University Sports Federation (FISU), told Xinhua during the recent Heads of Delegation meeting in Changchun.
Speaking as representatives gathered to finalize preparations for the Games, Remund said this was his fourth visit to Changchun and that he had been impressed by the region's winter sports resources. "We learned that Jilin Province has more than 60 ski resorts, and the scale is really impressive," he said.
Having worked in winter sports for many years and competed in four Winter Universiades as a Swiss cross-country skier, Remund said he had visited facilities around the world but was struck by Jilin's potential.
"I didn't know enough about Jilin before. After coming here, I found that Jilin really is a winter sports destination," he said. "For FISU, it's a great opportunity to come to Jilin, come to Changchun and celebrate the Winter Universiade in 2027."
Remund said preparations were progressing smoothly and expressed confidence in the organizers.
"I never had doubts about the service delivery," he said. "We have had a short time to prepare. FISU has also sent representatives to Changchun several times to help address related issues, and we have worked very well together. I am very impressed by what has already been achieved."
The Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade will run from Jan. 15 to 25, 2027. Guided by the principles of economy, efficiency and sustainability, the Games will feature competitions in Changchun and Jilin City, with 93 events across 12 sports. Cross-country running will make its debut at the Winter Universiade.
For Remund, the inclusion of cross-country running carries special significance. Some countries and regions lack the natural conditions traditionally associated with winter sports, and the addition of the discipline could open up new opportunities for more young people to engage with the Winter Universiade. Remund said the move could also send a message to parts of the world without ice or snow, helping extend the reach of international university sports.
"The platform will be great, and the bridge will be built," he said. That idea of building connections lies at the heart of what Remund hopes Changchun 2027 can achieve.
Remund emphasized the Games' broader legacy: bringing leading university athletes together to compete, exchange and learn, while encouraging local people to experience winter sports.
He highlighted the importance of renovating existing venues and keeping them accessible to residents, visitors and international tourists after the event.
"It's not only the Games themselves that matter, but also the projects around the Games," Remund said, adding that keeping venues open to the public after the event would be an important part of that legacy.
Beyond the Games, Remund said he had also been deeply impressed by Jilin's distinctive mountain landscape.
"At Beidahu Ski Resort, I saw green grass and cattle in the mountains in summer, while in winter there are ski tracks and winter tourism. It's really the same situation we have in Switzerland," he said, adding that he hopes to return after the Games as a tourist to hike and enjoy the mountains. ■

Thousands of suspicious accounts followed Swedish political voices, researchers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:19:09 UTC
18:19:09 KST

More than 8,500 X accounts were identified as suspicious in the run-up to Sweden's general election, in which the centre-left opposition secured a narrow preliminary lead.
At first glance, this X account below appears to belong to a Swedish woman named Ingrid Karlsson.
But the profile uses a stolen photograph, according to researchers, rarely publishes its own content and is actually listed by the social media platform as being based in Benin, West Africa.
It is one of more than 8,500 accounts identified by Dutch analysis company Trollrensics and the non-profit organisation Alliance4Europe, in collaboration with Swedish broadcaster SVT.
The researchers say the profiles display signs of coordinated behaviour, including similar identities, reused photographs and overlapping patterns in the Swedish political accounts they follow.
Rather than originating in Sweden, these accounts are listed on X as being based in Nigeria, Ghana, and parts of Asia.
They emerged in the run-up to Sweden's general election, held on Sunday. Preliminary results from the vote put the opposition bloc, led by former prime minister Magdalena Andersson's Social Democrats, narrowly ahead of the governing right-wing alliance.
With 95% of districts counted, opposition parties were projected to win 176 of the parliament's 349 seats, compared with 173 for the bloc led by current leader Ulf Kristersson, of the centre-right Moderate Party.
The results remain provisional, with the final result expected a week after election day, according to the Swedish Election Authority.
How were the accounts identified?
Trollrensics co-founder Robert van der Noordaa told The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, that his company uses 26 indicators to assess whether a collection of profiles constitutes a coordinated network.
This includes unusual spikes in accounts created on a certain date, stolen photographs, and accounts publishing identical posts simultaneously.
The Swedish accounts studied generally published little to no original content. Instead, they followed large numbers of genuine Swedish accounts involved in political debate in the run-up to the election.
Van der Noordaa said some profiles with thousands of followers appeared to derive as much as 30% of their following from suspicious accounts listed in Nigeria, Benin and parts of Asia.
The accounts followed people from different parts of the political spectrum, with a greater concentration on right-wing voices and those associated with the Moderate Party.
Researchers say mass-following can inflate a profile's popularity, as well as amplify posts through coordinated likes and reposts.
Who's behind the network?
Trollrensics says accounts with similar characteristics were identified in elections around Europe, including in the Netherlands and Hungary. Some even changed their identities when moving between different national political debates.
"They have a German name, a German bio, and then at some point they're sort of repurposed," van der Noordaa said. "We've also found accounts in Sweden that are following a lot of Swedish people that started as Dutch accounts."
Van der Noordaa believes that the accounts form part of a commercial "guns for hire" operation that can be deployed for different clients.
The majority of people hired to generate these troll accounts are either from Africa or the US, according to van der Noordaa.
Darren Linvill, co-director of Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub, separately examined a sample of the accounts. He told The Cube that their behaviour appeared consistent with paid amplification services increasingly used by political and state-linked actors.
Such operations can involve small marketing businesses or individual contractors running accounts and automated bots, whose services are then sold through larger companies or online marketplaces, according to Linvill.
These services include paid-for followers, comments, likes, reposts and automated bots.
"They were giving accounts followers so that those accounts appear more legitimate, appear to have a larger portion of the conversation," Linvill said. "They appear to represent a larger community than they do in real life."
According to Linvill, their activity represents amplification methods seen in Russian influence operations, which also use a network of disposable accounts to promote fake content.
Wider election security concerns
The findings emerged during an election held against a backdrop of heightened concern over foreign interference.
Swedish authorities said before the vote that the country was not considered a priority target for Russian influence. Nevertheless, they warned that the election was taking place amid a serious security situation and that hostile actors could seek to deepen existing divisions or undermine confidence in the electoral process.
Separate pro-Russian activity was detected ahead of the vote, with Alliance4Europe reporting that the pro-Russian influence operation known as Matryoshka circulated fabricated videos targeting the governing coalition and Ukrainian refugees.
During the election, unproven claims of widespread electoral fraud spread after a technical error affected the registration of around 500 advance voters. Other posts falsely alleged that a senior Election Authority official was affiliated with the Social Democrats, and others falsely claimed that Swedes without an identity document would be able to vote several times.
Sweden's Psychological Defence Agency said authorities had undertaken extensive preparations to protect the public from disinformation, propaganda and attempts to manipulate public debate.

Mecca Security Pact not to affect Pak ties with Iran: spox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:18:48 UTC
18:18:48 KST

Pakistan’s military agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, known as "Mecca Agreement," is purely defensive in nature and is not expected to affect relations with the Islamic Republic of Iran, he emphasized.
Speaking in an interview with English Al-Arabiya, the spokesman added this agreement is formulated as a joint defensive shield aimed at establishing regional peace, stability, and security; it is not intended for aggression or offensive action.
He also emphasized that the agreement would not complicate Pakistan's relations with Iran, nor would it affect the country's strategic ties with China.
In response to a question about what action Pakistan would take if a member state of the agreement were attacked, the Pakistan Army spokesperson stated that the operational details of the defense agreement would not be released.
No country or military force publicly discloses the details of its military operations or the manner in which it would fulfill specific defense obligation, he said, adding that practical response to an attack would be determined by Pakistan itself, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey.
There are numerous defense agreements worldwide that entail specific commitments, yet the manner in which military operations are conducted within their framework is not publicly disclosed, Chaudhry stressed.
He added that the goal of this agreement is to establish stability, peace, and security in the region, not to form a coalition exclusive to Muslim countries.
“There is nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is a collective deterrence, and it is complementary because all these countries have independent relations with other alliances, other countries, other blocks,” he said.
Chaudhry said the agreement is not directed against any particular country and should be viewed as complementary to Pakistan’s existing international relationships.
Asked whether the new defense arrangement could complicate Pakistan’s relations with Iran, Chaudhry rejected the suggestion.
“I don’t think, not at all,” he said, describing the agreement as the product of decades-old strategic relationships between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey.
He said Pakistan’s relations with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye have not “come out of the blue”, but are based on longstanding political, military, cultural and people-to-people ties.
“These relationships that Pakistan has with both these countries are special,” he said. “They are based on people-to-people relationship. There is an emotional connection, there is a cultural connection, there is a government-to-government, a military connection which spans over decades.”

Canada to become first 'associate member' of the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:18:47 UTC
18:18:47 KST

The status announced by von der Leyen during the State of the Union is an entirely new one, with details yet to be made clear. The European Commission’s President also proposed a new alliance with Ottawa covering tech, critical raw materials, energy and defence.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced on Wednesday that Canada has been invited to become the first “associate member” of the EU.
She announced the move during her 2026 State of the Union address in Strasbourg, to an audience including not only MEPs but also Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who attended her speech in the midst of a trade war with the US.
Since late August, the Canadians have been pushing hard for the Europeans to build a closer relationship with them, though full EU membership is not an option as Canada is not a European state.
During her speech before the MEPs on Wednesday, von der Leyen invited the country to become “the first associate member of the European Union".
“We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well,” she added.
A new status
Expectations had been high over the last week after Carney spoke about building a “unique alliance” with the EU.
Canada is not a European state geographically, but it shares the same values as the EU – human rights, democracy, rule of law – which are necessary criteria for becoming a member state.
Several options already exist for countries that don’t have full membership. Norway, for instance, is part of the single market, the EU’s borderless area of free movement of goods, persons, services and capital. Oslo and Brussels also collaborate on joint defence initiatives.
Switzerland also has access to the single market through several agreements – and in the years since Brexit, the United Kingdom and the EU have secured the largest and broadest trade and cooperation deal in the bloc's history, coverering a wide range of sectors. The UK is now taking part in several EU programmes such as Horizon Europe, the EU’s research and innovation programme.
Euronews has learned that Ottawa is already in talks with Brussels to join the Erasmus+ exchange program, Horizon Europe research grants, and mutual recognition of workers’ qualifications.
However, “associate member” is a completely new status, and key questions have not yet been answered – chief among them, whether Canada will have voting rights in EU institutions. Despite their regulatory harmonisation with the bloc, Norway and Switzerland have no say on EU legislation.
A new alliance with Ottawa
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz floated the idea last May of an “associate membership” for Ukraine, which is urgently seeking to enter the EU. In a letter sent to EU leaders, he argued that this status would grant Ukraine access to the decision-making bodies – the European Council, the European Commission and the European Parliament – without voting rights or a dedicated portfolio.
It would also allow the country to tap into certain EU-funded programmes on a "step-by-step" basis.
It’s hard to see Canada in the same category as Ukraine, a country which is at war, but von der Leyen's announcement on Wednesday nonetheless sent a strong political signal in a volatile world where historical alliances are shifting.
“Europe and Canada believe in democracy. That power does not belong to the strongest, the richest, or the loudest – but to all of us,” she said. “Democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work.”
She also called for a new alliance with Ottawa, which could include tech, defence, Arctic joint projects, but also energy, critical minerals and artificial intelligence.
“We will move from CETA to an Alliance for the Future to create a common prosperity and economic security space,” she said, referring to the 2016 EU-Canada trade agreement that removed tariff barriers between both sides and has been provisionally applied.
The economic and security cooperation between both partners is set to be pushed further during a summit in Montreal in October.

Instead of Helping Ukraine’s Poor, Ferrexpo’s Charitable Donations Flowed to Companies Associated With Its Then-CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:18:00 UTC
18:18:00 KST

Some of the transfers were large and instantaneous, including one payment worth approximately $986,000 that was moved out of Khimreaktyv within 45 minutes of the charitable funds hitting the company’s account in December 2016, the Crowe report shows. 
In other cases, money trickled out over a period of months. For instance, Khimreaktyv made eight transfers to a Ukrainian company called DRI LLC between July and November 2017 totaling around $480,000 worth of hryvnia, according to the Crowe report and a 2024 ruling by Kyiv’s Commercial Court relating to Khimreaktyv’s eventual bankruptcy. 
The contracts underpinning those payments, which were marked as fulfilling a loan assignment agreement, had no clear economic purpose, according to the court ruling. 
At the time of the transactions, DRI was majority owned by a U.K. company in which Zhevago owned shares in 2015, and which he told a U.K. High Court in 2021 he was the “owner or controller” of. Zhevago did not respond to OCCRP’s questions about whether he owned DRI at the time of the transactions. OCCRP contacted DRI via post, as well as its listed legal representative, but did not receive a response.
In total, OCCRP contacted more than two dozen other companies mentioned in the Crowe report seeking their response to allegations that they received charitable funds from Blooming Land, but did not receive a response. 
Khimreaktyv and Gas Turbine Technologies declared bankruptcy in 2020 and 2024, respectively, and are now under administration. Their largest creditors are Blooming Land’s sub-funds. 
The bankruptcy administrator for Khimreaktyv told OCCRP that the company received the majority of its income between 2013 and 2018 from Blooming Land, and that they had found no evidence that the funds were spent on implementing the company’s contracts with the charity.
“Khimreaktyv LLC did not conduct its own economic activity and did not have a real source of income,” the administrator noted. 
“Significant amounts of money were almost never retained in Khimreaktyv’s bank accounts,” the administrator added. “My analysis of the company's financial documents gives reasonable grounds to believe that it performed the function of a so-called ‘transit company’ - that is, one link in a chain of transactions.” 
The bankruptcy administrator for Gas Turbine Technologies confirmed the company received funds from Blooming Land and said that Ukrainian courts found it “did not take any actions aimed at the implementation of charitable programs and projects.”
Although OCCRP contacted multiple former employees of Blooming Land, apart from former director Temchenko only one other former manager at the charity, and a former director for one of the subfunds agreed to speak. 
Both rejected the findings that the charities had sent sizable funds to Gas Turbine Technologies and Khimreaktyv, while the former manager of Blooming Land from 2013-2014 said the organization “worked strictly within the framework of charitable activity” during her tenure. 
Banking Data Suggests Charity Funds Went to Troubled Bank
The National Bank of Ukraine classified Zhevago’s Finance and Credit Bank as “troubled” in January 2015 due to “risky operations,” including a significant increase in potentially non-performing loans. 
In response, Ukraine’s National Bank and Zhevago, who was the bank’s main shareholder but had no management role at the time, injected capital into the bank in an effort to save it. 
Around the same time, six of the companies which, based on the Crowe report, received Blooming Land’s funds, sent money — often of similar or near-identical amounts — to Finance and Credit Bank or to other firms that subsequently made transfers to the bank,  banking data seen by OCCRP shows. 
These payments were marked mostly as investments in the bank’s share capital. The data shows that none of these companies had comparable funds in their accounts at the time, and that the transactions took place either the same day or shortly after they received the money that the Crowe report traced back to Blooming Land. 
In total, by mid-February 2015, the final companies in these transaction chains had spent the equivalent of some $22 million buying shares in Zhevago’s struggling bank in this manner.
Then on a single day in July 2015, around $26 million worth of hryvnia was transferred from the three Blooming Land sub-funds to Gas Turbine Technologies, Khimreaktyv, and another company in payments marked for charitable services. 
All three companies sent the funds to a financial services company, FK Faktoring LLC. 
Later that same day, FK Faktoring LLC transferred the equivalent of $19 million to Finance and Credit Bank, the data shows.
According to the payment reference, the money was not provided for any charitable initiative. Instead, it was designated as a repayment for a commercial loan that FK Faktoring LLC had drawn from the bank in November 2010.
At the time, FK Faktoring LLC was partially owned by a Ukrainian insurance company, Omega, which Ferrexpo noted was under “common control” by Zhevago in its annual report that year. 
When asked about the transaction, Zhevago’s lawyers said that OCCRP’s characterization of the events was “not correct” and “not confirmed” by Ferrexpo’s review into Blooming Land. 
The National Bank of Ukraine stated it couldn’t comment on the $19 million loan repayment or confirm the entire transaction chain showing the purchases of the bank’s shares in 2015. 
Neither FK Faktoring, which is now in bankruptcy, nor Omega responded to requests for comment from OCCRP. When reached by phone, the director of FK Faktoring at the time of the transactions said he had never heard of the charities and that his company had not received any funds from them. Neither he nor the bankruptcy administrator for FK Faktoring responded to a written request for comment.
Finance and Credit Bank ultimately failed, with the National Bank declaring it insolvent in September 2015, stating that Zhevago “did not fulfil his written obligations to support bank liquidity.”  
Zhevago’s lawyers told OCCRP that it was decisions by National Bank officials which caused the collapse of Finance and Credit. 
Blurred Lines
From its inception, Blooming Land employed personnel who had a history of working at businesses associated with Zhevago, OCCRP found. 
Blooming Land’s incorporation documents show the charity was first established in March 2013 by two people who had served as senior legal personnel for AvtoKrAZ, a manufacturer of heavy-duty vehicles owned by Zhevago until the Ukrainian state took control of the business in 2022. (One of those founders has since died, while the other told OCCRP she was “not interested” in discussing the matter.)

Belarus frees more prisoners after US envoy's visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:17:56 UTC
18:17:56 KST

Trump's envoy wins release of 25 Belarus prisoners, expects hundreds more soon
VILNIUS, Sept 16 - Belarus freed 25 prisoners on Wednesday in return for a further easing of U.S. sanctions, and U.S. envoy John Coale told Reuters that hundreds more could be released in a month.
The deal was the latest to emerge from a series of negotiations stretching back more than a year between Coale and Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Coale has been tasked by President Donald Trump with securing the release of hundreds of people including human rights campaigners, political activists, journalists and lawyers.
The U.S. diplomacy is sensitive because Lukashenko, in charge of the former Soviet state since 1994, has long been shunned by the West for repressing his opponents and supporting Russia's war in Ukraine.
"This (process) has been very successful. President Trump's very happy with this," Coale told Reuters in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius, where the freed prisoners were taken.
ENVOY HOPES FOR MORE RELEASES SOON
The figure of 25 releases was much lower than the 250 that Coale negotiated when he last visited Minsk in March.
But the American said in an interview that he expected to return in about a month and hoped at that point that "hundreds" would be freed.
Human rights group Viasna, which is banned in Belarus as an extremist organisation, said many of those released on Wednesday had been sentenced to many years in prison. One of them, journalist Andrei Alyaksandrau, had been serving a 14-year term.
Also released were a trio of musicians, arrested in 2022, whose songs were designated as "extremist materials".
A source familiar with the situation told Reuters that, in addition to the 25, a significant number of prisoners were expected to be freed and remain inside Belarus.
Viasna said relatives of some detainees had been told they could collect their loved ones from penal colonies on Wednesday morning.
LUKASHENKO DENIES REPLACING SOME PRISONERS WITH OTHERS
Viasna says Belarus still holds 886 political prisoners, although Lukashenko rejects that label and denies charges by the exiled opposition that he is steadily arresting more people to replace those he releases.
Asked if he was sticking to an earlier prediction that all the prisoners could be freed this year, Coale told Reuters: "Well, I think so. (I'll) give it a try."
The 79-year-old has previously admitted to resorting occasionally to crude humour in order to win over Lukashenko, and discreetly emptying his glass on the floor in order to avoid getting drunk at long vodka sessions.
U.S. LIFTS SANCTIONS ON TWO BELARUSIAN COMPANIES
Coale said earlier that the U.S. was lifting sanctions on Lakokraska, a manufacturer of paints and industrial coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned industrial concern that oversees the forestry, pulp and paper sectors.
He also promised Lukashenko on Tuesday to get U.S. banks to hand back tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets.
Coale's humanitarian efforts have earned gratitude from many Belarusians, but rights groups and opposition politicians say arrests continue and Lukashenko has yet to end repression.
"Today, alongside our joy for those released, we remember those who remain behind bars," exiled opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya posted on X.
Asked what obstacles remained in the way of his diplomacy, Coale cited the wars in the Gulf and Ukraine.
"Look, if these wars weren't going on, we would get everybody out by next Tuesday. But the wars complicate our government, they complicate Belarus' government and everybody else in the world right now," he said. REUTERS

Lebanon's Aoun seeks security deal with Israel, peaceful Hezbollah disarmament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:16:06 UTC
18:16:06 KST

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun says Beirut wants to negotiate a security agreement with Israel after its withdrawal from southern Lebanon, while insisting that Hezbollah’s weapons must be brought under state control without triggering a confrontation.
In an exclusive interview with AFP ahead of his visit to France on Wednesday, Aoun said Lebanon had “no choice but negotiations” because war would be too costly for the country.
He said a security agreement with Israel should initially focus on ending the state of hostility and securing the border, potentially paving the way for a future peace agreement.
“We cannot jump directly to a peace agreement,” Aoun said.
Aoun calls for temporary force in south
Aoun also called for the creation of a temporary international force to prevent a security vacuum in southern Lebanon after the UN peacekeeping mission there ends its mandate at the end of the year.
“What matters is that there is no vacuum,” he told AFP.
He said the force could be European, American, Asian, Arab or a combination of countries and would remain in place only until the Lebanese army is capable of deploying throughout the area.
The UN peacekeeping mission, known as UNIFIL, has operated in southern Lebanon since 1978. The UN Security Council voted in 2025 to end its mandate following pressure from the United States.
Aoun is due to attend a meeting in Paris hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron and attended by Jordanian King Abdullah II. The meeting will seek international support for the Lebanese army as it expands its deployment across the country.
Aoun urged the US, European Union and Arab countries to help strengthen Lebanon’s military and state institutions.
Hezbollah disarmament to be peaceful
Aoun reiterated that Lebanon is determined to disarm Hezbollah, an Iran-backed armed group that has long maintained its own military capabilities alongside the Lebanese state.
He described the decision as “neither negotiable nor open to discussion,” but said the government does not want to achieve it through confrontation.
“The objective is not a confrontation,” Aoun said. “We are determined to resolve this issue peacefully.”
He said the process should not come at the cost of “a bloody conflict” or another civil war.
Aoun also said Lebanon’s international partners must share responsibility for strengthening the Lebanese army and state.
“Our Arab and European partners, as well as the United States and our friends, must share with us the responsibility of supporting the army and strengthening the Lebanese state,” he said.
