Iran: Architects of crimes against humanity to suppress protests must face international justice to deter further massacres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:43:14 UTC
17:43:14 KST

- New report finds Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their bloody suppression of the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising
- In-depth investigation exposes chain of command responsible for implementing state policy of lethal force to crush protests and identifies 87 officials who should be investigated for crimes against humanity
- Iranian authorities disproportionately targeted Kurdish and Baluchi communities with lethal repression and subjected them to the crime against humanity of persecution
- UN General Assembly should create an international criminal justice mechanism to tackle impunity for repeated mass protest killings culminating in January 2026 protest massacres
- Report released amid armed hostilities since unlawful US and Israeli attacks, underscoring the need for enduring ceasefire and accountability for violations of the UN Charter and international humanitarian law
In a landmark new report marking the fourth anniversary of the start of the Woman Life Freedom uprising, Amnesty International warns that those responsible for crimes against humanity committed to brutally crush nationwide protests in 2022 continue to control Iran’s deadly state machinery of repression today.  
The report, Architects of Atrocities: State Machinery Orchestrating Crimes Against Humanity in Iran’s 2022 Woman Life Freedom Uprising –more than 1,000 pages long – details how Iranian authorities committed the crimes against humanity of murder, torture, enforced disappearance, imprisonment, rape and persecution on political, gender, ethnic and religious grounds in order to crush the uprising. It also documents deadly protest repression operations and command structures, identifying 87 officials who should be criminally investigated for crimes against humanity.
Amnesty International is calling for an international criminal justice mechanism to be established urgently by the UN General Assembly to ensure Iranian authorities responsible for crimes against humanity are held to account and to deter further atrocities such as the large-scale protest massacres committed on 8-9 January 2026.
In light of the ongoing hostilities following unlawful attacks by the USA and Israel on Iran, Amnesty International also reiterates its call for an enduring ceasefire and independent investigations into attacks committed during the conflict. The organization calls for the UN to address accountability for violations of the UN Charter and of international humanitarian law, including possible war crimes.
“The extensive evidence gathered and analysed in our report leaves no doubt: Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity to crush the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising. They waged a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population demanding dignity, human rights and fundamental political change, pursuant to a state policy of using lethal force to obliterate dissent,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
Our report unveils how crimes against humanity in Iran are sustained by an architecture of impunity built into the country’s constitutional, legislative, political and judicial frameworks.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
“Our report also unveils how crimes against humanity in Iran are sustained by an architecture of impunity built into the country’s constitutional, legislative, political and judicial frameworks. The horrifying result has been intensifying cycles of mass protest killings, culminating in the massacres of thousands of protesters within just 48 hours on 8-9 January 2026. The UN General Assembly must end the unconscionable normalization of mass protest killings in Iran and create an international criminal justice mechanism aimed at prosecuting those most implicated in crimes against humanity.
“This report is being published at a time when people in Iran are also facing the devastating consequences of unlawful attacks by the USA and Israel. Amnesty International unequivocally opposes violations of international law by all parties and rejects any attempt to instrumentalize the suffering of victims of human rights violations in Iran to justify unlawful attacks that inflict further civilian harm.
“For years, Iranian people have faced brutal repression, persecution and impunity at the hands of their own authorities. Today, many are also bearing the human cost of unlawful military action carried out by the USA and Israel. A principled response requires rejecting both impunity for crimes against humanity and unlawful use of force. The international community must pursue people-centred diplomatic strategies that place civilian protection, atrocity prevention, justice and accountability at their core. After more than six months of air strikes that have killed and injured civilians, damaged the environment, and caused significant destruction of civilian infrastructure, an enduring ceasefire is urgently needed alongside independent investigations and action by the UN General Assembly to address accountability for violations of the UN Charter and of international humanitarian law and possible war crimes committed by all parties to the conflict.”
Amnesty International’s report, released four years after the death in custody of Zhina Mahsa Amini at the hands of the “morality” police sparked nationwide protests, documents how the Iranian authorities mobilized security forces armed with military-grade firearms and shotguns loaded with metal pellets and issued orders that facilitated the unlawful killing of hundreds of protesters and bystanders, including dozens of children. The crimes against humanity also included the arbitrary arrest, enforced disappearance, torture or other ill-treatment of thousands of men, women and children as well as persecution of bereaved relatives.
Alongside the report, Amnesty International is also publishing Lives Cut Brutally Short: Victims of Crimes Against Humanity During Iran’s 2022 Woman Life Freedom Uprising, a document recording the deaths of 377 protesters and bystanders, 56 of them children, based on information and evidence gathered as part of the organization’s investigation into nationwide patterns of killings by the security forces. The document includes victims’ photographs and images of their grave sites where available.
In addition to calling on the UN General Assembly to create an international justice mechanism given the political deadlock at the UN Security Council, the gravity and scale of crimes committed, and high risk of recurrence, Amnesty International also urges states to call on the UN Security Council to refer the situation in Iran to the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court.
The organization also urges prosecution authorities around the world to initiate investigations, under universal or other forms of extraterritorial jurisdiction, against Iranian officials allegedly responsible for crimes against humanity, including the officials named in this report, and, where sufficient evidence exists, to issue arrest warrants.
Amnesty International’s years of research for this report involved interviews with 270 people, including protesters, former detainees, relatives of those killed or detained, eyewitnesses, lawyers, human rights defenders, journalists and medical workers. The organization also analysed over 2,000 videos and extensive documentary evidence, including official statements, leaked official documents, prosecution orders, court verdicts and forensic records.
Amnesty International wrote to Iran’s Supreme Leader and senior security officials to share its findings and notify the 87 officials identified in the report. At the time of publication, it has received no response.
A nationwide attack carried out pursuant to state policy
Amnesty International’s investigations into crimes against humanity committed to crush the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising revealed that two main security forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) and the Police Command of the Islamic Republic of Iran (known by its Persian acronym, FARAJA), led lethal protest dispersals, implementing the state policy devised through the Supreme National Security Council, State Security Council and provincial and county security councils.
FARAJA and IRGC agents repeatedly fired into crowds, using military-grade assault rifles, handguns and shotguns loaded with metal pellets. In addition to firing into crowds, they chased fleeing protesters and bystanders, closing in on unarmed victims who posed no threat to the security forces or others and fatally shooting them at close range.
Among the FARAJA branches involved were the Prevention Police, including its Assistance Cohorts, and the Special Cohorts. The IRGC branches involved included the operational divisions, the provincial Security Cohorts and various Basij battalions, such as the Imam Ali Battalions and the Beit Al-Moghaddas Battalions. These IRGC branches operated under the relevant IRGC provincial corps, overseen in turn by a regional IRGC headquarters.
Official statements and leaked documents analysed in the report reveal the state policy as reflected in strategy meetings, binding orders, deployment plans, allocations of money and weapons, and instructions for a “firm and severe” response. One leaked order instructed forces to “respond mercilessly and go as far as causing death”.
Witnesses repeatedly described streets resembling battlefields as a result of relentless gunfire by the security forces. Mahshid, who protested in Mahabad, West Azerbaijan province, told Amnesty International: “I had never seen such scenes before… The situation was very frightening and felt like a war zone. The security forces just kept shooting.”
Most of the 377 protesters and bystanders, whose deaths Amnesty International recorded, were killed by security forces during protest dispersals between September and December 2022. Others died in custody, after release from custody or in suspicious circumstances suggesting state responsibility.
Consistent with long-standing patterns of denial and cover-up, the authorities have acknowledged only 202 deaths and falsely attributed most to non-state actors, “rioters” or “armed terrorists”, despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary. Far from acting to stop crimes as evidence mounted, senior officials repeatedly praised security forces and instructed the continuation of operations.
Total of 87 officials identified for criminal investigation
Based on detailed documentation of the security forces involved and in-depth analysis of their command structures, Amnesty International has identified 87 Iranian officials who should be criminally investigated for crimes against humanity.
The list, while not exhaustive, extends from the highest levels of Iran’s security apparatus to officials operating at provincial and county level.
The list of 87 individuals comprises 62 security force commanders – including 33 commanders from the IRGC and 27 commanders from FARAJA – and 25 Ministry of Interior officials including provincial and county governors. Among them are 10 national-level officials and 77 officials at regional, provincial and county levels holding responsibilities related to the 17 counties in Kurdistan, Kermanshah and West Azerbaijan provinces on which Amnesty International conducted in-depth investigations.
Among those identified is the late Supreme Leader and commander-in-chief of all armed forces, Ali Khamenei; and the late head of the General Staff of the Armed Forces, Mohammad Bagheri, both of whom were killed in February 2026 in air strikes carried out during the US-Israeli military attack against the Islamic Republic of Iran. Amnesty International also names the then minister of interior, Ahmad Vahidi, who has since become the General Commander of the IRGC, and the then deputy minister of interior for police and security, Majid Mir Ahmadi.
This investigation exposes the layers of command and coordination behind the Iranian authorities’ deadly protest crackdowns.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International
“This investigation exposes the layers of command and coordination behind the Iranian authorities’ deadly protest crackdowns. The agents on the streets operated within a hierarchical and coordinated chain of command linking them to officials who directed, enabled, facilitated and supported crimes committed on a massive scale,” said Agnès Callamard.
“The officials named remain beyond the reach of justice in Iran. Most remain in positions from which they can unleash further deadly repression while some even climbed the chain of command after the crimes against humanity in 2022. The cost of continued impunity has been devastating. It is beyond time to establish an international criminal justice mechanism for Iran before another protest massacre.”
Devastating toll on Kurdish and Baluchi communities
Protesters from Iran’s persecuted Baluchi and Kurdish communities suffered a devastating share of the lethal repression, accounting for 62% of the total number of recorded victims while they constitute 5% and 10-15% of the country’s population, respectively.
Amnesty International recorded the unlawful killing of 106 Baluchi protesters and bystanders, including 20 children, by security forces in Sistan and Baluchistan province (33% of recorded victims). On 30 September 2022 alone, 87 were unlawfully killed as security forces opened fire following Friday prayers in Zahedan – a crackdown widely known as “Bloody Friday”.
The organization also documented the circumstances surrounding the unlawful killing of 95 Kurdish protesters and bystanders, including 13 children, in the context of protest dispersals or in militarized areas near protests that were ongoing or had recently occurred across 17 counties in Kurdistan, Kermanshah and West Azerbaijan provinces (29% of recorded victims). Most were fatally shot; others were fatally beaten, struck by tear gas canisters or deliberately run over by security force vehicles.
Iman, an eyewitness in Sanandaj, Kurdistan province, said: “The agents would shoot anyone in their sight, not caring if they were women, children, passersby or protesters.”
Amnesty International found that in the provinces of Kermanshah, Kurdistan and West Azerbaijan, security forces consistently deployed designated marksman rifles, assault rifles, sub-machine guns and heavy machine guns mounted on top of pickup trucks.
Amnesty International has concluded that acts of murder and torture were committed against Kurdish and Baluchi protesters with discriminatory intent on political and ethnic grounds, and that that the elements of the crime against humanity of persecution are met for these targeted groups.
Impunity by design
In Iran, impunity for crimes under international law and other serious human rights violations is systemic and intentional.
Iran’s constitution places the justice system under the direct control of the Supreme Leader, who is not only the commander-in-chief of the security forces, but also appoints the head of the judiciary, who in turn appoints senior judges and prosecutors. Cases involving serious human rights violations by members of the security forces are handled by military prosecution offices and courts, where judges and prosecutors can themselves come from the security forces and routinely rely on accounts from the very security bodies implicated in crimes.
Iran’s Law on the Use of Firearms by Armed Forces in Necessary Incidents allows firearms to be used to disperse protests, in blatant disregard of international law, which permits the use of firearms only as a last resort to counter an imminent threat of death or serious injury. The law also generally exempts state agents from civil and criminal liability.
“Survivors and victims’ families in Iran have been trapped in a system where the very institutions meant to deliver justice are controlled by authorities with blood on their hands. Families who seek truth and justice are persecuted,” said Agnès Callamard.
Directing calls for accountability to Iranian judicial authorities complicit in crimes against humanity is detached from reality. The international community must advance international pathways to justice now.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International
“Directing calls for accountability to Iranian judicial authorities complicit in crimes against humanity is detached from reality. The international community must advance international pathways to justice now. The UN General Assembly must confront the crisis of impunity that exposes people in Iran to recurring and escalating mass protest killings.”
Background
Amnesty International is launching this report while people in Iran are at risk of crimes under international law on two fronts. On one front, they are exposed to violations of international humanitarian law since the USA and Israel unlawfully attacked Iran in violation of the UN Charter on 28 February 2026.
On the other, they risk further crimes against humanity in the context of protest crackdowns. Iranian authorities have used the cover of “wartime conditions” to intensify internal repression, further militarizing public spaces, openly threatening to carry out mass killings against protesters and dissidents, and escalating politically motivated arbitrary executions.
Iran has been gripped by successive waves of anti-establishment protests since December 2017, as protesters have repeatedly taken to the streets demanding human rights, dignity, freedom, the end of the Islamic Republic system and transition to a new rights-respecting system of governance. Amnesty International’s extensive research into the authorities’ response to successive waves of protests in December 2017-January 2018, November 2019, September-December 2022 and January 2026 reveals a recurrent pattern of mass unlawful killings, torture, enforced disappearance and other crimes under international law.

Türkiye awards first military type certificate to domestically developed aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:42:01 UTC
17:42:01 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye has issued its first Military Type Certificate for a domestically developed air platform following a comprehensive certification process conducted in line with international standards and relying entirely on national expertise.
The certificate was awarded to HÜRKUŞ-II on Sept. 9 by a Certification Board comprising personnel from the Secretariat of Defense Industries (SSB) and the Turkish Air Force, according to an SSB statement.
SSB head Haluk Görgün described the certification as both a technical and strategic milestone, saying it demonstrated Türkiye’s ability to design, produce, test, verify and certify its own aircraft.
He added that the experience gained through HÜRKUŞ-II would provide lasting institutional expertise for the certification of future national air platforms.
The certification process covered 12 disciplines, including avionics, electrical systems, propulsion and fuel, human factors, cabin safety, system safety, aircraft systems, flight performance, structures and software. A total of 1,790 certification requirements were verified, while 950 supporting documents were technically reviewed.
The aircraft also underwent 153 certification tests, comprising 38 laboratory tests, 71 ground tests and 44 flight tests.
 
The work brought together specialists from the SSB, the Turkish Air Force, the Defense Ministry, TR Airworthiness Services and Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAŞ), the aircraft’s manufacturer. Their combined expertise covered the process from design and production to testing, verification and technical assessment.

There will be a full-time Australian rider in motorcycle racing's premier class for the 43rd consecutive year with 21-year-old Senna Agius signing on to race for KTM Tech3 next year.

Australia has had a full-time rider in the premier class since 1985.
In the modern era of grand prix motorcycle racing, which began in 2002 when 500cc two-stroke bikes were replaced with 990cc four-stroke engines, Agius will become the 11th full-time Australian rider.

Von der Leyen calls for a 'European Security Council' to counter threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:38:31 UTC
17:38:31 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday called for the creation of a European Security Council that could bring together EU countries, Britain and Ukraine as Europe confronts growing security threats, particularly from Russia.
“For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent,” von der Leyen told the European Parliament in Strasbourg. “This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play.”
She said the European Commission would set out proposals to make the council a reality.
EU seeks NATO-style response to hybrid threats
Von der Leyen also called for a NATO-like mechanism to help European countries respond to drone incidents, sabotage and cyberattacks that fall short of conventional armed aggression but threaten national security.
“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said, calling for an urgent agreement on how governments should respond to such incidents.
She proposed a system modeled on Article 4 of the NATO treaty, which allows member states to request consultations when they believe their security or territorial integrity is threatened.
European governments have attributed or linked a number of recent acts of sabotage, cyberattacks and other hybrid activity to Russia, while responsibility for many incidents remains unconfirmed
Europe steps up AI oversight
Von der Leyen also said the EU would invite the world's largest AI laboratories for talks on how to manage increasingly capable systems and support industry efforts to develop them safely.
“The dangers of self-improving models are becoming ever more apparent,” she said, warning that incidents involving AI agents escaping controlled environments or inserting malicious code could offer a glimpse of more serious risks.
Her comments come amid growing concerns about AI systems operating with greater autonomy and calls from some researchers and technology figures for stronger safeguards.
EU plans emergency migration framework
The Commission president also announced plans for a European Emergency Response Framework aimed at dealing with what she described as “engineered and weaponised” mass movements of migrants.
The mechanism would be activated only under strictly defined conditions and allow limited, time-bound flexibility in standard procedures during exceptional situations.
“The events of this summer show that our tools need to evolve, especially for emergency situations,” von der Leyen said.
She stressed that any measures would have to comply with European values and fundamental rights while strengthening the bloc's ability to protect its external borders.

European Union invites Canada to become first ever ‘associate member’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:38:26 UTC
17:38:26 KST

Canada has been invited to become the first “associate member” of the EU by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.
In an unprecedented offer, von der Leyen said on Wednesday that the EU and Canada “see the world with the same eyes” through shared democratic values and common approaches to many big issues, from AI to climate breakdown, the Ukraine war and geopolitics.
Speaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, at the European parliament in Strasbourg, she said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships. So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU.”
Carney, who is due to address the parliament on Thursday, has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU as Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.
He later tweeted: “Canada and the EU are natural partners, united by shared values.”
The EU and Canada are due to hold a summit in late October to develop the future relationship.
Canada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedly talking about Canada becoming the 51st US state and lambasting the EU.
Von der Leyen said the existing EU-Canada trade deal would be upgraded to an “alliance for the future” to create a “common prosperity and economic security space”.
She said the two sides would also create a tech alliance, integrate defence industrial bases and make the Arctic a “flagship joint project”. EU officials are especially interested in Canada’s energy and natural resources. Von der Leyen pitched joint work on energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.
The offer of associate membership is certain to raise questions among other EU allies, including the UK, which has long sought a more flexible approach from Brussels.
The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules.
It remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market. When the UK was negotiating its departure from the bloc and post-Brexit relationship, EU officials repeatedly said there was no status that enabled a foreign country to be half in and half out of the single market.
The phrase itself took EU insiders by surprise since von der Leyen had not used the term when she briefed senior EU diplomats ahead of her speech last Friday.
One EU diplomat said member states were “generally very supportive of ambition” in the EU-Canada relationship, but had been slightly worried in recent weeks that von der Leyen was overpromising on Canada. “‘Associate membership’ sounds like a nice headline but in reality 10 member states have still not ratified Ceta,” the person said, referring to the EU-Canada trade agreement that was agreed 10 years ago. A second EU diplomat described associate membership as “an empty phrase”.
Carney’s approach to dealing with Trump has however attracted widespread praise among MEPs.
Last month, Carney announced he was breaking off trade talks with the US, saying Canada would not be subjugated, and then introduced retaliatory tariffs on billions worth of US goods. By contrast, the EU last year accepted 15% tariffs on many European goods while dropping its own duties to avoid a trade war with Trump.
Javier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said “for sure” the EU had lessons to learn from Carney’s approach, because “Trump respects people who are strong”. He added: “Canadians are the most European people outside Europe and that is the key point for the development of our relationship.”
Martin Leng at the Brussels Institute for Geopolitics thinktank said a world in flux was “pushing the EU towards far greater flexibility in its relations with third states”.
He said von der Leyen’s speech, with its focus on different sectoral areas of cooperation “points to the ambition and strategic breadth of the associate membership which the parties have in mind but also suggests that, in reality, Canada’s ‘membership’ may consist of ‘plugging in’ to existing programmes and frameworks, such as the European Defence Agency, rather than joining the union in any traditional sense”.
Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the term “associate member” has taken too much focus and “doesn’t really matter” in the long term.
“My hunch is that von der Leyen was hoping to rally supporters of much closer cooperation with Canada by using that label. In the end, what I expect is that we’re going to see a collection of agreements rather than membership in any institutional sense,” he said.
Carney’s decision to formalise close ties with Europe however prompted outrage from Conservatives at home.
Pierre Poilievre, the Tory leader, posted on social media that he feared Canadians “struggling to pay their rent” would have to pay more taxes “to fund the European Union’s heavy bureaucracy”.
“The welder from Welland didn’t elect a Eurocrat to regulate our steel. The farmer from Saskatchewan and the fisher from the Atlantic provinces didn’t choose a Brussels food regulator who has never seen our prairies or our coasts,” he wrote. “We will NEVER be the 51st American state. And we will NEVER be the 28th state of the European Union.”
Another, Jamil Jivani, posted that Conservatives “will NEVER support Mark Carney’s Liberal plan to have Canada join the hopelessly run, over-regulated, and self-destructive EU”.
Paris said no Canadian leaders “would be interested in formal EU membership if it involves subordinating Canadian law and regulatory structures” to Europe.
“I don’t think that’s on the table right now. There has long been a bipartisan push in Canada to deepen trade connections between Canada and Europe,” he said. “We’re now seeing now is a logical extension of those trade discussions into other areas.”

12 killed when building damaged in Israel's war on Gaza collapses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:38:00 UTC
17:38:00 KST

Five children were among 20 killed overnight Wednesday when a building – damaged in Israel's genocidal war on Gaza – came crashing down on dozens of Palestinians sheltering there.
The incident highlights the ongoing danger for tens of thousands of Palestinians who live in an estimated 2,000 damaged buildings due to Israeli airstrikes across coastal enclave.
Rescue workers from the civil defense said at least 20 people, including five children, were killed and 14 others injured when the seven-story building collapsed. Nearly 100 more people were believed to be trapped under the rubble.
A video obtained by Reuters showed rescue workers trying to pull out two people from under a collapsed wall. Another video circulated on social media showed Gaza's civil defense spokesperson, Mahmoud Basal, carrying a little girl, wrapped in a blood-stained scarf, in his hands.
Raed al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City's civil defense service, said at least 10 families lived in the collapsed building and there was still hope of finding survivors.
"We are still hearing voices from under the rubble, so there is still hope to find people," said Dahshan.
Alessandro Mrakic, head of the U.N. Development Programme's Gaza office, said rescuers from some U.N. agencies were taking part in the rescue efforts, which he described as difficult due to the lack of proper machinery. Egypt's relief agency was also taking part in rescue efforts.
"The situation, as you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed. So there are actually people that are digging with their bare hands. We need to prepare (for more deaths)," said Mrakic.
"There are approximately 400 buildings at risk of collapse. And we know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter," he added.
Palestinian and U.N. officials blame Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery in the territory. Israel says its curbs aim to keep equipment out of the hands of Hamas.
Israel's genocidal war on Gaza – launched after the Hamas incursion into Israel in October 2023 – has generated around 61 million tons of wreckage and debris that could take seven years to clear, according to the United Nations.
Dahshan warned residents to stay away from wrecked buildings due to the risk of collapse. The local rescue service says about 2,000 damaged buildings are inhabited by families.
"The limited availability of shelter options forced residents to move into this building, believing it was safe. However, at one point it collapsed entirely, tragically crashing down on people as they slept," said Dahshan.
Many families have told Reuters in the past months that they resorted to living in partially damaged buildings to protect themselves against wind and rainstorms, and because of the lack of new tents for the homeless.
An October 2025, U.S.-backed cease-fire halted large-scale fighting in Gaza, but it Israeli has carried out daily strikes and there has been little progress on steps toward permanent peace.
Hamas accuses Israel of violating the truce and undermining efforts to implement U.S. President Donald Trump's broader plan to end the Gaza conflict, which includes an Israeli withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and the disarmament of Hamas.
Israel says Hamas has been violating the deal.
More than 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since the cease-fire took effect, according to the territory's health officials, while the Israeli military says four if its soldiers have died.

Who should serve Israel? How parties propose solving the Haredi draft crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:37:53 UTC
17:37:53 KST

Since the establishment of the state, compulsory IDF service has been a central principle of Israeli society. Over the years, Zionist parties on both the right and left have voiced support for integrating yeshiva students into military service. In practice, however, the arrangement that began in 1948 as a compromise allowing about 400 yeshiva students to defer enlistment gradually expanded. Through legislation and coalition agreements, a framework was preserved for decades that allowed the overwhelming majority of ultra-Orthodox men to dodge military service.
Time and again, governments and Knessets tried to change that reality through enlistment targets, quotas and various arrangements, but the de facto exemption remained broad.
The dramatic change came during the current Knesset term. In June 2024, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that, in the absence of a legal framework for an exemption, the state had no authority to refrain from broadly drafting yeshiva students. It also ruled that state funding could no longer be transferred to yeshivas for students who had not received a lawful exemption or whose service had not been legally deferred.
The ruling effectively changed the legal situation, requiring the state to move away from a policy of broad deferments and exemptions to one in which the draft obligation also applies to yeshiva students, alongside enforcement mechanisms and sanctions.
Ahead of the election for the 26th Knesset, Zionist parties are once again promising that this time they will actually enlist ultra-Orthodox men. They say doing so will not undermine women’s integration in the IDF, while also arguing that Arab citizens should now be required to perform civilian service.
Likud
Likud chose not to respond to inquiries from ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth regarding the draft law and draft dodging among yeshiva students.
Yashar!
The party plans to advance a “National Service for All” law after the election, under which “anyone who does not serve in the IDF will be required to perform mandatory civilian service.”
On ultra-Orthodox enlistment, Yashar! said: “The only mechanism for deferring service will be an allocation of up to 3% of each annual cohort for outstanding individuals in various fields, including Torah scholars, through an open and equal selection process, with those individuals also undergoing induction and basic training.”
On sanctions against draft evaders, the party said: “A draft evader or deserter will be subject to broad revocation of civil and economic benefits and to criminal proceedings. Sanctions will include disqualification from state tenders, scholarships from the Council for Higher Education and Labor Ministry, municipal tax discounts, housing benefits and tax benefits.”
Beyachad
“Every citizen of the State of Israel will enlist in the IDF or perform national civilian service under the Defense Service Law, without exemptions — that applies to Arabs and to the ultra-Orthodox alike,” the Beyachad party said, adding: “There are no quotas and no targets. Anyone who does not enlist will not receive a shekel from the state.”
On sanctions, the party said: “We will change the incentive mechanisms so that citizens who serve and work receive priority. The formula is simple: anyone who does not enlist will not receive a shekel from the state. Not Zionist — not on my dime.”
Among other measures, stipends for married yeshiva students would be abolished, while daycare benefits, municipal tax discounts and subsidized housing benefits would be redirected toward those who serve.
Yisrael Beytenu
The party says that “every young man and woman at age 18 — Jews, Muslims, Christians, Druze and Circassians — will be required to perform military or civilian service. The IDF will determine who serves in the military track and who performs civilian service according to security needs. Those assigned to civilian service will serve, among other places, in the Prison Service, Fire and Rescue Authority, medical services and community assistance. No exemptions, no quotas and no deals.”
The party proposes a series of sanctions against draft evaders, including: “They will be barred from leaving Israel, will not receive benefits, will lose tax benefits, will not be eligible for municipal tax discounts or state participation in daycare payments and will not be permitted to work in the civil service or local government.”
The Democrats
“The obligation to serve the state should apply to all citizens, within a national and equal framework,” the Democrats said. “The IDF’s needs will receive priority in the screening process, and anyone not required for military service will be directed to meaningful civilian-national service according to the needs of the state. Expanding the pool of those who serve must be done without harming the status of women or their service opportunities in the IDF.”
Regarding sanctions against draft evaders, the party said: “The state must stop incentivizing non-service. Anyone who does not regularize their status and fulfill their service obligation should no longer be able to enjoy the same preferential benefits currently granted by the state, including benefits related to daycare, after-school programs and municipal taxes.
“At the same time, we will work to ensure that public funding is not transferred to institutions or organizations that systematically encourage draft evasion or seek to thwart the service obligation. The details of the enforcement mechanism will be determined through legislation, but the principle will be clear: the state will reward service, not draft evasion.”
Otzma Yehudit
Party head, Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, said: “We have proven that it is possible to integrate ultra-Orthodox men into meaningful service and strengthen Israel’s security without harming their way of life. We opened dedicated tracks in the police and Border Police, with full observance of Shabbat, kashrut, prayers and Torah study, appropriate gender separation and the establishment of the ultra-Orthodox ‘Avnet’ company in the Border Police.
“I sat with rabbis, we removed obstacles and created frameworks that allow a young ultra-Orthodox man to enter service as Haredi and leave it as Haredi.”
Amcha Yisrael
The party said: “Amcha Yisrael supports integrating ultra-Orthodox men into the IDF and will work to advance a Service Members Law that represents justice and fairness. Passage of this law before the government is sworn in is a prerequisite for our participation in any government. We will not be Goldknopf’s flak jacket, but the reservists’.”
The Joint List
The Joint List opposes drafting ultra-Orthodox men or any form of compulsory enlistment and believes that “sanctions should not be imposed on someone who chooses not to enlist. Instead of punishing citizens, we should work to end the occupation and wars and build a reality in which there is no need to draft more and more people into the military.”
Ra’am
Ra’am, naturally, opposes a draft law that would require young Arab citizens to serve in the IDF or perform civilian service. The faction also declined to respond on the issue of ultra-Orthodox enlistment, even though three Ra’am lawmakers voted in January 2022 in favor of a draft law that included annual enlistment targets for the ultra-Orthodox community.
The Reservists-Economic Party
The party says that “every citizen will report to the induction center, and from there will be assigned according to the military’s needs and the preferences of the prospective recruit, with military service receiving priority and national service tracks available for national missions. Except for medical exemptions, anyone who does not serve will face sanctions and lose state benefits.”
Those who do not enlist would lose a broad range of benefits, including “cancellation of tax and municipal tax discounts, denial of benefits such as participation in subsidized housing and daycare subsidies, revocation of a driver’s license, a ban on leaving the country, exclusion from public-sector and government jobs and denial of funding to educational institutions that do not support service.”
Religious Zionism
Religious Zionism declined to address the question of sanctions against ultra-Orthodox draft evaders. It said Bezalel Smotrich’s plan includes “passing a Basic Law for Service Members under the principle of ‘first in equality’ — those who serve receive everything. We will anchor in a Basic Law the status of IDF service members and reservists, while granting priority to them and their spouses in housing and daycare.”
The party also said that “expanding the pool of those who serve” would be achieved in part by drafting ultra-Orthodox men.
Shas
For years, most Shas lawmakers said that those who do not study Torah should enlist, but in practice they did not act to enlist students who had dropped out of yeshivas. In 2024, a recording was published of Sephardi Chief Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef saying: “Even someone who does not study is exempt from going to the army.”
Now, following the Supreme Court sanctions, Shas acknowledges that it will no longer be possible to avoid drafting yeshiva students who have left their studies, and Knesset lawmaker Yinon Azoulay has said the military will need to adapt itself.
United Torah Judaism
Both the Hasidic Agudat Yisrael faction and the Degel HaTorah faction, which represents the Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox community, continue to oppose the enlistment of students who have dropped out of yeshivas and, of course, oppose a universal draft law.
United Torah Judaism says the law it seeks to pass is intended solely to regulate the status of those who study Torah. From its perspective, it is not the party’s role to instruct those who do not study to enlist — that is the military’s responsibility.

Russian attacks across Ukraine kill at least 9, injure 36 as drone strike on bus kills 5
At least nine people were killed and 36 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, including five people killed when a Russian drone struck a passenger bus in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, local authorities said on Sept. 16.
A Russian drone struck a passenger bus in the Nikopol district of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on the morning of Sept. 16, killing five people at the scene and injuring at least seven others, local Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
"Almost every day, we see Russia striking civilian transport. People who were simply going about their business are killed and injured," Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
In the morning, Preisdent Zelensky said, "Each of these strikes is about the lives of ordinary people who need to be protected by forcing Russia to stop its stupid war."
The morning attack followed another wave of Russian strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast the previous evening. Two people were injured on Sept. 15 as Russian forces attacked three districts more than 10 times with drones, artillery, and aerial bombs, Hanzha added.
Russian forces launched 80 drones overnight, including Shahed-type attack drones, jet-powered variants, Gerbera drones, and decoy drones, the Air Force said. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 63 drones, while strikes were recorded at seven locations. Debris from downed drones fell at two locations, according to the Air Force.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, one person was killed and seven others were injured in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding district, Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the Regional Defense Council, said. Russian forces launched 746 strikes against 52 settlements in the region over the past day, according to Fedorov.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured seven others, regional authorities said. Russian forces targeted critical infrastructure as well as residential areas, damaging three apartment buildings, agricultural machinery and vehicles.
In Donetsk Oblast, two people were killed in Sloviansk and one person was injured in the region over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks injured 12 people over the past day, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russian forces used 12 guided aerial bombs, a Geran-2 drone, a Molniya drone, and more than 100 drones of types that authorities were still working to identify, according to Syniehubov.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian drone attacks damaged 17 sites over the past day and the morning of Sept. 16, with damage recorded in the Bila Tserkva, Boryspil, Brovary, Bucha, and Obukhiv districts, according to local authorities. A driver in the Obukhiv district suffered a concussion from the blast wave after a house, tractor, and vehicle were damaged.

There will be no new fines for speeding: Parliament rejected the bill
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:35:00 EEST
17:35:00 KST

There will be no new fines for speeding: Parliament rejected the bill
Kyiv • UNN
Lawmakers fell one vote short of adopting Bill No. 15348 as a basis. The document provided for fines of up to 3,400 hryvnias and 17,000 hryvnias for repeat offenders.
The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine has rejected a bill introducing new fines for speeding. MPs did not support Bill No. 15348 in its first reading - 225 votes "in favor" out of the required 226. This was reported by UNN.
Details
The bill provides for new fines for speeding violations, including:
-  exceeding the speed limit by 20+ km/h - a fine of 680 hryvnias; 
-  exceeding the speed limit by 40+ km/h - a fine of 2,040 hryvnias; 
-  exceeding the speed limit by 60+ km/h - a fine of 2,720 hryvnias; 
-  exceeding the speed limit by 80+ km/h - a fine of 3,400 hryvnias.  
It is also proposed to impose a fine of 17,000 hryvnias on drivers who have been subject to administrative penalties for speeding by more than 60 and 80 km/h five or more times during a year.
The bill stipulates that drivers held liable for speeding by more than 60 and 80 km/h will not be able to pay the fine with a 50% discount.
Additionally
It should be noted that currently, under Article 122 of the Code of Ukraine on Administrative Offenses, speeding by more than 20 km/h entails a fine of 340 hryvnias.
Speeding by more than 50 km/h carries a fine of 1,700 hryvnias.
If the violation is recorded automatically (by photo and video enforcement cameras), the driver may pay the fine within 10 days with a 50% discount.
Reminder
In June 2026, the Verkhovna Rada registered a bill on fines for exceeding the permissible noise level of vehicles. During martial law, the fines may range from 17,000 to 34,000 hryvnias.

Swiss set to reject tighter neutrality rules barring NATO cooperation, polls show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:32:56 UTC
17:32:56 KST

Swiss set to reject tighter neutrality rules barring NATO cooperation, polls show
- Polls show around 68% of Swiss voters oppose stricter neutrality rules barring NATO cooperation and sanctions in a September referendum.
- The proposal, backed by the right-wing Swiss People's Party, aims to tighten neutrality but is rejected by the government and many voters.
- Opponents warn the change would limit Switzerland's foreign policy flexibility and harm its global reputation by preventing sanctions on aggressor states.
AI generated
ZURICH – Voters looked set to reject constitutional changes that would bar Switzerland from cooperating with NATO or imposing sanctions on other countries, two polls showed before a referendum on the issue later in September.
Around 68 per cent were set to reject the adoption of a stricter definition of the country’s official neutrality, proposed in a plebiscite launched by the right-wing Swiss People’s Party (SVP), according to a survey by 20 Minuten and Tamedia.
Only 31 per cent were in favour of the proposals set out in the “Preservation of Swiss Neutrality” vote, that poll that was published on Sept 16 said.
A separate poll conducted by GFS Bern for broadcaster SRG showed 63 per cent against the proposal with 34 per cent in favour.
Both polls showed rising opposition to the proposal, which have been rejected by the Swiss government but which will be put to the public in a referendum on Sept 27 under the Swiss tradition of direct democracy.
“The current figures point very clearly towards a rejection,” and support was waning even among SVP voters, Corina Schena from GFS Bern said.
Swiss neutrality, internationally recognised since 1815 and part of the country’s constitution since 1848, kept Switzerland out of both world wars.
Christoph Blocher, a veteran politician and backer of the SVP, told Reuters in August that Switzerland’s neutral status was under threat after Bern imposed sanctions on Russia over its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Supporters of the change said tightening the definition of neutrality in the Swiss constitution would prevent the government from watering it down, and help Switzerland act as a credible mediator in conflicts, according to the Tamedia study.
But opponents said the initiative would severely restrict Switzerland’s ability to respond to foreign policy challenges and would weaken the country’s defence.
Nearly a quarter of those surveyed in the Tamedia poll also said that refraining from imposing sanctions in cases of violations of international law would be seen as taking sides with aggressor states and would damage Switzerland’s reputation around the world.

Mecca defense pact intended for 'collective deterrence' with no 'regional aspirations': Pakistan army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16

Aamir Latif
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Pakistan's army on Wednesday said the trilateral Mecca defense pact between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan is intended for "collective deterrence," and has no “regional aspirations."
“It formalizes Pakistan’s decades-old relationship with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the brotherly country of Türkiye in the domains for collective deterrence and defense of the three countries,” army spokesman Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said in an interview with Saudi broadcaster Al Arabiya.
Asked whether the pact inked in Mecca last month is primarily a defensive cooperation or the beginning of a broader strategic alliance, Chaudhry asserted that the pact was "defensive, as its name implied."
The pact provides that an attack on one member state would be treated as an attack on all.
The alliance's inaugural meeting was held in Istanbul on Aug. 31, where it was decided that Pakistan would initially head the alliance’s secretariat for three years.
“It is defensive.There’s nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is collective deterrence,” he said, adding that the agreement was also “complementary”.
“So this mutual defence agreement is complementary in nature. It is not competing with any other relationship of these countries,” he said, adding that the three allies have independent relationships with other nations, blocs and alliances.
 
Operational details not to be made public
In response to a question about how Pakistan would respond if one of the countries in the alliance came under attack, he said that the operationalization of defensive commitments were never made public in any discourse.
“You see, you have multiple other agreements which are defensive in nature, which are committal in nature. But no country comes out and starts sharing its operational details."
“It is for the three countries to decide, and it is for them to know and for them to actualize it,” Chaudhry maintained.
On whether the alliance was “complementing or competing” with Pakistan’s decades-long relationship with China, he said: “We need to understand that the Pak-Saudi and the Pak-Türkiye relationship has not come out of the blue. The Chinese understand it. The world at large understands it, that how historic these relationships are. We have formalized that."
To a question on whether the defense agreement would become part of the wider, Muslim-world security architecture, Chaudhry said that there was nothing in the pact that stated that it was a Muslim alliance, adding that it was an alliance for regional stability.
“It is not a club that is being made for only Muslim countries,” he said, adding that decisions on its expansion would be taken by the leadership of the three countries.
The alliance, he further said, can always encompass new, willing partners who also believe in regional peace, stability and security, and who have the shared vision of non-aggression, non-interference and collective deterrence.

US moves millions of military aid to Trump-aligned Americas

Breadcrumb
US strips millions in military aid from Europe and Mideast to back Trump-aligned nations in Americas
The Trump administration is stripping tens of millions of dollars in US military assistance from countries in Europe and the Middle East to support conservative-leaning governments in Central and South America.
The State Department on Tuesday notified Congress that it will reprogram $52 million in foreign military financing from Slovakia, North Macedonia, Tunisia and Iraq to Panama, Peru, Ecuador and Colombia.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Colombia, Ecuador and Peru last week and pledged to them additional support as the Trump administration has prioritized the Western Hemisphere in its foreign policy with an emphasis on combating drug trafficking and illegal immigration.
It is just the latest in a series of moves that have reduced either money or troop deployments to Europe in response to President Donald Trump's complaints about NATO allies not spending enough on their defense budgets and other matters. Both North Macedonia and Slovakia are NATO members.
But it also comes as the administration has put particular attention on the Western Hemisphere, aligning deeply with right-wing governments as Trump celebrates a renewal of the 19th century Monroe Doctrine establishing Washington's dominance in the Americas.
Foreign military financing provides recipient countries with US taxpayer dollars to allow them to purchase military equipment from American defense contractors.
The State Department said the funds would be used to "combat narcoterrorism in our backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal," adding that the Western Hemisphere has been historically neglected in US military assistance.
"These funds will prevent adversaries from establishing strategic footholds in our hemisphere," the department said in a veiled jab at China, which has increasingly sought to boost its presence in Latin America.
The shift of money does not eliminate foreign military financing for Tunisia, Iraq, North Macedonia or Slovakia, although the exact amount remaining for those countries was not immediately clear.
The State Department said, though, that the current distribution of financing does "not align with the administration’s prioritisation of" the Western Hemisphere.

KINSHASA, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Ebola transmission is showing starkly different trends across affected areas in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with the epidemic peak having passed in Ituri, the main epicenter of the outbreak, while transmission continues to rise in the eastern province of North Kivu, a leading Congolese Ebola expert said late Tuesday.
Jean-Jacques Muyembe, a veteran Congolese virologist heading the country's National Institute of Biomedical Research, said there had been "a clear improvement" in the fight against Ebola in Ituri.
"The peak is behind us (in Ituri). We are already on the downward slope," Muyembe said at a press briefing in Kinshasa. By contrast, he said the epidemic curve in North Kivu was still rising and "has not yet reached the plateau."
He stressed that the epidemic was unfolding at different stages in different provinces, making it difficult to assess the situation simply by combining case numbers nationwide.
Muyembe nevertheless cautioned that bringing the epidemic under control did not mean it was over, stressing the need to further strengthen contact tracing and other response measures.
Placide Mbala Kingebeni, director of Research, Clinical Trials and Innovation at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said at the briefing that progress in Ituri remained uneven, with cases and deaths declining in some hotspots while incidence was still rising slightly in other health zones.
The World Health Organization (WHO) offered a similar assessment earlier Tuesday.
"There are some, perhaps very early, signs that the epidemic is beginning to decline in some areas, while increasing exponentially in others," Olivier le Polain, head of Epidemiology and Analytics for Response at WHO, said at a UN briefing in Geneva.
He said some affected areas were more under control than others and could be viewed as separate epidemics rather than a single epidemiological challenge, warning that early improvements could still be followed by renewed flare-ups.
North Kivu has emerged as one of the main areas of concern. Le Polain said weekly cases reported in the province had roughly doubled within weeks.
"Although the response has been unprecedented in its scale, the epidemic continues to expand," he said, warning that the high caseload and wide geographic spread meant it would take "many, many months" to bring the outbreak fully under control.
Muyembe did not give a new deadline for containing the outbreak, saying only that response teams should "do everything possible so that we can celebrate the New Year under better conditions."
The DRC government's latest situation report, with data through Sept. 13, showed that the country had recorded 7,258 confirmed Ebola cases, including 3,510 deaths, across 62 health zones in seven provinces.
The current outbreak has become the largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic in the DRC's history and the second-largest globally, after the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

A total of 56 firefighters responded to the incident, the LAFD said. The fire was completely extinguished and did not spread to any structures. Four automobiles and two storage containers were damaged by the fire.

Los Angeles County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath told reporters Tuesday night that there were "serious questions about what happened tonight."
"Tonight is not the time to speculate about those answers, tonight is the time to care for the people who are hurting, to support our first responders and to stand together as a community," she added.

"This is a tragic night for Los Angeles. My thoughts are with those impacted by the bus collision and the helicopter crash, and with the entire NBC4 family who lost members of their team while they were doing their jobs," Mayor of Los Angeles Karen Bass said. ■

China issues world's first medical-device standard for AI-powered brain-computer interfaces
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:31:30 CST
17:31:30 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China has approved and issued the country's third medical-device standard for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), which is also the world's first such standard for BCI medical devices using artificial intelligence (AI) to process electroencephalogram (EEG) data.
BCI technology establishes a direct communication route between the brains of humans or animals and external devices. By capturing and decoding neural signals, BCI enables seamless interaction between brain and machine, ultimately allowing control over assistive devices to execute intended actions.
China's BCI sector is accelerating its transition from the laboratory to industrialization, making steady progress via the market launch of diverse related products and thanks to surging investment in the sector.
The standard, issued by the National Medical Products Administration, specifies quality requirements and evaluation methods for EEG datasets used by AI algorithms in BCI medical devices. It applies to datasets used in research and development, production, quality control and other stages of BCI medical device technology that uses AI algorithms to post-process EEG signals.
The standard covers requirements for the collection, processing, annotation, storage and access of EEG data, as well as methods for testing dataset quality. It will help address common industry challenges, including inconsistent quality-control criteria and non-standardized dataset development.
The administration said AI-powered BCIs depend on large and high-quality EEG datasets to train algorithms to decode brain signals and identify patients' intentions. In medical applications, the quality and consistency of such data can directly affect the performance and safety of the devices.
To support major innovations in BCI medical devices and meet the urgent needs of the industry, the administration adopted an expedited procedure for the development and approval of this standard.
China previously issued two BCI medical-device standards in 2025, covering terminology and test methods for the sensing and response performance of implantable neural stimulators with closed-loop functions.
The new standard will take effect on Sept. 1, 2027. ■

====================================================================================================

Solar activity can manipulate deep-sea climate: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:31:26 CST
17:31:26 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Solar activity not only affects temperatures on Earth's surface, but can also "control" climate change in the deep sea, according to a group of Chinese researchers.
Using eight decades of ocean reanalysis, they showed that the 11-year solar cycle robustly modulates the volume of a subsurface water mass in the North Pacific Ocean, the North Pacific Eastern Subtropical Mode Water (NPESTMW), said the researchers in an article published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters.
The NPESTMW, connecting the subtropics and tropics, forms at the ocean surface in winter and sinks, transferring heat and carbon to the deep ocean and influencing climate variability on timescales of years to decades.
Researchers at the Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (IOCAS), found that one to two years after the solar maximum, the formation of this mode of water was significantly suppressed.
The mechanism of this process is not as simple as solar heat directly warming the ocean, said Wang Jianing, a researcher at the IOCAS. During periods of high solar activity, anomalous cyclonic circulation over the formation region weakens surface winds and reduces ocean heat loss, suppressing winter mixed layer deepening and mode water formation.
However, the strength of this solar influence varies over time, according to the research article. A long-term natural climate fluctuation in the Atlantic Ocean further amplifies it, helping explain why the sun's imprint on climate has been particularly pronounced since the 1990s.
These findings reveal a new mechanism for incorporating solar activity, a predictable external forcing source, into decadal climate prediction. ■

====================================================================================================

Opinion: Southern Europe's recovery holds lessons for Europe today
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:31:05 CST
17:31:05 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- More than a decade ago, Portugal, Italy, Greece and Spain stood at the center of Europe's sovereign debt crisis. High debt, fiscal imbalances and soaring unemployment turned southern Europe into a symbol of the continent's economic difficulties.
Today, the picture looks different. Spain's economy expanded 2.8 percent in 2025, well above the eurozone average. Greece and Portugal recorded government surpluses of 1.7 percent and 0.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), respectively. Italy continues to face the challenge of public debt, but its manufacturing and export base has shown resilience.
As the continent grapples with a new competitiveness challenge, southern Europe's experience offers an interesting reference point: Recovery has depended not only on improving domestic conditions, but also on remaining connected to wider markets and sources of growth.
The debt crisis exposed structural problems that had accumulated for years in southern Europe. Under enormous economic and political pressure, countries across the region began tackling long-standing structural challenges embedded in their own economies.
Spain overhauled its labor market, giving firms greater flexibility while drawing on immigration to expand its workforce. Portugal cut red tape and streamlined licensing requirements for businesses. Greece consolidated its fragmented pension system and strengthened tax collection. Italy has sought to tackle cumbersome public administration through judicial and administrative reforms.
The process was painful. But these countries sought to restore competitiveness by repairing public finances, improving domestic institutions and reducing structural inefficiencies instead of looking abroad for scapegoats.
At the same time, southern Europe remained closely connected to the outside world.
Southern Europe's rebound has drawn strength from tourism, foreign investment, migration and access to the international market. Against a backdrop of rising protectionism globally, southern European economies have remained open to mutually beneficial cooperation, as illustrated by Volkswagen's multibillion-euro electric-vehicle push in Spain and Microsoft's investments in artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud infrastructure in Italy.
China has also played a role in this recovery story. At Greece's Piraeus port, Chinese investment and management have helped develop the port into a major European container hub. In Spain, CATL and Stellantis are investing up to 4.1 billion euros (4.72 billion U.S. dollars) in a battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, while Chinese automaker Chery has partnered with Spain's Ebro to revive vehicle production in Barcelona.
These examples matter as Europe confronts a new competitiveness challenge.
The EU today faces weak productivity growth, high energy costs, insufficient investment, demographic pressures and persistent fragmentation of its single market. At the same time, the policy debate has increasingly focused on tariffs, trade defenses, investment restrictions and reducing dependence on foreign suppliers, particularly China.
These defensive policies may offer an illusion of security, but in the long run they only drain the dynamism an economy needs to prosper.
The more fundamental approach is to create the conditions for European businesses to become more productive, innovative and competitive. That means tackling high costs, weak investment and regulatory barriers, while continuing to engage with global markets and make the most of the opportunities for international cooperation.
A decade ago, southern Europe, in the face of the debt crisis, decided not to erect walls of protection, but to accelerate reforms while keeping the door open for cooperation. That experience offers a timely reminder for today's struggling Europe. ■

We need to start discussing when work may need to stop, who should be compensated when it does and how the cost of adaptation can be shared
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
At the beginning of August, when temperatures in Hong Kong hit highs not seen for at least 140 years, the Labour Department’s Heat Stress at Work Warning system remained at the amber level, the lowest of three tiers. The controversy that followed raised a broader question: are our heat warnings adequately protecting people who work outdoors?
The Labour Department has since announced changes that will lead to earlier heat-stress warnings. These improvements to worker protection are welcome. But they also force us to confront a harder question: what happens when dangerous heat becomes common enough that protecting workers’ health begins to conflict with construction schedules, noise controls, workers’ incomes and the normal functioning of the city?
Let us for a moment consider the wider impact of the updated rules. After this summer, it is not hard to believe that heatwaves will become increasingly long and common.

‘Smart’ Nanoparticles Deliver mRNA Directly to Tumors in New Cancer Therapy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

Our immune systems don’t just fight bacteria and viruses invading the body. They are responsible for keeping our own tissues in check, taking out cancerous cells before they have a chance to grow. Once a tumor forms, however, it can create an environment that declaws cancer-fighting immune cells—in some cases even reprogramming them to suppress other parts of the immune system.
Overcoming the oppressive tumor environment remains a barrier for even some of the most promising treatments. “One of the biggest challenges in cancer immunotherapy is that the immune system may be capable of attacking a tumor, but the tumor environment can stop those immune cells from doing their job,” University of Adelaide professor Chunxia Zhao explained in a press release.
In a study published this week in Science Advances, Zhao’s team developed a system that can precisely deliver an mRNA therapy to transform immune cells back into allies. The researchers focused on tumor-associated macrophages, which—when rewired by signals from the cancer—hinder the arrival and activity of T cells, one of the body’s main weapons against cancer. The mRNA carries the instructions for producing CXCL9, a chemical signal for recruiting T cells.
Flipping this switch is the easy part. mRNA technologies have been rapidly advancing, especially in the realm of cancer treatments, since they were first introduced to the public as Covid vaccines. However, you don’t want an immune-activating signal going just anywhere in the body. A risk of any immunotherapy is amping up the immune system too much, which can cause dangerous and potentially deadly side effects.
To make sure the mRNA made it directly to the site of the tumor and nowhere else, the researchers developed a delivery method they dubbed “smart” nanoparticles. In any mRNA therapy, including a standard Covid shot, the mRNA is encased in some kind of nanoparticle, usually a lipid envelope. This fatty structure helps the molecules enter cells. In this case, the researchers took this basic technology and added a targeting mechanism to ensure the mRNA only got into the right cells.
The smart nanoparticles were studded with antibodies that bind to TREM2, a protein present on the surface of tumor-associated immunosuppressive macrophages. A tumor’s environment tends to be a messy place full of many different cell types, so not only does this honing mechanism help get the therapy to the right part of the body, but only into macrophages in that region that need reprogramming.
In addition to the mRNA, the smart nanoparticles also carried a drug called resiquimod, which can stimulate certain immune pathways. Initial laboratory results showed that not the previously lethargic macrophages began producing CXCL9 as well as other markers of an active immune state, such as NOS2, expression of which increased by a factor of 89.5. Signals of a more immunosuppressive state also notably decreased.
The researchers then administered the smart nanoparticles to mice with aggressive breast cancer. After three doses, tumor growth slowed. The concentration of CXCL9 was approximately four times higher than in the control group, and the researchers detected the presence of T-cell activity. The treatment also reduced the proportion of macrophages with immunosuppressive characteristics by 63 percent.
Often, cancer treatments are combined to attack the tumor from different directions. The researchers tested their new therapy in combination with two types of immunotherapy already used called immune checkpoint inhibitors. The combination did not further reduce the tumor size, but it did generate important changes in the immune system. Different types of T cells increased within the tumors and nearby lymph nodes—a finding associated with the potential for a more lasting immune response.
The researchers also did not detect any negative effects to other organs, but they urged caution that more studies are needed to evaluate the safety before human trials can begin.
“This is an important proof of concept that we can use mRNA and nanoparticle technology to reprogram the immune environment of a tumor,” said Professor Zhao. “There is still significant work to do before this approach could be considered for patients, but these results provide an encouraging foundation for developing more targeted cancer immunotherapies.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

BoM issues a fresh 'super' El Niño reality check for Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:29:47 UTC
17:29:47 KST

IN BRIEF
- Australia's El Niño could see Pacific sea surface temperatures climb more than 3C above average.
- The BoM says rainfall will vary across Australia, with parts of the south-east facing a drier end to the year.
Australia's current El Niño could become the strongest on record, but the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) has cautioned that doesn't necessarily mean the country is headed for an exceptionally hot and dry summer.
The BoM says models indicate the El Niño underway in the Pacific Ocean could produce the highest central tropical Pacific sea surface temperature anomaly since reliable records began in 1950.
But it has stressed the strength of an El Niño does not directly determine how severe its impacts will be in Australia, with several other climate drivers influencing rainfall and temperatures.
Could this be the strongest El Niño on record?
An El Niño occurs when sea surface temperatures in parts of the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, triggering changes in atmospheric circulation and weather patterns.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The BoM says the current event is likely to become the strongest recorded based on forecast sea surface temperatures in the central tropical Pacific.
During the 1982-83 El Niño, which currently holds the record, sea surface temperature anomalies peaked at around 2.6C above average in January 1983.
The current event is forecast to potentially exceed 3C above average.
However, the BoM has warned against assuming a stronger El Niño automatically means more extreme conditions for Australia.
"Every El Niño is different," it said in an advisory it released on Tuesday.
"A strong event can produce only modest effects in some regions, while a weaker event can have significant impacts."
Australia's weather is influenced by a combination of climate drivers, including El Niño, the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), surrounding sea surface temperatures and seasonal changes, as well as the longer-term effects of climate change.
The previous El Niño, which developed in spring 2023 and continued into early 2024, was considered a moderate-to-strong event.
What could El Niño mean for Australia's summer?
The current El Niño is likely to continue through spring and summer, although its influence on Australian rainfall typically diminishes around early summer.
The BoM's latest long-range forecast, issued on 10 September, shows most of Australia is likely to experience above-average temperatures over the coming months.
Rainfall, however, is expected to vary considerably across the country
Between October and December, below-average rainfall is likely across parts of south-eastern Australia, including southern NSW, Victoria and Tasmania.
Most of Western Australia, as well as some central and northern parts of the country, are instead forecast to receive above-average rainfall.
The IOD is currently neutral, but all climate models suggest a positive IOD could develop later in spring. A positive IOD can increase the likelihood of drier spring conditions, particularly across southern and eastern Australia.
Climate change is also increasing the likelihood of hotter summers and more frequent extreme heat events.
While El Niño can increase the chance of higher temperatures, the BoM says local conditions and short-term weather patterns will also be important in determining bushfire risk.
Why has it still been raining during El Niño?
Despite El Niño's association with dry conditions in Australia, 2026 has so far been wetter than usual across large parts of the country.
The year began with an active La Niña climate pattern and a very wet northern wet season before conditions rapidly transitioned towards El Niño during autumn. El Niño was underway by June.
Parts of Australia's interior also received unusually high winter rainfall, largely due to significant weather systems including two north-west cloudbands and strong cold fronts drawing tropical moisture from the north-west.
While winter rainfall was unusually high for an El Niño year, the BoM said it was not record-breaking overall. Large parts of eastern Australia and south-west Western Australia still experienced a dry winter.
The BoM also pointed to unusually warm oceans around Australia and globally, which can provide additional moisture and energy for rain-producing weather systems.
Australia's overall water storages were around 71 per cent full in early September. Capital city storages were above 80 per cent, with the exceptions of Melbourne at around 70 per cent and Perth at around 40 per cent.
Conditions have been drier than average this year in parts of north-eastern NSW and south-eastern Queensland, south-west Western Australia and Tasmania.
The BoM also cautioned against drawing direct comparisons between Australia's coming summer and the extreme heat experienced recently across Europe and North America.
There is no predictive link between a northern hemisphere summer and the Australian summer.
However, it said recent overseas conditions demonstrated how extreme heat could rapidly dry vegetation, increase fire intensity and cause fire conditions to escalate quickly.

Ukraine
