'Red line': Saudis down suspected Houthi drone near Mecca
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:12:00 UTC
17:12:00 KST

Saudi Arabia declared the security of Islam's holiest city a "red line" Wednesday after military air defenses intercepted an attempted drone attack near Mecca, accusing Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels of escalating the widening Middle East conflict into sacred territory.
The incident sparked immediate condemnation across the Muslim world, even as the Houthis vehemently denied launching weapons toward Mecca and dismissed Riyadh's allegations as a manufactured falsehood.
The alleged strike marks a dangerous surge in hostility that threatens to pull key regional allies deeper into the multi-front war, with crude oil prices remaining stubbornly above $100 a barrel amid escalating disruptions to global shipping and energy infrastructure.
According to the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the rebels in Yemen, air defense systems intercepted and destroyed an armed drone at approximately 6:50 p.m. local time Tuesday before it entered restricted airspace over Mecca, located roughly 1,100 kilometers (680 miles) from the Yemeni border. Coalition spokesperson Col. Turki al-Maliki said debris from the intercepted aircraft fell in an unpopulated area south of the city.
The attempt marks the second time Saudi Arabia has accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca, following a 2017 incident in which the coalition reported intercepting a ballistic missile fired toward the holy site.
"The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line," the Saudi-led coalition said in a statement, vowing that it "will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the Terrorist Houthi Militia."
In Mecca, brief public alert warnings triggered localized panic among residents. "I saw a few people panicking, running to the window to see what happened," one Mecca resident told reporters on condition of anonymity. "I think the alarm system creates panic ... Life is normal in Mecca, and there have been previous incidents in Mecca so this isn't the first one."
Another resident noted feelings of shock over the alleged targeting of the site, which draws millions of Muslim pilgrims annually and is guarded by heavy security deployments and advanced air defense batteries. "I won't hide that we were scared," the resident said, "or you can say surprised." "Aren't they Muslims? They're targeting the holiest city. What's inside to target?"
Houthi officials, however, swiftly rejected the coalition’s account. Hazem al-Assad, a member of the Houthi politburo, posted on social media that "the claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone."
Despite the denial, the rebels continued to press military operations elsewhere. Later Wednesday, Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree claimed that rebel forces had shot down a Saudi-led coalition F-15 fighter jet over Yemen's central Marib province. Saree provided no evidence or specific timeframe for the downing, and coalition spokespeople did not immediately confirm or comment on the claim.
The ground conflict inside Yemen – dormant since 2022 – has flared dramatically since July, when the Houthis launched a massive offensive against government forces, forcing more than 82,000 people to flee their homes since early September, according to the United Nations.
Yemen’s permanent representative to the U.N., Abdullah al-Saadi, stated that government troops are fighting to restore "national institutions across every inch" of the nation while appealing for international intervention.
Simultaneously, the Houthis have established control over Yemen’s entire Red Sea coastline and seized key islands near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, declaring a maritime blockade strictly against Saudi-flagged vessels.
The reported targeting of Mecca, meanwhile, drew swift, fiery condemnation from international diplomatic bodies and regional powers.
The Jeddah-based Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), representing 57 member states, denounced the "heinous attacks ... against the city of Mecca and the Madinah region," stating the action violated the "sanctity of holy sites."
Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy warned that "compromising the security of Mecca and the sanctity of Islamic holy sites is a matter of extreme gravity" and noted that escalating Houthi strikes "threaten the region's security and stability."
Pakistani Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif delivered an impassioned response, praising the Saudi armed forces for their "extraordinary vigilance, courage, and professionalism" during what he termed a "swift and heroic action."
"I condemn in the strongest possible terms the dastardly and heinous attempted drone attack against the Holy Site of Makkah Al-Mukarramah," Sharif said on X, calling on all parties to exercise "maximum" restraint. "Our region has already suffered far too much from conflict. Dialogue and diplomacy remain the only sustainable path toward peace."
Sharif added that "Pakistan stands unwaveringly, shoulder to shoulder with the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, in the defense of its sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as for the security and sanctity of the Haramain Sharifain (cities of Mecca and Medina) – a duty that every Pakistani carries close to their heart."
The escalation will also test a new trilateral security pact finalized in August between Saudi Arabia, nuclear-armed Pakistan, and NATO member Türkıye, which followed a bilateral mutual defense agreement signed between Islamabad and Riyadh last year.
However, senior Turkish and Pakistani officials told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity that Riyadh has not formally requested military assistance under the alliance.
A Turkish official noted that efforts to "institutionalize" the pact must be completed before the alliance becomes operational.
As Riyadh faces mounting pressure, the United States has shown reluctance to enter a direct military confrontation with the Houthis. While Washington maintains billions of dollars in arms contracts with Saudi Arabia and a U.S. military task force continues providing intelligence-sharing and planning assistance, top American leadership signaled a desire to stay out of active combat.
"The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us," U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday, adding that the rebel group remains focused on Saudi Arabia.
U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance confirmed Monday that Washington maintains "constant contact" with Saudi officials while engaging in "direct conversations with the Houthis themselves," describing the crisis as "a very fluid and dynamic thing."
U.S. media reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman personally requested U.S. military intervention during a call with Trump last week, but the request was turned down.
With Washington stepping back from direct intervention, rival Iran sought diplomatic backing in Beijing. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in China.
Wang expressed concern over the spread of hostilities into Yemen and the Red Sea while urging both Tehran and Washington to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Chinese President Xi Jinping also reiterated Beijing's willingness to assist in mediating an end to the conflict during the BRICS summit in New Delhi.
The strategic fallout is compounding global economic strain. A major Saudi pipeline remains offline following a weeks-old strike by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, and Iranian strikes continue to target merchant ships near the Strait of Hormuz.
Tanker traffic through Hormuz has dropped to between 5 million and 7 million barrels per day (bpd), less than half of pre-war levels, despite U.S. naval escorts.
In the Red Sea, Houthi naval operations threaten the gateway to the Suez Canal, cutting Egypt’s vital transit revenues to half of pre-2023 levels.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi jointly called for "ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation" through both Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Qatar warned that any prolonged closure of the Bab el-Mandeb waterway would prove "catastrophic for the entire world," as global energy markets brace for prolonged instability.

Russia Sanctions Bill Clears Another Hurdle, Heads Toward Final Vote In US Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:10:06 UTC
17:10:06 KST

WASHINGTON -- A sweeping Russia sanctions bill championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham cleared a key procedural hurdle in the US House of Representatives on September 15, setting up a final vote on legislation that supporters say would increase pressure on Moscow and strengthen US support for Ukraine.
The House voted 214-211 to approve a rule allowing consideration of Senate amendments to the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, with two Democrats joining Republicans voting in favor. Many Democrats oppose the bill because it would give President Donald Trump additional power to impose tariffs.
The vote cleared the way for the House to consider the version approved by the Senate with strong bipartisan support in August, and a final vote in the 435-seat chamber is expected on September 16. If it approves the Senate text without changes, the bill would go to Trump.
"We're going to get done tomorrow," Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska told RFE/RL, expressing confidence that the House would pass the bill. "At least that's the least we could do. We've got to do more."
The legislation would impose sanctions on Russian officials and military figures, foreign suppliers supporting Russia's defense sector, and networks helping Moscow evade existing sanctions.
It would also target Russia's so-called shadow fleet of oil tankers, restrict new US investment in Russia and exports that could support the Russian military, and authorize sanctions against people responsible for abducting Ukrainian children. The measure also extends sanctions on Iran.
In addition, it would allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries purchasing Russian energy or helping Moscow evade sanctions.
The tariff provisions have drawn opposition from mostly Democratic lawmakers concerned about granting additional trade authority to Trump and about potential effects on US fuel prices.
The Senate rejected an effort to remove the provisions before passing the legislation.
'Scorching Sanctions'
Republican Representative Michael McCaul of Texas, who is managing the legislation on the House floor, portrayed its expected passage as part of Graham's legacy.
"One of the proudest accomplishments I think I've had is the bill we're going to pass tomorrow that Lindsey Graham said, in his words, if I'm not mistaken, the biggest legislative accomplishment of his career," McCaul said at an event at Ukraine House in Washington marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's restored independence.
Graham, a South Carolina Republican and prominent supporter of Ukraine, died in July.
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, who worked with Graham on the legislation, said at the same event that the measure would impose "scorching sanctions" intended to "throttle Putin's war machine."
Divisions over the tariff provisions have complicated the bill's path through the House.
Republican Representative Tim Burchett of Tennessee said he had received assurances that Republican leaders would consider measures aimed at reducing fuel costs.
'A Symbolic Win For Ukraine'
Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and a supporter of the legislation, has urged the House to approve it, saying it would target financial resources sustaining Russia's war and increase pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin to negotiate.
The sanctions push comes as Ukraine continues to seek US military and economic support more than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
Andrew D'Anieri, associate director of the Atlantic Council's Eurasia Center, told RFE/RL that enactment of the bill would be "a symbolic win for Ukraine," but said Kyiv also needed continued military assistance, particularly air defenses.
At the Ukraine House event, US Under Secretary of the Treasury for International Affairs Jonathan Greenstein said Washington remained committed to "achieving a negotiated settlement and a durable peace" while supporting an "independent and prosperous future for Ukraine."
Greenstein said the United States had disbursed $7.5 billion to Ukraine in 2026 and expected to provide nearly $300 million more in the coming months.

From nail hammering to drilling, Japan’s new robots push physical AI forward

2026-09-16
08:08:56 UTC
17:08:56 KST

Robots are getting to grips with the physical world in Tokyo, where technology companies are showcasing machines designed to handle objects, perform industrial tasks and work alongside humans.
The demonstrations offer a glimpse of how AI could move beyond screens and software, giving machines the ability to interact with their surroundings and carry out physical tasks.
Among the prototypes on display is a machine developed by THK, which picks up bottles, bags and boxes under the remote control of a single operator. Its articulated arms and grippers also allow it to hammer a nail into a piece of wood, demonstrating the precision and dexterity needed for more complex tasks.
Nachi, HatsuMuv and ugo are also presenting their latest robotic systems. Ugo is showcasing its semi-humanoid ugo Nova, which performs a drilling task under remote control.
Designed to work in environments built for humans, the robot has two seven-axis arms as well as additional joints in its head and waist. It is also designed to collect real-world data that can be used to train physical AI models.
But the demonstrations also reveal the technology’s current limits. Many of the robots still depend on human operators, with developers now working to give them greater autonomy as investment in AI-powered machines grows in Japan.

Piazza under pressure as Iran’s Olympic path narrows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:08:05 UTC
17:08:05 KST

Piazza under pressure as Iran’s Olympic path narrows
TEHRAN - Iran’s silver medal at the 2026 AVC Men’s Volleyball Continental Championship should have been celebrated as a positive step. Instead, the defeat to Japan in the final has left head coach Roberto Piazza and the Iranian federation facing a much more complicated question: what exactly is the team building toward?
Japan’s 3-0 victory in Fukuoka did more than settle the Asian title. It also handed the hosts a direct ticket to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, while Iran lost their clearest route to volleyball’s biggest stage. The silver medal was respectable, but the timing of the defeat makes it a painful one.
 
 Iran are not mathematically out of the Olympic race. Twelve teams will compete in Los Angeles: the United States as hosts, five continental champions, three teams from the 2027 World Championship and three more based on the world ranking after the preliminary phase of the 2028 Volleyball Nations League.
 
 For Iran, the remaining routes are extremely demanding.
 
 The World Championship route would require a top-three finish in 2027, an achievement that currently looks more aspirational than realistic. The ranking route is therefore likely to become the central target. Iran are currently around 18th in the world, while several potential Olympic rivals including Slovenia, Bulgaria, Ukraine, Turkey, Germany, Finland, Argentina and Serbia, sit ahead of them.
 
 That makes every match over the next 18 months significant. Wins matter, but so do sets and individual points, because the ranking system leaves little room for careless losses against supposedly weaker opponents.
 
 *The Piazza question
 
 This is where the debate over Piazza becomes unavoidable. The Italian is an experienced and respected coach, and replacing him simply because Iran failed to beat Japan would be an overly simplistic reaction. Former Iran international and coach Mahmoud Afshardoust has argued that Piazza is not a minor figure in world volleyball and that the federation should judge him against the objectives established when he was appointed.
 
 The more important question is whether Piazza’s Iran are developing an identity capable of competing with the best teams consistently—not merely producing competitive stretches in individual matches.
 
 Against Japan, Iran stayed close deep into all three sets but repeatedly failed to turn those moments into victories. The problem was not a total lack of quality. It was the inability to make the decisive plays when the margin for error disappeared.
 
 Piazza has also invested heavily in younger players, a strategy that carries both risk and potential reward. Iran cannot remain dependent forever on an ageing generation, but rebuilding while simultaneously chasing an Olympic qualification requires exceptional timing and execution.
 
 The upcoming Asian Games and the 2027 World Championship will provide further evidence.
 
 The Olympic door is still open. But after Fukuoka, Iran no longer control their destiny. Piazza’s challenge is to turn a team with potential into one that can win the moments that matter.

India's goods trade deficit narrows as gold imports fall
India's goods trade deficit narrowed unexpectedly to $26.86 billion (€23.28 billion) in August, government data showed on Tuesday, as a sharp drop in gold imports offset a slight decline in exports.
While total imports fell to $70.67 billion from $76.22 billion, gold imports nearly halved to $2.3 billion from $4.16 billion in July.
In recent weeks, Prime Minister Narendra Modi had renewed calls for Indians to avoid buying gold unless necessary and postpone non-essential foreign travel, as he promotes self-reliance amid global disruptions to trade, energy markets and supply chains following the Iran war.
Meanwhile, crude oil imports rose 25.8% year-on-year to $16.69 billion.
Total goods and services exports rose nearly 25% year-on-year to $82.68 billion, according to the trade ministry.
The US remained the top destination for Indian exports.
2 women killed in ongoing Manipur violence
Two women were killed in the northeastern Manipur state, police said on Wednesday, bringing the civilian death toll from three weeks of ethnic violence to 10.
The women were killed near their home in Tamenglong district on Tuesday, about 150 kilometers (93 miles) west of the state capital, Imphal.
Police said the attack appeared linked to recent clashes between Naga and Kuki groups.
Ethnic violence between Manipur's predominantly Hindu Meitei majority and mainly Christian Kuki minority has killed more than 250 people since it erupted in 2023.
Recent clashes have also involved Naga groups.
The latest killings came days after eight people died in three separate incidents across the state.
Authorities have struggled to restore calm, despite efforts by the Indian government.

After 10 years, India introduces UPI charges for merchants
Ten years after the launch of the popular instant digital payment system Unified Payments Interface (UPI), the Indian government announced charges on transactions on Tuesday.
However, the charges will only be on merchants and payments between two individuals remain free.
The charges, known as the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR), are taking effect from October 15.
According to the government circular:
- Person-to-person UPI payments will remain free regardless of the amount
- Merchant payments of up to ₹2,000 (€18.06) will also remain free.
- Merchant transactions above ₹2,000 will have 0.4% MDR levied
- MDR will be capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 or more.
- Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh (€903) a month through UPI will continue to pay zero MDR
- Sectors such as railways, fuel and telecommunications will have a flat ₹5 fee for transactions above ₹2,000.
Last month, the Indian parliament passed a bill allowing the government to levy charges on UPI.
According to the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), the MDR framework will enable further investment in "infrastructure resiliency, innovation, cybersecurity and customer service."
As of June, India had 554.9 million UPI users, according to NPCI. Meanwhile, UPI transactions worth ₹29,82,355.95 crore (about €269.3 billion) were recorded in August, NPCI data showed.
Some experts fear the new charges could prompt merchants to shift back toward cash payments.
India protests 'unacceptable and unprofessional conduct' by Pakistan Navy
India on Wednesday summoned Pakistan's top diplomat to protest what it called "unacceptable and unprofessional conduct" by Pakistani naval units that led to a collision with an Indian warship in the Arabian Sea, India's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
According to India, a Pakistani naval ship approached its warship at high speed, causing a collision on Tuesday in international waters. No major damage was reported.
The Indian ship was on a routine surveillance mission, officials said.
"The Charge d'Affaires of Pakistan was advised to convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents," the ministry said.
India said the incident violated a 1991 agreement requiring the countries' naval vessels and submarines to maintain a distance of at least three nautical miles in international waters.
Pakistan has not issued a statement regarding the incident.
This incident marks the first overt military tension between the nuclear-armed rivals since their four-day conflict last year, which threatened to turn into a full-blown war.
US bill sanctioning Russia could adversely impact India
India-US ties could come under pressure as the US lawmakers consider a Russia sanctions bill that would allow President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas. India, a major consumer of Russian energy, could be affected by the measure.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 cleared a key procedural hurdle in the House of Representatives on Tuesday in a 214-211 vote, media reports said. The House is expected to hold a final vote on Wednesday.
The bill, imposing sanctions on Russia's leadership, energy and defense sectors and "shadow fleet" accused of helping Moscow evade oil sanctions, was passed by the Senate last month.
If approved by the House, the bill would go to Trump to be signed into law.
The proposed tariffs seek toincrease economic pressure on Moscow by targeting countries that continue buying Russian energy.
India-US ties facing test
While India and Russia ties have grown stronger since the start of the war in Ukraine, driven largely by Russian oil exports, the same cannot be said of India-US relations under Prime Minister Narendra Modi as tensions mounted over New Delhi's purchases of Russian oil.
Last August, Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian imports over those purchases, on top of a 25% reciprocal tariff.
However, the additional Russia-related tariff was removed in February 2026, while the reciprocal tariff was reduced to 18% as part of a US-India trade framework.
However, the landmark bilateral trade agreement between the two countries remains in limbo, with no significant breakthrough.

Over UAH 131 billion in additional revenue: which taxes they want to raise in 2027
Kyiv • UNN
The government has budgeted for over UAH 131 billion in additional revenue from tax changes. These include increases in VAT, excise duties, and taxation of parcels.
In Ukraine’s draft state budget for 2027, government officials have envisaged a number of tax changes that are expected to generate more than UAH 131 billion in additional revenue. This was reported by Roksolana Pidlasa, chair of the Verkhovna Rada Budget Committee, on September 16, UNN reports.
Details
In particular, the changes include raising the VAT rate, increasing excise duties on fuel, and introducing VAT on international parcels. According to Pidlasa, the government expects to receive the largest amount of additional revenue by raising the value-added tax rate by 1 percentage point.
The expected effect on the budget is estimated at UAH 58.7 billion
Another UAH 38.5 billion is planned to be raised by taxing banks’ profits at a rate of 50%. In addition, the budget calculations include UAH 11.8 billion in revenue from VAT on international parcels and UAH 8.3 billion from a 4% increase in excise duties on fuel.
Separately, the government has budgeted UAH 64.9 billion in additional revenue from bringing customs activities out of the shadow economy. These funds are expected to be received if the customs revenue plan is exceeded.

bethan laura wood, max lamb and andu masebo rethink the material language of home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:03:06 UTC
17:03:06 KST

ALTERNATIVE MATERIAL LANGUAGES AT HOME
How can material innovation and unexpected forms bring joy to the homes we inhabit every day? Three London-based designers are rethinking materials from radical new perspectives and exploring how the idea of home is shaped by community and the act of making. In rejection of uniformity, the home of today becomes a vehicle for pleasure, personality and creative liberation. From ceramic dining chairs to a sofa woven from nautical rope, familiar materials are recontextualized in new forms as the spirit of unpredictability reigns supreme. Embracing experimentation and the element of surprise, these alternative material languages evoke a sense of carefree abandon.
Bethan Laura Wood’s ‘Extra Trimmings’ explores ornament through braided rope | image: courtesy of Shore Studios
BETHAN LAURA WOOD WEAVES ORNAMENT INTO STRUCTURE
Take the humble sofa. At the center of every living space, it’s become a symbol for comfort, connection and community. Designer Bethan Laura Wood brings new meaning to the sofa in “Extra Trimmings”, a collaboration with Shore Studios, featuring woven lounge chairs, settees and stools made with nautical braided rope. Taking its cue from the exuberance of 1970s interiors, where color, pattern and texture collided, the seating collection combines Wood’s technicolor approach and Shore’s structural weaving. Ruffles, scallops and loops are sculpted in braided rope and hand-knotted silicone, creating a new kind of upholstery, both tactile and architectural.
In “Extra Trimmings”, ornament is no longer simply decoration; it is woven into the structure, texture and narrative. Vibrant color and pattern come together in a rejection of all things beige, in favor of a more generous vision of home: more playful, more human and unapologetically personal.
Bethan Laura Wood seated on her ‘extra trimmings’ creation
DB: What can material expression and ornament bring to domestic life beyond aesthetics?
Bethan: It can tell a story that connect you with the past and memories. It can create comfort and pleasure; it can give function and information.
DB: What is the most unconventional object in your own home?
Bethan: Haha, too many to mention! I collect many things from my travels and the cities I visit, from tiny two-tone cracker whistles in the shape of clarinets to beautifully woven straw rain coats from Japan. Vases by Jochen Holz in the shape of psychedelic root vegetables to name only a few. I love creating compositions of these objects together to connect different colours textiles and patterns together.
Bethan Laura Wood working on her ‘extra trimmings’ creation
braided rope, ruffles and loops shape bethan laura wood’s exuberant seating collection
MAX LAMB PUSHES CERAMIC BEYOND TABLEWARE
Master of unconventional materials, designer Max Lamb’s latest collection, “Crockery”, rethinks the familiar notion of ceramic, being a fragile and delicate material, with a series of chairs crafted from stoneware. The designer collaborated with 1882 Ltd, a ceramics manufacturer based in England’s historic pottery region of Stoke-on-Trent, to develop a collection of dining chairs made entirely of clay. Here, earthenware moves beyond the realms of tableware and into furniture, supporting the presence of the human body.
“Crockery” is a collective undertaking, with 23 potters involved in the production of each chair, every stage of the meticulous process requires a fine balance of specialist knowledge and collaboration. From preparing and releasing the molds to drying and firing, the process is shared across a community of makers. This ethos of collective production is central to Lamb’s work, as material experimentation thrives under the culture of making. The resulting chairs occupy a space between sculpture and furniture, bringing craft into the domestic environment in unexpected forms. Lamb’s chairs celebrate not only the possibilities of ceramic, but the people, processes and shared knowledge involved in the production of design.
Max Lamb’s ‘Crockery’ collection transforms stoneware into sculptural seating | image: courtesy of Gallery Fumi
ANDU MASEBO BRINGS AUTOMOTIVE MATERIALS INDOORS
Meanwhile, Andu Masebo’s Tubular Chair begins with another act of reappropriation: materials normally found on a car are reimagined in the context of the home. Sourced from London’s mechanic and exhaust workshops, stainless steel tubes normally used for car exhaust systems are transformed into chairs with voluptuous, curving frames, while recycled chip rubber becomes a soft, tactile seat.
Working closely with exhaust manufacturers, Masebo adapted the limitations of their machinery into an opportunity for invention, bending and joining two sections of tube to create the chair’s distinctive silhouette. The finished seat embraces its industrial origins, down to the deliberately exposed welded joins, which are celebrated rather than concealed.
Andu Masebo reimagines automotive materials through his Tubular Chair
LEAVING DOMESTIC CONVENTION AT THE DOOR
Across the distinct work of each designer, there is a shared refusal to follow the prescribed language of domestic furniture. Materials are recontextualized and familiar forms are disrupted in objects that question our assumptions about what the home should be made from. There is a sense of liberation to be found in approaching the home as a place for experimentation, humor and surprise. In this version of domesticity, convention can be left at the door.
Andu Masebo’s design combines stainless steel exhaust tubing with recycled chip rubber | image: Yeshen Venema

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wants Canada to become the first “associate member” of the European Union, she said in her annual State of the Union address on Wednesday.

Advertisement
The nine-year-old CETA accord has, however, yet to be ratified by national and regional parliaments in 10 EU member states.
Von der Leyen’s initiative comes as Brussels and Ottawa seek to forge closer ties while both grapple with a costly trade war with the United States. Von der Leyen nonetheless insisted that the new partnership is “not against anyone else.”

In addition, the two sides will “make the Arctic a flagship joint project. We will work on energy, critical minerals and batteries. On AI, quantum, cyber and economic security," she said.
Carney will address the European Parliament on Thursday.
Canada and the EU will hold a summit at the end of October in Montreal. They also aim to reach a deal on digital trade by the end of the year.

$42b fund manager Cathie Wood sees interest rates topping 7pc on AI boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
08:01:12 UTC
17:01:12 KST

ARK Invest manages around $42b. Its CEO Cathie Wood believes interest rates could top 7pc
In short:
Fund manager Cathie Wood tips economies to boom and prices to fall, but interest rates to surge as the AI revolution gathers pace.
It could result in interest rates exceeding 7 per cent.
What's next?
Ms Wood does not think calls for regulation will be heeded and predicts that US President Donald Trump will veto any such efforts that might pass Congress.
The manager of a $US30 billion ($42 billion) investment fund believes artificial intelligence and related disruptive technologies will lead to both deflation as well as short-term interest rates pushing 7 per cent.
In Australia to spruik a new investment partnership with Australian fund manager Associate Global Partners, ARK Invest CEO and chief investment officer Cathie Wood argues that "technology is inherently deflationary" by increasing productivity and pushing down the cost of production.
She believes the current AI expansion will translate to an economic boom alongside "good deflation", as opposed to the price falls generated during economic crises when demand is collapsing.
"We think short rates will approximate nominal GDP growth, which was true during the industrial revolution — the last time we had a technology revolution of this size," she told ABC's The Business in a one-on-one interview during her visit.
"Real growth could move into the 7 to 8 per cent range, nominal maybe the 6 to 7.5 per cent range.
"Short rates would, over time, I'm not saying tomorrow, move towards that 6.5, 7.5 per cent rate.
"Long rates, they'd still go up as well, but not as much."
Overnight, US 10-year government bond interest rates again briefly moved above 5 per cent.
Aside from a brief period in 2023, this month has been the first time that rate has breached that level since before the global financial crisis of 2008.
"Once we have psychologically passed the 5 per cent yield threshold in the US 10-year … then we can see that all kinds of doors have suddenly been opened up, and all kinds of possibilities about where yields could sit are just waiting for us to explore," Rabobank global strategist Michael Every told The Business.
Loading...
Will rising interest rates blow up the AI boom?
Conventional wisdom and previous experience have generally shown rising interest rates to be poison for the value of tech firms, especially those yet to generate profits.
Financial commentator Satyajit Das recently said that he expected a financial crisis within the next two years, driven by a combination of rising interest rates and a realisation that AI was not delivering on its promised or required returns on investment.
Loading...
However, Ms Wood argues that major US AI companies are already starting to generate revenues above ARK's optimistic expectations.
"We're all looking for proof points and we are getting some already, and they're astounding," she said.
"Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate in December of last year was $9 billion, in July it was $65 billion."
ARK's Venture Fund holds stakes in Anthropic and Open AI, which Ms Wood said is based on the belief that the trillions of dollars of investments going into artificial intelligence will ultimately pay off.
"There are rumours, and we think they are well-founded, that Anthropic's gross [profit] margins are 80 per cent," Ms Wood said.
"That's a software-like gross margin."
When asked if those kind of profit margins are sustainable given the tendency of competition to erode them as technologies become more mature and widespread, Ms Wood argued the AI boom is "very different" from earlier boom-bust cycles such as railroads and the internet.
"Between 1873 and 1893 in the United States, 200 railroads went out of business," Ms Wood explained.
"There was a lot of hope and a lot of capital deployed, and investors just didn't know if it would pay off. Ultimately it did, but too late for most of those railroad companies.
"In the case of AI we've already narrowed the market down so much to four big players.
"This is not on a wing and a prayer like railroads were. The revenue generation started immediately."
She said that revenue generation has so far surpassed ARK's relatively optimistic forecasts.
"If it's a big surprise to us it's a shock to everybody else," Ms Wood remarked.
'If you win AI you win the 21st century'
Another potential threat to the AI boom is the debate about regulation, stoked in the past week by comments from industry leaders.
Michael Every believes some of those within the industry talking about the need for a slow down in AI development and increased regulation, such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, may be doing so with a strong element of self-interest.
"Either they've only just watched The Terminator and The Matrix, having completely avoided those movies up until now in their life. That's one particular option," he told The Business.
"Or they are looking for regulation because they want to have the drawbridge raised in terms of where they are, which is ahead of almost everybody else, and not allow open source technology to see other companies, both within America and particularly within China, catch up."
Ms Wood does not think the calls for regulation will be heeded and predicts that US President Donald Trump will veto any such efforts that might pass Congress while he remains in office.
Loading...
Mr Every agrees that the US is unlikely to handicap itself in the AI race with China.
"The White House openly says if you win AI you win the 21st century," he said.
"It's not only the US saying that, China is saying exactly the same thing in slightly different words.
"Many other people recognise that truth too, both in economic and national security terms."

====================================================================================================

Russian drone killed five people on a scheduled minibus in southeastern Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:59:43 UTC
16:59:43 KST

A Russian drone struck a scheduled passenger minibus in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on the morning of 16 September, killing and injuring people on board, the oblast military administration reported. The vehicle was running an intercity route when the drone reached it on the open road. Prosecutors opened a criminal case, and the head of the oblast council called the attack a cynical strike on people going about their day.
Five killed on the Pokrov to Dnipro run
Five people died at the scene, and doctors are treating at least seven injured, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration, Oleksandr Handzha, said. Russian forces struck Nikopol district with an FPV drone, damaging a route minibus that was travelling on the highway, the Prosecutor General's Office said.
Mykola Lukashuk, who heads the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Council, wrote that the strike was aimed and cynical.
"Russians cynically struck a passenger bus. Just a minibus in which people were travelling on their own business," he wrote.
The photograph Handzha published shows the windows torn out along one side of the white van, with blood running down the panel below them. In Lukashuk's image of the front end, the destination board behind the cracked windshield reads Pokrov, via Nikopol, to Dnipro, three towns strung along the same road.
The Dnipropetrovsk Oblast prosecutor's office opened proceedings under Article 438 of Ukraine's Criminal Code, which covers violations of the laws and customs of war, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
Drones had also attacked the district center and the Marhanets community in the same region, damaging an apartment building without hurting anyone, the administration said.
Buses on these roads have been hit all year
Nikopol district lies on the Dnipro River directly across from Russian-occupied territory, which puts its roads inside the range of short-range drones. A drone hit a city bus in central Nikopol in April, killing four people and injuring 17, after which the mayor cut services and ran the rest off the fixed schedule. In June, a drone struck a minibus in Nikopol, killing two people and injuring 12, among them two 12-year-old girls, and in August a drone burned out another route minibus elsewhere in the district, injuring at least seven passengers.
The pattern runs past this district. A drone hit a bus near Dnipro in May, injuring six people including a child and a pregnant woman, and war analysts have assessed that Russian forces use harm to civilians as an instrument of the war in southern Ukraine rather than as its by-product.
An FPV drone, short for first-person view, sends a live video feed back to whoever is flying it. The operator watches the target grow in the frame and steers the drone into it. A bus in motion is a target that has to be chosen and followed. FPV models are not the only cheap weapon over these roads: Russia also flies Molniya strike drones, which reach further and are switching to digital video that Ukraine's current detectors cannot pick up.
The Prosecutor General's Office documented more than 11,000 attacks by short-range drones on civilians, medics, rescuers, and police, with criminal cases rising from 2,427 in 2024 to 6,771 in 2025 and another 2,010 opened in the first four months of 2026.

Von der Leyen pitches European Security Council in response to Trump and Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:59:26 UTC
16:59:26 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday said she would propose a new security forum for EU and like-minded leaders in response to escalating Russian attacks and fraying transatlantic relations.
It's part of a broader rethink of security policy that includes a more robust response to hybrid attacks attributed to Russia and a greater effort to build up Europe's own defense capabilities — although in conjunction with NATO.
“For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent with partners like Ukraine, the U.K., Norway, Canada and others involved,” she said in her annual State of the European Union address.
Advertisement
“This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play — this is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality,” she said. "The urgency is clear."
The proposal underscores growing fears that Europe is struggling to deal with rapidly proliferating airspace violations, cyberattacks and sabotage attempts amid tensions linked to the Kremlin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with NATO wary of escalating its response amid fears of setting off a war with Russia.
The transatlantic alliance has also been strained by growing tensions between U.S. President Donald Trump and European allies and Canada. Trump threatened to annex Greenland earlier this year, is recalibrating U.S. forces in Europe and has threatened Canadian sovereignty, fueling doubts over Washington’s commitment to the transatlantic alliance.
“This is a Europe that stands up for each other,” von der Leyen said, “like when we stood up for Greenland when threatened.”
Various versions of a European Security Council have been floated since the 1980s but none have gained traction. The idea resurfaced after an EU split over the 2003 Iraq war and was given fresh impetus in 2017 by former EU executive chief Jean-Claude Juncker and French President Emmanuel Macron, but failed because of U.K. reluctance.
Green MEP Sergey Lagodinsky resuscitated a formal proposal for a UN-style security council this year, arguing for an intergovernmental treaty that would bring together Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland and the U.K. alongside two rotating seats for smaller countries to speed decision-making in crises.
Advertisement
EU capitals have generally been skeptical of handing over their jealously guarded powers on defense to new institutions. The pitch also risks a clash with NATO, which has repeatedly warned Brussels against duplicating the alliance's security mission.
The Commission chief also said she would propose an EU emergency security protocol modeled on NATO’s Article 4 urgent consultation procedure to respond to hybrid attacks that fall below the threshold of armed aggression but still threaten national security.
“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said. “When triggered by one member state, all member states would convene to coordinate a European response — to deter further escalation and to mitigate the impact.”
To bolster Europe’s efforts to take charge of its own defense, von der Leyen also floated a new scheme for building European strategic military capabilities such as air-to-air refueling and air and missile defense — areas where the continent still relies heavily on U.S. technology.
“I can announce a new European Instrument for strategic enablers — fully aligned with NATO,” she said. “These systems are essential, and we need more of them. Only together does Europe have the scale to deliver them.”
Manfred Weber, who leads the center-right European People’s Party group in the European Parliament, echoed that call and warned of the danger posed by Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Advertisement
“The threat is clear — Putin won’t stop,” he said, speaking after von der Leyen's address. “Our answer is unity … joint command structures, European drones, European satellites so closely connected that no one can ever undo this cooperation.”
Weber said such joint action should reduce the fragmentation of European defense efforts, which leads to waste and duplication among member countries. The goal is not to create "27 bonsai armies," he said.

The President of the European Commission centred climate early on in the speech, before mentioning AI or migration.
Ursula von der Leyen says this summer of extreme heat was a "mere preview" of the high temperatures to come.
The President of the European Commission spoke about climate very early in the speech, before mentioning AI or migration.
She did not mince her words when she listed the many places around Europe that experienced extreme weather this summer leading, she said, to 35,000 excess deaths.
She called the the repeated heatwaves "a summer of truth" in the annual State of the Union speech, in which policy and plans for the year ahead are laid out.
In a moving moment, she introduced the family of a firefighter who died fighting flames. The parliament gave a prolonged standing ovation in honour of the fallen hero.
What action will EU take after summer of extreme heat?
Von der Leyen said Europe "can, must and will stay the course of our climate targets".
She said mitigation, adaptation and preparedness must lie at the heart of Europe's approach to tackling extreme weather.
Von der Leyen announced a European Heatwave Plan, saying "there can be no repeat of this summer."
"We need better early warning systems and better health preparedness. We need urban adaptation and cooling. And we need to support the most vulnerable," von der Leyen said. The most common type of cooling - air conditioning - was the subject of intense debate around Europe this summer, as many questioned whether they should install it int he face of unprecedented temperatures.
'We will identify 100 of the most vulnerable territories in Europe'
Von der Leyen recognises that climate adaptation is becoming an immediate economic and public policy challenge rather than a long-term environmental issue, reports Euronews' Marta Pacheco, who is based in Brussels.
"We will present a new framework for climate resilience next month. We will identify 100 of the most vulnerable territories in Europe. And we will assess the risks — and at which level they should be managed," the Commission chief recalled as 660,000 hectares were burnt to the ground and roughly 12 million tonnes of crops were lost.
Von der Leyen also announced a new Climate Insurance Alliance.
"Today, only around 25 per cent of catastrophe losses in Europe are covered by private insurance. This means that, far too often, national budgets become the insurer of last resort. We need to take action to close this gap," the Commission chief told MEPs in Strasbourg.

Schools in England to get almost £500m extra in bid to avoid strike by teachers over pay
Schools in England are set to receive additional funding to cover the costs of the teachers’ pay award, the UK’s largest teaching union has claimed. The Press Assocation reports:
The leader of the National Education Union (NEU), which has been preparing a formal ballot of its members on strike action, said the move signalled “a welcome return to reality” and a “message of hope” for school staff.
In July, the government accepted the recommendations of the School Teachers’ Review Body (STRB) for teachers to receive a 3.5% pay rise from this month, but the Department for Education (DfE) said schools would be expected to fund some of the pay award out of their existing budgets.
But in a letter to the NEU on Wednesday, education secretary Lucy Powell said schools can use savings in employers’ contributions to the local government pension scheme to help cover the costs of pay rises for school staff.
The letter, seen by the Press Association, said the 4.9 percentage point reduction in what employers are expected to contribute will deliver “significant savings” on the pay bill for support staff.
Powell said: “We can confirm this reduction in costs will not be clawed back and as such, we are confident that schools will be able to cover the costs of the teacher pay award, at a national level.”
In the letter to the NEU, she added: “Given the material change to the affordability position, I would ask that the NEU revisits its proposed ballot of members planned for October and moves away from strike action.”
On Wednesday, the NEU claimed it had secured “a fully funded pay increase” for all teachers throughout England, and called it a “significant step”.
The NEU has been preparing a formal ballot for strike action, which was due to begin on 3 October and close on 15 December.
The union’s national executive will now meet on 24 September to discuss its response to the letter.
Daniel Kebede, general secretary of the NEU, said: “Finally, we have a government that accepts the reality that any teacher pay award must be fully funded.
“Plugging the £460m black hole in school budgets signals a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community.
“Be in no doubt that the significant ground conceded by government is a consequence of NEU members’ willingness to take a stand.”
Burnham says UK's commitment to Nato 'unwavering' as he meets its secretary general, Mark Rutte
Andy Burnham assured Nato chief Mark Rutte that the UK’s commitment to the alliance remains despite the change in prime minister. As the Press Association reports, the Nato secretary general wished Mr Burnham “good luck” in the job as the two met face-to-face for the first time to discuss defence issues.
Burnham said:

DHSC announces local health partnerships as part of shifting focus from treatment to prevention
The Department of Health and Social Care has announced that it is going to pilot a new form of local, health partnership. They will focus on joined-up prevention.
The initiatives will involve NHS organisations, councils and community groups working together to tackle health inequalities. They will launched in: Bristol; Lewisham; north-east Lincolnshire; 19 boroughs of London; North Nottinghamshire; and York and Scarborough.
The projects will help more people receive joined-up support earlier, avoid unnecessary hospital admissions and remain independent for longer.
The six sites will develop and test new neighbourhood health models that bring together NHS services, councils, community organisations and local people to improve outcomes and tackle inequalities.
They will pave the way for the future so more areas can benefit from the innovative partnership model. The funding will help sites develop and test new neighbourhood health models, creating the foundations for larger-scale investment and wider adoption across the NHS in future.
The government has partnered with Social Finance, Macmillan Cancer Support and West Hertfordshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust. This will bring together expertise in cancer care, system transformation, innovative finance and neighbourhood health. The projects will be backed £1.5m in funding from the Office for the Impact Economy, a government body that works with “impact investors” – people wanting to invest private capital for a social good.
The government argues that these models could provide a model for the future because current health funding models don’t incentivise health providers to spend money on preventative measures that will stop people going to hospital.

The programme is a key part of our 10-year health plan, helping us shift from treating sickness to preventing it in the first place, and giving people the help they need in the heart of their own communities.
Burnham should appoint a deputy PM, says former cabinet secretary Simon Case, as he calls for written constitution
Andy Burnham should formally appoint a deputy PM, the former cabinet secretary Simon Case has said.
Case said he thought the appointment was necessary because in a country like Britain there should be absolutely no doubt about who might take over in the event of the PM being incapacitated.
He made his comment in evidence to the Lords constitutional affairs committee where he also said he had gradually come round to the idea that Britain needs a written constitution – in part because of the risk of informal constitutional conventions being ignored by rogue actors.
Case said he first became convinced of the need for the government to have a deputy PM when Boris Johnson became so ill with Covid in 2020 that his life was at risk. At the time Dominic Raab was the de facto deputy, as first secretary of state.
Raab was made deputy PM in 2021 and since then every PM before Burnham appointed a deputy.
Burnham does not have a deputy. But Louise Haigh is first secretary of state, and second to Burnham in the cabinet order of precedence.
At the committee hearing, John Cryer put it to Case that everyone assumed that, in the event of something happening to Burnham, Haigh would take over.
Case replied:
My assumption is the same as yours. This title, first secretary of state … is conveying the sense that this person fulfills that deputy role. But, as you said, these are assumptions that we’re making
We’re a $4 trillion economy, a nuclear power, a P5 nation [one of the five permanent members of the UN security council]. You and I shouldn’t be sitting here having to make assumptions about who’s in charge if the prime minister is unavoidable. I mean, come on.
Case said that over time his views on the need for written constitution had changed. He said that he did not think important process decisions should be left up to “the whim of a prime minister of the day”.
As an example of how some constitutional rules are unclear, Case confirmed reports that, when Johnson was facing a leadership challenge, some of his team thought he could avoid being forced out by his own MPs by calling a snap election. Case said:
When Boris Johnson’s cabinet ministers were resigning left, right and centre and his government was falling apart, some – well, I’ll leave them unnamed - uninformed individual around Boris Johnson decided to float the idea of whether it would be time to call a general election as a way of avoiding him being sort of brought down by his own party.
Case said he had to see off the idea by digging out a copy of the so-called Lascelles principles – a letter to the Times, sent anonymously by the king’s private secretary in 1950, that explains when it is appropriate for the monarch to refuse a request from a PM to call an election. The letter has no legal status, but is now taken as part of the unwritten constitution.
Explaining how his views had changed, Case said:
As time has gone on, I’m one of those people who’ve been on a rather long journey on this, becoming more and more convinced that we should be heading towards a more codified and written constitution.
But Case also said he was a “pragmatist”, and did not think this would happen for “a very, very long time”.
At the committee, Lord Strathclyde, the chair, suggested to Case that a cabinet secretary could stop a PM acting inappropriately by resigning, or threatening to resign.
In his reply, Case said:
I’m not entirely sure that the resignation of a cabinet secretary would have that impact. Perhaps in years gone by that might be true.
But cabinet secretaries these days are becoming a little bit like prime ministers and London buses - they come and go.
At Westminster it is normal for MPs who defect from one party to another to resist calls for a byelection, partly by arguing that they were personally elected.
But in the Senedd elections in May, MSs (members of the Senedd) were for the first time elected by the closed proportional list system, with each constituency electing six members.
Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, the lead candidate for Reform UK, Pen-y-Bont Bro Morgannwg (Bridgend and Vale of Glamorgan) was elected as a direct result of people voting for Reform UK. But she will now sit as a Plaid Cymru MS and vote for Plaid policies.
Under this election system, Cooper-Lesadd cannot resign and trigger a byelection. If she were to resign, her seat would be taken by the next person on the Reform UK list in that constituency.
In a post on social media, Joe Martin, a Reform UK MS, said her position was “completely untenable”. He went on:
No one, literally no one, voted for her in May’s election. The votes that put her in Parliament were for Reform UK. Specifically, they were to scrap the nation of sanctuary, prevent the breakup of the UK, and to deliver Reform’s manifesto.
This means she has no mandate to represent those people any longer. The people of Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannog wanted a voice in Reform. Instead, they’ve been used as a springboard for the political ambitions of Sarah Cooper-Lesadd. That simply isn’t right.
If you believe in Plaid Cymru, stand for Plaid Cymru. Don’t deceive your way through a selection process to stand where you think is most opportune to realise your own ambitions. A party with any sense would drop her like a stone at the next election.
In a separate post, Matthew MacKinnon, Reform UK’s director of external affairs, said Cooper-Lesadd should resign.
She was elected on a list system under a Reform banner with a clear intention to pursue her own agenda and not @RUKWales
She was not elected as an independent.
She has shamefully manipulated the party and the electorate.
She should resign.

Jenner is Kipper royalty: a long-marcher whose husband is a good friend of Nigel Farage. Likeable and modest, she was working as a school teacher just weeks before being selected for the Senedd.
Pip more prone to abuse compared to equivalent disability benefits abroad due to design flaws, report says
The government is under pressure to cut the amount of money spent on disability benefits, particularly the personal independence payment, a non-means tested benefit that helps people with the costs they incur as a result of their disability.
In a report out today, Re:State, a centrist/right-leaning thinktank focusing on public sector reform, says the amount being spent on Pip is too high. It says other, equivalent benefits in prosperous democracies have much tighter rules and, as a result, work more effectively.
In particular, it highlights the fact that, while Pip claimants have to provide evidence of their disability, they do not have to provide evidence of the extra costs they are incurring as a result. “The requirement for evidence of extra costs is common in international models, but entirely absent from Britain’s model,” it says.
The report concludes:
Britain stands alone on a number of fundamental decisions. Pip has been designed to maximise administrative simplicity at the cost of accuracy, transparency, and perception of fairness. No other country relies solely on a functional assessment to determine extra-cost entitlement, without requiring evidence of the costs the benefit is intended to help meet. This creates a system which is vulnerable to gaming, and poorly equipped to distinguish between different levels of genuine need.
Additionally, Pip’s broad definition of extra costs means that its daily living component overlaps substantially with services that other countries address through social care and local provision. Elsewhere, clearer boundaries allow different parts of the state to perform different functions and reduce the risk of paying twice for the same need.
In incapacity benefits, versus the comparison countries, Britain appears to have a low bar for access; a less rigorous application and assessment process; and much weaker work incentives. Some of the comparator countries also make much greater use of employer responsibilities, intended to prevent people requiring incapacity benefits in the first place. It appears highly likely these design choices contribute to a greater proportion of Britain’s working-age population claiming incapacity benefits and a much greater proportion claiming incapacity benefits without any conditionality, as well as Britain’s comparably high disability employment gap.
The lesson from international experience is therefore not simply that Britain spends too much or that other countries have better systems. It is that design choices have consequences. How need is defined, where responsibility sits, what evidence is required, and what incentives are created all affect caseloads, expenditure, employment, and public confidence.

Last year the Home Office announced that prison officers would be allowed to use Pava, a form of pepper spray, to incapacitate children at young offender institutions.
Today the Howard League for Penal Reform, which opposed the move, has released figures showing that Pava has been used disproportionately against black boys. In a news release, it says:
In April 2025, Shabana Mahmood, the then secretary of state for justice, gave the green light for Pava spray to be used in three prisons in England, holding boys as young as 15 – Feltham A, Werrington and Wetherby. The Howard League understands that deployment began in August for Werrington and Wetherby and in September for Feltham A.
Figures provided to the Howard League in response to a Freedom of Information Act request show that in the first few months of deployment, up to the end of March 2026, Pava spray was drawn and used against 33 children and young people in total – 19 in Feltham A and 14 in Werrington. In Wetherby, Pava spray was drawn on at least one occasion but not used.
Of the 33 children and young people who had Pava spray used against them, 18 were Black and six were white. Despite comprising only about 30% of the population in Feltham A and Werrington, Black children and young people were on the receiving end about 55% of the time.
Gemma Abbott, legal director at the Howard League, said:
Pava is a chemical irritant spray that can cause severe pain, and it is classified as a prohibited weapon under the Firearms Act 1968. It is shameful that prison staff have been given the power to use it against children.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said that Washington is carrying out the “greatest economic isolation campaign” against Iran and its enablers, arguing that the pressure is taking a growing toll on the Iranian economy.
“The strength of our economy has allowed the United States to wage the greatest economic isolation campaign in history against the Islamic Republic of Iran and its enablers,” Bessent said in opening remarks before the House Financial Services Committee on Tuesday.
The committee held its annual hearing with the Treasury Secretary on the state of the international financial system.
Bessent said President Donald Trump had taken action against Iran that previous administrations had deferred.
“Under his leadership, America is no longer managing the Iranian threat; we are ending it,” he said, adding that US economic strength was allowing Washington to exert pressure “from a position of strength.”
Bessent later said Iran’s economy was in “dire straits,” citing what he described as a collapse in the currency, surging inflation and long lines for gasoline.
“We have seen the currency collapse, we have seen inflation through the roof,” he said, claiming that Iranians were facing three- to four-hour gasoline lines because the country had to import fuel.
‘Very vigorously’
Bessent attributed the pressure to a combination of the US blockade on Iran and Operation Economic Outcast, a Treasury campaign launched in August to target Iran’s financial connections and entities accused of helping Tehran evade US sanctions.
“Economic Outcast is possible because of the blockade,” he said, adding that Treasury had spent months mapping nodes in payment networks used by Iran.
Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast on August 24, saying its aim was to sever financial channels used by Iran to sell oil, evade sanctions and generate revenue.
Bessent also said Washington would intensify enforcement against entities accused of facilitating Iranian trade and helping Tehran circumvent sanctions.
He said measures targeting such facilitators would “start biting” on September 23 and would be fully enforced.
“We know, for those of you who are enabling the regime, you know who you are, we know who you are,” Bessent said, adding that Treasury would exercise its sanctions authorities “very vigorously.”
Bessent said the UAE had announced steps to cut financial transactions and trade with Iran. He also said Treasury had sanctioned branches of an Egyptian bank in Dubai that transferred more than $1.8 billion to Iran since 2025.
“With China, we have had some very good private discussions,” Bessent said, adding that he expected them to continue when he meets Chinese Vice Minister Liao Min this weekend and during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned spring state visit.

State of emergency declared in Russian Arctic village after 200-ton diesel spill reaches the sea
Authorities have declared a regional state of emergency in Taymyr after a diesel fuel spill in the settlement of Syndassko, the Krasnoyarsk Krai government reported.
The spill occurred on the morning of September 15, when a diesel fuel storage tank was damaged in Syndassko, on the shore of Khatanga Bay. Law enforcement sources in the region told the Russian state news agency TASS that a storm caused the accident, with rising water levels in Khatanga Bay flooding and damaging the tank on the coastline.
Between 170 and 200 tons of diesel fuel leaked from the tank, according to various estimates, and reached the bay, the region’s Emergency Situations Ministry reported.
Local authorities said there is no threat to residents’ life or health, and that the petroleum products have not entered the body of water from which Syndassko residents draw their water.
The tank belongs to Taymyr Alliance Trading (TAT), a Khatanga-based company that supplies electricity to several settlements. Investigators have opened a criminal case over violations of environmental protection rules governing the operation of industrial facilities, sources who spoke to TASS said.
Taymyr’s head, Alexey Chlenov, said “no obvious signs of environmental damage have been found.” He added that Syndassko’s power supply has not been disrupted, with fuel in reserve tanks expected to last 10 days.
Syndassko, one of Russia’s northernmost settlements, is home to about 500 people.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Advanced Lithium Electrochemistry Co. plans to set up a production facility in Tainan to fulfill growing orders for cathode materials used in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, CTEE reported Wednesday.
LFP batteries are known for their stable structure and high safety and are widely used in electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and power systems. The cathode is a key battery component that affects safety and performance, according to Anue and Hoyu Resources Technology.
Aleees plans to lease an existing factory in Tainan and install new equipment to make LFP precursor materials, which are used to produce LFP cathodes. The company has signed a pricing agreement with a North American customer to manufacture and supply the materials.
The agreement covers 20 years of shipments starting July 1, 2027. Trial production at the Tainan plant is scheduled to begin in January next year, with shipments expected to start in July.
Aleees has not disclosed the customer's identity due to a confidentiality agreement. Supply chain sources said the order is related to the expanding use of energy storage systems and electric vehicles in North America.
The Tainan plant is expected to play a key role in Aleees' restructuring as battery supply chains move to reduce reliance on China. The company is one of the few LFP cathode material manufacturers outside China with patents covering LFP composition, structure, and manufacturing processes.
The facility is initially planned to have an annual production capacity of 25,000 to 50,000 metric tons of precursors, with the figure potentially rising to 100,000 tons as orders increase. Aleees expects the North American agreement to begin contributing to revenue in mid-2027, with its contribution potentially increasing in 2028.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Labor groups have called on the government to standardize penalties for employers who pay below the minimum wage, saying inconsistent local rules weaken enforcement, CNA reported Wednesday.
The Taiwan Labor Front said fine standards vary among local governments and industrial parks overseen by the Ministry of Economic Affairs. It said the differences could reduce the effectiveness of the Minimum Wage Act.
Taiwan Labor Front Secretary-General Yang Shu-wei (楊書瑋) said enforcement varies widely across the country. Under current guidelines for economics ministry industrial parks, he said an employer could commit more than 50 violations before receiving the maximum fine.
Yang said similar differences exist among Taiwan’s six special municipalities. Tainan and several counties have yet to establish specific fine guidelines for minimum wage or Labor Standards Act violations.
Taipei Confederation of Trade Unions Deputy Chair Wang Yen-chieh (王燕杰) said authorities recorded 153 minimum wage violations nationwide last year. Under the fine standards used in economics ministry industrial parks, only a small number of repeat offenders would have received the maximum penalty, per Rti.
Labor groups said consistent enforcement is especially important for younger workers, who often have less bargaining power and may fear losing their jobs if they report violations.
Taiwan Alliance for Advancement of Youth Rights and Welfare Secretary-General Chang Yu-chia (張祐嘉) cited a 2024 labor ministry survey showing 59% of workers aged 15 to 29 did not state an expected salary when applying for jobs, per UDN.
Among young workers who received pay raises, 23.5% said minimum wage increases were one factor. Chang said the findings showed the minimum wage remains an important safeguard for workers with limited bargaining power.
The Taiwan Labor Front urged the labor ministry to work with local governments and the economics ministry to create a nationwide penalty standard. It proposed imposing the maximum fine after an employer commits five or more violations, per Nownews.
The group also urged financial regulators to review sustainability reports filed by listed companies. It said companies that violate minimum wage rules but fail to disclose the cases should be publicly identified, per CTS News.
The labor ministry said it has asked local authorities to follow common penalty principles under the Labor Standards Act when handling minimum wage cases. It has proposed formally adding the Minimum Wage Act to the guidelines, and local labor authorities have agreed to follow the revised standards once the changes are completed, per Tai Sounds.

Marine Corps tests new robot boat to hunt underwater mines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:52:02 UTC
16:52:02 KST

- U.S. Marine Corps explosive ordnance disposal teams tested a new Unmanned Surface Vessel at Camp Pendleton in late August as part of the LEON hazard-clearing system.
- The Marine Corps expects to begin fielding the USV to EOD companies in fiscal year 2027, with the rest of LEON following within two years.
Marine Corps explosive ordnance disposal teams tested a new unmanned boat at Camp Pendleton in late August, part of an effort to clear mines and other explosive hazards from coastal waters without putting divers directly in harm’s way. The Explosive Hazard Defeat Team, working under Program Manager Combat Support Systems, ran the Unmanned Surface Vessel through two weeks of trials off the Southern California coast.
The boat is a commercial unmanned surface vessel fitted with sonar, forward-looking infrared cameras, and both line-of-sight and acoustic communications gear. It can drive itself along programmed routes.
It is the fourth piece of a five-part system the Marine Corps calls Littoral Explosive Ordnance Neutralization, or LEON. The full system also includes a remotely operated vehicle, diver equipment, an unmanned underwater vehicle, and an amphibious unmanned ground vehicle, each meant to extend how far Marine explosive ordnance disposal technicians can operate from a hazard before they have to approach it directly.
“The USV is a key part of the LEON System of Systems (SOS). While it provides a search capability, it will primarily enable the other LEON systems to conduct operations below the surface, locating and identifying potential hazards, then relaying that information to the surface for real time updates. The LEON SOS will enable maneuver by identifying safe routes for transit within the littorals,” said Capt. Timothy Guinan, project officer, Explosive Hazard Defeat Team.
The boat’s main job is to scan for hazards and serve as a communications relay, called a Mobile Gateway Buoy, linking the underwater and shallow-water parts of the LEON system to command elements on shore or afloat. It can run missions for up to 14 hours at a stretch, according to Guinan, covering large stretches of coastline with little more than a small crew monitoring it from a distance.
“Unmanned systems allow operations to continue without fatigue. These systems can be launched and left to conduct a mission for upwards of 14 hours covering large areas of the littorals, while it requires minimal manpower to monitor the system,” Guinan said.
Marines from 7th Engineer Support Battalion’s explosive ordnance disposal company took part in the testing, known formally as a Field User Evaluation. That gave fleet Marines, rather than engineers alone, a chance to run the system through waypoint navigation, target deployment, and location verification before offering feedback to the program office.
The teams started in calm water, learning the controls and setting up mock mine targets, then moved into a wider-area search through varying sea conditions off the Pacific coast.
“The events were very successful. Everyone was communicating well. The platform itself was running well, had long endurance and gave us good results to refine and further develop the capability,” said Chief Warrant Officer 2 Alfredo Andrade, officer in charge, Explosive Ordnance Disposal Company, 7th Engineer Support Battalion.
Andrade said the push toward unmanned maritime systems reflects a broader goal within the EOD community: reducing how often Marines have to physically approach a suspected explosive hazard, and cutting the strain that repeated deployments put on a limited pool of trained technicians.
“Some of the conflicts that we are engaged in take a toll on the force, and surging in new forces is costly. It turns into a logistical problem. To preserve the safety and the health of the forces…the USV and the [LEON] program exist to ensure that we have readily available combat power,” Andrade said.
The Marine Corps expects to begin fielding the USV to explosive ordnance disposal companies in fiscal year 2027, with the rest of the LEON family of systems set to follow over the two years after that.

U.S. Army spends $18M turning cavalry regiment into tank brigade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:47:29 UTC
16:47:29 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Akima Facilities Operations $18 million to repair and refit equipment for a cavalry regiment converting into a heavy brigade combat team.
- Army Contracting Command expects the work to be completed by Oct. 18, 2027, with locations and funding set individually for each order.
The U.S. Army is spending $18 million to repair and refit equipment as one of its cavalry regiments transforms into a heavy brigade combat team, trading in lighter reconnaissance vehicles for the tanks and armored fighting vehicles that define the Army’s most heavily armed formations. Army Contracting Command awarded the contract modification to Akima Facilities Operations, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The switch from a cavalry regiment to a heavy brigade combat team is not a simple relabeling. A cavalry regiment is built for scouting and screening, using wheeled and lightly armored vehicles to find the enemy and report back. A heavy brigade combat team is a different animal entirely, organized around M1 Abrams tanks and M2 Bradley infantry fighting vehicles, designed to fight through resistance rather than avoid it. Moving a unit from one structure to the other means overhauling much of what it owns, from vehicles to support equipment, so it matches the new formation’s requirements.
That overhaul work is what this contract pays for. In Army contracting language, it is called induction and repair, a process in which vehicles and equipment are brought in, inspected, and either fixed or refurbished so they are ready for use under the unit’s new configuration. Some of what comes in may already belong to the Army and simply needs reconditioning. Other items may need more extensive rebuilding before they can be issued to soldiers.
The modification, worth $17,927,838, adds funding to an existing contract, W52P1J-20-F-0137, rather than creating a new one. Only one company submitted a bid for the work, and the Army awarded it to that sole bidder, a detail the contract announcement discloses but does not explain further.
The Department of War did not identify which cavalry regiment is undergoing the conversion, nor did it say where the repair work will take place. That is not unusual for a contract structured this way. Locations and funding will be worked out separately for each order placed under the agreement, rather than fixed in advance, and the current phase of work is expected to be finished by Oct. 18, 2027, giving the Army roughly a year to complete it.
Akima Facilities Operations is based in Herndon, Virginia, and is part of Akima, a group of companies that holds a range of federal contracts covering logistics, facilities support, and equipment maintenance work for the U.S. government. The company’s role here fits that broader business line: keeping military hardware serviceable rather than manufacturing it.
What remains unclear is the scale of the work. The Army did not disclose how many vehicles or pieces of equipment the induction and repair effort will cover, nor did it release the total value of the underlying contract beyond this modification. Army Contracting Command, which manages the agreement from its headquarters at Rock Island, Illinois, has not said whether additional modifications are expected as the conversion moves forward.
